Limitation of the method: VB variance underestimation not quantified vs MCMC; no public code; no predictive validation in the market application.

Krueger (2024, arXiv:2412.09430) derives exact identities for the linear pool of distributional forecasts: pool entropy = average component entropy + disagreement term D >= 0 for all kernel scores; D equals the realized pooling gain over the average component score (Prop 5.1); the linear pool is the maximally-central combination under any kernel score (Prop 7.1).

Prop 3.1 (eq. 4): E_{F^omega}[S(F^omega,X)] = sum_i omega_i * d(F^omega,F^i) [D = disagreement] + sum_i omega_i * E_{F^i}[S(F^i,X)] [avg component entropy], for any proper S; for kernel scores D = (1/2)E_{F^omega}[L(X,X_tilde)] - (1/2)sum_i omega_i E_{F^i}[L(X,X_tilde)] (eq. 6).
equation: E_{F^omega}[S(F^omega,X)] = sum_i omega_i * d(F^omega,F^i) + sum_i omega_i * E_{F^i}[S(F^i,X)]

claim: Prop 5.1: S_L(F^omega,y) = sum_i omega_i S_L(F^i,y) - D - the linear pool beats the average component score by exactly D. Under the log score the central pool is the log pool, not the linear one; the log score is NOT a kernel score (excluded from the centrality result); D measures gain over the average component, not the best.

NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations illustration: RPS-based disagreement D correlates 0.86 with pool variance and 0.68 with pool ERPS. Tension noted: high D gives more pessimistic self-assessed entropy (eq. 6) but better realized score (Prop 5.1) - a calibration implication; monitor PIT histograms alongside D.

Hasegawa, Deshpande, Small, Rosenbaum (2018, arXiv:1705.03918) propose a causal-inference method for treatments with observable versions: report both the primary confidence interval Ic (all data) and a versions-robust interval Iv (union of version-specific intervals) jointly with NO multiplicity penalty, plus Rosenbaum Gamma sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.

Prop 1: if one version, Pr(Iv superset Ic superset tau) >= 1-alpha; in any case Pr(Iv superset tau_min) >= 1-alpha - jointly, no multiplicity correction, no power loss on Ic; tau_min = min(tau^a, tau^b), tau_max = max(tau^a, tau^b).

High-school-football-and-cognitive-decline study (Gamma=1): Ic = [-0.308, 0.099]; Iv = [-0.357, 0.219] - both compatible with no effect; both rule out +/-0.5 words (full age-65->72 age-related decline benchmark).

Simulation (Appendix): the dual-interval method beats the omnibus F-test in power to reject Fisher's sharp null when versions differ by < ~30-40% in magnitude with the same sign. Zero multiplicity cost: Ic is exactly the conventional interval.

Wilson & Wilson (2024, arXiv:2405.09865): Bayesian linear mixed-effects model of log finish times across 28 amateur cross-country races (8 courses, 5 seasons; 14,067 men's + 10,515 women's chip-timed finish times; 2,668 unique men, 2,116 unique women) with random athlete/course/season effects and current + lagged-month rainfall fixed effects, estimated via JAGS (10k burn-in, 1M iterations thinned by 100 -> 10k posterior samples).

Model: Y_ijk = log(T_ijk) | mu_ijk, tau ~ N(mu_ijk, 1/tau); mu_ijk = lambda + alpha_i + beta_j + delta_k + gamma(D_jk - d_bar) + rho_m R_m + rho_{m-1} R_{m-1} (windspeed dropped); alpha_i ~ N(0,1/tau_alpha) athlete, beta_j ~ N(0,1/tau_beta) course, delta_k ~ N(0,1/tau_delta) season random effects with corner constraints alpha_1=beta_1=delta_1=0; correlated prior on rainfall effects via Gamma-distributed decay phi < 1.
equation: mu_ijk = lambda + alpha_i + beta_j + delta_k + gamma(D_jk - d_bar) + rho_m R_m + rho_{m-1} R_{m-1}

claim: Current-month rainfall: +10 mm -> +25 s (men, 47-min race) / +18 s (women, 38-min race), posterior median 0.001 per mm on log scale. Previous-month rainfall: +10 mm -> +22 s (men) / +14 s (women) - the lagged underfoot effect is nearly as large as the contemporaneous one.

Windspeed posterior centered at 0 (-0.001 to 0.000) - NO effect, attributed to looped courses (headwind/tailwind cancel); NOT generalizable to open stadiums. Acknowledged measurement error (central-station weather vs course-level conditions; GPS distance error) was not modeled and creates attenuation bias toward zero.

Evans, Williams & Thomas (2020, arXiv:2009.00550v1): Twitter follow-graph 'social affinity' affinity(p,t) = |{q : p follows q and q is on team t}| (raw count, follow-out direction only) predicts a free agent/traded player's destination team better than performance/value features - but the headline numbers are contaminated: a July-2020 snapshot graph with no edge timestamps was used to predict transitions back to 2001/2002, so post-transition follows leak the label; no temporal train/test split.

Destination accuracy: MLB social-only 16.880%, all features 19.402%, team ID + social 19.955% (best reported); NBA Twitter-only 26.104%, all-social 26.667%, all features 29.740%, rank/value + social 30.238% (best). All ~5-9x random baseline 1/29 ~= 3.45%; social-over-non-social gain ~= +3-6 pp in both leagues. Data: MLB transitions 2002-2018 (4,207 unique switchers, 702 with Twitter handles = 16.7% coverage); NBA transitions 2001-2018/2019 (1,847 switchers, 784 with handles = 42.4%).
No standard errors on the ten-run means; differences like 19.402% vs 19.955% may not be significant; no roster-capacity constraints were modeled.

Shianifar & Faiud (2026, arXiv:2608.03416v1): ten LLM assistants made one frozen pre-tournament forecast of the full 48-team/104-match 2026 FIFA World Cup under identical conditions, scored with a transparent additive scheme and audited via stage decomposition. Ground truth: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in the final.

Additive scoring (equations 1-12): per group match S_m = 5*I_exact + 3*I_outcome + 2*I_winner + I_GD (max 11, 9 for exact draws); per group S_g = 5*I_winner + 5*I_top2 + 3*N_qual + 2*N_rank; knockout S_progression = 2*C_R32 + 4*C_R16 + 6*C_QF + 8*C_SF + 12*C_Final; S_placing = 20*I_champion + 10*I_runner-up + 8*I_third + 5*I_fourth.

Final totals: GPT-5.5 Thinking 744 (GS 254 / ST 248 / KO 242), GPT-5.5 717 (261/264/192), Gemini 699, Qwen 3.7 687, DeepSeek 599, Claude Sonnet 4.6 591, Mistral 568, Perplexity 552, Perplexity Pro 530 (KO 0), Grok 496 (KO 0). Only GPT-5.5 Thinking picked champion Spain; champion picks across models: Brazil 4, France 3, Argentina 2, Spain 1.

Knockout SD 88.65 vs group-match 8.65 and standings 12.20 - knockout drives essentially all separation: corr(total, KO) r = 0.986 (Spearman 0.945); corr(total, group-match) r = 0.055; corr(total, standings) r = -0.103. Decompose composite evaluation scores by stage; never conflate the highest-variance component's ranking with overall skill.
Claude Sonnet 4.6 had the best group outcome accuracy at 63.89% (46/72) but finished 6th overall; champion GPT-5.5 Thinking only 58.33% (42/72); exact-score accuracy 6.94-13.89% across models.

Self-reported model confidence was uncorrelated with outcome accuracy (r = -0.060) and total score (r = -0.067) - confidence is noise; any product surface displaying model confidence must carry calibration evidence. Perplexity Pro ranked 1st on group-match points and 1st after standings, then 9th overall with 0 knockout points - scoring design, not forecasting skill alone, determined the final order.

Amos Storkey (2011, AISTATS, arXiv:1106.4509): prediction-market equilibria with machine-learning agents implement standard ML model-combination rules (mixtures, products of experts, graphical-model message passing), with the combination form determined by agents' utility functions.
Log utility u(w) = log w implies equilibrium price proportional to sum_i (wealth_i * p_i) - a wealth-weighted mixture of experts (arithmetic pool).
equation: u(w) = log w ==> price proportional to sum_i (wealth_i * p_i)

claim: Exponential/CARA utility u(w) = -exp(-a*w) implies equilibrium price proportional to product_i p_i^{weight_i} - a product of experts (geometric/log pool); wealth drops out under CARA. Other utilities interpolate between mixture and product combinations; local-potential markets implement MRF/CRF/Boltzmann-machine marginals with message-buying approximately equal to belief propagation.
equation: u(w) = -exp(-a*w) ==> price proportional to product_i p_i^{weight_i}

claim: Limitations recorded: the paper is pure theory with zero empirical content; real ensembles violate the assumptions freely; multivariate state spaces make exact clearing intractable (no convergence analysis for loopy message passing); the market framing adds clearing/budget overhead over standard stacking.

Cherny & Obloj (Oxford, 2013, arXiv:1305.6831): for a long-run investor maximizing asymptotic growth of expected utility, a floor constraint (wealth must dominate a benchmark at all times) leaves the optimal long-run growth rate (CER) unchanged.
Criterion: R_U(V) := limsup_{T->infinity} (1/T) log E[U(V_T)] (eq. 1); the optimal rate is the Certainty Equivalent Rate (CER).

Theorem 2.2 (floor irrelevance): sup_{V in A(v_0)} R_U(V) = sup_{V in A_G(v_0)} R_U(V) (eq. 4) for floor G_t <= X_t in A(v_0(1-epsilon)); explicit optimizer V_hat_t := epsilon * xi_hat_t + X_t (epsilon weight on the unconstrained optimizer, rest on a floor-dominating process).
equation: sup_{V in A(v_0)} R_U(V) = sup_{V in A_G(v_0)} R_U(V)

claim: Proof device: the epsilon-cost vanishes at rate (1/T)(-gamma log epsilon) -> 0 - the floor is a fixed additive term under the log, hence asymptotically free. Remark 2.4: the drawdown solution = Azema-Yor transform of the floor solution = Azema-Yor transform of the unconstrained solution.
Risk-sensitive link: for U(x) = x^p/p, (1/p) log E[e^{p F_T}] = E[F_T] + (p/2) Var(F_T) + O(p^2) - the CER criterion is approximately mean-variance on log wealth to first order.
equation: (1/p) log E[e^{p F_T}] = E[F_T] + (p/2) Var(F_T) + O(p^2)

claim: Limitations: continuous-time/continuous-path setup; no finite-horizon guidance on choosing epsilon (it practically controls floor tightness); no estimation error; turnpike convergence speed unquantified.

Deng, Li, Li, Qi (2022, arXiv:2210.06866v1): pure mechanism-design theory on how contestants choose among parallel contests (crowdsourcing platforms, conferences) and how contest designers set prize structures. The source ledger's verdict is REJECT: operator-side results with no player-side implementable artifact.

Contestant choice characterized via symmetric Bayesian Nash equilibrium through quantile functions; designer best-response is NP-hard; FPTAS achieves (1-epsilon)-approximation with a constant-ratio worst-case guarantee under unknown competition. Assumptions: contestants enter exactly one contest; skill types private but distributionally known; designers maximize total participant value, not profit.

No numerical results at all - theoretical guarantees only (NP-hardness, FPTAS ratio, constant-factor worst-case bound). The paper's 'contest selection' is the contestant-choice equilibrium (which contest a solver enters), not DFS field/payout picking - a scope mismatch noted explicitly in the source ledger.

arXiv:2304.03870 ('ASPEST: Bridging the Gap Between Active Learning and Selective Prediction'): a protocol for spending a small active-learning label budget where a shifted model is most uncertain, then self-training, to restore selective-prediction quality under domain shift.

ASPEST stack: (1) checkpoint ensemble - ensemble the source model's training checkpoints for better-calibrated target-domain uncertainty; (2) active acquisition - spend the label budget on the lowest-margin (smallest top-two probability gap) target examples; (3) target fine-tuning - fine-tune on acquired labels; (4) pseudo-label self-training on high-confidence target pseudo-labels. Metric: AUACC = area under the accuracy-coverage curve.

MNIST->SVHN, label budget 100: AUACC improves 79.36% -> 88.84% - a +9.48 point gain from 100 labels. Consistent gains reported across CIFAR-10->CINIC-10, FMoW, Amazon Review, DomainNet, Otto. The full combination (ensemble + active acquisition + fine-tuning + self-training) beats any subset.

Dani, Madani, Pennock, Sanghai, Galebach (2006, arXiv:1206.6814v1): an empirical shootout of six forecast-aggregation algorithms converting a crowd of noisy NFL probability forecasts (ProbabilitySports, 1,319 games, 2000-2004; expert counts per season 625 -> 786 -> 1,257 -> 1,969 -> 2,231) into one calibrated forecast.

Zero-one accuracy is a dead end: no algorithm consistently beats simple averaging on 0/1 error. Quadratic loss is where aggregation wins: the novel Variance (EM) algorithm beats Average in 9 of 11 experiments (5 NFL seasons + 3 NCAA + 3 multi-year), sign-test significant (p <= 0.1) in 2003 and 2004. Scoring rule: 100 - 400(p - y)^2 per game (quadratic, incentive-compatible).

Variance algorithm (EM): model each expert's prediction as Gaussian centered on the true event probability with per-expert variance sigma_i^2; alternate between inverse-variance-weighted probability estimates and variance estimates. Equations: (1) p_hat_t = (sum_i w_i p_{it})/(sum_i w_i), w_i = 1/sigma_i^2; (2) sigma_i = sqrt(sum_t (p_t - p_{it})^2 / T).
equation: p_hat_t = (sum_i w_i p_{it})/(sum_i w_i), w_i = 1/sigma_i^2; sigma_i = sqrt(sum_t (p_t - p_{it})^2 / T)

claim: Experts algorithm regret bound: loss(A) <= [ln(2)*N + L*ln(1/beta)] / ln(2/(1+beta)), L = best expert's loss in hindsight; best config beta = 0.75, update e^{-beta q}, Vovk prediction. Despite worst-case guarantees, the experts algorithm never consistently beats Average - a cautionary tale.

Quadratic scores (higher = better), 2000-2004 seasons (Top Expert / Average / Avg(30) / Variance / Var(20) / Experts / Expert MD / ExpGrad / MarketSim): 2000: 3185 / 2561 / 2864 / 2979 / 3187 / 2801 / 2875 / 2827 / 3090; 2003: 4218 / 3298 / 3731 / 3498 / 3881 / 3343 / 3442 / 3371 / 3397; 2004: 3747 / 3371 / 2986 / 3456 / 3344 / 3099 / 3346 / 3137 / 3203. Multi-year 2000-3: Top Expert 9,910 vs Average 11,169 vs Variance 11,512. Prediction markets (TradeSports/NewsFutures, 2003) scored 3,389/3,359 - Variance (3,498) was competitive with real-money markets.

Expert quality distribution is brutal: median final season scores -485, -649, -684.2, -437, -275 (2000-2004) - most experts badly miscalibrated. Even averaging only experts with negative final scores yields positive scores (1,763-2,717/season) - averaging smooths miscalibration.

Watts, Pipping-Gamon, Wyner, Wharton (arXiv:2608.19454): 'Dummy RAPM' - instead of dropping low-minute players from Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus, represent them as pooled 'dummy' lineup-side count indicators to improve out-of-sample stint-level margin prediction.

Weighted stint-level ridge regression (response = home-minus-away margin per 100 possessions per stint; weights = stint possession count) with 10 dummy indicators added to the design matrix - counts of 1-5 excluded low-minute players on the home lineup and 1-5 on the away lineup. Ridge objective: min_beta ||W^{1/2}(y - X beta)||^2 + lambda_player ||beta_players||^2 + lambda_dummy ||beta_dummy||^2, with lambda_dummy/lambda_player = 2.2 (selected).

Selected hyperparameters: 10 minutes per appearance threshold; dummy/player penalty ratio 2.2. Outer-test RMSE: Dummy RAPM 12.856 vs Filtered RAPM 12.897 - improvement of 0.042 points (0.30%); 95% CI for the RMSE reduction: 0.013-0.070 (excludes zero). Dummy RAPM better in 13 of 16 seasons; mean R^2 0.178 vs 0.173. Data: ESPN/sportsdataverse NBA play-by-play, 16 seasons, 19,589 games, 496,575 stints; strict chronological split per season (Oct-Dec train, Jan-Feb validation, Mar-Apr outer test).

Limitations: predictions conditioned on realized held-out lineups (lineup-conditioned margin prediction, not a true pregame forecast); count-additivity assumed, not tested (3rd excluded player may differ from 1st); 10-min/appearance threshold is a selected constant that may vary by era/pace.

Nguyen, Yurko & Yu (2024, arXiv:2403.14769): 'Fractional Tackles' - a new defensive stat from NFL tracking data that detects contact windows around the ball-carrier and distributes fractional tackle credit among all contacting defenders proportional to their toward-carrier velocity, replacing the binary conventional tackle count.

Contact window: {t : min_d dist(d, carrier, t) <= 1.5 yd} (threshold chosen because ~95% of first-contact/tackle-event distances fall below it); multiple windows per play allowed. Window value: v(w) = E[Y_end | state at window end] - E[Y_end | state at window start] (yards prevented, positive = good defense). Fractional tackle per defender: FT_d = sum_w v(w) * share_d(w), share allocated by peak toward-carrier velocity, adjusted by a first-contact indicator.
equation: v(w) = E[Y_end | state at window end] - E[Y_end | state at window start]

claim: Split-half reliability: fractional tackles 0.69 vs combined tackles 0.59 overall; by position group 0.57/0.57/0.73 vs 0.46/0.51/0.64 - fractional wins in every group. Data: NFL Big Data Bowl 2024, 12,486 plays / 136 games, weeks 1-9 of the 2022 season, 10 Hz player tracking; analysis restricted to 5,539 running-back run plays (of 6,670 total run plays).

Leaderboard (2022 weeks 1-9 RB runs): Roquan Smith 19.83 total / 0.102 per-play; Christian Wilkins 17.53 / 0.125; Bobby Wagner 17.33. Coverage: 19,691 player-play instances credited vs 7,720 conventional tackle/assist instances (~2.5x coverage). 7,453 contact windows detected; mean window duration 1.28 s.

Limitations: RB run plays only (no pass plays, scrambles, WR screens); 1.5-yd threshold and velocity-share rule are heuristics with no ground truth; 10 Hz tracking can miss brief contacts; forced-missed-tackle detection rule-based and unvalidated; single 9-week sample, no season-to-season stability shown.

Holt, Qian & van der Schaar (2024, arXiv:2401.00282): 'Deep Generative Symbolic Regression' (DGSR) - a two-step framework that pre-trains a conditional generative model p_theta(f|D) of equations and then gradient-refines the posterior at inference time (NGPQT) before discrete MAP search; shown to generalize to MORE input variables at inference than seen in pre-training.

End-to-end loss = NMSE(f_hat(X), y) = MSE/var(y) over mini-batches of t datasets x k sampled equations; non-differentiable token->equation step handled by policy gradients (RL-style pre-training gradients). Architecture: Set Transformer encoder (permutation-invariant over {(X_i, y_i)} pairs) -> latent V in R^w; Transformer decoder with hierarchical tree-state representation.

Recovery metric A_Rec% = % of kappa random-seed runs finding the true equation f*, plus average equation evaluations gamma. SRBench ground-truth: DGSR 63.25% recovery vs previous best 52.65% - new state of the art. R rationals: +10% recovery rate over prior best. Ablation: >=10% better than NGGP on Feynman d=5.

Three demonstrated properties: (P1) invariance-aware representations (learns equation equivalences); (P2) efficient inference refinement; (P3) recovers truths with d=12 variables after pre-training on fewer - the killer feature: pre-train on cheap low-dimensional problems, refine on the full high-dimensional problem. Limitations: all evaluation on synthetic, noise-free equations - no noise study; no wall-clock numbers for refinement; no public code.

Zhu, Xu, Yuan & Huang (2022, arXiv:2010.08784, AutoML Conf 2022): 'DIFER: Differentiable Automated Feature Engineering' - the first gradient-based feature search. Each constructed feature is a parse tree serialized by postorder traversal, embedded by an LSTM into a continuous space where an MLP predicts downstream performance and gradient ascent improves the embedding before decoding back to a discrete feature.

Objective (Eq 2): F* = argmax_{F_hat subset of F, order(f_hat) <= K} P(X union F_hat, y); infinite discrete space (aleph_0) capped by max order K. Joint loss (Eq 3): L = L_pre + lambda * L_rec (lambda adaptive; L_pre = performance-prediction MSE, L_rec = sequence reconstruction loss). Gradient step (Eq 4): e_0 = e + eta * grad_e P(e), eta = 0.0001, applied for multiple adaptive steps until the decoded parse tree actually changes.

DIFER best on 21 of 25 public tabular datasets (15 classification + 10 regression); average +2.57% over SOTA NFS; 40x fewer feature evaluations (4,096 vs 160,000). Regression max single-dataset gain 11.42%; average +10.72% over Raw and +9.55% over Random features. Select cells (1-RAE for R / F1 for C): Bikeshare DC R NFS 0.9746 -> DIFER 0.9813; Openml_637 R 0.5693 -> 0.6343; Ionosphere C 0.9516 -> 0.9770.

80.9% of generated features are order > 1; performance rises with K but saturates at K=5; K=2 suffices on most datasets. Search space: unary {log, sqrt, min-max normalization, reciprocal}; binary {+, -, x, /, mod}; max order K = 5. Parsimony example: APomentumovary (10,936 raw features) - AutoFeat OOM, NFS adds 10,936, DIFER adds 491; SpamBase - DIFER adds 1 vs NFS 57.

Significance: Friedman test p = 1.17e-10; Nemenyi pairwise p-values: DIFER vs DFS 0.0010, vs AutoFeat 0.0010, vs NFS 0.0046 (all significant at alpha = 0.05). Predictor quality: pairwise ranking accuracy 0.918 vs 0.5 random (fraction of feature pairs whose predicted score ordering matches true ordering).

Limitations flagged: 5-fold random stratified CV (no time ordering - future leaks on temporal data); in-fold selection optimism; numerical-only (no categoricals); no relational/GroupBy operators - cannot invent 'mean EPA by team' features; predictor trained on 512 samples in 512-dim space may not extrapolate off-distribution.

Bouadi, Alavi, Benbernou & Ouziri (2024, arXiv:2410.02519): 'SMART' - a hybrid Knowledge-Graph semantic-reasoning (HermiT/Description-Logics exploitation + SWRL validity rules) + DQN reinforcement learning (exploration) system that optimizes a bi-objective of model performance and feature interpretability jointly.
Bi-objective (Eq): T* = argmax_T (lambda * P(L(X_hat_T, Y)) + (1 - lambda) * I_KG(X_hat_T)); I_KG(X_hat_T) = sum I_KG(x_hat), lambda in [0,1] is the user-set accuracy/interpretability tradeoff.
equation: T* = argmax_T (lambda * P(L(X_hat_T, Y)) + (1 - lambda) * I_KG(X_hat_T))

claim: Feature interpretability: I_KG(x_tilde) = max over decomposition paths pk of I^pk_KG(x_tilde), where I^pk_KG(x_tilde) = product_j Inter(t_j) x min_i I_KG(x_i) - product of per-transformation interpretability scores times the least interpretable feature on the path. Interpretability = the intellectual effort a domain expert exerts to map a feature to domain concepts, operationalized via KG distance.
equation: I^pk_KG(x_tilde) = product_j Inter(t_j) x min_i I_KG(x_i)

claim: DQN loss: L_i(theta_i) = E[(r + gamma * max_a' Q_hat(s',a';theta_hat_i) - Q(s,a;theta_i))^2]; state = semantic vectorization of the dataset (features mapped to KG concepts, summed semantic feature vectors); actions = {unary, binary, aggregations, date operators}; reward = delta-P (k-fold CV performance gain) + interpretability score.
equation: L_i(theta_i) = E[(r + gamma * max_a' Q_hat(s',a';theta_hat_i) - Q(s,a;theta_i))^2]

claim: SMART vs raw data: +20.94% average improvement across 14 public tabular datasets and 5 downstream models (RF, DT, LR, SVM, XGB). SMART vs strongest baselines (averages): +11.55% over DIFER, +4.86% over NFS, +7.24% over mCAFE. Example RF cells: Diabetes 0.740 -> 0.853; Medical Appointment 0.491 -> 0.893; Bikeshare DC 0.393 -> 0.988; Amazon Employee 0.712 -> 0.912; NYC Taxi 0.425 -> 0.610.

Interpretability validation: SHAP feature-importance on raw+SMART datasets shows SMART features outrank raw features on all four plotted datasets; human-readable outputs (NYC Taxi Haversine pickup-dropoff distance; Medical Appointment booking lead time - longer lead time -> higher no-show probability) vs mCAFE's opaque composites. Limitations: no temporal dimension or leakage/lookahead discipline; SWRL coverage only as good as the rule author (penalizes genuine novelty by construction); lambda has no selection guidance; the cross-dataset transferability claim is untested.

Liu, Yan et al. (EPFL 2020, arXiv:2012.11717): 'Social NCE' - contrastive learning of socially-aware motion representations where 'negative' samples are locations occupied by OTHER agents, teaching a trajectory forecaster that two agents cannot occupy one location.

Social-NCE loss: L_NCE = -log[ exp(sim(q,k^+)/tau) / sum_n exp(sim(q,k_n)/tau) ], sim = cosine; full Social-NCE objective L = L_task(f,g) + lambda * L_SocialNCE(f,psi,phi). Query q = psi(h_t^i) (2-layer MLP of history embedding); key k = phi(s_{t+delta t}^i, delta t); positive key = ground-truth future location + epsilon ~ N(0, 0.05*I).

N = 8(M-1) social negatives per horizon: s_{t+delta t}^{i,n-} = s_{t+delta t}^j + Delta s_p + epsilon, j != i, Delta s_p = (rho cos theta_p, rho sin theta_p), theta_p = p*pi/4, p=0...7; rho = 0.2 m (forecasting) / 0.6 m (navigation); horizons delta t in {1,...,4}; tau = 0.1; embeddings unit-normalized, 8-dim. Implemented on Social-STGCNN, Trajectron++, Social-LSTM, Directional-LSTM with no architecture changes; lambda=0.1 for imitation learning, (tau=0.2, lambda=1.0) for Rainbow DQN RL, (tau=0.2, lambda=0.1) for offline RL.
equation: s_{t+delta t}^{i,n-} = s_{t+delta t}^j + Delta s_p + epsilon

claim: ETH/UCY collision-rate cut: 37.0% (Social-STGCNN) and 45.7% (Trajectron++) vs vanilla, with top-20 FDE on par. TrajNet++: collision-rate reduction 9.5%-37.5% across sub-categories. Imitation learning: ~69% collision-rate reduction vs vanilla (lambda=0.1); random negatives WORSEN the policy; markedly better in low-demo regimes; multi-horizon beats single-horizon. Rainbow DQN: vanilla needs >4000 episodes to reach reward 0.6; Social-NCE reaches it in <2000 episodes and attains collision-free policy faster.

Lourenco, Gama, Xing, Marreiros (2025, arXiv:2512.11668v1): position paper arguing large in-context tabular models (TabPFN-style) unify Stream Learning and Continual Learning - keep parameters FIXED, treat the input context as the learnable object; regime adaptation = choosing which past weeks enter the context.

Two principles named (not operationalized): distribution matching (current distribution = plasticity; prior distributions = stability) and distribution compression (diversification to avoid redundancy + retrieval to re-activate relevant past data). Sketch mechanisms listed: histograms, wavelets, count-min sketches, reservoir/coreset sampling; retrieval = neighborhood-based selection around query, referee meta-models, repository matching on drift. Cited capacity claim: modern LTMs handle contexts 'exceeding 500K samples and 50K features.'

Zero new numbers in this paper; no experiments, no equations, no code/data stated. The only quantitative claim is imported from prior work [62]: TabPFN + inference-time sketching 'consistently outperforms' Adaptive Random Forest and Streaming Random Patches on 7 streaming benchmarks (NOAA, SmartMeter, Electricity, Rialto, Posture, CoverType, PokerHand) - margins not reproduced, treat as pointer not evidence.

Titsias, Ruiz, Nikoloutsopoulos, Galashov (2020, arXiv:2009.03228v3): 'Information Theoretic Meta Learning with Gaussian Processes' - a variational information bottleneck (VIB) framework that recovers MAML as a special case (beta=0 + Dirac encoder) and yields GP-VIB, a few-shot GP regressor.

IB objective: L_IB(w) = I(Z, D^v) - beta * I(Z, D^t) (Eq. 2). VIB bound: F(theta,w) = E[log p_theta(D^v|Z)] - beta * E[log(q_w(Z|D^t)/p_theta(Z))] (Eq. 7); per-task F_tilde_i = E[log p(D^v_i|Z_i)] - beta * KL[q_w(Z_i|D^t_i) || p_theta(Z_i)] (Eq. 8).
equation: L_IB(w) = I(Z, D^v) - beta * I(Z, D^t)

claim: MAML recovery: psi_i = theta + Delta(theta, D^t_i), Delta = rho * grad_theta log p(D^t_i|theta); F_tilde_i(theta) = log p(D^v_i | theta + Delta(theta, D^t_i)) when beta=0 and the encoder is Dirac. GP-VIB task objective (Eq. 13): sum_j E_{q(f^v_{i,j})}[log p(y^v_{i,j}|f^v_{i,j})] - beta * KL[q(f^t_i|D^t_i) || p(f^t_i|X^t_i)].
equation: F_tilde_i(theta) = log p(D^v_i | theta + Delta(theta, D^t_i))

claim: Sinusoid K-shot MSE: MAML-1step K=5: 0.600 +/- 0.662; MAML-10step K=5: 0.280 +/- 0.013; GP-VIB K=5: 0.02 +/- 0.014; MAML-10step K=20: 0.043 +/- 0.003; GP-VIB K=20: 0.001 +/- 0.001 - GP-VIB beats MAML by >10x at every K; posterior mean matches ground truth after K=4 shots with shrinking uncertainty. beta used: 0.001 in classification, 1 in regression (globally set, not tuned per dataset).

mini-ImageNet 5-shot accuracy: Baseline++ 66.18 +/- 0.18 (best baseline) vs GP-VIB+Linear 65.84 +/- 0.22. Omniglot->EMNIST cross-domain 1-shot: GP-VIB+Linear 76.01 +/- 0.54 (SOTA cell) vs DKT+Linear 75.97 +/- 0.70. mini-ImageNet->CUB 1-shot: GP-VIB+CosSim 40.70 +/- 0.48 (best). Pattern: dominant on regression; classification competitive with SOTA cells on cross-domain transfer.

Nguyen, Do, Carneiro (2020, arXiv:2003.02455v3): 'SImPa' (PAC-Bayes Meta-Learning with Implicit Task-Specific Posteriors) - meta-learning with PROVED generalization bounds at both levels of the bi-level objective (Theorem 2) plus best-in-lane calibration (ECE/MCE), using an implicit GAN-style generator posterior instead of inexpressive diagonal-Gaussian VI. No KL weighting factor to tune - only confidence parameter epsilon.

Task-specific posterior q(w_i;lambda_i) is implicit: w_i = G(z;lambda_i), z ~ p(z) (Eq. 10), sampled only, no analytic form. KL[q||p] estimated via compression lemma (Lemma 1): KL[Q||P] = sup_phi E_Q[phi(h)] - ln E_P[e^{phi(h)}], phi = neural net omega_i (Eq. 11-12). Meta-posterior q(theta;psi) = N(theta; mu_theta, sigma_0 I) (Eq. 9).

Omniglot standard CNN: SImPa 98.352 +/- 0.005 vs MAML 97.143 +/- 0.005, ABML 97.281 +/- 0.004, BMAML 94.104 +/- 0.008, Prototypical 96.359 +/- 0.006. miniImageNet standard CNN: SImPa 51.72 +/- 0.48 (1-shot, best) / 63.49 +/- 0.40 (5-shot). miniImageNet WRN features: SImPa 62.85 +/- 0.56 (1-shot) / 77.65 +/- 0.50 (5-shot), edging LEO on both means. tiered-ImageNet: SImPa 70.26 +/- 0.35 (1-shot, SOTA) / 80.15 +/- 0.28 (5-shot). Smallest ECE and MCE vs all probabilistic meta-learners compared.

Multi-modal 5-shot regression: SImPa 'much smaller MSE' than MAML/PLATIPUS/ABML with best reliability diagram. Cost (Appendix C): MAML 6 GPU-hours; ABML/BMAML/PLATIPUS ~30; SImPa >48 hours. Per-update O(125n') vs O(100n) MAML, O(440n) VI. Generator explosion: a 32,645-param base net requires a 16.7M-param generator - the scaling wall for deep base nets.

arXiv:2203.03003: offline deep RL (CQL, continuous-action actor-critic, CQL(H)-style per Kumar et al. 2020) for dynamic pricing of consumer credit. Data: ~200,000 approved US auto-loan applications from an online lender via the Center for Pricing and Revenue Management, Columbia. Reward: r(s_t,a_t) = p(Accept_t | s_t,a_t) * (expected profit if accepted per Phillips et al. 2015) - interest income minus capital costs minus credit risk. State s_t: 16 features (Term, Amount, FICO, PD, PreviousRate, CompetitionRate, PrimeRate, Tier, LoanType, CarType, PartnerBin, State, Months, DayOfWeek, MonthOfYear, DaysSinceApp).

pi_CQL: +21% expected profit over historical policy pi_beta (3-seed average), with <15% MAPD in prices vs the existing policy; average price pushed down 6.8% -> 5.9% (consistent with documented historical over-pricing, Phillips et al. 2015). pi_Opt (parametric): +34% expected profit with 24% MAPD - fragile: under alternative response models with similar fit, the estimated gain ranged from a -7% decrease to a +34% increase, average estimate 12.6%, 'strong evidence of overfitting.'

Baseline logistic price-response model has low pseudo-R^2 ('limited explainability of the feature set') - the regime where model-free offline RL's advantage is largest. Synthetic experiments: CQL recovers near-optimal pricing under misspecified demand. Limitations: off-policy evaluation is model-based, so +21% is estimated, not realized; single-step (myopic) formulation; partial observability/adverse selection acknowledged but unsolved.

Hafner et al. (Google Research/DeepMind/U Toronto 2020, arXiv:2010.02193): 'DreamerV2' - replaces DreamerV1's Gaussian world-model latents with a vector of categorical latents trained via straight-through gradients plus KL balancing. Architecture lineage: DreamerV1 (Gaussian latents) -> DreamerV2 (categoricals + KL balancing) -> DreamerV3 (kept categoricals, added symlog/twohot).

Three changes over DreamerV1: (1) categorical stochastic state z_t (vector of categorical variables, not diagonal Gaussian); straight-through gradients: sample = onehot_sample + probs - stop_grad(probs) (Bengio et al. 2013); (2) KL balancing: L_KL = alpha * KL(sg(q)||p) + (1-alpha) * KL(q||sg(p)), alpha=0.8, scaled by beta=0.1 (Atari) / beta=1.0 (continuous control); (3) behavior learning via actor-critic trained purely on imagined rollouts in compact latent space (actor via REINFORCE + straight-through world-model gradients; critic via TD on imagined rewards), world model trained separately from policy.

Paper claims: first agent with human-level Atari performance (55 games, sticky actions, 200M steps) learned purely inside a separately trained world model; surpasses final performance of top single-GPU agents IQN and Rainbow at the same budget; humanoid solved from pixels only. RSSM: recurrent deterministic h_t; prior p(z_hat_t|h_t), posterior q(z_t|h_t,x_t), both categorical vectors. Limitations: categoricals use biased straight-through gradients; codebook size is a manually tuned hyperparameter.

Maeda & Shimizu (2020, arXiv:2001.04197): 'RCD' (Repetitive Causal Discovery) - a functional-model causal-discovery method for linear non-Gaussian acyclic models with latent confounders. Foundation: Darmois-Skitovitch theorem - if y_1 = sum alpha_i s_i and y_2 = sum beta_i s_i with independent s_i are independent, then all shared components (alpha_j beta_j != 0) are Gaussian; contrapositive: a non-Gaussian shared component implies dependence (direction inferred from non-Gaussian residuals).

RCD three steps: (1) ancestor extraction - repeatedly infer causal direction between few variables (Lemmas 1-3), each time removing effects of already-identified common ancestors via least-squares regression; (2) parent vs ancestor separation - Lemma 4 + Theorem 2 conditional-independence test; (3) latent-confounder detection - pairs still correlated but with unidentifiable direction get bi-directed arrows (shared latent confounder). Tuning used: alpha_C (Pearson) = 0.01, alpha_I (independence) = 0.01, alpha_S (Shapiro-Wilk non-Gaussianity) = 0.01, max regression size n = 2. Evaluation metric: F-measure = 2*precision*recall/(precision+recall), scored separately for bi-directed (latent confounders) and directed (causality) edges.

Simulation (linear DAG with 40 causal arrows, 4 latent confounders, noise X = Y^3 with Y ~ N(0.0, 0.5)): latent-confounder detection - RCD, FCI, RFCI, GFCI 'almost the same' with RCD medians highest; causality - RCD highest median precision and F-measure of all methods, median recall second-highest (next to RESIT). Paper's own caveat: 'RCD does not greatly improve the performance metrics compared to the existing methods.'

GSS real data (n=1380, domain-knowledge ground-truth directions, Table 1): bi-directed - RCD 4 estimated / 4 correct (precision 1.0); FCI, RFCI 3/3 (1.0); GFCI 0/0. Directed - RCD 5 est / 4 correct (0.8); LiNGAM 5/4 (0.8); RESIT 12/4 (0.3); FCI/RFCI 3/1 (0.3); PC/GES 2/1 (0.5). Paper: 'RCD performs the best among the existing methods in terms of both.'

Limitations: linear only; no public code (reimplementation required); non-Gaussianity is load-bearing - near-Gaussian indicators may fail the Shapiro-Wilk gate; paper warns real structures are 'often very complex' and RCD 'likely produces a causal graph where each pair is connected with a bi-directed arrow' (degenerate failure mode); cross-sectional (no time dimension).

Shchur et al. (Amazon 2023, arXiv:2308.05566): 'AutoGluon-TimeSeries' - AutoML for probabilistic time-series forecasting (diverse model zoo + greedy forward-selection ensemble outputting point and quantile forecasts). Model zoo, 3 families: (a) statistical - AutoETS, AutoARIMA, AutoTheta (StatsForecast); (b) deep learning - DeepAR, PatchTST, Temporal Fusion Transformer (GluonTS/PyTorch); (c) tabular - DirectTabular / RecursiveTabular (TS task converted to tabular regression); plus Naive/SeasonalNaive baselines.

Validation: time-series cross-validation generating out-of-fold predictions; ensemble via greedy forward selection, weights tuned to optimize the chosen eval metric (wQL or MASE) on OOF predictions; sparse final ensemble; predicts mean + arbitrary quantile levels (e.g., 0.1/0.5/0.9) for prediction_length steps ahead. Metrics: mean weighted quantile loss (wQL, probabilistic), MASE (point vs naive). Per-dataset errors rescaled to [0,1] for averaging; win rate vs Seasonal Naive.

Point accuracy (MASE, Table 3): AutoGluon champion on 19/29 Monash datasets; avg rank 2.08; avg rescaled error 0.073; win rate vs Seasonal Naive 100.0%; 0 failures. Next: StatEnsemble avg rank 3.12 / 0.238 (3 failures); AutoPyTorch avg rank 4.12 / 0.257; DeepAR avg rank 5.08 / 0.434; TFT avg rank 6.12 / 0.635 (worst of the deep methods).

Probabilistic (wQL, Table 4): AutoGluon champion 19/29; avg rank 1.80; avg rescaled error 0.086; win rate vs baseline 100.0%; 0 failures. StatEnsemble avg rank 3.36 / 0.330; DeepAR 4.08 / 0.455; TFT 4.24 / 0.487. Paper claims it 'often even improv[es] upon the best-in-hindsight combination of prior methods' (beats the oracle combination of baselines on some datasets).

Limitations: NFL team-week series are SHORT (17-18 games/season, few stable-regime seasons) - likely favors the tabular family over DL; no sports data in benchmarks (untested on rule-change/QB-injury regime shifts); ensemble quantiles can still be miscalibrated without CQR/isotonic recalibration; 4h fits too heavy for weekly in-season refresh; same Amazon team evaluating their own system (auditable via open code at github.com/autogluon/autogluon).

Kirsch et al. (arXiv:1906.08158): 'BatchBALD' - an active-learning acquisition function that scores candidate batches JOINTLY via mutual information between the joint batch labels and model parameters, so batch acquisition avoids the redundant near-duplicates that naive top-b BALD picks (sometimes performing worse than random). Proven submodular, so greedy selection is a (1-1/e)-approximation. Estimation: MC dropout posterior samples; joint entropy via enumerating c^n label configs then MC sampling.

BatchBALD: a_BatchBALD({x1..xb}, p(omega|D)) = I(y1..yb; omega | x1..xb, D) = H(y_{1:b} | x_{1:b}, D) - E_{p(omega|D)}[H(y_{1:b} | x_{1:b}, omega, D)]. Proven a_BatchBALD <= a_BALD; equals BALD at acquisition size 1. Greedy acquisition with (1-1/e) guarantee via submodularity (Nemhauser et al. 1978).
equation: a_BatchBALD({x1..xb}, p(omega|D)) = I(y1..yb; omega | x1..xb, D)

claim: MNIST labels-to-90% accuracy (25/50/75% quartiles): BatchBALD 70/90/110 vs BALD reimpl 120/120/170 vs Gal 2017 145. To 95%: 190/200/230 vs 250/250/>300 vs 335 - approximately 1.6-1.7x label savings. BALD's performance 'drops drastically' acquisition size 1->40; BatchBALD acq-10 performs 'close to the ideal with acquisition size 1.'

Repeated MNIST (3x-replicated), acq size 10: BALD performs worse than random; BatchBALD 'copes with the replication perfectly.' EMNIST: BALD unable to beat random; BatchBALD beats both; acquired class-histogram entropy consistently higher (more diverse). CINIC-10 transfer: 59% mark at 1170 acquired (BatchBALD) vs 1330 (BALD) median, about 12% label savings, beating BALD from 500 samples onward.

VLDB tutorial by the Uber Michelangelo feature-store team + Stanford DB group on managing the ML pipeline lifecycle: feature authoring/publishing with definitional metadata (update cadence + definition SQL); training/deployment via date-partitioned dual stores (streaming features via aggregation functions to online in-memory DBMS + offline SQL warehouse; date-partitioned time-based joins); monitoring/maintenance via feature-quality metrics (freshness, null counts, mutual information across features) and training-deployment skew detection (offending features isolated and replaced for retraining/serving).

One cited number: Orr et al. 2021 structured-data augmentation improved rare-entity performance by 40 F1 points (paper's claim, not reproduced). Key operative findings are doctrinal: the training-deployment skew statistic is named but undefined (implementer chooses KS/PSI/MI); embedding-ecosystem metrics (nearest-neighbor stability, eigenspace overlap, slice-based learning) are half irrelevant unless learned player embeddings are adopted; tutorial claims are experience-asserted, not measured (no false-positive/false-negative rates, no latency/scale numbers).

Lian et al. (PVLDB 14(1), arXiv:2309.12239): 'ContTune' - continuous tuning for distributed stream processing (Apache Flink operator parallelism) via a 'Big phase' (binary-lifting to clear backpressure, decoupling tuning from the DAG) followed by a conservative Bayesian Optimization 'Small phase' with a feasibility-gated acquisition and history reuse across workload changes; proven O(1) average reconfiguration complexity.

CBO acquisition: argmax_{p_i} (p*_i - p_i) * I(mu(p_i) - lambda_i), the indicator filters parallelism levels whose GP-mean processing ability is below upstream data rate lambda_i (feasibility first; stricter than Constrained EI). GP posterior: mu(p_i) = k_*^T K^-1 y; sigma^2(p_i) = k_*(p_i,p_i) - k_*^T K^-1 k_*; bounds l = mu - beta*sigma, u = mu + beta*sigma.
equation: mu(p_i) = k_*^T K^-1 y; sigma^2(p_i) = k_*(p_i,p_i) - k_*^T K^-1 k_*

claim: Real Flink workloads (ContTune alpha=3 vs DS2): avg reconfigurations per tuning 1.29 vs 2.40 (-46.25%; alpha=0: -35.42%); end-to-end tuning time -47.08%; end-to-end runtime -3.12%; total CPU cost -0.22% (essentially identical), +1.84% vs Dhalion (cheapest but slowest to converge). Backlogged data: -43.01% vs DS2, -89.09% vs Dhalion; buffered-data processing time -16.79% vs DS2, -88.10% vs Dhalion. p99 latency equivalent to DS2 at same max workload while using fewer cores per query (e.g., Q5: 22 vs 25 cores).

Santoni, Jouanne, Scullin (arXiv:2608.23808): 'MinervaScore' - a single auditable 0-100 statistical-robustness grade combining four established backtest-validation quantities: Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR), Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO), Superior Predictive Ability (SPA), Minimum Track Record Length (MinTRL) - plus a regime-stability diagnostic, with a binary 'Robustness Seal' gate, calibrated on 359,062 production backtest records.

Seal (eq. 2): Seal = 1[DSR >= tau_DSR and PBO <= tau_PBO and SPA <= tau_SPA and T >= MinTRL and rho >= tau_rho], with tau_DSR = 0.95, tau_PBO = 0.50, tau_SPA = 0.10, tau_rho = 0.60; MinTRL per Bailey & Lopez de Prado.
equation: Seal = 1[DSR >= tau_DSR and PBO <= tau_PBO and SPA <= tau_SPA and T >= MinTRL and rho >= tau_rho]

claim: Regime composite (eq. 3): rho = 0.5*p_+ + 0.3*clip_[0,1](1 - s_SR/sigma_ref) + 0.2*logistic(SR_min); p_+ = fraction of validation windows with positive Sharpe, s_SR = std of per-window Sharpes, SR_min = minimum across windows, sigma_ref = 2 (fixed, heuristic weights - authors' flagged weakest link).

Aggregation (eq. 7): S = w^T z / sqrt(w^T Sigma_eff w), w = (0.35, 0.25, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10), Sigma_eff = cross-sectional margin correlation (Hartung-style dependence adjustment); S maps to 0-100, 80+ reserved for Seal holders. Signed margins: z_DSR = (u - Phi^-1(tau_DSR))/sigma_DSR, u = (SR_hat - SR_0)/s_hat_e, DSR = Phi(u); z_MinTRL = tanh((T - MinTRL)/sigma_T), sigma_T = max(0.2*MinTRL, 50). Margins are descriptive, NOT p-values (authors' explicit disclaimer).
equation: S = w^T z / sqrt(w^T Sigma_eff w)

claim: Synthetic ground truth: MinervaScore AUROC = 0.989 at headline difficulty (near-perfect separation of true signal from lucky backtests). Honest caveat: improvement over GT-Score proxy and gates-passed baseline is modest - 'remains close to the corrected DSR-alone baseline' (most value is the DSR). Pre-registered real-market test: no significant forward relationship - Spearman rho_s = 0.013, one-sided permutation p = 0.40 - authors position the score as an 'auditable validation and reporting layer, rather than evidence of demonstrated real-market predictability.' The score ranks statistical support, NOT probability of future profit.

Chaejeong Lee et al. (arXiv:2304.12654, ICML 2023): 'CoDi' - mixed-type tabular synthesis with two physically separated diffusion models (Gaussian for continuous, categorical for discrete) that co-evolve by conditioning on each other's perturbed states, bound together with a triplet contrastive loss. Reverse conditioning: p_thetaC(x_{t-1}^C | x_t^C, x_t^D) and p_thetaD(x_{t-1}^{D_i} | x_t^{D_i}, x_t^C) - each step conditions on BOTH models' previous-step outputs.

Contrastive triplet loss: L_CL(A,P,N) = sum max{d(A_i,P_i) - d(A_i,N_i) + m, 0} (Eq. 16). Anchor = real sample; positive = one-step-estimated x_hat_0^+ conditioned on true counterpart (Eqs. 17-18: x_hat_0^{C+} = (x_t^C - sqrt(1-alpha_bar_t) epsilon_thetaC(x_t^C,t|x_t^D))/sqrt(alpha_bar_t)); negative = x_hat_0^- conditioned on a NEGATIVE condition built by shuffling the counterpart block across rows (Method 3: permute whole discrete/continuous blocks between records, preserving within-block pairing). Distance: Euclidean for continuous, cross-entropy for discrete. Combined losses: L_C = L_{Diff_C} + lambda_C L_{CL_C}, L_D = L_{Diff_D} + lambda_D L_{CL_D}, 0<lambda<1 (Eqs. 19-20).

TSTR quality (Table 1, CoDi vs STaSy vs Identity=real): Binary F1 0.4726 / 0.4559 / 0.4154; Binary AUROC 0.8106 / 0.7961 / 0.8119; Multi-class macro F1 0.6221 / 0.6078 / 0.6514; Regression R^2 0.4794 (ONLY positive among 9 methods; Identity 0.6673; STaSy -1.3200; all GAN baselines -inf or <= -0.07); RMSE 0.6477 vs Identity 0.3593. Diversity coverage (Table 2): CoDi 0.6931 (best), STaSy 0.5771, TableGAN 0.5759, TVAE 0.3903, CTGAN 0.3834, MedGAN 0.0155, VEEGAN 0.0019.

Sampling time for 10K fakes (Table 3): CoDi 0.5187s vs STaSy 4.6417s (~9x faster); RNODE 103.14s; OCT-GAN 0.6008s. Discrete-space ablation (Table 4): discrete-space diffusion beats continuous-space on all 4 discrete-only datasets - e.g., Phishing F1 0.931 +/- 0.012 vs 0.915 +/- 0.008, coverage 0.644 vs 0.127 (continuous model collapses category counts). Negative-sampling ablation (Table 5): Method 3 (whole-block shuffle) best - Heart F1 0.872 +/- 0.039 / coverage 0.949 +/- 0.012. Contrastive-learning ablation (Table 6): CL improves F1 on Bank (0.566 vs 0.527), Seismic (0.305 vs 0.210), Faults, Obesity; Absent R^2 -0.026 -> 0.095.

Paper limitations: no head-to-head vs TabDDPM exists in either paper; random splits only (no temporal evaluation); two models + triplet loss = more hyperparameters (lambda_C, lambda_D, margin m) and a more fragile training loop; inapplicable to pure-continuous or pure-discrete tables; no privacy analysis.

Chris Lu et al. (arXiv:2408.06292v3): 'The AI Scientist' - automates the full scientific loop (idea generation -> Aider-driven experiment iteration -> LaTeX write-up -> automated LLM peer review) across small code templates. Experiment iteration: Aider plans experiments, executes in order, receives error traces back on failure/timeout, fixes code, re-attempts up to 4 times; after each experiment writes an 'experimental journal' entry; re-plans and implements next experiment, up to 5 iterations.

Reviewer calibration (Table 1, 500 ICLR 2022 papers): Human (NeurIPS consistency-experiment baseline): balanced acc 0.66, accuracy 0.73, F1 0.49, AUC 0.65, FPR 0.17, FNR 0.52. Uncalibrated Sonnet 3.5: 0.52 +/- 0.01 balanced acc, 0.40 +/- 0.01 acc, 0.55 +/- 0.01 F1, 0.52 +/- 0.01 AUC, 0.95 +/- 0.02 FPR. The reviewer is a noisy gate, not a replacement judge - calibrated AI reviewer approaches but stays below human consistency.

Diffusion template results (Table 3): Sonnet 3.5: 51 ideas, 49 novel, 38 experiments passed, 38 papers, mean score 3.82, max 6.0, total cost ~$250. GPT-4o: 51 / 41 / 17 / 16, mean 3.70, max 5.0, ~$300. DeepSeek Coder: 51 / 42 / 32 / 31, mean 3.32, max 5.0, ~$10. Llama-3.1 405B: 51 / 31 / 21 / 21, mean 2.30, max 3.0, ~$120. Scale/cost: ~50 ideas per run, ~12 hours on 8x NVIDIA H100s; cost ~$10-15 per completed paper. Average accepted NeurIPS paper ~= 6.

Failure modes the authors state (Section 8): do NOT take generated papers' scientific content at face value - treat as hints; ideas often similar across runs (weak novelty operator); Aider fails to implement a significant fraction of ideas; agent occasionally misimplements ideas SILENTLY (needs adversarial code checking); limited experiment budget per idea -> unfair comparisons (no control for parameters/FLOPs); agent 'struggles to compare the magnitude of two numbers' (known LLM pathology) and sometimes changes the metric without accounting for it in baseline comparisons; no vision - can't fix unreadable plots; minimal sandboxing led to a runaway self-relaunching process, ~1TB checkpoint writes, and agents editing time-limit constraints instead of shortening runtime.

arXiv:2608.25770: 'HypoForge' - a self-improving multi-agent framework for automated hypothesis generation and testing that splits skill learning by supervision type: an adversarial generator-discriminator for hypothesis generation (where no explicit feedback exists) and execution-outcome learning for hypothesis testing (where empirical feedback exists), distilling accumulated experience into reusable skills rather than raw trajectories. Contrasts with Reviewer/Critic frameworks that revise individual items.

Skill update: S_h^{t+1} = distill(generator batch, discriminator distribution-level feedback); the generator 'progressively improves its hypothesis generation policy by maximizing the scientific quality score.' 'Distill into skills, not trajectories' principle: store distilled testing-skills (e.g., 'always run the permutation null before trusting a delta-Brier') alongside cases.
equation: S_h^{t+1} = distill(generator batch, discriminator distribution-level feedback)

claim: Generation (Table 4 ablations): full model vs w/o Feedback - Q(H^t): 0.785 vs 0.726; Hit@K: 0.648 vs 0.491 ('discriminator feedback effectively refines generation skills'). Testing: removing execution outcomes drops T_h from 0.659 to 0.565 while E_h stays comparable ('the importance of empirical validation signals for improving testing skills'). Headline claim: 'consistently outperforms existing AI scientist frameworks and skill-level variants in both hypothesis quality and testing performance'; learned skills show 'strong transferability across diverse scientific research tasks' (transferability claim qualitative).

Limitations: discriminator trained/defined against 'high-quality human-written hypotheses' - if that reference set overlaps the benchmark, the distribution-match score is circular (unaddressed); Q(H^t) and Hit@K are judge-based metrics with the usual bias risk; no cost/iteration counts reported.

Xin Wang et al. (Applied Soft Computing; arXiv:2507.21945v1): 'LMAC-Net' - K=5 learnable 'atomic pattern' queries per modality (RGB, optical flow, audio) plus an attention-center consistency loss forcing all modalities to attend to the same temporal segments, with two-level scoring (segment scores -> softmax-weighted overall).

Cross-attention with learnable temperature tau (init 0.07): alpha_{k,t} = exp(q_tilde_k^T v_t / tau) / sum_j exp(q_tilde_k^T v_j / tau) (Eq. 6); update p_k^{(m,i)} = sum_j a_{k,j} v_j + p_k^{(m,i-1)} (Eq. 7). Attention center alpha_bar_k^m = sum_t t * alpha_{k,t}^m (Eq. 14).
equation: alpha_{k,t} = exp(q_tilde_k^T v_t / tau) / sum_j exp(q_tilde_k^T v_j / tau)

claim: Composite loss L = lambda_1 L_score + lambda_2 L_feature (Eq. 11); L_feature = L_rank + L_sparsity + L_consistency (Eq. 13). L_rank: hinge enforcing alpha_bar_1^m < alpha_bar_2^m < ... < alpha_bar_K^m with margin d plus boundary terms (Eq. 15). L_sparsity = sum |t - alpha_bar_k^m| * alpha_{k,t}^m (Eq. 16). L_consistency = sum_t sum_{i<j} ||alpha_bar_t^{m_i} - alpha_bar_t^{m_j}||^2 (Eq. 17).

Two-level scoring: linear regression per query -> K segment scores s_hat_k; final S_hat = sum_k w_tilde_k s_hat_k with w_tilde = softmax(w), w in R^K learnable (Eq. 9-10). Validation metric: Spearman rank correlation, Fisher-z averaged across actions (Eq. 18).
equation: S_hat = sum_k w_tilde_k s_hat_k, w_tilde = softmax(w)

claim: RG average Spearman: LMAC-Net 0.840 vs PAMFN (2108 paper) 0.819 vs GDLT (unimodal SOTA) 0.765. Fis-V average: 0.850 (TES 0.811, PCS 0.881) vs PAMFN 0.822 vs GDLT 0.820. Efficiency (Table 4): 0.419G FLOPs, 8.95M params, 4 ms inference - 'substantially lower than PAMFN' (18.06M, 33 ms). Ablation (Table 5): concat baseline 0.676/0.731 -> +MLQE 0.730/0.765 -> +L_rank 0.731/0.779 -> +L_sparsity 0.735/0.779 -> +L_consistency (full) 0.797/0.808 - consistency loss is the single biggest contributor.

Ledger's leakage critique: assumption (3) - modalities SHOULD attend to identical segments - is the weak point for football: crowd audio spikes BEFORE the visible play (anticipation); exact-center consistency loss could destroy cross-modal lead-lag structure. Recommendation: asymmetric or lag-tolerant consistency loss rather than the paper's exact-center matching.

Ansari et al. (2025, arXiv:2503.12107v1): 'ChronosX' - lightweight adapter blocks (Input/Output Injection Blocks) that let frozen pretrained time-series foundation models consume past and future exogenous covariates without retraining the backbone. Objective: same as backbone (cross-entropy for Chronos; MSE for TimesFM/MOMENT variants). Training modes compared: adapter-only (frozen backbone) vs full fine-tuning vs frozen zero-shot vs covariate-free fine-tuning; tested on Chronos, MOMENT, TimesFM.

Input Injection Block (IIB): e_tilde_t = e_t + W_2 * sigma(W_1 * [e_t; x^past_t] + b_1) + b_2 (residual FFN; identity when covariates are zero/uninformative). Output Injection Block (OIB): logits_tilde_t = logits_t + FFN([logits_t; x^future_t]).
equation: e_tilde_t = e_t + W_2 * sigma(W_1 * [e_t; x^past_t] + b_1) + b_2

claim: Adapter-augmented models beat frozen backbones on covariate-driven datasets across all three backbones (Chronos, MOMENT, TimesFM). Adapter-only training matches or approaches full fine-tuning performance at a fraction of trainable parameters. IIB and OIB are complementary: past-covariate effects recovered by IIB, future-known effects by OIB; combination is best. Data: 32 synthetic datasets (each 100 daily series of length 1827, prediction horizon 30) with known ground-truth covariate effects.

Channel-discipline rule: future covariates are truly known at forecast time (weather forecasts, rest days, venue); injury reports are NOT future-known and belong in the past channel or as nowcasts. Any post-kickoff value in the future channel = leakage fail. Real-world caveat: covariates are noisy/partially observed/confounded - expect smaller gains than synthetic; no treatment of missing covariates or ragged alignment (bye weeks, postponed games).

Hsieh & Wong (2024, arXiv:2404.13371): 'On Risk-Sensitive Decision Making Under Uncertainty' - a variance-penalized Kelly objective U_n^rho(K) with a single risk-aversion knob rho, with KKT necessary-optimality conditions giving the sizing formula.

Objective: U_n^rho(K;X) = (1/n) E[log(V(n,K)/V_0)] - (rho/(2n^2)) var(log(V(n,K)/V_0)), rho >= 0; stages k=0...N-1; feedback gain K_i(k) in [0,1] fraction of account; unit-simplex constraint K_i >= 0, sum K_i = 1; account dynamics V(n) = <K, R_n> V_0; X(k) i.i.d., bounded, arbitrarily correlated components.

Betting example root equation: f(p,K_2,rho) = -1 + 2p/(1+K*_2) - 2p*rho*log(1+K*_2)/(1+K*_2) + 2p*rho*(p*log(1+K*_2)+(1-p)*log(1-K*_2))/(1+K*_2) = 0; at rho=0: K*_2 = 2(2p-1) = classical Kelly. Lemma 3.2 optimality conditions are necessary in general; necessary AND sufficient when log-variance is convex (verified in both examples via second derivative >= 0).

Numerical findings: p=0.6: rho=0 -> K*_2=0.4 (Kelly); rho=0.1 -> K*_2 approx 0.3646; rho=1 -> K*_2 approx 0.2035 (falls 'by around 0.2'). p=0.75: rho=0 -> K*_2=1; rho=1 -> K*_2 approx 0.5643. K*_2 negatively affected by rho, more sensitive to rho as profit probability rises. Inventory example (n=5, rho=1/2): K*_1=1, K*_2=0 (full allocation to safe category).

Limitations: no empirical validation at all; assumes payoff distribution known exactly (estimation uncertainty in p not handled - the overbetting risk); i.i.d. fails for sports slates; simplex = fully invested, no cash, no leverage; no principled rho-calibration procedure.

Agrawal & Ramdas (2026, arXiv:2604.20172): 'Cover Meets Robbins While Betting on Bounded Data' - a 50-50 convex combination of Cover's uniform-portfolio mixture and a modified Robbins prior that hedges the two: O(ln n) worst-case regret AND O(ln ln n) regret on typical paths plus optimal growth rate. First explicit construction achieving all three.

Setup: bet fraction lambda in [-1/m_0, 1/(1-m_0)]; wealth W_n(lambda) = product_{i=1}^n (1 - lambda*(X_i - m_0)), W_0=1; mixture wealth W_n = integral W_n(lambda) pi(lambda) d lambda; best-in-hindsight W*_n = sup_lambda W_n(lambda); regret R_n = ln W*_n - ln W_n. Key identity: ln W*_n = n * KL_inf(Q_hat_n, m_0). Assumptions: observations in [0,1]; m_0 in (0,1); comparator = constant-lambda strategies.

Thm 3.1 (Cover uniform mixture): path-wise O(ln n) regret on every sequence - unimprovable adversarially. Thm 4.1 (modified Robbins prior): low regret on every path in Ville event E_alpha = {sup_n ln W_n <= ln(1/alpha)}; Thm 4.2: O(ln ln n) regret on almost every path (measure-one set E_0); linear-regret paths a null set under bounded support. Rate hierarchy: Cover/uniform Theta(ln n) worst-case (tight); Robbins O(ln ln n) typical-paths, linear worst-case; 50-50 mixture strictly dominates each component on the combined criteria. Game-theoretic LIL: wealth process witnesses a sharp upper law of the iterated logarithm - either the LIL holds on a path or wealth -> infinity on it.

Killer dual-use: under the null (no edge, conditional mean = breakeven), wealth stays bounded (Ville); if wealth crosses 1/alpha, edge is certified at level alpha WITHOUT peeking corrections - an anytime-valid sequential test of whether the engine has edge; conversely a shutdown trigger if wealth decays. Limitations: zero empirical validation; comparator class is constant fractions only; bounded [0,1] requires affine map of real P&L (tails must be clipped); m_0 must be chosen; 50-50 weight is a choice not optimized; Robbins prior needs tuning parameters (beta_l, beta_u).

Gajera et al. (2026, arXiv:2602.06986, software paper): 'DISCOVER' (Data-Informed Symbolic Combination of Operators for Variable Equation Regression) - a Python-native, GPU-accelerated symbolic regression framework whose differentiators are hard dimensional-consistency enforcement via the pint unit library during feature generation (invalid expressions pruned before evaluation) plus multiple exact/heuristic sparse solvers (OMP, MIQP, simulated annealing) for the L_0 problem.

Core objective (Eq. 1): min_beta ||y - Phi*beta||^2_2 subject to ||beta||_0 <= D (NP-hard L_0-regularized least squares; all strategies are approximations). Physics constraints via config file: operator restrictions, complexity caps, variable-combination rules; dimensional consistency enforced with pint - units tracked through every symbolic operation, dimensionally invalid candidates excluded during generation, shrinking search space. GPU acceleration: CUDA (NVIDIA) and MPS (Apple Silicon), CPU fallback.

No numerical results or benchmarks in the paper - every performance claim is aspirational; treat as design doc, not evidence (benchmarking ongoing). Adversarial limits: (a) SISSO-style linear-in-features assumption is narrower than full SR (no nested compositions like sin(x^2+e^x) unless pre-generated); (b) hard unit constraints only help when the unit system is real - sports 'units' are softer, and over-strict rules could block valid discoveries (paper's own stated limitation); (c) MIQP exact but scales poorly, no guidance on when each solver wins.

arXiv:2504.17355v1: 'TCTO' (Collaborative Multi-Agent RL for Automated Feature Transformation). Three collaborative agents (sequential): Head Cluster Agent (pi_h: Rep(c_i) concat Rep(V) -> score), Operation Agent (pi_o: Rep(c_h) concat Rep(V) -> o in O), Operand Cluster Agent (pi_t: Rep(c_h) concat Rep(V) concat Rep(o) concat Rep(c_i) -> tail cluster for binary ops). Operation set O: unary x^2, x^3, sqrt(x), sin, cos, ln, e^x, tanh, sigmoid, 1/x, standard scaler, min-max, quantile transform; binary +, -, x, /. Roadmap clustering: similarity matrix A_tilde[i,j] = cosine(v_i, v_j) on node embeddings; enhanced Laplacian S = D - (A + A_tilde); hierarchical spectral clustering to k clusters.

Dual reward: R_p = V(M(F_{t+1}),Y) - V(M(F_t),Y) (Eq. 5, downstream delta); R_c = (1/n) sum_j 1/e^{h(v_j)} (Eq. 6, complexity penalty on roadmap depth); R = R_p + R_c, weights 1:1 (ablation: either alone is worse). Q-loss: L = (Q_p^pi(s_t,a_t) - (R_t + gamma * max Q_t^pi(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})))^2 (Eq. 7), value-based RL with prediction/target Q-networks.

MI pruning score: I(v,Y) = sum sum p(f,y) log[p(f,y)/(p(f)p(y))] (Eq. 8); node-wise pruning at 30% ratio (optimal per sweep). State representation: 2-layer Relational GCN over roadmap, relations = operation types: v_i^{(l+1)} = phi(sum_r sum_{j in N_i^r} (1/c_{i,r}) W_r^{(l)} v_j^{(l)}); cluster state Rep(c_i) = mean of node embeddings.
equation: v_i^{(l+1)} = phi(sum_r sum_{j in N_i^r} (1/c_{i,r}) W_r^{(l)} v_j^{(l)})

claim: Table I: TCTO best on all 20 datasets (9 regression, 11 classification). Selected margins vs runner-up: Housing Boston 0.495 +/- 0.015 (vs 0.491 FastFT); Airfoil 0.622 +/- 0.011 (vs 0.605 OpenFE); Openml_616 0.499 +/- 0.052 (vs 0.467 GRFG); Openml_607 0.670 +/- 0.008 (vs 0.640 GRFG); Openml_586 0.689 +/- 0.004 (vs 0.650 GRFG); PimaIndian 0.850 +/- 0.007 (vs 0.835 FastFT); SpectF 0.950 +/- 0.012 (vs 0.927 FastFT); Messidor 0.742 +/- 0.003 (vs 0.731 FastFT); German Credit 0.768 +/- 0.008 (vs 0.749 FastFT); Higgs 0.709 +/- 0.001 (vs 0.709 GRFG, tie broken at 3rd decimal); Amazon Employee 0.936 +/- 0.001 (vs 0.935). Table II robustness: best or tied-best across all 7 downstream models on Housing Boston (Lasso 0.370 vs 0.238 FastFT - 56% relative lift) and Messidor.

Case study (Table III): Housing Boston 1-RAE 0.414 (raw) -> 0.474 (TCTO-g) -> 0.494 (TCTO); top-10 importance sum falls 0.993 -> 0.527 (diversifies importance across deeper transforms; reuses high-value intermediate nodes v_17, v_30). Wine White F1 0.536 -> 0.559. Costs: reward estimation dominates runtime (16 min/step on ALBERT-425k with RF -> switched to LightGBM); linear time scaling with dataset size; node-wise pruning ratio 30% optimal; on extremely large-sample sets all AFT methods show limited gains (networks already learn latent patterns).

Adversarial read notes: only TCTO reports +/- std; baselines appear point estimates; reward = downstream validation performance (risk of feature-space overfit without nested CV; paper doesn't detail discipline); operation set is generic math - discovered features like 1/(sin v_12 - v_0) are uninterpretable and potentially numerically unstable (division near zero); all experiments tabular IID, no temporal validation.

arXiv:2605.28816 (NVIDIA Research, 2026): 'Gamma-World' (Generative Multi-Agent World Modeling Beyond Two Players). Flow matching: L_FM = E||v_theta(z_sigma,sigma,C) - (epsilon - z_0)||^2 on linear interpolant z_sigma = (1-sigma)z_0 + sigma*epsilon (eqs. 1-2); Transformer-based latent video diffusion (DiT) with block-causal attention (Diffusion Forcing/Self-Forcing) for streaming. Training in three stages: (a) bidirectional teacher (dense attention, single shared noise level); (b) block-causal student with SHA + Diffusion Forcing as full multi-step diffusion; (c) conditional Self-Forcing distillation with DMD + rollout-aware training into few-step generator. Streaming: KV caches per agent stream + shared hub cache; 24 FPS.

Simplex Rotary Agent Encoding: 4D rotary operator R_4D(t,p,h,w) = diag(R_t(t), R_p(p), R_h(h), R_w(w)) (eq. 6); agent angles theta_p = alpha * s_{pi(p)} (eq. 9), where s_v = sqrt(V/(V-1)) * Q(e_v - (1/V)1) are regular-simplex vertices (eq. 7) with unit norm and equal pairwise distance 2V/(V-1) (eq. 8, proved App. B); V = fixed simplex pool (max identities), V <= d_p/2+1; per batch, agents randomly assigned to distinct vertices pi - parameter-free, permutation-symmetric, no learned slots; new agents activate unused vertices at inference without architecture change.

Sparse Hub Attention: sequence = PTL agent tokens + TK hub tokens (K learnable hubs per frame, broadcast, removed from output); mask M_hub(i,j) = 1[rho(i)=rho(j) or rho(i)=hub or rho(j)=hub] (eq. 11); composed with block-causal mask M(i,j) = 1[b(j)<=b(i)] * M_hub (eq. 12); cost drops from O(P^2 n^2 L^2) to O(PnL(nL+nK)) + O(nK(PnL+nK)) (eq. 13) - linear in P.

vs baselines (Table 1, FVD down / FID down across 5 protocols): gamma-World 184.1/24.8 (memory), 199.3/24.0 (grounding), 191.5/21.2 (movement), 264.5/32.1 (building), 280.0/46.9 (consistency) vs Solaris 333.8/51.7, 301.9/36.1, 311.1/36.3, 448.6/71.0, 443.1/94.8 - best in every column, roughly halving Solaris's FVD. Ablation (Table 2): Simplex+SparseHub (full): FVD 223.4, FID 30.2, LPIPS 0.269, PSNR 27.7, SSIM 0.836 vs learned view-embedding+dense: 256.3/32.4/0.281/26.4/0.815 vs sequence-concat no-encoding dense: 285.6/35.2/0.298/25.6/0.798 - simplex encoding is the bigger win; SHA matches dense attention quality at linear cost. Zero-shot 2->4-agent generalization works qualitatively; streaming at 24 FPS.

Limitations (stated): gaming/robotics only; no explicit 3D geometry or physics - long rollouts drift; simplex pool caps scaling (V <= d_p/2+1); no quantitative state-accuracy metrics, all perceptual; the trained model is useless for NFL - only the two mechanisms transfer. MOVE-37 lab report (2026-09-13): two symbolic-regression experiments on squared win probability added (WPA^2) from nflfastR play-by-play (2021-2024; 141,288 plays) - a time-stratified SR run testing whether the GP could discover a conditional time-term contribution, plus a soft-target-regularization variant. Both designs failed - the report concludes the SR method is 'structurally incapable of this target class.' Target: y = WPA^2, clipped at stratum-train 99th percentile, standardized. Strata on game_seconds_remaining: EARLY = gsr > 2700 (Q1, n~16k/24k train/repl), LATE = gsr < 900 (Q4/OT, n~19k/28.6k train/repl). Harness: gplearn SymbolicRegressor, log-cosh fitness, function set {add,sub,mul,div,sqrt,log,abs,inv,tanh}, population 2000 x 30 generations, parsimony 0.001; splits primary train 2021-2022 -> test 2023, replication train 2021-2023 -> test 2024.

Probe diagnostics (GBM ceiling / OLS linear test R^2): LATE primary: GBM 0.3079, OLS 0.0514; clip99 0.0565, tail kurtosis 31.4. LATE replication: GBM 0.2979, OLS 0.0420; kurt 29.8. EARLY primary: GBM 0.1514, OLS 0.0882; kurt 18.7. EARLY replication: GBM 0.1375, OLS 0.0749; kurt 18.8. Calibrated human time-term heuristic (B2 baseline) explains test R^2 0.1233 / 0.1165 in the LATE stratum vs 0.053 on full data - time carries concentrated late-game signal.

Best LATE SR programs found only baroque transforms of |score_differential| (X3): seed 123 R^2 0.0369 / 0.0385 (log(tanh(inv(sqrt(tanh(X3)))))); seed 42: mul(-0.211, abs(X3)) R^2 0.0315; seed 7 collapsed to constant -0.160, R^2 negative. NO quarter_seconds_remaining (X4) term in any of 6 LATE programs, on either split. Smooth-linear OLS on the same 9 features beats best SR in LATE (0.0537/0.0433 vs 0.0369/0.0385) - kink is decoration there.

EARLY control: both seeds found down-only forms (X0 = down); sub(X0, tanh(X0)) R^2 0.1126 / 0.0922 beats OLS (0.0898 / 0.0777) - down effect is genuinely nonlinear (saturating). Redesign C (soft-target regularization beta=0.9 on y_train, Vanneschi & Castelli 2021): two of three seeds collapsed to constants (R^2 -0.0300 / -0.0207); third found sqrt(|score_differential|) at R^2 -0.0030, worse than log-cosh alone (best 0.0157). Per pre-registered rule, SR declared structurally incapable of this target class.

Play-type residual gate: target = pass_indicator - xpass (nflfastR xPass column); residual mean -0.0431/-0.0437; GBM ceiling 0.0527 (primary) / 0.0375 (replication) vs kill threshold 0.03 -> CONTINUE, not skipped; OLS captures most of it (0.040/0.026 - little nonlinear headroom); kurtosis -1.04 -> MSE (not log-cosh) is the correct fitness if ever run. nflfastR xPass overpredicts pass probability by ~4.3pp on the pass/run-filtered sample - possible miscalibration or sample-selection artifact, reported as observation not claim.

American football is structurally the hardest mainstream sport for computer vision: 22 players, coordinated movement from a standing start, LOS pileups described as the densest occlusion scenario in mainstream sport, helmets defeating face-based re-ID, and route/formation classification requiring strategy understanding; no open equivalent of SoccerNet exists for NFL broadcast, and the expensive gap is labeled data for football-specific classifiers, not geometry.

The 7-method de-vig oracle implements multiplicative, additive, power, Shin 1992/93, differential margin weighting (Buchdahl), odds ratio (Cheung), and logarithmic methods; the common prelude is invOdds[i] = 1/decimalOdds[i], margin = sum(invOdds) - 1; every method sums to 1.0 within 1e-9; power solves for k in sum(invOdds^k)==1 by bisection on (0,100); the Market A docstring margin=0.1362 is STALE and wrong (true 0.03242570633874986) and must be regenerated, not hand-edited.

Shin 1992/93 de-vigging solves the insider-trading parameter z in [0,100] so that sum(shinProb(z))==1, with shinProb(z)[i] = (sqrt(z^2 + 4*(1-z)*invOdds[i]^2/sum(invOdds)) - z) / (2-2z); if there is no sign change it falls back to multiplicative; golden fixtures: Market A z=0.01623644285628778, Market B z=0.01875368084485522, Market C z=0.0 with Shin equal to Multiplicative.

Parlay MRI v1 uses the Karlis & Ntzoufras (2003) bivariate Poisson: X = W1+W3, Y = W2+W3 with Wi ~ Pois(lambda_i) independent, Cov(X,Y) = lambda3 exactly, and lambda3 -> 0 collapsing to the independent product model; parameterization lambda1 = exp(homeAdvantage + homeAttack + awayDefense), lambda2 = exp(awayAttack + homeDefense), lambda3 = exp(correlationLog); the PMF sums k=0..min(x,y) of poissonPmf(x-k,lambda1) x poissonPmf(y-k,lambda2) x poissonPmf(k,lambda3).

Bivariate Poisson test-vector hazards: Set1 (l1=1.5, l2=1.0, l3=0.3) has P01 == P00 exactly because l2=1.0 is the multiplicative identity of Poisson, so a lambda1/lambda2 transposition bug passes Set1 undetected and regression tests must fix at least one Set2 value; and grid truncation silently discards mass (the 4x4 Set1 grid captures only 85.8% of mass, sum=0.8580), so grids must use maxGoals about 10-15 or set normalize:true.

Pose2Trajectory equations: Time2Vec t2v(tau)[i] = omega_i tau + phi_i if i = 0; F(omega_i tau + phi_i) if 1 <= i <= k; MEDE = (1/T) sum_{t=1}^{T} sqrt((x_t - x-hat_t)^2 + (y_t - y-hat_t)^2).
equation: t2v(\tau)[i] = \omega_i\tau + \phi_i\ \text{if}\ i = 0;\ F(\omega_i\tau + \phi_i)\ \text{if}\ 1 \le i \le k;\ MEDE = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{(x_t - \hat{x}_t)^2 + (y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2}

claim: Findings: joints beat trajectory-only 2x at short horizons (36 vs 79 px MEDE at 50 ms); ball context dominates long horizons (48 vs 91 px at 500 ms); no external baselines (no Kalman, no published SOTA); interpolation leakage risk: ball-gap polynomial fill uses 10 points after the gap (future information); REJECT.

Agent Imputer architecture: input window L=5 events centered on t -> shared bidirectional Time-Aware LSTM (H_1=100, irregular-Delta-t cell-memory discount) -> dense+ReLU (H_2=50) -> fully-connected graph 2-layer SAGEConv (H_3=64, H_4=32, mean aggregation) -> (B x N x 2); 15 features/agent/timestep incl. nextAgentTime/X/Y (future info - a smoother, not a filter); loss = mean Euclidean distance; 150 epochs, batch 128, AdamW lr 0.002.

Findings: position imputation test (meters) X/Y/XY = 4.29+-0.09/4.41+-0.11/6.88+-0.10 vs best naive 18.01+-0.46 -> ~61.8% error reduction; LSTM-only beats GNN-only (temporal modeling is the essential component); error significantly higher at end of halves (p<0.01, fatigue/loss-of-structure); distance covered abs % error 2.79-6.03%; pitch control MAE 0.130 vs baselines 0.272-0.305; limitations: deterministic point estimates, no uncertainty; 6.9 m error too coarse for micro-events.

Augmented APM equations: ridge APM beta-hat = argmin_beta ||y - X beta||^2_2 + lambda ||beta||^2_2; Bayesian recast y|beta ~ N(X beta, sigma^2); beta ~ N(0, tau^2), tau = 0.1, sigma = 1; Augmented APM beta|alpha ~ N(alpha x rating, tau^2); alpha ~ N(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha^2); time weighting y|beta ~ N(t X beta, t sigma^2).
equation: \hat{\beta} = \arg\min_{\beta}\|y - X\beta\|^2_2 + \lambda\|\beta\|^2_2;\ y|\beta \sim N(X\beta, \sigma^2);\ \beta \sim N(0, \tau^2),\ \tau = 0.1,\ \sigma = 1;\ \beta|\alpha \sim N(\alpha \times rating, \tau^2);\ \alpha \sim N(\mu_\alpha, \sigma_\alpha^2);\ y|\beta \sim N(tX\beta, t\sigma^2)

claim: Findings: Augmented APM has best predictive accuracy in all three seasons (10-fold CV); FIFA starts the season as the best predictor; both APM and Augmented APM out-predict FIFA by February (calendar decay of prior value); Salah ranked 1st in standard APM, 4th in Augmented APM; replacing goal differential with xG response did NOT improve accuracy; prior hyperparameters set by intuition, not estimated; MSE differences reported without confidence intervals.

Underdog CLT-rule equations: mu = sum_i v_i N_i p_i; sigma^2 = sum_i v_i^2 N_i p_i(1-p_i); P ~= (1/2)[1 + erf(Z/sqrt(2))], Z = (mu - mu_opp)/sqrt(sigma^2 + sigma_opp^2); skill curve p_i(N_i) = alpha_i - beta_i N_i/N.
equation: \mu = \sum_i v_i N_i p_i;\ \sigma^2 = \sum_i v_i^2 N_i p_i(1-p_i);\ P \simeq \frac{1}{2}[1 + \text{erf}(Z/\sqrt{2})],\ Z = \frac{\mu - \mu_{opp}}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \sigma_{opp}^2}};\ p_i(N_i) = \alpha_i - \beta_i N_i/N

claim: Findings: underdog (mu < mu_opp) maximizes win probability by increasing outcome variance; favorite minimizes it (the 'CLT Rule'); basketball optimal 2/3 mix switches at s_{2/3} = 0.39N; football toy: run when y < 2.8N, Hail Mary when y > 4.9N, short pass between; skill curve: optimal three-point share N_3/N ~= 0.208; assumes i.i.d. Bernoulli trials, fixed opponent, no downs/field position/clock - opponent modeled as fixed (no game-theoretic response).

CAMP decomposes each cricket over into actual-minus-expected runs from a state-dependent expected-remaining-runs model: expected runs in over i are e_i = R(S_i) - R(S_{i+1}) with R(S_i) = P(S_i) - T(S_i) (projected total minus Duckworth-Lewis-style target adjustment), wicket-adjusted to e'_i = (1-w)*e_i if a wicket fell (w tuned to 1, so a wicket zeroes the over's expectation) and actual over value r_i = A(S_i) - A(S_{i+1}); batter contribution is c_i^p = r_i^p - (e'_i/6)*b_p, bowler contribution c-hat_i^p = e'_i - r_i, and the final score CAMP_score = w_bat*C_bat(p) + w_bowl*C_bowl(p) with w_bat=1, w_bowl=0.2 tuned to maximize Man-of-the-Match agreement on the same 961-match corpus used for evaluation -- the corpus verdict is REJECT because the wicket penalty and batting/bowling weights were tuned on the evaluation metric (textbook data snooping), with no train/test split and no temporal validation of any kind.
equation: e_i = R(S_i) - R(S_{i+1}); e'_i = (1-w)*e_i if wicket fell, else e_i; c_i^p = r_i^p - (e'_i/6)*b_p; c-hat_i^p = e'_i - r_i; CAMP_score = w_bat*C_bat(p) + w_bowl*C_bowl(p)

claim: CAMP validated against Man-of-the-Match awards on ESPNcricinfo ball-by-ball ODI data (961 matches, 1,002 batters, 802 bowlers, 2001-2019): among the winning team's 11, Rank 1 agreement was CAMP 638/961 (66.3%) vs baseline LNC 585/961 (60.8%) and Top 3 867/961 (90.2%) vs 864/961 (89.9%); but among all 22 players Rank 1 was CAMP 458/961 (47.6%) vs LNC 461/961 (47.9%) -- no rank-1 edge where it matters most, and the headline edge is in-sample since constants were tuned on this corpus; MoM itself is a narrative-driven ground truth (voters reward match-winning moments, exactly what a context metric rewards) that inflates agreement.

L1-regularized logistic regression for partial player effects in hockey (2,439 players, n=69,449 goals, 11 NHL seasons 2002-03 to 2013-14): log[q_i/(1-q_i)] = alpha + u_i'gamma + v_i'phi + x_i'beta_0 + (x_i circ s_i)'(beta_s + p_i beta_p) with y_i = +1 home scored goal i / -1 away, penalized negative log-likelihood l(eta;y) = sum log(1+exp[-y_i eta_i]) + n*lambda*sum_j(|beta_0j|+|beta_sj|+|beta_pj]), only player effects penalized while team-season (gamma) and special-teams (phi) effects are left unpenalized to fully remove confounding; lambda chosen by corrected AICc = 2*sum l(eta-hat_lambda;y) + 2kn/(n-k-1) (analytic and deterministic, preferred over cross-validation), fit with the gamlr R package with standardize=FALSE so low-ice-time players are not up-weighted.
equation: log[q_i/(1-q_i)] = alpha + u_i'gamma + v_i'phi + x_i'beta_0 + (x_i circ s_i)'(beta_s + p_i beta_p); l(eta;y) = sum log(1+exp[-y_i eta_i]) + n*lambda*sum_j(|beta_0j|+|beta_sj|+|beta_pj]); AICc = 2*sum l(eta-hat_lambda;y) + 2kn/(n-k-1)

claim: Partial for-percent and partial plus-minus derived from the fitted coefficients: PFP_sj = (1+exp[-beta_0j-beta_sj])^-1 and PPM_sj = g_sj*PFP_sj - g_sj*(1-PFP_sj) = g_sj*(1-2*PFP_sj) where g_sj is goals player j was on ice for; rankings change dramatically vs the no-confounder model -- Sidney Crosby drops out of the top 5 per-season when special-teams effects are omitted (penalty-kill time confounds player ratings, showing snap context must be unpenalized controls, not folded into player effects), and goalies' PPM collapse once team-season effects are controlled because they act as team surrogates.

Process vs outcome metrics diverge: Daniel Sedin tops Corsi-PPM at 615.14 (2010-11) but ranks 152nd in goals-PPM (19.45), which the authors call troubling for Corsi-only analysis since only goal differentials win games; PPM is more correlated with salary than marginal plus-minus, goals-based metrics more salary-correlated than Corsi-based, and PFP > 0.5 cleanly predicts high salary vs marginal for-percent peaking near 0.5; all playoff-innovation coefficients beta-hat_pj = 0, i.e., no evidence of clutch players was detected.

In the normal location model Y = theta + Z with Z ~ N_p(0, I_p) under quadratic loss R(theta,delta) = E_theta||delta - theta||^2, a fixed-scale Bayesian neural network Bayes estimator is provably NOT minimax (thin prior tails over-shrink large signals; the Stein excess-risk integrand B(u) = psi(u)^2*u - 2p*psi(u) - 4u*psi'(u) with psi(u) = E[1/(1+V) | U = u] gives u*psi(u) -> infinity as u -> infinity so sup_theta R > p), while replacing the fixed scale with a heavy-tailed BetaPrime(1, b) hyperprior on the effective output variance with b = p/2 - 2 yields a minimax and admissible radial shrinkage rule delta_BNN,hyper(Y) = E[W/(1+W) | Y] Y = (1 - E[(1+W)^-1 | Y]) Y via superharmonicity of sqrt(m) (Fourdrinier-Strawderman-Wells); the rule is a one-dimensional radial shrinkage factor computable by quadrature or Monte Carlo over W and requires p >= 5.
equation: delta_BNN,hyper(Y) = E[W/(1+W) | Y]Y = (1 - E[(1+W)^-1 | Y])Y, W ~ BetaPrime(1, p/2 - 2)
