Fifteen team-selection strategies in 3 families (Variable: Random 1/2, Fav Team, Allrounder Select All, Career Averages, Tournament Stats, Popularity; Deterministic: Career Points, TOPSIS x3, Mean-Var Optimization; Learning/Deterministic form-based: MA5 = avg points last 5 matches, MA1 = last match, Allrounder Pref) simulated across IPL 2024 (71 completed matches, playing XI + impact players as the selection pool) under two contest payoff structures with 8 metrics (Win% Best Rank, Win% Average Rank, mean/median average points, average rank, best rank) normalized to (0,1) via x'_ij = (x_ij - (min_i x_ij - 1))/(max_i x_ij - min_i x_ij + 2) and rank-based metrics flipped via 1 - x'; dynamic tournament: 100 iterations x bootstrap-sampled matches with agent reweighting via softmax w_i = e^{x_i/25}/sum_j e^{x_j/25}, agents_i = round(w_i x 1500), 6 repetitions averaged.
equation: x'_ij = (x_ij - (min_i x_ij - 1))/(max_i x_ij - min_i x_ij + 2); w_i = e^{x_i/25}/sum_j e^{x_j/25}

claim: Contest-structure-dependent strategy results: variable strategies took rank 1 in ~95% of matches but Win%(Average Rank) ~= 0 (Random 1: Win% Best Rank 23.944%, Win% Average Rank 0.000%), while deterministic strategies had the best average rank in ~89% of matches and MA5 had Win%(Average Rank) 21.127% (highest); Average-4 ranking: Career Averages 1st, then Tournament Stats, MA5 -- all beating Random 1; Mega Contest (top-heavy, top 60% paid, steep drop-off): MA5 consistently high across all metrics while Random 1 had the highest maximum payoff but strongly negative mean/median, and MA1/Mean-Var/Allrounder Pref/Career Points/TOPSIS Synthesis/Popularity Selection had NEGATIVE maximum payoffs (every agent lost money); 4x-or-Nothing (flat, top 20% get 400): MA5's MINIMUM payoff was positive -- every MA5 agent profited; dynamic tournament: Mega converged to variable strategies + MA5 as the only strong deterministic survivor, 4x converged in 3-5 iterations to a single dominant strategy (most often MA5 or MA1); Popularity Selection performed poorly in both contests -- popularity was driven by weak strategies' picks (caution about ownership-based selection).

AbstainBoost for distribution-free sequential prediction with abstentions under an adversarial corruption threat model (Yu & Blanchard 2026): weak learners WL(T,z) partition rounds into m groups, estimate k-shattering probabilities rho-hat^S_k(F) via U-statistics + median-of-means, abstain when min_y rho^S_k(F^{x->y}) >= 0.9 rho^S_k(F) (the instance does not shrink the version space); boosting (Alg. 6) deletes each expert's first s predictions, majority-votes survivors, abstains if < C experts predict; error counts MisErr = sum_t 1[y-hat_t not in {y_t, bottom}] and AbsErr = sum_t 1[c_t = 0 and y-hat_t = bottom]; Theorem 2 (oblivious): MisErr ~< T^{3 alpha}, E[AbsErr] ~< d^2 log^{5/3}(T)*T^{1-alpha} for alpha in [0,1/3]; Theorem 5 (adaptive) same MisErr with AbsErr ~< d^2(D log D + log T)^{2/3} log(T)*T^{1-alpha}; Theorem 3 (lower bound, tight up to poly factors): some VC-1 class forces E[MisErr] >= T^alpha/32 or E[AbsErr] >= T^{1-alpha}/2 -- the polynomial tradeoff is necessary -- corpus verdict REJECT: deep correct theory for a problem GSE does not have (GSE does batch prediction on a stochastic sports process, not adversarial sequential injection), no experiments, no data, no code, and the portable mechanisms are already covered by ledgers 1153/1154/1157 with certification by 1330.
equation: Thm. 2: MisErr ~< T^{3 alpha}, E[AbsErr] ~< d^2 log^{5/3}(T)*T^{1-alpha}; Thm. 3 lower bound: E[MisErr] >= T^alpha/32 or E[AbsErr] >= T^{1-alpha}/2

claim: Closed-form dynamics for how social influence (coupling to others' opinions, alpha) and individual conviction (anchoring to initial opinion, beta) affect wisdom-of-crowds error and diversity over time (Mavrodiev & Schweitzer 2020): dx_i(t)/dt = alpha[<x(t)> - x_i(t)] + beta[x_i(0) - x_i(t)] + A xi_i(t), alpha = social influence, beta = conviction, xi_i Gaussian white noise, A = noise strength; collective error E(t) = [ln T - <ln x(t)>]^2; group diversity D(t) = Var[ln x(t)] ~= <delta^2(t)>/<x(t)>^2 (delta method); long-term diversity D_LT = <delta^2(0)>*beta^2/[<x(0)>(alpha+beta)]^2 with sensitivities dD_LT/dalpha = -2<delta^2(0)>beta^2/[<x(0)>^2(alpha+beta)^3] < 0 (social influence always destroys diversity) and dD_LT/dbeta = 2 alpha beta<delta^2(0)>/[<x(0)>^2(alpha+beta)^3] > 0 (conviction preserves it); long-term collective error E_LT is an infinite series in initial moments with (alpha,beta) weights (Eqn. 19) and d<ln x(t)>/dt > 0 always.
equation: dx_i(t)/dt = alpha[<x(t)> - x_i(t)] + beta[x_i(0) - x_i(t)] + A xi_i(t); D_LT = <delta^2(0)>*beta^2/[<x(0)>(alpha+beta)]^2

claim: Parameter-sweep scenarios (Fig. 3, exact): (a) E(0) = 0.80, <ln x(0)> < ln T: increasing alpha always improves, increasing beta worsens; (b) E(0) = 0.02, <ln x(0)> > ln T: any alpha deteriorates, beta counterbalances; (c) E(0) = 0.01, <ln x(0)> < ln T: non-monotonic -- E_LT = 0 achievable with alpha < 0.5 and sufficient beta, alpha > 0.5 deteriorates; qualitative: social influence helps only when initial collective error is large AND the initial mean is below truth -- in most cases it deteriorates -- while conviction always mitigates; the corpus ADAPT is an ensemble-diversity governance rule for GSE's model pool (ensemble members sharing nflverse data, features, and retraining pipelines are the analog of high-alpha agents -- 'diversity rot', with no repo file currently auditing cross-model dependence): audit via alpha_proxy = mean pairwise correlation of week-to-week prediction changes across component models, beta_proxy = each model's correlation with its private signal vs the ensemble mean, weekly delta^2(t) tracking of cross-model log-odds variance, a model-independence registry (each model keeps >= 1 unshared feature family/source), and a new-model gate requiring mean pairwise |correlation| < 0.85 on holdout.

Peer expectations (each expert's expectation of OTHER experts' forecasts) cut worst-case regret in forecast aggregation (Kong 2024, arXiv:2402.06062v1): regret R(f, pi) = excess Brier loss over the Bayesian aggregator knowing pi (binary state, quadratic loss); proposed aggregators over (forecast x_i, peer-expectation p_i) pairs: average expectation, weighted expectation, weighted hard sigmoid, plus a dedicated C.I.I.D. aggregator and hard-sigmoid variant; the level-one (forecasts only) minimax regret floor cited is 0.0225; in the refinement-ordered (Blackwell-informativeness) setting peer expectations drive minimax regret to 0 (theorem, not numerical).
equation: R(f, pi) = excess Brier loss over the Bayesian aggregator knowing pi

claim: Reported worst-case regrets (starred = Matlab numerical estimates, not proved maxima): two conditionally independent experts -- average expectation 0.0072*, weighted expectation 0.0040*, weighted hard sigmoid 0.00255*, information-theoretic lower bound 0.00144; C.I.I.D. setting -- dedicated aggregator 0.00391*, hard sigmoid 0.00211*; the paper claims peer expectations cut regret by roughly an order of magnitude vs the 0.0225 level-one floor, but all gains are worst-case regrets inside synthetic discretized games, not accuracy gains on real panels; assumptions: experts truthfully report forecast and peer expectation, binary state, squared loss, conditionally independent (or C.I.I.D.) signals (strategic misreporting and correlated signals out of scope); iterating higher-order expectations may converge to the prior, with XOR as an explicit counterexample where it does not; the GSE translation is to use each engine component's 'expectation' of the market/median-model forecast as the peer proxy (computable offline, no elicitation needed) and aggregate with the weighted hard-sigmoid rule (adoption gate: >= 0.002 Brier improvement, Diebold-Mariano p < 0.05, walk-forward on 2024-2025 picks).

Exact statistical properties of the MAE table-prediction metric under random guessing (Haugen & Owren 2018): MAE = (1/n) sum_{i=1}^{n} |P(i) - i| over predicted permutation P of n teams; Theorem A.1: max_P S(P) = n^2/2 (even n), attained by the reversed permutation P_0 = [n,n-1,...,1], hence max MAE = n/2; E[MAE] = (1/3)*(n^2-1)/n (eq. A.6) and Var[MAE] = (n+1)(2n^2+7)/(45n^2) (eq. A.7) under uniform random guessing -- for n = 20: E[MAE] = 6.65, max = 10, P(exact table by chance) = 1/20! ~= 4e-19; Paul Merson's 2016/17 Premier League pre-season prediction achieved MAE = 2.8 vs the random-guess expectation 6.65.

On the Norwegian top flight (2009-2016, round-by-round tables): per round r, regressing final rank on round-r rank -> R^2_pos(r) and final rank on round-r goal difference -> R^2_gd(r); Tippeligaen 2016: R^2_pos(r) reaches 0.80 by round 7 -- 80% of final-table variation explained 7 rounds in; across 2009-2016 goal difference beats table rank (R^2_gd > R^2_pos) early in the season in 7 of 8 seasons (the exception is 2016, where rank dominated all rounds), with roughly 80% explanatory power by mid-season for most seasons -- supporting the strategy: sort by goal difference early, switch to latest table later; caveat: R^2 values are in-sample per season (fit and evaluated on the same season's rounds) and there is no controlled comparison against simulation-based methods; the GSE transfer is to build the NFL analog (2015-2025 weekly R^2 curves of final win totals on week-r standings vs schedule-adjusted point differential) and to adopt the MAE-null formulas into season-product methodology docs as exact chance baselines.

Descriptive ice-hockey tracking study (Yu, Boucher, Bornn & Javan 2019, SPORTLOGiQ proprietary data: ~3,650 events/game, NHL/AHL/SHL 2016/17-2017/18, 0.50M 5v5 passes) measuring pace arithmetically as distance traveled by the puck between successive same-team possession events divided by elapsed time, decomposed into phi_T (total speed), phi_EW (east-west), phi_NS (north-south), phi_N (north-only; backward movement counted as zero), analyzed zonally and via a polygrid (rink in 668 cells of 5x5 feet, 2D Gaussian smoothing sigma = 0.5): phi_T highest in the neutral zone with offensive/defensive zones ~10-13% slower; OZ forward pace (phi_N) 35% slower than DZ and 43% slower than NZ (offered as explanation for the previously reported negative correlation between forward pace and offense); second-period 'long change': DZ forward pace up ~7%, odd-man rushes up ~35%; zone entries: high-danger entries 24.3 ft/s vs dump-ins 21.6 ft/s (~13% faster); pre-shot pace quintiles 10 -> 42 ft/s: true shooting 2.9% -> 4.1% (+38%) with shot distance constant at ~37-40 ft; failed receptions occur at significantly higher speeds than successful ones (exception: slot passes); AHL phi_T 1-2% slower than NHL; McDavid fastest in OZ (driven by phi_NS), Jagr slowest (-13.7% OZ WOWY) -- corpus verdict REJECT (wrong sport, proprietary unreplicable data, purely descriptive, no forecast, no calibration, no market test).

Investment strategy minimizing the probability wealth ever falls to a fixed fraction alpha of its running maximum (drawdown) in a Black-Scholes market with deterministic payout (Angoshtari, Bayraktar & Young 2015): wealth dW_t = [rW_t + (mu-r)pi_t - c(W_t)]dt + sigma pi_t dB_t (eq. 2.1) with payout c(w) continuous, non-decreasing, unique 'safe level' w_s where rw = c(w) (Assumption 2.1); drawdown time tau_alpha = inf{t: W_t <= alpha M_t} with M_t = running max; the optimal strategy (Prop. 2.1, Thm. 3.1) pi*(w) = 2(c(w)-rw)/(mu-r) (eqs. 2.3, 3.8) -- the DOLLAR amount (not fraction) invested in the risky asset -- is independent of m and alpha and is provably identical to the ruin-minimizing rule even with a moving ruin level alpha M_t; minimum drawdown probability phi(w,m) = 1 - g(w,m)/g(w_s,m) for m >= w_s and phi = 1 - k(m)g(w,m)/g(w_s,w_s) for m < w_s (eq. 3.6) with scale function g (eq. 2.6), k (eq. 3.7), and delta = 1/2((mu-r)/sigma)^2.
equation: dW_t = [rW_t + (mu-r)pi_t - c(W_t)]dt + sigma pi_t dB_t; tau_alpha = inf{t: W_t <= alpha M_t}; pi*(w) = 2(c(w)-rw)/(mu-r)

claim: Universality (Remark 3.2): the identical strategy pi*(w) = 2(c(w)-rw)/(mu-r) minimizes E[f(min, max)] for ANY f non-increasing in the minimum and non-decreasing in the maximum -- the objective shape only changes boundary conditions; under mild conditions the safe level w_s is never reached (Feller explosion test, v(w_s^-,m) = inf; Props. 4.1-4.3), and if c(w)-rw stays bounded away from 0 (w_s = inf) drawdown probability is identically 1; no numerical results (theorem paper), but qualitatively the optimal risky amount shrinks linearly to zero as wealth approaches the safe level; the infinite-horizon assumption is load-bearing -- finite-horizon variants can behave differently, and a betting season is finite; the GSE translation is a per-slate bankroll risk budget (alpha = 0.8 stop, 'payout' c(w) as per-slate unit-withdrawal/target-profit function) R(w) = 2*(c(w)-r*w)/(mu-r) with (mu-r)/sigma mapped to the engine's per-slate edge/volatility, auto-derisking as bankroll approaches the safe level, split across approved edges proportionally to edge/vol^2, with phi(w,m) monitored as a bankroll risk metric.

In the Garivaltis (2019) continuous-time Kelly model with borrowing, a Kelly gambler facing a loan rate r_L chooses optimal leverage b*(r_L) = (μ − r_L)/σ²; Nash bargaining between broker and gambler yields the outcome that the gambler sizes as if borrowing at the broker's call rate, b* = (μ − r)/σ², and the bargained rate is r_L* = (3/4)r + (1/4)(ν − σ²/2); in the paper's illustrative example (σ = 15%, r = 3%, ν = 9%) the outputs are leverage 3.17, negotiated rate 4.2%, net interest margin 1.2%, gambler growth 12%/year, and broker profit 2.6% of client equity/year. The corpus ledger verdict was REJECT (broker margin-loan pricing, no sports content) and it does not count toward the valuable target.

Li (2023, arXiv:2302.13979v1) makes Kelly portfolio choice robust to distributional uncertainty by solving max_w min_{P: W(P,ς_n) ≤ δ} E_P[log(1 + wᵀR)], where W is the Wasserstein distance between the adversarial distribution P and the empirical log-return distribution ς_n; the paper derives an exact finite-dimensional convex dual reformulation so no adversary sampling is needed, and in an out-of-sample test (10 random S&P 500 stocks per universe, 1,000 repetitions, trained on 2019 daily log-returns, tested 2020-01-01 through 2023-02-20 including the COVID crash) the robust version shows directional improvements over standard Kelly on all five metrics (annualized return, volatility, Sharpe, max drawdown, log final wealth), with larger δ (δ ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4}) being more conservative and better protected during the COVID crash. Caveats: all results are graphical only (no numeric tables), δ is chosen on an ad hoc grid with no data-driven rule, and transaction costs/leverage constraints are not modeled.
equation: max_w min_{P: W(P,ς_n) ≤ δ} E_P[log(1 + wᵀR)]

claim: Szabó, Gascón & Baran (arXiv:2212.12504v1) post-process dual-resolution ECMWF precipitation forecasts (one 9 km deterministic run + 51-member 18 km ensemble) with censored shifted gamma EMOS (CSG), linking ensemble statistics to a gamma distribution shifted and left-censored at zero and estimating parameters by minimizing mean CRPS over a rolling training window, scored with CRPS(F,x) = ∫(F(y) − 1{y≥x})² dy, CRPSS vs the raw ensemble, and Brier scores; semi-locally trained CSG EMOS (stations clustered by climatological/ensemble characteristics) fully catches up with state-of-the-art quantile mapping without needing the extra historical data quantile mapping requires, while raw dual-resolution differences shrink to non-significant levels after post-processing. Limitations: CSG is precipitation-specific, the configuration is ECMWF-specific, and verification is European-domain only.

Wu, Yan & Chen (arXiv:2603.21163v2) simultaneously estimate MLB ballpark effects and team defensive quality from Statcast total-bases residuals (2015–2024) in two stages: (1) Total Bases Residual R_i = TB_i − μ_g(i), where μ_g(i) is expected total bases given the batted ball's exit-velocity/launch-angle group; (2) a weighted least-squares regression of TBR on ballpark indicators plus defensive-team indicators, producing a Defensive Bases Saved (DBS) metric with standardized 95% uncertainty intervals; average 95% interval half-widths are 19.97 standardized points for park factors and 30.84 for defense, DBS correlates with Outs Above Average at 0.5327 vs 0.4409 with the Def metric, and where TBR-based park estimates disagree with official MLB park factors, home–away scoring patterns are more consistent with the new estimates. Caveats: additive separable park/defense assumption, EV/LA measurement error, weighting-scheme dependence, MLB-specific.

Dubach (arXiv:2604.24366v2, pre-registered) studies Polymarket limit-order-book microstructure on 30.29 billion order-book events over 52 days joined to 255.43 million on-chain trades across 600 pre-registered markets, documenting: a longshot spread premium (SF1) with median quoted half-spread ~400 bps in mid probability deciles rising to 650–900 bps below 0.10 probability, an order of magnitude wider than racetrack premia; depth that is layered not top-heavy (median top-of-book share 0.136 vs 0.10 uniform null; only 9% of markets top-heavy with L1 > 0.5); median maker HHI 0.031 (~32 effective makers); category median effective half-spreads of 0.0075 (Sports), 0.0001 (Geopolitics), −0.0004 (Other), −0.0393 (Crypto) prob pp; a wash-share lower bound with median self-counterparty share 0.97%, p99 10.6%, max 22.2%; and a depth regression with coefficients +0.222 on log duration (SE 0.073), −1.02 on log p(1−p) (SE 0.180), +0.41 on log volume (SE 0.046) and +0.008 on time-to-close (t=0.08, no residual effect).

In Dubach's Polymarket microstructure study, trade direction inferred from the public feed via the STRICT algorithm agrees with on-chain aggressor sign (from makerAssetId/takerAssetId) only ~59% of the time (volume-weighted 0.592, 95% CI [0.542, 0.659]; panel mean 0.615, CI [0.579, 0.653]) vs ~80% for Lee-Ready on equities, meaning feed-only microstructure measures on Polymarket are direction-blind and direction must be sourced from on-chain OrderFilled events; additionally the measures are window-fragile, with the effective half-spread sign-flipping on 67%/50% of comparable markets across two windows and Kyle's λ flipping on 60%/43%, while Glosten–Harris decomposition S^(eff)_(1/2) = c + φ on the top-100 markets with on-chain signs gives a median effective half-spread of ≈ −0.0003 prob pp, i.e., essentially zero systematic spread on the largest markets.

Lototsky & Pollok (arXiv:2002.03448v1) extend the Kelly criterion to general return distributions with the growth rate gr(f) = E[ln(1 + f·r)] (eq. 2.5) maximized for the optimal fraction f*, wealth asymptotics W_n^f = exp(n·gr(f)·(1 + ε_n)) with ε_n → 0 a.s., a CLT refinement (Thm 2.1, eq. 2.10) W_n^f = exp(n·gr(f) + √n·σ_r(f)·ζ_n + ϵ_n) with σ_r(f) = (E[ln²(1+fr)] − gr²(f))^{1/2} for finite-horizon wealth confidence bands, concavity dgr/df = E[r/(1+fr)] and d²gr/df² = −E[r²/(1+fr)²] < 0 with interior optimum conditions giving a unique f* ∈ (0,1), a high-frequency limit (Thm 4.1, eq. 4.5) W_t^f = exp((fμ − f²σ²/2)·t + fσ·B_t) under r_{n,k} = μ/n + (σ/√n)·ξ_{n,k}, and a lognormal closed form (Thm 4.2, eq. 4.16) f* = b/σ² + 1/2 for P_t = e^{bt+σB_t}, with the binary case recovering f* = 2p − 1 and max gr = p·ln(p/(1−p)) + (2−p)·ln(2−2p); numerics at n=10 bets per unit time match the closed form closely for b ∈ (−1/2, 1/2). Limitations: fat-tailed Lévy cases derived but not simulated, closed form is lognormal/GBM-only, and Thm 4.1's T=+infinity version is explicitly unavailable.

Lototsky & Pollok's Thm 2.1 finite-horizon refinement W_n^f = exp(n·gr(f) + √n·σ_r(f)·ζ_n + ϵ_n), with σ_r(f) = (E[ln²(1+fr)] − gr²(f))^{1/2}, gives rigorous finite-horizon bankroll confidence bands for Kelly-sized wealth; the admissibility conditions are P(r ≥ −1) = 1 (losses bounded at 100%), P(r>0)>0 and P(r<0)>0, E|ln(1+r)| < ∞, and no-short/no-leverage f ∈ [0,1].

Varin & Firth (2024, arXiv:2406.09597) solve ridge-penalty selection for paired-comparison strength models via 'pairwise empirical Bayes' (PEB): the penalized likelihood ℓ_λ(μ) = ℓ(μ) − (λ/2)Σᵢμᵢ² with working prior μ ~ N(0, λ⁻¹I) is paired with the closed-form penalty selector λ̂ = [1 − 2sin(πτ̂/2)]/sin(πτ̂/2), where the small-sample-adjusted concordance is τ̂ = (c−d)/(c+d+2p), so no high-dimensional marginal integration or repeated CV refits are needed; across 120 simulation scenarios (p ∈ {20,40,60}, λ from 2⁻¹ to 2⁶, training fractions 20–80%, 1,000 replications each, order effect δ=0.2) PEB was uniformly best among displayed methods and visually indistinguishable from leave-one-round-out CV ridge at zero refit cost, and it is robust to misspecification (negligible penalty difference under t_8 true strengths, small differences even under t_3).

In Varin & Firth's PEB application to 28 English Premier League seasons (1995–2023, 10,640 matches, 20 teams × 38 match-weeks; train on first 10/15/20/25/30 weeks, predict remaining; naive baseline of outcome frequencies 46% home/25% draw/29% away gives log score 1.06), bias-reduced MLE (Firth BRMLE) beat plain MLE in all 28 seasons at all training sizes, PEB usually beat BRMLE with the largest gains after only 10–15 weeks of training data (the early-season sparse regime), while plain MLE could predict worse than the naive baseline in sparse data and Firth bias reduction under-shrank relative to the predictive optimum; the reader proposes a naive-baseline gate that automatically rejects any rating configuration whose sparse-data log-loss exceeds naive outcome frequencies.

Andrae et al. (ICLR 2025, arXiv:2410.05431v2) forecast ensemble weather with a single conditional diffusion model over arbitrary continuous lead times, using correlated/fixed noise across lead times so each ensemble member traces a temporally coherent trajectory; their ARCI hybrid (autoregressive 24h anchors + continuous diffusion interpolation between anchors) beats pure 6-hour autoregressive rollout at 10-day lead with 4x sampling speed. On WeatherBench ERA5 (train 1979–2015, validation 2016–2017, test 2018): day-10 z500 ARCI achieves 765.6 RMSE / 355.2 CRPS / 0.93 spread-skill ratio vs AR-6h 811.8 / 391.9 / 0.88; day-10 t850 ARCI 3.29 / 1.63 / 0.95 vs AR-6h 3.39 / 1.69 / 0.92. Sampling cost for a ten-day 6-hourly ensemble member: AR-6h 32 s vs ARCI 8 s. Limitations: ERA5 is a model product inheriting assimilation biases, 5.625-degree resolution is coarse, fixed-noise coherence is a sampling heuristic with no physical-constraint guarantee between anchors, single test year (2018).

Peel & Clauset (2015, arXiv:1504.05872) fit generative latent-skill Bradley–Terry models to within-game scoring-event sequences across four leagues; the empirically winning NFL structure is the independent anti-persistent model P(ψ_i=r|ψ_{i-1}=r)=π^def_r/(π^def_r+π^off_b), P(ψ_i=r|ψ_{i-1}=b)=π^off_r/(π^off_r+π^def_b) (Eq. 10), encoding forced possession change after a score with separate offensive/defensive skills. Findings: bigram self-rates (rr+bb) are NBA 0.35, CFB 0.45, NFL 0.44, NHL 0.49; NFL held-out log-likelihood (2000) favors independent anti-persistent (−1,278) over independent (−1,286) with restorative models always worse for the NFL (8/10 seasons favor independent anti-persistent) — NFL shows anti-persistence yes, lead-size restoration no. Cross-sport: NBA restorative anti-persistent best all 9 seasons; CFB independent best (2000: −7,487 vs restorative −8,114); NHL no clear winner. Best-model who-wins AUC reaches ≥80% accuracy at halftime in all four leagues, beating static BT early; first-order Markov is the strongest baseline and the best NFL predictor early in season until ~30% observed. Data: STATS LLC proprietary scoring-event data, NFL 10 seasons 2000–2009 (32 teams, 2,561 games, 20,115 events, mean 7.85/game); OT removed; timestamps discarded; AUC values read from plots, not tabulated.

Peel & Clauset (2015) model equations: lead L_i = Σ_{j=1..i} φ_j δ(ψ_j,r) − φ_j δ(ψ_j,b) (Eq. 1); independent model P(ψ_i=r) = d_rb = π_r/(π_r+π_b) with π ∈ [0,1] latent skill (Eq. 2–3); restorative model P(ψ_i=r) = d_rb + ℓ^r_i c_rb with c_rb = γ_r+γ_b (Eq. 4–5), logisticized to σ(m_rb ℓ+v_rb) with m_rb=4c_rb, v_rb=−4(1/2−d_rb) (Eq. 6–9); rotational symmetry P(ψ_i=r|L_{i-1}) = 1 − P(ψ_i=b|−L_{i-1}); fit per season via MCMC with goodness-of-fit = 10-fold CV held-out log-likelihood per season per sport, and online prediction (train on first T games with T ≥ 10%, predict remaining events) scored by AUC.
equation: L_i = Σ_{j=1..i} φ_j δ(ψ_j,r) − φ_j δ(ψ_j,b) ; P(ψ_i=r) = π_r/(π_r+π_b)

claim: Xia et al. (2024, arXiv:2402.15862v2) built SportQA, a 70,592-question sports benchmark: Level-1 (21,385 one-correct MC), Level-2 (45,685 4-way MC across 35 sports), Level-3 (3,522 multiple-select, 1–4 correct, 24 tasks across 6 sports, manually authored by experts). GPT-4 (5-shot CoT) scores L1 85.63, L2 78.82, L3-easy-single-hop 73.58, L3-hard-single-hop 64.08, L3-easy-multi-hop 34.40, L3-hard-multi-hop 23.01; GPT-4 leads other models by >15% on average yet lags human experts (L3 96.63/96.02/94.90/91.84) by roughly 30–65% on scenario tasks. Error analysis: deficiency in conceptual understanding is the most frequent L1/L2 error (40%); on L3, 82.5% of incorrect questions showed inadequacy in multifaceted answer identification, and conceptual misunderstanding accounts for 55% of single-hop and 50% of multi-hop errors. Caveats: L1/L2 questions come from public text likely in training corpora (scores likely overstated), models are 2023-vintage, scores rest on sampled subsets, and L3 covers only 6 sports with no NFL-deep scenarios.

Sudhir & Tran-Thanh (2024, arXiv:2402.14021) is a pure philosophy-of-mathematics theory paper on prediction markets for first-order-logic sentences that are neither verifiable nor falsifiable, using Hintikka verification-falsification game semantics and an equilibrium price setter; key results are Lemma 1.2 (no computable asset/scoring-rule mechanism for Σ_4/Π_4+ sentences via Tarski's theorem), Lemma 3.1 (inexploitability of the price setter), Theorem 3.2 (equilibrium prices converge for every sentence), and Theorem 3.4/Corollary 3.5 (market learns constructive truth: computably-verifiable-true sentences converge to price 1). The corpus ledger verdict was REJECT (no sports content, no data, no empirical mechanism); the paper explicitly sets aside sports-like claims, noting prediction markets serve 'probabilities of claims whose truth will be revealed at some fixed time.'

Johnstone & Nettleton (2022/rev. 2026, arXiv:2208.08598) build honest, distribution-free single-game win probabilities from a conformal predictive distribution (CPD) over margin of victory: the conformal p-value π(y_c, τ) = (n+1)^{-1} Σ_{i=1}^{n+1} [𝕀{R_i(y_c) < R_{n+1}(y_c)} + τ·𝕀{R_i(y_c) = R_{n+1}(y_c)}] (Eq. 11) with conformity scores R = y − ŷ (signed residuals, τ=1/2 mid-p-value smoothing); home win prob u = 1 − π_w(0, 1/2); coverage guarantee P(y_{n+1} ∈ C_{1−α,τ}(x_{n+1})) ≥ 1 − α (Eq. 13) requiring only exchangeability. Tournament-win probabilities use the Edwards recursion q_uJ = q_u(J−1)·Σ_s p_us·q_s(J−1) (Eq. 3) with zero Monte Carlo error, and field probability P(F_u=1) = P(C_u=1) + P(L_u ≤ t_u) − P(C_u=1, L_u ≤ t_u) where the upset count L_u is a Poisson-binomial sum. Calibration is defined as E_p̂[|P(ẑ=z | p̂=p) − p|] = 0 (Eq. 21) and log-loss as logL(p̂, z) = z·log(p̂) + (1−z)·log(1−p̂) (Eq. 22).

In Johnstone & Nettleton's NCAA basketball study (7 seasons of Division 1 men's and women's margin-of-victory data, 2014–15 through 2020–21), pooled relative log-loss shows conformal win probability (1.00) beats linear (1.01 women / 1.02 men) and logistic (1.02 women / 1.03 men); conformal is best in every season×league combination except women's 2015–16 and men's 2020–21, where it is within 1% of the best method; reliability plots show all three methods comparable at high win probabilities but conformal markedly better calibrated at low win probabilities (points closest to the diagonal). The 2020 case study: women's top strengths Baylor 40.68, South Carolina 40.30, Oregon 39.32; men's Kansas 25.26, Gonzaga 22.79, Duke 22.31. Exchangeability within a season is noted as shaky (injuries, form, schedule) but empirical calibration holds.

Cataldo (2026, arXiv:2609.10589) 'Halo' shows that adding a scale head to any existing deep time-series forecaster and training under the matching negative log likelihood improves the point estimate itself, not just uncertainty quantification. Identities: MSE ≡ Gaussian NLL with constant variance (Eq. 5); MAE ≡ Laplacian NLL with constant scale (Eq. 6); heteroscedastic models learn per-sample σ̂_i or b̂_i; β-NLL = (1/2N)Σ sg(|σ_i|)log(σ_i²) + (1/2N)Σ sg(|σ_i|)(y_i−μ_i)²/σ_i² (Eq. 7) with β=0.5 fixed and stop-gradient stabilization has the same optimum as NLL with stabler backprop. On five electricity price forecasting markets (Nord Pool, PJM, Belgian, French, German EPEX SPOT) across three base models, Halo improves MSE and MAE in 28 of 30 model–market–metric comparisons with average MSE cuts of 2.6%–16.5% and MAE cuts of 1.7%–11.0% per model; dual-head vs. parallel wirings differ by <1.5% (dual-head preferred, half the parameters); retuning helps in 2/5 markets and hurts in 3/5. One exception: TimeXer on the German market (baseline MSE 0.4527 beats Halo-tuned 0.4790). Caveat: every number is a single training run with no seed variance reported.

Calvo, Palmí-Perales, Armero & Gómez-Rubio (2026, arXiv:2608.09824) jointly model interrelated player-performance variables over an NBA season in a longitudinal Bayesian network with the joint p(y, z, φ, θ) = p(y, z | φ, θ) p(φ | θ) π(θ) (Eq. 1) with player random effects φ, and compare static, dynamic AR(1) (minutes depend on previous game's minutes via β_M^(+)), and hidden-Markov variants by WAIC on Philadelphia 76ers 2005–06 player-game data (13 players × 82 games). WAIC: static 21274.69, dynamic 21194.13, hidden Markov 21274.60 — the dynamic AR(1) variant is preferred; the minutes AR(1) coefficient β_M^(+) = 0.097 (95% CI 0.076–0.119, entirely positive), player random-effect SD σ_M = 0.688, common mean μ_0^(M) = 2.616; make-probability player-effect SDs σ_{C_1} = 0.475 (FT), σ_{C_2} = 0.190 (2PT), σ_{C_3} = 0.302 (3PT); participation posteriors Iverson 0.870, Iguodala 0.988, Webber 0.905, Korver 0.988, Lou Williams 0.369. Posterior predictive f(y_* | D) = ∫ f(y_* | θ, φ) π(θ, φ | D) d(θ, φ) (Eq. 16) supports reverse queries such as minutes | points ≤ 10. Limitations: one team, one season (generalizability untested), no held-out game prediction scoring, structure assumed known, and heavy MCMC cost (3 chains × 1,000,000 iterations, 500,000 burn-in, thin every 500).
equation: p(y, z, φ, θ) = p(y, z | φ, θ) p(φ | θ) π(θ)

claim: Li, Kang, Li, Zhang & Petropoulos (2021, arXiv:2012.01643) 'Forecast with Forecasts: Diversity Matters' learns ensemble combination weights from pairwise disagreement among pool members' own out-of-sample forecasts via XGBoost + softmax, replacing FFORMA's 42 hand-crafted time-series features; the ambiguity decomposition is MSE_comb = Σᵢ wᵢ MSEᵢ − Σ_{i<j} wᵢ wⱼ Div_{i,j} with Div_{i,j} = (1/H) Σ_h (f_{ih} − f_{jh})², and scale-normalized diversity (Eq. 3) Div_{i,j} = [Σ_h (f_{ih} − f_{jh})²] / [Σ_{p<q} Σ_h (f_{ph} − f_{qh})²] sums to 1 across pairs; weights use softmax w(Div_n)_i = exp{y(Div_n)_i}/Σ_i exp{y(Div_n)_i} and the joint cost (Eq. 6) is Err = ½ (MASE/MASEnaive2 + MSIS/MSISnaive2). 56 diversity features per series come from upper/lower 95% prediction intervals over an 8-method pool; point-forecast diversity is deliberately omitted (midpoints carry no extra information).
equation: MSE_comb = Σᵢ wᵢ MSEᵢ − Σ_{i<j} wᵢ wⱼ Div_{i,j} ; Div_{i,j} = [Σ_h (f_{ih} − f_{jh})²] / [Σ_{p<q} Σ_h (f_{ph} − f_{qh})²]

claim: On the M4 competition dataset (100,000 series), the Diversity method in Li et al. (2021) achieves overall mean MASE 1.5478 / MSIS 14.0197 vs FFORMA 1.5586 / 14.5934 and simple average 1.9040 / 17.5077, with the paper reporting Diversity's mean MASE 18.71% lower and MSIS 19.92% lower than simple average; MCB significance tests show Diversity vs FFORMA not statistically significant (mean ranks FD 2.36, Diversity 2.40, FFORMA 2.40, SA 2.85), while diversity+FFORMA features (FD, 1.5507 / 14.0254) is significantly better than all baselines, showing historical features and future diversity are complementary. In the FMCG case study (955 SKU×location series), Diversity reaches MASE 0.9365 / MSIS 8.0066 vs FFORMA 0.9599 / 8.1254. Caveats: M4 results benefit from post-sample experimentation (authors' admission), the diversity-to-weight map must be retrained when pool members change, and XGBoost hyperparameters are not reported.

Sasan & Swartzentruber (2024, arXiv:2412.08840) estimate the causal effect of the NBA end-of-quarter two-for-one (TFO) strategy on quarter-end score differential Y_i = Y_{i,EOQ} − Y_{i,TFO-O} (Eq. 1) with estimands ATE/ATT/ATC: E[Y_i(1)−Y_i(0)] (Eqs. 2–4), using covariate-balancing propensity scores e(X)=P(W=1|X) (Eq. 8), IPW weights W_i/ê(X_i)+(1−W_i)/(1−ê(X_i)) (Eq. 9), 1:1 optimal pair matching with τ̂_ATT = n_1⁻¹Σ_{i:W_i=1}(Y_i−|M(i)|⁻¹Σ_{j∈M(i)}Y_j) (Eq. 13), CATE τ(x)=E[Y_i(1)−Y_i(0)|X=x] (Eq. 14), causal forest (Athey/Wager) with DML orthogonalization and honest estimation, and RATE heterogeneity tests TOC(q)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)|S(X_i)≥F⁻¹(1−q)]−E[Y(1)−Y(0)], RATE=∫_0¹TOC(q)dq (Eqs. 15–16). On NBA play-by-play for 2018-19 (1036 TFO-A / 529 TFO-NA) and 2021-22 (950 / 462): ATC via IPW is 0.55 (0.43, 0.66) p<0.001 for 18-19, 0.57 (0.45, 0.69) p<0.001 for 21-22, 0.55 (0.47, 0.64) pooled; matching gives 0.60/0.64/0.63, all p<0.001; causal forest ATE 0.61 (SE 0.11). Each unconverted TFO opportunity costs slightly more than half a point of score differential. Heterogeneity tests find nothing significant: RATE 0.035 (SE 0.112), calibration-on-differential p=0.1741. Assumptions checked: consistency, no interference, conditional exchangeability, positivity; balance via Love plots with a 0.1 standardized-mean-difference rule. Limitations: coach play-calling ability unmeasured, NBA 2K ratings subjective, no tracking/spatial data, 4th quarters excluded.

An arXiv 2022 paper (arXiv:2205.04343, Univ. of Augsburg / Univ. Hospital Tübingen) attempting to predict self-reported running fatigue (Borg RPE 6–20) from smartphone armband audio (CNN14 on 30 s log-Mel spectrograms, 64 bins, 32 ms window, 10 ms hop) achieved only CNN14-pretrained MAE 2.35 / CCC 0.287 and CNN14-random MAE 3.48 / CCC 0.208 on the KIRun dataset (48 runners, 185 sessions; 56/23/21% train/dev/test splits, subject-DEPENDENT). The corpus ledger verdict was REJECT: subject-dependent splits let the model learn runner identity (voice, gait acoustics, device) rather than fatigue, invalidating the headline result; individual test-runner MAEs reach up to ~5.0 vs the global 2.35; age 51–60 had the worst MAE despite good representation; KIRun was never released, so the work is not reproducible. Its only value is cautionary: use subject-dependent-split failure as a negative audit test for workload models.

Inoue & Kawabata (Mon. Wea. Rev.; arXiv:2507.18937) show member-wise CNN correction of coarse 40 km JMA GEPS ensemble surface-temperature forecasts beats Kalman-filter baselines and operational 5 km models while preserving ensemble information: deterministic CF–CNN cuts RMSE by 1.2 K (46%) vs raw control forecast with mean error within ±0.05 K (vs KF's residual positive bias); GSM–CNN cuts 0.99 K (39%) vs GSM–KF only 0.76 K (29%); CRPS reduced ~0.8 K (47%) vs original GEPS with spread/skill ratio approaching 1.0 via RMSE reduction; Energy Score reduced >50% and Variogram Score ~75%; the FI–NE–ACC decomposition (ACC = p/(SDAF·SDAV), FI = p/SDAF², NE = SDAF√(1−ACC²), IE = |1−FI|·SDAV) shows the CNN reduces noise error while maintaining/increasing forecast information — genuine error reduction, not smoothing. A key efficiency result: training on the control member vs a perturbation member vs the ensemble mean gives no statistically significant differences, so training on the control member only halves training cost. Limitations: the 30 Jun 2022 heatwave (>39°C) CRPS improved 3.19→2.62 K but max intensity was underestimated (low-resolution input information); residual warm-tail bias in Q–Q plots; code only available on collaborative request.
equation: ACC = p/(SDAF·SDAV) ; FI = p/SDAF² ; NE = SDAF√(1−ACC²) ; IE = |1−FI|·SDAV

claim: MatchTime (Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ., 2024, arXiv:2406.18530) repairs large text–video timestamp misalignments in soccer commentary with a two-stage pipeline: coarse alignment (WhisperX ASR → LLaMA-3 narration summaries per 10-s clip → LLaMA-3 re-timing by sentence similarity) then fine alignment with frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 encoders and trainable MLPs to 512-d trained with contrastive InfoNCE-style loss L_align = −(1/k)Σ_i log[Σ_j Y[i,j]exp(A[i,j]) / Σ_j exp(A[i,j])] on affinity matrix A[i,j] = C_i·V_j/(‖C_i‖‖V_j‖), with inference ~t_i := ^t_j, j = argmax A[i,:] over 1 FPS candidates in [t−45 s, t+30 s] (replay-robust). On SN-Caption-test-align (49 matches, 3,267 manually re-aligned pairs; raw offsets range −108 to +152 s, mean abs offset 16.63 s, only 26.29% within 10 s), MatchTime reduces mean abs offset 13.89 s → 6.89 s, 10-s window compliance 35.32% → 80.73%, 60-s 88.07% → 98.17%. The MatchVoice generator (2-layer Perceiver-style temporal aggregator with 32 learnable queries → MLP to 768-d prefix tokens → LLaMA-3 decoder, ^C = Ψ_dec(Ψ_proj(Ψ_agg(v_1..v_n))), LoRA r=16, 30-s window) trained on aligned data reaches BLEU-1 33.22, BLEU-4 10.10, METEOR 26.79, ROUGE-L 26.06, CIDEr 39.27, GPT-score 7.32, beating the same model on unaligned data and the SN-Caption baseline. Limitations: anonymous commentary (no player names), GPT-score is an LLM judge not human eval, alignment evaluated on only 4 matches (292 samples).
equation: L_align = −(1/k)Σ_i log[Σ_j Y[i,j]exp(A[i,j]) / Σ_j exp(A[i,j])] ; A[i,j] = C_i·V_j/(‖C_i‖‖V_j‖)

claim: Nechepurenko (2026, arXiv:2605.00459) stress-tests the deadline-resolved Information Leakage Score ILS^dl(M) = (p(T_event^−) − p(T_open)) / (p_T_resolve − p(T_open)), with hazard-decay adjustment ILS^{dl,adj}(M) = (p(T_event^−) − E[p(T_event^−) | T_open, D, λ̂]) / (p_T_resolve − p(T_open)) subtracting the survival-probability-implied baseline, across 12,708 Polymarket markets (2020–2026). Findings: only 88 of 12,708 (0.7%) yield computable ILS^dl and 12 of 88 (13.6%) pass the anchor-sensitivity gate (no sign change and shift ≤ 0.3 under 30-min/2h/6h/24h anchor offsets), so the effective interpretable domain is ~12/12,708 markets; of 32 documented insider episodes, only 1 is in scope (Bitcoin ETF approval, ILS^dl = 0.012, at the cell median not the right tail); raw ILS^dl medians are negative across all six cells (range −0.88 to −0.16); anchor robustness shows Spearman rank correlation 0.30 between article-derived and 24h anchors with an 86% anchor-fragility rate; T_event recovery agrees with exact dates only 57.8% of the time (below the ≥90% ex-ante criterion); the pooled post-2024 hazard λ̂ = 0.042 (half-life 16.4 days), corporate-disclosure-only λ̂ = 0.156 (half-life 4.5 days), Weibull over pooled data AIC 454.66 vs exponential 476.59 (Δ=21.9); pooled detectors face a 1:7.9 selection penalty against structurally-irrelevant controls (sports, crypto price, weather), so detection must be category-conditional. Pipeline scope conditions: lead time τ > 0, edge-effect |p(T_open)−0.5| ≤ 0.4, non-trivial move |Δ_total| ≥ 0.05.

Long (2026, arXiv:2604.17577) derives the exact finite-horizon Kelly stake optimizer for repeated multi-outcome events by maximizing a quantile (e.g., median) of terminal wealth X_n(W) = ∏_{i} W_i^{N_i} with N multinomial(n, p) and W_i the state-price wealth profile per outcome, via Arrow–Debreu wealth-profile geometry: partition the count-vector space into 'chambers' (fixed outcome-wealth ordering), within each chamber the α-quantile of terminal wealth is a single monomial in the count vector, maximize it as an ordinary Kelly problem on the chamber's empirical law k/n ('shadow-Kelly'), enumerate chambers, solve each exactly, and take the global optimum. Worked ternary example (p=(0.6,0.3,0.1), q=(1/3,1/3,1/3), n=2, α=1/2): quantile optimizer (1.5,1.5,0) gives median terminal wealth 2.25 vs ordinary Kelly profile (1.8,0.9,0.3) which puts 0.3 on the third outcome the quantile optimizer zeroes out; binary example: median-optimal shadow point (2/3,1/3) for median count vector (2,1). Limitations: requires exact p and q (miscalibrated probabilities inherit full Kelly's fragility to edge misestimation), chamber enumeration grows combinatorially, quantile objectives accept large left-tail outcomes by construction (a median maximizer can have severe downside beyond the quantile), no correlated events, no empirical validation.

A Bayesian stop-loss calibration procedure bins the empirical distribution of trade maximum drawdowns by win/loss, computes conditional expected values per bin, and takes the cumulative argmax bin edge as the threshold T = right edge of the bin maximizing the cumulative conditional-expected-value vector (eq. 4), with the stop implemented as a trailing stop at (1−T) × (maximum price since entry); construction uses l=20 hours holding period, m=250 trades, n bins chosen by a square-root rule on trade count. On 114 assets, the rolling-window R method vs signal-only baseline improved 57.02% of cases, with average gains +6.37% on winners, average losses −6.94% on losers, and overall expected change in NLV +0.65% (eq. 5–6) — the paper's own conclusion is that the method is 'on average quite successful, but imperfect' and +0.65% is a thin margin. Caveats: l and m were chosen with knowledge of the data, no time-ordered splits described, the T method suffers sparse data, and the R method's overlapping artificial trades create correlated samples the paper does not adjust for. The corpus verdict was ADAPT (weak): only the binning machinery transfers (to bankroll-drawdown stake throttling), since discrete −110 bets cannot be stopped mid-trade like equity longs.

Conformal PID control for time-series prediction intervals (Angelopoulos-style) upgrades adaptive conformal inference (ACI, pure integrator) to a full PID design: the quantile tracker is q_{t+1} = q_t + η(err_t − α), and the general controller is q_{t+1} = ϑ_{t+1} + r_t( Σ_{i=1}^t (err_i − α) ), where ϑ_{t+1} is the 'scorecaster' (any forecaster of the next score from observable features) and r_t is a saturating integrator (bounded, e.g. tan/tanh-based) on cumulative errors; the long-run error bound for bounded scores |s| ≤ b is | (1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T (err_t − α) | ≤ (b + η)/(ηT), and the theorem gives deterministic long-run coverage for any score sequence and any scorecaster satisfying boundedness/saturation conditions, with no stochastic assumptions. On COVID-19 4-week-ahead US state-level death forecasts (late 2020–late 2022, nominal 80%): during a 10-week winter shock stretch the base ensemble missed 8 of 10 (20% coverage) while the PID controller missed 3 of 10 (70% coverage), with intervals widening as the scorecaster anticipated the shock. On NSW half-hourly electricity demand (nominal 90%), PID maintains coverage through demand-regime changes where the Transformer's raw intervals fail. Limitations: still needs Y_t revealed each step, the guarantee is long-run not finite-window, and a bad scorecaster adds noise.

A Bayesian in-game NBA home-team win-probability estimator uses a dynamic beta prior elicited from 14 NBA experts, updated with binned play-by-play outcomes via the posterior mean p̂ = (n + α)/(N + α + β) at each elapsed second t = 0..2879 and score lead ℓ, then blends with a pregame probability through the optimized logistic blend logit(p_blend) = −1.10633 − 0.02313·I0(ℓ) + 0.00027·t + 0.06618·|ℓ| − 0.00139·ℓ², coefficients optimized to minimize Brier score. Windowing is [t−3,t+3]×[ℓ−2,ℓ+2], narrowing to [ℓ−1,ℓ+1] in minutes 3–1 and no score binning in the final minute. On ESPN NBA play-by-play (training 7,376 games, 2012/13–pre-COVID 2019/20; test 2018/19 and 2019/20 with 6,590,576 second-level observations each): blend-model Brier 0.1622 (linear-time), 0.1613 (linear time+score), 0.1598 (quadratic B3); blended dynamic Bayes total Brier 0.1598 vs ESPN's 0.1582 — within ~0.0016 of ESPN. Critical flaw: the B3 blend coefficients were optimized on the same test seasons used for evaluation, so reported gains are optimistic and true out-of-sample performance is unknown. The ℓ² term captures garbage-time nonlinearity and the expert prior anchors early-game estimates where data are sparse.

The Quantile Super Learner (QSL) ensembles multiple candidate quantile algorithms by minimizing cross-validated quantile loss L^α(ψ)(x,y) = α|y−ψ(x)| if y>ψ(x) else (1−α)|y−ψ(x)|, with risk R_P^α(ψ) = E_P[L^α(ψ)] minimized by the true conditional quantile; discrete QSL selects κ̂_n = argmin_k of V-fold CV empirical quantile risk, continuous QSL combines ψ̂_π^α = Σ_k π_k ψ̂_k^α over a finite grid on the K-simplex, and online QSL trains on all data before t and scores on the new batch. Theorem 1 (i.i.d.) gives an oracle inequality: excess risk ≤ oracle excess risk + O(log n / √n) when K = O(n^a) and candidates output uniformly bounded functions; Theorem 2 (online): excess risk ≤ oracle excess risk + O(log log t / √t). Empirical results: in i.i.d. simulation QSL is best or tied-best quantile risk at all quantiles × sample sizes (N1=1000, α=0.5: QSL 0.092 vs GBM 0.092, GRF 0.20, QGAM 0.27, QRNN 0.31, QReg 0.40); on perovskite formation-energy data QSL has the lowest CV quantile risk at all 7 quantiles (α=0.5: 0.065 vs GBM 0.078); on solar GHI data QSL is lowest in most location×quantile cells. Weight inspection shows no single candidate dominates — GBM gets higher weight for tail quantiles (10%/90%) and weights vary by location. Caveat: intervals from paired quantile estimates have NO finite-sample coverage guarantee (QSL undercovers 73.0% at nominal 80% in simulation), and Theorem 2's stationarity assumption is violated by sports data.

A factor graphical model (FGM) for combining forecasts strips common error factors via PCA from the forecast-error panel (e_t = Bf_t + ε_t; Σ = BΣ_fB′ + Σ_ε), estimates the sparse precision of idiosyncratic residuals with weighted GLASSO Θ̂_{ε,λ} = argmin trace(W_εΘ_ε) − logdet(Θ_ε) + λΣ_{i≠j}d̂_{ε,ii}d̂_{ε,jj}|θ_{ε,ij}| with W_ε = Σ̂_ε + λI, reconstructs full precision via Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury Θ = Θ_ε − Θ_εB[Θ_f + B′Θ_εB]⁻¹B′Θ_ε, and forms optimal Bates–Granger weights w = Θι_p/(ι_p′Θι_p) with MSFE(w,Σ) = w′Σw; the weight-estimation error bound (3.9) says ‖ŵ−w‖_1 is controlled by ‖(Θ̂−Θ)ι‖_1 so precision consistency implies weight consistency. λ is tuned by EBIC: λ_EBIC = argmin_λ {−2l(Θ_{ε,λ}) + log(T)·df(Θ_{ε,λ}) + 4·df(Θ_{ε,λ})·log(p)·η}, η=1 (CV overfits, STARS overselects); factor count q via Bai–Ng IC1 (usually α̂=1 in the macro application). On 100 Monte Carlo simulations, Factor GLASSO and Factor MB dominate equal weighting, plain GLASSO, and plain nodewise regression in precision and weight error; in the macro application (McCracken–Ng 128 series, 1960–2020, 120 FAR models, 7 indicators), both beat EW/GLASSO/nodewise across horizons with the factor benefit larger at longer horizons (h≥2). Key diagnostic: plain GLASSO under factor structure shrinks almost all partial correlations to zero and degenerates (it is worse than EW for FEDFUNDS, while Factor GLASSO beats EW) — never run vanilla GLASSO on raw model-error precision.
equation: w = Θι_p/(ι_p′Θι_p) ; Θ = Θ_ε − Θ_εB[Θ_f + B′Θ_εB]⁻¹B′Θ_ε

claim: VAIR (Lee et al. 2025, arXiv:2512.17446), a visual-analytics system for joint-level injury risk in sports video (3D pose reconstruction via Co-Motion/SMPL → OpenSim biomechanical simulation → threshold-based risk flags in a multi-view UI), was REJECTED by the corpus ledger: the paper concedes in Sec. 7.5 'Lack of Objective Performance Evaluation' that it has zero quantitative metrics — no pose-estimation accuracy, no risk-detection precision/recall, no baseline comparisons — evaluation consists of three experts' quotes, there is no released code or data, and its failure modes (limb errors, overlapping players, partial framing) are exactly the conditions of broadcast NFL footage. Literature thresholds it cites include Achilles risk at ankle dorsiflexion ≈ 40° with knee flexion ≈ 22.5°, and ACL anterior loading during knee flexion 30–90° with internal rotation/valgus; its case-study reconstructed angles are ACL: knee flexion ~74°, abduction ~95°, internal rotation ~67° (valgus collapse), Achilles: plantar flexion ~−32° with knee rotation.

Bhattacharya, Ghosal & Ghosh (2018, arXiv:1810.00908) build a better cricket rain-rule resource table via Bayesian nonlinear regression with order-constrained priors that enforce exact monotonicity, beating the ICC Duckworth–Lewis table on first-innings score prediction: likelihood R̄(u,w) ~ N(m(u,w;θ), σ²/n_uw) (Eq. 4) with mean function m(u,w;θ) = a_w(1 − e^{−b_w u}) (Eq. 5), and monotonicity priors (Eq. 7) a_0 ~ U(0,A_0), b_0 ~ U(0,B_0), a_{w+1}|· ~ U(0,a_w), b_{w+1}|· ~ U(0, a_w b_w/a_{w+1}), 1/σ² ~ Ga(a,b), proven (Appendix B) to enforce monotonicity with probability 1. On 947 ODI first innings (2005–2017, cricsheet.org; 500 (u,w) cells, 26.8% unobserved), the RSS ratio (Bayes/D/L, Eq. 8 RSS_u = Σ_w Σ_i (R^A − R^P)²) is < 1 in the majority of overs-left scenarios from u=30 down to u=1; the Bayesian table is monotone in both dimensions by construction while the D/L table is flat at 11.9% for 8 wickets lost across u=50..15 and 4.7% for 9 wickets, and the naive empirical table is non-monotone with wild values (e.g., 101.71% at 47 overs/3 wickets). Tail-state differences are large: 10 overs/9 wickets = 18.12% (Bayesian) vs 4.70% (D/L). Limitations: evaluation is in-sample; MAR assumption untestable in extreme states; D/L parameters never public so the claim is against the table, not the method.

Cao et al. (2024, arXiv:2402.11191v1) generate automatic NBA game news from live-text feeds (494 games, 58,745 sentences; train 340 games / 43,211 sentences; test 154 / 15,534) via KEE event segmentation plus knowledge-graph enrichment: segmentation is a threshold-crossing detector (passage boundary when cumulative score difference within a window crosses an 8-point threshold, or when key max/min largest scoring run/drought is detected in the score-differential time series), and generation compares CNN vs KEE-template vs KEE+KG. Results: ROUGE-1/2/L of CNN 0.264/0.065/0.182, KEE 0.392/0.138/0.197, KEE+KG 0.563/0.372/0.447 — KG enrichment roughly doubles ROUGE-2 over KEE alone (0.138 → 0.372); human-panel fan 'excellent' rate rises 17.80% → 41.60% (KEE → KEE+KG), journalist 'good' 39.50% → 52.00%. The NBA KG (4,027 player nodes, 30 team nodes, 43,510 game nodes, 1,836 match nodes; not released) is static while news is game-specific, so if KG season stats incorporate the game being written about, post-game knowledge leaks into 'news' — the paper does not document the KG snapshot date relative to the games. TransE-style scoring score(h,r,t) = −||h + r − t|| with margin ranking loss L = Σ max(0, γ + score_neg − score_pos) is used for KG completion. Caveats: the 8-point threshold is hand-tuned on NBA data with no sensitivity analysis, entity linking is assumed solved and linking errors never measured, and the human panel is small (n=20, journalists n=4) with no inter-rater agreement reported.
equation: score(h,r,t) = −||h + r − t|| ; L = Σ max(0, γ + score_neg − score_pos)

claim: Brogly et al. (2025, arXiv:2504.08764v1) test whether zero-shot phi-3-mini scoring 9.35M Canadian news headlines 1–10 on health topics can triage sports-injury texts, finding the SLM wildly overconfident on sports injury: human mean 1.87 vs SLM mean 9.87, with binary agreement (human concurs text is related) of 54.68% / 74.58% (medicine/health low/high filter) but only 6.69% / 24.01% for sports injury — sports-injury positives are wrong ~93% unfiltered, ~76% even with the Boolean high filter; Spearman ρ for sports injury collapses from 0.3413 (low filter) to 0.0318 (high filter). Human eval: 7 raters on 1,144 medicine/health + 1,117 sports-injury texts with inter-rater ICC 0.758/0.640 and Fleiss's κ 0.789/0.648, so the disagreement is the SLM's problem. A serendipitous finding: the SLM rated some 'junk' texts (e.g., 'Reporter_Name, The Associated Press') highly — investigation showed they were sports/health reporters' bylines, a real latent signal (reporter identity) the task did not intend. Throughput: ~475K texts/week per GTX 1080Ti instance, ~950K/week per RTX 4090; 9.35M texts took ~4 weeks on 2×1080Ti + 1×4090. The verdict: zero-shot phi-3-mini is ADAPT only as a recall-oriented triage filter in a cascade with downstream review (recall ≥ 0.95 gate), never as a labeler.

Nakharutai, Caiado & Troffaes (2019, arXiv:1901.03645) model bookmaker odds and free-coupon promos as desirable gambles in an imprecise-probability framework: gamble g_i(ω) = −a_i if ω = ω_i, else b_i (Eq. 26) for fractional odds a_i/b_i; desirability ⟺ Σ_ω g_i(ω)p(ω) ≥ 0 ⟺ b_i/(a_i+b_i) ≥ p(ω_i) (Eqs. 27–30), with upper probability mass p̄(ω_i) ≔ b_i/(a_i+b_i) (Eq. 31); a bookmaker's odds avoid sure loss ⟺ Σ_i b_i/(a_i+b_i) ≥ 1 (Theorems 1, 5, 6), and the multi-book version uses per-outcome maximal odds. Worked examples on real market odds: 4/(3+4) + 5/(13+5) + 5/(16+5) = 1.087 ≥ 1 → the bookmaker's odds avoid sure loss; and a £5 qualifying bet at 13/5 on D plus a £5 free coupon on a single other outcome creates a sure gain for the customer (bookmaker losses up to £16 on the coupon leg), with the optimal exploiting portfolio extracted via complementary slackness on the LP dual. Limitations: illustrative examples, not a market-wide scan; no account-limitation/arb-ban modeling; the plain-odds check is textbook, the value-add is the coupon/terms extension.
equation: g_i(ω) = −a_i if ω = ω_i, else b_i ; sure loss avoided ⟺ Σ_i b_i/(a_i+b_i) ≥ 1

claim: Angoshtari, Bayraktar & Young (2015, arXiv:1507.08713) minimize the probability that wealth ever falls below a fraction α of its running maximum before death, φ(w,m) = P(τ_α < τ_d), with constant consumption: the safe level is c/r (wealth whose riskless interest covers consumption); optimal feedback investment (case m ≥ c/r, Eq. 4.1) is π_t = (μ−r)/σ² · 1/(γ−1) · (c/r − W_t^π), with γ = 1/(2r)[(r+λ+δ) + √((r+λ+δ)² − 4rλ)] > 1 and δ = ½((μ−r)/σ)². Three regimes: (i) αm < w < c/r ≤ m: optimal = lifetime-ruin-minimizing strategy; (ii) αm < w ≤ m ≤ m* < c/r: optimally NEVER let maximum wealth increase above current m (raising the max would make the α-level drawdown too great given constant consumption); (iii) αm < w < m with m* < m < c/r: allow the maximum to increase to c/r. In regime (ii) the minimum drawdown probability equals the Legendre dual of a controller-stopper problem's value function. Structural note: π_t ∝ (c/r − W_t) — investment is MORE aggressive when wealth is far below the safe level, the classic ruin-minimization shape, opposite of Kelly's wealth-proportional sizing; it is NOT growth-optimal and the paper does not price the growth cost. Pure analytic theory, no empirical data; the m* threshold is implicit with no closed form quoted.

Drugov & Ryvkin (2026, arXiv:2507.16348v1) characterize the prize structure maximizing minimum effort in a rank-order tournament when the designer knows nothing about the noise distribution except an upper bound on its Shannon entropy: the robust prize has p_k − p_{k+1} ∝ 1/k (asymptotically harmonic prize differentials), p_n = 0 (last place gets nothing), p_1 a distinct top prize, the dual induces a worst-case exponential noise distribution with rate e^{−H̄}, and the Gini coefficient of the prize profile → 1/2 as participants n → ∞. The corpus ledger verdict was REJECT: it is principal-side (designer-side) prize-design theory for contest operators with no player-side payout-exploitation method, no sports data, no empirical validation, and nothing implementable for a DFS operation; the harmonic-schedule-as-contest-selection-benchmark idea was considered and rejected because deviation from a robust-design benchmark does not imply player-exploitable edge.

RISAN (Robust Instance Specific Deep Abstention Network, arXiv:2107.03090) jointly learns a prediction function f(x) and a per-input rejection width ρ(x) — each input gets its own abstention band |f(x)| ≤ ρ(x) — via a smooth double-sigmoid surrogate of the 0-d-1 loss L_d(yf(x), ρ) = 1{yf(x) ≤ −ρ} + d·1{|f(x)| ≤ ρ} with abstention cost d ∈ (0, 0.5); the surrogate is classification-calibrated (excess 0-d-1 risk bounded by excess surrogate risk) and the joint (f, ρ) learner has generalization bounds. On Cats vs Dogs and CIFAR-10 with synthetic label noise: at 20% label noise and low rejection rates RISAN's accepted accuracy is 6–7 percentage points higher than baselines; at 40% noise about +10 points on Cats vs Dogs and +5 on CIFAR-10; 5–10 points better than DAC on unrejected samples. Limitations: binary 0-d-1 only (a moneyline-dog loss ≠ a spread loss), fixed d can't express asymmetric sports costs, double-sigmoid is non-convex, synthetic uniform noise vs structured sports noise, and ρ(x) doubles output complexity and gate-overfit capacity. The instance-specific width (not a global ρ) plus the calibrated surrogate drives the win, and the abstention mechanism refuses to fit noisy labels.

Groll et al. (2024, arXiv:2410.09068v1) predict UEFA EURO 2024 by linearly combining three learners (LASSO-Poisson, conditional-inference random forest, XGBoost) on team-covariate differences plus three separately-estimated 'enhanced' team-strength variables: combined model ŷ_i = w_1·exp(β_0+x_iβ) + w_2·(1/B)Σ_b ŷ_i^{(b)} + w_3·Σ_kηf_k(x_i) with Σw=1, weights grid-searched (step 0.05) minimizing a min-max-normalized average of ML/CR/RPS; enhanced variables include HistAbility λ_{i,m} = exp(β_0 + (r_i − r_j) + h_i·⑪(team i at home)) with Σ_i r_i = 0, time-decay w_{time,m}(x_m) = (1/2)^{x_m/1095.75} (3-year half-life) and match-importance weights 4/3/2.5/1, plus logability from inverse-simulation on bookmaker tournament odds, and ridge-estimated plus-minus. Expected goals convert to W/D/L via the Skellam distribution P(K=k) = e^{−(λ_1+λ_2)}(λ_1/λ_2)^{k/2} I_k(2√(λ_1λ_2)), with metrics ML_i = Π_r π̂_{ri}^{δ_{r,ỹ_i}}, CR_i = ⑪(ỹ_i = argmax_r π̂_{ri}), RPS_i = (1/2)Σ_{r=1}^{2}(Σ_{l=1}^{r}(π̂_{li} − δ_{l,ỹ_i}))², followed by 100,000 tournament simulations. Leave-one-tournament-out results: bookmakers beat all models on every metric (ML 0.4047 / CR 0.5179 / RPS 0.1973 vs combined 0.3994 / 0.4923 / 0.2015); best weights are 0.15 LASSO + 0.85 Cforest + 0.00 XGBoost (XGBoost in only 2 of top-10 combos); final LASSO coefficients: intercept 0.1308, logability 0.4037, market.value 0.0943, GDP 0.0876, CL.players 0.0162, FIFA.rank −0.0017 (ξ ≈ 0.0183). EURO 2024 simulation: France 19.2%, England 16.7%, Germany 13.7%, Spain 11.4% — Spain actually won, as the 4th favorite. Overround removal: quoted_odds_i = odds_i·δ + 1 with median δ-margin 16.8%; p_i = 1/(exp(l_i)+1). Caveats: convex weights chosen on the same CV predictions used for comparison (selection bias uncorrected); Skellam independence assumption.

Wapner, Dalpiaz & Eck (arXiv:2005.07742) introduce SEAM for batter–pitcher matchups with few direct observations: the batted-ball location density is estimated as a convex combination f̂_BP = w_1f̂_direct + w_2f̂_batter-vs-synth-pitchers + w_3f̂_synth-batters-vs-pitcher with w_i ≥ 0, Σw_i = 1, w_1 increasing in n_direct (MSE-motivated; collapses toward the direct KDE as the direct sample grows); similarity kernels are Gaussian-type weights on standardized pitch-characteristic vectors (velocity, movement, spin) and batter contact-profile vectors. On Statcast data (train 2017–2020, temporal holdout 2021), conditional coverage nominal → empirical: SEAM 0.579/0.641/0.779 at nominal 0.50/0.75/0.90 vs batter-only 0.513/0.574/0.662 vs pitcher-only 0.549/0.595/0.713 — SEAM wins at every level, with the largest gains at nominal 0.90 (+0.117 over batter-only, +0.066 over pitcher-only); fixed-size (2,000-cell) region coverage: SEAM 0.758 vs batter-only 0.741 vs pitcher-only 0.750. Caveats: conditional validation covers only matchups with ≥ 10 balls in play in the holdout (the sparsest and most common matchups excluded from the headline metric), selected covariates are assumed to fully capture player style, and the pitch-mix metagame is not modeled.

Gao, Shen & Zhang (arXiv:2110.03874) give sharp non-asymptotic expansions for the Bradley–Terry–Luce MLE and spectral estimator in the sparsest identifiable comparison-graph regime: win probability P(y_ijℓ = 1) = ψ(θ*_i − θ*_j) with ψ(t) = e^t/(1+e^t); BTL MLE θ̂ ∈ argmin_{θ: 1_nᵀθ=0} ℓ_n(θ), ℓ_n(θ) = Σ_{i<j} A_ij [ȳ_ij log(1/ψ(θ_i−θ_j)) + ȳ_ji log(1/ψ(θ_j−θ_i))]; spectral (rank centrality) estimator from the stationary distribution π̂ of Markov chain P_ij = A_ij ȳ_ji/d with θ̃_i = log π̂_i − (1/n)Σ_k log π̂_k; per-team precision ρ_i(θ) = √(L·Σ_{j≠i} A_ij ψ′(θ_i−θ_j)) giving data-driven SE_i ≈ 1/ρ_i(θ̂), ψ′(t) = ψ(t)(1−ψ(t)); MLE expansion (Theorem 2.2) θ̂_i − θ*_i = (1+ε_{1,i}) b_i/d_i + ε_{2,i} with b_i = Σ_{j≠i} A_ij(ȳ_ij − ψ(θ*_i−θ*_j)), d_i = Σ_{j≠i} A_ij ψ′(θ*_i−θ*_j). Key results: the MLE attains the exact locally minimax optimal ℓ_2 constant ‖θ̂−θ*‖² = (1+o(1))/(pL)·Σ_i(Σ_{k≠i} ψ′(θ*_i−θ*_k))⁻¹ (Prop. 4.4) matching the van Trees lower bound (Theorem 4.7), while the spectral estimator has a strictly larger constant (Prop. 4.5); finite-dimensional CLT: k fixed normalized coordinates converge jointly to N_k(0, I_k); the rank CI (Prop. 4.3) has data-driven lengths — better-connected teams get tighter intervals. Simulations validate CLT from n=500 and the MLE risk curve lies below the spectral curve; operating regime requires κ = O(1) bounded dynamic range and np ≫ (log n)^α on an Erdős–Rényi comparison graph. Limitations: static θ* (no dynamics/injuries/QB changes), NFL schedule is not Erdős–Rényi, binary outcomes only, no home-field advantage, ties, or covariates; rank-CI finite-sample coverage for n=32 teams untested.
equation: P(y_ijℓ = 1) = ψ(θ*_i − θ*_j) ; ψ(t) = e^t/(1+e^t) ; ρ_i(θ) = √(L·Σ_{j≠i} A_ij ψ′(θ_i−θ_j))

claim: GFN-SR (Li, Marinescu, Musslick; arXiv:2312.00396) recasts symbolic regression as a GFlowNet problem, sampling expression trees with probability π(s) ∝ R(s) over complete trees s (learned partition function Z = Σ R) instead of maximizing expected reward, returning a diverse set of high-quality candidate equations rather than collapsing onto one mode (the failure mode of DSR under noise); vanilla reward R(s) = 1/(1+RMSE(s)); the novel adaptive reward baseline R_B(s) uses baseline B > 0 and scaling γ ∈ [0,1], initialized to the mean vanilla reward of the first batch and annealed toward the mean reward of top performers, concentrating sampling on modes without collapse. The policy is an LSTM forward policy P_F(·|s) = categorical over library tokens fed one-hot parent+sibling tokens with DSR-style in-situ constraint masking, trained with trajectory balance (TB) loss on pre-order node addition from the empty tree. On a noisy synthetic benchmark (6 equations in 3 near-degenerate pairs, 10% Gaussian noise), recovery rates GFN-SR/DSR/BSR are f_1: 100/75/30; g_1: 15/5/5; f_2: 15/5/0; g_2: 95/40/90; f_3: 95/5/5; g_3: 85/90/75 — GFN-SR beats both on 5 of 6; on noiseless Nguyen 12 benchmarks DSR leads most but GFN-SR is outright best on Nguyen-5 and Nguyen-12. Diagnosis: DSR's return-maximization locks onto the wrong-but-high-reward mode of each near-degenerate pair. Caveats: asymmetric recovery strictness strengthens the claim but the benchmark is author-designed; 25M evaluations/run with no wall-clock comparison; SRBench/Feynman and real noisy data are future work.

The autofeat Python library (Horn, Pack, Rieger; arXiv:1901.07329, JMLR) generates tens of thousands of nonlinear features via SISSO-inspired symbolic expansion: Step A applies transforms {log(x), √x, 1/x, x², x³, |x|, exp(x), 2^x, sin(x), cos(x)}, Step B combines pairs with {+, −, ·}; growth 3 raw features → step 1 ~20, step 2 ~750, step 3 4000+; physical units enforce dimensionally 'legal' features via Pint with Buckingham π-theorem dimensionless groups. Selection: (1) drop features highly correlated with original/simpler ones; (2) noise filtering — fit L1 model on real + synthetic noise features (shuffled copies or N(0,1)), keep only real features with |coefficient| exceeding the largest noise coefficient; (3) chunked selection (chunks each < n/2 features, refit per chunk plus promising set); (4) stability voting on subsamples with correlation pruning — typically a few dozen features retained from several thousand. On five UCI regression datasets (R² train/test): diabetes AFR1 0.553/0.400 vs RR 0.541/0.383; boston AFR2 0.893/0.791; concrete AFR2 0.913/0.868 (best non-RF test); airfoil AFR2 0.863/0.842; wine quality AFR2 0.397/0.384 — 2 engineering steps is the sweet spot and AFR3 overfits catastrophically when features ≫ samples (diabetes AFR3 test −12.4 with 32,161 features from 442 samples; boston AFR3 test 0.048 with 54,631 features from 506 samples). Most-selected feature forms: ratios x_1/x_2, 1/(x_1x_2), products x_1·x_2², exp(x_1)/x_2, log(x_1)/x_2, |x_1−log(x_2)|. Limitations: no time-awareness (pooled selection leaks on temporal data), single train/test split with no error bars, and Pint unit legality unused in reported experiments.

SMARTFEAT (Lin, Ding, Jagadish, Zhou; arXiv:2309.07856) is a two-stage LLM feature-engineering system: a GPT-4 operator selector picks transformations from an operator library at the feature level (API cost scales with features, not rows), and a GPT-3.5 function generator turns selections into executable pandas code, with proposal vs sampling prompting chosen by search-space richness; operator types are unary (normalization, bucketization, get_dummies, date splitting), binary (+, −, ×, ÷), high-order (groupby aggregations over categorical columns), and extractor (weighted indices, external-source lookups). On 8 Kaggle binary-classification datasets, average AUC (Table 4): SMARTFEAT wins 5/8 — Adult 76.81 → 87.00 (+13.3%), Tennis 77.93 → 87.39 (+9.5%), Heart 67.38 → 72.15 (+7.0%), Housing 86.72 → 92.19 (+6.3%), Diabetes 82.20 → 86.76 (+4.3%), West Nile Virus 78.96 → 82.12 (+4.0%); Bank ≈ unchanged; Lawschool −0.4% (honest null on well-constructed features). CAAFE beats SMARTFEAT on Tennis (+13.6% vs +9.5%) — numerical-combination tasks favor free-form code gen — while Featuretools and AutoFeat frequently hurt AUC (AutoFeat −10.5% on Housing, −15.6% median on Tennis), showing context-agnostic enumeration is actively harmful. Tennis feature-importance: SMARTFEAT's 25 generated features yield IG@10 90%, RFE@10 80%, FI@10 80% (vs AutoFeat 1,978 generated/5 selected, 10%); binary and extractor operators contribute most of the Tennis gain; removing feature descriptions drops Tennis AUC to 77.86 (−1.4%). Both SMARTFEAT and Featuretools finish under 10 min on all datasets while AutoFeat exceeds the 60-min timeout. Leakage cautions: the extractor's external-source path has no timestamp guard and there is no temporal/lookahead discipline (tabular-classification only).

TrajTok (USC; arXiv:2605.20134) is an adaptive multi-resolution spatial tokenizer for trajectories: hierarchical H3 hex grid where cells whose point counts exceed a capacity threshold are recursively split until count < threshold or r_max (Porto: r6–r9, |V| = 1494 vs 46 cells at fixed r7); tokens are (cell ID, resolution, original coords, timestamp). It pairs this with a factorized encoder separating geometric ('where', g_j = e_{c_j} learned cell embedding with Spatial-Temporal RoPE over lat/lon/time) from kinematic ('how', x^kin_j = [v_j/v_max, sinθ_j, cosθ_j] with haversine speed and circular heading, k_j = MLP(x^kin_j), temporal-only RoPE), fused by self-attention then cross-attention, pretrained with co-masked token modeling: shared mask set M across channels with L_geom = −(1/|M|)Σ log p_θ(c_j|G) (masked cell-ID prediction) and L_kin = β_speed·MSE(v̂, v/v_max) + ½β_heading·MSE(sin/cos heading), J = L_geom + λ·L_kin; run-aware span masking rejects candidate spans lying entirely inside a single repeated-cell run. On Porto taxi data only: similarity retrieval HR@1 0.435, R5@20 0.983, MRR 0.588 (+0.127/+0.176/+0.140 over strongest baseline; NDCG@50 0.658, second to NeuTraj 0.672); call-type classification macro-F1 0.773 (best), micro-F1 0.811; prefix ETA 42.27 s MAE; full-trajectory travel time 38.4 s MAE. Ablations: adaptive tokenizer best overall; geo-only wins similarity/classification, kin-only wins ETA; mask ratio 0.30 best. A critical pretraining–transfer mismatch: 120k steps reduce validation loss 25% (0.098→0.073) but zero-shot retrieval drops 0.351→0.257 — longer pretraining hurt transfer, so early stopping must be transfer-validated, not loss-validated. Limitations: Porto taxi only (road-constrained trips unlike free player movement), no cross-dataset transfer.
equation: L_geom = −(1/|M|)Σ log p_θ(c_j|G) ; L_kin = β_speed·MSE(v̂, v/v_max) + ½β_heading·MSE(sin/cos heading) ; J = L_geom + λ·L_kin

claim: An empirical benchmark (arXiv:2308.10328, 2023) of 9 rehearsal-based online continual learning methods (AGEM, ER, ER+LwF, ER-ACE, MIR, SCR, RAR, DER++, GDumb) on Split-CIFAR100 and Split-TinyImageNet (5 seeds; protocol batch 10 new + 10 replay per step, 3 training passes/mini-batch on CIFAR100 and 9 on TinyImageNet, memory 2000/4000) with metrics WC-ACC_t = (1/k)·A(E_k, f_t) + (1 − 1/k)·min-ACC_{T_k} (Eqs. 1–2), AAA_t = (1/t)·Σ_j (1/k)·Σ_i A(E_i, f_j) (Eq. 3), AA = (1/k)·Σ_i A(E_i, f_t), and average forgetting finds: no method wins across metrics or memory sizes; final accuracies cluster within ~5% of the i.i.d. reference; ER+LwF best on CIFAR100 by a tiny margin, ER-ACE best on TinyImageNet; AGEM is the clear loser. Stability ≠ accuracy: MIR beats SCR by 1% final accuracy on CIFAR100 but SCR beats MIR by ~9% on WC-Acc. Probed representation quality ≈ the i.i.d. reference (45.8% CIFAR100 / 34.3% TinyImageNet) and plain ER has the BEST probed accuracy despite below-average stability — the paper's conclusion is that the classifier head, not the representation, is the main failure point. Underfitting, not forgetting: classical forgetting rises across the stream (misleading in class-incremental settings since task difficulty grows); cumulative forgetting shows steady backward transfer. Memory ablations: even 5 samples/class suffices for decent representation strength (probed gap only 1%→2% between memory sizes). GDumb (retrain from scratch on the buffer before each inference) is a strong reference, implying the online constraint may buy little vs periodic from-scratch refits.

MetaVRF (arXiv:2006.06707v2, 2020) meta-learns random Fourier feature bases by treating them as latent variables inferred variationally from the task support set plus LSTM-accumulated cross-task context, yielding task-adaptive kernels with a closed-form kernel-ridge base-learner and no gradient steps at meta-test: KRR closed form α = Y(λI+K)⁻¹; Ŷ = f_α(X̃) = αK̃ (Eqs. 3–5); RFF map z(x) = D^-1/2[cos(ω_1ᵀx+b_1),…,cos(ω_Dᵀx+b_D)] (Eq. 7) with D=780 vs 2048 for regular RFFs; ELBO log p(y|x,S) ≥ E_{q_φ(ω|S)} log p(y|x,S,ω) − D_KL[q_φ(ω|S) || p(ω|x,S)] (Eq. 11); context [h^t, c^t] = g_LSTM(S̅^t, h^{t−1}, c^{t−1}) (Eq. 14); reparameterization ω = ω_μ + ω_σ ⊙ ε, ε∼N(0,I). miniImageNet 5-way 1-shot (shallow net): bi-LSTM MetaVRF 54.2 ± 0.8 vs VERSA 53.3 ± 1.8, vanilla LSTM 53.1 ± 0.9, MAML 48.7 ± 1.8; 5-shot: bi-LSTM 67.8 ± 0.7 vs RFFs 65.4 ± 0.9; with WRN-28-10 embeddings 1-shot: bi-LSTM 63.80 ± 0.05 (SOTA) vs LEO 61.76 ± 0.08; 5-shot: 77.97 ± 0.28 vs TADAM 76.70 ± 0.30. CIFAR-FS 5-way 5-shot: R2-D2 77.4 ± 0.2 vs MetaVRF bi-LSTM 76.5 ± 0.9. Ablations: bi-LSTM > vanilla LSTM > w/o LSTM consistently, and MetaVRF(780d) beats plain RFFs(2048d) at every sampling rate — adaptive kernels work at far lower sampling rates. Robustness: trained 20-way-5-shot → tested up to 100-way, retains 94% accuracy. Few-shot sine regression beats MAML at k=3,5,10. Limitation: no calibration metrics (accuracy only, no NLL); λ meta-learned globally with no per-task noise modeling.
equation: α = Y(λI+K)⁻¹ ; Ŷ = αK̃ ; z(x) = D^-1/2[cos(ω_1ᵀx+b_1),…,cos(ω_Dᵀx+b_D)] ; log p(y|x,S) ≥ E_{q_φ(ω|S)} log p(y|x,S,ω) − D_KL[q_φ(ω|S) || p(ω|x,S)]

claim: The foundational distributional-RL paper (arXiv:1707.06887, 2017) models the full distribution of the random return via the categorical C51 algorithm (51-atom softmax over fixed return support) instead of only its expectation: distributional Bellman operator TZ(x,a) =^D R(x,a) + γ Z(X′,A′), equality in distribution; γ-contraction in maximal Wasserstein form (policy evaluation) but NOT a contraction in total variation, KL, or Kolmogorov distance; the control (optimality) operator is NOT a contraction in any distribution metric (stability in control is empirical, not guaranteed). Categorical parametrization: Z_θ(x,a) = z_i w.p. p_i(x,a) = exp(θ_i(x,a))/Σ_j exp(θ_j(x,a)); support z_i = V_min + i·Δz, Δz=(V_max−V_min)/(N−1), N=51, V_max=−V_min=10; categorical projection (ΦT̂Z_θ(x,a))_i = Σ_{j=0}^{N−1} [1 − |[T̂z_j]^{V_max}_{V_min} − z_i|/Δz]_0^1 · p_j(x′,π(x′)) (Eq. 7) with cross-entropy loss vs the projected target and greedy policy w.r.t. E[Z_θ]; trains at ~75% of DQN speed for N=51. On 57 Atari games (mean %human / median %human / games > human baseline / games > DQN): C51 (ε=0.01) 701% / 178% / 40 / 50 vs DQN 307% / 118% / 33 / 43; within 50M frames C51 outperformed a fully trained (200M-frame) DQN on 45 of 57 games. Atom ablation: more atoms always increase performance; even the 1-parameter Bernoulli variant beats DQN in 3/5 games; Seaquest reaches state-of-the-art; sparse-reward games (Venture, Private Eye) show strong performance since value distributions propagate rarely occurring events better; Pong's learned distribution is bimodal, reflecting intrinsic unobservable randomness of reward timing. Limitation: main-table results use best-evaluation-score reporting (favors lucky seeds).
equation: TZ(x,a) =^D R(x,a) + γ Z(X′,A′) ; Z_θ(x,a) = z_i w.p. p_i(x,a) = exp(θ_i(x,a))/Σ_j exp(θ_j(x,a)) ; z_i = V_min + i·Δz

claim: A 2025 theory-only paper (arXiv:2507.12657) reframes path-dependent derivative pricing (e.g., Asian options, payoff = function of the running average, max(average − strike, 0)) as distributional RL with recursive quantile updates and RBF-based quantile-function approximation: the distributional Bellman operator is a γ-contraction in the Wasserstein metric ('errors in the learned distribution at one time step do not amplify through recursion'); quantile SGD gives unbiased stochastic gradients of the pinball loss and quantile parameters converge to Bellman-operator fixed points under regularity assumptions. The corpus ledger verdict is effectively no-build: zero empirical validation (no experiments, tables, or benchmarks — all claims theoretical), RBF approximators scale poorly to high-dimensional state spaces, a single-author 2025 paper not peer-reviewed, and the authors' own caveat that minimizing Wasserstein distance alone may not reflect financially critical tail behavior or extreme-quantile accuracy — directly relevant to any drawdown use case.

The Trajectory Transformer (arXiv:2106.02039, 2021) reduces offline RL to sequence modeling: a GPT-style transformer decoder (4 layers, 4 heads) trained by teacher forcing to maximize E[Σ_t log P_θ(x_t | x_{<t})] over per-dimension discretized (state, action, reward) token sequences, with beam search as planner (argmax_{y ∈ Y_T} log P_θ(y | x) with reward-biased beam expansion; variations yield imitation, goal-reaching, and offline RL). Discretization: uniform (bin width (max s^i − min s^i)/V) vs quantile (each token accounts for 1/V of empirical data mass); a key stated property is that joint state-action modeling biases generation toward in-distribution actions, removing the need for explicit pessimism/conservatism. On D4RL: substantially better error compounding than the PETS feedforward Gaussian ensemble on length-100 humanoid trajectories (generated trajectories 'visually indistinguishable' from real while the single-step model produces physically implausible predictions); offline RL performs on par with or better than all prior methods (BRAC, CQL, MBOP, Decision Transformer, BC) on locomotion and, combined with DP, SOTA on sparse-reward long-horizon AntMaze. Discretization ablation: uniform ≈ quantile except HalfCheetah-Medium-Expert, where quantile achieves more than twice the return of uniform (large velocity range strands uniform bins). Limitations: per-dimension discretization explodes vocabulary for high-dim states; beam search is a planner not a sampler (argmax, not unbiased samples); NFL games run 150+ plays in token count.

DAGuerreotype (Zantedeschi et al. 2023, arXiv:2301.11898) learns causal DAG structure by continuous optimization of a topological ordering over the permutahedron: any DAG = topological ordering (permutation) + edges only from lower to higher nodes in the order, the ordering learned via sparse relaxations over the permutahedron (sparsemax/sparseMAP-style; Gumbel-Sinkhorn/Birkhoff connections), keeping every learned graph a valid DAG and allowing edge estimation via any (even non-differentiable) subroutine; theorem bound SHD(R^{σ(θ)}, R^{σ(θ′)}) ≤ ∫ ΣΣ δ_{H_ij} dt (global sensitivity bound on SHD between induced orderings). Edge estimators tested: masked linear, masked MLP (NoTears-nonlinear style), LARS; evaluation uses SHD (favors sparse) vs SID (structural intervention distance; favors dense) with Pareto analysis. On Sachs (d=11, 853 obs, 17-edge ground truth) + SynTReN (10 networks, d=20, 20–25 edges, 500 obs each), DAGuerreotype sits on the SHD-vs-SID Pareto front: NOTEARS/GOLEM/NPVAR have best SHD but worst SID (too sparse); VI-DP-DAG has best SID but worst SHD (too dense); performance strongly depends on the edge estimator (linear better on Sachs, MLP needed for SynTReN); space complexity ≥ O(d²) edge-mask matrix. The paper itself cites the Reisach et al. critique: synthetic linear-DAG benchmarks are flawed because marginal variance grows with DAG depth, so sort-by-variance + sparse regression matches SOTA — hence standardize variables and validate orderings against domain knowledge.

auto-sktime (Zöller et al. 2023, arXiv:2312.08528) is an AutoML system for time-series forecasting with per-family pipeline templates, a time-aware multi-fidelity budget, and warm-starting HPO from prior runs: pipeline templates define search space Λ_i = Λ_i^1 ∪ ... ∪ Λ_i^n ∪ {λ_{i,r}} per forecaster family; multi-fidelity budget b ∈ [b_min, b_max] with 0 < b_min < b_max ≤ 1 and fidelity proxy f̃_D(·, b) with f̃(·, b_max) = f(·), where the budget maps to a lookback window y_{i, T_i − l_b : T_i} (short recent window at low budget, expanding backward to the full series at b_max), allocated by successive halving; Bayesian optimization initialized from prior runs (meta-learning). On 64 diverse real-world time series (MASE, 5-min budget, 5 seeds): auto-sktime 1.59±1.61, rank 3.22±1.94, 326s — significantly best on MASE and rank; APT-TS 3.12±5.41; AutoTS 4.26±10.94; HyperTS 2.88±5.03; pmdarima 2.63±3.21; ETS 2.57±2.78; PyAF 3.23±5.33; AutoGluon 6.00±18.17; DeepAR 11.54±51.51; TFT 9.80±50.62.
