SUM_{k=0}^{min} C(y_k^h,k)C(y_k^a,k)k!(lambda_3/(lambda_1 lambda_2))^k, with lambda_1 = exp(alpha^h + x^{att,h} - x^{def,a}), lambda_2 = exp(alpha^a + x^{att,a} - x^{def,h}), lambda_3 = exp(beta).
equation: G_k(y_k | x^h, x^a) = e^{-(lambda_1+lambda_2+lambda_3)} (lambda_1^{y_k^h}/y_k^h!)(lambda_2^{y_k^a}/y_k^a!) SUM_{k=0}^{min} C(y_k^h,k)C(y_k^a,k)k!(lambda_3/(lambda_1 lambda_2))^k; lambda_1 = exp(alpha^h + x^{att,h} - x^{def,a}); lambda_2 = exp(alpha^a + x^{att,a} - x^{def,h}); lambda_3 = exp(beta)

claim: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck mean-reverting skill dynamics: M_{t,t'} = N(x_{t'} | x_t . e^{-tau(t'-t)} + mu_0(1-e^{-tau(t'-t)}), sigma_0^2(1-e^{-2tau(t'-t)})); EM M-step closed forms exist for sigma-hat_0^2 and tau-hat^2, with a Gauss-Hermite M-step for epsilon; the paper derives but never fits the OU dynamics.

Skill-rating benchmark numbers (average negative log-likelihood, train/test, protocol 3 years train to 1 year test): WTA tennis - Elo-Davidson 0.640/0.636, Extended Kalman 0.640/0.635, TrueSkill2 0.650/0.668, SMC 0.640/0.639, Discrete 0.639/0.636; EPL football - Elo-Davidson 1.000/0.973, Extended Kalman 0.988/0.965, TrueSkill2 1.006/0.961, SMC 0.988/0.962, Discrete 0.987/0.961; bivariate Poisson EPL variants - EK 0.975/0.954, SMC 0.978/0.950, Discrete 0.984/0.954, beating the win/draw/win-only SSM on match-winner prediction despite not being optimized for it; chess - Elo-Davidson 0.802/1.001, Extended Kalman 0.801/0.972, TrueSkill2 0.802/0.978, SMC 0.801/0.974, Discrete 0.801/0.976. The 65% chess draw rate makes cross-sport NLL magnitudes meaningless, and there are no significance tests on the NLL differences.

EM on the tennis 2-D likelihood landscape (Fig. 3): TrueSkill2's Gaussian approximation 'evades the global optimum' while SMC and discrete identify it ('no systematic bias beyond the factorial approximation'); smoothing case study (Fig. 4): Tottenham's 2011-2023 skill ascended under Villas-Boas/early Pochettino and descended late Pochettino, with the 2022 decline driven by defence weakening while attack stayed proficient.

Stival, Bernardi, Dellaportas (2022) 'Doubly-online changepoint detection for monitoring health status during sports activities' (arXiv:2206.11578v1) is a Gaussian state-space model with a latent changepoint chain S_1:N over repeated athletic activities that detects distributional regime changes both between activities (after each completed session, updating parameters and retrospective segmentation) and within an activity in real time; demonstrated on 85 consecutive warm-up runs (first 10 minutes on flat routes, sampled every second, T=600) from one well-trained athlete via Polar v800 watch plus Polar H10 heart-rate monitor, with variables heart rate (bpm) and speed (m/s).

Doubly-online changepoint model structure: latent changepoint chain S_1:N with S_1=1 and S_n - S_{n-1} = 1 iff a changepoint occurs at activity n; transition p(S_n|S_{n-1}) = lambda for a new segment (lambda=0.5 in the application); measurement y_{n,t} = [Z^(S)_theta Z^(A)_theta][alpha_t^(s); alpha_{n,t}] + epsilon_{n,t} with epsilon ~ N_P(0, Sigma_theta) (Eq. 1), combining a segment-specific latent trend alpha_t^(s) with an activity-specific disturbance alpha_{n,t} and block-diagonal state transitions (Eqs. 2-4); inference by online EM with SMC approximation of changepoint predicted probabilities (constant complexity) plus Kalman filter/smoother for latent states.
equation: p(S_n|S_{n-1}) = lambda for a new segment, lambda=0.5; y_{n,t} = [Z^(S)_theta Z^(A)_theta][alpha_t^(s); alpha_{n,t}] + epsilon_{n,t}, epsilon ~ N_P(0, Sigma_theta)

claim: Changepoint decision rule (Eq. 14): p-hat(D_n = 1 | y_{1:n,1:T}) > delta, with delta=0.5 in the application; within-online monitoring reports the posterior P(D_n = 1 | y_{n,1:t}, past) at every time point t during an activity.
equation: p-hat(D_n = 1 | y_{1:n,1:T}) > delta, delta=0.5; within-online posterior P(D_n = 1 | y_{n,1:t}, past)

claim: Changepoint-detection real-data results: 34 estimated changepoints in 85 activities, of which 19 are single-activity segments (high between-activity variability); 15 of the 19 fall in the last 43 activities and are attributed partly to systematic measurement errors (probable device malfunction), so the method detected a device problem, not just physiology. Within-online case studies: activity 21 flagged (P ~ 1 after about 20 s, elevated HR at the same speed); activity 33 flagged after about 2 min (low HR plus low speed = low effort); activity 39 flagged (low HR, normal speed = improved fitness); activity 32 correctly not flagged (P ~ 0 throughout).

Within-online detection difficulty: detection is hard early at t=40 and 'satisfactory' after observing 2/3 of the series (t=80); sensitivity decreases as delta increases, significantly for T=60/120 but stable for T=240; sensitivity is prioritized over specificity (missing a health problem is worse than a false alarm); the paper has no head-to-head against simpler alternatives (CUSUM, BOCPD, offline PELT) on real data, and lambda=0.5 is fixed arbitrarily.

Chatterjee, Ibsen-Jensen & Tkadlec (2016, arXiv:1604.05090, IJCAI 2016) define the epsilon-perturbation set P(P,epsilon) = {P' : |P'_ij - P_ij| <= epsilon}, the epsilon-guaranteed win probability wp_epsilon(i*,P,sigma) = inf_{P' in P(P,epsilon)} wp(i*,P',sigma), and the epsilon-worst drop d_epsilon = wp - wp_epsilon as a robustness primitive for tournament win probabilities.
equation: P(P,epsilon) = {P' : |P'_ij - P_ij| <= epsilon}; wp_epsilon(i*,P,sigma) = inf_{P' in P(P,epsilon)} wp(i*,P',sigma); d_epsilon = wp - wp_epsilon

claim: Drop approximation d-hat_epsilon via the multilinear decomposition wp = alpha_ij . P_ij + beta_ij: deterministic d-hat_epsilon = c . epsilon where c = number of crucial (0,1)-matches whose flip loses the tournament, O(N log N); probabilistic d-hat_epsilon = SUM_{i!=j} |alpha_ij|, O(N^4); the worst perturbation always lies on the l-infinity boundary.
equation: d-hat_epsilon = c . epsilon, c = # crucial (0,1)-matches; d-hat_epsilon = SUM_{i!=j} |alpha_ij| with wp = alpha_ij . P_ij + beta_ij

claim: Robust-tournament-draw examples: Example 2 (N=64 hard tournament, unique winning draw) gives wp_0.01 < 0.54, wp_0.05 < 0.07, wp_0.1 < 0.02, so a 'guaranteed' win collapses under 1% probability error, and the linear coefficient of the drop polynomial is N-1 = 63; Example 3 (two draws, both wp=1 exactly) gives wp_0.01 > 0.89 for the robust draw versus < 0.73 for the fragile one, i.e., identical point estimates with sharply different worst-case guarantees; Example 4 shows a delta-suboptimal draw (wp 0.502 vs 0.506) guarantees more under epsilon=0.02 (>0.432 vs <0.429), so suboptimal point estimates can be superior once robustness is priced in.

The linear-term drop approximation requires epsilon < cN^{-2}, which for N=64 means epsilon much less than 0.0002, an extremely restrictive regime; the underlying RTFP/RPTFP draw problems are NP-complete, with poly-time approximation only in Aziz et al.'s special cases.

Issac et al. (2023, arXiv:2305.05423) built a Lambda-architecture Azure big-data pipeline for cotton bloom detection with YOLOv5-large (46.5M params) on 1,300 hand-labeled images (80/20 split), reporting mAP 0.96, precision 0.84, recall 0.99, F1 0.904 at IoU 0.55; the ledger verdict is REJECT as a precision-agriculture vision paper with nothing transferring to sports-statistics modeling (no external test set, single farm/season/cultivar, generalization unproven).
equation: precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN); F1 = 2.precision.recall/(precision+recall); IoU = overlap/union, correct iff IoU >= 0.55

claim: Chatton et al. (2024, arXiv:2412.10245v3) propose sPoRT, a nonparametric diagnostic for sequential positivity violations in longitudinal causal inference: per treatment rule times per time point, fit regression trees predicting rule-adherence from covariate history; flag covariate-defined subgroups with estimated adherence probability < beta as positivity violations; exclude subgroups with relative size < alpha (minimum-size guard); cap tree complexity at gamma variables. Hyperparameters: alpha in {0, 0.05, 0.1}; beta in {0.01, 0.05, 5/(sqrt(n).ln n)}; gamma in {2, 3, all}; main run alpha=0.05, beta=5/(sqrt(n_t).ln n_t), gamma=2.

The sequential positivity assumption diagnosed by sPoRT is that at each time t, P(follow rule at t | covariate history, followed rule so far) > 0 for all covariate strata; on a clinical cohort of 2,352 HIV-positive children (South Africa, Malawi, Zimbabwe; visits at 0/1/3/6/9/12 months), Rule 3 (ART when CD4 < 750 or CD4% < 25%) had 2 violations at 6 months and 13 at 9 months, Rule 4 (CD4 < 350 or CD4% < 15%) had 1 at 6 months and 7 at 9 months, and no violations appeared when pooling over time, showing temporal aggregation masks sequential violations. Adaptive beta examples: Rule 3 n1=2060 -> beta=.014, n2=1346 -> beta=.019, n3=794 -> beta=.027, n4=565 -> beta=.033.
equation: sequential positivity: P(follow rule at t | covariate history, followed rule so far) > 0 for all strata

claim: sPoRT is explicitly a diagnostic, not an estimator: it reports no effect estimates, and the extract contains no simulation validation with known ground-truth violations.

Grady et al. (2026, arXiv:2604.27865) introduce KellyBench, a walk-forward full-season EPL simulation where frontier LLMs act as sequential decision-makers maximizing log-wealth, on EPL 1993-94 through 2023-24 with closing bookmaker odds at about 5.3% overround; per-matchday reward r_t = log W_{t+1} - log W_t with cumulative R = SUM r_t = log(W_{T+1}/W_1); Kelly growth W(b) = SUM_{x,y} p(x,y) log(b(x|y)o(x)) with optimal b*(x|y) = p(x|y) and W* = I(X;Y); edge decomposition g(p;p*,q) = D_KL(p*||q) - D_KL(p*||p), so growth is positive iff the model is closer to truth than the market-implied probabilities; binary Kelly fraction f* = (rp - (1-p))/r with the reference implementation using fractional Kelly 0.25.
equation: r_t = log W_{t+1} - log W_t; R = SUM r_t = log(W_{T+1}/W_1); W(b) = SUM_{x,y} p(x,y) log(b(x|y)o(x)); b*(x|y) = p(x|y); W* = I(X;Y); g(p;p*,q) = D_KL(p*||q) - D_KL(p*||p); f* = (rp - (1-p))/r

claim: KellyBench headline result (2023/24 test season, 5 models x 5 seeds): every frontier LLM loses money on average - GPT-5.4 -7.9% ROI (best +34.1%, worst -32.9%, 115 bets), Opus 4.6 -11.2% (best +21.5%, worst -44.7%, 202 bets), GLM-5 -51.6% (ruin), Gemini 3.1 Pro -66.0% (ruin), Kimi K2.5 -89.6% (ruin); only 3/25 seeds positive, and delta log-loss versus the market is positive for all five, so predictive underperformance versus the market drives the losses.

KellyBench failure-mode prevalence across 25 seeds: ruin 6/25; no principled sizing at execution 9/25; Kelly code written but never invoked 7/25; no promoted-team handling 22/25; never retrained 7/25; declared task complete while the season was still running 8/25; label leakage 7/25; draw/longshot miscalibration 22/25.

KellyBench adaptivity results: fully adaptive seeds averaged -11.1% ROI versus -70.0% for fully static seeds; only Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 avoided ruin (both retrained and cut size when no edge was found). Sophistication scores of 52: Opus 4.6 26.5%, GPT-5.4 22.3%, GLM-5 17.3%, Kimi K2.5 12.7%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 8.8%, human quant 73.1%; seeds scoring 11-18/52 went bankrupt at about 8% versus about 55% for seeds scoring 0-5/52 (logistic regression p < 0.001). Human baselines: Human Quant +5.1% ROI (39 bets, Sharpe 0.96), the only profitable strategy; AI Researcher -4.3%; Dixon-Coles -15.4% yet beats 3 of 5 frontier models; rubric-access ablation raised sophistication to 55.0% and mean ROI to -0.7% (3 seeds).

KellyBench methodology: a 52-point expert sophistication rubric (45 criteria, not fully published); Mann-Whitney U tests on pooled per-matchday log returns with Holm-Bonferroni correction; hierarchical bootstrap with 50K simulations; five full-season episodes (2000/01, 2010/11, 2020/21 train; 2023/24 test plus/minus literature).

Bandyopadhyay & Mukherjee (2026) 'An Augmented Rating System for Test cricket' adapts the Glicko rating system with a recalibrated logistic scale d=85 (vs chess's 400), additive home/toss effects combined via an FGM copula, and margin-of-victory-scaled rating updates; verdict ADAPT as four portable mechanics for team-strength ratings.

Glicko core used in the augmented rating system: E_A = 1/(1+10^{-(R_A-R_B)g(RD_B)/d}); g(RD) = 1/sqrt(1+3RD^2/pi^2); RD_A' = 1/sqrt(1/RD_A^2+1/d^2); r_A' = r_A + g(RD_B)(S_A-E_A)/sqrt(1/RD_A^2+1/d^2). Scale recalibration by grid search over d on Brier, MAE, log loss, and ECE gives d=85 for Test cricket versus the chess default 400.

Home/toss additive adjustment inside the expected score: E_{i,home} = 1/(1+10^{-(R_i-R_j+h_{i,j})g(RD_j)/85}) with h_{i,j} = (won-lost)/played pairwise; the FGM copula combining home (H) and toss (T) effects is E = F(H)G(T)[1+omega(1-F(H))(1-G(T))] with omega=-0.5436 from empirical Spearman rho=-0.1812=omega/3, chosen over Gaussian/Frank/Plackett by log-likelihood and AIC.

MOV-scaled actual score: S_A = (1+MOV)/2 for a win, (1-MOV)/2 for a loss, 1/2 for a draw, with MOV_i = ((R_i-R_min)/range_R)^{beta_i} . ((W_i-W_min)/range_W)^{1-beta_i} + I_i . (E4P_i+ERM_i)/TR_i; MOV values exceeded 1 in the table (e.g., 1.886), breaking the probabilistic interpretation and never renormalized.

Augmented rating system results: scale d=85 vs d=400 gives Brier 0.1601 vs 0.1929 (17% improvement), log-loss 0.5946 vs 0.6645 (10.52%), MAE 0.3629 vs 0.4047 (10.33%), ECE 0.1594 vs 0.1844 (13.56%); home advantage 82 home wins vs 41 away wins (chi-square p=3.386e-7); toss advantage 75 wins after winning toss vs 50 after losing (p=0.002399); winner-prediction accuracy 44 of 56 non-drawn matches (~78.6%) in the WTC 2021-23 test cycle; Spearman rank correlation 0.9624 between Glicko ranks and ICC ranks; bootstrap-permutation robustness over 100 permutations gives average CV 0.44% and SD ~0.436 rating points.

Chernis, Koop, Tallman & West (2024) 'Decision Synthesis in Monetary Policy' introduces Bayesian Predictive Decision Synthesis (BPDS): combine models by weighting on realized decision outcomes rather than predictive fit alone, using decision-dependent weights, outcome calibration functions, and entropic tilting to target expected scores; demonstrated on three monetary-policy VARs (3-variable, larger VAR, time-varying-parameter VAR, 5 lags, sign restrictions) with US macro quarterly data 1990-2024 in pseudo-real-time sequential forecasting at horizons k=8 quarters.

BPDS mixture: f(y|x) proportional to SUM_j pi_j(x) alpha_j(y|x) p_j(y|x,M_j), with pi_j(x) decision-dependent model probabilities and alpha_j(y|x) outcome-dependent calibration modifiers; equivalently f(y|x) = SUM pi-tilde_j(x) f_j with f_j = alpha_j p_j / a_j and pi-tilde_j = k(x) pi_j a_j. Entropic (exponential) tilting: alpha_j = exp{tau(x)' s(y,x)} so that E_f[s(y,x)] = m_f(x), with tau(x) solved numerically per candidate decision.
equation: f(y|x) propto SUM_j pi_j(x) alpha_j(y|x) p_j(y|x,M_j); f(y|x) = SUM pi-tilde_j(x) f_j; f_j = alpha_j p_j / a_j; pi-tilde_j = k(x) pi_j a_j; alpha_j = exp{tau(x)' s(y,x)}; E_f[s(y,x)] = m_f(x)

claim: BPDS bounded score functions: s_{jh}(y_h) = exp{-(y_h-y*)^2/(2z_y^2)} with z = d/sqrt(-2 log eps), eps=0.4, d_y=2, d_g=2, d_x=1; case-study dual-mandate utility U(y,g,x) = -SUM_{h=1:8} {theta(y_h-y*)^2 + (1-theta)(g_h-g*)^2 + (x_h-x_{h-1})^2} with y*=2% inflation and g*=2.5% GDP growth.

BPDS results: expected utility exceeded BMA in virtually every period (Figure 8), with the gap largest pre-financial-crisis when BPDS/BMA recommendations diverged most; BPDS recommendations were more constrained (less extreme) than BMA's; BPDS predictive mixtures were less dispersed than BMA (BMA more heavy-tailed, especially at long horizons). Importance-sampling ESS stayed 90-95% pre-COVID, collapsed during the COVID recession (targets unrealistic given the state) but recovered, and mixture ESS stayed above individual-model ESS throughout; there is no formal statistical test of the utility differences, the evidence is graphical and trajectory-based.

Manski (2021) 'Probabilistic Prediction for Binary Treatment Choice' develops Wald minimax-regret (MMR) statistical decision theory for binary treatment choice: as-if optimization with estimated probabilities, closed-form MMR rules, and weighted estimators with optimized weights; illustrated with a two-covariate example (p_m0=0.2, p_M0=0.6, lambda=+-0.1, U_0B=0.6) and Monte Carlo max-regret with 20,000 draws on a 50x50 parameter grid.

Wald criteria: Bayes risk, maximin, and minimax regret over states of nature s, sampling distributions Q_s, and decision functions phi(psi). Clinical threshold rule: p_x* = 1 - U_B; choose treatment B iff p_x > p_x*. Regret: R_s[phi(psi)] = |(1-p_s) - U_B| . e[p_s, phi(psi), U_B], where e is the probability the rule chooses the inferior treatment.
equation: p_x* = 1 - U_B; choose B iff p_x > p_x*; R_s[phi(psi)] = |(1-p_s) - U_B| . e[p_s, phi(psi), U_B]

claim: MMR closed forms: no-data MMR = min[(1-p_m) - U_B, U_B - (1-p_M)]; uninformative-data randomized rule with q = [U_B - (1-p_M)]/(p_M - p_m); one-observation max regret = 1/4 . max[(1-U_B)^2, U_B^2]; Hoeffding bound: max_s E_s[R_s(n/N)] <= delta + max[(1-p_m)-U_B, U_B-(1-p_M)] . exp(-2N delta^2). Weighted (kernel) estimators with optimized weights; ecological inference via constrained least squares.
equation: no-data MMR = min[(1-p_m) - U_B, U_B - (1-p_M)]; q = [U_B - (1-p_M)]/(p_M - p_m); one-observation max regret = 1/4 . max[(1-U_B)^2, U_B^2]; max_s E_s[R_s(n/N)] <= delta + max[(1-p_m)-U_B, U_B-(1-p_M)] . exp(-2N delta^2)

claim: ITP weighted-estimator minimized maximum regret (Table 1, exact values): (N0,N1)=(10,10): 0.030 at w=0.751; (5,15): 0.034 at 0.863; (15,5): 0.023 at 0.752; (20,20): 0.021 at 0.858; (10,30): 0.026 at 0.911; (30,10): 0.016 at 0.800, so optimal weights favor the own-group sample but borrow substantially from the other group. Ecological example: maximum regret 0.011 for (10,10), 0.008 for (20,20).
Manski's critique: biostatistics and ML evaluations (accuracy, AUC, calibration) miss decision quality because the probability is an instrument and the decision is the target.

Manski (2021) 'Econometrics for decision making: building foundations sketched by Haavelmo and Wald' (Haavelmo Lecture, Univ. of Oslo) argues econometric models should be evaluated by regret across the full state space (all feasible states of nature), not by fit within the model space; applies Wald decision theory to prediction and binary treatment choice with new numerical maximum-regret findings.

Wald statistical-decision-function criteria: (1) maximize average welfare; (2) maximin welfare; (3) MMR = min_c max_s [max_d w(d,s) - w(c,s)]. Hodges-Lehmann (1950) MMR predictor for [0,1] outcomes: (mu_N sqrt(N) + 1/2)/(sqrt(N)+1). Missing-data midpoint predictor max regret: 1/4[P(delta=1)^2/K + P(delta=0)^2]. MMR fractional allocation: z_MMR = E[y(b)|delta(b)=1].p + {1-E[y(a)|delta(a)=1]}(1-p); max regret z_MMR(1-z_MMR) fractional versus min(z_MMR,1-z_MMR) deterministic singleton. Binary-choice regret: R_{c(.)s} . |w(a,s) - w(b,s)|; as-if optimization: c[s(psi)] in argmax_c w[c,s(psi)]. Numerical max-regret via Monte Carlo (5,000 samples per state) over discretized state-space grids, N=25-100.
equation: MMR = min_c max_s [max_d w(d,s) - w(c,s)]; HL predictor = (mu_N sqrt(N) + 1/2)/(sqrt(N)+1); missing-data midpoint max regret = 1/4[P(delta=1)^2/K + P(delta=0)^2]; z_MMR = E[y(b)|delta(b)=1].p + {1-E[y(a)|delta(a)=1]}(1-p); fractional max regret = z_MMR(1-z_MMR); deterministic = min(z_MMR,1-z_MMR)

claim: Utah juvenile sentencing illustration (Manski & Nagin 1998; males born 1970-1974, convicted before 16; 11% confined, 23% of those with no reoffense in 2 years; 89% non-confinement, 41% no reoffense): max regret of mandate-confinement (a)=0.45 versus mandate-no-confinement (b)=0.55, so (a) minimizes maximum regret, yet the empirical-success rule picks (b) because 0.41>0.23, showing as-if optimization can select the MMR-inferior treatment.

AMMR max regret is roughly invariant in p but rises from about 0.34 (N=25) to about 0.40 (N=100), so more data makes the deterministic rule less randomized and more regrettable, approaching 1/2 as N approaches infinity (footnote: N=1 gives 1/4 for all p). The midpoint predictor beats the sample-average-of-observed-outcomes: max MSE about 1/4 the size at observability <=0.8 and about 1/2 at 0.9 (Table 1A N=100: 0.1952 at P(delta=1)=0.1, 0.0620 at 0.5, 0.0025 at 1.0; Table 2A: 0.7779, 0.2404, 0.0025). Identification (missing-data bias) dominates imprecision when observability <0.7; the empirical-success rule max regret equals exactly max(p,1-p) in the known-distribution case; coarse-grid max regret is a lower bound on true max regret (paper's own footnote).

Xie & Muppidi (2026) 'Forecasting the Winner of a Live Tennis Match' compares five approaches integrating pre-match strength and live in-match information within a strictly chronological evaluation (train 2011-2021, validation 2022, test 2023-2024), introducing the hybrid Trace architecture: Markov recursion plus Elo pre-match prior plus Bayesian-shrinkage live updates, stacked with live features in a histogram gradient-boosting model. Data: Jeff Sackmann Grand Slam point-by-point data (8,222 matches, 1,505,355 point-level prediction states after cleaning, 21.8% excluded); ATP/WTA Elo matched to 96.0% of matches; code at github.com/cx-57/live-tennis-research.

Trace live-tennis components: Markov score recursion V(s) = q(s)V(T1(s)) + (1-q(s))V(T2(s)); deuce D(q) = q^2/(q^2+(1-q)^2). Elo: q_{i,t} = 1/(1+10^{(Rj,t-Ri,t)/400}); R_{i,t+1} = R_{i,t} + K_{i,t}(S_{i,t}-q_{i,t}), K_{i,t} = 250/(m_{i,t}+5)^{0.4}. Elo-to-serve-edge mapping: e = clip(alpha.d, -0.15, 0.15); pa = clip(beta+e, 0.45, 0.88), pb = clip(beta-e, 0.45, 0.88); selected (beta,alpha) = (0.64, 1.3e-4) at 25% match progress, (0.59, 1.3e-4) at 50% and 75%.

Bayesian shrinkage of the live serve rate toward the Elo prior: theta-hat = (n/(n+kappa))theta-hat_live + (kappa/(n+kappa))theta_prior, with kappa grid {40,80,160,320,640} selected as 640/160/40 at 25/50/75% match progress, so shrinkage weakens as the match progresses. Trace stack input: x(s) = [p_M, p_S, logit(p_M), logit(p_S), p_S - p_M, z(s)] into an HGBM with configs (lr, max_leaf_nodes, l2) in {(0.03,7,1.0),(0.03,15,1.0),(0.05,7,1.0),(0.05,15,3.0)}, early stopping, max 250 iterations.
equation: theta-hat = (n/(n+kappa))theta-hat_live + (kappa/(n+kappa))theta_prior; x(s) = [p_M, p_S, logit(p_M), logit(p_S), p_S - p_M, z(s)]

claim: Trace results: accuracy (test, 25%/50%/75%/all-points) 0.7606/0.8215/0.8834/77.84%, highest in every column with the largest lead mid-match (about 40-70% progress); log loss (test, 25/50/75%) 0.4753/0.3530/0.2002, lowest at all checkpoints; serve-shrink beats Elo-asymmetric on log loss at every checkpoint (0.5142/0.4266/0.2842 vs 0.5210/0.4549/0.3096); HGBM alone is weak early (below symmetric Markov at 25%: accuracy 0.6944 vs 0.6851) but the strongest single model late (75%: accuracy 0.8738, log loss 0.2299); Trace is well calibrated, especially at 25% and 50% progress; DeepTennis LSTM comparison: 79.5% overall on a leakage-suspect non-chronological split versus Trace 81.30% all-points on the same split; WTA accuracy curves fluctuate more than ATP (hypothesis: 66% vs 79% service-hold rates, untested).

Skripnikov, Cemek & Gillman (2026) 'Leveraging Minute-by-Minute Soccer Match Event Data to Adjust Team's Offensive Production for Game Context' models per-minute offensive production with a Negative Binomial GAM on game context (score differential, red-card differential, home, pre-match strength, game minute) and projects team stats onto a neutral 'tied, full-strength' baseline via the multiplicative factor e^{-(eta-hat_s - eta-hat_0)}. Data: ESPN minute-by-minute event commentary 2008-2023 (15 seasons), 5 leagues (EPL, La Liga, Bundesliga, Ligue 1, Serie A), about 4.97M minute-team observations; pre-match win probabilities from OddsPortal (Selenium scrape) as strength control; about 70 games excluded for corrupted commentary; data plus R code at github.com/UsDAnDreS/JQAS_LeveragingMinuteByMinute_Soccer_Event_Data_Paper.

Negative Binomial GAM specification: log(Shots) ~ s(Diff.S) + s(Diff.RC) + Home + s(Diff.WP) + s(GM|Half=1) + s(GM|Half=2) + s(Team) + s(season), chosen over Poisson (DHARMa overdispersion/zero-inflation failures), ZIP (BIC plus miscalibration), and Gaussian (KS failures). Adjustment factors: e^{-(eta-hat_s - eta-hat_0)} for score differential s; e^{-(eta-hat_rc - eta-hat_0)} for red-card differential; e^{-gamma-hat} for away-to-home; 95% CIs from GAM Bayesian posterior covariance. No adjustment for win-probability differential (do not penalize strength) or minute (do not penalize timing). Extreme bins: |score|>3 -> +-3, |RC|>2 -> +-2, minute 45+ -> 45; GCV for spline df; team/season random-effect smooths; game-level random effects tested per season and rejected (75 tests); score-by-minute interaction tested season-by-season with Holm correction across 75 tests, significant only a handful of times, so the additive model stands.
equation: log(Shots) ~ s(Diff.S) + s(Diff.RC) + Home + s(Diff.WP) + s(GM|Half=1) + s(GM|Half=2) + s(Team) + s(season); adjustment = e^{-(eta-hat_s - eta-hat_0)}

claim: Game-context multiplicative coefficients: trailing teams' shots x0.70-0.90; leading teams x1.10-1.75; up a man x0.75 (down 1), x0.40-0.70 (up 2+); down a man x1.7-1.9 (down 1), x2-3 (down 2+); Serie A has the steepest score-differential slope ('catenaccio'). Extreme examples: Bordeaux 31 shots -> 13.8 [12.5,15.1]; Bayern 15 -> 31.9 [30.1,33.7]; Real Madrid 40 -> 60.7; PSG 18 corners -> 9.5; Getafe 22 shots/14 corners -> 12.8/8.7. England-France 2022 World Cup: 16 -> 14.35 vs 8 -> 8.15, so the adjustment narrows but does not erase the gap. Season-level: 8 of the 10 strongest positive adjustments were league winners, 8 of the 10 strongest negative were relegated teams.

Context-adjusted stats correlate more with points earned than raw stats: shots 0.787 vs 0.718, corners 0.737 vs 0.603, and significantly beat raw stats in forecasting future score differentials (paired t-test, Holm p<0.01 in all leagues). LOSOCV per-game totals: shots MAE 3.24-3.53 (27-28% of mean), R^2 21-31%; corners MAE 1.9-2.1 (40% of mean), R^2 17-22%. Forecasting RMSE reduction 0.004-0.04 goals per game (1.5-15.2 over 380 games), significant everywhere but, per the authors, of marginal practical magnitude.

The r06 variant of the Terawong & Cliff (2024) deep read adds the deployment protocol: the XGBoost imitation policy is redeployed as a new agent and evaluated on profit against all baselines in two scenarios of 100 races each, beating every baseline in both scenarios including the Privileged agent that runs private forward race simulations, largest p=0.0017 (Privileged vs XGBoost, scenario 2); the simulator uses 110 bettors (ZI, Leader-Wins, Back-The-Favourite, Linear-Extrapolator, Underdog, Privileged RP(1,10,15)) and a 1-D discrete-time stochastic race process with blocking/hurrying.

Caveats from the r06 read of the imitation-learning betting paper: the authors explicitly caution against real-money use because BBE race dynamics are 'convincing' but not calibrated to real races, so profitability inside the ABM transfers to nothing in reality; stakes are fixed throughout and stake sizing is entirely unaddressed; and there is circular-simulator risk since the policy is trained and tested inside the same ABM with no real-data validation.

The r06 variant of the SportsGrounder deep read adds architecture details: the proposal branch uses OV-DINO decoding M=900 queries with domain-guided top-K selection via cross-modality similarity S = F_c(Q_sf) tensor E_t^top, retaining K=15; IGF (Eq. 5): H_vis = [Z-tilde_1^vit concat Z-tilde_1^obj concat ... concat Z-tilde_T^vit concat Z-tilde_T^obj], frame-by-frame interleaving of global features with hybrid entity tokens; AAS maps the final EOS hidden state through a softmax action head (Eq. 6) with a masked cross-entropy loss L_act (Eq. 7) and a task-conditional indicator, L_SFT = L_vqa + lambda.L_act with lambda=0.1; Stage 3 MPO: L_MPO = L_p + alpha.L_q + beta.L_g (Eq. 11), a DPO-style preference loss with margin tau and beta=0.1 (Eq. 12); LoRA SFT for 3 epochs.
equation: S = F_c(Q_sf) tensor E_t^top; H_vis = [Z-tilde_1^vit concat Z-tilde_1^obj concat ... concat Z-tilde_T^vit concat Z-tilde_T^obj]; L_SFT = L_vqa + lambda.L_act, lambda=0.1; L_MPO = L_p + alpha.L_q + beta.L_g

claim: The r06 SportsGrounder read adds: on SoccerNet with bbox-as-text prompt injection MiniCPM-V reaches 49.1 and InternVL3.5 45.2; subtask head-to-heads (SportsGrounder vs best baseline): Action 42.5 vs 41.2, Team 71.2 vs 64.1, Jersey 33.4 vs 37.8 (MiniCPM-V wins), Spatial 54.2 vs 46.8; the hyperparameters lambda=0.1, K=15, tau/beta=0.1 are empirical and not swept; the conference (ACM MM '26) is November 2026, after the read date, so treat as preprint with peer review pending; and fine-grained identity (jersey OCR 33.4% vs 25% chance) remains unsolved even at SOTA.

Sinha, Dyer, Gimpel & Smith (2013, arXiv:1310.6998) test whether Twitter output (team-assigned tweet volume and unigrams, 2010-2012 NFL seasons) can predict game winners, winners-against-the-spread, and over/under outcomes as well as traditional game-stat features, using logistic regression with a strictly online protocol: test week k in [4,16] of 2012, train on 2010-2011 all weeks plus 2012 weeks [1,k-3], tune L1/L2 in {0,1,5,10,25,50,100,250,500,1000} on dev weeks [k-2,k-1]; weeks 1-3 and 17 excluded. Data: Twitter garden-hose (10%) stream 2010-2012 with team assignment via manually-built hashtag lists (multi-team hashtag tweets discarded; Japanese-baseball #giants contamination removed via Unicode script filters); NFLdata.com 2010-2012 regular seasons with bookmaker spreads and totals; 2012 data volumes: weekly tweets 1,014,473 (pregame 266,382 / postgame 290,879), garden-hose about 42M messages/day.

Twitter-volume rate features: rateS(v_old, v_curr, Delta) = sign(v_curr - v_old) . floor(|v_curr - v_old|/Delta), Delta=500 (tuned on 2010-11), output in {-2,-1,0,1,2}; rateP(v_old, v_curr, theta) = sign(v_curr - v_old) . floor(|v_curr - v_old|/(theta . v_old)), theta in {0.1..0.5}, v_old in {v_prev, v_prev_avg}; Twitter unigrams: (home/away, unigram) log(1+frequency), 0.1% occurrence threshold, reduced via CCA (1/2/4/8 components); statistical baselines are 10 feature sets F1-F10 (spread line; O/U line; avg points beaten/missed spread; beaten/missed O/U; avg scored; avg given up; avg total; avg(spread+scored); home/away WTS%; avg INTs/fumbles/sacks) plus all 55 pairwise unions.
equation: rateS(v_old, v_curr, Delta) = sign(v_curr - v_old) . floor(|v_curr - v_old|/Delta), Delta=500; rateP(v_old, v_curr, theta) = sign(v_curr - v_old) . floor(|v_curr - v_old|/(theta . v_old)), theta in {0.1..0.5}

claim: Twitter NFL prediction results (online accuracy): Winner - F1 (spread line) 60.6, F5 (avg points scored) 65.9, union of all F_i 63.0, Twitter unigrams 52.3, rateS 51.0; Winner-against-the-spread - F1 47.6, F4 54.8, union 47.6, unigrams 47.6, CCA(4 components) 51.9, rateS 55.3 (above the 53% profit threshold), rateP theta=0.1 (v_prev) 52.4; Over/under - F1/F2 48.6, Twitter unigrams 54.3 (best single-set O/U number), rateS 52.4; oracle conjunctions (starred): F5+ F9 + rateP(theta=.2) winner 65.9*, F3+F10+rateP(theta=.1) WTS 57.2*, F3+F4+rateS(Delta=200) O/U 58.2*.

Adaptive weekly feature selection on a trailing-2-week window (177 games): winner 63.8%, against-the-spread 52.0% (below profitability), over/under 44.1%; the trailing-2-week selection is unstable (best set changed in 8 of 13 weeks). A postgame-tweet win/loss classifier using a domain lexicon ('win/victory/WIN' vs 'refs/lost/bad') reached 67% average accuracy. The 53%+ against-the-spread accuracy profitability assumption is used throughout, and the rateS hyperparameters tuned on 2010-11 transferred to 2012.

Liu et al. (2026, arXiv:2603.13397v2) introduce TennisVL (a 471.9-hour tennis commentary benchmark over 202 matches) and TennisExpert, a framework combining a video semantic parser (scoreboard OCR, GRU event spotting, RF-DETR detection plus homography) with hierarchical memory (short-term FIFO of K=4 rallies plus deterministic long-term stat consolidation) feeding a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B (SFT 3 epochs, lr 1e-5, cosine schedule, 4x H200 GPUs, BF16, vision encoder and projector frozen) to generate expert-level analytical tennis commentary.

TennisExpert equations: C_t = MLLM(V_t, M_t, H_t) (Eq. 1); short-term memory S_t = {(V_i,M_i,C_i) | i=t-K,..,t-1}, K=4 (Eq. 2); long-term L_t = Phi(L_{t-1}, M_{t-K}), deterministic consolidation; objective log p(C_t|V_t,M_t,H_t) = SUM_j log p_theta(w_j | w_{<j}, Z_v, Z_s) (Eq. 3). Parser: per-rally scoreboard state s_t = (rho_A, rho_B, v); GRU event detector Edit Score 81.2; RF-DETR player/ball detection plus court keypoints plus homography.
equation: C_t = MLLM(V_t, M_t, H_t); S_t = {(V_i,M_i,C_i) | i=t-K,..,t-1}, K=4; L_t = Phi(L_{t-1}, M_{t-K}); log p(C_t|V_t,M_t,H_t) = SUM_j log p_theta(w_j | w_{<j}, Z_v, Z_s)

claim: TennisExpert results: BLEU-4 7.98, METEOR 31.54, ROUGE-L 29.16, CIDEr 43.71, LLM-judged total 88.05 (accuracy 15.79, coherence 19.29, excitement 16.84, professionalism 16.73, pacing 19.40) versus best proprietary zero-shot Gemini-3-Pro 1.78/20.02/17.41/10.11/total 59.89 and GPT-5.2 total 56.59. Ablation (fine-tuned): V_t alone 42.74 total, then V_t+M_t 73.74, then +S_t 85.97, then +S_t+L_t 88.05 (CIDEr 7.86 -> 24.15 -> 41.92 -> 43.71), showing structured metadata and memory contribute the bulk of the gain.

Critical caveat (paper's Section 9): TennisExpert's ground-truth commentary is LLM-synthesized (Gemini 3 Pro), not human-written, so the model learns to imitate an LLM's synthesis; the metric gains partly measure LLM-to-LLM style matching, not expert judgment, and the factual reliability of tactics and stats is unmeasured. Efficiency: about 14k tokens O(1) versus O(T) dense video, about 20 GB VRAM, MLLM inference under 2 s, parser up to 40 FPS on a single GPU.

TennisVL dataset: 202 matches, 471.9 hours of YouTube broadcast video (2019-2025, 1280x720, 25-30 FPS), 40,523 rally clips (average 7.68 s), average commentary 31.42 words, 94 players, 162,503 shots; audio-based rally segmentation (racquet-impact signatures, crowd/announcer-noise augmentation); commentary synthesized by Gemini 3 Pro from WhisperX transcripts plus TennisAbstract shot data plus score context; human review of 2,000 random pairs with >95% acceptance; match-level split 182/35,687 train and 20/4,836 test; code/data at github.com/LZYAndy/TennisExpert.

Katkuri, Kawada, Wachs (2026, arXiv:2608.25350v1) train RL reward models from VLM-generated listwise rankings (K in {3,4,5}) under a Plackett-Luce likelihood for Meta-World robotic manipulation (Sawyer arm; Drawer Open, Door Close, Button Press; 5 seeds, 100,000 env steps per config; VLM = GPT-5.6 Luna); verdict REJECT as a robotics paper with no sports-relevant claim, data, or transfer path.

Plackett-Luce likelihood (Eq. 3): P_psi[sigma^{(1)} > ... > sigma^{(K)}] = product over k of exp(r-hat_psi(sigma^{(k)})) / sum_{j=k..K} exp(r-hat_psi(sigma^{(j)})); segment reward r-hat_psi(sigma) = sum_t r-hat_psi(s_t, a_t); reduces exactly to Bradley-Terry for K=2. Baselines: BT-Kwise (rank-broken into C(K,2) implied pairs), BT-Pairwise (K=2), RL-VLM-F (two-stage VLM analysis, 2M=8 VLM requests), oracle SAC on ground-truth rewards.
equation: P_psi[sigma^{(1)} > ... > sigma^{(K)}] = product_k [ exp(r-hat_psi(sigma^{(k)})) / sum_{j=k..K} exp(r-hat_psi(sigma^{(j)})) ]; r-hat_psi(sigma) = sum_t r-hat_psi(s_t, a_t)

claim: Listwise VLM reward-model results: the best PL config (K=4) achieves 86% mean final success (Drawer Open 86+-3.7, Door Close 48+-19.3, Button Press 41+-18.4), matching the oracle baseline on Drawer Open; either PL or BT-Kwise tops preference-based methods in 2 of 3 environments (Drawer Open: BT-Kwise K=5 89+-7.1; Door Close: PL K=5 54+-13.2; Button Press: BT-Kwise K=4 45+-8.2); no universal advantage by K or formulation; PL significantly beats BT-Kwise only for Button Press at K=5, which the authors call significance 'nominal'; longer rankings introduce VLM reasoning noise.

Torrente et al., Sony AI (2026, arXiv:2607.06989v2) generate ITTF-legal elite table-tennis serves with an 8-DoF robot arm via motion primitives, minimum-jerk MPC, and HEBO Bayesian optimization; verdict REJECT as a robotics motion-planning paper ('impressive, irrelevant') with no predictive model or transferable statistical method; data sources are 1,243 professional-player serves (Apr 2025-Apr 2026, Japanese league, including Paris 2024 silver medalist Miu Hirano) and the elite points-won-while-serving baselines of 52.78% (men) / 53.28% (women) from Gomez et al. 2017.

ACE motion-planning parameterization: Eq. 1 parameter vector xi_s = (u_0, u-dot_0, u-double-dot_0, X_0, tau, p_tau, n_tau, v_tau, tau_f, u_{tau_f}); Eq. 2 minimum-jerk program min_z 1/2 j_z^T j_z + lambda_p eps_p + lambda_n eps_n + lambda_v eps_v subject to joint constraints with tolerances Delta p_tau = 5 mm, Delta phi_tau = 0.5 degrees, Delta v = 0.01 m/s / 0.01 relative, and slack weights lambda_p = 2 m^{-1}, lambda_n = 1, lambda_v = 0.2 (m/s)^{-1}; Eq. 3 serve reward F = r_pos + r_vel + r_top/back + r_side + r_height + s_leg with genome at most 10 dims, population 20, 100 iterations, about 1.5 min per serve.
equation: xi_s = (u_0, u-dot_0, u-double-dot_0, X_0, tau, p_tau, n_tau, v_tau, tau_f, u_{tau_f}); min_z 1/2 j_z^T j_z + lambda_p eps_p + lambda_n eps_n + lambda_v eps_v; Delta p_tau = 5 mm, Delta phi_tau = 0.5 deg, Delta v = 0.01 m/s / 0.01 rel; lambda_p = 2 m^{-1}, lambda_n = 1, lambda_v = 0.2 (m/s)^{-1}; F = r_pos + r_vel + r_top/back + r_side + r_height + s_leg

claim: ACE robot-serve results: robot serve point-win 95% Wilson CI rose from [40.8-55.3]% (Apr 2025) to [51.5-58.7]% (Apr 2026 vs Miu Hirano), comparable to the elite human 52.78%/53.28% serve-point baselines; ace rate 11% (Apr 2025) -> 21% (Mar 2026) -> 20% (Apr 2026); spin up to 550 rad/s and ball speed 6.7 m/s, with robot spin exceeding professional players' from Feb 2026; task-specific generation on real hardware: topspin+velocity 263.4+-70.0 rad/s, 4.4+-1.1 m/s; backspin -131.8+-176.9 rad/s; aiming error 299+-313 mm real (166+-285 sim); sim-to-real gap: only 12-15 of 25 trained serves valid on hardware per task (48-60% transfer).

Lee, Makur, Singh, Purdue (2026, arXiv:2605.23854v1) prove entrywise (l-infinity) error bounds for spectral Bradley-Terry ranking (rank centrality) under a semi-random adversary model, plus an MMWU edge-reweighting scheme that restores Erdos-Renyi-like guarantees on clustered comparison graphs; the NFL schedule is exactly a 'semi-random-like' non-uniform comparison graph (dense intra-division blocks, sparse inter-division edges). Theory only plus synthetic simulations (3-block SBM with block edge-probability matrix P = [[1,1,0],[1,2log n/n,2log n/n],[0,2log n/n,2log n/n]], n in {30,...,135}, 25 repetitions; ER with p = 2log(n)/n); no empirical dataset, no released code.

Spectral ranking error bounds: unweighted Theorem 3.1: ||pi-hat - pi||_inf / ||pi||_inf <= (c_1/gamma + c_2) . sqrt(log(n)/(npk)), w.p. >= 1 - O(n^{-5}), for np >= c_0 log(n), k >= 5. SBM Proposition 3.4: same bound under np >= c_0 log^5(n), q_m <= r.p (assortative SBMs). Weighted Theorem 4.1: ||pi-hat - pi||_inf / ||pi||_inf <= c_1/lambda_{n-1}(L^W) . sqrt(n log(n) p/k) + c_2/lambda_{n-1}(L^W)^2 . sqrt(n^2 log(n) p^2/k) + c_3/lambda_{n-1}(L^W)^3 . sqrt(n^4 log(n) p^3/k). MMWU Theorem 4.2: <= c_1 sqrt(log n/(npk)) + c_2 sqrt(n log n/((np)^3 k)); Corollary 4.3 (np >= c sqrt(n)): ER-optimal <= C sqrt(log n/(npk)). MMWU SDP (Yang et al. 2024, Algorithm 2): 1/2-approximation in near-linear time; monotone coupling (Def. 5.2, Lemma 5.3) shows a semi-random graph contains an ER-like subgraph w.h.p. Key phenomenon: adding edges can reduce the normalized Laplacian's spectral gap (Braess paradox, Eldan et al. 2017), so more data does not equal better spectral ranking.
equation: Thm 3.1: ||pi-hat - pi||_inf / ||pi||_inf <= (c_1/gamma + c_2) . sqrt(log(n)/(npk)); Thm 4.1: ||pi-hat - pi||_inf / ||pi||_inf <= c_1/lambda_{n-1}(L^W) . sqrt(n log(n) p/k) + c_2/lambda_{n-1}(L^W)^2 . sqrt(n^2 log(n) p^2/k) + c_3/lambda_{n-1}(L^W)^3 . sqrt(n^4 log(n) p^3/k); Thm 4.2: <= c_1 sqrt(log n/(npk)) + c_2 sqrt(n log n/((np)^3 k)); Cor 4.3: <= C sqrt(log n/(npk))

claim: SBM simulation results: on the heterogeneous 3-block SBM, MMWU-weighted spectral ranking keeps the spectral gap at about 0.07 while the unweighted gap decays 0.03 -> 0.01 as n grows; weighted l-infinity error about 0.46 vs unweighted about 0.48 at n=135; the weight heatmap shows the dense block downweighted and the sparse block upweighted, i.e., reweighting normalizes degrees. On ER graphs there is no significant difference (error about 0.4-0.415 for both), so reweighting is harmless but unnecessary. Simulation 1 deliberately violates the theory's own assumptions (p=0 allowed) yet reweighting still works empirically. Stated assumptions: score dynamic range bounded by constant h; uniform base probability p > 0 (adversary can only boost); k comparisons per pair uniform; spectral gap lower bounded by constant gamma w.h.p. (unweighted); weighted graph must be connected.

Asztalos, Balazs, Palla, Vicsek (2026, arXiv:2508.19848v1) measure hierarchy (flow hierarchy, global reaching centrality from 2-reach, random-walk hierarchy) and 3-cycle structure in tennis/fencing pairwise-contest networks, and compare network-based prediction scores against Elo and official rankings. Data: men's/women's tennis 1968-2024 (194,996 men's matches, 158,092 women's, Jeff Sackmann public data; Grand Slams, tour events, Davis Cup); fencing foil/epee/sabre x men/women 2015-2024 (43,571-73,068 bouts per category). Prediction: five scores per player (2RC, RWC, SFS official ranking, recomputed Elo, reversed PageRank) mapped to win probabilities via a fitted score-difference function, fit on trailing years, predicting the next year; metrics are fraction of mistakes (FM; 0.5 = random), average squared error (SE; 0.25 = random), average linear error (LE), with p=0.5 counted as half a mistake.

Men's tennis prediction (Table 4): FM - ELO 0.344 (best), 2RC 0.345, RPR 0.345, SFS 0.356, RWC 0.450; SE - ELO 0.213 (best), RPR 0.217, 2RC 0.219, SFS 0.224, RWC 0.245; women's tennis FM: 2RC 0.347, ELO comparable; fencing: the official ranking (SFS) beats Elo on the most accurate measures. Structural: real networks show large hierarchy gaps versus Erdos-Renyi nulls for all three measures; versus the configuration model, flow hierarchy and random-walk hierarchy are higher and global reaching centrality is mixed. Format effect: elimination (single-elim/DE phase) networks have lower hierarchy and more 3-cycles than round-robin/pool-phase networks, so elimination formats produce more circular win-loss patterns. Caveats: the recomputed Elo is not real Elo (elite-only subset), which flatters the network measures; yearly snapshots ignore within-year form; NFL yearly win graphs are extremely sparse (about 256 edges on 32 nodes), so hierarchy measures would be noise-dominated.

Cycle-enrichment diagnostic: 3-cycle density (cycles divided by all node triads) and the cycle-versus-feedforward-loop ratio, with cycle enrichment defined as observed 3-cycles versus expected 3-cycles under resampled outcomes from a given ranking score's implied win probabilities.

Zhang & Naidu (2024, arXiv:2403.04873) introduce SIDO, a hierarchical-Bayesian player-attribution framework for League of Legends that decomposes a player's gold/damage impact into own, ally, and enemy effects, validated with the discrimination/independence/stability metric-quality discipline (Franks et al. 2016). Data: Riot API solo-queue games from top-1000 accounts (Grandmaster/Challenger) on NA/KR/EUW, patches 13.14-13.18 (July 18-Sep 27, 2023); filters: at least 50 games per role per account, champions played by at least 30 accounts, disconnects removed (<500 damage by 7 min); pro labels from players on top-level NA/EU/KR/CN pro teams.

SIDO model algebra: player model (Eq. 1): gold_pg = beta_0 + b_c + b_p + eps_pg (b_p = skill metric); damage model (Eq. 2): dmg_pg = beta_0 + beta_dmgt x_pg + b_c + b_p + eps_pg (x_pg = damage taken, controlling aggression); ally models (Eq. 3): residualize each ally via re-fit player models (AXE approximation), sum residuals Delta = SUM_a(Y_ag - E[Y_ag]), then Delta = beta_0 + b_c + b_p + eps_g; enemy models: same procedure on enemies, metric = -b_p. Priors: beta_0 ~ N(0,1); b_c ~ t_3(0,phi), b_p ~ t_3(0,tau); phi,tau ~ HalfC(0.5); sigma ~ HalfC(0.3) (t_3 for outlier-robust random effects, half-Cauchy scales). Champion proficiency heuristic (Eq. 4): delta_pc = (1/n_pc) SUM_{g in G_pc}(Y_pg - beta-hat_0 + b-hat_c), centered/scaled. Meta-metrics (Franks et al. 2016): discrimination (fraction of between-player variance not due to sampling noise), independence (fraction of variance uncorrelated with other metrics, via Gaussian copula), stability (concordance index of pairwise orderings across time windows).
equation: gold_pg = beta_0 + b_c + b_p + eps_pg; dmg_pg = beta_0 + beta_dmgt x_pg + b_c + b_p + eps_pg; Delta = SUM_a(Y_ag - E[Y_ag]); Delta = beta_0 + b_c + b_p + eps_g; enemy metric = -b_p; beta_0 ~ N(0,1); b_c ~ t_3(0,phi); b_p ~ t_3(0,tau); phi,tau ~ HalfC(0.5); sigma ~ HalfC(0.3); delta_pc = (1/n_pc) SUM_{g in G_pc}(Y_pg - beta-hat_0 + b-hat_c)

claim: SIDO results: SIDO separates pros from non-pros across all roles (most FDR-significant in the 0-7 and 7-15 min windows); basic averages show smaller, less consistent differences; Plus-Minus shows small inconsistent differences, often scoring pros below average. Gold differential predicts winners: 69% (0-7 min), 79% (7-15), 83% (15-25); damage: 63%, 73%, 72%. The SIDO player model has lower RMSE than basic-average on held-out patches 13.10/13.11 despite lower discrimination, so shrinkage trades discrimination for accuracy. Meta-metrics: discrimination (Top EUW 0-7 min gold) - player SIDO 0.77/BA 0.87, ally SIDO 0.30/Plus-Minus 0.00, enemy SIDO 0.46/Plus-Minus 0.01; independence - Plus-Minus ~0.98-1.00, BA ~0.06-0.09, SIDO ~0.48-0.68; stability (concordance) - gold player SIDO 0.53-0.75, ally/enemy SIDO 0.47-0.65. The authors' honesty rule: with low ally/enemy discrimination, use 5-category bucketing (high/low positive, neutral, low/high negative) instead of continuous scores. Role insights: support pros differentiate via enemy damage prevented; jungle pros' biggest edge is enemy gold prevented in 7-15 min (LCK 0.17, LEC 0.12); bot-lane pro edge about 2:1 technical-vs-teamplay, jungle about 1:2, others about 1:1.

Zanco, Szczecinski, Kuhn, Seara (2022/2023, arXiv:2212.12015v2) treat the Elo update as stochastic gradient descent on a logistic loss and derive, via adaptive-filter theory, closed-form skill-evolution, mean-square-deviation, and loss trajectories plus principled design rules for the step size beta; validated on 10 seasons of real league data (Italian volleyball SuperLega 2009/10-2018/19, pandemic seasons excluded, M=12-15 teams, K=132-210 games per season, regular season only; estimated HFA eta-hat 0.06-0.77 and skill spread v-hat 1.2-3.7 per season).

Elo-as-SGD: theta_{k+1} = theta_k + beta[y_k - sigma(x_k^T theta_k + eta)]x_k (Eq. 9), on the Bradley-Terry model Pr{y_k=1|theta} = sigma(x_k^T theta + eta). Mean skill (Eq. 33): E[theta_{k,m}] = (1 - alpha1^k)theta*_m, alpha1 = 1 - 2beta h-bar/(M-1); time constant tau1 ~= (M-1)/(2beta h-bar) (Eq. 59). MSD (Eq. 48): d-bar_k = alpha2^k(d-bar_0 - d-bar_inf) + d-bar_inf, alpha2 = 1 - 4beta(h-bar - beta h-bar^2)/(M-1) (Eq. 47), d-bar_inf = beta h-bar(M-1)/[2(h-bar - beta h-bar^2)] (Eq. 50); tau2 ~= (M-1)/[4beta(h-bar - beta h-bar^2)] (Eq. 60). Bias-variance split (Eqs. 52-53): b-bar_k = alpha1^{2k} d-bar_0, omega-bar_k = (alpha2^k - alpha1^{2k})d-bar_0 + (1 - alpha2^k)d-bar_inf. Loss: l-bar_k ~= l-bar_min + l-bar_ex,k, l-bar_ex,k = h-bar d-bar_k/(M-1) (Eqs. 55-57); v_th = 2ln2 ~= 1.4 separates high/low skill-spread regimes (Eq. 62). Laplace approximation: h-bar = 1/4(v+1)^{-1/2}exp(-eta^2/[4(v+1)]) (Eq. 30).

claim: Improvement-over-initialization bound (Eqs. 67-69): 0 < beta < [(1-1/M)/(2v) + h-bar^2/h-bar]^{-1}, with rule of thumb beta < 2v. Optimal step size (Eq. 71): beta_{o,k} ~= 1/2[(1-1/M)/(2v) + h-bar^2/h-bar + 2h-bar^2(k-1)/(M-1)]^{-1}; for small v, beta_{o,k} ~= v. Step sizes tested: beta=0.1 (FIFA/FIDE range), beta=0.87 (optimal via Eq. 71 at k=K/4, averaged over seasons), beta=2.49 (improvement-bound threshold via Eq. 67).
equation: 0 < beta < [(1-1/M)/(2v) + h-bar^2/h-bar]^{-1}; beta < 2v (rule of thumb); beta_{o,k} ~= 1/2[(1-1/M)/(2v) + h-bar^2/h-bar + 2h-bar^2(k-1)/(M-1)]^{-1}; for small v, beta_{o,k} ~= v

claim: Elo SGD results: with v-hat about 1.2-3.7 the optimal beta_{o,k} is about 0.93-1.09 in natural-logistic units; dividing by s' = 400/ln10 ~= 173.7 gives K_opt about 160-190 Elo points, much larger than the FIFA/FIDE range, which under-converges within a season. Theory matches simulated MSD/loss in transient and steady state across all tested beta values (Fig. 6); beta=0.87 (optimal) converges within the season while beta=0.1 (FIFA/FIDE scale) does not. End-of-season MSD/loss versus beta (Fig. 7): the model tracks experiment over beta in (0.01, 4); beta beyond the improvement bound inflates MSD and loss sharply, so such values should not be used. Per-season per-team skill trajectories follow the theory's mean curve (Fig. 8); per-season beta_{o,k} in {0.939, 0.998, 0.93, 1.09} for the four displayed seasons.

Yan et al. (2022, arXiv:2201.04480v2) cast top-player identification as a dueling-bandits problem: MaxIn-Elo / MaxIn-mElo maintain a UCB candidate set and always schedule the maximum-uncertainty pair, replacing per-round MLE refits with online batch SGD (constant time and memory in T) while keeping an O-tilde(sqrt(T)) regret bound. Data: twelve real-world games from Czarnecki et al. (2020), mostly OpenSpiel - transitive (Transitive game, Triangular game, Elo game plus noise 0.01/0.05/0.1; 100 policies, top SSCC size 1) and intransitive (Kuhn-poker 64 policies/SSCC 64, AlphaStar 100/SSCC 1, tic_tac_toe 100/SSCC 2, hex 3x3 100/SSCC 2, Blotto 100/SSCC 99, 5,3-Blotto 21/SSCC 18), plus a 4x4 '2 Good, 2 Bad' game for the alpha-IG comparison; code at github.com/yanxue7/MaxIn-Elo.git.

MaxIn-Elo equations: Elo model (Eq. 2): p-hat_xy = sigma(r_x - r_y), sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x}); Elo cross-entropy loss (Eq. 3); standard SGD Elo update (Eq. 4): r_x^{t+1} <- r_x^t + eta(o_{xy}^t - p-hat_{xy}^t). Cumulative regret (Eq. 5): R(T) = SUM_{t=1}^T [r*_{x*} - 1/2(r*_{x_t} + r*_{y_t})]. Batch projected SGD (Eq. 8): r-tilde_j <- Pi_C(r-tilde_{j-1} - eta_j grad_r l_{j,tau}(r-tilde_{j-1})), eta_j = 1/(alpha j), r-bar = (1/j) SUM r-tilde_q. UCB pair score (Eq. 9): h(x_t,y_t) = r-bar_{x_t} - r-bar_{y_t} + gamma ||e_{x_t} - e_{y_t}||_{V_t^{-1}}; candidate set (Eq. 10): S = {x | h(x,y) > 0, for all y != x}; max-uncertainty selection (Eq. 11): (x_t,y_t) = argmax_{(x,y) in S x S} ||e_x - e_y||_{V_t^{-1}}. mElo prediction (Eq. 12): p-hat_xy = sigma(r_x - r_y + c_x^T Omega_{2k x 2k} c_y); mElo SGD updates (Eqs. 18-20); mElo UCB score (Eq. 13). Regret bound (Theorem 1): R(T) <= tau Delta_max + (2+tau)g_1(T) sqrt(2nT log((2tau+T)/n)) + 4g_2(J) sqrt(tau T), w.p. >= 1-10/T; R(T) ~ O-tilde(sqrt(T)). Complexity (Table 1): MaxIn-Elo O(n^2 T) time, O(n^2) memory vs MaxInP O(nT^2+n^2 T) time, O(nT) memory, so memory is constant in T.
