Cavus & Biecek (2022, arXiv:2206.07212v2) explain xG via aggregated ceteris-paribus profiles: classifier f: X -> Y minimizing L(f) = P[Y != f(X)]; aggregated profile g_AP^j(z) = E_X^{-j}[f(X^{j|z})] with estimator g_hat_AP^j(z) = (1/k) sum_i f(x_i^{j|z}); xG_{player/team} = sum_i f(X_i).

The xG paper's engineered features: distance to goal X_i^{DTG} = sqrt([105 - (L_i x 105)]^2 + [34 - (W_i x 68)]^2) and angle to goal X_i^{ATG} = |a_i/b_i x 180/pi| with a_i = arctan[7.32 x [105-(L_i x 105)]] and b_i = [105-(L_i x 105)]^2 + [34-(W_i x 68)]^2 - (7.32/2)^2.

Cautionary finding from the paper's own numbers: the ORIGINAL-data random forest had better Brier (0.051) and log-loss (0.173) than the 'winning' ROSE over-sampled model (0.071, 0.270) - the headline metrics (recall 0.958, AUC 0.985, F1 0.940) were inflated by evaluating on over-sampled test data; verdict: permanently reject ROSE-style over-sampling for GSE probability models, since resampling changes model behavior (PDP curves for distance-to-goal differed across sampling treatments), not just class balance.

Schalke 04 vs Bayern Munich (2021-01-24): Schalke 0 goals on xG 2.67 (13 shots, mean angle 25.23 deg, mean distance 17.99m); Bayern 4 goals on xG 9.59 (31 shots, 27.79 deg, 16.96m); AP what-ifs: Schalke reducing mean shot distance 18m->15m raises per-shot xG ~40%, mean angle 25 deg->35 deg raises per-shot xG ~20%.

The paper's dataset: 315,430 shots (33,656 goals, ~10.66%) from 12,655 matches across 7 seasons (2014-15 to 2020-21) of the top-five European leagues; league conversions: Bundesliga 11.2% (55,129 shots), EPL 10.4% (66,605), La Liga 11.0% (62,028), Ligue 1 10.5% (61,053), Serie A 10.3% (70,615).

Sakaori & Abe (2026, arXiv:2609.12468v1) build a fully Bayesian Generalized Poisson matrix factorization with closed-form Gibbs updates: the GP pmf is p(y) = eta(eta+xi*y)^{y-1} exp(-(eta+xi*y))/y! restricted to 0<xi<1 (overdispersion only); mean/variance E[y_ij]=s_ij with V = s_ij(1+theta_i)^2 (theta-param) or s_ij/(1-xi_i)^2 (xi-param); priors w_ik, h_jk ~ Gamma and xi_i ~ EBeta(alpha_xi,beta_xi,gamma_xi).

The EBeta (exponentially tilted beta = Esscher transform of beta) pdf is p(xi) = xi^{alpha-1}(1-xi)^{beta-1}exp(-gamma*xi) / [B(alpha,beta)*1F1(alpha;alpha+beta;-gamma)]; its novel infinite-mixture representation (mixture of Beta(alpha, beta+m) for gamma>=0 or Beta(alpha+m, beta) for gamma<0) has recursive weights w_{m+1} = (beta+m)gamma/((alpha+beta+m)(m+1))*w_m, truncated at M=200 with machine-precision accuracy even at gamma=100 - cheaper than SIR (4706s vs 6202s on an M5 MacBook).

Bayesian GPMF beats GPMF-MLE on MSE in all simulation settings with gains growing in dispersion (at xi=2/3: W-MSE 84.1 vs 251 random-init / 335 NNDSVD; S-MSE 2.66 vs 7.61); 95% credible-interval coverage is near nominal (S ~ 0.954-0.966, xi ~ 0.934-0.953); the EPL gegenpressing application is qualitative only (Factor 1 = league-wide pressing baseline; Factors 2-3 = team tactical signatures peaking at matchweeks 20/25/28/29; xi largest for Watford/Swansea/Chelsea/Spurs, smallest for Leicester). Ledger verdict: REJECT for GSE adoption - no prediction mechanism, no sports-forecasting result.

Pipping-Gamon & Wyner (2026, arXiv:2601.18774v4): model the live win-probability sequence as the Doob martingale p_k = P(Y=1 | F_k) bounded in [0,1] with p_0 = P(Y=1) and p_N = Y in {0,1}; path maximum M_N = max_{0<=k<=N} p_k. Discrete-time unconditional: F_{M_N}(x) >= 1 - p_0/x for x in [p_0, 1), F_{M_N}(x) = 0 for x < p_0, with atom P(M_N = 1) = p_0.
equation: F_{M_N}(x) ≥ 1 − p_0/x  for x ∈ [p_0, 1); atom P(M_N = 1) = p_0

claim: Conditional law (given eventual loss): F_{M_N|Y=0}(x) >= 1 - (p_0/(1-p_0))*((1-x)/x) for x in [p_0, 1); the continuous-path versions are exact identities. Two-player eventual-loser maximum (p_0 >= 1/2): F_{M_lambda}(x) = 1 - (1-p_0)/x on [1-p_0, p_0), 2 - 1/x on [p_0, 1); symmetric case p_0 = 1/2: P(M_lambda >= 2/3) = 1/2 - half of all evenly matched games see the eventual loser reach >= 67% win probability.

Applied to ESPN's 78.4% peak WP for the Eagles in Super Bowl LVII: F_{M_lambda}(0.784) = 2 - 1/0.784 ~ 0.7245, so P(M_lambda >= 0.784) ~ 0.2755 - mildly unusual but far from extraordinary under correct calibration, refuting the naive 'collapse' framing; the diagnostic's feature is that misspecification of the WP model shows up as empirical deviation from these exact laws.

Trading diagnostic (eq 9): M_loss on losing trades obeys the conditional law - at p_0 = 1/2, P(M_loss >= 2/3 | Y = 0) = 1/2; limitations: NFL WP updates are coarse (a pick-six can move WP 30+ points, loosening discrete-time bounds), ~1% NFL ties are unhandled (binary outcomes only), and small p_0 error propagates through the kink at x = p_0.

Dominitz & Manski (2025, arXiv:2403.11016v3) argue ML's K-fold/Common-Task out-of-sample evaluation should be replaced by Wald's statistical decision theory: evaluate the pick rule ex ante as a statistical decision function by minimax regret across a state space S of (training-population, prediction-population) pairs.

Decision criteria: Bayes risk min_c integral L(c,s) d pi (eq. 1); minimax min_c max_s L(c,s) (eq. 2); minimax regret (MMR) min_c max_s [L(c,s) - min_d L(d,s)] (eq. 3); statistical versions use sample data psi ~ Q_s over feasible SDFs Gamma, e.g. MMR min_{c(.)} max_s (E_s{L[c(psi),s]} - min_d L(d,s)) (eq. 6).

Binary-choice regret decomposes (Appendix A, eqs. A1-A6) as expected regret = error probability x loss magnitude: for MSE, regret = V_s[p(psi)] + {E_s(y)-E_s[p(psi)]}^2; for MCR, regret = P(misclassify) - min[P_s(y=1), 1-P_s(y=1)]; with cross-covariate restriction P_s(y=1|x') + lambda-(x,x') <= P_s(y=1|x) <= P_s(y=1|x') + lambda+(x,x') for all s in S (eq. 9).

Clinical illustration: threshold px# = [U_x(A,0)-U_x(B,0)] / ([U_x(A,0)-U_x(B,0)] + [U_x(B,1)-U_x(A,1)]) (eq. 13); neutralized-disease special case px# = 1-U_xB (eq. 17); and the cautionary quantitative fact that Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani (2024) found naive 90%-coverage CIs for prediction error actually miscover 31%, needing ~1.6x widening - CV-based uncertainty quantification is unreliable.

Cautions from the authors themselves: optimizing over SDFs Gamma has 'no generally applicable approach' and high-dimensional ML settings are 'not currently computationally tractable'; maximum regret is only as credible as the analyst-specified state space S; MMR optimizes for the worst state, potentially sacrificing gains in likely states (Savage's critique of minimax); in betting, utility (bankroll growth, risk tolerance) is chosen, not known; and NFL seasons are not i.i.d. draws (schedule structure, rule changes, evolving meta).

Xenopoulos, Coelho & Silva (2021, arXiv:2109.12990v1) value Counter-Strike team 'buy' decisions by counterfactual win-probability deltas (optimal vs actual choice): game-level WP models (multiclass CT win / T win / draw from round-start state) - logistic regression baseline, Hyperopt-tuned XGBoost, and a 2-layer ReLU neural network with dropout and softmax - trained per-map and with one-hot-encoded map features, early stopping patience 10.

Weighted log-loss on the buy-decision task (Table 2, exact): logistic regression 0.793, XGBoost 0.739, neural network 0.736, OHE-map XGBoost 0.730 (winner), OHE-map NN 0.732; the OSE metric is printed as OSE_T = sum_r (W_{T,r} - O_{T,r})^2 (Eq. 2) though the prose describes it as a mean-squared error - a formula/prose mismatch noted by the reader.

Observed round win rates by buy type: Eco 3%, Low Buy 27%, Half Buy 34%, Hero Low Buy 25%, Hero Half Buy 48%, Full Buy 59%; CT eco rounds: the predicted-optimal buy was low/half buy in over 90% of cases, with ~3% average lost win probability per suboptimal eco; second round after losing the pistol: actual T buys 27%/10%/63% eco/low/half vs optimal 0%/0%/100%, actual CT buys 6%/3%/91% vs optimal 4%/0%/96%.

Team decision quality: OSE correlates with round win rate at r = -0.45 (better decisions -> more wins); the held-out-map experiment showed more-data (fine-tuned) models matched or beat prior per-map models on 6 of 7 maps; limitations: counterfactual substitution into an associational WP model is not a causal estimate - the 'optimal' buy may just be the buy good teams choose.

The NFL adaptation spec: restrict counterfactual substitution to game states with overlap (only evaluate decisions where both actual and candidate choices are observed with adequate support - propensity-trimmed); decision types are 4th-down go/kick, 2-point conversions, timeout usage, challenges; aggregate to team-season Decision Quality Error (DQE, the OSE analog - defined explicitly as a mean, fixing the sum/mean ambiguity); adopt only if cross-season stability r >= 0.3 and it adds Delta R^2 >= 0.02 to next-season wins over the EPA/luck baseline.

Manski (2019, arXiv:1909.06853v1) is the superseded draft of the paper fully read as ledger 0477 (arXiv:1912.08726v4, Feb 2021); ledger verdict: REJECT as a separate adaptation target - its unique findings are folded into 0477's experiments.

ES-rule max-regret bounds (Manski & Tetenov 2016, Props. 1-2), K arms, outcome range M, n/arm balanced: (10) (2e)^(-1/2) M (K-1) n^(-1/2) - tighter for K=2,3 treatments; (11) M (ln K)^(1/2) n^(-1/2) - tighter for K>=4; worked numerical comparison (N=145 per arm): ES rule max regret 0.01 vs one-sided z-test 0.05, with ES regret peaking at effect size ~+-0.03 (error prob ~0.35) and z-test regret peaking at effect size ~0.08 (error prob ~0.6).
equation: (10) (2e)^{−½}M(K−1)n^{−½}  (tighter for K=2,3); (11) M(ln K)^{½}n^{−½}  (tighter for K≥4)

claim: Midpoint predictor max regret: 1/4[P(delta=1)^2/N + P(delta=0)^2] (STATA program wald_mse, Manski & Tabord-Meehan 2017); and the curious finite-sample result (Prop. 2): under its assumptions there is no MMR advantage to large sample size - one observation per treatment is as good as the full sample, though the reader flags this as resting on the artificial setting where p is known.

Cancer treatment-choice illustration: conventional test (Type I error 0.05, Type II 0.20) gives Type I regret 1/30 yr, Type II regret 4/5 yr, max regret 4/5 yr; reversed test (0.20, 0.05) gives regrets 2/15 and 1/5 yr, max regret 1/5 yr - the unconventional test has 4x smaller max regret (reader flags: artifact of the extreme 1/3-vs-5-year asymmetry in a stylized two-point state space).

Sim2Win (Zemzoumi & Abouaomar 2026): CatBoost trained on rolling 5-match shifted team behavioral profiles (no team names or Elo) reached 60.90% accuracy / 0.9289 log loss / 0.7268 AUC on soccer pre-match home-draw-away prediction holdout (1,411 team-match rows, 178 teams, 11 competitions, StatsBomb open event data).

Sim2Win rolling tactical profile definition with no-leakage shift: profiles are computed as the mean of the previous k=5 matches shifted one match back, and the matchup vector concatenates home and away profiles.

Sim2Win ablation: window length 5 is the key choice — window 3 cost −4.11% accuracy, window 7 cost −3.93%; removing xG volatility cost −1.66%; raw unshifted per-match features added +7.10% accuracy but are pure leakage, reported only as a diagnostic upper bound.

Sim2Win LOCO (Leave-One-Competition-Out, 7 folds): mean AUC 0.704 vs ELO 0.567, Pi-Rating 0.551, GAP 0.548 — 21/21 AUC wins and 19/21 accuracy wins; draw prediction is a structural failure (Draw F1 = 0.238 on holdout; best mitigation XGBoost + class weights reaches 0.400 at a cost of accuracy).
Sim2Win engineered ratios: Pressing Efficiency PE = ball recoveries/(pressures+ε); Shot Quality SQ = xG/(shots+ε); Directness D = passes/(possession events+ε); Chaos C = fouls + 3·yellows + 5·reds.
equation: PE = ball recoveries/(pressures+ε); SQ = xG/(shots+ε); D = passes/(possession events+ε); C = fouls + 3·yellows + 5·reds

claim: DIAMOND baseball highlight selector (Kang et al. 2026) defines Win Expectancy WE(s) = W_s/N_s, Win Probability Added WPA = WE_after − WE_before, and Leverage Index LI = |WE_after − WE_before| / Avg(|WE_after − WE_before|).
equation: WE(s) = W_s/N_s; WPA = WE_after − WE_before; LI = |WE_after − WE_before| / Avg(|WE_after − WE_before|)

claim: DIAMOND (n=5 KBO games): full pipeline P 0.748 / R 0.846 / F1 0.793 vs WPA-only 0.635/0.716/0.673; Preparation+Decision stages contribute +9.2pp F1 over WPA-only, Reflection adds +2.8pp; expert preference 66.6% = 2 of 3 curators, all TVING employees (conflict of interest unaddressed).

CLVision CVPR-2023 continual-learning challenge (Hayes et al. 2024): under class-incremental streams WITH repetition, ensemble-of-frozen-experts dominated replay methods (winner HAT-CIR 62.75% vs ER-2000 21.91% vs joint upper bound 65.12%); when repetition was removed the strategy ranking inverted (ER-2000 25.35% beat all finalists).

DWGRNet ensemble logit: the ensemble logit for class k is the maximum over branches of (branch logit divided by branch entropy, times the number of classes that branch saw, times the branch feature norm).
equation: ensemble_logit_k = max_{i ∈ M} (logit_{i,k} / entropy_{i,k} · N_C^{(i)} · feature_norm_{i,k})

claim: FLAT (Zhu et al. 2023) dataset embedding: permutation-invariant over rows AND columns via nested meta-encoding means passed through learned maps.
FLAT column embedding for column j is the mean over meta examples of the learned row-column encoding passed through map g.

FLAT results (118 UCI datasets): medical 29 datasets at N^meta=3 — FLAT 66.54±0.11 vs Iwata 65.82±0.60, KNN 64.99±0.27, CatBoost 62.86±0.28; FLATadapt adds +0.5–2.33pp via few inference-time gradient steps; inference 0.45s vs FT-Transformer 40.61s; limitation: classification only, O((N^col)²) GAT cost.

FLAT Graph Attention Network attention weights and target prediction: attention from LeakyReLU-scoring of concatenated projected node pairs, node update as attention-weighted neighbor sum, prediction as softmax over a projected mean of final-layer node embeddings.
equation: α_jk = exp(LReLU(a^{l⊤}[W^l h^l_j || W^l h^l_k])) / Σ_r exp(LReLU(a^{l⊤}[W^l h^l_r || W^l h^l_k])); h^{l+1}_j = Σ_k α_jk W^l h^l_k; p(ŷ^target) = softmax(W^L((1/N^col)Σ_j h^{L-1}_j))

claim: Decision Transformer (Chen et al. 2021): returns-to-go R̂_t = Σ_{t′=t}^{T} r_{t′}; trajectory modeled as the sequence τ = (R̂_1, s_1, a_1, R̂_2, s_2, a_2, …, R̂_T, s_T, a_T); at inference, seed with a target return and decrement R̂_{t+1} ← R̂_t − r_t after each executed action.

Decision Transformer results: Key-to-Door with 1K random trajectories — DT 71.8% vs CQL 13.1%, BC 1.4%; desired target returns and observed returns are highly correlated (near-perfect match on Pong/HalfCheetah/Walker); on Seaquest DT extrapolates beyond the dataset's max episode return when prompted higher; K=1 context significantly worse than K=30.
Optimal stopping as deep RL (Fathan & Delage): risk-neutral GBM discretization S_t = S_{t−1} e^{(r−σ²/2)Δt + σ√Δt ε} with ε∼N(0,1); state = price history/time-to-maturity, actions = {exercise, wait}.
equation: S_t = S_{t−1} e^{(r−σ²/2)Δt + σ√Δt ε}, ε∼N(0,1)

claim: Fathan & Delage optimal stopping: distributional RL (C51/IQN) beat DDQN on real S&P 500 paths (111 stocks, 2014–2019); test set — best IQN achieved 2.91% relative option payout vs 2.17% exercising on the last day and 2.53% binomial tree; C51 achieved 22.0% average return, 8% higher than any classical benchmark; prioritized replay/dueling degraded IQN/C51 and were omitted.

Genie (DeepMind, Bruce et al. 2024): three-component generative model (spatiotemporal video tokenizer + unsupervised Latent Action Model + MaskGIT dynamics) scaled from 40M to 2.7B parameters and to a final 11B-parameter model trained on 200,000+ hours of Internet gameplay video filtered to 30,000 hours.

Genie Latent Action Model: encoder q(ã_{1:t} | x_{1:t}, x_{t+1}) infers latent actions from consecutive frames; decoder p(x̂_{t+1} | x_{1:t}, ã_{1:t}) exists ONLY for the training signal and is discarded at inference; VQ-VAE objective limits actions to a small discrete codebook |A|=8.

Dual-likelihood confidence regions for total causal effects (Strieder & Drton 2024): linear SCM X = BX + ε with ε ~ N(0, σ²I) — equal error variances are the identifiability restriction; dual LR test statistic equals the classical LR statistic for a modified problem and has a closed-form solution; simulations achieve desired 95% coverage in all settings including low sample sizes, with regions essentially as tight as expensive LRT-inversion.

FastBO (Jiang & Mian 2024): per-configuration adaptive fidelity — efficient point e_i = min{ r | C_i(r) − C_i(2r) < δ_1 } (doubling resources past this point yields < δ_1 improvement); saturation point s_i = min{ r | ∀ r′>r, |C_i(r′)−C_i(r)| < δ_2 } (performance plateaus); claims any single-fidelity method extends to multi-fidelity — but the source is an extended abstract with qualitative claims only, no numbers.
equation: e_i = min{ r | C_i(r) − C_i(2r) < δ_1 }; s_i = min{ r | ∀ r′>r, |C_i(r′)−C_i(r)| < δ_2 }

claim: Core-set active learning (Sener & Savarese 2018, ICLR 2018): redefines batch AL as core-set selection; minimizing the covering-radius loss bound is equivalent to k-center minimax facility location, and greedy furthest-first gives a 2-OPT solution; robust variant is a MIP feasibility program with outlier allowance Ξ = 1e-4 × n.

Core-set Theorem 1 bound: core-set loss ≤ δ(λ^l + λ^ηLC) + √(L²log(1/γ)/(2n)) with probability ≥ 1−γ; outperformed all baselines on CIFAR-10/100/SVHN; k-Medoids is ineffective because cluster centers sample already-well-covered points rather than tails; oracle uncertainty and DBAL beat empirical uncertainty, but random still beat them in the batch setting due to correlated queried labels.

Data-lakehouse architecture paper (Mazumdar, Hughes & Onofré 2023, three Dremio employees): maps every traditional RDBMS-OLAP warehousing requirement to lakehouse components (object storage + Parquet/ORC + Iceberg/Hudi/Delta table format + catalog + decoupled compute); argues the lakehouse satisfies warehousing and adds time travel, ACID via optimistic concurrency, schema evolution without rewrites, and data-as-code branching; zero quantitative results anywhere in the paper.

What-went-wrong data lakes (Gahi 2026): operational swamp defined as 3+ of 6 measurable indicators (>50% assets without ownership, metadata completeness <40%, >40% datasets unused in 90 days, untraceable lineage, duplicates >20%, no automated ingestion quality validation); cites convergent failure signals: Gartner 60–85% big-data project failure, NewVantage 2020 (98.8% of Fortune 1000 investing, only 37.8% data-driven), VentureBeat 87% of data-science projects never reach production.

2026-06-24 GSE session handoff: first real-data out-of-sample backtest of the GSE player-projection engine vs naive points-persistence — 2023 model MAE 4.9928 vs naive 4.7573 (n=2,955); 2021–2023 boosted-log1p 5.1802 vs naive 4.9999 (n=10,301); genuine Tweedie loss improved 4.99 → 4.87 without flipping the result; honest verdict — canPublishProjections stays off, everything stays shadow.

2026-09-18 WIRE-40 stat-intake audit: 40 external inputs live-verified — 1 cleared, 14 cleared-with-attribution, 25 use-with-caution; every use-with-caution source defaults OFF behind an env flag; pbp_participation and ftn_charting on RIGHTS-HOLD (CC-BY-SA-4.0); NGS and PFR advstats are persisted as systems of record but not yet scoring inputs; genuine breadth gaps are college football data and Big Data Bowl tracking.

ADR-009 randomized publication protocol (2026-08-14): daily board-day-level randomized experiment (candidate board vs de-vigged market-mirror baseline), baseline-slate rate ε = 0.15 (~85% of days candidate board), π_t = 0.85 → Hoeffding width w = B/(π(1−π)) ≈ 7.84B; coin = committed-seed HMAC-SHA256(seed, 'publication-coin:v1:' + date) with monthly epochs; e-processes for value (plug-in λ capped 1/(4B)) and shift (Beta(1,1) per-arm-per-stratum); rollout is shadow-first with both slates logged.

Jarvis Agent Council spec (2026-06-12): 23 governed agent seats across 6 departments (6 registered draft-only, 3 manual, 14 designed-but-not-wired) with authority tiers 0–4 (default 0/1 unless wired and approved); AUDIT (performance & calibration auditor) must stay independent of pick/metric producers; acceptance criterion: no simulated/not-wired capability presented as real.

API v1 disposable-rehearsal packet: deliberately non-executable owner-review packet (all 8 command intents executableNow=false, livePromotionAllowed=false); forbidden targets include production database, shared staging database, raw API key material, partner billing/onboarding path, provider account, and live API v1 routes.

API v1 live-route promotion packet: 10 required owner gates before any live route can even be discussed; the payload-envelope gate (filterApiV1MetricPayloadFields()/filterProprietaryMetricPayloadEnvelope()) is the API-layer enforcement point for the public/private surface doctrine — no proprietary metrics, metric names, or methodology may leak through public endpoints.

Mahoney & Paniak (2023): neural-network FPTS projections + MILP optimizer for NFL DraftKings — against real DraftKings users the generated lineups 'generally fell in approximately the 31st percentile (median)', a documented negative result showing point-estimate maximization cannot find high-ceiling, low-duplication tail events in top-heavy GPPs; gaps: no ownership/leverage, no stacking/correlation, no ceiling/floor asymmetry, no payout structure, no portfolio handling.

PIDTC tennis landing-point prediction (Huang et al. 2026): with court-boundary priors from Hough lines — 85.71% in/out accuracy, 94.59% recall; without priors 52.86% accuracy with 100% recall (effectively fails to converge); label-fed regression MSE 372.39 vs no-prior 1183.39 (claimed 68.53% MSE reduction) — but baselines (RNN/LSTM/Transformer/GRU) received no priors, confounding architecture with information; training sweep at tiny N is non-monotonic (no CIs).

PIDTC uses dot-product attention softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V with standard sinusoidal positional encoding in its Transformer classify-then-regress cascade (BCE for in/out classification, MSE for landing-point regression).

SkillSight (Vijayan et al. 2025): gaze-only student model 44.4% accuracy at 9.5 mW vs teacher 50.1% at 943 mW and TimeSformer 45.5% at 697.5 mW on Ego-Exo4D — 73x lower energy for a 1.1% accuracy drop; student without distillation drops to 40.0% from 44.4%; power modeled not measured.

SkillSight gaze-modified attention: temporal attention softmax is augmented with a gaze attention map weighted by λ_c, where the gaze attention is a Gaussian centered on the gaze patch; power modeled as P = alpha*N/T + beta*B/T + sum_m gamma_m*delta_m.
equation: A_m^t = softmax(A_v^t + lambda_c A_g^t); P = alpha*N/T + beta*B/T + sum gamma_m*delta_m

claim: Rane (2025) time-decayed ridge (RAPM) on F1 2014–2024 Hybrid Era: constructors explain 64.0% of race-outcome variance (DNF-excluded), 76.1% DNF-inclusive, and only 47.0% in qualifying (driver matters more where machinery can't break); validation metric is Kendall's Tau = (concordant − discordant)/C(n,2) averaged across races; τ = 0.625 for the best race model; McFadden's pseudo-R² = 1 − LL(full)/LL(null).
equation: Kendall's Tau = (concordant - discordant)/C(n,2); McFadden's pseudo-R^2 = 1 - LL(full)/LL(null)

claim: F1 RAPM time decay (grid-searched): exponential season decay 0.75, round decay 0.075; coefficient stabilized via LOESS-blended update with weight capped at 0.7; the partial-Tau decomposition pipeline (per-race Kendall Tau against team/car/team-driver splits) is portable as a component-isolation pattern for problems like QB vs offensive line vs coach.

MambaTrack (2024): learned bi-Mamba motion predictor replaces the Kalman filter in tracking-by-detection; SportsMOT HOTA 72.6 vs ByteTrack 62.8 (+9.8); DanceTrack HOTA 56.8 vs OC-SORT 54.6; motion-model shootout HOTA: IoU-only 44.7, KF 45.9, LSTM 51.3, Transformer 52.5, MTP 54.9; 67 ms/frame on laptop RTX 4060, on par with KF.

equation: o = [delta_cx, delta_cy, delta_w, delta_h]; p_hat_{t+1} = MTP(T, p_hat_t)

mAFTER guarantee (Prop 1): (1/T)Σ E[(y_t−ŷ_t^(M))²] ≤ inf(inf_i risk_i + c1 log K/T, risk_SA + c2/T, risk_LR + c2/T); inner forecast ŷ_t,w = Σ_i w_i ŷ_{t,i}; in the SPF evaluation risk is normalized against the simple average (SA = 1.00, mAFTER = 0.90 on PGDP).
equation: ŷ_t,w = Σ_i w_i ŷ_{t,i}; (1/T)Σ E[(y_t−ŷ_t^(M))²] ≤ inf(inf_i risk_i + c1 log K/T, risk_SA + c2/T, risk_LR + c2/T)

claim: WALLA wagering mechanism (arXiv 2607.04389v1): net payout π_i(p,w,y) = w_i (s(p_i,y) − b_{−i}(p_{−i},w_{−i},y) − c_3 w_i); Theorem 3.2: truthful prediction is a dominant strategy; Theorem 3.3: best-response wager w_i*(p_i) = (A_i / 2c_3)^+ with A_i = E[s(p_i,Y) − b_{−i} | F_i] — non-positive advantage self-excludes (zero weight); Theorem 3.5: operator deficit bounded by (s̄−s̲)²/4c_3.

WALLA results: homogeneous scenario AUC 81.07±0.58 / ACC 87.00±0.47 (matches StackedGen 81.99/87.76); as participants grow 4→12, UniformAvg AUC collapses 70.29→63.10 while WALLA I holds 81.07→82.10; MRR = 100.00 at all M (always identifies the informed model); BayesX KLD 2.22 vs Uniform 25.64.

Goldberg & Mahmoud: Conditional Expected Drawdown CED_α(X) = TM_α(μ(X)) — the tail mean of the maximum-drawdown distribution, a drawdown analog of Expected Shortfall; convex (Prop 3.3) and positively homogeneous (Prop 3.5); Euler attribution MRC_i^{CED_α}(P) = E[(F_{i,t*} − F_{i,s*}) | μ(P) > DT_α(P)] where (s*,t*) locate the portfolio's maximum drawdown.
equation: D_t^(X) = M_t^(X) − X_t; CED_α(X) = TM_α(μ(X)); MRC_i^{CED_α}(P) = E[(F_{i,t*} − F_{i,s*}) | μ(P) > DT_α(P)]

claim: CED empirical (1982–2013 daily): CED_0.9 over 6-month paths — US Equity 47%, US Bonds 29%, 60/40 33%; equity's drawdown-risk contribution spikes in crises (2008), co-moving with VIX; estimation: T-length series → T−n overlapping paths of length n → CED_α = average of largest (1−α)% drawdowns.

Ryan (2026, registered report): conformal-Kelly sizing f = 0.15·μ̂/σ̂² (conformal interval half-width as σ̂); sealed 2022–2024 lockbox — calibration transferred (empirical coverage 0.7450 vs 0.75 nominal) but the growth edge did not: DEV 0.2845 growth / 1.336 Sharpe / 27.7% drawdown vs lockbox Config A 0.0847 / 0.453 / 36.6%; naive equal-weight 2× won on growth (0.1679); cautionary: ~200 DEV configs searched (selection bias), cap bound 97.7% of DEV days.

WorldCupArena Scoreline partial-credit: S_score = 45·I_r + 25[1 − e_d/5]_+ + 20[1 − e_t/6]_+ + 10[1 − e_team/8]_+ (exact = 100; result class worth 45); best LLM result accuracy 70.7% vs human fans 69.7% and BetVictor 68.3% — the edge is near-miss calibration (Scoreline 68.49 vs 53.35), not hit rate; search effect −0.26 to −4.26 (no reliable gain); exact-score leader only 2.2%.

WorldCupArena availability-aware aggregation: S_A = Σ_{j∈A} w_j S_j / Σ_{j∈A} w_j over available components only — missing truth excluded, never zero-filled; minimum-coverage rule ≥52 valid predictions; lock-predictions-24h-before/score-after verification protocol (prevents post-hoc backdating).
equation: S_A = Σ_{j∈A} w_j S_j / Σ_{j∈A} w_j

(JQAS 2023): frame-level (~4 Hz) generative horse-race simulator — hierarchical cubic B-spline trajectories θ_h ~ N(μ_θ, Σ_θ), jockey/track effects, CFD drafting model; win probability = fraction of posterior-predictive simulated races won; lane-draw counterfactual: lane 2 expected rank 3.28 / win prob 0.21 vs lane 6 worst at 3.88; retrodiction caveat — trajectories are spline-fits, jockey decisions are exogenous.

Ötting et al. (2022): on 212 Bundesliga matches reaching 1–1, bettors staked ~12.7pp higher relative stakes on the equalizer-scorer (+35.7% at covariate means; second half +19.4pp) while momentum had zero effect on outcomes (β₂ = 0.115, n.s.) and zero effect on bookmaker odds (β₂ = −0.017, n.s.); logit Pr(win_i,m=1) = β₀ + β₁·impprob + β₂·equaliser + β₃·minute + β₄·redcard.
equation: logit Pr(win_i,m=1) = β₀ + β₁·impprob + β₂·equaliser + β₃·minute + β₄·redcard

claim: Momentum-staking minute after equalizer: 47.0% of stakes on scorer, 37.2% conceder, 18.6% draw — while the draw is most likely (39.3%), then conceder win (33.2%), then scorer win (27.5%); ROI of always backing the equalizer: −20.1% (moderate favorites) to −23.3% (strong longshots) vs 7.9% average overround.

Motegi & Masuda (2012): dynamic win-lose score extends Park–Newman with online updates w_{t_n} = A_{t_n}ᵀ1 + e^{−β(t_n−t_{n−1})}(I + αA_{t_n}ᵀ) w_{t_{n−1}} (loss vector ℓ built symmetrically; score s = w − ℓ); on 137,842 ATP matches: dynamic 0.659–0.661 accuracy (α 0.08–0.20, β=1/365) vs static 0.623, beats official ATP rankings 0.637 over α ∈ [0.11, 0.39]; game order matters more than decay rate; caveat: no convergence guarantee (temporal network is acyclic), α is a pure tuning knob.

Csató (2023): Football Club Elo (k=400/K=20, all matches) beats the UEFA club coefficient (European results only) at predicting 19 seasons of Champions League — group matches AUC 0.814 vs 0.784, knockout 0.690 vs 0.617, group ranking 0.784 vs 0.754; but in the both-model regression UEFA's coefficient stays significant for group ranking (0.012***) — 'European experience' adds value beyond domestic-weighted Elo.
Elo update E_1 = E_0 + K(R−W) with R ∈ {1, 0.5, 0}, W = 1/(1+10^{Δ/s}); model fit compared via Cox & Snell R² = 1 − (L_0/L_M)^{2/n} and McFadden = 1 − ln(L_M)/ln(L_0).

Michels, Bajons & Fischer (2026): NFL pre-snap man/zone prediction — non-homogeneous HMM decodes defender→offensive-player assignments from y-coordinate time series with reaction lag l=4 (0.4 s at 10 Hz, AIC-selected), μ_{t,j} = y_{t−l}(off_j); transitions γ_{ij} = exp(η_{ij})/Σ_k exp(η_{ik}), η_{ij}^{(t,r,d,p)} = β₀ + β₁|y_{t−l}(off_i) − y_{t−l}(off_j)| + u_r + v_d + w_p; n=3,963 motion plays (2,980 zone / 983 man).

HMM defensive-scheme results: GCM omnibus test p ≈ 0.0002 — HMM features significantly associated with coverage given all other features; position random effects: CB −0.178 (follow receivers) vs FS 0.175, ILB/MLB/OLB ≈ 0.006–0.007 (pass off assignments); total switches median 1.00, mean 1.82, max 21; 2,980 zone / 983 man plays; descriptives only establish the assignment signal, not out-of-sample prediction accuracy.

GCM conditional-independence test (Shah & Peters): GCM ≔ E[Cov(Y,X|Z)] = E[(Y − E[Y|Z])(X − E[X|Z])] for testing Y ⊥ X | Z; test statistic is asymptotically N(0,1); works with arbitrary regression learners for E[Y|Z] and E[X|Z].

BBE (Cliff 2021): race-event preference-modulated step S_c(t, f_r) = (k − |f_r − p_c|) · U(d_min, d_max); exchange with back/lay aggregated into per-competitor ladders, time-priority matching, ~5% commission on winnings only, unmatched bets cancelled at race start; minimum population bound B ≥ 4DN bettors (needed for non-empty market at N=5: prob 0.038).

Kaggle 2014 March Mania winner (Glickman & Stern): logistic on Las Vegas spread logit(Pr(y_g=1)) = β₀ + β₁·spread_g ensembled with KenPom-efficiency logistic S₂ = 0.25·M₁ + 0.75·M₂ won with log-loss 0.52951 (1st of 433); luck simulation: if S₂ were truth, median rank 14, P(win) = 11.65% — even perfect probabilities win a 433-entry contest only ~12% of the time; skill multiplies win odds ~50–60× vs random (P(win) 11.65% vs 0.23%).

March Mania contest scoring: LogLoss_ij = −(y_i log(ŷ_ij) + (1−y_i)log(1−ŷ_ij))·I(Z_i=1); LogLoss_j = (1/63)Σ_i LogLoss_ij; ensemble weights grid-searched on 2008–2013 tournament log-loss (optimum 0.69 on M₂ / 0.31 on M₁).

MoPLEx (Li et al. 2026, LLM preference alignment): +43.7% clustering-accuracy and +15.2% ranking-accuracy improvement over mixture-of-BT baselines; k-PL mixture unidentifiable when k > m/2 (fixed by augmenting to m′ ≥ 26); gradient approximation within 5% error up to 34B params; zero sports transfer (verdict: REJECT).

Xing (Stanford): cycle-consistency test (Prop. 1) — a scalar BT representation exists iff Σ_k ℓ_{i_k i_{k+1}} = 0 for every directed cycle; Chatbot Arena: cyclic energy share 4.2% vs bootstrap null 95th pct 3.5% (p=0.008) — scalar-score representation rejected at 1%; one-eighth law: inf_r Σ_e ρ_e D_KL(Bern(σ(ℓ_e))‖Bern(σ((Br)_e))) = (1/8)‖ℓ^cyc‖²_W + O(ε³); misfit priced 0.0034 bits vs predicted 0.0038 (ratio 0.89).

Attention channel for preference data: ℓ_z = η_z + β_z Δ*_z, β_z ≥ 0; generalized logit: log[π_z(1|ω)/π_z(0|ω)] = α_z + β_z{u_z(1,ω)−u_z(0,ω)}; BT pseudo-true limit: r†(ℓ) = (BᵀWB)⁺BᵀWℓ + O(ε³); sample complexity: distinguishing Δ=δ from −δ needs ~1/(β²δ²) labels.
equation: ℓ_z = η_z + β_z Δ*_z; log[π_z(1|ω)/π_z(0|ω)] = α_z + β_z{u_z(1,ω)−u_z(0,ω)}

claim: Whelan & Klein (2021): unified multi-outcome BT θ^I_ij = σ({p_J(λ_i−λ_j) + o_J τ | J})_I; four-outcome θ^RW_ij = π_i/D; θ^OW_ij = ν π_i^{2/3}π_j^{1/3}/D; θ^OL_ij = ν π_i^{1/3}π_j^{2/3}/D; θ^RL_ij = π_j/D; exponents chosen so the MLE moment condition makes expected points equal actual points under 3-2-1-0 scoring; Bayesian inference via Laplace with analytic Hessian's Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse (handles singular λ-shift, enforces Σλ_i = 0) and HMC in Stan with successive-differences parametrization ω_i = λ_i − λ_{i+1}.
equation: θ^I_ij = σ({p_J(λ_i−λ_j) + o_J τ | J})_I; θ^RW_ij = π_i/D; θ^OW_ij = ν π_i^{2/3}π_j^{1/3}/D

claim: Bradley-Terry–Davidson tie model: θ^W_ij = π_i/(π_i + ν√(π_iπ_j) + π_j); tie probability between even teams = ν/(2+ν); four-outcome OT probability between even teams = e^{τ̂}/(1+e^{τ̂}); log-likelihood: L = (1/2)Σ_iΣ_jΣ_I n^I_ij ln θ^I_ij.

Jadbabaie, Makur & Shah (2020): skill score = negative differential entropy −h(P_α) = ∫P_α(t)log(P_α(t))dt = D(P_α‖unif([0,1])); cricket World Cup negative entropy → near 0 by 2019 (most unpredictable); EPL 2018–19 highest of five European leagues (most competitive).

Skill-distribution two-stage estimator: rank centrality α̂_i = π̂*(i)/‖π̂*‖∞ (leading left eigenvector of the empirical stochastic matrix), then Parzen–Rosenblatt KDE P̂*(x) = (1/nh)Σ_i K((α̂_i−x)/h) with Epanechnikov K_E(x)=¾(1−x²)𝟙{|x|≤1}; minimax lower bounds Ω̃(n^{−1/2}) (Thms 1–2).

Deb (2021): GBI = [1/((2N−1)·λ̂)]·Σ_{i≠j}Σ_{k∈{0,1}} (X_ijk − λ̂)²; under perfect balance (2N−1)·GBI ~ χ²_{2N−1} asymptotically; panel regression (5 leagues × 10 seasons): GBI coefficient −1.52* (SE 0.72) — the only significant balance coefficient (C6, HICB not significant); GBI–C6 correlation 0.52, C6–HICB 0.90.

GBI perfect-balance theorem: with 3/1/0 points and iid Poisson(λ), league perfectly balanced; goal difference Y_ij ~ Skellam(λ,λ), pmf P(Y_ij=k) = e^{−2λ}·I_{|k|}(2λ); draws: P(Y1=Y2|λ) = e^{−2λ}·I_0(2λ); simulation: GBI test type-I ≈5% at all λ, power >99% even when only 1 of 20 teams differs.

Alexandari, Kundaje & Shrikumar (2018/2020): post-hoc abstention framework — calibrate + label-shift-adapt (Platt; Saerens EM/MLLS), estimate metric gain via calibrated p(y|x) as label proxy, abstain on the largest-gain subset under budget; IMDB label-shift: sensitivity@99% spec 0.3571±0.004 → 0.7067±0.0067 @30% abstention (significantly best, Wilcoxon p<0.05); miscalibrated abstention can HURT (entropy/max-prob worse than base at high abstention); works beyond binary (multiclass/multi-label) unlike Saerens.

Abstention optimizers: sensitivity-at-specificity t* = min{i : 1 − nᵢ⁻/n₀⁻ ≥ s}; auROC = (1/(n⁻n⁺))Σᵢ yᵢsᵢ⁻, sᵢ⁻ = Σ_{i′<i}(1−y_{i′}); weighted Cohen's κ: κ(S,f) = 1 − [Σ_{x∈S} W_{y(x),f(x)}]/[ΣᵢΣⱼ W_{i,j}(Nⁱ/N)Fʲ]; baseline: abstain on lowest Jensen–Shannon divergence between predicted probs and class prior.

Mao, Mohri & Zhong (2023): two-stage predictor-rejector wins everywhere on multiclass abstention — SVHN abstention loss 0.94%±0.02% vs Mozannar 1.61%±0.06% / Cao 2.16%±0.04%; CIFAR-10: two-stage 3.31%/2.69%/22.83% (abstention loss / accepted error / rejection ratio) vs Cao 3.62%/3.08%/28.27% — better selection, not more abstention; all gains in the two-stage variant (single-stage P-R no better than baselines).

Calibration-gap lemma (Lemma 20): C*_Labs(H,R,x) = 1 − max{max_{y∈H(x)} p(x,y), 1−c}; two-stage variant freezes predictor h and trains rejector r from a possibly different function family on possibly different features; H-consistency: abstention excess risk ≤ Γ(surrogate excess risk).

AthletePose3D (~1.3M frames, 165K unique postures, MoCap ground truth): SOTA 3D pose models fail on athletic motion without sport-specific data — MotionAGFormer MPJPE 257.26 mm (trained on H3.6M) → 100.12 mm after AP3D fine-tuning (~60% reduction); kinematic validation: joint-angle correlations 3D upper limb r=0.90 / lower r=0.82 (trustworthy) vs velocities 3D r=0.28/0.11 (untrustworthy); all SPM paired t-tests p<0.05 — every estimated waveform differs significantly from GT.

Csató: proved that under UEFA-style coefficient-based seeding, a team can be punished with a worse seed for performing better in qualification (violates incentive compatibility); proved the remedy c̃_i = max{c_j : rank_j ≥ rank_i} restores monotonicity (pot assignment can never worsen with better qualification).

In the Bayesian home-advantage model (Benz, Bliss, Lopez; NFL, four NCAA divisions, all 50 states of high school football, 2004-2023, ~1.28M games), the score differential Y_ijkt for home team i vs away team j in league k, season t is modeled as normal: Y_ijkt ~ N(μ_ijkt, σ_k^2), where θ_ikt and θ_jkt are season-specific team strengths, and home advantage (HA) takes three forms: constant (Model 1), linearly drifting (Model 2), or time-varying (Model 3). Model 2 adds a posterior probability of decline, P(β_1k < 0).
equation: Y_ijkt ~ N(μ_ijkt, σ_k^2); Model 1: μ_ijkt = θ_ikt − θ_jkt + α_k; Model 2: μ_ijkt = θ_ikt − θ_jkt + β_0k + β_1k(t − t_0); Model 3: μ_ijkt = θ_ikt − θ_jkt + γ_kt

claim: The Bayesian home-advantage model's priors are θ_ikt ~ N(0, ζ_k^2) for team strengths, with half-normal variance priors ζ_k, σ_k ~ HalfNormal(0, 5^2), α_k ~ N(0, η_k^2) for the constant home-advantage term, and β_0k, β_1k ~ N(0, λ^2) with half-normal variance priors for the linear-drift form.
equation: θ_ikt ~ N(0, ζ_k^2); ζ_k, σ_k ~ HalfNormal(0, 5^2); α_k ~ N(0, η_k^2); β_0k, β_1k ~ N(0, λ^2)

claim: 2023 estimated home advantage (points per game) was FCS 2.49, FBS 2.39, DIII 2.37, DII 1.86, and NFL 1.73 with a 95% credible interval of (1.07, 2.39) — well under the folklore 3-point figure.

Home advantage is declining in NFL and top college football: FBS slope β_1 ≈ −0.097 points/year (~1 point per decade) with P(decline) = 1.000; NFL slope β_1 = −0.032 points/year with P(decline) = 0.857 (NFL home advantage down ~0.65 points over 20 years). High-school home advantage is flat or rising (38 of 50 states have positive β_1). Attributed drivers: replay review expansion (NFL challenge success rate 31% → 58%; NCAA adopted replay 2004-2006; high school prohibited until 2019) and improved travel.

Unadjusted empirical home-vs-away score differentials are severely biased upward relative to team-strength-adjusted estimates (gaps often exceeding 3 points), because better teams host more home games; any home-edge feature must be strength-adjusted. On NFL data, Model 2 (linear home-advantage drift) won the ELPD model comparison via loo() with ΔELPD = 0, vs Model 1 at −1.31 (SE 1.75) and Model 3 at −4.93 (SE 4.83). The supplementary hierarchical Model 2H (shared trend β_1k ~ N(β_1*, λ_1^2)) over-shrinks when state sample sizes differ wildly.

Knee joint moments (an ACL-risk indicator) can be estimated from motion-capture kinematics without force plates by encoding 8 marker (x,y,z) trajectories as an RGB image (8 markers → image width, 125 time samples → height, warped to 227×227 via cubic spline interpolation), fine-tuning CaffeNet (pre-trained on 1.3M ImageNet images) with its final 1,000-dim SoftMax replaced by a Euclidean loss layer for multivariate regression, and PCA-compressing the 6 output KJM waveforms (e.g., RKJMz from 90 to 59 features at threshold t = 0.999).

Double-cascade transfer learning (fine-tune from ImageNet, then from an earlier ground-reaction-force/moment model's weights, then on knee joint moments) improved sidestep-left correlation from 0.9179 to 0.9277 and sidestep-right from 0.8168 to 0.8512 (+4.2%, p < 0.01), with a mean improvement of +1.8% across movement types; sidestep pair combined r(KJMmean) = 0.8895.

The weakest component throughout knee joint moment estimation is KJMz (internal/external rotation): run right 0.7430 (single-tune), sidestep right 0.7304 (double-cascade). Five-fold cross-validation on sidestep right gave mean r(RKJMmean) = 0.8472 vs single-fold 0.8512, indicating overfitting was avoided. Cited epidemiology: non-contact ACL events are 51-80% of team-sport ACLs, >80% in sidestepping/single-leg landing.

ScoutGPT serializes a football match as an event-token sequence: a 54-dimensional match-context vector c (team IDs, 22 player roles, 22 player IDs, 8 match-state tokens) plus each event as a 10-token tuple (team ID, role, player ID, action type, start x/y, end x/y, elapsed time δt, outcome), flattened to s = (c1..c54, s1,1..s1,10, ..., sT,1..sT,10), with continuous fields quantized into shared integer bins 0-105. It uses a NanoGPT (GPT-2 decoder-only) backbone with per-field sub-vocabularies, learnable positional embeddings, and causal masked multi-head self-attention.

ScoutGPT trains with a composite loss L = L_next + L_goal with no weighting coefficient: L_next is next-token cross-entropy and L_goal is a goal-prediction head at each event's last token predicting binary indicators g_t^+ and g_t^- (whether the acting team scores or concedes within 15 seconds). Constrained decoding enforces ownership-lock on the ball-carrier across in-possession events and dynamic episode termination on EOS, set-piece restart, goal, foul, or own goal.

ScoutGPT counterfactual transfer simulation (swap a transferred player's ID/role tokens into the target team's context, Monte Carlo-generate episode sequences, aggregate residual on-ball value into simulated episode VAEP) cut mean absolute error of post-transfer episode VAEP from 1.84 (naive carry-over) to 1.25 across 40 players by post-transfer minutes in 2025 (K League 2021-2025 event data, 1,320 training matches). Case: Jinsu Kim (left back) — naive 7.00 vs ground truth 11.07 vs simulated 11.63 (errors 4.07 naive vs 0.56 simulated).

ScoutGPT next-event prediction beat the LEM-Transformer baseline with start-x MAE of 4.59 → 0.97 and time MAE of 1.42 → 0.75. Ablations: removing lineup info degrades role accuracy/F1 by −0.090/−0.156; removing the context block degrades time R² by −0.184 and inflates time MAE by +0.069; removing both is worst on time (−0.212 R², +0.097 MAE).

In the parimutuel (fair-odds) Kelly re-derivation, the expected log-profit is E(z_k)(l_1,l_2) = p_1·ln(1 + (IN_2/IN_1)·l_1 − l_2) + p_2·ln(1 + (IN_1/IN_2)·l_2 − l_1), where l_k is the fraction of capital staked on event k, p_k the true probability, and IN_k the pool total for event k.

The unconstrained Kelly optimum for parimutuel bets is (l̄_1 − p_1)·IN_2 = (l̄_2 − p_2)·IN_1 — a line of optimal strategies in (l_1, l_2) space, where l̄_k is the optimal stake fraction and p_k the true probability.

Maximum profit under parimutuel Kelly decomposes as E(z_k)(l̄_1,l̄_2) = −Σ_{k=1,2} p_k·ln((IN_1+IN_2)/IN_k) − S, where S = −Σ_k p_k·ln p_k is the Boltzmann/Shannon entropy: max profit = 'unpopularity profit' (the seer's profit from staking against the crowd) minus entropy. It is nonnegative — profit is zero iff p_1·IN_2 = p_2·IN_1 (crowd matches true probabilities).
equation: E(z_k)(l̄_1,l̄_2) = −Σ_{k=1,2} p_k·ln((IN_1+IN_2)/IN_k) − S, where S = −Σ_k p_k·ln p_k

claim: The no-short Kelly optimum is (l_1* = p_1 − (IN_1/IN_2)·p_2, l_2* = 0) when p_1·IN_2 > p_2·IN_1 (indices swapped otherwise); under Laplace indifference (IN_1 = IN_2) this reduces to (l_1* = p_1 − p_2, l_2* = 0), the classic Kelly result.

Glickman's strength-dependent extension of the Bradley-Terry-with-ties-and-order-effects model (motivated by chess, where draws are more common between stronger players) makes both tie probability and the order (home/white) effect vary with the average strength of the competitors: P(win) ∝ exp(θᵢ + xᵢⱼ[α₀ + α₁(θᵢ+θⱼ)/2]/4), P(loss) ∝ exp(θⱼ − xᵢⱼ[α₀ + α₁(θᵢ+θⱼ)/2]/4), P(draw) ∝ exp(β₀ + (1+β₁)(θᵢ+θⱼ)/2), where θᵢ, θⱼ are strengths and xᵢⱼ = ±1 encodes the order advantage. When α₁ = β₁ = 0 the model collapses exactly to David (1988). The IIA property is preserved: P(win)/P(loss) odds are unaffected by tie parameters.
equation: P(win) ∝ exp(θᵢ + xᵢⱼ[α₀ + α₁(θᵢ+θⱼ)/2]/4); P(loss) ∝ exp(θⱼ − xᵢⱼ[α₀ + α₁(θᵢ+θⱼ)/2]/4); P(draw) ∝ exp(β₀ + (1+β₁)(θᵢ+θⱼ)/2)

claim: The Davidson–Beaver order effect is logit P(win) = θᵢ − θⱼ + (α/2)xᵢⱼ, and the strength–Elo link is Rᵢ = 1500 + (400/log 10)·θ̂ᵢ, with Elo-scale prior conversion μᵢ = (Rᵢ − 1500)/(400/log 10).
equation: logit P(win) = θᵢ − θⱼ + (α/2)xᵢⱼ; Rᵢ = 1500 + (400/log 10)·θ̂ᵢ; μᵢ = (Rᵢ − 1500)/(400/log 10)

claim: On 24,888 US Chess Open games (2006-2019), the full strength-dependent model had DIC = 43,821 vs 44,658 for David (1988) and 44,553 for the constant-tie-probability variant — substantially better. Posterior means (95% central intervals): α₀ = 0.363 (0.289, 0.434), so white win-to-loss odds are exp(0.363/2) ≈ 1.20 for average players (0.545 vs 0.455 decisive); α₁ = 0.037 (0.000, 0.074), so white advantage grows slightly with strength (evenly matched strong players θᵢ=θⱼ=2: odds 1.244, P(white win) 0.554); β₁ = 0.120 (0.103, 0.138) gives decisive positive evidence for strength-dependent ties: draw probability is 0.238 for evenly matched average players vs 0.489 for evenly matched strong players (θᵢ=θⱼ=2).

Automatic Risk Adaptation (ARA) replaces the hand-tuned static CVaR risk level in distributional RL with a per-state risk level from the agent's own parametric uncertainty: risk-neutral value Q(s,a) = E_{τ∼U(0,1)}[Z_τ(s,a)] from the quantile function, risk-distorted value Q_β(s,a) = E_τ[Z_{β(τ)}(s,a)], CVaR distortion β_CVaR(τ;α) = τ·α keeping the worst-α fraction of quantiles, novelty u(s) = ‖f(s)−g(s)‖² (Random Network Distillation prediction error between frozen target f and trained predictor g), and β_ARA(τ) = β_CVaR(τ; ψ(u)) with ψ(u) = e^{−u} ∈ (0,1] mapping novelty to risk level — novel states get conservative action selection, familiar states get risk-neutral.
equation: Q(s,a)=E_{τ∼U(0,1)}[Z_τ(s,a)]; Q_β(s,a)=E_τ[Z_{β(τ)}(s,a)]; β_CVaR(τ;α)=τ·α; u(s)=‖f(s)−g(s)‖²; β_ARA(τ)=β_CVaR(τ; ψ(u)), ψ(u)=e^{−u}

claim: Static CVaR risk levels are provably suboptimal under changing conditions: in tabular Windy GridWorld LavaGap, the optimal α wandered 0.4 → 0.5 → 0.1 → 0.9 across four wind settings with no predictable pattern, and the best-vs-worst static α gap widened from 0% (train setting) to 10% under unseen wind directions. On DynamicAnt, ARA's final return was ≥14% better than neutral DSAC and every static-CVaR agent (α=0.75 reached only ~60% of ARA's performance). On BipedalWalkerHardcore, ARA had the lowest failure rate at every point of training — 4× lower than neutral, 7× lower than static risk-aware agents by end of training — while conceding slightly on return to static α=0.5/0.75.

ARA limitation: conservative-by-default can stall exploration (bad seeds in fixed-dynamics Ant stayed conservative and never learned to walk), and the uncertainty↔risk proxy requires failure states to be rare — if failures are common, the proxy inverts. ARA adds one RND network pair, needs no extra episode evaluations, and its cost is independent of state/action-space size.

SINDy-SI adds domain side information (equilibria, monotonicity, symmetries, invariant sets) as hard sum-of-squares constraints inside sparse nonlinear-dynamics discovery: parameterize f̂(x) = W^⊤φ(x) with a monomial library, minimize ‖Y−ΦW‖²_F + ξ‖W‖₀ (thresholded refit), and solve the side-information-constrained regression min_W ‖Y−ΦW‖²_F subject to f̂(x) ∈ P_d ∩ {S_i}, lifted to a convex semidefinite program via the Schur complement. An SOS encoding example is {−∂f̂_i/∂x_i(x) − z_i(x)g(x)} ∈ Σ with SOS multipliers z_i and bounding ball g(x) = R²−‖x−c₀‖² (Putinar's Positivstellensatz).
equation: f̂(x)=W^⊤φ(x); min ‖Y−ΦW‖²_F + ξ‖W‖₀; min_W ‖Y−ΦW‖²_F subject to f̂(x) ∈ P_d ∩ {S_i}; {−∂f̂_i/∂x_i(x) − z_i(x)g(x)} ∈ Σ; g(x)=R²−‖x−c₀‖²

claim: SINDy-SI beats both plain SINDy and unconstrained SOS-constrained fitting in scarce-data regimes: on the Lorenz system, leave-one-trajectory-out cost J_k was — low noise: OLS 5.63×10⁴, SINDy 3.19×10⁶, side-information-only 822.42, SINDy-SI 2.0432; medium noise: OLS 5.59×10⁵, SINDy 1.28×10⁶, SI-only 1.89×10⁴, SINDy-SI 1.66×10³; high noise: OLS 5.13×10⁶, SINDy 1.49×10⁷, SI-only 2.16×10⁵, SINDy-SI 1.15×10⁵. Side information alone beats sparse-only by ~2 orders of magnitude; the combination wins everywhere and the gap widens with noise. On the single-machine infinite-bus power system, SINDy-SI emergently recovered the 7th-order Taylor expansion of the true sin dynamics (f̂₂(x) = 0.1790x₁⁷−1.944x₁⁵+34.09x₁³−203.8538x₁−1.415x₂+47.171 vs true 0.0404x₁⁷−1.6987x₁⁵+33.97x₁³−203.841x₁−1.415x₂+47.1698) without being told the expansion existed.

The directed cross-set behavioral-overlap metric is S(T|B) = mean_i max_j |Spearman ρ(f_i^T, f_j^B)| — the mean over test features i of the maximum absolute Spearman correlation with any benchmark feature j, computed across ~800 series; high S(T|B) means test set T adds little beyond benchmark B.

Median computation time on a 1000-sample series across the seven time-series auto-extraction libraries spans four orders of magnitude: catch22 < 10 ms, TSFEL 0.03 s, Kats 0.06 s, feasts 0.47 s, tsfresh 2.53 s, tsfeatures 6.18 s, hctsa 16.5 s; per-feature, catch22 and TSFEL cost ~10^-4 s while tsfeatures costs ~3 s per feature.

Within-set redundancy measured by PCA to 90% variance is highest for TSFEL and tsfresh — in TSFEL, 90% of variance across 390 features is captured with just 4 principal components — while catch22 (designed for low redundancy) is the least redundant. Average best-match |ρ| vs the hctsa benchmark: catch22 0.96, feasts 0.84, Kats 0.84, tsfeatures 0.88, TSFEL 0.88, tsfresh only 0.55; tsfresh is the most distinctive test set (S(tsfresh|B) = 0.25-0.5 for all other benchmarks).

128 tsfresh features had max |ρ| < 0.2 against any hctsa feature, and 118 of 128 (92%) were raw FFT coefficients (real/imaginary components and angles); S(TSFEL|tsfresh) = 0.5 because TSFEL computes absolute FFT magnitudes but not real/imag/angle components. Feature-computation failure rates: tsfresh 25.2% of features failed at T=100 (all FFT coefficients 51-99 components); Kats had 3 Holt-Winters failures on white noise; hctsa ~0.6-0.9% failed at short lengths. Caveat: no predictive task was evaluated — 'distinctive' ≠ 'predictively useful' — and overlap numbers are on univariate uniformly-sampled series, not multivariate/irregular series like play-by-play.

Five classical screening criteria were rebuilt as one-pass online algorithms: T_j = (μ₁−μ₂)/√(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂) and Fisher_j = Σ_c n_c(μ_c−μ)² / Σ_c n_c σ_c² are incrementally exact via running averages (variance = MS − μ²), while MI, Chi-square, and Gini come from bin counts of an ε-approximate quantile summary with exact weight-preservation adjustment and on-demand aggregation into K=5 bins.
equation: T_j = (μ₁−μ₂)/√(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂); Fisher_j = Σ_c n_c(μ_c−μ)² / Σ_c n_c σ_c²

claim: The online quantile summary satisfies the ε-approximate guarantee |r̃⁺(x) − r̃⁻(x) − w̃(x)| ≤ ε·w(Q), and concept drift is handled by a fading factor α ∈ (0,1) penalizing history via μ_n = α(n−1)μ_{n−1} + x_n (with a sparse variant using time anchors and universal weight maps), also applied to tuple weights in the quantile summaries.

Online-vs-offline parity: bin-count differences → 0 for ε ≤ 0.001 on all 7 benchmark datasets, and top-10% rank mismatch = 0 at ε < 0.01 even on the hardest sets. Online quantile (ε=0.001) vs offline timing — url: 19,094 vs 130,177 ms (~7×); dorothea: 4,285 vs 11,961 ms; gisette: 1,176 vs 4,018 ms — but at ε=0.0005 the url runtime explodes to 934,553 ms, worse than offline: precision has a sharp cost cliff.

With adaptation (α=0.9), online feature screening strictly dominates no-adaptation at every shift rate on a synthetic 1000-D drifting stream; even at the fastest shift (true feature set changes every 250 samples), adaptation detects all 100 true features with fewer selected features. On 3.2M-feature URL data with SGD, T-score with adaptation gave error 0.0073 vs 0.0080 no-screening vs 0.0097 without adaptation (Fisher with adaptation 0.0072 vs 0.0092), with screening runtime 63-205 s vs SparseFSA training 12,484 s (~2% of training cost). On 20NewsGroups, MI with adaptation gave error 0.061 vs 0.064 no-screening vs 0.062 without adaptation.

The binding media-automation risk doctrine forbids fully automated media generation and posting under any circumstances ('Never permitted'), and classifies automation risk in five tiers: Manual (Low) → Draft-assisted (Medium) → Template-assisted (Medium-High) → Scheduled posting (High) → Fully automated (CRITICAL — FORBIDDEN). It forbids the MoneyPrinter-style pipeline (AI scripts → programmatic slides → AI voiceover → auto-upload) for four stated reasons (claim governance bypass, fake persona risk, platform ToS, copyright), and requires every AI-voiced content to carry visible/audible disclosure 'AI-narrated content.'

The calibration feedback loop's confidence-band calibration table (per model version, per 50-pick window): 80-100 (Strong) → expected win rate ~65-75%, acceptable actual 58-80%; 65-79 (Moderate) → ~55-65%, acceptable 48-72%; 50-64 (Lean) → ~50-55%, acceptable 43-62%; 0-49 is withheld and not tracked for win rate. calibrationError is the difference between the confidence-band implied win rate and the actual outcome (negative = overconfident); calibrationDirection is OVERCONFIDENT | UNDERCONFIDENT | CALIBRATED; win rate = win count / total settled, where total settled counts WIN + LOSS only (excludes PUSH, VOID).

The alert rule: if a confidence band's actual win rate falls outside its acceptable range for two consecutive 50-pick windows, a calibration alert is raised, and the operator decides to (1) accept current calibration, (2) adjust the confidence scoring algorithm (requires a model version increment), or (3) widen the acceptable range (requires documented justification) — the system never autonomously adjusts confidence scores.

Win rate is never displayed until 30 picks are settled for the version, and is not projected forward or annualized. Forbidden public claims include 'Our model has proven predictive accuracy', 'Past win rate predicts future performance' (must not appear on any public surface in any form), and 'The model is improving' — the approved phrasing is only 'calibration data is accumulating.' A model version reaching 100 settled picks with a win rate below 45% triggers an operator alert — a warning, not automatic retirement.

Source reliability scores update within 24 hours of settlement confirmation; no single settlement event changes a source's score by more than ±5 points; scores are smoothed over a 30-pick rolling window; a source correct 90%+ on a specific claim type (e.g., injury status) gains a claim-type reliability bonus. Calibration triggers only on game completion, for ACTIVE picks with result WIN/LOSS/PUSH/VOID confirmed by a Tier 1 or licensed Tier 2 source; if no Tier 1/2 confirmation arrives within 6 hours, the pick is flagged SETTLEMENT_PENDING; PUSH/VOID are excluded from win rate but not from the ledger, and a >15% VOID rate triggers a review.

The 2026-09-05 market-anchored display-probability proposal argues the only honest public win probability is market-anchored: each book's quoted price per side → implied probability → average across books in the snapshot → normalize two-sided to sum to one (proportional de-vig), fixed at publish time in the pick's immutable proof receipt, while the 0-100 confidence selection score must never be shown as a percent. The de-vig method is PROPORTIONAL (receipt tag proportional_devig_v1); the Shin-per-book median (consensusNoVig) was measured and withdrawn.

Measured calibration failure of confidence-as-probability: confidence Brier 0.2689 / ECE 0.116 (production scoreBakeoff, 2026-09-05); on the 80+ confidence band — n 235, claimed 0.8663, realized 0.5191, gap −0.3472, SE 0.0326, z = −10.7; confidence-as-probability Brier on the 80+ band = 0.3617 (a constant 0.5 scores 0.25). The structural reason: confidence is non-monotone in realized outcome — realized win rate peaks at conf 75-79 (0.6146) and falls to 0.4643 by conf 90-94, below the 0.5280 of the lowest band — so no monotone calibrator (isotonic/PAVA) can repair it.

Shin vs proportional de-vig head-to-head (n=621): ALL paired Brier diff +0.002151 (t = 1.798), moneyline diff +0.012808 (t = 1.797) — not significant; the entire moneyline Shin advantage lives in 11 rows with |gap| > 0.1 (degenerate/lopsided books), and excluding those 11, Shin is slightly worse (−0.001361, t = −1.125). Receipts must name their method (proportional_devig_v1), and MODEL_VERSION stays v5.2.7 (no scoring path changes; a gratuitous bump would reset the deployed-version calibration slice to n 0).

marketFairProb (n=622, bookmakerCount ≥ 2) is monotone with every band gap within 0.07 — e.g., the 0.90-0.99 band: n 50, claimed 0.9399, realized 0.8800, Brier 0.1047. rankingP (n=1,390) is monotone and calibratable but over-confident in the upper-middle band (0.68-0.76: claimed 0.7138, realized 0.5828). Spread/total calibration must be reported per market, never pooled with moneylines (pooled Brier floor 0.22 is unreachable since spread/total cover probabilities sit near 0.25 by construction).

nfelo (Robby Greer) = Elo + QB Elo + HFA/rest/weather + SRS from win-total futures + nfelounits (EPA by unit translated to Elo via EWMA with offseason regression, combined by an EloTranslator trained to minimize log-loss on win probability). In the MuZero audit (He, Moerland, de Vries & Oliehoek, arXiv:2306.00840), the h-horizon action-sequence value is v^{a_{t:t+h−1}}(s_t) = Σγ^k r_{t+k} (eq. 3), and the value prediction error is |v^π_h(s_t) − v̂^π_h(s_t)| of the learned model vs ground truth (Def. 2, eq. 7), estimated by Monte Carlo over states from the behavior policy's state distribution.

MuZero value equivalence FAILS: even on its own behavior policy, the learned model's prediction error grows quickly with horizon ('does not imply that we learn models that are actually value equivalent'). For unseen policies, error grows as action sequences become less probable under the behavior policy — the model cannot evaluate what it has not executed. Free search (uniform prior + learned model) fails completely in Lunar Lander and Breakout; in Breakout, learned-model MCTS never beats the prior alone. With a policy prior, learned-model MCTS improves over the prior alone in Cart Pole/Lunar Lander given enough simulations, but the improvement is small vs the ground-truth model.

MuZero mechanism finding: the policy prior lowers TV/KL divergence between the policy prior and the MCTS visit distribution, which makes MCTS visit actions the prior favors and therefore lowers value prediction error — 'apart from biasing the search, the policy prior may also serve to prevent the search from exploring directions where the learned model is less accurate.' Authors' caveat: results are specific to value-equivalence losses; reconstruction-based (Dreamer) or temporal-consistency (EfficientZero) losses may generalize better in low-data regimes — an untested hypothesis — and the experiments are deterministic toy environments only (no stochastic/partial-observability/multi-agent tests).

Conformalized quantile regression (CQR; Romano, Patterson & Candès 2019): (1) train two quantile regressors at α/2 and 1−α/2; (2) compute calibration scores E_i = max{ q̂_α/2(X_i) − Y_i, Y_i − q̂_{1−α/2}(X_i) }; (3) expand the band by the (1−α)(1+1/n)-th empirical quantile of the scores. Interval: C(x) = [ q̂_α/2(x) − Q̂_{1−α}(E), q̂_{1−α/2}(x) + Q̂_{1−α}(E) ]. Guarantee: P(Y ∈ C(X)) ≥ 1−α under exchangeability. CQR appears explicitly or implicitly in ≥20 of the 100 surveyed papers — the single most influential method in the batch.

Jackknife+ (Barber, Candès, Ramdas & Tibshirani 2019): interval = [ α-th quantile of { μ̂_{−i}(X_{n+1}) − |Y_i − μ̂_{−i}(X_i)| }, (1−α)-th quantile of { μ̂_{−i}(X_{n+1}) + |Y_i − μ̂_{−i}(X_i)| } ], guaranteeing ≥ 1−2α coverage for any symmetric algorithm and any distribution; the original jackknife can have zero/vanishing coverage. In a forward-collision-warning evaluation (Hu et al., NGSIM), inference was 73% faster than Transformer methods with ADE 0.73 m (42.2% better than Social_LSTM), and CQR intervals achieved 91.3% coverage at 90% nominal.
equation: interval = [ α-th quantile of { μ̂_{−i}(X_{n+1}) − |Y_i − μ̂_{−i}(X_i)| }, (1−α)-th quantile of { μ̂_{−i}(X_{n+1}) + |Y_i − μ̂_{−i}(X_i)| } ]

claim: Missing-values conformal theorem (Zaffran, Dieuleveut, Josse & Romano 2023): if the data satisfy exchangeability (A1) and the imputation satisfies symmetry (A2), then imputed variables are exchangeable and the conformal guarantee holds — impute-then-predict+conformalize is marginally valid for any missingness distribution (even MNAR). Caveat: mask-conditional coverage can fail dramatically. Also surveyed: nested conformal + QOOB (avoids train/calibration split inefficiency); reweighting w_i = ρ(x_i, x_{n+1}) / ((1/n) Σ_j ρ(x_j, x_{n+1})) adapting intervals to local difficulty; KOWCPI (kernel-based, optimally weighted conformal time-series prediction with conditional coverage under strong mixing); TQA (post-hoc wrapper preserving cross-sectional coverage, improving longitudinal coverage); and SEMF (EM-style, VAE-like Monte Carlo sampling, works with XGBoost/MLPs, evaluated on 11 tabular datasets).

RES-aware calibration identity: BS = UNC − Var[P]; minimizing Brier is equivalent to maximizing RES under REL ≈ 0. The calibration framework decomposes the Brier score into reliability (REL), resolution (RES), and uncertainty (UNC); probability maps may only expand underconfident probabilities when outcome-fitted under a REL guard.

Online beta recalibration: OGD on (a,b) for g = σ(a·logit p + b) under log-loss (convex). fitResAwareBeta: grid maximize validation RES subject to REL ≤ 0.015 + λ(a−1)². Brier-OGD ensemble: simplex OGD on Brier for ensemble weights. Adaptive delta hedge: hedge experts over δ candidates; sit-out loss ≈ 0.25. Free stretch p′ = 0.5 + k(p−0.5) without outcomes is forbidden.

The design's central claim: probability maps cannot invent ranking from pure market-echo noise; they can raise Var[P_cal] = RES when the raw model is underconfident (mass squeezed toward 0.5) and the true posterior is sharper — provided expansion is outcome-fitted under a REL guard, never free stretch. Promotion path: GREEN×3 only on live eligibility floors — never on shadow alone; RES-calibration only when holdout REL holds and RES gain is real. Target: Brier ≤ 0.22.

Continuous-time portfolio theory (Agarwal & Sircar, arXiv:1610.08558) maximizing expected utility of wealth relative to its running maximum under a hard drawdown constraint: objective V(t,l,m,x,y) = sup_π E[U(L_T/M_T)] subject to L_s ≥ αM_s a.s., where l is wealth, m is the running maximum, and U(ξ) = ξ^{1−γ}/(1−γ) with γ=3.0 (and a two-term mixture with γ_1=3.0, γ_2=1.5). Dimensionality is reduced via ξ = l/m ∈ [α,1] (wealth-to-peak ratio) to a PDE for Q(t,ξ,x,y).
equation: V(t,l,m,x,y) = sup_π E[U(L_T/M_T)] subject to L_s ≥ αM_s a.s.; U(ξ)=ξ^{1−γ}/(1−γ); ξ = l/m ∈ [α,1]

claim: Policy findings across ξ∈[0.4,1] and volatility regimes: near the high watermark (ξ→1) the optimal policy gradually liquidates the risky position; with the stochastic-volatility correction the investor holds the risky position longer near the peak, then liquidates sharply to guard downside. At elevated vol (y=1.05θ): invest more than the constant-vol policy π_0 and build up faster away from the barrier; at y=0.95θ: invest less but hold more near the peak. The stochastic-vol correction to the VALUE function is small, but the corrected strategy π_0+π_1 is 'remarkably different' from π_0.

Weighted split conformal prediction under covariate shift (Tibshirani, Barber, Candès & Ramdas, NeurIPS 2019): when the covariate distribution shifts between calibration and test but the conditional outcome law P(Y|X) is stable, reweight calibration scores by the likelihood ratio w(x) = dP̃_X/dP_X. Weighted split conformal uses nonconformity scores on the calibration fold with the weighted empirical distribution Σ_i p̃_i δ_{V_i} + p̃_{n+1} δ_∞ where p̃_i ∝ w(X_i) normalized INCLUDING the test point's weight; the interval is the weighted (1−α)-quantile. Theoretical backbone: weighted exchangeability (joint density factorizes as Π w_i(v_i)·g(v) with symmetric g).
equation: w(x) = dP̃_X/dP_X; Σ_i p̃_i δ_{V_i} + p̃_{n+1} δ_∞ with p̃_i ∝ w(X_i)

claim: Weighted quantile lemma: P{ V_{n+1} ≤ Quantile(β; Σ_i p̃_i δ_{V_i} + p̃_{n+1} δ_∞) } ≥ β; corollary: with correct weights, target marginal coverage ≥ 1−α. Effective sample size heuristic: n̂ = ‖w‖_1²/‖w‖_2². Practical weight estimation uses probabilistic classification (e.g., logistic regression) distinguishing calibration vs test covariates. Assumptions: (i) P_{Y|X} invariant between calibration and test; (ii) w(x) known or well-estimated; (iii) absolute continuity (finite weights).
equation: P{ V_{n+1} ≤ Quantile(β; Σ_i p̃_i δ_{V_i} + p̃_{n+1} δ_∞) } ≥ β; n̂ = ‖w‖_1²/‖w‖_2²

claim: On the Airfoil self-noise dataset (UCI, 1,503 observations, 5 covariates, target = sound pressure level, nominal 90% coverage, 5,000 random trials, shifted test resampled with w(x)=exp(xᵀβ)): average empirical coverage was 90.2% for ordinary split conformal with no shift (sanity check); under shift, ordinary split conformal gave 82.2% (severe undercoverage), while weighted conformal with oracle weights restored 90.8%. The weighted histogram is more dispersed (reduced n̂); an n̂-matched unweighted comparison lines up closely — dispersion is the price of weighting, not a defect.

The bivariate-Poisson home-advantage model (Benz & Lopez, arXiv:2012.14949): (Y_H, Y_A) ~ BP(λ_1, λ_2, λ_3) with log λ_1 = μ_ks + T_k·I_pre + T'_k·I_post + α_H + δ_A (home attack + away defense + home-advantage term), log λ_2 = μ_ks + α_A + δ_H, log λ_3 = γ_k (constant covariance); team attack/defense strengths are seasonal random effects centered at 0. Priors: μ_ks ~ N(0,25); α,δ,τ ~ N(0,σ²), σ ~ Inverse-Gamma(1,1); T_k, T'_k ~ N(0,25). The λ_3=0 (independence) variant was used since observed goal correlation was −0.16 to 0.07.
equation: (Y_H, Y_A) ~ BP(λ_1, λ_2, λ_3); log λ_1 = μ_ks + T_k·I_pre + T'_k·I_post + α_H + δ_A; log λ_2 = μ_ks + α_A + δ_H; log λ_3 = γ_k; μ_ks ~ N(0,25); α,δ,τ ~ N(0,σ²), σ ~ Inverse-Gamma(1,1); T_k, T'_k ~ N(0,25)

claim: In a simulation study of 1,800 simulated seasons (100 per cell × 18 cells, ρ* ∈ {−0.8,−0.4,0}, T* ∈ {0,0.25,0.5}), mean absolute bias of home advantage (goal-difference scale): bivariate Poisson 0.051-0.084 across all cells; linear regression 0.382-0.549 (~6× larger bias — ~85% bias reduction from BP); paired comparison 0.059-0.094 (close to BP).

Covid ghost-games home-advantage posterior means (log scale, pre → post): Austrian Bundesliga 0.161 → −0.202 (−225.7%, P(decline)=0.999); German Bundesliga 0.239 → −0.024 (−110.2%, 0.995); Greek Super League 0.409 → 0.167 (−59.3%, 0.972); Spanish La Liga 0.306 → 0.149 (−51.3%, 0.959); English Championship 0.234 → 0.114 (P=0.912); six leagues showed increases (Swiss Super League 0.180 → 0.362, +101.1%, P(decline)=0.043; Serie A 0.204 → 0.292, P=0.125). P(decline) > 0.9 in 7/17 leagues, > 0.5 in 11/17 — a 'mixed' verdict vs the pooled literature's uniform-drop finding. Pre-Covid heterogeneity was 2.5× (Greek 0.409 vs Austrian 0.161), justifying league-specific estimation.

The FC-WQ two-step tail-risk framework (Storti & Wang, arXiv:2104.04918v2): Step 1 combines a universe of VaR models separately at each quantile level via Q̂_t^{(C,α_j)} = c_{0,j} + Σ_i c_{i,j} Q̂_{t,i}^{(α_j)} (Eq. 10), with grid α_1=0.005 < … < α_M=0.025 (M=3 or 5), n_mod=8 models, weights ĉ_{j,N+h} fit per level by minimizing rolling-window quantile loss (Eqs. 12-13), and Chernozhukov et al. (2010) monotonization to prevent quantile crossing. Step 2 converts combined quantiles into an Expected Shortfall forecast: EŜ_t^{(FC-WQ)} = w_0 + Σ_{j=1}^M w_j Q̂_t^{(C,α_j)} (Eq. 11), where w_j = Beta(j/M; a, b) density weights (Eq. 8), w_0 absorbs left-truncation bias, and (w_0,a,b) are estimated by minimizing the Fissler–Ziegel strictly consistent joint VaR–ES log-score (AL log-score, Eqs. 15-16) via Matlab fminunc. Design insight: model uncertainty lives in Step 1 (each level gets its own weights); Step 2 follows from the definition of ES as a tail-quantile average, so the combined ES is 'purged of model uncertainty.'

Beta weight function: w(x;a,b) = x^{a−1}(1−x)^{b−1} Γ(a+b)/(Γ(a)Γ(b)). Joint VaR–ES score: S_t = −log((α−1)/EŜ_t) − (r_t − Q̂_t^{(C,α)})(α − I(r_t ≤ Q̂_t^{(C,α)}))/(α EŜ_t), jointly minimized at the true (VaR, ES). Quantile combination loss: QL̄_{t,N}(α_j, c) = (1/N) Σ_{k=1}^N (α_j − I_{t−k,j})(r_{t−k} − X̂_{t−k}c), X̂ = [1, Q̂^{(U,α_j)}].

FC-WQ evaluation on 6 equity indices through the 2008 crisis (out-of-sample H = 2000 days from January 2008): VaR 2.5% violation MAD (VRate/α, target 1.0): FC-WQ 0.0028 (best), CARE-AS 0.0031, EGARCH-t-HS 0.0035, CAViaR-AS 0.0038, GJR-GARCH-t 0.0128 (worst); per-market VRate/α: S&P 1.04, Hang Seng 0.98, FTSE 1.00, DAX 1.18, SMI 1.32, ASX 0.90. VaR quantile loss (average): FC-WQ 164.2 (best) vs GJR-GARCH-t 166.6 (worst); S&P 500: FC-WQ 160.7 vs GJR-GARCH-t 162.9. Joint VaR–ES AL log-score (average): FC-WQ-3 4257.6 (best), FC-WQ-5 4257.8, FC-SA-5 4265.8, ES-CAViaR-Mult-AS 4266.5, GJR-GARCH-t 4314.8 (worst). The win decomposes: combination beats individuals (FC-SA < CAViaR-AS-SA); Beta weighting beats simple averaging (FC-WQ < FC-SA); combining models beats single-model WQ. Stability: FC-WQ's per-step losses visibly more stable through 2009-2012; M=3 ≈ M=5 (negligible gain from finer grids).

In the NBA timeout causal study (Gibbs, Elmore & Fosdick, arXiv:2011.11691), a scoring run is defined as ≥9-point change in score difference Δ(t) within the prior 2 minutes; run duration δt = min{argmax_d(|Δ(t)−Δ(t−d)| : 0<d≤2)}; signed run total s(t) = Δ(t)−Δ(t−δt). The novel outcome (Eq. 5) is yi = −sgn(s(ti)) ∫_{ti}^{ti+1} [Δ(x)−Δ(ti)] dx — the integrated, centered score difference over the 1-minute post-treatment window, where positive means the run was stopped or reversed.
equation: δt = min{argmax_d(|Δ(t)−Δ(t−d)| : 0<d≤2)}; s(t) = Δ(t)−Δ(t−δt); yi = −sgn(s(ti)) ∫_{ti}^{ti+1} [Δ(x)−Δ(ti)] dx

claim: The causal estimand is ATT = E[Yi(1)−Yi(0) | Ti=1], with franchise ATT (Eq. 6): ATTf = E[Yi(1)−Yi(0) | Ti=1, Bi=1] computed with non-parametric bootstrap 95% CIs, paired permutation tests, and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control. Units: plays meeting 4 criteria (run occurring; no timeout in the 2-min pre-treatment window; no timeout in the 1-min post-treatment window; windows not truncated by period end); final sample 4,684 runs (834 treated with timeout, 3,850 controls); |moneyline|>2400 units dropped for positivity. Propensity came from a GAM on 13 covariates (teams, run point total, run duration, time left, win probability, signed score diff at run start/end, possession, home, week, over/under, spread, moneyline) with 1,000 Monte-Carlo 70/30 splits giving PPV 0.612, NPV 0.847; matching was genetic matching (R Matching package) minimizing generalized Mahalanobis distance on covariates + propensity score, one-to-many with replacement.
equation: ATT = E[Yi(1)−Yi(0) | Ti=1]; ATTf = E[Yi(1)−Yi(0) | Ti=1, Bi=1]

claim: Findings: the naive (unmatched) estimate was −0.08 (insignificant), but the matched ATT was −0.35 (Abadie–Imbens SE 0.07, p < 0.001) — calling a timeout during an opposing run is slightly disadvantageous on average (the opposing team continues to outscore at a faster rate than in matched no-timeout runs). 20 of 30 franchises had negative point estimates; after FDR control, the Indiana Pacers and Utah Jazz were significantly negative; no positive franchise effect survives correction. The effect was negative and significant for every alternative run definition (7-10 points × 1.5-3 min grid); 20 genetic-matching re-runs were consistent. Rosenbaum sensitivity: the 95% CI includes 0 at Γ ≈ 1.50 (authors note the bound is conservative). Chicago Bulls had the most treated runs (41); median 27.5 per franchise.

MiGNet 2.0 detects true head impacts from instrumented-mouthguard false triggers with a deep 1D CNN: 2× [1D conv (64/128 filters, 5×1/10×1), maxpool 2, batchnorm, dropout 40%], reshape to 2D, 2D conv (64 filters, 3×15, stride 3×1), global average pooling, batchnorm, dropout 40%, softmax. Sensor: Stanford MiG2.0 mouthguard — triaxial accelerometer (±400 g @ 1000 Hz) + triaxial gyroscope (±4000 °/s @ 8000 Hz); 10 g trigger; 200 ms windows (−50 ms pre, +150 ms post); 6 input channels (ax, ay, az, αx, αy, αz). The physics-informed component adds synthetic true impacts from a finite-element head-neck model generated to match mouthguard output style; training strategies compared: field only, field + 25% synthetic, field + 100% synthetic, and pretrain on synthetic (+verified falses) then fine-tune on field — the pretrain-then-fine-tune strategy won.

The F-score metric used is Fβ = (1+β²)·(precision·recall)/(β²·precision + recall), with F2 emphasized because missing true impacts is costlier; the replacement bar was F2 ≥ 0.90. Test results: MiGNet 2.0 F1 0.95 / F2 0.98 vs Wu et al. 2018 (SVM) 0.90/0.88, Gabler et al. 2020 (AdaBoost CART) 0.89/0.84, Domel et al. 2020 (CNN) 0.79/0.75 (cross-dataset comparison, acknowledged imperfect). Training strategies (test NPV/PPV): field only 0.69/0.97; +synthetic max 0.72/1.00; augmented + 25% synthetic 0.76/0.97; balanced + 100% synthetic 0.87/0.86; pretrain-then-finetune 0.89/0.86 (best NPV). Workflow trial (6 participants, 88 mouthguard events): manual video review took ~12 hours vs automated ~0 hours; both found all 61 true impacts; false impacts: manual 27, auto 20; auto had 7 false positives and 0 false negatives — clearing the F2 ≥ 0.90 replacement bar.

The ice-arena study solves the transient heat-conduction PDE ∂u/∂t = α_I ∂²u/∂x² on 0<x<30 mm with u(0,t)=T_S(t), u(L,t)=T_I(t), by eigenfunction expansion with time-dependent Dirichlet boundary conditions fitted from measurements: solution = linear quasi-steady profile + eigenfunction series Σ{∫₀ᵗ e^(−αλₙ²(t−τ))Ŝₙ(τ)dτ + e^(−αλₙ²t)cₙ}sin(λₙx), λₙ=nπ/L. It assumes 1-D conduction, known-from-data Dirichlet BCs, and constant thermal diffusivity; only the first ~6-7 eigenfunction terms matter, with correction maximal at t=0 and minimal ~50 s.
equation: ∂u/∂t = α_I ∂²u/∂x², 0<x<30 mm; u(0,t)=T_S(t), u(L,t)=T_I(t); Σ{∫₀ᵗ e^(−αλₙ²(t−τ))Ŝₙ(τ)dτ + e^(−αλₙ²t)cₙ}sin(λₙx), λₙ=nπ/L

claim: Ice-arena findings (Reebok Arena, Leppävaara, Finland): heat-load split was ceiling thermal radiation 74%, lighting 14%, convection ~10%, condensation ~2%; refrigeration was ≈ 43% of hall energy use, ~1,800 MWh/yr. One resurfacing event (450 kg water at 40°C on ice at −4.5°C surface): Q_w = 231.21 MJ total (Q1 water cooling 75.28, Q2 freezing 152.1, Q3 ice cooling 3.69 MJ). Energy-balance closure: theoretical 142.37 kJ/m² vs measured 140.49 kJ/m² (1.32% error); steady-state flux 42.87 vs 41.85 W/m². Air was strongly stratified: −3.5°C at 5 mm, +4.2°C at 5 m. The ledger's verdict is REJECT — no sports-outcome data, no weather observations used for prediction, no transferable mechanism for a prediction engine.

The SR-RAG sports-rehabilitation retrieval system (Zhang et al., arXiv:2601.00216v1) structures retrieval around evidence-based-medicine principles: (1) PICO-schema GraphRAG — retrieve from a knowledge graph by matching the question's PICO structure (357,844 nodes, 371,226 edges, 44,033 PICO-aligned medical nodes); (2) PICO-guided HyDE — hypothetical PICO-structured answer as dense retrieval query; (3) ColBERT + BGE reranking; (4) separate evidence-grade pools — retrieval runs independently within each grade A–E so weak evidence cannot drown out strong evidence; (5) BETR reranker with monotone grade biases. Generator: DeepSeek-V3 (also tested with other backbones).

The BETR (Bradley–Terry evidence reranker) is P(d+ ≻ d−|q) = σ(a·Δs + u_{t+} − u_{t−}), where Δs is the base relevance-score gap and u_t are learned grade biases constrained monotone in evidence grade (u_A ≥ u_B ≥ … ≥ u_E), with MAP priors, trained on pairwise human preference labels.

SR-RAG evaluation on a new 1,637-question sports-rehab benchmark (983/327/327 train/val/test): DeepSeek-V3 + SR-RAG (test) achieved R@10 0.812, nugget coverage 0.830, faithfulness 0.819, semantic similarity 0.882, PICOT match 0.788 — leading on every metric vs naive RAG (0.643 / 0.718 / 0.769 / 0.841 / 0.582), Youtu-GraphRAG (0.741 / 0.773 / 0.798 / 0.868 / 0.659), and Med-R2 (0.724 / 0.758 / 0.803 / 0.861 / 0.678). Ranking ablation (four quality metrics): full BETR 3.51 / 0.473 / 0.847 / 0.641 vs semantic-only 3.18 / 0.362 / 0.781 / 0.523 vs heuristic grade weighting 3.34 / 0.418 / 0.814 / 0.586 — full BETR wins on all four, but heuristic weighting gets most of the way there. Human-verified n=80: SR-RAG 0.762 vs Med-R2 0.649. No latency/cost analysis of the five-stage pipeline was provided.

The forecast-accuracy assumption (martingale): E[p_t | p_{t−1} = a] = a — prices are unbiased forecasts. The winner-conditioned update is E[p_t | E, p_{t−1} = a] = a + Var(p_t | p_{t−1} = a)/a — price changes are proportional to conditional uncertainty.
equation: E[p_t | p_{t−1} = a] = a; E[p_t | E, p_{t−1} = a] = a + Var(p_t | p_{t−1} = a)/a

claim: In log-likelihood space, work with logit(p) = ln(p/(1−p)); price changes in this space are approximately symmetric and power-law distributed; the winner/loser movement ratio is predicted ≈ e^ε (ε = log-likelihood step size) and was empirically 'reasonably close.' A coin-flip information-arrival simulation (22 synthetic markets, n=1200 flips) showed log score rising linearly with time, accelerating near resolution.
equation: logit(p) = ln(p/(1−p)); winner/loser movement ratio ≈ e^ε

claim: Expected entropy loss (information gain) for a term w is E[IG] = Σ P(w) · KL(class distribution | w || class distribution) — it ranks event-explaining words/phrases around market-move dates. Limitations of the 2002 paper: old, small, political-market sample; no held-out prediction test; retrospective and outcome-conditioned; the martingale assumption fails under the favorite-longshot bias and time-varying risk premia documented in sports markets.
equation: E[IG] = Σ P(w) · KL(class distribution | w || class distribution)

claim: The account-level sign-randomization skill test: per account, permute trade signs (long/short) 10,000 times holding magnitudes/timing fixed; compare realized P&L against the 10,000-draw null distribution to get a skill p-value; accounts above the null are 'skilled winners' (persistent directional skill conditional on opportunity selection). The insider heuristic is single-event lifecycle + conviction (position size relative to account) + recent account creation — it catches the single-event population the skill classifier excludes by design.

Sign-randomization results on full Polymarket transaction history 2023-2025 (1.72M accounts, 210,322 markets, $13.76B volume): 54,477 skilled winners (3.14% of 1.72M accounts) with 44% out-of-sample retention; 110,703 unskilled losers (6.4%); lucky winners 29.0%; unlucky losers 61.4%; makers 0.1%.
