Skilled winners + makers (<3.5% of accounts) capture >30% of gains.

Composite statistical screen: $143M anomalous profit over 210k+ wallet–market pairs. Insider heuristic on 1,950 flagged accounts: mean profit $15,012.92, median $2,758.29; imbalance predicted the next price move (t=2.54) and outcomes (t=8.65). Information Leakage Score Iran-conflict case: ILS_dl = +0.113 vs resolution proxy −0.331 (0.444 apart); the Iran conflict cluster had >$832M cumulative volume across 18 markets, but only 1 of 18 met all ILS pipeline conditions — the pipeline is brittle on real data. Sports is 42.05% of Polymarket markets / 35.37% of volume.

Greedy Gibbs sampling for KL-regularized contextual bandits (Wang et al., arXiv:2609.13564): the greedy policy is π_t(a|x) ∝ π_ref(a|x)·exp(η·R̂_t(x,a)) (Eq. 4), where R̂_t is the least-squares reward estimate over history. The KL-regularized regret is Reg_RF(T) := Σ_{t=1}^{T} (J_RF(π*) − J_RF(π_t)) (Eq. 2), with regret decomposition Reg_RF(T) ≤ η·Σ_{t=1}^{T} S_t (Lemma 4, Eq. 5).
equation: π_t(a|x) ∝ π_ref(a|x)·exp(η·R̂_t(x,a)); Reg_RF(T) := Σ_{t=1}^{T} (J_RF(π*) − J_RF(π_t)); Reg_RF(T) ≤ η·Σ_{t=1}^{T} S_t

claim: Theorem 1: Reg_RF(T) = O(η e^{2η} log T log(N_R T/δ)); GP: O(η e^{3η} log T log(N_P T/δ)); BT: O(η e^{2η} log T log(N_R T/δ)). Trade-off: greedy Gibbs beats UCB when e^{2η} log T ≲ d_RF (eluder dimension); UCB wins at large η (weak regularization). The Bradley–Terry preference model is P*(x,a¹,a²) = σ(R*(x,a¹) − R*(x,a²)) with σ(z) = (1+e^{−z})^{−1}.
equation: Reg_RF(T) = O(η e^{2η} log T log(N_R T/δ)); P*(x,a¹,a²) = σ(R*(x,a¹) − R*(x,a²)), σ(z) = (1+e^{−z})^{−1}

claim: On a synthetic contextual bandit (|X|=3 contexts, |A|=3 actions, |R|=5 reward functions, horizon T=5000, 10 seeds, η ∈ {0.5, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 500, 1000, 2000}), RF-GS achieves 'substantially lower regret' than K-UCB for small/moderate η; as η increases the Gibbs policy concentrates, RF-GS under-explores, and K-UCB 'eventually outperforms.' The GP result sharpens Wu et al. 2025 by removing their η³e^{9η} term (Corollary: Õ(min{η d_GP, √(d_GP T)})). No numeric regret values are reported in the text (figure only); the crossover η is not stated.

The Lens2Zernike model (Jhawar et al., arXiv:2603.04999) blindly recovers physical optical aberration parameters — a 36-dim Zernike coefficient vector (Z2–Z37, Noll indexing) — from a single blurred smartphone image, with total loss L_total = λz·Lcoeff + λp·Lphysics + λm·Lmap (Eq. 1): Lcoeff is MSE in normalized Zernike coefficient space; Lphysics is MSE on the wavefront/PSF derived via a differentiable optics layer (Fourier transform of predicted coefficients); Lmap adds auxiliary decoder heads predicting high-resolution wavefront and PSF maps. Hyperparameters (LR, optimizer, epochs, λ weights) are not stated in the paper.

Optics findings: full model (z+p+m) MAE 0.00128λ / MSE 4.20×10⁻⁵ vs baseline coeff-only 0.00197λ / 5.82×10⁻⁵ — ~35% MAE improvement; beat literature baselines DLWFS (Xception) 0.00173λ and DLAO (LAPANet) 0.00324λ. Downstream Wiener deconvolution: mean PSNR 24.66 dB (predicted PSFs) vs oracle 25.02 dB (−0.36 dB gap). Synthetic-only training (110,090 synthetic blurred images via Fourier-optics forward simulation; IDMxS Mobile Camera Lens Database of 109 smartphone lens designs, proprietary); real-hardware validation is future work. The ledger's verdict is REJECT — no sports, betting, or prediction content.

The darts study compares five win-probability models: Null π_NULL = ½·(1 + (s1−s2)/100), truncated [0,1] (0.5 pp per score point); Logistic π_REG = 1/(1 + e^{-(c0 + c_{p1} − c_{p2} + c1·s1 + c2·s2)}); Basic simulation (Monte Carlo, 1000 games from current score, π_SIM = W/1000); Time-adjusted sim with a distance vector + multiplier vector m = ⟨m0, m1, m2, m3⟩; and Score-dependent Massey (SDMM, new): perceived strength at score s_i is (271−s_i)/271·r_i^(1) + s_i/271·r_i^(2), π_SDMM = ½·(1 + Δperceived), truncated [0,1].

The head-to-head betting-game evaluation protocol (model A posts odds, model B bets, profit decides): the expected payout for betting on an event is |α_t−β_t|·(p_t − α_t) — positive iff the true probability exceeds model α's estimate. It is a portable, economic model-comparison tool: the null model showed a betting edge over every model except SDMM, indicating the other models systematically overestimated the favorite — a finding Brier can mask.

Darts results (1,131 games, 2,465 round-predictions): Brier — Null 0.1902, Logistic 0.1980 (worst, overfit on low-sample players), Basic Sim 0.1849, Adjusted Sim 0.1857, SDMM 0.1807 (best); Round-1: SDMM 0.2372 vs Null 0.2500. Recalibrated null π'_NULL = ½·(1 + (s1−s2)/85) gave Brier 0.1889 (marginal effect 100·Δr/542 = 0.59 pp/point). The paper's conclusion (exact): 'we conclude that the probabilities generated by the score-dependent Massey model most accurately reflect reality, although the model may systematically err on the conservative side.'

KASportsFormer (Yin et al., arXiv:2507.20763) is a 2D→3D pose-lifting transformer with an explicit kinematic-anatomy stream: input X ∈ ℝ^{F×J×3} (F=27 frames, J=17 joints, 2D coords + confidence); bone features H_bone and limb tokens H_limb via an MLP composer L = P(B), including fused 'hyperlimb' cross-body connections; multi-stream spatiotemporal transformer with Token Blending H^i = α^i_AC ⊙ H^i_AC + α^i_AS ⊙ H^i_AS + α^i_G ⊙ H^i_G.
equation: H^i = α^i_AC ⊙ H^i_AC + α^i_AS ⊙ H^i_AS + α^i_G ⊙ H^i_G

claim: KASportsFormer losses: L_pos = Σ_tΣ_j‖P̂_t − P_t‖₂; L_vel = Σ_tΣ_j‖ΔP̂_t − ΔP_t‖₂; total L = L_pos + λL_vel (λ not stated in paper). Training: 120 epochs, batch 32, AdamW lr 5e−4, wd 0.01; 29.3M params (N=26 layers, d=128, h=8). Metrics: MPJPE and P-MPJPE (mm, lower better) under DET (HRNet-estimated 2D) and GT (ground-truth 2D) conditions.
equation: L_pos = Σ_tΣ_j‖P̂_t − P_t‖₂; L_vel = Σ_tΣ_j‖ΔP̂_t − ΔP_t‖₂; L = L_pos + λL_vel

claim: KASportsFormer results: SportsPose 27-frame DET 58.0/44.3 vs MotionAGFormer-L 59.5/47.1 (−1.5mm MPJPE) and D3DP 60.0/45.1 (−0.8mm P-MPJPE); GT 30.9/27.9; it loses on the Soccer action (+0.7mm, attributed to limited perception of limb acceleration in kicking). WorldPose DET 34.2/22.0 vs MotionAGFormer-B 35.6/22.9; GT 8.5/6.2 vs MotionBERT 9.3/6.8. Ablations (DET MPJPE): baseline 59.6, w/o bone 58.6, w/o limb 58.9, softmax-blending 59.0, ours 58.0. The ledger's verdict is REJECT — CV infrastructure with no path to game-outcome prediction.

The cricket speed–accuracy tradeoff is modeled as a power law r = K_bat · τ^{−α}, where r is the run scoring rate ('speed') and τ is the innings half-life ('accuracy'); the proportional form is (∂r/r)/(∂τ/τ) = −α (Eq. 4); the total-runs scaling S ∼ r^{1−1/α} implies for α>1 total runs increase with rate, for α<1 they decrease, and α=1 leaves them unchanged (form uncertain — PDF extraction garbled).

The drift–diffusion forward model of cricket score evolution: recurrence P_S(S,B) → Fokker–Planck ∂P_s/∂b = −r ∂P_s/∂s + D ∂²P_s/∂s² − r_e P_s; first-passage density ψ(s,b) = ∫_0^b [s/√(4πDt³)] exp[−(s−rt)²/(4Dt) − r_e t] dt; chase metric P/b_m. It assumes identical balls, ignores bowler effects, predicts average batter performance, and was never validated against held-out match data.
equation: ∂P_s/∂b = −r ∂P_s/∂s + D ∂²P_s/∂s² − r_e P_s; ψ(s,b) = ∫_0^b [s/√(4πDt³)] exp[−(s−rt)²/(4Dt) − r_e t] dt

claim: Cricket tradeoff estimates: collective fit batters α = 0.618 (Pearson R = −0.902, p < 10^{−15}); bowlers α = 0.695 (R = −0.898, p < 10^{−15}); individuals: batters mean α = 0.680 (95% CI [0.617, 0.743], R < −0.880), bowlers mean α = 0.679 (95% CI [0.623, 0.734], R < −0.930), range 0.4-1.1. The average batter (α=0.62<1): increasing scoring rate reduces total runs; α>1 players are rare and 'always perform better irrespective of the game format.' Format suitability: high α → shorter formats (T20I), low α → longer formats (Tests); flips between b=20 and b=100 balls, and targets s=50 vs s=300. The ledger's verdict is REJECT — cricket-only, no predictive validation.

The soccer predictability model (Maimone & Yasseri, arXiv:1908.08991): build a directed graph loser→winner weighted by points, take strength as eigenvector centrality, set x = home centrality − away centrality, and map to a probability with y = 1/(1 + exp(−(x−μ)/s)) (Eq. 4.1); μ is fitted by OLS, y=1 for a home win, y=0 for an away win; ties are excluded; μ quantifies home-field advantage.
equation: y = 1/(1 + exp(−(x−μ)/s)); x = home centrality − away centrality

claim: Market and Elo benchmarks from the predictability study: market benchmark (Eq. 4.2) Prob(HomeWin) = (1/h)/(1/h + 1/a), Prob(AwayWin) = (1/a)/(1/h + 1/a); Elo comparison E_i = 1/(1 + 10^((R_j−R_i)/400)), R'_i = R_i + K(S_i − E_i) with K=32, start 1500; Brier (Eq. 4.6) P = 1/((1−n)T)·Σ_jΣ_i (f_ij − E_ij)²; training window is past N matches normalized by season length T: n = N/T (headline n = 0.5).

Soccer predictability findings (87,816 matches, 11 European leagues, 1993/94–2018/19): football became more predictable, tracking rising inequality (Gini) and declining home-field advantage — positive AUC trend in England, France, Germany, Netherlands, Portugal, Scotland, Spain; first-10-vs-last-10 t-test significant for England (AUC p=0.0330), Germany (0.0326), Portugal (0.0044), Spain (0.0097); Gini t-test significant for England (0.0009), Germany (0.0367), Portugal (0.0000), Spain (0.0001); all leagues 'tend to converge towards 0.75 AUC.' Gini–AUC correlation: Spain 0.874, England 0.823, Germany 0.805, Scotland 0.723, Portugal 0.694, Turkey 0.686, Netherlands 0.676, Italy 0.622, France 0.563, Greece 0.561, Belgium 0.413. Home advantage declined in all leagues. The network model beats Elo AUC in ~61% of cases (170 of 280 league-seasons); it 'underperforms the market on average,' but Brier/AUC differences are 'statistically indistinguishable at the 2% significance level for the majority of year-leagues.'

TA-3DGS uses a time-indexed fixed-size 3D Gaussian representation G_t = {g_{t,k}} with covariance Σ_{t,k} = R(q_{t,k}) diag(s_{t,k}²) R(q_{t,k})ᵀ and densification DISABLED (‖G_t‖ = K for all t); the warm-chain initializes Θ_t^{(0)} ← Θ*_{t−1} (forward) or Θ*_{t+1} (backward) — initialization ONLY, no temporal constraint. Per-frame objective (Eq. 15, reconstructed — notation uncertain): L_t(Θ_t) = Σ_i L_img(Θ_t; I_t^{(i)}) + λ_reg R(Θ_t), R = Σ_k (‖s‖² + α² + ‖b‖²).
equation: Σ_{t,k} = R(q_{t,k}) diag(s_{t,k}²) R(q_{t,k})ᵀ; L_t(Θ_t) = Σ_i L_img(Θ_t; I_t^{(i)}) + λ_reg R(Θ_t), R = Σ_k (‖s‖² + α² + ‖b‖²)

claim: 3D Gaussian Splatting results (Blender 4.0 synthetic renders): D-WS 42.50 PSNR / 0.0110 LPIPS vs TACV 34.28/0.0275, 4DGS 28.17/0.0800, D-3DGS 18.45/0.1396, D-NeRF 6.44/0.5726; S-PK 44.59/0.0023; S-MP 43.84/0.0023. Ablation: Warm+Densify splats grow 188,393→846,094 over 5 frames (44.56→200.11 MB) vs Warm+NoDensify fixed 100,000 splats (23.65 MB, ~194–202 s/frame). The ledger's verdict is REJECT — no calibrated synchronized multi-camera NFL capture exists, broadcast footage is excluded, and AI-synthesized video conflicts with the standing video rule.

The supply-chain LLM+MIP case study: maximize Σ_tΣ_i (safety-stock reward − shortage penalty) − Σ_tΣ_{i,j} (fixed transfer cost · Y_{i,j,t}), subject to inventory balance inv_{i,t} = inv_{i,t−1} + inbound − outbound − demand + replenishment, safety-stock constraint inv ≥ ss − short, and big-M linking 0 ≤ x ≤ cap·Y, Y ∈ {0,1}. The two-LLM pipeline layers over the classical MIP: LLM1 builds role-specific context (planner/finance/warehouse views); LLM2 reflects/checks LLM1's context for consistency; the optimizer's outputs are the only numbers the LLMs may present.
equation: 0 ≤ x ≤ cap·Y, Y ∈ {0,1}; inv_{i,t} = inv_{i,t−1} + inbound − outbound − demand + replenishment

claim: The supply-chain case study claimed savings of $394,734 vs the no-transfer baseline — a single proprietary case with no counterfactual methodology shown; there is no baseline optimizer comparison, no LLM hallucination/explanation-accuracy evaluation, and no ablation of two-LLM reflection vs a single LLM; the constraint notation is internally inconsistent (index i for SKU and DC; y/Y casing). The transferable asset is the architecture pattern: deterministic optimizer as the sole source of truth, LLM as explainer checked against the optimizer's numbers.

The EURO hybrid tournament-forecasting model (Groll et al., arXiv:2106.05799): historic abilities via log(λ_ijm) = β_0 + (r_i − r_j) + h·1(home) (Eq. 1), bivariate Poisson with time-decay weight w_time,m = (1/2)^(x_m/half-period), half-period 3 years, Σr_i=0, weighted MLE. Random forest via ranger (Breiman) and cforest (conditional inference trees), B=5000, mtry=√p=4; XGBoost via xgb.train with 10-fold CV tuning; baseline lasso Poisson via cv.glmnet. Expected goals become Poisson intensities λ; win/draw/loss via the Skellam distribution; extra time λ×1/3; penalties = coin flip.

The bookmaker-consensus ability estimate: strip the overround (median 17.3%), average log-odds across 19 books, then run inverse tournament simulation (100k runs) with Bradley-Terry pairwise probabilities to find abilities matching consensus. Plus-minus ratings: ridge regression of segment goal differences on player presence indicators (±1) with country home advantage, red-card, age, and league adjustments, with triple weighting (recency, duration, goal state).

EURO results (leave-one-tournament-out, 144 matches, EURO 2004–2016): cforest likelihood 0.382 / classification rate 0.486 / RPS 0.213; xgboost 0.380 / 0.486 / 0.217; ranger 0.372 / 0.458 / 0.216; lasso 0.379 / 0.458 / 0.210; bookmakers 0.400 / 0.493 / 0.203. MAE of goals: lasso best 0.846 (cforest/xgboost 0.862–0.883). Variable importance: market.value top (~0.055 mean decrease in accuracy), then logability, CL.players, ave.PM, UEFA.points, FIFA.rank ≈ HistAbility, GDP. 100k EURO 2020 simulations (win %): France 14.8, England 13.5, Spain 12.3, Portugal 10.1, Germany 10.1, Belgium 8.3, Italy 7.9, Hungary 0.0. xgboost showed 'higher sensitivity and instability during tuning,' attributed to small sample; cforest chosen as 'best and most reliable.' Benchmark asymmetry: bookmaker odds fixed days pre-match embed late info (injuries) the model cannot see.

FieldConverter's geometry initialization (§3.4): select the lowest valid lower-limb keypoint j*, back-project through the calibrated camera, intersect with the pitch plane (z=0), and subtract the relative-pose offset: r^{c,init}_{i,t} = q^c_{i,t} − x̂^{rel}_{i,t,j*} (Eq. 18). Temporal residual refinement: a TCN (5 residual blocks, dilations 1,2,4,8,16, k=3, 1.278M params) or Transformer (2 encoder layers, 4 heads, 1.252M) over 41-frame windows, stride 8, outputs residual Δr̂^c with r̂^c = r^{c,init} + Δr̂^c (Eq. 33); overlapping windows are mean-aggregated (Eq. 34).
equation: r^{c,init}_{i,t} = q^c_{i,t} − x̂^{rel}_{i,t,j*}; r̂^c = r^{c,init} + Δr̂^c

claim: FieldConverter loss: L = λ_root L_root + λ_vel L_vel + λ_acc L_acc + λ_cam3D L_cam3D, with L_root = Smooth-L1 (β=1) on root residuals (Eqs. 35–36) plus velocity/acceleration auxiliaries (37–41). Input vector f_{i,t}: flattened pelvis-centered 3D skeleton + 2D keypoints + box geometry/log-aspect + camera descriptor (intrinsics, distortion, center, view direction) + world ray–ground intersection + validity mask (370/345 dims). Training: AdamW lr 1.6788×10⁻⁴, wd 3.2001×10⁻⁴, batch 64 windows, ≤60 epochs, early stopping patience 10, grad clip 1.0.
equation: L = λ_root L_root + λ_vel L_vel + λ_acc L_acc + λ_cam3D L_cam3D

claim: FieldConverter results on FIFA Skeletal Tracking Light 2026 (~2.41M player–frame observations; strictly match-disjoint splits): root error / World MPJPE / reprojection (cm/cm/px) — geometry-only 48.58 / 48.36 / 5.39; MLP residual 13.63 / 15.76 / 3.69; TCN residual 10.12 / 13.20 / 3.49; Transformer residual 11.04 / 13.21 / 3.43. Residual learning cuts root error ~72% vs geometry alone; temporal context matters more than the specific backbone. Direct absolute-root regression MLP gives 256.00 cm root error vs residual MLP 13.63 — the decomposition does the heavy lifting. Airborne failure: TCN root error ~10 cm grounded → ~15 cm at 10–13 cm foot clearance → 29 cm at 15–18 cm → 37 cm at highest clearance (geometry-only degrades 46 cm → ~1 m).

The undergraduate soccer video pipeline (MSOE, 2025) combines pretrained object detection + SAM2 tracking + a small custom keypoint CNN + DLT homography for 2D pitch positions: YOLOv5x selected with IoU 0.7644 / recall 0.7995 / precision 0.8963 / F1 0.8451 (best balance); all YOLOs beat Faster R-CNN (F1 0.7194) on every metric; 17/22 players identified with no fine-tuning. Keypoint CNN: visibility accuracy 99.89% train / 97.18% test; masked MAE 0.0107 train / 0.0138 test (normalized), 5.96px/7.65px. System: keypoint MAE 0.225m (ground truth) / 0.26m (predicted); average projection error 0.499m.

The soccer pipeline's admitted failures: ballboy/referee false positives; K-means team classification (k=2 on 5×5 RGB patches) flips under glare/shadows; no re-ID, no ball detection, no jersey numbers, and no tracking metrics (MOTA/IDF1 absent). Negative evidence: K-means on jersey-color patches is brittle under glare — supervised jersey-number OCR + appearance embeddings are needed. The source paper's 'Zhang et al. 2024' 95.62% keypoint claim is a citation mismatch (bibliography maps to an underwater-image paper) and was REMOVED. The ledger's verdict is REJECT.
equation: keypoint loss = MAE over visible keypoints (weight 10) + binary cross-entropy on visibility (weight 1)

claim: GridMind (Telemetry Sports vendor paper, 2025) is a multi-agent NLP system over NFL data: (1) Prompt Augmentation Agent, (2) Query Interpretation Agent (T5-class + sentence embeddings, few-shot NL→MongoDB/SQL), (3) Data Retrieval Agents (structured / semi-structured NGS+CV / unstructured embedding search), (4) Synthesis Agent. Techniques: RAG, Sentence-BERT + OpenAI embeddings, Whisper speech-to-text, Pinecone vector DB, Chain-of-Thought query decomposition, dialogue memory. Anti-hallucination rule: ground numeric claims in structured data models.

GridMind evaluation: 58% good/bad retrieval accuracy in a 10-person closed alpha; latency 17.5s mean sequential with 20s+ outliers on complex queries. Worked examples (illustrative, not evaluated): Mahomes vs Purdy season yards 2,454 vs 2,208 with 12 TDs each; Anthony Richardson tWAR 0.10 (39th of 48 QBs); Ravens run blocking 19th/32; Vikings pass coverage 17th, rush defense 28th. Admitted failures: terminology mismatch ('OB-LB' confused users), metadata dependence, compute overhead. Proprietary metrics named (Passing Composite, QB Accuracy, QB Decision Making, QB IQ, tWAR) are vendor-locked and non-reproducible. No baselines vs competing systems, no ablation of agent contributions.

ShuttleSet (KDD '23) is a badminton dataset: 44 professional matches (2018–2021) annotated stroke-by-stroke by 6 experts (104 sets, 3,685 rallies, 36,492 strokes; 27 top players), with benchmark models ShuttleScorer, ShuttleNet, and DyMF. The only equation stated is the camera-to-world homography p' = Hp (H in R^3×3 from ≥4 court-corner correspondences; court 13.4m × 6.1m). Annotation consistency: temporal MAE 0.24 (serve) / 0.02 (return) / 0 (dead bird) frames; spatial MAE 0.18 (shuttle) / 0.86 (player); shot-type accuracy difference 0 / 0.05 / 0.11.

ShuttleSet benchmark results: ShuttleScorer shot-influence AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, Brier 0.1574 (vs Bi-GRU 0.6603/0.7054/0.2158 — 26.8% AUC, 11.6% ACC, 27.1% Brier improvement per paper); ShuttleNet stroke forecasting τ=8: cross-entropy 2.4125 / MSE 1.8121 / MAE 1.3582; DyMF movement forecasting τ=8: 2.3566/1.0963/1.5875. Most common men's shots: net shot 3,781 (15.45%), lob 3,124 (12.76%), return net 2,130 (8.70%). Case study: Ng Ka Long Angus's right side identified as a weak area. Per the file: no fixed train/test split; player coverage highly imbalanced; the 'used by national teams' deployment claim is unverifiable. The ledger's verdict is REJECT — zero transferable concept to NFL prediction.

Soccer critical-situation RL (Rahimian, Oroojlooy & Toka 2021): possession value PV(s) = P(shot|X)·P(goal|shot,X) (Eq. 1); reward r = PV(s) if shot, PV(s')−PV(s) if kept, −0.1 if lost (Eq. 2); return R(τ) = Σγᵗr / Σγᵗ with γ=0.99 (Eq. 3). Off-policy policy gradient: ∇_θE[f] = E[(p(x)/q(x))·f(x)·∇_θ log p(x)] (Eq. 4). Doubly robust estimator (Jiang & Li 2016): V_DR^{H+1−t} = V̂(s_t) + ρ_t(r_t + γV_DR^{H−t} − Q̂(s_t,a_t)), ρ_t = π₁/π₀ (Eq. 5). Behavior policy: CNN-LSTM (100-unit LSTM + softmax) over possession endings; defensive pressure via spectral clustering (kNN k=5 → Laplacian → K-means, ball holder as initial centroid, 3 zones, elbow method).
equation: PV(s) = P(shot|X)·P(goal|shot,X); R(τ) = Σγᵗr / Σγᵗ, γ=0.99; ∇_θE[f] = E[(p(x)/q(x))·f(x)·∇_θ log p(x)]; V_DR^{H+1−t} = V̂(s_t) + ρ_t(r_t + γV_DR^{H−t} − Q̂(s_t,a_t)), ρ_t = π₁/π₀

claim: Soccer RL results: the behavioral-policy classifier with hand-crafted + pressure features (state III) reached 81% accuracy, 0.56 loss, 56,036 params — pressure features beat exact locations (state II: 75%/0.65, fails to converge; state I: 68%/0.71). The trained policy's mean reward was ≈ +0.45 vs the behavioral ≈ −0.1 expected goals/episode, with all 104 games improved (in-sample OPE). Scenario analyses: the fouled player (−0.16) should have shot (0.4 expected); an error-conceded-goal situation should have fouled; bad control should have sent the ball out. The xG logistic regression reached AUC 0.798, Brier 0.012 (5-fold CV, beat XGBoost/RF/SVM). Honest failure modes noted: OPE evaluated on the same 104 training games (in-sample); the −0.1 loss penalty was hand-tuned; no IS weight diagnostics/clipping; no held-out matches for policy evaluation.

The Pythagorean win formula is W-L% = RS²/(RS²+RA²) with empirical exponent ≈ 1.83. The paper (Luo & Miller 2016) models runs scored/allowed as a linear combination (mixture) of two Weibull distributions: density f(x;α,β,γ) = (γ/α)((x−β)/α)^{γ−1} e^{−((x−β)/α)^γ}, x ≥ β; mixture win probability (Theorem 2.2, closed form): P(X>Y) = Σ_iΣ_j c_i c'_j · α_{RS_i}^γ / (α_{RS_i}^γ + α_{RA_j}^γ), with c_1+c_2 = 1. Fitting: 7 free parameters per team-season by least squares on half-integer-binned per-game runs; χ² goodness-of-fit (16 df, Bonferroni thresholds 37.7/42.5).
equation: W-L% = RS²/(RS²+RA²); f(x;α,β,γ) = (γ/α)((x−β)/α)^{γ−1} e^{−((x−β)/α)^γ}, x ≥ β; P(X>Y) = Σ_iΣ_j c_i c'_j · α_{RS_i}^γ / (α_{RS_i}^γ + α_{RA_j}^γ)

claim: Pythagorean mixture results (MLB 2004–2012): the fitted γ mean was 1.83 (sd 0.18, median 1.79) — reproducing the empirical exponent from theory; mean |games off| 2.89 (sd 2.34) in 2011; 2004–2012 mixture mean games off 3.11 (sd 2.33) vs single Weibull 4.22 (sd 3.03) — ~25% improvement, significant (p < 0.01). BUT vs baseball-reference pythWL (1979–2013): mixture 3.03 (sd 2.21) vs pythWL 3.09 (sd 2.26) — only 0.06 games better, NOT significant (very large p-value). Era split: pythWL better 1979–1989 (7/11 years); mixture better 1990–2013 (15/24 years, ~0.3 games when it wins). Simplification attempts failed: mixture weights highly volatile (c_1 mean 0.21, sd 0.39); fixing parameters gave 'significantly worse' predictions. χ² tests: independence of runs scored/allowed holds modulo structural zeros. The ledger's verdict is REJECT — the significant improvement is only over the paper's own single-Weibull strawman, not over the one-line formula everyone uses.

GraphQL query-cost learning (Mavroudeas et al., 2021): estimate(s,c,q) = m(h(s,c,q)) ≈ tcx(r, Query, c), where tcx is type complexity. Feature extractors: h_f (bag-of-words field counts), h_g (graph2vec AST embeddings), h_s (six summary features: static-analysis upper bound, query size, width, nesting, list count, sum of list limits). Three Lale AutoML pipelines (StandardScaler → {No-Op, polynomial, Nystroem} → {linear, tree, Ridge, RF, kNN k=3, GBR}), 43 hyperparameters, 5-fold CV with Hyperopt (60h / 1,500 combos per dataset), then a Wolpert stacked ensemble over the three estimates. Metrics: MAE = 1/n Σ|c_i − ĉ_i|; Error% = (ĉ−c)/c.
equation: estimate(s,c,q) = m(h(s,c,q)) ≈ tcx(r, Query, c); MAE = 1/n Σ|c_i − ĉ_i|; Error% = (ĉ−c)/c

claim: GraphQL cost results: GitHub GraphQL API — static bound MAE 31.5 ± 263.8 vs ML 8.2 ± 35.5; Yelp — static 14,180.5 ± 30,827.9 vs ML 60.7 ± 180.4. Ablation: summary features alone nearly match the stack (GitHub MAE 8.7 vs final 8.2); graph2vec embeddings were worst alone (GitHub 31.58, Yelp 880.9). Hyperopt preferred gradient boosting in most pipelines. Rate-limit simulation: threshold violations ≤6% of accepted queries on GitHub (≤80% over) and ≤15% on Yelp. Robustness: the ML estimate rises rapidly as the static-bound feature enters the malicious regime; GBR plateaus outside the training range (no extrapolation). The ledger's verdict is REJECT — GSE consumes metered-by-request APIs, so rate-limit needs are solved by request counting and caching, not ML cost prediction.

The Proximity-Aware Contextual Transformer (Prakash & Kothari 2024) for tabular prediction: objective L̂ = min_f Σ_i L(P_i, P̂_i) with P = f(U, R, C), where U is user features, R is round features, and C is proximity-aware contextual features (rounds t−5..t+5 around the current round). Tokenizer: T_j^(num) = b_j^(num) + x_j^(num)·W_j^(num); T_j^(cat) = b_j^(cat) + x_j^(cat)·W_j^(cat); T = stack of tokens → Transformer + [CLS] head. Training: Optuna Bayesian optimization on validation, 10 random seeds averaged, no model-agnostic DL tricks (no pretraining/augmentation/distillation/LR schedules) to isolate architecture.
equation: L̂ = min_f Σ_i L(P_i, P̂_i); P = f(U, R, C); T_j^(num) = b_j^(num) + x_j^(num)·W_j^(num); T_j^(cat) = b_j^(cat) + x_j^(cat)·W_j^(cat)

claim: Dream11 tabular results (7,074,749 train / 1,165,011 validation / 831,583 test tuples): test MAE / MSE — GBDT Baseline 42.4 / 500.35; MLP 40.4 / 362.53; ResNet 41.34 / 397.48; TabTransformer 37.99 / 442.74; FT-Transformer 38.07 / 448.90; Proposed 37.13 / 351.01 (best on both) — 2.5% MAE and 21.8% MSE over FT-Transformer. Train-fraction → MAE: 0.05 → 38.56; 0.5 → 37.13; 0.9 → 36.78 (monotone). Error-distribution reading: MLP has higher MAE but lower MSE (fewer extremes); TabTransformer/FT-Transformer have good MAE but worse MSE (more large errors). Gaps: the split is not stated to be time-ordered (leakage risk); the missing ablation is FT-Transformer + contextual features as plain inputs (no architecture change) — test features-vs-architecture separately before crediting the transformer; weak GBDT baseline (no Optuna-level tuning disclosed); no calibration/uncertainty.

ParlayMarket (Rana, Nadkarni, Moshrefi & Viswanath, Princeton/Kaleidoscope Blockchain, 2026) supports parlay-style joint contracts over M binary events with coherent pricing via a pairwise exponential-family (Ising) model: belief state (Eq. 11) P_φ(x) ∝ exp(Σ_i θ_i x_i + Σ_{i<j} W_ij x_i x_j) — the max-entropy distribution matching first/second moments; prices via belief propagation. Online dependence learning from trade flow: φ_{t+1} = φ_t − η∇_φ CE(p_m*, p_m^{φ_t}) (Eq. 13) — each trade treated as cross-entropy error on the composite pseudo-likelihood (Eq. 12); 'shadow trades' propagate information across markets. Contracts: f_S(x) = ∏_{i∈S} x_i (Eq. 1); prices p_S(φ) = E_{P_φ}[f_S(x)] (Eq. 2). Trader model: correlated arithmetic Brownian scores (Eq. 3).
equation: P_φ(x) ∝ exp(Σ_i θ_i x_i + Σ_{i<j} W_ij x_i x_j); φ_{t+1} = φ_t − η∇_φ CE(p_m*, p_m^{φ_t}); f_S(x) = ∏_{i∈S} x_i; p_S(φ) = E_{P_φ}[f_S(x)]

claim: ParlayMarket theorems: parameter contraction 0.9/round (Thm 1); mean per-market loss ℓ̄_M = O(bη/2^M) halves per added market (Prop 2); higher-order parlays raise μ_eff and accelerate convergence (Prop 3); loss is quadratic in parameter error (Lemma 1). Loss scaling results (M ∈ {4..9} correlated binary assets, Gaussian score model ρ=0.3, 100 runs, η=0.2): per-market loss halves per added market (ℓ_{M+1}/ℓ_M ≈ 0.49–0.50); ℓ_M·2^M ≈ 0.15 constant for M=4..9 — aggregate loss flat, polynomial not exponential; it is the only non-oracle model whose loss decays with M. Ablation: without parlay flow the ranking reverses — ParlayMarket has the HIGHEST non-oracle loss; parlays are the primary information channel for dependence learning. Limitation: Ising cannot represent higher-order dependence (unquantified floor); mutually exclusive outcomes need a structural preprocessing layer.

Kalshi RFQ audit (220,746 native trades, 2026-02-03, 16 days): 13/33 = 39% of near-independent combo quotes violate the Fréchet upper bound P(A∩B) ≤ min(P(A),P(B)), some by 5.7×; aggregating 4.5 quotes/maker tightens spreads by only 0.19¢. Kalshi NBA replay (2026-03-07; 732 base markets, 5,918 combo tickers, 2-10 legs): standalone MM (θ_corr) had 3,973 accepted trades, 86.8% win, $113,984.58 PnL, Sharpe 1.0049 — the best risk-adjusted non-native strategy (vs Kalshi execution $244,190.77, Sharpe 0.7151); native LP backtest execution was $591,485.31 PnL, 52.35% ROI, Sharpe 0.2177. Spreads: 5.12¢ on 999 base markets vs 11.89¢ on 549 combo markets.

The EPL staking study (Vélez Jiménez et al., ITAM/CETYS, 2023) compares Sharpe-ratio (quadratic utility) vs Kelly (log utility) portfolio staking: Return R(ℓ̄) = 1 + ℓ̄′ϱ̄ with ϱ̄ = D_o·m − 1; Sharpe S(ℓ̄) = (ℓ̄′μ̄ − R_f)/√(ℓ̄′Σℓ̄), convexified via ȳ = κℓ̄ (Eq. 7); Kelly max log-growth = D_KL(p‖p̃) (Eq. 10); bivariate ℓ* = (op−1)/(o−1). The multivariate simultaneous Kelly formulation (claimed novel, Eq. 13): max p̄′log(1 + W′ℓ̄ − Σℓ_i·1) s.t. Σℓ_i ≤ 1, ℓ̄ ≥ 0 — concave and SQP-solvable. Fraction calibration: 200 Dirichlet(1) simulations on validation → 17% fractional. Assumptions: no short selling/borrowing, infinitely divisible money, odds/probabilities fixed, match independence, true probabilities known.
equation: R(ℓ̄) = 1 + ℓ̄′ϱ̄; S(ℓ̄) = (ℓ̄′μ̄ − R_f)/√(ℓ̄′Σℓ̄); max p̄′log(1 + W′ℓ̄ − Σℓ_i·1) s.t. Σℓ_i ≤ 1, ℓ̄ ≥ 0; Kelly max log-growth = D_KL(p‖p̃)

claim: EPL staking results (2,660 games 2014/15–2020/21; test second half 2020/21, 20 matchweeks × 10 matches, 30 bets, 59,049 outcome combos per matchweek): the neural net reached 54% accuracy vs crowd (Pinnacle-implied) 51.5% and nulls 38/20/42%, but its cross-entropy was 1.0318 vs the crowd's 0.9966 — the model is WORSE than the market on information loss (accuracy edge without calibration edge). Portfolios: best was restricted + 17% fractional Sharpe → 135% final wealth (+35.8% profit); restricted fractional Kelly 111%; complete fractional Kelly 102%; complete fractional Sharpe 97%. Full-stake: 24%, 16%, 3%, 0% — Sharpe complete went to ruin two weeks before the end (final wealth 0%, log-growth −∞). Betting/wealth p-values were 0.16–0.50 — NONE significant; profit is indistinguishable from luck. The model beat 78/100 Dirichlet random sims. Arbitrage was found 3 times (e.g., Everton–Aston Villa 2021-06-05, tt = −0.0085); Sharpe converges to the arbitrage vector with infinite Sharpe. Kelly max bet averaged 29.7% of portfolio stake (vs Sharpe 25.9%); SQP took 20.9 s/fixture (Kelly), 5.3 s (Sharpe); matchweek 23 Kelly SQP failed (gradient overflow, last-iteration patch). Caveat: Pinnacle final odds were used as INPUT features, so the accuracy-vs-crowd comparison is contaminated; multivariate Kelly scales as N = Πm_k outcomes (intractable for full NFL prop portfolios without factorization).

The Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model (Zhang, Rastelli & Friel, UCD/Insight, 2026) generalizes the Maher Poisson goal model with a spike-and-slab prior on team-specific dispersion: CMP pmf (Eq. 1) f(y|μ,ν) = (μ^y/y!)^ν / Z_f(μ,ν); ν=1 recovers Poisson; E(Y) ≈ μ + 1/(2ν) − 1/2, Var(Y) ≈ μ/ν. Likelihood (Eq. 3): y^H|μ^H,ν_i ~ COM-Poisson(μ^H,ν_i) — dispersion follows the scoring team. Maher centring (Eq. 4): log(μ^H_{i,j}) = α_i + β_j + γ; log(μ^A_{j,i}) = α_j + β_i; Σ-constraints (Eq. 6).
equation: f(y|μ,ν) = (μ^y/y!)^ν / Z_f(μ,ν); E(Y) ≈ μ + 1/(2ν) − 1/2; Var(Y) ≈ μ/ν; log(μ^H_{i,j}) = α_i + β_j + γ; log(μ^A_{j,i}) = α_j + β_i

claim: The spike-and-slab prior (Eq. 5): Z_i|p_i ~ Bern(p_i), p_i ~ Beta(1,1), η_i ~ N(0,1), ν_i := exp(Z_i η_i) — the spike at ν=1 is the Poisson regime, the slab LogNormal around 1 is the non-equidispersed regime. Inference: Metropolis-within-Gibbs (binary-flip MH + Exchange for Z_i; correlated bivariate (α_i,η_i) proposal ρ=0.85; 250,000 iterations, 50,000 burn-in). Fit: WAIC (Eq. 17); prediction: Ignorance score IGN = −log2(f̃(y*)) (Eq. 18) evaluated on Outcome / O-U 2.5 / Goal Difference; RPS checked. Code: github.com/nzhang98/compoisson_goal.
equation: Z_i|p_i ~ Bern(p_i), p_i ~ Beta(1,1), η_i ~ N(0,1), ν_i := exp(Z_i η_i); IGN = −log2(f̃(y*))

claim: CMP simulation: TP at 0.5 threshold was 1.00 at ν=0.2, 0.94 at 0.3, then collapsed to 0.58 at 0.5 and 0.14 at 0.8; FP ≈ 0.04–0.16 stable. WAIC at ν=0.3: Poisson 2836.5 vs CMP-SAS 2640.5; near equidispersion (ν=0.9) Poisson best but CMP-SAS close (2130.5 vs 2131.3) — SAS robustness. The ledger's verdict is ADOPT — the count-data model GSE should run for NFL scoring distributions, most directly for totals where dispersion is the entire game.

EPL 2023/24 results (threshold 0.5): 3 over-dispersed teams (Fulham P(Z)=0.94, ν̂=0.323; Brighton 0.58, ν̂=0.729; Wolves 0.51, ν̂=0.766) + 1 under-dispersed (Nott'm Forest 0.53, ν̂=1.395). Fulham's attack shifts from −0.090 (Poisson) to −1.831 (CMP-SAS) — extreme overdispersion (boom/bust) masked by Poisson. In-sample WAIC: CMP-SAS 2370.0 < CMP-Full 2386.1 < Poisson 2400.3. Out-of-sample IGN: Outcome 1.326 vs 1.327; O/U 2.5 0.929 vs 0.974 (largest gain); GD 2.937 vs 2.940; CMP-Full was worse than Poisson on Outcome/GD. Man Utd–Fulham 1–2: CMP-SAS exact-score P 4.68% vs Poisson 4.22%; away-win prob 0.270 vs 0.196 (+8pp). Across five seasons: CMP-SAS WAIC best every season (e.g., 2024/25: 2293.1 vs 2312.8); CMP-SAS IGN ≤ Poisson every season × market; ~3 dispersed teams/season (mostly overdispersed); Liverpool dispersed 3/5 seasons (direction changes); Nott'm Forest underdispersed 2 straight seasons. Limitations: detection power collapses near equidispersion; NFL's 17-game season is thinner than 38-game EPL; no recency weighting; conditional independence under-predicts draws; 250k-iteration MCMC is too heavy for weekly production (needs VI/Laplace).

Neural Relational Inference (NRI; Kipf et al., arXiv:1802.04687v2) is a variational autoencoder whose latent code is a discrete interaction graph over agents, decoded by a graph neural network: ELBO L = E_{q_φ(z|x)}[log p_θ(x|z)] − KL[q_φ(z|x)‖p_θ(z)]; latent z_ij = discrete one-hot edge type between objects i and j, sampled with Gumbel-softmax/concrete z_ij = softmax((h²_{(i,j)} + g)/τ), τ = 0.5; encoder = 2-round GNN message passing on the fully-connected graph; decoder = per-edge-type MLPs predicting Δx with Gaussian noise σ²I, plus a recurrent (GRU) decoder variant for non-Markovian data. Anti-degeneracy trick: predict M = 10 steps into the future so the decoder cannot ignore z.
equation: L = E_{q_φ(z|x)}[log p_θ(x|z)] − KL[q_φ(z|x)‖p_θ(z)]; z_ij = softmax((h²_{(i,j)} + g)/τ), τ = 0.5

claim: NRI results: unsupervised edge-recovery accuracy on 5 objects — Springs NRI(learned) 99.9% (matches supervised 99.9%; correlation baselines ~52%); Charged 82.1% (supervised 95.0%; baselines ~54–56%); Kuramoto 96.0% (supervised 99.7%). 10-object: springs 98.4%, charged 70.8%, Kuramoto 75.7%. Path prediction: NRI(learned) beats both LSTM baselines at 10–20 steps on all three physics tasks (springs 20-step MSE 2.13e-5 vs LSTM(joint) 7.02e-4); LSTM wins only 1-step Kuramoto but 'goes out of sync' long-term. Motion capture: NRI beats full-graph and LSTM baselines long-term; dynamic graph re-evaluation significantly improves over static; the learned graph beats the anatomical skeleton graph; the 4-edge-type model finds an interpretable hand↔opposite-extremities edge.

On NBA SportVU 2016 pick-and-roll tracking (12k segments, 5 nodes: ball, ball handler, screener, two defensive matchups), NRI beats LSTM and is on par with the full graph; learned edges separate the ball + ball handler (off-ball) from the other three players — semantic structure discovered unsupervised. NFL transfer caveats: 22 players + ball = 506 directed edges/frame vs the paper's 5 nodes/25 frames (two orders of magnitude smaller); football interactions are dynamic (the paper trains on static graphs — its own headline limitation); zone drops are ball-less coordination that pairwise coupling captures only weakly. The ledger's verdict is ADAPT — man vs. zone coverage framed as a latent interaction graph over the 22 players that NRI can infer unsupervised from NGS tracking trajectories.

The skill-adjusted expected-goals model (Noel, arXiv:2511.07703v2) injects recency-weighted player-skill estimates into a context-only LightGBM shot model (NHL): shooter GAX = (weighted goals) − (cumulative weighted xG); goalie GSAX = (cumulative weighted xG) − (weighted goals allowed); shooter talent ratio = (weighted goals)/(weighted xG); goalie talent ratio = (weighted xG against)/(weighted goals against); 'true' talent = sum of total + locational + situational variants. Recency weighting: linear decay over each player's prior shot history; shots aggregated into nine spatial bins; Gower similarity between players stabilizes sparse histories. Baseline: LightGBM binary classifier on context-only shot features, tuned with Optuna; skill features added as inputs; evaluated per skill bracket (low p≤0.5, mid 0.5<p≤0.75, high p>0.75) on log loss, AUC, Brier.
equation: Shooter GAX = (weighted goals) − (cumulative weighted xG); goalie GSAX = (cumulative weighted xG) − (weighted goals allowed); shooter talent ratio = (weighted goals)/(weighted xG)

claim: Skill-adjusted xG results (Table 5, adjusted vs baseline): high bracket (p>0.75): log loss 0.2982→0.2844 (−0.0138), AUC 0.7238→0.7616 (+0.0378), Brier 0.0849→0.0816 — largest gain; mid bracket: log loss 0.2831→0.2792, AUC 0.7424→0.7519, Brier 0.0809→0.0798; low bracket: log loss 0.2126→0.2100, AUC 0.7531→0.7630, Brier 0.0567→0.0560 — consistent directional improvement across all 9 metric–bracket cells, but low/mid gains are small and the baseline is self-admittedly not state-of-the-art (part of the gain may be skill features compensating for an underfit baseline). Limitations: talent ratio uses the same weighted xG model being evaluated (self-referential circularity risk); sparse players' talent is set to exactly zero (crude — shrinkage to league average would be standard); 5v5 only; no defender-proximity tracking; loose temporal validation (possible leakage); hockey shots are discrete binary events while NFL props are continuous accumulations — transfers as player-context residuals, not directly.

Team-skill aggregation study (Dehpanah et al., arXiv:2106.11397v1): a team's skill rating is computed from member ratings by SUM (μ_t = Σμ_i, equal contribution), MAX (μ_t = max(μ_i), best member 'carries'), or MIN (μ_t = min(μ_i), weakest link), inside Elo, Glicko, and TrueSkill. Elo team win probability generalized to N-team fields: Pr(t_i wins, F) = [Σ_{j≠i} (1 + e^{(μ_tj − μ_ti)/D})⁻¹] / C(N,2); Elo team update μ′_ti = μ_ti + K[R′_ti − Pr] (K=10, D=400); player update μ′_j = μ_j + w_pj(μ′_ti − μ_ti), w_pj = μ_j/Σμ_members. Rank normalization: R′_ti = (N − R^obs_ti)/C(N,2).
equation: μ_t = Σμ_i (SUM); μ_t = max(μ_i) (MAX); μ_t = min(μ_i) (MIN); Pr(t_i wins, F) = [Σ_{j≠i} (1 + e^{(μ_tj − μ_ti)/D})⁻¹] / C(N,2); μ′_ti = μ_ti + K[R′_ti − Pr], K=10, D=400; μ′_j = μ_j + w_pj(μ′_ti − μ_ti), w_pj = μ_j/Σμ_members

claim: Glicko team update: μ′_ti = μ_ti + [0.0057565/(1/σ²_ti + 1/d²_ti)]·[Σ g(σ_tj)(R′_ti − Pr)], with d²_ti = [(0.0057565)² Σ g(σ_tj)² Pr(1−Pr)]⁻¹. TrueSkill non-draw win update: μ′_ti = μ_ti + (σ²_ti/c)·[N(t/c)/Φ(t/c)], c = √(2β² + σ²_ti + σ²_tj), β=4.16, τ=0.833. Evaluation was purely online/walk-forward (matches sorted by timestamp) with NDCG (PUBG) and accuracy (LoL, CS:GO); three setups: all players, best 1000 (top by final rating, first 10 games — survivorship/lookahead flag in sample construction), most frequent (>100 games, first 100 games).
equation: μ′_ti = μ_ti + [0.0057565/(1/σ²_ti + 1/d²_ti)]·[Σ g(σ_tj)(R′_ti − Pr)]; d²_ti = [(0.0057565)² Σ g(σ_tj)² Pr(1−Pr)]⁻¹; μ′_ti = μ_ti + (σ²_ti/c)·[N(t/c)/Φ(t/c)], c = √(2β² + σ²_ti + σ²_tj), β=4.16, τ=0.833

claim: Aggregation findings: PUBG (%NDCG, all players) — Elo SUM 60.2 / MAX 61.5 / MIN 61.3; TrueSkill SUM 61.7 / MAX 62.2 / MIN 61.8; frequent players: TrueSkill 60.3 / 62.8 / 60.4. LoL (%Accuracy, all) — Elo 49.2 / 50.2 / 49.5; Glicko 49.3 / 50.1 / 49.8; TrueSkill 49.8 / 50.4 / 49.3; best: TrueSkill MAX 76.1 vs MIN 26.1 (extreme gap driven by best-player sample selection on final ratings). CS:GO (%Accuracy, all) — Elo 64.7 / 64.3 / 60.8; TrueSkill 64.3 / 62.7 / 59.7; PreviousRank 46.6 — MAX roughly tied with SUM here. The paper's headline: MAX wins in the majority of cases (all PUBG and LoL setups; CS:GO less consistent — authors attribute to higher density/smaller rating range); the 'carry' interpretation is that team performance is primarily determined by the most skilled member. Caveats: esports teams of 2–5; NFL has 11 simultaneous roles with more substitution and specialization — the 'carry' mechanism does not transfer cleanly; no confidence intervals; margins like 62.2 vs 61.7 are within noise; SUM 'even shows more inaccurate predictions compared to PreviousRank' for PUBG all-players under Elo/Glicko.

DLS-Cal (Roy, arXiv:2609.04754v1) is an interpretable MLP calibration layer on cricket's Duckworth-Lewis-Stern target-revision method that predicts DLS residuals: r̂_{DLS-Cal} = r̂_{DLS} + Δ(x) (eq. 1), x ∈ R^18 (DLS prediction + empirical training-set per-bucket bias prior + 16 enriched features). Architecture: 4-layer MLP (widths [18,128,128,64,1], GELU, dropout 0.25, 27,265 params, final layer zero-initialized), trained on Huber loss (δ=10) with AdamW (η=1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 512, cosine annealing, ≤50 epochs, patience 8); the gender-aware variant trains separate male/female calibrators routed at inference.

The Win-Flip Rate metric (eq. 2): WFR_k(M) = (1/N) Σ_i 1[|r̂_{M,i} − r_i| > k], reported at k ∈ {3,5,10,15} — a thresholded-error fairness-style metric distinct from ECE/LRD. The audit machinery: temporal splits (train ≤2022, val 2023, test 2024–Mar 2026); match-level block bootstrap (B=2,000 whole-match resamples) for all audit intervals; bucket-matched gender-gap estimate over 59 cells with ≥30 examples per gender; ablation ladder (lookup vs linear vs MLP-without-prior vs full MLP).

DLS audit results (8,150 international matches, 2,781,465 ball records, 27 June 2002 – 5 March 2026; synthetic interruption sampling yields 233,550 examples; 417 real rain-affected matches held out). Test (N=69,090), lower-is-better: DLS original RMSE 37.41 / MAE 30.54 / bias +17.40; DLS canonical RMSE 28.92 / MAE 22.61 / bias +7.57 (22.6% RMSE cut); stacking ensemble RMSE 21.49 / MAE 16.19 / bias −0.20 (best); DLS-Cal gender-blind RMSE 23.72 / MAE 17.72 / bias −1.62. DLS-Cal has the lowest ODI WFR5 of any method: 83.0% vs XGBoost 84.0%, stacking 85.0%.

DLS bias audit (training split): DLS mean error +4.79 runs (median +7.98); per-bucket mean bias spans −111 to +26 runs (ODI), a 137-run total span; ODI ANOVA F=527.16, Kruskal–Wallis H=9,797.69. Gender gap (ODI): men's mean bias +1.51 (N=60,660), women's +7.63 (N=10,350) → gap +6.13 runs; match-clustered 95% CI [+3.70,+10.07], bootstrap p(gap≤0)<0.001; bucket-matched gap +8.34 unweighted / +9.64 weighted; women's bias exceeds men's in 55 of 59 cells; T20I gap +0.51 runs, not significant (95% CI [−1.10,+2.12], p≈0.27). DLS-Cal bias reduction (test): mean |bias| ODI 33.74→23.29 runs (31.0% reduction); T20I 20.58→16.71 (18.8%); gender-aware DLS-Cal cut women's residual bias +6.19→+0.65 runs (5.54-run cut). Real rain-affected matches (417): DLS under-predicts ODIs (bias −11.1, RMSE 45.8), over-predicts T20Is (+8.7, RMSE 25.1).

The 'Quantitative Methods in Finance' lecture notes (Vansteenberghe, arXiv:2601.12896v3, 86,845 extracted lines) cover standard textbook blocks: weak stationarity (E(y_t)=μ, Var=σ², Cov(y_t,y_{t+s})=γ(s)); SARIMA–GARCH Φ_P(L^s)φ_p(L)(1−L)^d(1−L^s)^D y_t = Θ_Q(L^s)θ_q(L)ε_t, ε_t=σ_t z_t (explicit warning: do not estimate ARMA then GARCH on residuals sequentially); Wold IRFs IRF(h)=E(y_{t+h}|ε_t=1,…); Engle–Granger cointegration two-step + ECM; event studies AR_{i,t}=R_{i,t}−α−β_i R_{m,t}, AAR/CAR; VaR_q=inf{x:P(R>x)≤1−q}; Frank copula C(u,v,δ)=−δ^{−1}log[1+(e^{−δu}−1)(e^{−δv}−1)/(e^{−δ}−1)]; DiD with continuous treatment intensity; synthetic control; Monte Carlo hypothesis testing. No training procedure, no hyperparameters, no validation design.

The lecture notes report zero original numerical results of their own and carry the author's own disclaimer that methods are 'developed for pedagogic purpose only and would not be recommended for actual investment decision making.' Empirical-finance machinery (GARCH volatility clustering, cointegration) assumes liquid-market DGPs that do not map to NFL game outcomes (short seasons, discrete scores, no continuous price). Notably: grep found zero mentions of the Kelly criterion. The ledger's verdict is REJECT — zero novel methods, zero empirical results, zero sports-domain content.

SportsNGEN (Thorpe et al., arXiv:2403.12977v3) is an autoregressive transformer decoder that jointly simulates all players and the ball from tracking data: output representation = grid classification over discrete spatial offsets (61 bins/dimension; players use 3,721 bins total, ball 226,981 bins, bin size {46,13,10} mm); categorical distribution over bins + nucleus (top-p) sampling at generation. Context inputs: context tokens, player identity embeddings, velocities, ball-to-player distances, elapsed time; auxiliary event classifier + sport-specific stopping logic. Architecture: token MLP 30→256→512→2048; decoder 4 layers, 2048 hidden, 8 attention heads, expansion factor 4, dropout 0.2; training ~2 days on one NVIDIA A100. Preprocessing: max history 6 s; dataset doubled by simultaneous x/y court flips; positional noise ±25 mm (x), ±12.5 mm (y/z).

SportsNGEN results: top-p sweep optimum 0.8–0.9; ~20% of generated rallies judged non-realistic after training convergence; player identity embedding realism improves until ~20, then plateaus. Counterfactual example: corner-placement choices yielded ~58% win probability vs <50% for the original middle shot, from 100 rollouts per choice. Limitations: proprietary 25 Hz tennis tracking (3 male pros, 6 best-of-3 matches per pair, 3 tournaments/3 surfaces) — unreplicable and unsanity-checkable; unreliable OOD behavior for unseen players (identity embeddings are player-specific — fatal for NFL roster turnover, needs a generic fallback); 100 rollouts per state is expensive; 61 bins/dimension is coarse vs fine NFL field-position value.

The CORP calibration hierarchy (Gneiting & Resin, arXiv:2108.03210v3) for real-valued outcomes (auto-calibration → threshold/quantile/CEP/probabilistic/marginal): conditional T-calibration T(L(Y|T(F))) = T(F) for identifiable functionals (means, quantiles, expectiles, moments, Huber); Thm 2.11 says auto-calibration implies conditional T-calibration for identification-function functionals. The T-PAV algorithm (Alg. 1) is pool-adjacent-violators isotonic regression producing increasing recalibrated values x̂_i = T(δ_{k:l}), conditionally T-calibrated and optimal under any consistent scoring function of mixture form.

CORP score decomposition: S̄ = MCB_S − DSC_S + UNC_S (MCB=miscalibration, DSC=discrimination/resolution, UNC=uncertainty; Thm 3.3 guarantees nonnegativity under PAV); extended form: S̄ = MCB_u + MCB_c − DSC + UNC. Empirical skill score: S_skill = 1 − S̄̂/Ŝ_mg = (D̂SC − MĈB)/ÛNC (eq. 30). Universal coefficient of determination: R* = (DSC − MCB)/UNC (eq. 31), in [0,1] only under in-sample loss-minimization-with-intercept conditions (Assumption 3.5). Canonical losses: mean → (x−y)²; α-expectile → 2|1{x≥y}−α|(x−y)²; α-quantile → 2(1{x≥y}−α)(x−y). Code: github.com/resinj/replication_GR21; R package reliabilitydiag (CRAN).
equation: S̄ = MCB_S − DSC_S + UNC_S; S_skill = 1 − S̄̂/Ŝ_mg = (D̂SC − MĈB)/ÛNC; R* = (DSC − MCB)/UNC

claim: CORP demo results: butterfly (MSE) — null model 0.263, MCB 0.031, DSC 0.461, UNC 0.693; ridge 0.224, 0.033, 0.502, 0.693 ('both reliable; ridge has considerably higher discrimination'). Bank of England CPI inflation forecasts Q3 2005–Q1 2020 (n=59 quarters), 1-quarter-ahead: threshold at 2% — BS 0.113, MCB 0.024, DSC 0.135, UNC 0.224; 75%-quantile — QS 0.331, MCBu 0.009, MCBc 0.121, DSC 0.497, UNC 0.698. R*/skill decays with lead time and goes negative at k≥4 quarters ('informative at ≤3 quarters only'); 4Q-ahead threshold: BS 0.307, MCB 0.091, DSC 0.008. Limitations: CORP flattens non-monotone miscalibration into horizontal segments; consistency bands assume forecast–residual independence (violated by serially correlated NFL errors — use block resampling by week); R*∈[0,1] fails out-of-sample (use the possibly negative skill score instead); variance functionals are excluded (identifiability counterexample).

The two-point PTZ camera calibration method (Chen, Zhu, Little, arXiv:1801.09005v1) for broadcast cameras when fewer than four field-marking correspondences are visible: camera model P = KQ_φQ_θ · S[I|−C] (PTZ part · fixed-base prior); pixel from ray: p = [f·tan(θ_p − θ) + u, f·tan(φ_p − φ) + v]ᵀ; focal length from two points via the image-of-absolute-conic quadratic cos α = x₁ᵀωx₂/(√(x₁ᵀωx₁)√(x₂ᵀωx₂)), ω = K⁻ᵀK⁻¹; initial pan/tilt from one point via the closed-form quadratic in tan(pan): a·t_p² + b·t_p + c = 0, with a = (V²+1)Z² − U²(X²+Y²), b = −2XZ(U²+V²+1), c = (V²+1)X² − U²(Y²+Z²); Levenberg–Marquardt reprojection refinement; pan-tilt forest = random forest (5 trees, max depth 20, info-gain on angular variance) regressing SIFT descriptors → pan/tilt ray labels; pose optimization min Σ‖p_i − P(r̂_i)‖² with RANSAC (2-point minimal set → 16 iterations at 99% success, 50% outliers, vs 71 for 4-point). Assumptions: fixed known camera base; square pixels, principal point at image center; focal length the only intrinsic unknown; no lens distortion.
equation: P = KQ_φQ_θ · S[I|−C]; p = [f·tan(θ_p − θ) + u, f·tan(φ_p − φ) + v]ᵀ; cos α = x₁ᵀωx₂/(√(x₁ᵀωx₁)√(x₂ᵀωx₂)), ω = K⁻ᵀK⁻¹; a·t_p² + b·t_p + c = 0

claim: Two-point calibration results: highlights dataset mean IoU ± std 0.83±0.16 vs CalibMe 0.68±0.30 (per sequence 0.88±0.06 / 0.81±0.21 / 0.69±0.36 / 0.94±0.04 vs CalibMe 0.75±0.22 / 0.73±0.27 / 0.61±0.37 / 0.62±0.33); speed 0.3 s/frame (0.2 SIFT + 0.1 prediction/optimization) vs 3.0 s/frame. World Cup 2014: 0.99±0.01 (BRA–MEX) and 0.98±0.01 (BRA–NED) vs CalibMe 0.84±0.24 and 0.69±0.37. Synthetic at σ=3.0 px feature noise: mean rotation error <0.02°, mean focal error <2.5 px; >85% of real images have rotation error <1°. Feature-distance thresholding: inlier rate (angular error <0.5°) 0.33 vs 0.09 without; mean IoU 0.83 vs 0.53. Narrow FOV (<~25°) still fails (IoU <0.6). The ledger's verdict is REJECT — pure CV broadcast-camera calibration with no transfer to win/spread/total probability modeling.

Factorized-attention transformers for NFL defensive coverage (Song et al., arXiv:2603.25901v1): temporal attention per agent + agent ('social') attention per timestep (Scene Transformer / HoopTransformer style) instead of full spatio-temporal attention; learnable embeddings for categorical metadata (position, offense/defense) fused with transformer output → per-player latent vectors → feed-forward head; temporal pooling (average over time) → play-level per-player representations. Three cross-entropy losses: matchup loss L = −(1/D) Σ_d Σ_r z*_{d,r} log(exp(Z_{d,r})/Σ_{r'} exp(Z_{d,r'})) with a 'no matchup' class; coverage loss over C=20 classes (19 responsibilities e.g. hook curl left, deep right + 'no assignment'); target-defender loss over N players (receiver logit masked −1e9 pre-softmax) plus post-processing rules (confidence <50% in prevent → 'no target defender'). Training augmentation: random trajectory truncation — 11 fixed strategies (start ∈ {−30,−20,−10,0}, end ∈ {snap, pass forward, pass arrival}) at 60% + fully random at 40%.
equation: L = −(1/D) Σ_d Σ_r z*_{d,r} log(exp(Z_{d,r})/Σ_{r'} exp(Z_{d,r'}))

claim: Coverage-decoding results (NFL Next Gen Stats tracking, 2020–2024; 2020–2023 train, 2024 test; PFF ground-truth labels, proprietary; 21,567 eligible pass plays in 2024): receiver–defender matchup up to 0.894 accuracy / 0.894 F1 full context (−30 → pass arrival); post-snap windows 0.872–0.873; pre-snap-only ~0.750–0.752 accuracy, 0.745–0.746 F1. Coverage assignment: ~0.918–0.919 accuracy / 0.877–0.879 F1 with post-snap context; pre-snap-only ~0.882–0.883 / 0.825–0.827; ~70% of 2024 plays had all coverage defenders correct at pass arrival; ~20% had 1–3 errors ('judgment calls'); Top-2 accuracy 97% across 20 classes. Target defender: rule-based nearest-defender 0.764 → transformer 0.862 → transformer + post-processing 0.882 (~12pp lift).

Double-coverage findings (2024): 1,179 instances across 21,567 eligible pass plays (5.5% rate); top-5 model-ranked double-covered receivers: Ja'Marr Chase, Garrett Wilson, CeeDee Lamb, Justin Jefferson (plus one more, aligned with human labels); the model flagged 9 double coverages on Tre Tucker vs 0 in human labels (paper suggests human 'reputation bias'); Mike Evans had only 10 all season. Disguise proxy: Kansas City (Spagnuolo) had the lowest pre-snap prediction accuracy (most deceptive); Tampa Bay and San Francisco were most predictable. Limitations: play-level end-of-play labels vs frame-by-frame prediction; inference substitutes a predicted team scheme for the ground-truth scheme used in training (error cascade); PFF labels have charting-guideline violations; inter-annotator agreement never reported; rare schemes concentrate errors (Prevent: 3% of plays with 6+ errors); quick-game passes (<2s) are unassignable.

The FIFA World Cup study (Al-Bustami & Ghazal, arXiv:2505.01902v1): overall accuracy 59.38% (proposed: logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, AdaBoost, k-NN with majority vote) vs 56.25% (baseline) — a 3.13pp gap (~2 games on a ~64-game test set, within noise); high-scoring games 81.25% vs 81.25% (tie); low-scoring games 52.08% vs 47.92%; of the 28 matches the baseline got wrong, the proposed model got 7 correct (25.00%). No confidence intervals, no sample sizes for subsets, no significance tests, and no comparison against Elo, FIFA rankings, betting odds, or any published soccer rating model. The ledger's verdict is REJECT: draws were excluded (~25–30% of real soccer outcomes removed, inflating accuracy); leakage controls absent (attributes through 2022/2023 may postdate predicted tournaments; features not as-of-knowable); the 1930-history baseline is far below obvious benchmarks; internal model-list inconsistency (the ensemble section names XGBoost, which is not in the listed model set); feature/split opacity blocks any porting.

The cricket LSTM architecture (Chakwate & Madhan, arXiv:2011.02122): three-block network — shared Input Transformation block per ball + LSTM block + Output Transformation block mapping to a 2-dim win/lose vector, softmax → win probability, mean Binary Cross Entropy over all balls as the training objective. Four variants tested: A (all-input/single output), B (all-input/multi-output — one output head per timestamp, selected best, converges in 100 epochs), C (randomly sampled prefixes/single output), D (cumulative-sum features/single output). Best model appends three ablations to inputs: pre-match LGBM classification result, first-innings target score, wickets fallen.

Cricket LSTM results (1,597 international ODIs from 1971 onward; ball-level + match-level attributes). Architecture comparison (test accuracy % at J=300/250/200 balls): Model A 93.7/63.5/57.2; Model B 95.7/75.1/66.4; Model C 79.6/66.7/59.2; Model D 60.8/52.6/52.6. Pre-match classification test accuracy: AdaBoost 47.2%, LGBM 61.3% (train 76.3%). Ablation gains on Model B (test, J=300/250/200): baseline 95.7/75.1/66.4 → +pre-match result 96.3/77.6/68.2 (~+2% avg) → +target score 98.0/90.1/87.1 (~+13% avg) → +wickets fallen 98.4/92.5/88.2 (~+2% further). Reader flags: test accuracy exceeding train at several checkpoints signals a small/odd test split; late-match accuracy is near-deterministic arithmetic (score vs target), so only early-ball accuracy (62–82%) is real signal; no calibration metrics reported (no Brier, log loss, AUC); hyperparameters unstated; train/test split methodology unstated. The +13% ablation argues score-differential conditioning is the dominant feature class for in-play models.

Dayaratna & Miller (arXiv:1205.4750) prove the linear MLB win% model WP = 0.500 + beta(RS − RA) is the first-order Taylor approximation of Bill James's Pythagorean formula WP ≈ RS^gamma / (RS^gamma + RA^gamma), pinning the slope to a closed form: beta = gamma / (4·R_avg). Partial derivatives at (R_avg, R_avg): df/dx = gamma/(4·R_avg), df/dy = −gamma/(4·R_avg). Appendix identity: WP = (1 + (RA/RS)^gamma)^−1 ≈ 1/2 + (gamma/4)(ln RS − ln RA) ≈ 1/2 + (gamma/(4·R_avg))(RS − RA). Empirical: per-season OLS of WP on (RS − RA) with intercept at 0.500; gamma_hat recovered via gamma_hat = beta_hat · 4 · R_avg; 95% CIs with Bonferroni correction (alpha = 0.05/20 = 0.0025).
equation: WP ≈ RS^gamma / (RS^gamma + RA^gamma); WP = 0.500 + beta(RS − RA); beta = gamma / (4·R_avg); df/dx = gamma/(4·R_avg), df/dy = −gamma/(4·R_avg); gamma_hat = beta_hat · 4 · R_avg

claim: Linearized Pythagorean results (MLB 1991–2011, 20 seasons, 600 team-seasons): per-season beta_hat ranges 0.084–0.126 (1991: beta_hat=0.119, R²=0.922; 2010: 0.094, R²=0.950; 2011: 0.104, R²=0.867); R² across all 20 seasons from 0.807 to 0.950. Recovered gamma_hat ranges 1.634 (2010) to 2.108 (2004); every season's 95% CI except 2010 contains 1.82, and with Bonferroni correction 2010's CI [1.399, 1.870] also contains it. All estimates significant at the 0.0025 level. Jones & Tappin cross-check: beta_bar=0.00065 with gamma=1.81 implies 696 runs/team/year (matches observed scale ~4.3 runs/game). Reader flags: retrospective in-sample OLS only — no out-of-sample prediction; n=30 teams/season gives wide CIs; MLB-only constants do not transfer to NFL (accepted NFL gamma ≈ 2.37).

DashArena (Wang & Deng 2026, arXiv:2608.10567) is a benchmark for LLM-generated interactive analytic dashboards evaluated via replayable interaction trajectories and a distilled VLM judge with Bradley-Terry aggregation; the ledger verdict is REJECT because it is an LLM code-generation benchmark with no math, model, or dataset transferring to NFL team-rating prediction.

DashArena's evaluation protocol: (1) task briefs derived from Tableau Public dashboards (Claude Opus 4.6 writes task intent); (2) candidate generates one HTML dashboard + JSON interaction trajectory; (3) Playwright executor replays trajectory and reports renderable/replayable deterministic validity; (4) VLM pairwise judge outputs A/B/tie preference with rationale; (5) Bradley-Terry aggregation with leaderboard scaled 1000 + 400*theta and task-bootstrap 95% CIs.

DashJudge-8B (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) is distilled from a Claude Opus 4.6 teacher with LoRA rank 16, scale 32, dropout 0.05, lr 1e-4, batch 8, cosine schedule, 2 epochs, ~50 min on one 80GB A100; judge agreement with humans on 99 pairs is 79.8% (kappa 0.600), vs teacher 78.8% (kappa 0.590) and base model 70.7% (kappa 0.419); adding interaction evidence to screenshots raised agreement 71.7% to 79.8% (+8.1 pts).
In DashArena's Bradley-Terry judge aggregation, P(i > j) = sigma(theta_i - theta_j) is the logistic link between latent dashboard strengths theta_i and theta_j, with sigma the sigmoid function.

DashArena findings: no model exceeds 86% render rate or 74% replay rate (GPT-5.5: 85.8%/73.3%; Grok 4.3 last); leaderboard order is GPT-5.5 first (CI overlaps human baseline), then human baseline and GLM-5.2, then Claude Opus 4.6, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Kimi K2.7 Code mid-tier; in a 100-candidate failure audit, 95.7% of 70 signal-enriched candidates had a confirmed model-attributed defect and 21 of 30 execution-clean candidates still had defects deterministic checks cannot detect; task-subsampling stability mean Kendall tau = 0.810 at 25 tasks, 0.867 at 50, 0.945 at 100.

Kargi & Salinas (2026, arXiv:2606.13221) fix LLM-leaderboard rating miscalibration: hard win/tie/loss labels in Bradley-Terry fitting produce correctly-ordered but mis-scaled Elos (battle agreement kappa 0.147-0.231 yet Spearman rho 0.868-0.976, 'good rankings, bad ruler'); the ledger verdict is ADAPT because calibrated soft targets in BT via a fitted score-to-probability map and split-conformal intervals on ratings port to GSE's NFL team-rating and margin models.

Soft-Elo's regularized Bradley-Terry objective is theta_hat = argmax over theta of sum over pairs of [y_ij log sigma(theta_i - theta_j) + (1 - y_ij) log(1 - sigma(theta_i - theta_j))] minus lambda||theta||^2 with lambda=0.01, and ratings are rescaled as Elo_i = 1500 + (400/ln 10)*theta_i.
equation: theta_hat = argmax sum[y_ij log sigma(theta_i - theta_j) + (1 - y_ij) log(1 - sigma(theta_i - theta_j))] - lambda||theta||^2, lambda=0.01

claim: Soft-Elo's soft target y_tilde(x) = sigma(beta*s(x)) maps a judge score difference s(x) through a temperature beta fit per fold by MLE on human non-tie battles (beta* in [0.36, 0.60] across judges, fold std <= 0.005); fitted sigma(beta*s) reduced ECE from 0.14 to 0.03 and cut held-out Elo MAE 39-73% per judge (cross-judge mean 45.9 to 17.9 Elo; DeepSeek-V3.2 63.4 to 17.1, -73%), preserving rank order (Spearman delta in [-0.011, +0.014]).

Soft-Elo's split-conformal rating intervals use normalized nonconformity S_i = |epsilon_i|/SE_hat_i where epsilon_i = Elo_LLM,i - Elo_Human,i and SE_hat_i is the bootstrap standard error over 20 battle subsamples, giving intervals [Elo_LLM - q_hat*SE_hat, Elo_LM + q_hat*SE_hat] with q_hat the ceil((1-alpha)(n+1))-th smallest S_i; at 90% nominal they narrowed median widths 39-70% vs Hard-Elo (131.9-261.0 to 74.4-143.1 Elo) with coverage 92.1-96.4%.

Soft-Elo diagnostic warning: on the ComparIA French-language distribution shift, Qwen beta* collapsed to 0.13-0.14 and soft targets damaged rankings — a flat score-agreement curve means soft targets should not be trusted; root cause is median |s| ~ 0.61 for top-vs-top-quartile battles vs ~1.54 for top-vs-bottom, which Hard-Elo treats as identical unit wins, and residuals correlate with human Elo at Pearson +0.49 to +0.90 (stretched ruler).

STAMP (Yamada & Fujii 2026, arXiv:2603.24015) models basketball team shot-type-specific spatial tendencies with a hierarchical Poisson GLMM (INLA-fitted) that separates stylistic tendency from pace via a possession exposure offset; ledger verdict ADAPT as a template for NFL team x field-zone x play-type rate modeling (the basketball application itself is not GSE-relevant).

STAMP likelihood: Y_{isadk} ~ Poisson(mu_{isadk}) with log mu_{isadk} = log E_{is} + eta_{isadk}, where E_{is} is team possessions (exposure offset), and the linear predictor eta = beta_0 + season + side + shot-type fixed effects + team i.i.d. u_i + area i.i.d. v_a + seasonally-correlated team x area w_{ias} (equicorrelation) + season-specific team x side z_{ids} + shot-type loadings gamma_m(k) on random slopes r^{(m)}_{ias} for jump shots and step-back/pull-up, with sum-to-zero constraints on all random-effect blocks and Penalized Complexity priors calibrated via prior predictive checks; one INLA fit takes ~1 minute wall-clock.

STAMP validation on B.LEAGUE play-by-play (2023-24 and 2024-25; 2,352 games, 306,444 field-goal attempts; train regular-season, evaluate out-of-sample on postseason via Monte Carlo expected log predictive density elpd_post^MC + LPML): full model elpd_post^MC = -3,383 and LPML_reg = -49,967 vs no-random-effects baseline -6,581 (LPML -130,617), a full-model gain of about 3.2x10^3; team x area only reaches -6,422, and adding jump+step slopes (no team x side) reaches -3,385 (only ~2 units worse out-of-sample than full) with substantially better LPML (-37,835), so the team x side effect is marginal; prior sensitivity shows best elpd always one of the two richest structures across 7 prior settings with Kendall's tau > 0.97 between model rankings across priors.

STAMP outputs per-team x area x shot-type posterior relative-rate maps vs league plus left-right bias log(Right/Left) with ~95% credible intervals; reader flags: no opponent adjustment (tendencies conflate style with schedule), frequency-only (efficiency not modeled), only 2 seasons so equicorrelation is barely identified, postseason eval set is only 3.16% of data, and NFL cells are far sparser (~1,000 plays/team/season vs 300k+ shots) so partial pooling is even more necessary.

Alimohammadi & Asgari (2025, arXiv:2507.08108) generalize the Mallows ranking model so the distance metric itself is learned: d_alpha(pi,sigma) = sum_i |pi(i)-sigma(i)|^alpha, with an FPTAS sampler, joint MLE for (alpha, beta, central ranking), and consistency proofs validated on college football/basketball power rankings; ledger verdict ADAPT because a learnable upset-shape parameter alpha is new capability for GSE poll-aggregation/tournament simulation (it explains ranking dispersion, not matchup outcomes).

The learned-distance Mallows law is P_{alpha,beta,sigma}(pi) = e^{-beta d_alpha(pi,sigma)}/Z_n(beta,alpha), with log-likelihood L_m(alpha,beta,sigma) = -(beta/m) sum_l d_alpha(pi^(l),sigma) - log Z_n(beta,alpha); two-step MLE first finds central ranking sigma_hat via min-weight perfect matching on a bipartite graph with edge weights sum_l |pi^(l)(i) - j| (consistent for any true alpha_tilde > 0), then fits (alpha, beta) from the score equations.

The learned-distance Mallows central-ranking error bound is P(sigma_hat_m != sigma_0) <= n! * exp(-m/(3n^4)), improving to <= n! * exp(-m/(54n^2)) when alpha_tilde = n/3; (alpha_hat, beta_hat) are asymptotically normal with sqrt(m)((alpha_hat-alpha_0),(beta_hat-beta_0)) -> N(0, I^{-1}) where the Fisher matrix is [[beta^2 Var[dot d], beta Cov[dot d, d]],[beta Cov[dot d, d], Var[d]]]; marginals decay as P(pi(i)=j) <= c(alpha,beta)^{|j-i|} for alpha >= 1; the FPTAS sampler requires alpha >= 1 and alpha < 1 sampling is stated open.

On college football 2019-2021 Massey composite top-10s, the learned-distance Mallows fit alpha_hat = 0.442 (+/-0.061), beta_hat = 0.455 (+/-0.051), with held-out top-1 8.0% and top-5 41.9% vs Mallows-tau (6.9%, 41.1%) and Plackett-Luce (3.5%, 30.5%); on 100-team college basketball, alpha_hat = 0.002 (+/-0.002) gives top-1 12.873% vs Mallows-tau 2.212% and PL 1.749% (over 5x top-1 improvement); sampler partition-function relative error (1.25 +/- 0.03)e-4 at n=6 and (2.94 +/- 0.06)e-4 at n=10, with time ratio vs exact Ryser 32.0 at n=6, 1194.5 at n=8, 113531.6 at n=10.

Learned-distance Mallows reader flags: top-10 teams pre-selected from known end-of-season polls (survivorship bias); 100-team alpha_hat ~= 0.002 means the model nearly 'learns away' the metric; the sports-relevant alpha_hat (0.44) is below 1, outside the sampler's proven regime; NFL has 32 teams and far fewer weekly ranking sources than Massey's composite corpus.

Ismail (2023, arXiv:2312.12700) introduces the Estimated Performance Rating (PRe) via constrained binomial-probability maximization, proved equivalent to Tournament Performance Rating (TPR) whenever TPR is defined but remaining defined for perfect/zero scores where TPR is undefined; ledger verdict ADAPT as the mathematical basis for 'peak-performance' ratings of NFL teams/units over streak windows.

PRe machinery: Elo win probability W(A,B) = 1/(1 + 10^((B-A)/400)); average opponent rating R_a = (1/k) sum_j b_j; TPR defined by m = n/(1 + 10^((R_a - TPR)/400)); binomial score probability S(w,m,n) = C(n,m) w^m (1-w)^(n-m); PRe = max_{w in [0,1]} S(w,m,n) subject to S(w,m,n) <= t with default t = 0.75; back-translation w* = 1/(1 + 10^((R_a - A*)/400)) and A* = R_a - 400 log10((1-w*)/w*); draws handled by doubling m,n; alternative objective S_bar(w,m,n) = sum_{k=m}^{n} C(n,k) w^k (1-w)^(n-k).

PRe main theorem: for 0 < m < n, a rating R is the TPR iff W(R, R_a) in argmax_w S(w,m,n) (proof: d/dw of the binomial gives w* = m/n, matching TPR's defining equation); empirically TPR and PRe coincide for every m and n <= 30.

PRe empirical illustrations: Alcaraz Wimbledon 2023 7/7 (R_a=1927) -> PRe 2478 (highest, strongest field); Djokovic French Open 7/7 (R_a=1867) -> 2417; Brazil 1970 World Cup 6/6 (R_a=1900) -> 2424 vs Brazil 2002 7/7 -> 2369; Fischer 20-win chess streak (R_a=2705) -> PRe 3441 vs Steinitz 25-win -> 3356 (quantifies the informal judgment that Fischer's was more impressive); Caruana 7-win (R_a=2793) -> 3344; at R_a=2700, n=2: PRe = 3024 for 2/2, 2891 for 1.5/2 (agrees with TPR), 2700 at 1/2, 2509 at 0.5/2, 2376 for 0/2.

PRe reader flags: average-opponent collapse discards opponent variance (Jensen gap); per-game independence assumed; t=0.75 threshold is arbitrary and entirely drives long-streak PRe; no predictive validation as a forecaster; the text's w*=0.29 for 0/2 contradicts the table's w*=0.13 (table value used).

NETS (Hauri & Vucetic 2022, arXiv:2209.00451) recognizes pick-and-rolls and handoffs from NBA tracking data with per-object LSTM trajectory embeddings, Transformer self-attention, permutation-invariant team pooling, and a three-stage recipe (self-supervised trajectory pretraining -> weak-label fine-tuning -> manual-label fine-tuning); ledger verdict ADAPT because the architecture pattern ports to NFL tracking data for play-concept/formation recognition (the basketball label taxonomy does not transfer).

NETS transformer layer: z_o^{l+1} = LN(FF(LN(Att(Q,K,V)))) + z_o^l with attention head_i = softmax((QW_i^Q)(KW_i^K)^T/sqrt(d_k)) V W_i^V; classification head y = softmax(FF(z_B^N concat sum_{i=1..5} z_{A_i}^N concat sum_{i=1..5} z_{D_i}^N)); class-weighted NLL L = -(1/|D|) sum_D sum_k alpha_k y_k ln(y_hat_k) with alpha = (0.77, 2.34, 0.77); trajectory pretraining loss L_MSE = (1/2H)||nu - nu_hat||^2_2.

NETS weak-label rules: possession if a player is closest to ball >=5 consecutive frames with ball within 5 ft, height <10 ft, speed <25 ft/s; pick-and-roll if triangle distances delta_a, delta_d1 < 6 ft and delta_d2 < 3 ft; handoff if possession changes between two offensive players within 6.5 ft; weak-label specificity vs manual labels: 82% pick-and-roll, 90.5% handoff.

NETS hyperparameters: d_h=256, N=8 layers, h=64 heads, Adam lr 5e-5, batch 512, early stopping (50 epochs), ~400 epochs (~30h on one GPU) pretraining; input windows L=10 frames (1.2s) at 0.12s after 3x downsampling of 25 Hz NBA SportVU data (632 games of 2015-2016, 113,760 possessions, 869,905 non-overlapping 1.2s sequences); 45,802 weak pick-and-rolls, 15,251 handoffs, 808,852 other; manual labels 1,800 sequences (600/class, 50/50 train/test).

NETS results: trajectory ADE/FDE (feet), best at all horizons — H=10 NETS 1.08/2.34 vs LSTM 1.61/2.98 and SocialGAN 1.25/2.75; H=20 NETS 2.78/5.87; H=40 NETS 5.70/10.88. Weak-label 3-class F1 (p&r, handoff, other): NETS (0.856, 0.768, 0.988) vs GBoost (0.398, 0.443, 0.915) and LSTM (0.360, 0.490, 0.905). Ablation: removing pretraining -> (0.802, 0.675, 0.982); removing LSTM embed -> (0.803, 0.731, 0.983); removing pooling -> (0.829, 0.718, 0.985). Manual-label test F1: rules alone (0.869, 0.874, 0.893); NETS on weak labels (0.915, 0.863, 0.908); NETS on 900 manual labels only (0.784, 0.813, 0.844) — worse than rules; pretrain->weak->manual sequential fine-tune (0.951, 0.938, 0.902) — best, beating the rules; without team pooling, t-SNE splits into C(5,2)=10 sub-clusters keyed on player indices.

NETS reader flags: random 80/10/10 split (not time-ordered) inflates scores; the recipe needs a weak-label rule engine first (manual labels alone fail); NFL tracking is 10 Hz x 22 players with play segmentation, not continuous possessions.

Drummond & Popinga (2021, arXiv:2111.08140) perform full Bayesian MCMC inference (Stan) of a dynamic Bradley-Terry model on climbing ascents to quantify what one grade increment means in difficulty, with climber ability following a Wiener process; ledger verdict ADAPT because the Wiener-drift dynamic-rating model and data-driven rating-scale calibration port to GSE team strengths (the climbing domain itself has no NFL transfer).

Climbing success model: Pr(y=1) = p_send = e^{m C(t)}/(e^{m C(t)} + e^{m R}) = logit^{-1}(m C(t) - m R), so log-odds of success are linear in the grade difference between climber ability C(t) and route grade R with slope m; ability dynamics C(t+1) ~ N(C(t), w^2) (Wiener process); expected failures before redpoint E[a] = (1 - p_send)/p_send; session-grade convention uses the best outcome per climber per route per day.
equation: Pr(y=1) = p_send = e^{m C(t)}/(e^{m C(t)} + e^{m R})

claim: Climbing difficulty finding: Australia-Sport m_hat = 0.85 [0.83, 0.86], i.e. d = e^m = 2.33 [2.29, 2.37] times more failed attempts per success per grade increment (vs no-drift log-linear mean 0.65); New Zealand-Sport m_hat = 0.80 [0.76, 0.84] (2.22 [2.13, 2.31] x); abstract-level estimates by grade system: one increment = 2.1x (Ewbank), 2.09x (French), 2.13x (UIAA), 3.17x (Vermin bouldering); community ascent-count slopes 0.7-0.79 across countries/styles match the Bayesian analysis; median explicit fails per climber 126 (range 18-642); fails were 29.9% of ascents (IQR 4.7%-72.0%); MCMC runtime 1 hr 8 min on an iMac 3.6 GHz 8-core i9.

Climbing-grade reader flags: all inference in-sample with no held-out prediction; route grades treated as truth; per-attempt success assumed constant with no learning — authors flag this as 'the most questionable detail'; selection bias shifts the intercept up to ~1 grade but flattens slope only ~(k-1)/k ~= 10%; selective failure logging overestimates slope (known complete loggers show slopes slightly below 2).

Nag et al. (2020, arXiv:2005.12524) propose a three-stage hybrid pipeline (gradient-magnitude/directional-coherence temporal candidate detection, Bayesian skin detection with Viola-Jones face-to-torso geometry, adaptive pixel-linking deep text detector) to detect bib numbers on marathon runners and sports players in video; ledger verdict REJECT — bib-number OCR on marathon runners has no viable transfer path to GSE's numerical/odds NFL engine.

Bib-detection Stage 1: gradient magnitude GM(i) = log(1 + (sum Sx^2 + sum Sy^2)/2) (eq. 1) and directional coherence DC(i) = ((lambda_1 - lambda_2)/(lambda_1 + lambda_2))^2 (eq. 3) from the covariance matrix of Sobel gradients with eigenvalues lambda_1, lambda_2; GMdiff/DCdiff via 5x5 max-min; Fuse = GMdiff + DCdiff; frame differencing + K-means k=3 (Max/Min/Average clusters); key frames from cluster statistics (eqs. 7-9).

Bib-detection Stage 2: Bayesian skin P(skin) = MODE(Avg)/(MODE(Avg)+MODE(Max)) (eq. 10), posterior P(skin|window) thresholded >= 0.50 (eq. 11); torso geometry Height_Torso = 7 * Height_Head (eq. 12) and Width_Torso = 2 * Height_Head (eq. 13), multipliers fit on 500 samples; Stage 3 adaptive pixel-linking loss L = 2 alpha(t) L_pixel + (1 - alpha(t)) L_link (eq. 14) with VGG16 backbone, SGD momentum 0.8, weight decay 6e-6, lr 0.0001 for 20K iterations then 0.001 for 40K; F-measure with alpha = 0.5 (eq. 17).

Bib-detection findings on 9,115 videos/images across six datasets: torso detection F-measures RBNR 0.92, MMM 0.79, CTW1500 0.79, MS-COCO 0.76, R-ID 0.87, own 0.78 — beats prior RBNR/MMM methods on nearly every dataset; text/bib detection F best-on-all-six (RBNR 0.75, MMM 0.79, Re-ID 0.90, CTW1500 0.71, MS-COCO 0.37, own 0.82); '-Torso' variants of EAST/RRD/TextSnake/Re-ID/CRAFT all improve over '-Full' (e.g., CRAFT-Torso 0.81 vs 0.80 on own data), confirming torso pre-segmentation helps every detector; torso-region recognition input beats full-image for every method on every dataset (e.g., SEE-Torso 0.83 vs SEE-Full 0.80); all methods fail on MS-COCO (F <= 0.37).

FEBAMA (Li, Kang, Li 2021, arXiv:2108.02082v3) sets forecast-combination weights via softmax of a linear function of time-varying time-series features, fit by maximizing Bayesian log predictive score; ledger verdict ADAPT — a regime-dependent ensemble weighting scheme portable to GSE model blending with sports-native regime features.

FEBAMA equations: combined density p(y_t|Y_{t-1},M) = sum_i w_{i,t} p(y_t|Y_{t-1},M_i); weight equation w_{i,t} = exp(x_t'beta_i) / (1 + sum_{j=1}^{m-1} exp(x_t'beta_j)) (Eq. 4); log score LS(Y_T,M) = sum_t log p(y_t|Y_{t-1},M) (Eq. 2); pool log score = sum_t log[sum_i w_{i,t} p(y_t|Y_{t-1},M_i)] (Eq. 5); log posterior log p(beta|Y_T,X_T,M) = const + sum_t log[sum_i w_{i,t} p(y_t|...)] + log p(beta) (Eq. 7) with MAP via BFGS and priors N(0, sigma^2=10^3); Metropolis acceptance (Eq. 10) for variable-selection indicators; MASE (Eq. 11) for point forecasts; validation via DM tests and MCB rank tests at 95%.

FEBAMA S&P 500 results (daily log returns 2010-01-04 to 2019-09-18; 1,193 one-step density forecasts evaluated): out-of-sample avg log score FEBAMA -1.2770, FEBAMA+VS -1.2740 vs GP -1.2950, OP -1.3036, SA -1.3067 — FEBAMA top-two in all 4 model combos, MCB-significant at 95% vs all benchmarks; in-sample FEBAMA best LS in all 4 combos, DM-significant at 90% in 3/4 (p = 0.1749, 0.0326, 0.0821, 0.0075). M3 monthly (1,428 series, 18-step horizon): LS SA -3.529, OP -3.542, GP -3.546, FEBAMA -3.377, FEBAMA+VS -3.320; MASE SA 2.249, OP 2.224, GP 2.233, FFORMA 2.217, FEBAMA 2.206, FEBAMA+VS 2.192; FEBAMA+VS best LS in 9/11 combos, DM-significant at 95% in 7/11 combos both metrics. Interpretability example: garch_r2 coefficient +12.96 for the GARCH model drives its weight peaks; high entropy pushes higher SV-model weight in volatile 2015. Caveats: hyperparameters (feature count, window=100) tuned on in-sample LS; OP/GP jury-rigged for multi-step (unfair to baselines).

Douven (arXiv:2607.18269v1) tests whether wisdom-of-crowds transfers to LLM ensembles: 15 LLMs elicited on 254 binary Manifold Markets questions, comparing classical vs learned aggregators and quantifying training-cutoff contamination; ledger verdict ADAPT — weight models by error decorrelation (not accuracy), keep biased sources as contrastive negative weights, enforce cutoff hygiene.

Wisdom-of-LLM-crowds methods: aggregators arithmetic/harmonic/geometric/log-odds mean, median; MLP 15->64 (ReLU, dropout 0.2)->32 (ReLU, dropout 0.2)->sigmoid (Adam lr 5e-3, 25 epochs, BCE); logistic regression L2 lambda=0.01; symbolic regression (SymbolicRegression.jl, 50 runs); metrics Brier score (primary), accuracy, AUC, sign/Wilcoxon/permutation tests, Spearman rank correlation; contamination measured via within- vs outside-cutoff accuracy differentials, probability extremity |p-0.5| Welch t-tests, and cutoff-matched market baselines.

LLM-crowd aggregation results on the clean 94 items (resolving after 1 Sept 2025, post all training cutoffs): Brier arithmetic mean 0.313, median 0.343, MLP 0.264 (15.6% reduction), logistic regression 0.241 (23% reduction) — LR beats every individual model and all classical methods; MLP vs arithmetic mean: sign test 62/94, p=.002; Wilcoxon z=-2.48, p=.013; permutation p=.049.
