Mechanism: LR weight vs individual Brier rank r_s=-0.075 (not accuracy); 9 of 15 models get negative weights (used contrastively); models selected in 100% of symbolic-regression runs include both the best (Sonnet, Opus, Flash, Gemini Pro, GPT-5.4 Mini) and the worst locals (Qwen 2.5 7B, LLaMA 3.1 8B, Phi-4 14B) — a U-shape consistent with complementary error patterns; LR weight diagnostic: absolute weight vs error decorrelation (negative mean pairwise Pearson correlation of squared errors), r_s = +0.482.

The best low-complexity LLM-crowd formula is σ(p_Gemini Pro − p_Claude Haiku), a pure model-disagreement signal, achieving Brier 0.231 on 203 full items (12.9% reduction vs 15-model arithmetic mean 0.265).

LLM-crowd contamination findings: accuracy differentials within- vs outside-cutoff range +0.05 to +0.26 (Claude Sonnet +0.256); full-vs-clean ranking Spearman rho=0.532; the cloud-vs-local mean accuracy gap collapsed 35.8% to 8.9% on clean items; human market vs LLMs: final market Brier 0.098 vs LLM mean 0.266 (2.72x); cutoff-matched LLM 1.61-2.64x worse (mean 1.95x); clean subset only 94 items — individual rankings underpowered.

Dombrovskii & Obedko (2014, arXiv:1410.8042) apply model predictive control (receding-horizon) portfolio optimization with correlated returns, position constraints, quadratic transaction costs, and different borrow/lend rates; ledger verdict ADAPT for the long-only + constraints portion as a structural template for GSE's slate-level staking (correlated simultaneous picks, vig as transaction cost) — the borrowing/shorting machinery has no sportsbook analog; the paper's own results are figure-only with zero exact numbers.

MPC portfolio receding-horizon QP: minimize J(k+m/k) = E{[V(k+m)-V^0(k+m)]^2/F_k} + shortfall penalty (rho=0.1) + quadratic transaction-cost term (Eq. 8), horizon m=10, apply first control then re-solve; reference path V^0(k+1) = (1+mu_0)V^0(k) with mu_0=0.0015/day (Eq. 7); QP form (Eq. 19): Y = [2V(k)G(k) - F(k)]U(k) + U(k)'[H(k)+R(k)]U(k) under linear constraints with R=diag(10^-4) and bounds beta_i=-0.6, gamma_i=3 (proportional to wealth); predictor is VAR(2): eta(k+1) = nu + A_1 eta(k) + A_2 eta(k-1) + omega(k+1), OLS on trailing 200-day windows. Assumptions: finite conditional first/second moments, positive-definite R, no return-distribution assumptions.

MPC portfolio data: MICEX (Russian Stock Exchange) daily prices via finam.ru — Sberbank, Gazprom, VTB, LUKOIL, NorNickel, Rosneft, Sibneft — ~1,500 trading days, illustrated 2007-07-20 to 2014-09-11; risk-free rates r_1=0.0001 (lending), r_2=0.0002 (borrowing) per day; solved with MATLAB quadprog. Claims are qualitative only: a smooth wealth-growth curve tracking the 0.15%/day target over 2007-2014 across 5-asset combos. Reader flags: parameter choices (mu_0, rho, R, beta, gamma, m) asserted by hand with no optimization or sensitivity analysis; VAR(2) parameters frozen for 6 years after a 200-day fit; no train/test split, no baseline, no statistical tests.

Polakow & Gebbie (2006, arXiv:physics/0601166v3) use SVD/random-matrix theory on the correlation matrix with the Kaiser-Gutman rule (retain factors with eigenvalue >= 1 as effective dimensions, separating signal from noise) to count effectively independent bets, replacing naive breadth sqrt(N) with sqrt(N_effective) for Kelly-style aggregate sizing; ledger verdict ADAPT — GSE should run the breadth diagnostic on correlated pick slates before aggregate Kelly sizing.

Independent-bets method: eigendecomposition/SVD of the return/correlation matrix; effective breadth ~= sqrt(N_effective); scale total aggregate stake exposure by sqrt(N_effective/N) instead of sizing picks independently. Assumptions: correlation matrix stable over the estimation window; returns approximately stationary.

Independent-bets findings: 41 Johannesburg Stock Exchange equities over 4.3 years daily data (from March 2003) yield 8 effective dimensions -> breadth ~= 3 vs naive sqrt(41) ~= 6; equities + SA government bonds: 9 dimensions -> breadth 3 vs conventional ~= 7; mixed universe (+13 international assets): 13 dimensions -> breadth ~= 4 vs conventional ~= 8 — the consistent message is the true independent-bet count is roughly half the naive count. Caveats: no out-of-sample validation, purely demonstrative; bet-outcome correlations (binary) need a different estimator, e.g. tetrachoric or bootstrap.

Mori & Hisakado (2009, arXiv:0911.3249) show efficiency emerges non-monotonically in a parimutuel racetrack market as betting progresses (concentration -> dispersion -> re-concentration); ledger verdict ADAPT — the AR/EAR/DL(x) time-resolved efficiency diagnostic is portable to NFL line-movement phases from open to close.

Racetrack efficiency math: win bet fraction from odds x_{i,k}^r = 0.788/(O_{i,k}^r - 0.1) (eq. 1), renormalized; scale invariance via ROC curve (x_0(s), x_1(s)) fitting x_1 = a*x_0^alpha in the small-x_0 region (eq. 8), with the double scaling limit giving exact x_1 = x_0^alpha over the full range (eq. 22); efficiency via Lorenz curve L(x) (eq. 9) and expected Lorenz EL(x) (eq. 11); AR = (integral L - 1/2)/[(1/2)(1 - N_1/N)] (eq. 10) with EAR analog (eq. 12); AR = EAR is the necessary-but-not-sufficient efficiency condition; the sign of DL'(x) tells over/under-estimation by rank. Polya urn voting model: vote prob P_{i,t}^mu = X_{i,t}^mu/Z_t (eq. 13), Z_t = N_1 s_1 + N_0 s_0 + t (eq. 14); beta-binomial vote counts (eq. 15); thermodynamic limit gamma (eq. 17); x_1 ~ x_0^alpha with alpha = s_1/s_0 (eq. 21).

Racetrack data: JRA 2008 win-bet time series — 3,542 races -> 3,250 used (final pool 10^5 <= V_r <= 10^6); N=47,273 horses, N_1=3,251 winners, K=285,269 announcements; full-sample replication JRA 1986-2006: 71,549 races, N_1=71,650, N_0=829,716; almost half of all votes arrive in the last 10 minutes.

Racetrack findings: ROC fits t_0: alpha=1.03 (diagonal, no information); t_3: alpha=1.77 over 0.03 <= x_0 <= 0.3; 1986-2006: alpha=1.81 over 0.003 <= x_0 <= 0.3 — the scale-invariance exponent is stable across decades. AR rises monotonically, saturating at t_2; EAR starts ~=0.9 (extreme concentration), falls to minimum at t_2, rises after; AR=EAR at t_1 AND at t_3 — efficiency is attained twice with an inefficient interval between. DL(x) anatomy: t_1 — top 10% overestimated, next 10% underestimated; t_2 — popular 30% underestimated, 70% unpopular overestimated (favorite-longshot bias state, max AR-EAR gap); t_3 — near-efficient, top 20% mildly overestimated. 1986-2006: degree of inefficiency very small; top 0.4% underestimated, next 10% overestimated (contrary to simple favorite-longshot bias). Companion paper 1006.4884 extends with independent/herding voter decomposition.

Szczecinski (2026, arXiv:2604.03840v1) gives closed-form statistical analysis of the Elo update: steady-state variance, convergence time, and the core separation of the ranking scale from the prediction scale; ledger verdict ADAPT — split GSE's Elo into a published ranking scale vs an empirically-fit prediction scale, and use the convergence constant as a rating-trust flag.

Elo statistics: steady-state Elo estimate variance v ~= sK/2 (s = logistic scale, K = K-factor); convergence constant tau = 4s/K (in units of games) — the time constant with which a rating forgets its initialization; win probability from rating differences uses a separately fitted scale (optimal scaling via logistic regression), not the ranking scale s. Variants tested: conventional Elo, no-HFA Elo, HFA Elo, optimal-scaling Elo, fully adaptive online variant; evaluation by log score on a walk-forward stream. Assumptions: latent strengths drift slowly relative to tau; conditionally independent Bernoulli/logistic outcomes; logistic link correctly specified up to scale.

Elo findings on 5,719 FIFA international matches (2018-06-04 to 2024-07-14): log scores (lower better) conventional 0.998; no-HFA 0.904; HFA 0.894; optimal scaling 0.893; online/fully adaptive 0.891 — the ranking/prediction scale separation drives the 0.998 -> ~0.89 improvement. By 2024, 80% of teams had less than one convergence constant (tau) of experience — most published ratings had not converged, quantifying rating unreliability for low-volume teams. Caveats: optimal-scaling/adaptive hyperparameters tuned on the same walk-forward stream evaluated on; single FIFA dataset; v ~= sK/2 assumes slow strength drift (breaks under coaching/roster regime change); tau theory is stationary-regime only.

Csurilla & Csato (2026, arXiv:2609.21674v1) compare performance-based Elo ratings vs lagged Transfermarkt squad market values for forecasting 1,503 UEFA Champions/Europa League matches; ledger verdict ADAPT — equal-weight forecast pooling of a performance rating with a market-implied strength measure is a cheap, proven upgrade for GSE's NFL team-strength blend.

Elo-vs-Transfermarkt setup: targets goal difference GD (eq. 1), expected-goals difference xGD (eq. 2), ordered outcome R in {0,1,2} (eq. 3); Elo_it = Elo^h_t - Elo^a_t (1-September snapshot, eq. 4); TM_it = log V^h_{t-1} - log V^a_{t-1} (eq. 5); models per target: OLS (eq. 6), ordered probit (eqs. 7-8), multinomial logit (eq. 11); equal-weight pool Y^eq = 0.5 Y^Elo + 0.5 Y^TM (eq. 17); stacking Y^stack = a_t + b_E Y^Elo + b_T Y^TM (eq. 19); RPS-minimizing convex weight omega in {0,...,1} (eq. 20); metrics RMSE, OOS R^2 (eq. 12), RPS (eq. 13, x100), Brier (eq. 14), log loss (eq. 15); clustered loss-differential t-tests (eq. 16, DM-style); expanding-window recursive validation with headline eval 2023/24 (238) + 2024/25 (362) = 600 matches, 2022/23 (238) for combination parameters, 7 sample-restriction robustness checks.

Elo-vs-Transfermarkt in-sample (N=1394): GD adj-R^2 = 0.254 (Elo), 0.236 (TM), 0.261 (joint); standardized coefs 0.977/0.938 single, 0.662/0.358 joint; corr(Elo diff, log-TM diff) = 0.877. OOS GD RMSE/R^2: Elo 1.710/0.237; TM 1.710/0.237; Joint 1.698/0.248; Equal-weight 1.695/0.251; Stacked 1.686/0.259. OOS 100xRPS/Brier/log loss: Elo 19.729/0.183/0.932; TM 19.533/0.182/0.928; Joint 19.539/0.182/0.926; Equal-weight 19.431/0.182/0.923; Estimated 19.480/0.182/0.925. Equal-weight vs Elo: Delta=-0.297 RPSx100, 95% CI [-0.588,-0.007], p=0.045; vs TM: p=0.499 (not significant). Equal-weight pool has best RPS under all 7 sample restrictions; estimated weights never significantly beat fixed 0.5 (stacking fit on only 238 forecasts — high variance); probability-pool weight omega = 0.35-0.40 on Transfermarkt. Calibration flaw (all models): observed home-win frequency exceeds predicted in every bin (e.g. [0.0,0.2): predicted 0.133 vs observed 0.236). Raw Elo difference beats the canonical Elo expected-score transform; no league-phase slope break (all p>0.2).

Brown (2017, arXiv:1704.00583v1) builds a PageRank model on per-game event graphs (reversed pass arcs, goal-node scoring arcs, turnover arcs) to quantify playmaking that box scores miss, via an Integrated Playmaking Metric (IPM); ledger verdict ADAPT — ports to NFL target networks for WR/TE involvement metrics and team-aggregated flow differentials (team strength).

PageRank playmaking construction: directed graph with n player nodes + 1 goal node; pass i->j drawn as arc j->i (rank flows to the playmaker); a score creates n arcs goal->scorer; dispossession is an arc victim->dispossessor; contested miss is an arc shooter->defender; initialization arcs (player<->goal + goal self-loop) guarantee primitivity; the Markov chain stationary vector satisfies T^T v = v; Integrated Playmaking Metric IPM_i = 50n*r_i/(1-r_g) (goal-node rank factored out; mean 50, scale 0-1000, cross-game comparable); propositions 2.1-2.2 give spacing guarantees (some bench player always non-negligible; some pair always close); validation is qualitative — IPM ordering vs P/A/R/S/FG% stat lines across 9 games, no predictive target.

PageRank IPM findings on nine manually-transcribed NBA games (2014-2016): Klay Thompson's 41-pt game -> IPM 50.27 (average); game-toppers Curry 122.91-132.74, Westbrook 125.96, Lowry 123.55; 93% of players with >=5 assists had IPM >= 50; 40% of top-10 IPMs had <=20 P+A+R+S — surfacing 'invisible' contributors (Dellavedova, Ronnie Price); aggregate: 87% of IPM<30 players had P+A+R+S <= 10; 64% of IPM>70 had P+A+R+S >= 25; team signal: winning team's starters had higher average IPM in 8/9 games (full-team average only 6/9); top-ranked player was on the losing team 4/9. Limitations: 9 games only, manual transcription, no prediction experiment, equal arc weights, scaffolding arcs arbitrary.

Bober-Irizar, Dua, McGuinness (2024, arXiv:2410.02831) benchmark Elo, Glicko2, TrueSkill (team and per-player), and WinRate on 9,929 pro CS:GO matches, with matchmaking framed as acquisition functions affecting rating quality; ledger verdict ADAPT — per-player TrueSkill across roster moves and information-weighted updates are the two transferable findings.

CSGO rating emulators: WinRate E[A|B]=(1+w(A)-w(B))/2; Elo E=1/(1+10^{(R_B-R_A)/400}); Glicko2 (mu, phi RD, sigma volatility, tau): v=[g(phi')^2 E(mu,mu',phi')(1-E)]^{-1}, Delta=v g(phi')(s-E); TrueSkill (mu, sigma, beta, tau); TrueSkillPlayers (per-player, updated jointly). Acquisition functions: AF_draw = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p) (binary entropy, max at p=0.5); CrossEntropy (surprisal vs seen matchups); Weighted = alpha*draw_factor + beta*seen_factor, alpha=beta=1; LeastSeen; TSQuality. Simulator: 100 runs per emulator x AF; train on AF's top pick of 25 drawn matches; accuracy on non-draw test matches; TrueSkill sensitivity via log grid search +-1 order of magnitude, GP-smoothed.

CSGO rating results (9,929 pro/semi-pro matches, hltv.org, >=1-star team rating, 2017-2022; random 50/50 train/test): accuracy at 500/1000/2000 training matches — at 500: Glicko2 60.1->61.2 (best team-based), TrueSkillPlayers 59.6->62.1 (best overall); at 2000: Glicko2 62.6->63.1, TrueSkillPlayers 61.8->64.1 (best achieved). Weighted acquisition function best for every emulator; LikeliestDraw/CrossEntropy +1-1.5% over random; MostSeen and LikeliestWin worse than random; TSQuality (fun matchmaking) worse than random (56.5-62.9%). TrueSkill sensitivity: beta and sigma dominate, tau minor; optimal beta=sigma/0.5 and beta=sigma/1.6 vs default beta=sigma/2; per-player emulator robust (1.3% range vs 7.5% for per-team); defaults near-optimal — tuning gains small, mistuning costs large. Weighted-AF accuracy declines late in training (informative matches consumed early; uninformative leftovers skew ratings). Caveats: random non-temporal 50/50 split; accuracy-only eval (no log loss); draws excluded; single pro dataset.

Rasp & Lerch (2018, arXiv:1805.09091, Monthly Weather Review) do NN distributional regression with closed-form Gaussian CRPS loss and station embeddings for post-processing ensemble weather forecasts; ledger verdict ADAPT — directly feeds GSE's weather-impact lane: calibrated stadium-level weather distributions as a first-order input to totals/spread models.

NN postprocessing frame: y_{s,t}|X_{s,t} ~ F_{theta_{s,t}} with theta_{s,t} = g(X_{s,t}); EMOS link (mu,sigma) = (a_s + b_s*xbar^{t2m}, c_s + d_s*s^{t2m}); boosting link (mu,sigma) = ((1,X)^T beta, exp((1,X)^T gamma)); NN output = Gaussian (mu,sigma) parameters with no activation, trained with the closed-form CRPS of a Gaussian (eq. B2) as SGD loss; station ID -> 2-dim embedding (n_emb=2) concatenated with predictors and trained jointly; regularization via early stopping on 20% training holdout (dropout/weight decay failed to help); ensemble of 10 NNs with different inits averaging distribution parameters; Adam; one hidden layer (deeper overfit without gain); calibration checked with PIT/verification-rank histograms; significance via Diebold-Mariano + Benjamini-Hochberg across stations; permutation feature importance (Breiman-style on validation CRPS).

NN postprocessing data: ECMWF 50-member ensemble, 00 UTC init, 48h lead, TIGGE archive; DWD surface stations Germany (537; 499 with 2016 validation data); 2007-01-03 to 2016-12-31 daily; 42-predictor vector; splits: train 2007-2015 (1,626,724 samples) or 2015-only (180,849), validation = all of 2016 (182,218 samples); code at github.com/slerch/ppnn.

NN postprocessing results — mean CRPS (2015-train / 2007-2015-train): raw 1.16/1.16 -> EMOS-gl 1.01/1.00 -> EMOS-loc 0.90/0.90 -> EMOS-loc-bst 0.85/0.80 -> FCN-aux-emb 0.88/0.87 -> NN-aux 0.90/0.86 -> NN-aux-emb 0.82/0.78; best NN improves 29% over raw and 3% over best benchmark; NN-aux-emb best at 65.9% of stations (2015) / 73.5% (2007-2015); significantly better than EMOS-loc-bst at 30% of stations, worse at <=2%; long training helps nonlinear models most (EMOS-loc-bst and NNs gain 4-5%; linear gains ~nothing); cost: NN-aux-emb >=2x faster than EMOS-loc-bst including the 10-run ensemble; QRF ~10x slower than EMOS-loc-bst; GPU ~=6x CPU speedup. Top permutation-importance predictors after t2m mean: station altitude, orography, shortwave radiation flux, 850 hPa specific humidity (cloud-cover proxy); ensemble sigma unimportant (spread-error correlation only r=0.15; spread-error ratio 0.51->0.95 after post-processing, mostly additive); raw ensemble under-dispersed (U-shaped rank histogram); all post-processed distributions well calibrated.

Wang, Tzeng, Fan, Huang (2026, arXiv:2609.19035) introduce CPIT, turning a sample-only Monte Carlo forecaster into a calibrated predictive distribution via affine bias correction plus conformal PIT recalibration; ledger verdict ADAPT — CPIT is a drop-in post-processing layer for GSE's Monte Carlo game samples to get threshold-coherent exceedance probabilities for margin of victory.

CPIT equations: bias-corrected conformal PIT with randomized PIT u_i=(N_i+V_i(N_i^*+1))/(m+1); conformal calibration map C_hat(t)=(1+sum 1{u_i<=t})/(N+1); calibrated CDF F_tilde^e_x(y)=C_hat_m(F_tilde^adj_x(y)); rank-cell weights w_j=C_hat_m(j/m)-C_hat_m((j-1)/m); Gaussian smoothing tau_x=4^{1/3} s_x m^{-1/3}; PIT-centrality wrapper (score 2 F_tilde^e_x(y)-1) for nested intervals. Theorem 3 gives a uniform error bound with probability <=2exp(-2N eps^2); Proposition 1: W1(P_tilde^e tau_x, P_tilde^e_x) <= tau_x sqrt(2/pi).

CPIT validation metrics: PIT CvM distance, QErr (mean |empirical-nominal| coverage over {0.05,...,0.95}), mean CRPS, central-90% coverage/length, Brier skill scores at thresholds; baselines: raw ensemble, global/GAM affine correction, three interval-only split-conformal scores.

CPIT results: Simulation 1 — CvM 474.56->0.59, QErr 0.2745->0.0098, CRPS 0.1915->0.0854; CPIT 90% coverage 0.890/0.891. Simulation 3 (shape misspecification): affine correction inert (CvM >31); CPIT CvM->~1.02, QErr 0.0757->0.0120; upper-tail QErr 0.033->0.013. WeatherBench-2 (50-member ECMWF IFS-ENS 24h precipitation vs ERA5, n=3,649 cases 2018-2022): CPIT(GAM) average CvM 0.154 (98% reduction), QErr 0.012, coverage 0.886 unsmoothed / 0.928 smoothed. CPIT's single CDF yields threshold-coherent monotone exceedance probabilities pi_hat(10)>=pi_hat(20)>=pi_hat(40)>=pi_hat(80) — interval-only baselines cannot do this. Caveats: affine bias correction can worsen things when misspecified (Taiwan NW: BC(Global) CvM 7.40->10.26); GAM correction is the safe default; marginal diagnostics can mask local miscalibration (Sim 2). Reference implementation github.com/egpivo/bc-cpit and PyPI bc-cpit.

Lee, Tama, Cha (2022, arXiv:2206.13246) predict soccer players' SOFIFA market values with a LightGBM regression tuned by Optuna TPE hyperparameter search; ledger verdict REJECT — no Bayesian forecasting, and the transfer-fee target has no mapping to GSE's picks or projections. Methods: LightGBM regressor with Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) in Optuna (independent and multivariate TPE, pruning on/off); baselines linear regression, lasso, elastic net, kernel ridge, GBDT, default LightGBM; 10-fold CV on RMSE/MAE; SHAP on the best model; no model equations stated; search spaces: learning rate [0,1] default 0.1, n_estimators [50,3000] default 100; 100 training repetitions per result.

Player-value data: 2,720 players from 20 top-division European clubs (top-4 of five leagues) in 2021-2022 UCL; 2022 SOFIFA dataset (~55 ability attributes) merged with 2021-2022 WhoScored big-five data; ground truth = SOFIFA market value.

Player-value results: best validation RMSE 716.38 (I-TPE LightGBM) vs 949.94 (best GBDT); optimized LightGBM claimed ~3.8x/1.4x/1.8x better than regression baselines/GBDT/plain LightGBM on RMSE; I-TPE ~1.8x better than unoptimized GBM on RMSE and MAE; SHAP top features 'Overall', 'Release_Clause', 'Age', 'BOV'; Release_Clause correlation 0.96 with target. Ledger adversarial notes: 'Release_Clause' (r=0.96) and 'Wage' are near-price variables (borderline tautological); cross-sectional design predicts listed values, not realized future fees; 'Bayesian' is only Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, not Bayesian inference; SOFIFA values are video-game estimates.

Briz-Redon (2023, arXiv:2304.01538) proposes a doubly self-exciting Poisson model for describing scoring levels in NBA basketball: an INGARCH(1,1) Poisson model with a hierarchical game->minute structure testing whether scoring is 'contagious' at game and minute scales, estimated Bayesianly with a Wasserstein-barycenter divide-and-conquer scheme; ledger verdict ADAPT as a portable template for NFL weekly fantasy volume feeding drive-level scoring rates, with self-excitation parameters quantifying within-game 'hot' volume dynamics.

DSE Poisson dynamics: INGARCH(1,1) with Y_t ~ Po(lambda_t) and lambda_t = d + kappa lambda_{t-1} + eta Y_{t-1}; stationary if kappa+eta < 1; unconditional mean mu = d/(1-(kappa+eta)); Var(Y_t) = mu(1-(kappa+eta)^2+eta^2)/(1-(kappa+eta)^2) >= mu. Game level: lambda_g = exp(alpha_S + alpha_Home I_{Home}) + kappa_S lambda_{g-1} I_{g>1} + eta_S Y_{g-1} I_{g>1}; minute level: lambda_{gm} = exp(alpha_G + sum quarter-half effects alpha_{QH} + lambda_hat_g/48) + kappa_G lambda_{gm-1} I_{m>1} + eta_G Y_{gm-1} I_{m>1} (game-level posterior mean as offset).
equation: lambda_t = d + κ λ_{t−1} + η Y_{t−1}

claim: DSE Poisson estimation: Bayesian with N(0,1000) priors on intercepts and U(0,1) on (eta, kappa), NIMBLE MCMC; Wasserstein barycenter p-bar(theta|data) = WB(p(theta|G_1),...,p(theta|G_K)) across 4 season periods (games 1-21, 22-42, 43-62, 63-82); WAIC comparison vs non-self-exciting baseline; hierarchical clustering on Wasserstein distances of eta_S, kappa_S posteriors.

DSE Poisson findings on 2018-19 NBA regular-season made/missed FGs (8 teams x 82 games x 3,936 minutes; 8 top scorers; overtime discarded): game level — DSE improves WAIC only for 3 players (Harden 391.25->388.63, KAT 394.67->382.11, Paul George 377.04->376.63) and no team improves (Celtics 499.56->504.30); minute level — DSE improves WAIC for many units/periods (e.g. KAT: 893.64->885.82, 1019.17->1018.14, 1031.85->1031.55 first three periods), though absolute gains are small (<3 points on ~1000-scale WAIC); clustering: KAT's kappa_S posterior far from all others; Harden and Paul George most similar on eta_S (the two highest eta_S values). Takeaway stated in file: self-excitation in scoring volume is a within-game phenomenon for most units, not a game-to-game one — except for a few high-usage players. Caveats: explanatory only — no out-of-sample forecast evaluation (author's own admission); Poisson ignores zero-inflation; only makes modeled (efficiency vs volume confounded).

Remlinger, Alasseur, Briere, Mikael (2023, arXiv:2111.15365) test Bernstein Online Aggregation (BOA), an online regret-bounded convex combiner of 13 ML stock-return forecasters, on 30 years of data; ledger verdict ADAPT — BOA is the online, regret-bounded ensemble combiner GSE needs for a non-stationary multi-model engine, with weights updated from realized expert losses at a fast log(K)/T rate.

BOA (Wintenberger 2017) update: online convex combination w_{k,t} with update w_{k,t} proportional to w_{k,t-1}*exp(-eta l_{k,t}(1+eta l_{k,t}))/exp(-eta l_{w,t}(1+eta l_{w,t})), where l_{k,t} is the excess loss of expert k over the current mixture; the second-order term eta l^2 penalizes large errors; regret R_T -> 0 at rate log(K)/T.

BOA protocol (Gu et al. 2020): yearly refits, expanding training from 1957-1974, rolling 12-yr validation, 1-yr out-of-sample test 1987-2016 on WRDS (CRSP + Compustat): >30,000 US stocks, 1957-2017, 94 firm characteristics per stock-month rank-transformed to [-1,1], publication lags respected (+1/+4/+6 months); portfolio = long top-decile / short bottom-decile per model, equally weighted (main) and value-weighted (appendix). 13 experts: OLS+H, OLS3+H, GLM+H, ENet+H, PLS, PCR, RF, GBRT+H, NN1-NN5 (+H = Huber loss); comparators uniform mixture PtfUNI (1/K), best fixed convex combo on validation, 1-yr rolling best combo, oracle. Extensions: pre-trained BOA (validation-year weight init); expert specialization (split a beating expert into 2K'=10 bagged variants, re-aggregate over K+2K'=33); leave-one-expert-out importance. Metrics: annualized return, vol, Sharpe, skew, kurtosis, max drawdown, max 1-month loss, turnover. Reference implementation: R package OPERA.

BOA findings: best expert NN2 — annualized return 0.50, vol 0.18, SR 2.74, max DD 0.17, max monthly loss 0.16, turnover 1.23; PtfBOA — return 0.49, vol 0.18, SR 2.77 (best), skew 3.11 (best), max DD 0.08, max loss 0.08 (tail risk roughly halved vs NN2), turnover 1.23 (same); PtfUNI SR 2.56; fixed best-convex on validation 2.28; 1-yr rolling 2.60; oracle 2.92 (little headroom); pre-trained BOA SR 2.78; extended 33-expert SR 2.82, max monthly loss 0.07 (best overall). Weight dynamics: NN2 + OLS+H take ~67% of average weight; adapted quickly at the 2001 dot-com regime break (OLS+H ~40% pre-2001 on short side -> NNs after); 2008 crisis barely moved weights. Caveats: transaction costs not modeled; within-regime behavior concentrates on 1-2 experts (~67%) so the benefit is mostly regime-switching, not averaging; 2008 did not de-risk; expert models themselves are not online (only the mixture is).

Bastian, Basu, Dette (2025, arXiv:2502.08430) construct simultaneous bootstrap confidence bands around phase-mean curves after change-point detection on lab treadmill knee-angle data — a functional-data-theory note; ledger verdict REJECT: no predictive component, no injury outcome, requires per-stride biomechanical curves GSE cannot obtain at NFL scale; replaced by 2309.00756.

Uniform-confidence-band pipeline: BINSEG change-point detection -> relevant-change selection (||mu_i - mu_{i-1}||_inf > Delta, data-driven Delta = ||mu_hat_final - mu_hat_initial||_inf/3) -> simultaneous bands mu_hat^+-_i(t) = mu_hat_i(t) +- sigma_hat(t) q_hat*_{1-alpha/2}/sqrt(n_hat_i), quantile from multiplier (Gaussian) block bootstrap on residuals with long-run variance sigma_hat^2 = sum_{l=-c}^{c} sigma_hat^2_l K(l/c). Theorem 2.1: liminf coverage >= 1-alpha-beta (beta = change-selection level), exactly 1-alpha when no jump sits at Delta. Assumptions: Dette & Kokot 2022 conditions (A1)-(A4) (stationarity, mixing, moments), sigma(t)^2>0, consistent change-point estimators.

Uniform-confidence-band results on marker-based optical motion-capture knee-angle data from runners on a treadmill lab fatigue protocol (runners A and B, n=1830 strides; data not public; no code link): Runner A: Delta=6.6, 3 phases; runner B: Delta=8, 1 change; left-knee comparison Delta=5.9. Qualitative: fatigue phase shows reduced knee bending while foot is in air (second peak shift), consistent with Zandbergen et al. 2023 'protection mechanism.' No numeric accuracy results, no baselines, no train/test split, no numeric metric tables — theoretical validation only (asymptotic coverage). Ledger adversarial notes: Delta threshold ad hoc; coverage asymptotic (finite-sample behavior on short series unstudied); input is per-stride joint-angle curves from optical mocap — NGS provides aggregate speed/acceleration, not stride curves; lab treadmill exhaustion != NFL game fatigue.

Fuentes-Jimenez et al. (2026, arXiv:2602.11668) detect knee injuries (PFPS/ITBS vs healthy) from full stance-phase joint-angle time series with a hybrid CNN and triple explainability (SHAP/saliency/Grad-CAM) under strict volunteer-separated CV; ledger verdict ADAPT — a portable, interpretable injury-screening pipeline adaptable to NGS-derived stride kinematics for soft-tissue (hamstring) risk.

Knee-injury CNN: two-branch architecture — temporal branch (joint-temporal tensor (T,A,C) -> Gaussian noise 0.05 -> 2x Inception-residual blocks (64 filters) + SE modules + dropout 0.3) + point-value branch (dense 8->16, BN/SiLU/dropout 0.3); fusion -> dense 16 -> sigmoid; RMSprop 1e-4, binary crossentropy, class-imbalance data generators. Tasks: three binary (PFPS+ITBS / PFPS / ITBS vs healthy) x three input regimes (time series only, point values only, hybrid); 10 models (KNN, linear/poly SVM, GP, DT, AdaBoost, RF, ANN, CNN, LSTM); 5-fold CV with strict volunteer separation (80/20 volunteers). Explainability: SHAP (SVM_L) + saliency + Grad-CAM as 2D joint x time heatmaps with cross-method consistency check.

Knee-injury data: Ferber et al. 2024 public database — 1,798 runners, treadmill, high-speed Vicon optoelectronic mocap; analyzed 137 PFPS + 126 ITBS + 576 healthy records; per sample: demographics + raw marker trajectories of 7 structures; X-Y-Z Cardan angles for 6 joints + 3 segments; stance phase via PCA-based touch-down/toe-off (Osis et al. 2014); cubic interpolation to 101 samples. No model-code link.

Knee-injury findings: CNN best accuracy — PFPS 77.9% (hybrid), ITBS 73.8% (time series), PFPS+ITBS 71.4% (time series); classical best SVM_L (PFPS hybrid 71.7%, F1 73.5), GP (PFPS+ITBS hybrid 66.0%). CNN high-recall screening profile: PFPS recall 90.3% / precision 41.3% / F1 56.5; ITBS recall 81.9% / precision 34.3%. Hybrid helps PFPS (+1.7pp over time series alone) but slightly hurts ITBS (-0.5pp); full temporal dynamics beat point-value reduction. SHAP (SVM_L): longer stance time (both feet) -> injury risk in all three tasks; PFPS adds lower stride rate + high MF/HF power (foot/ankle/pelvis); ITBS adds stride length (longer = protective) + lower knee abduction peak velocity (protective). CNN heatmaps: midstance 20-60% most relevant; three explainability methods consistent. Limitations: treadmill (not overground) gait; retrospective case-control — detects correlates, not predictors of future injury; CNN precision 34-52% limits clinical use; authors state the maps 'do not allow for the determination of a clear specific running pattern.'

Lakatos (2025, arXiv:2509.02784) builds a GraphSAGE network trained on a weighted Energy-Score + Variogram-Score composite loss producing multivariate calibrated ensembles in one step, beating the standard two-step (univariate calibration + ECC/Schaake shuffle) approach; ledger verdict ADAPT — the one-step recipe for spatially coherent joint weather scenarios across all 30 NFL stadiums in a single forward pass.

dualGNN: GraphSAGE with mean aggregator; graph edges by distance threshold chosen to minimize CRPS (50 km irradiance / 100 km visibility); 1 hidden SAGEConv layer (1024 units) irradiance / 2 (64) visibility; batch norm, ReLU, dropout 0.2; output = K ensemble members directly (non-parametric). Loss: L = w_1*ES + w_2*VS, w_2 = 1-w_1, VS normalized by mean(ES)/mean(VS); irradiance best 0.9/0.1, visibility best 0.3/0.7. Training: <=500 epochs, early stopping (patience 15/10), validation 0.3, batch 64, lr 0.03, one model for all lead times, 10 replications; training windows 30 d (irradiance) / 530 d (visibility); PyTorch Geometric. Formulas: sample CRPS = (1/K)sum|f_k-y| - (1/2K^2)sum sum|f_k-f_l|; ES = (1/K)sum||f_k-y|| - (1/2K^2)sum sum||f_k-f_l||; VS_p = sum_i sum_j omega_ij(|y^(i)-y^(j)|^p - (1/K)sum_k|f_k^(i)-f_k^(j)|^p)^2, p=0.5; ECC reorder f_tilde_k^(d) = f_hat_{pi_d(k)}^(d). Evaluation: ES, VS_0.5, sample CRPS, coverage/width, multivariate rank histograms, DM tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

dualGNN data: solar irradiance — WRF v4.4.2 8-member, 3 km, 48 h hourly, 18 stations Atacama/Coquimbo Chile, 2021; visibility — ECMWF IFS (control + 50 exchangeable), 30 SYNOP stations Germany/Czech/Poland, 2020-2021, 20 lead times 6-120 h, 84 WMO categories, CAMS covariates. No code link.

dualGNN findings: Irradiance — dualGNN #1 on ES and VS: beats GNN-ES by 4% (ES) and 5.2% (VS); beats MLP-ECC in 88.46% of DM cases (never worse); beats MLP-SSh in 76.92%; EMOS outperformed in 96-100% of cases. Univariate CRPS as % of raw: EMOS 51.62%, MLP 42.57%, dualGNN 42.85%, GNN-ES 43.23%, GNN-CRPS 40.79%. Adding VS did NOT hurt ES — improved both. Visibility — dualGNN #1 on VS (beats GNN-ES by 5%; beats POLR-SSh in 70% of DM cases); ES only 0.4% above GNN-ES (tied). Coverage: 90% intervals — GNN models deviate ~1% from nominal vs 2% POLR, 51% raw; dualGNN most uniform multivariate rank histograms. Key side finding: dualGNN's learned rank structure beats raw-ensemble and historical rank structures as a dependence template — the GNN learns real spatial dependence, not just marginals. Caveats: data hunger (530-day training for visibility); graph construction crude (distance threshold only); w_1/w_2 empirical per dataset (no universal rule); slight overestimated correlation in energy/dependence pre-rank histograms.

Wang, Zhang, Shi (2022, arXiv:2207.08635) introduce GOAL, the first and only English sports-game summarization dataset (goal.com football commentary->news, 103 labeled pairs, few-shot setting); ledger verdict ADAPT — the English-language testbed for the summarization pipelines from ledgers 1599/1600 before spending annotation budget on NFL.

GOAL methods: ROUGE-1/2/L (py-rouge) on a 20-sample test set (split 63/20/20 train/val/test); baselines Longest-k, TextRank, PacSum (extractive); PGN (LSTM abstractive); LED-base-16384 (4,096-token input, 1,024 output, beam 4, lr 3e-5, batch 4, 10 epochs, 20 warmup); PacSum beta=0.1, lambda1=0.9, lambda2=0.1, TF-IDF sentence reps. No new model. Data: 103 labeled English commentary-news pairs (goal.com, UCL/Europa/Premier/Serie A 2016-2020; <10% of the 2,263-match SOCCER collection have news); avg commentary 2,724.9 words / news 476.3 words; plus 2,160 unlabeled commentary docs for semi-supervised; English news machine-translated to Chinese by 4 volunteers + expert check for cross-lingual setting (63 samples). Released at github.com/krystalan/goal.

GOAL findings — test ROUGE-1/2/L: Longest 30.3/4.2/19.5; TextRank 27.6/2.9/18.8; PacSum 31.0/5.3/19.6; PGN 32.8/5.7/21.4; LED 34.7/7.8/24.3 (best). All absolute scores far below Chinese-dataset numbers (ROUGE-L ~47 in ledgers 1599/1600) — few-shot + longer inputs + missing score field makes this genuinely hard; English commentaries carry no per-timestamp score field (Chinese corpora use (t,c,s)), so models must infer game state implicitly. Qualitative: LED output has repeated phrases, misses important events; key-verb probing shows it handles common events ('beat') but fails on rarer ones ('blocking'). Limitations: only 20 test samples (wide confidence intervals); semi-supervised, multi-lingual, cross-lingual settings proposed but not actually benchmarked (reserved as future work); no human evaluation; LED repetition unaddressed.

Sugawara & Mori (2026, arXiv:2503.16470) derive the time-inhomogeneous Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process for betting-odds convergence from a microscopic model of herder vs. informed bettors, and estimate a time-varying informed-bettor fraction r_inf(n) on 3,450 JRA races; ledger verdict ADAPT — a parametric, fittable model of how betting markets converge toward efficiency as the event approaches: port from vote-share to NFL line-movement data to locate when 'sharp money' takes over.

OU herding micro rule: f_n(z) = r_inf(n)*q + (1-r_inf(n))*z (convex mix of informed f_inf=q and herder f_herd=z). SDE: dZ(n,q) = -[r_inf(n)(Z-q)/(n+1)] dn + [sqrt(q(1-q))/((n+1)sqrt(Delta t))] dW(n,q); potential U_n(z) = r_inf(n)/[2(n+1)](z-q)^2; closed-form solution + MSE decomposition; log-MSE approx ln(MSE(n)/MSE(1)) ~= (-2r_1 + 4 Delta r/(N-1)) ln((n+1)/2) - 2((n-1)/(N-1))Delta r. Constant r_inf: MSE ~ power law (exponent 2r_1 for r_1<1/2, 1 for r_1>1/2, log correction at 1/2 — 'super-normal transition'). Linear r_inf(n) = r_1 + (n-1)/(N-1)*Delta r: crossover to exponential decay at n > n_c = (N-1)/(2 Delta r) + 1 when Delta r > 0.

OU herding estimation: regress (n+1)(Z(r,h,n+1)-Z(r,h,n)) = -r_inf (Z(r,h,n)-q(r,h)) at n in {1,...,50}; macro validation = empirical log-MSE ratio vs Eq. 10 in four q-strata. Data: JRA 2008 win-bet data — 3,450 races, 50,180 horses, 3,453 winners; final pools 5.9x10^4-1.46x10^7 (mean ~=3.0x10^5); 14-401 announcements per race (mean ~=80); odds->vote share via JRA formula O = max(1.1, 0.788/Z) inverted with +0.05 truncation adjustment; normalized time n[r,i] = 100*t/T (n=1 ~= 480 min to post, n=50 ~= 20 min). Code: github.com/LABO-M/Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Process-for-Horse-Race-Betting.

OU herding findings: informed fraction r_inf(n) = 0.334 + [(n-1)/49]*0.658, R^2 = 0.90 (all horses); at n=50, r_inf = 0.992, herder fraction 0.008 — reverses prior assumption: herders decrease over time, market becomes more efficient approaching post. q-strata: q<0.01 (25.6%) and 0.01-0.1 (52.2%) match theory closely; q>=0.4 favorites (1.6%) converge slower than theory (MSE slope ~= -0.5 vs theoretical 2r_inf = 0.8): persistent herding on favorites -> slower convergence -> favorite-longshot bias (favorites undervalued). Crossover n_c ~= 77 (N=100, Delta r=0.658); low per-n regression R^2 acknowledged (q-heterogeneity, n<->real-time mismatch). Caveats: pari-mutuel vote-share != fixed-odds line (herder rule needs re-derivation for NFL); n is pool-normalized not clock-normalized; MSE(100) = 0 by construction so only n <= 50 analyzed; no holdout or forecasting test; single year/jurisdiction, win market only.

The Bayes-Kelly paper (2024, arXiv:2402.03035) is a pure-theory paper proving the Bayes-Kelly test martingale is exactly optimal for sequentially accumulating evidence that a forecast stream is miscalibrated (maximizes expected log test wealth at every horizon; the optimum equals a KL divergence); ledger verdict ADAPT — the statistical engine behind GSE's abstention / stake-shrink triggers. No empirical dataset, no simulations with stated sample sizes, no code repository link.

Bayes-Kelly: a conformal test martingale built from a prior over the miscalibration alternative, updated per observed forecast-outcome pair via a conformity measure. Theorem 3.2 (paper's numbering): for a fixed conformity measure and alternative, Bayes-Kelly maximizes E[log(test wealth)] at every horizon; the maximum equals D(alternative || null). Assumptions: exchangeability under the null (calibrated forecasts); conformity measure and prior over alternatives fixed in advance; the general algorithm may be computationally infeasible (paper's stated limitation — practical use needs a tractable special case). The optimality theorem itself is the result: no other test martingale (for the same conformity measure and prior) accumulates expected log-evidence faster at any horizon. Limitations: general algorithm may be computationally infeasible; no demonstration on real forecasts or betting data; optimality is relative to a fixed conformity measure and prior — a bad prior yields a valid but weak monitor; exchangeability under the null is strong for sports forecasts with regime shifts.

Ledger verdict REJECT for the STGCN-LSTM Olympic medal prediction paper (arXiv:2501.17711): a deep read found it to be a buzzword-stacked, non-reproducible modeling collage with factual hallucinations, wrong math, and internally inconsistent numbers — nothing in it can be adapted with engineering integrity.

The rejected paper claims a stack of STGCN (GATConv) -> bidirectional LSTM with attention/highway fusion -> DeepEnsemble (HistGradientBoosting, XGBRegressor, TemporalTransformer), Zero-Inflated Compound Poisson (EM + elastic net) for zero-inflated counts, BOCPD change points, DDD triple-difference for coach effects, DML/IPW/matching for hosting effects, and Markowitz mean-variance for resource allocation; its moderation model is given as Treatment Effect = 8.2 + 0.15xGDP + 1.2xCoach_Level + 0.8xHist_Medals (units never defined).

The rejected Olympic paper has mathematically wrong equations as stated: lambda=0.05 claimed as '20-year half-life' (true ~=13.9 years; e^(-0.05x20)=0.37 != 0.5); eta=0.33 claimed 'half-life ~3 Olympic cycles' (true ~=2.1 cycles); equations (13) and (14) are the identical formula duplicated under two identical subsection titles. Tables 2 and 3 are both mislabeled '2028 Paris Olympics' (Paris was 2024; 2028 is LA), and Table 2 shows fractional gold declines (-1.60) for countries winning essentially zero medals. The flagship causal example is a hallucination: Lang Ping (a volleyball coach) is claimed to have coached Chinese table tennis 2005-2016. Hosting total effect 24.5+-2.7 medals but section 6.2 claims a '2.3-medal average host country effect' — internally inconsistent; DML/IPW/matching host estimates 14.8/15.1/15.5 — suspiciously tight agreement. No dataset released, no schema, no repository, no code; the coach-mobility variable driving the central 'causal' claims has no described data source.

Bates et al. (2021, arXiv:2101.02703, JACM 2023), 'Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets', generalizes conformal prediction from controlling miscoverage to controlling ANY monotone risk with high probability 1-delta; ledger verdict ADAPT — the formal risk-control layer for GSE's abstention-gated public pick publishing (complements the Conformal Risk Control ledger, which controls risk only in expectation).

RCPS UCB calibration: fix a NESTED family of set predictors {T_lambda} (larger lambda -> larger sets -> loss nonincreasing in lambda); on calibration data compute empirical risks R_hat(lambda); form high-probability upper confidence bounds R_hat^+(lambda); choose lambda_hat = inf{lambda : R_hat^+(lambda') <= alpha for all lambda' >= lambda}. Formulas: R(T) = E[L(Y,T(X))]; Theorem: P(R(T_{lambda_hat}) <= alpha) >= 1-delta; example Hoeffding UCB: R_hat^+(lambda) = R_hat(lambda) + sqrt(log(1/delta)/(2n)). Supported UCBs: Hoeffding, Hoeffding-Bentkus, Waudby-Smith-Ramdas, Pinelis-Utev, CLT/asymptotic. GSE transfer noted in file: T_lambda = {games with |edge| >= lambda} is nested in lambda; loss L = fraction of posted picks that lose.

RCPS data: five vision problems — (1) ImageNet classification with class-varying loss, 30,000 calibration / 20,000 evaluation points, 100 random splits; (2) MS COCO multi-label (80 categories, TResNet); (3) ImageNet hierarchical (WordNet tree); (4) polyp image segmentation (per-polyp pixel recall); (5) protein structure (AlphaFold-style). Code in the angelopoulos-lab RCPS GitHub repo.

RCPS findings: ImageNet class-varying loss — risk controlled at nominal level across all 100 splits with 'reasonable' set sizes; realized-risk histogram concentrates just below alpha (near-tightness). COCO multi-label: risk controlled at reasonable set sizes. Hierarchical ImageNet: risk controlled with 'relatively precise (low depth)' predictions — safety not bought with trivially huge sets. Polyp segmentation: captures 90% of true polyp pixels per polyp per image with the CLT bound. No competing-method horse race; the empirical claim is tightness (risk ~= alpha from below). Caveat: with a 100-pick calibration window and delta=0.1, the Hoeffding penalty sqrt(log(1/delta)/2n) ~= 0.12 — enormous against alpha=0.45; the paper's own remedy is the tighter Waudby-Smith-Ramdas (empirical-Bernstein) UCB.

Ashburn & Colvert (2006, physics/0607064) build a Bayesian mean-value (posterior-mean, not MAP) college football rating model whose Normal prior is determined self-consistently from the data's own schedule structure (MSV/MTV) rather than hand-tuned; ledger verdict ADAPT as the portable prior-calibration module for GSE's Bayesian rating stack.

Bayesian mean-value rating formulas: win probability P(i beats j) = Phi(r_i - r_j, sigma_v) with sigma_v = 1 (1/2+1/2 per-team performance variance); ratings are posterior means via moment integrals m_i(n) = integral r^n Phi_p(r,sigma_p) prod_j Phi_ij(r) dr; r-tilde_i = m_i(1)/m_i(0); sigma_i^2 = m_i(2)/m_i(0) - (m_i(1)/m_i(0))^2. Prior: Normal(r_{i k-bar}, sigma_p) centered on mean scheduled opponent; sigma_p^2 = sigma^2 - sigma'^2/N_i (eq. 36), from mean schedule variance MSV (sigma'^2) and mean team variance MTV (sigma^2), iterated to convergence. Outcome correlation diagnostic: rho_i = [1/2 W_i(W_i-1) + 1/2 L_i(L_i-1) - W_i L_i] / [1/2 (W_i+L_i)(W_i+L_i-1)] (eq. 19). Home field h via Newton iteration on the win-count equation (eq. 42); mean h = 0.244, SD 0.016 (2001-2005). Published metric: r-tilde-tilde_i = mean over j!=i of P(r-tilde_i - r-tilde_j, sigma_i^2+sigma_j^2+sigma_v^2), a scale-free 'winning percentage' in [0,1].

Bayesian mean-value findings on all Division I-A, I-AA, II, III, NAIA college football games 2001-2005 (~700 teams, ~3,600 games/season in 2005; teams, winner/loser, home/away/neutral site only — no margins): outcome correlation model-implied vs actual per season: 0.161 vs 0.164, 0.158 vs 0.158, 0.164 vs 0.164, 0.153 vs 0.151, 0.151 vs 0.157 — differences -0.003, 0.000, 0.000, +0.002, -0.006 ('quite accurate and relatively unbiased'); actual rho precision sigma_rho ~= 0.010-0.011; sqrt(MSV) 0.93-1.02, sqrt(MTV) 0.76-0.85; model-implied upset frequency U: 21.2%, 21.3%, 20.7%, 21.6%, 22.2% — inside sanity bounds (16-19% ranking violations / 28% from Fair & Oster 2002); triplet splits (2007 addendum): estimated 9.24/9.26/8.78/9.51/9.84% vs actual 9.09/8.93/8.94/9.54/9.44%, within ~0.39% one-sigma precision; sum-of-squared ranking differences vs BCS computer average: 38.4 (model, no HFA) vs median 66.1 of six BCS computers — best by a comfortable margin; with HFA 62.9 vs 62.6 (second by a hair). No code or data published (atomicfootball.com defunct); method fully specified mathematically.

Yao, Vehtari, Simpson & Gelman (2018, arXiv:1704.02030) give the canonical theory for stacking Bayesian predictive distributions via log-score maximization with PSIS-LOO densities — the theoretical foundation of Stan's loo::stacking_weights(); ledger verdict ADAPT — directly replaces BMA for GSE's heterogeneous (M-open) Bayesian ensemble.

Log-score stacking: weights w-hat = argmax_w (1/n) sum_i log sum_k w_k p(y_i|y_{-i}, M_k) subject to w_k >= 0, sum_k w_k = 1 (general form (2.2): argmax over any proper scoring rule S); combined predictive p-hat(y-tilde|y) = sum_k w-hat_k p(y-tilde|y, M_k) (2.3). PSIS-LOO: importance ratios r_{i,k}^s = 1/p(y_i|theta^s, M_k), generalized-Pareto fit on largest 20%, smooth/truncate, exact-LOO substitution for Pareto k-hat > 0.7. Pseudo-BMA: w_k = exp(elpd-hat_loo^k)/sum exp(elpd-hat_loo^{k'}); Pseudo-BMA+ (2.6): Bayesian-bootstrap (Dirichlet(1,...,1)) averaging over elpd vectors, w_k = (1/B) sum_b w_{k,b} — regularizes weights away from 0/1. Diagnostic gate: distrust weighting when n < 5 x effective parameters.
equation: ŵ = argmax_w (1/n)Σᵢ log Σₖ wₖ p(yᵢ|y_{−i}, Mₖ)

claim: Stacking findings: Gaussian-mixture simulation (M-open, truth N(3.4,1), 8 candidates N(1..8,1)) — log-score stacking beats BMA on expected log predictive density except at extremely small n; stacking of distributions attains the same optimal MSE as stacking of means. Key robustness: duplicating a candidate model leaves stacking weights unchanged in theory while BMA/Pseudo-BMA concentrate on the duplicate and get worse. Linear subset regression (J=15, SNR 4:1): stacking beats all six competitors (stacking of means, Pseudo-BMA, Pseudo-BMA+, best-LOO, best-marginal-likelihood, BMA) across n=5->200. vs mixture models: stacking and Pseudo-BMA+ beat a full mixture model on log predictive density at every (rho,n) tested and are ~30x faster. Real datasets: US Senate voting 1988-92 (n=94); Bangladesh well-switching (n=3020, 8 logistic/B-spline models) — both methods put bulk weight on Model 5 (5th-degree splines) and ~0 on the most complex Model 8; stacking's ~0.09 weight on simple logistic Model 1 visibly smooths boundary fluctuation; example printed weights: stacking [0.25, 0.06, 0.09, 0.25, 0.35, 0.00] vs Pseudo-BMA+ [0.28, 0.05, 0.08, 0.30, 0.28, 0.00]. Caveats: LOO degrades when n < 5x effective parameters; log-score stacking is outlier-sensitive (CRPS alternative supported). Code: R/Stan loo::stacking_weights() / model_weights(log_lik_list, method='stacking').

Assis, Assuncao & Vaz-de-Melo (2020, arXiv:2009.06750) run a Pearl-DAG + back-door-criterion + same-game matching causal study finding NBA timeouts have no causal effect on short-term performance — the apparent effect is regression to the mean; ledger verdict ADAPT — the DAG/matching design is the portable template for debiasing GSE's in-game momentum features.

Timeout causal design: treatment A_t (timeout at game instant t); outcome Y_t^lambda = (P_{t+lambda} - P_t)/lambda - (P_{t-1} - P_{t-lambda-1})/lambda = Delta P_t^{t+lambda} - Delta P_{t-lambda}^t (post-trend minus pre-trend of scoring-margin rate; lambda in {2,4,6} possessions); effect TE = E[Y_t^lambda | A_t=1] - E[Y_t^lambda | A_t=0], estimated as TE_h (home) and TE_a (away). Confounders: quarter Q_t, scoring margin P_t, seconds since period start S_t, pre-trend Delta P_{t-lambda}^t; unobserved inter-game confounders U absorbed by same-game matching. Three matching estimators: exact on pre-trend within same game; Mahalanobis on X_t; propensity score via GBM with Euclidean distance; optimal matching via rcbalance; non-overlapping windows. Inference: 10,000-permutation Monte Carlo on difference-in-means, 99% CIs. Assumptions: conditional ignorability given (U, X_t, Delta P_{t-lambda}^t); SUTVA via non-overlapping windows; DAG completeness (asserted, not tested).

Timeout findings on NBA 2014-15 through 2017-18 play-by-play (main analysis 2016-17: 30 teams, 1,309 games incl. playoffs; 281,373 game instants; 17,765 timeouts — 7,754 home-called, 8,011 away-called, 2,000 mandatory/official): naive before/after mean short-term momentum change: +0.629 (lambda=2, n=14,031), +0.421 (lambda=4, n=12,225), +0.302 (lambda=6, n=10,296) — Wilcoxon/bootstrap p 'numerically equal to zero' (the conventional wrong evidence). Causal estimates (99% CIs): all |TE| <= 0.059 points/possession; largest magnitude = propensity matching lambda=4 away: TE_a = -0.059, CI (-0.098, -0.020); home lambda=4: -0.032 (-0.072, 0.008). Of 18 tests, only 6 significant at alpha=0.001 (no multiplicity correction), every significant effect negligible vs the 1-point practical relevance threshold. Last-5-minutes stratification: 'very similar' — no effect in clutch time either. Complements ledger 1684 (Gibbs et al., ATT -0.35 on a different outcome): convergent evidence timeouts don't help. Code/data: github.com/pkdd-paper/paper667 (R).

Gong, Zhao & Yang (2023, arXiv:2305.14612) build the first automated 2D-video implementation of the clinical Landing Error Scoring System (LESS) for ACL injury risk — OpenPose keypoints -> 5 biomechanical features -> 9/5/1 threshold scoring -> AHP-weighted composite, with public code and Jetson Nano edge deployment; ledger verdict ADAPT.

Automated LESS pipeline: 2D video -> OpenPose keypoints per frame -> 5 features: (1) knee flexion angle (sagittal), (2) trunk/hip flexion angle (sagittal), (3) lateral trunk angle (frontal), (4) ankle-knee horizontal distance, (5) ankle-shoulder horizontal distance; joint angles from keypoint vectors via cosine rule on projections. Each feature scored 9 (excellent) / 5 (good) / 1 (poor) via threshold intervals; composite via Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) pairwise-comparison weight matrix. Takeoff check: knee varus/valgus from |knee-ankle distance|: < 30 degrees = stable; 30-50 degrees = varus error; > 50 degrees = valgus error. OpenPose confidence threshold > 0.4 selected (PCKh@0.5 = 91.3% at 18.5% keypoint loss; 88.9% at 0.2/7.1% loss; 90.9% at 0.6/36.7% loss; 93.5% at 0.8/76.2% loss). Assumptions: LESS valid for ACL risk (Padua 2009); 2D projections suffice; OpenPose accurate enough at the chosen threshold. Code: github.com/ZiyuGong-proj/Assessment-of-ACL-Injury-Risk-Based-on-Openpose.

Automated LESS findings on 30 subjects (10 basketball players, 10 active, 10 less active; platform landing / drop vertical jump test, sagittal + frontal video; subject videos not released): group separation basketball > active (p = 0.0193), active > less active (p = 0.0486), basketball vs less active p = 3.59x10^-8. Example kinematics: max knee flexion ~= 65 degrees (excellent); max hip flexion ~= 70 degrees (excellent); frontal thigh-trunk cosine ~= -1 (parallel); peak frontal flexion cosine ~= -0.75 (30-60 degrees, good). No prospective injury outcomes — validation is group discrimination only, partly circular. Limitations: n=30, single lab setting, controlled landing test (far from broadcast video: occlusion, angles, multiple athletes); AHP weights are expert-subjective, not data-driven; LESS is a screening tool, not a validated individual-level injury predictor.

Curtis & Haines (2025, arXiv:2505.02990) fit a linear mixed-effects model of 2023 NYC subway ridership on weather covariates; ledger verdict REJECT — transit demand, not sports; methodologically strictly dominated by ledger 1703's sports-native equivalent (24,582 finish times, finer granularity). Replaced by ledger 1712.

Subway ridership model: linear mixed-effects (nlme/lme4): Y_ij = fixed borough intercepts/slopes + b_0i + b_1i*month + beta*weather + eps_ij; random intercepts/slopes per OD pair, compound-symmetry temporal correlation, REML; PCA on 11 weather covariates (PC1 ~65%, PC2 ~19%, PC3 ~6%); borough-stratified models; Manhattan x gust interaction; December-confounding check. Assumes linearity, monthly aggregation preserves signal, 50 sampled pairs representative. Data: MTA 2023 origin-destination ridership (115M+ rows via API, aggregated to monthly averages) joined to Weather Underground monthly weather (max/avg/min temp, dew points, total precip, max/avg wind, max/avg gust); analysis sample only 50 OD pairs with complete 12-month records. Dataset on GitHub (hainesdata/subway-ridership-longitudinal-analysis); full R code in appendix.

Subway ridership findings: max gust speed has a significant negative ridership effect (t ~= -2.7 to -3.1); total precipitation and max wind insignificant. Effect concentrated in Manhattan-originated trips (max_gust t = -2.52, n.s. elsewhere); Manhattan x gust interaction t = -3.07. December's significance disappears once max_gust is added — gust confounds the December calendar effect (AIC 995.87 -> 971.78). PC3 (steady-vs-gusty wind) x month interaction p = 0.03. Authors' own conclusion: weather has *minimal* influence on ridership since NYC depends on transit regardless. Limitations: n=50 of 111k possible pairs; one year of monthly data can't separate weather from seasonality; no holdout/CV; several models failed to converge; residual variance very high (sigma^2 up to 25).

Lee et al. (2024, arXiv:2408.05123v1) — Sportify: a system that answers sports-video questions by retrieving relevant clips, classifying the tactic (KNN + FastDTW over SportsVU trajectories), overlaying embedded visualizations (arrows/highlights for PASS/CUT/SCREEN/SHOOT), and narrating in first- or third-person voice; ledger verdict ADAPT — the 'evidence-grounded answer' pattern is the academic version of GSE's telestrated-clip doctrine.

Sportify pipeline: (1) question -> retrieve relevant clip; (2) tactic classification on SportsVU coordinates via KNN over FastDTW distances vs 134 human-annotated reference clips; (3) PASS/CUT/SCREEN/SHOOT event extraction and filtering; (4) embedded visualization rendering (trajectory arrows, player highlights, tactic labels); (5) ReAct retrieval of external context (Google/Wikipedia/Statmuse); (6) answer generation in three modes: plain text, third-person visual, first-person personified ('I cut baseline because the screen freed me'). No learned parameters beyond k and the DTW warping window. Assumption: SportsVU-grade coordinates available; 134 reference clips cover the question space. Data: SportsVU player-coordinate data (proprietary, STATS); 134 human-annotated reference clips covering basketball tactics; Google/Wikipedia/Statmuse via ReAct agent; user study: 13 basketball fans (12 completed timed tasks). No public code or dataset.

Sportify findings: tactic classifier 0.8533 accuracy (5-fold CV) on 134 clips. PASS/CUT/SCREEN/SHOOT extraction F1 0.7393. Action-sequence identification accuracy: text 72.22% (26/36), third-person visual 72.22% (26/36), first-person visual 69.44% (25/36) — essentially no difference; accuracy claims don't survive n=13. Watch time: text 69.44s, third-person 68.72s, first-person 86.27s; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.02, H = 7.765; Dunn text-vs-first p = 0.046 — first-person costs ~17s more with no accuracy gain. Visualization helpfulness: Cut 85%, Screen 77%, Pass 85% rated helpful. Key gaps: no test of whether personified narration distorts facts (fabricated player intent risk); no modern VLM baseline; basketball/SportsVU-only.

Xi, Moallemi, Pai & Wang (2026, arXiv:2607.08199) forecast the conditional volatility (next price-move scale) of binary prediction-market contracts from structural state variables — deadline-resolution (Wright-Fisher) + adverse-selection/order-flow (Glosten-Milgrom) — in a closed form that beats plain GARCH(1,1) by 34% on ~880,000 out-of-sample hourly forecasts; ledger verdict ADAPT.

Prediction-market structural variance (closed form): h_t^2 = p_t(1-p_t)/tau_t + K*nu(V_t)*s_t^2/4, with nu(V) = sqrt(V) (headline), K >= 0 fit by MLE. First term = Wright-Fisher deadline-resolution (Bernoulli boundary shape: variance max at p=0.5, forced to zero at resolution); second = Glosten-Milgrom order-flow: spread s_t scaled by activity proxy sqrt(V). Benchmarks: plain GARCH(1,1); deadline-resolution-only (DR); DR-AS(sqrt V); probit-Brownian variance shape (Archak & Ipeirotis 2010); GARCH+DR-AS hybrid. Evaluation: 95% prediction intervals for next-hour price, volume-weighted Winkler interval score (VW-IS; penalizes width plus a multiple of miss distance; lower better), paired bootstrap over contract-level clusters. 56-month expanding walk-forward (fit all prior active-update observations, test next month).

Prediction-market volatility data: hourly Kalshi panel, August 2021 - April 2026: binary contracts (Sports, Politics, Economics, Elections, Crypto, Entertainment); per contract-hour: mid implied probability p_t, bid-ask spread s_t, traded volume V_t, time to resolution tau_t; target = size of next-hour probability move conditional on an active update. ~880,000 OOS forecasts; 1,624 contract-hours unlabeled. Kalshi data via public API; no public code or data artifact.

Prediction-market volatility findings: plain GARCH(1,1) VW-IS 0.7675; deadline resolution alone 0.5829; DR-AS(sqrt V) 0.5085 — 34% better than GARCH, 13% better than deadline alone; GARCH+DR-AS 0.4620 — best overall, 9% better than DR-AS alone. Category portability: global fit best or near-best in most major categories; category-specific refitting does NOT systematically improve OOS. Sports contracts are more event-concentrated/jump-like than Economics (Economics: deadline alone nearly matches the winner; only 4.9% of large-move hours vs 8.0% observation share). Zero-update robustness checks (Appendix D) preserve the structural ranking. Limitations: headline conditions on an active update occurring; sportsbook odds lack a true bid-ask spread (books shade lines, limit bettors) — spread must be re-mapped to cross-book dispersion; no causal identification (manipulation vs information not separated); sqrt(V) is a modeling choice.

Jiayu Li (2026, arXiv:2608.23393) — KellyBoost: trains gradient-boosted trees directly on the growth-optimal (Kelly) decision objective instead of a prediction/classification surrogate, with closed-form gradients and a CRRA risk-aversion dial; ledger verdict ADAPT — directly portable to GSE's multi-pick simultaneous portfolio sizing, but only with the fractional-Kelly tempering dial engaged, per the paper's own boundary finding. (This brief is the c05-r13 read of the same paper as the c05-r08 read.)

KellyBoost (r13 read): one multi-output XGBoost emitting logit vector z(x_t) in R^K; portfolio weights w_t = softmax(z) on the simplex (long-only, fully invested; cash leg makes this unrestrictive). Loss (Eq. 1): l_t = -log(1+S_t), S_t = w_t^T y_t — negative log growth rate, the Kelly criterion as training objective. Population proposition: minimizer satisfies sigma(z(x)) in argmax_w E[log(1+w^T y) | x] a.e. — the conditional Kelly portfolio. Gradient: logit k pushed up when y_k > S (outperforms competing portfolio), force proportional to sigma_k * 1/(1+S). Hessian diagonal h_k can be negative (non-convex in z); safeguard uses |h_k|. CRRA dial: phi_gamma(S) = ((1+S)^{1-gamma} - 1)/(gamma-1), gamma->1 recovers -log(1+S) — 'the utility-side analogue of fractional Kelly.' Stabilizers: K_ens=4 leave-one-out ensemble (single tree fits unstable to one-row perturbations).

KellyBoost OOS 2013-01 -> 2026-07 (163 monthly decisions; log G bar = mean realized log growth per 20-day decision x100; Sharpe daily ann. vs T-bills): KellyBoost log G 0.47, ann. return 6.2%, vol 23.9%, Sharpe 0.30, max DD -46.2%; MLP same loss 0.56/7.1%/20.5%/0.35/-55.5% (Delta log growth vs KellyBoost -0.9 [-9.2,+8.9]); two-stage LGBM+optimizer 0.82/8.2%/20.9%/0.40/-40.4% (Delta -1.9 [-12.3,+10.0]); multiclass surrogate 0.35/4.0%/19.2%/0.21/-42.7% (Delta +2.0); unconditional Kelly 0.42/4.1%/19.3%/0.22/-50.9% (Delta +2.0). Every pairwise bootstrap interval straddles zero — 13.6 years of monthly decisions can't separate any two methods at conventional significance, so the paper argues from consistency. Growth objective beats the classification surrogate in all four 2x2 cells (trees 0.47 vs 0.35 searched; 0.39 vs 0.32 hand-built; MLPs 0.56 vs 0.20; 0.67 vs 0.49); pooled paired per-decision difference +0.18, bootstrap Pr(Delta>0) = 0.89 (0.84-0.96). Growth objective trades less in every cell, so transaction costs widen the gap. Boundary finding: end-to-end learners trail the two-stage pipeline (0.82 log G) because estimated full-Kelly concentrates too aggressively while two-stage squared-error forecasts shrink toward zero — 'the optimizer is not the problem; the estimated full-Kelly target is.' Exact Hessian beats first-order substitutes 3x on selection but loses deployed. Selection protocol committed gamma=1.14 (essentially logarithmic).

Katriel (2012, arXiv:1209.4203) gives an exact closed-form gambler's ruin probability for i.i.d. integer-valued payoff distributions with bounded per-game loss, expressed through the roots of the payoff generating function inside the unit disk — a strict generalization of the classical symmetric +-1 ruin formula. No empirical data — pure probability theory, no numerical results in the paper. Ledger verdict ADAPT — root-finding for p(z)=1 in the unit disk must be implemented numerically (paper provides none) and validated.

Gambler's ruin Theorem 1, Eq. (2): P_ruin(M) = sum_{n=1}^{nu} Phi_{n,M-n+1}(eta_1,...,eta_n) prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-eta_j), where eta_j are the nu roots of p(z)=1 in |z|<1 and Phi_{n,r} is the complete symmetric polynomial of order r (handles multiple roots). Distinct-roots form, Eq. (3): P_ruin(M) = sum_{j=1}^{nu} eta_j^M prod_{i!=j} (1-eta_i)/(eta_j-eta_i). Assumptions: i.i.d. integer payoffs with max loss nu, p_{-nu} != 0, E[X_t] > 0; ruin when wealth < nu; infinitely rich adversary (no profit target).

Gambler's ruin implementation spec in the file: discretize weekly settled P&L to 0.1u integers, estimate {p_k} empirically per market, find nu roots numerically (numpy polynomial roots on z^nu*p(z)), compute via Eq. (3), size stakes so P_ruin(bankroll) <= 1%, recompute monthly; ~1 day effort.

Knysh & Korkolis (2016, arXiv:1605.00998v2) give a methods note for parallel optimization of expensive continuous black-box functions using radial-basis-function response surfaces, Latin-hypercube initialization, and a modified CORS sampling algorithm with space rescaling; ships a Python implementation. Benchmark comparisons for the optimizer itself; nothing sports-related. Ledger verdict REJECT — generic 2016 continuous black-box optimizer, zero sports/DFS content, superseded by modern libraries (BoTorch, Ax, scikit-optimize), and the wrong problem class (DFS lineup optimization is discrete/combinatorial, not continuous black-box).

Blackbox optimizer method: RBF surrogate s(x) = sum lambda_i phi(||x-x_i||) + polynomial tail; CORS infill: optimize the surrogate subject to a distance constraint from evaluated points, with space rescaling; parallel batch evaluations for multicore scaling. Assumptions: smooth black-box function amenable to RBF interpolation; parallel workers available.
equation: s(x) = Σ λ_i φ(||x−x_i||) + polynomial tail

claim: The 'when in doubt, abstain' paper (arXiv:2510.13327) is a Stackelberg game analysis of how an abstention option affects a principal whose classifier is published and agents strategically manipulate features in response; it proves abstention never hurts and shows strategic agents force wider abstention bands. Ledger verdict ADAPT — the 'abstain more when the other side is strategic' theorem is a stress-test lens for GSE's public picks, since books/market react to posted edges; but the paper's manipulators are loan-applicant-style feature manipulators, not bookmakers, so the turning point must be re-estimated on real line data.

Abstention-game theorems: Theorem 3.1 — adding the abstention option cannot increase the principal's loss, even with strategic agents; Theorem 3.3 — the optimal threshold under strategic agents T-bar* > T* (truthful case), i.e. abstain more when the other side reacts. Simulation: turning point at abstention cost c = 0.5 — beyond it abstaining costs more than a random guess. Noise comparative statics: unconstrained T* rises monotonically with sigma; constrained T-bar* first dips (moderate noise weakens manipulation) then rises at high sigma.

Abstention-game simulation: 100,000 samples per threshold; x ~ Uniform[-2,2]; thresholds 0.01-2.0 in 0.01 steps; defaults gamma = 0.4444 (manipulation cost/benefit), c = 0.3 (abstention cost), sigma = 0.5 (label noise); metric Delta-H (harm reduction from the abstention option). Findings: T-bar* (strategic) consistently higher than T* (truthful) across the sweep — Theorem 3.3 confirmed numerically; Delta-H > 0 throughout.

Inacio et al. (2020, arXiv:2008.13005v2) study wisdom-of-crowds on the 64-match 2018 FIFA World Cup forecasting contest (511 registrants, 57 full panels), testing aggregation strategies (Top-n, local/global wisdom, Budescu-Chen contribution weighting, exponential-weights ISP) against statistical models and 100,000 simulated tournaments separating luck from skill.

World Cup crowd methods: scoring via linear transform of Brier score to 0-100 per match (100 = probability 1 on observed outcome); 64-match total. ISP-eta: p-hat_t = (sum_j w_{j,t} f_{j,t})/(sum_j w_{j,t}), w_{j,t} proportional to exp(eta R_{j,t-1}); regret R_{j,t-1} = sum_{t0<t}[l(p-hat_{t0},y_{t0}) - l(f_{j,t0},y_{t0})]; eta in {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1}. Budescu-Chen: contribution C_j = sum_{i=1}^N(S_i - S_i^{-j})/N; weighted average over forecasters with C_j > 0. Assertiveness: (3/2) sum_{i=1}^3(P_i - 1/3)^2 in [0,1]; 0 = maxi-min (1/3,1/3,1/3), 1 = vertex. Bootstrap-like extension to n = 1...1,024 matches (matches treated as exchangeable).

World Cup contest totals (of 64 matches): Esportes em numeros (Maher 1982 Poisson) 4650 (72.7 avg, rank 1); Groll et al. 2018 (random forest) 4644 (2); Global wisdom 4634 (3.5); FiveThirtyEight 4634 (3.5); Chance de Gol (bivariate Poisson) 4611 (5); Budescu-Chen 4601 (rank 6); Local wisdom 4567 (12.5); Top-1 'follow the leader' 4438 (rank 40 — chasing recent form fails). Data: fifaexperts.com 2018 World Cup contest (site defunct); bookmaker-odds-implied forecasts from 18 sites for 'Global wisdom'.

World Cup crowd luck findings: luck dominates at 64 matches — the actual winner, simulated under her own probabilities, wins only 28.2% of 100,000 tournaments (avg position 4.7 +- 4.8); she needs ~=576 matches for 95% win probability; Global wisdom needs ~=1,024. Assertiveness: best forecasters were less assertive; top users' assertiveness declined toward (1/3,1/3,1/3) as the tournament progressed; worst users stayed overconfident — Brier scoring punishes over-assertiveness. Third group-stage round hardest to predict (dead rubbers, strategic draws) — structural calendar effect. Forecast counts fell 363 (opener) -> 101 (third-place playoff) — attrition bias in late aggregates.

Hu, Yang & Xue (arXiv:2006.07513) propose a two-stage Bayesian method modeling each NBA player's shot locations as a Log-Gaussian Cox Process estimated via INLA/SPDE, then clustering players into shot-selection archetypes with a Mixture of Finite Mixtures (MFM) that jointly estimates the number of groups K and assignments. Ledger verdict ADAPT (not ADOPT — no predictive evaluation, two-stage uncertainty gap); improvement path = single-stage joint model or propagating Stage-1 posterior uncertainty.

Bayesian shot-selection method: Stage 1 LGCP — shot locations ~ Poisson process with log-intensity = Gaussian process (Matern covariance via SPDE). Stage 2: similarity s_ij = 1 - d_ij/max(d), d_ij = normalized ||lambda-hat_i - lambda-hat_j||_2; Fisher z-transform z = atanh(s); MFM with prior on K; collapsed MCMC + Dahl's partition summary. Assumptions: shot-attempt locations only (makes/misses, defenders, context ignored); one season fixes a player's style; two-stage (Stage-1 uncertainty not propagated).

Bayesian shot-selection findings: simulation (75 players, 3 true groups, 50 replicates) mean Rand index: MFM 0.9988 vs K-means 0.9005, DBSCAN 0.7642, mean shift 0.7380; 42 of 50 replicates recovered the true 3 clusters. NBA 2017-18 (191 players with >400 field-goal attempts, shot (x,y) locations from stats.nba.com / BigDataBall-style sources): 9 inferred groups; mean concordance Rand index across 50 chains: 0.948. No public code URL in text.

Cranmer (2023, arXiv:2305.01582) introduces PySR/SymbolicRegression.jl with an evolve-simplify-optimize loop (BFGS constant fitting), adaptive parsimony, and EmpiricalBench — a benchmark of rediscovering 9 historical physical laws (Hubble, Kepler, Newton, Planck, Leavitt, Schechter, Bode, ideal gas, Rydberg) from original noisy data without constants. Ledger verdict ADOPT — the production symbolic-regression stack for GSE's metric-invention program; ~1-2 engineer-days to wire.

PySR mechanics: adaptive parsimony (used) l(E) = l_pred(E)*exp(frecency[C(E)]), where frecency = frequency+recency count of expressions at complexity C(E) in a moving window / tunable constant (replaces classical l = l_pred + parsimony*C). Mutation acceptance (simulated annealing): q_anneal = exp(-(L*-L)/(alpha*T)), T = 1 - k/n_c. Evolve-simplify-optimize loop: evolve -> algebraic simplification (infrequent, so redundant intermediates survive to mutate) -> BFGS constant optimization inside every expression. Migration via global permanent 'hall of fame' (best expression per complexity across all island populations). GP denoising kernel: k(x,x') = sigma^2 exp(-|x-x'|^2/2l^2) + alpha delta(x-x') + C; complexity = nodes in expression tree. Custom operators: any 1-2 argument scalar operator with SymPy + JAX/PyTorch equivalents; backend fuses operators into SIMD kernels.

PySR EmpiricalBench (digitized 1929 Hubble original data via WebPlotDigitizer; Kepler, Newton, Planck, Leavitt, Schechter, Bode, ideal gas, Rydberg datasets — original public where available, else synthetic data from the equation with noise; code at github.com/MilesCranmer/PySR, SymbolicRegression.jl, github.com/MilesCranmer/pysr_paper): 9 laws x 5 trials = 45 runs/algorithm; correct rediscoveries: PySR 35/45, QLattice 21/45, Operon 9/45, EQL 5/45, DSR 0/45 (many failed/crashed), SR-Transformer 0/45 (pre-trained on billions of synthetic expressions — still last). Four classic-heuristic GP algorithms all beat the two pure deep-learning approaches. Hubble/Kepler/Newton/Leavitt/Bode/Ideal Gas: PySR 5/5 each; Planck and Rydberg: nobody solved (0/5 for all).

DrSR (Wang et al. 2025, arXiv:2506.04282) upgrades LLM-guided symbolic regression with two reasoning modules: pi_data (LLM analyzes raw data + residuals, coarse->fine) and pi_idea (LLM reflects on positive/negative/invalid candidates into a reusable idea library), fixing LLM-SR's prior-only proposals and repeated invalid expressions. Ledger verdict ADAPT — port the residual-driven insight update to GSE's metric-invention loop; needs sports adaptation (no textbook priors) and cost control (cap LLM calls; update insight only on new best).

DrSR mechanics: res_{t,i} = y_i - f*(x_i); D_t = {(x_i, y_i, res_{t,i})} -> resample 100 pairs -> refined insight D_new (local monotonicity changes, nonlinear interactions). Generation conditioned on cognitively enriched prior: p_LLM(f | D, I) replacing static p_LLM(f). Metrics: ACC_tau = (1/N_test) sum 1(|f(x_i)-y_i|/|y_i| <= tau); NMSE = sum(f-y)^2/sum(y-ybar)^2. Closed loop: generate -> evaluate -> update insights + ideas -> generate better; three LLM calls per iteration (pi_data, pi_main, pi_idea).

DrSR findings on six benchmarks (backbones Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct; baselines gplearn, PySR, DSR, uDSR, LLM-SR, LaSR): Oscillation 1 (Acc/NMSE) — DrSR-Mixtral 83.92% / 3.14e-7 vs LLM-SR-Mixtral 5.9% / 1e-4, PySR 3.80% / 3e-4, uDSR 1.78% / 2e-4, DSR 0.42%. Oscillation 2 — DrSR-Mixtral 99.94% / 1.80e-12 vs LLM-SR 7.62% / 4.59e-5, PySR 7.02% / 2e-4. E. coli (all struggle) — DrSR-Mixtral 5.12% / 0.0195 vs LLM-SR 2.08% / 0.2282. Stress-Strain — 88.28% / 0.0156 vs LLM-SR 68.10% / 0.0530, PySR 70.60% / 0.0347. LSR-Transform-2Avg: 92.51% / 0.0055; LSR-Synth-CRK0: 95.20% / 8.87e-8. DrSR-Llama3.1 backbone-robust (Oscillation 1: 77.98% / 5.40e-7); ablation: both pi_data and pi_idea contribute. No public repo URL confirmed in text.

LLM-FE (Abhyankar et al., arXiv:2503.14434, published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research 05/2026) casts feature engineering as evolutionary program search — an LLM proposes feature-transformation programs, validation fitness scores them, and a FunSearch-style island model with Boltzmann cluster sampling refines them; open code at github.com/nikhilsab/LLMFE. Ledger verdict ADOPT — adopt the harness wholesale; only the prompt layer is GSE-specific; add cutoff annotations (pre-kickoff only) and paired-permutation-test keep criterion with Holm correction to fix best-of-20 selection bias.

LLM-FE method: bilevel objective max_T E(f*(T(X_val)), Y_val) s.t. f* in argmin_f L_f(f(T(X_tr)), Y_tr); programs T ~ pi_theta(p) sampled from the LLM. Sampling: b = 3 programs/iteration, temperature 0.8; executed before evaluation, error-prone/timeout discarded. Island model: m = 3 islands, programs clustered by identical validation-score signature; Boltzmann cluster sampling P_i = exp(s_i/tau_c)/sum_j exp(s_j/tau_c); top-k programs become next prompt's in-context examples (implicit mutation/crossover); global budget 20 LLM samples. Boltzmann temperature schedule tau_c = T_0(1 - u mod N / N), T_0 = 0.1, N = 10,000; eval caps T = 30 s, M = 2 GB per program. Prompt recipe: role+instruction (explicitly 'use domain knowledge', 'generate complex features'), task description, feature names+descriptions, serialized samples ('If c_1 is x_i ..., then Result is y_i'), the evaluation function itself, one in-context demo, function stub.

LLM-FE data: 37 datasets — 19 classification + 10 regression (OpenML, UCI, Kaggle; 315-581k rows, 4-279 features) + 8 large-scale high-dimensional classification; 5 post-Sept-2021 sets for the memorization control; 80/20 splits x 5 seeds. Backbones GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; predictors XGBoost, MLP, TabPFN.

LLM-FE findings: classification mean rank over 19 datasets (XGBoost): LLM-FE 1.42 vs CAAFE 3.47, OpenFE 3.63, OCTree 4.05, Base 3.95, AutoFeat 5.11, FeatLLM 5.11. Standouts: balance-scale 0.856->0.990, jungle_chess 0.869->0.969, covtype 0.870->0.882. Regression mean rank over 10 datasets: LLM-FE 1.10 (best on all 10; e.g. housing RMSE 4.845->4.525, wine 0.639->0.612) vs OpenFE 2.80, Base 4.55. Ablation (normalized accuracy): full 0.70 -> w/o domain knowledge 0.626, w/o data examples ~0.66, w/o evolutionary refinement 0.587 — refinement is load-bearing; no-refinement plateaus by iteration ~5 while full keeps climbing through 20. Wilcoxon significance (95% CI) over base XGBoost: 10/10 regression (p < 0.001), 8/15 classification (p < 0.05). Memorization control: modest but consistent gains on post-cutoff sets (fico 0.715->0.719, healthinsurance 0.756->0.759, pharyngitis 0.655->0.660, acsincome 0.807->0.809); HPO control: gains persist on 3/5 datasets after Optuna 100-trial tuning. 16.67% of generated features land in top-10 by SHAP, 62.96% in top-50 (features are used, not spurious); features transfer across predictors (MLP 0.745->0.791, TabPFN 0.852->0.863); noise-robust at sigma in {0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1}. ~45% of LLM-FE's discovered features qualify as 'complex' per Kuken et al. (2024) vs negligible for CAAFE/OCTree (fixes LLM simplicity bias); discovered operators skew toward groupby-then-mean/min/max, residual, sigmoid vs CAAFE's 75% multiply/divide.

UniTraj (Zhu et al. 2024, arXiv:2411.03859): an MAE-style trajectory foundation model (~2.38M params, 8 RoPE encoder + 4 decoder blocks, d=128) pretrained with four masking strategies on WorldTrace (2.45M trajectories, ~8.8B GPS points, 70 countries) and evaluated zero-shot across regions, sampling rates, and four downstream tasks. Ledger verdict ADAPT — the most complete MAE trajectory recipe; needs adaptation from single-agent GPS to multi-agent play data; masking strategies map to NFL regimes (random -> dropped frames, block -> occlusions, RDP key-points -> route breaks, last-N -> ball-carrier forecasting).

UniTraj mechanics: dynamic resampling R(n) = R_min if n >= n_max; = 1 if n <= n_min; = 1 - (1-R_min)phi(n) otherwise, with phi(n) = ln(n-n_min+1)/ln(n_max-n_min+1). Four masking strategies (mask ratio r): (a) random, (b) contiguous blocks of size b, (c) key-points via RDP (I_key = {p_k | d_max(p_k, overline{p_1 p_n}) > eps}), (d) last-N (prediction-style). Tokenizer: spatial normalized to origin (x_i,y_i) = (lng_i-lng_1, lat_i-lat_1) -> Conv1D to h_i^s in R^d; temporal Delta t_i -> Linear to h_i^t in R^d; h_i = h_i^s + h_i^t; RoPE theta_i = i / 10000^{2k/d}. Training loss: L = (1/|I|) sum_{i in I} ||f_{theta,phi}(tau-tilde)_i - tau_i||^2 over masked positions only; Adam lr 1e-3, 200 epochs, batch 1024, on A100/L40s. Assumptions: masked coordinate reconstruction is a sufficient proxy for representation quality; mobility patterns transfer across regions; adapter heads suffice per task.

UniTraj data: WorldTrace (new, open ODbL via OpenStreetMap GPX): 1M train / 100K test high-quality subset; avg 358 points/trajectory, ~6 min, 5.73 km, 48.0 km/h. Eval: Chengdu (>1M taxi), Xi'an (millions of taxi), GeoLife (182 users), Grab-Posisi (84K ride-hailing), Porto.

UniTraj findings: Recovery MAE (meters): Xi'an — UniTraj(ft) 6.50 vs TrajFM 18.86, DeepMove 27.31; GeoLife — UniTraj(ft) 23.23, 'nearly halving TrajFM's error'; zero-shot UniTraj already beats all traditional baselines on every dataset.
