(2021) Automatic Model Selector (AMS) uses a decay epsilon-greedy multi-armed bandit over M candidate ML models with arm probabilities P(best) = (1-epsilon) + epsilon/M for the currently-best model and P(alt) = epsilon/M for each alternative, with decay schedule epsilon(t) = epsilon_0 * max(0, 1 - t/alpha); models rotate onto live ad-bidding traffic every 15 minutes and traffic concentrates on the best-performing arm by the live business KPI (CTR/CPC/CPA). It was chosen over Thompson sampling and UCB following Mäkinen 2017 (simplicity plus empirical performance) and is reward-agnostic (no Beta-Bernoulli or sub-Gaussian assumptions).
equation: P(best) = (1−ε) + ε/M; P(alt) = ε/M; ε(t) = ε₀·max(0, 1 − t/α)

claim: In two proprietary live-traffic experiments (Xaxis/Copilot AI RTB ad campaigns), Xie et al. (2021) showed offline AUC does not predict online performance twice: in experiment 1 a 7-day-lookback model led offline AUC early but the 60-day model took the AUC lead around day 7 while cumulative online CTR followed a similar but not identical trend (higher offline AUC at campaign start did NOT translate to higher live CTR); in experiment 2 the control model had slightly better test AUC yet 'significantly outperformed' the test model on the live KPI. The paper reports no exact numbers, p-values, or sample sizes - all results are qualitative figure readings.

Busseti, Ryu & Boyd (2016) Risk-Constrained Kelly adds a hard drawdown constraint to Kelly gambling via a sufficient convex bound: E[(r'b)^(-lambda)] <= 1 implies P(W_min < alpha) < beta, where r is the return vector, b the bet allocation vector, W_min the minimum wealth over the horizon, alpha the drawdown level, beta the allowed probability, and lambda = log(beta)/log(alpha); proved via stopping time tau = inf{t : w_t < alpha} with w_t = w_{t-1} (r_t'b) and a martingale/change-of-measure argument.
equation: E[(r'b)^{−λ}] ≤ 1 ⟹ P(W_min < α) < β, with λ = logβ/logα

claim: The Risk-Constrained Kelly program (Eq. 7) is: maximize over b the expected log growth E[log(r'b)] subject to 1'b=1 (budget), b>=0 (no shorting), and the drawdown constraint E[(r'b)^(-lambda)] <= 1; it is convex (concave objective, convex constraint) and lambda->0 recovers unconstrained Kelly. A quadratic Taylor approximation around b=e_n (the cash vector) gives QRCK, a Markowitz-like mean-variance form with lambda as the risk-aversion knob.

On synthetic experiments (n=20 bets with 19 risky plus cash, K=100 outcomes, returns uniform[0.7,1.3] with 0.2/2.0 spikes; 10,000 Monte Carlo trajectories of 100 rounds), with alpha=0.7 and beta=0.1, full Kelly had growth 0.062 but realized drawdown risk 0.397 (40% chance of a 30% drawdown); Risk-Constrained Kelly with lambda=6.456 had growth 0.043, bound 0.100, realized 0.073; with lambda=5.5 growth 0.047, bound 0.141, realized 0.099 (true constrained optimum growth lies in [0.047, 0.062]). At matched 10% risk the exact convex RCK (growth 0.047) beat its quadratic approximation QRCK (0.044), and the bound is typically about 30% higher than the actual risk.

Kampakis & Adamides (2014) predicted EPL match outcomes from Twitter text with this pipeline: CMU ARK TwitterNLP POS tagger keeping only adjectives, verbs, nouns, adverbs, interjections and emoticons, then Porter stemming, then chi-square-ranked bigrams with 1-35 terms per side (best around 11-15 terms per side), fed to random forest / naive Bayes / logistic regression / SVM evaluated with 100 random seeds, out-of-bag estimates and leave-one-out cross-validation on 1,975,614 tweets from 2014-03-21 to 2014-05-11.

Kampakis & Adamides (2014) measured: Twitter-only random forest 65.6% +/- 4.33% accuracy (range 56.3-74.7%) with kappa 0.25 +/- 0.093; historical-stats-only naive Bayes 58.9% +/- 5.97% accuracy with kappa 0.239 +/- 0.075; combined Twitter-plus-stats random forest 69.6% +/- 2.4% (64.4-74.7%) with kappa 0.28 +/- 0.065. Bigrams beat unigrams, performance peaked around 11-15 features per side then declined, and the Twitter RF may mostly predict the majority class (high accuracy but modest kappa). Limitations noted: only about 90 matches with high variance, feature selection likely outside the CV loop (optimistic bias), no time-ordered split, and never tested against odds as the real baseline.

Mori & Hisakado (2010) estimated the win-bet fraction in Japanese horseracing as x_{i,k}^r = 0.788/(O_{i,k}^r - 0.1) where O is the win odds, and the accuracy ratio as AR = 2*(Prob(alpha_w < alpha_l) - 1/2) = 2*(AUC_ROC - 1/2), i.e. twice the ROC area above chance.

Mori & Hisakado's two-type voting model writes the probability a vote goes to the winner at time t as P_t^w(n+s) = r_i*w + r_h*(n+s)/(Z+t), where r_i is the independent (informed) voter fraction, r_h the herding fraction, w the true win probability, n the announced vote count and s an early-vote parameter. Convergence regimes for the squared deviation of the empirical win fraction from truth are: (x_t^w - w)^2 ~ t^(-1) if r_i > 1/2 (normal diffusion), ~ t^(-2 r_i) if r_i < 1/2 (super-diffusion), ~ log(t)/t if r_i = 1/2. The measured exponent beta = 0.488 gives r_i = beta/2 = 0.244, i.e. an independent-to-herding ratio of about 1:3 - only roughly 1 in 4 bettors carries information.
equation: P_t^w(n+s) = r_i·w + r_h·(n+s)/(Z+t); (x_t^w − w)² ~ t^{−1} if r_i > 1/2; ~ t^{−2r_i} if r_i < 1/2; ~ log(t)/t if r_i = 1/2

claim: Mori & Hisakado showed value bettors who bet proportionally to (w - x) aggregate to look exactly like independent voters: the fundamental-voter mapping is P_t^w = r_f*(w + lambda*(w - x_t^w)) + r_h'*x_t^w, which yields effective parameters r_i = (1+lambda)*r_f and r_h = r_h' - lambda*r_f. Empirically on 2,471 JRA 2008 races (N=35,719 horses, 2,472 winners, ~200,000 announcements): [(x_alpha(t) - x_{alpha,f})^2] ~ t^(-0.488 +/- 0.007) rejecting normal diffusion, AR_f - AR(t) ~ t^(-0.589 +/- 0.005) with final AR_f = 0.6826, convergence rapid after t_c ~ 3x10^4, and early concentrated votes (s=3) carry almost no information (AR near 0 at t ~ 70).
equation: P_t^w = r_f·(w + λ(w − x_t^w)) + r_h′·x_t^w → r_i = (1+λ)·r_f, r_h = r_h′ − λ·r_f

claim: Moreland & Superdock (2018) extended Elo from win/loss to the full margin-of-victory distribution by fitting one Elo rating per handicap threshold h: R_i(h) is updated by K times (1_{margin_i > h} - E_h) with expected win prob E_h = logistic((R_i(h) - R_j(h) + HFA)/s); the spread CDF F(h) = P(margin <= h) is reconstructed from the collection of threshold win probabilities, with quantiles read off directly. Assumptions: threshold outcomes are conditionally independent given the latent margin (acknowledged incoherence - the CDF need not be monotone), a stationary margin distribution within season, and constant additive home-field advantage. On NFL 2009-2017 the model was 'comparable but slightly worse than Vegas' (paper's own characterization; no exact MAE table).
equation: R_i(h) ← K·(1_{margin_i > h} − E_h); E_h = logistic((R_i(h) − R_j(h) + HFA)/s); F(h) = P(margin ≤ h)

claim: Moreland & Superdock (2018) used offseason regression priors that spreads retain 60% and totals retain 70% of the prior-season rating, with home field worth 54 Elo points. The reusable constants adopted are: 0.60 spread retention, 0.70 totals retention, and 54-Elo-point HFA.

Blythe & Kiraly (2015) modeled individual athletic performance in log form as log t = lambda_1 f_1(s) + lambda_2 f_2(s) + lambda_3 f_3(s) with rank r=3 optimal, where t is time, s event distance, f_k distance functions and lambda_k athlete coefficients; the classic Riegel power law is the special case lambda_1=1.06 for all athletes and f_1 = log s.

Local low-rank matrix completion (LMC) predicts a missing athlete-event entry M[a,s*] by: taking the target event plus the r log-closest events, restricting to complete rows (plus athlete a), then 400 times sampling r athletes and solving det M[(a,a_1..a_r),(s*,s_1..s_r)] = 0 for the missing entry to get candidate m_i, each weighted by w_i = sigma_i^(-2) from a first-order variance estimate, and averaging with inverse-variance weights to get m*. On thepowerof10.info British Athletics data (164,746 individuals, 1,407,432 performances across 10 events through 2013-08-03), LMC rank 2 log-time RMSE (0-95th percentile) was 0.0515 +/- 0.003 versus EM 0.0566, Purdy 0.061, Riegel 0.0982, k-NN 0.122 and nuclear-norm 0.391 +/- 0.05 (LMC rank 2 best at p <= 1e-4 Wilcoxon); rank 3 was optimal when at least 4 events existed (0.0309 +/- 0.001) with no gain at rank 4; LMC is orders of magnitude faster than nuclear-norm/EM per completion.

Blythe & Kiraly (2015) found the individual power-law exponent lambda_1 has median 1.12 (5th/95th percentiles 1.10/1.15) versus Riegel's world-record values 1.08/1.06, and f_1 is linear in log-log space with R^2 = 0.9997, making the 'broken power law' an epiphenomenon of individual heterogeneity; relative errors were about 2% relative RMSE/MAE for top-25% athletes, with rank2-over-rank1 improvements of 26.3% short (100/200m), 29.3% middle (400/800/1500m), 12.8% mile-to-half-marathon, and 3.1% marathon (all p=1e-3). Their headline example: the fair Farah-Bolt race distance is 492m (95% CI 374-594m).

Aronson's 'TenisRank' weights each tennis match edge (directed loser->winner in the player graph) as W_edge = W_aging x W_surface x W_instance (multiplicative separability assumed): aging is exponential decay in years-back with 3-5 year windows, surface is 1 if the match surface equals the target surface else a tuned constant, instance is ATP-style round/tournament importance with a tuned lambda; win probability comes from a logistic fit of hit-rate on ranking difference with parameter a=45.321. On tennis-data.co.uk (~40,000 matches, 923 tournaments 2000-2013), the ATP ranking baseline 2005-2013 was 66.849% accuracy; aging alone (3yr, lambda=-5) added +1.3pp vs ATP (+0.8pp vs plain PageRank); surface alone (0.5) added +1.7pp vs ATP (+1pp vs PageRank); the combined model (4yr, aging -5, surface 0.3, instance lambda=1.7) reached about 70% hits (+3pp vs ATP, +2.2pp vs PageRank), with ANOVA p=0.000024 vs ATP and p=0.00079 vs PageRank; it won on every surface (grass best, about +2pp vs ATP), top-10 matchups (+3pp), and all 5 tournament types (Grand Slams ~74%).
equation: W_edge = W_aging × W_surface × W_instance; P(victory) = logistic fit of hit-rate on ranking difference (a=45.321)

claim: PandaSkill (De Bois et al. 2025) is a two-step esports rating: PScore (per-role XGBoost with 2,000 rounds, lr 0.01 and monotonicity constraints forcing worthless-death and contest-loserate negative, standardized inputs, 5-fold CV; predicted win probability goes through a train-learned percentile transform to a 0-100 grade) feeding free-for-all OpenSkill updates (players ranked by performance, not team outcome) with dual contextual-plus-meta ratings for isolated regional pools. Skill is Bayesian S_i ~ N(mu_i, sigma_i^2), initialized mu=25, sigma=25/3, summarized as theta_i = mu_i - 3 sigma_i; dual ratings mu_i = mu_i^ctx + mu_i^meta and sigma_i^2 = sigma_ctx^2 + sigma_meta^2, where intra-region games update ctx only and inter-region games update meta only with contextual-lower-bound offsets (TrueSkill2-style); head-to-head probability P(S_i>S_j) = Phi((mu_i-mu_j)/sqrt(sigma_i^2+sigma_j^2)).
equation: S_i ~ N(μ_i, σ_i²), init μ=25, σ=25/3; θ_i = μ_i − 3σ_i; μ_i = μ_i^ctx + μ_i^meta; σ_i² = σ_ctx² + σ_meta²; P(S_i>S_j) = Φ((μ_i−μ_j)/√(σ_i²+σ_j²))

claim: PandaSkill on professional League of Legends (2019-09-15 to 2024-09-15: 37,388 games, 4,927 players, all regions; inter-region games scarce at Worlds 592 + MSI 312 vs LCK 2,438, LPL 3,643): PScore accuracy 90.74% (SD 0.60) vs PlayeRank 91.00% and PI 91.30% (monotonicity costs about 1%); ECE 0.93% (SD 0.03) vs PlayeRank 1.28% and PI 2.28%; role fairness (Wasserstein) 0.09-0.44 vs PI 0.35-0.66 vs PlayeRank 2.44. Outcome forecasting (all/intra/inter): PScore+EWMA 63.06/63.33/52.34 vs PScore+Meta_FFA_OpenSkill 64.98/64.86/70.07 - the meta rating fixes inter-region play (52.34 to 70.07); FFA updates hurt team-outcome forecasting (61.71 vs 67.39 inter) but significantly improve expert concordance (majority 80.63% SD 6.52, unanimity 88.98% SD 5.99, best). Worked example: HLE vs T1 (T1 won) - HLE losers Peanut/Zeka gained rating while T1's Oner/Zeus lost rating despite winning, demonstrating performance-decoupled ratings.

Weyn et al. (2021) compared ensemble construction for subseasonal weather forecasting: stochastically perturbed (SP) ensembles built by retraining with perturbed model weights (32 models from 8 training cycles with different random seeds, 4 checkpoints each every 10 epochs after epoch 100 selected by 4-week T850 ACC; grand ensemble 32 SP x 10 ERA5 initial conditions = 320 members) beat initial-condition-perturbation (IC) ensembles on spread and RMSE. IC ensembles were under-dispersive (spread much less than RMSE, shrinking in the first 36h); SP spread was about 80% of RMSE at 8 days and 95% at 14 days; SP ensemble-mean RMSE stayed below climatology through 14 days versus only 7-8 days for IC. Checkpoint diversity approximately equals independent-retraining diversity (spread between checkpoints of one cycle ~ spread between cycles), so snapshot ensembling is a cheap substitute for retraining.

Weyn et al. (2021) measured subseasonal-to-seasonal skill of deep-learning weather prediction (DLWP): compute was a 320-member 6-week ensemble in ~3 minutes on one GPU and a one-week forecast ~0.1 s on a V100; at weeks 5-6 the DLWP T850 anomaly correlation was in statistical tie with the full ECMWF S2S ensemble (overlapping 95% CIs); ranked probability skill score RPSS (T2, days 12-18) was ECMWF 0.247 vs DLWP 0.121, and bias-corrected weeks 5-6 were 0.155 DLWP vs 0.287 ECMWF (close on land only). RPSS is defined as RPSS = 1 - <RPS>/(<RPS_C> + D_0/M) with D_0 = (K^2-1)/(6K), and the ideal-ensemble assumption is that ensemble spread should match ensemble-mean RMSE.

Sharma (2025) defined the Distance-to-Competitive-Balance index DCB(s) = sqrt((HHI - HHI_min)/(HHI_max - HHI_min)), where HHI = sum_i s_i^2 and s_i is team i's share of total league points; DCB is normalized 0 (balanced) to 1 (concentrated) and is regime-invariant across the 2-point vs 3-point eras.
equation: DCB(s) = √[(HHI − HHI_min)/(HHI_max − HHI_min)], HHI = Σ_i s_i²

claim: Sharma (2025) applied synthetic control to England's 1981 switch from 2 to 3 points per win: donor weights G* = argmin_G (X1 - X0 G)' V (X1 - X0 G) with g_i >= 0 and sum g_i = 1, synthetic England = Y0 G*, ATE = actual minus synthetic DCB averaged 1981-1993; the predictor-importance matrix V was chosen by pre-treatment RMSE minimization with weights DCB(1969) 0.3485, DCB(1965) 0.2119, avg win share 0.1587, team count 0.1544, avg draw share 0.0777, DCB(1979) 0.0488, and donor weights France 0.6010, Spain 0.3350, Netherlands 0.0650 (Germany/Italy zero).
equation: G* = argmin_G (X1 − X0G)'V(X1 − X0G), g_i ≥ 0, Σg_i = 1

claim: Sharma (2025) measured the main SCM ATE of the three-point rule as -0.051 on DCB (increased competitive balance), with alternative specifications -0.0571 to -0.073 and a DID with equal donor weights of -0.0545 (near-identical); placebo donor-league ATEs were Dutch 0.0097, Spanish 0.0124, French 0.0026, German -0.0219, Italian 0.0145 (all near zero), placebo year 1969 was -0.0175, leave-one-out unchanged, and the alternate NAMSI-hat index gave -0.0297 (same direction). Goals-per-match ATE was -0.0131 (no significant change): the rule changed point dispersion without changing scoring volume, in tension with Moschini (2010)'s 35-country panel finding more goals and fewer draws.

The GSE intelligence-core build journal records an empirical-Bayes shrinkage weight w = n / (n + k) with DEFAULT_PLAYER_RATE_SHRINKAGE_K = 12 as the pseudo-sample strength, used in the feature store (B1-B6) for player rate shrinkage.

The GSE Tweedie gradient-boosted baseline used negative-gradient pseudo-residuals under a log link: mu = exp(F), pseudo-residual = y*exp((1-p)F) - exp((2-p)F), power p = 1.5 default; Newton leaf update = -sum(grad)/(sum(hess)+ridge) with grad = e^((2-p)F) - y*e^((1-p)F) and hess = (2-p)*e^((2-p)F) + (p-1)*y*e^((1-p)F).
equation: pseudo = y*exp((1-p)F) - exp((2-p)F); leaf = -sum(grad)/(sum(hess)+ridge); grad = e^{(2-p)F} - y e^{(1-p)F}; hess = (2-p)e^{(2-p)F} + (p-1) y e^{(1-p)F}

claim: The GSE split-conformal uncertainty layer used the finite-sample quantile as the ceil((n+1)*p) order statistic of the calibration residuals; the model-promotion Clark-West gate requires >= 30 out-of-sample samples, a positive adjusted mean difference, a t-stat > 1.64, and model MAE < market MAE before 'beatsMarket' is declared.

GSE's definitive 2021-2025 backtest (71 walk-forward folds, 18,344 out-of-sample player-weeks, purged and embargoed) recorded model MAE 5.3087 versus naive 4.9064, so beats-naive = FALSE (Clark-West t=18.8 but model MAE higher, so the gate correctly withheld publication). The single-season 2023 backtest: 3,796 samples, 2,955 OOS, model MAE 4.9928 vs naive 4.7573 (FALSE); after genuine Tweedie loss 4.8679 vs 4.7573 (still FALSE); the correctly-implemented Newton leaf actually raised OOS MAE 4.87 to 5.04 (deviance-optimal is not MAE-optimal - overfit at fixed hyperparameters); opponent-defense ablation was never selected by the greedy booster with identical OOS MAE (5.0437 vs naive 4.76). The recorded honest verdict: beating naive points-persistence out-of-sample is genuine ML research, not a one-session win, and canPublishProjections stays off.

The GSE audit1 review found a real adversarial bug in the Tweedie GBM: the first-order mean-of-gradient leaf could overshoot or diverge for small power p; the fix was the Newton leaf plus a regression test asserting non-increasing deviance for p in {1.1, 1.5, 1.9}, and the backtest sped up ~3x (42s to 13s). The journal also records the fantasy-points identity: fantasy points = pass yds/25 + pass TD*4 + rush and receiving yds/10 + TD*6, with team yards/TDs split into PASSING and RUSHING pools via the C3 game-script pass/run rate and the RECEIVING pool equal to the passing pool.
equation: fantasy points = pass yds/25 + pass TD*4 + rush&rec yds/10 + TD*6

claim: The partial-abstention multi-label framework defines per-label uncertainty u_i = 2*min(p_i, 1-p_i) and a generalized loss L(y, yhat) = ell(y_D, yhat_D) + f(|A(yhat)|) where D is the predicted label set and A(yhat) the abstained set; the linear case is L = ell + |A|*c with abstention penalty c in [0,1], and a concave variant f_2(a) = (a*m*c)/(m+a). For decomposable losses like Hamming, the risk-minimizing rule is closed-form and O(m log m): sort labels by uncertainty and choose the optimal prediction size d = |{i : min(p_i, 1-p_i) <= c}|, a pure threshold rule; for rank loss the optimal predicted set is the top-d labels by p_i under label independence.

Partial-abstention Hamming loss was 'often much lower' than both full prediction and full abstention across six MULAN benchmarks (cal500, emotions, scene, yeast, mediamill, nus-wide) with 10-fold CV and competitors sharing the same binary-relevance plus sklearn logistic-regression probabilities; as penalty c rises, loss rises and abstention rate falls, and the SEP variant converges to full-prediction performance at c=0.5 while PAR converges at c=1 (sanity check: never abstain at maximum penalty). Results were figure curves only with no numeric tables extracted, and no significance tests were reported.

For binary classification with a reject option under l2 adversarial perturbations of radius gamma, the confidence-based reject classifier is h(f(x), rho): +1 if f(x) > rho, abstain if |f(x)| <= rho, -1 if f(x) < -rho, with reject cost d in (0, 0.5); the adversarial-robust target loss is ell_d^gamma = (1-d)*sup over B_2(x,gamma) of 1{yf(x') < -rho} + d*sup over B_2(x,gamma) of 1{yf(x') <= rho}, which for linear classifiers equals a gamma right-shift of the standard reject loss. Theorem 11 proved differentiable convex margin surrogates are NOT calibrated for this loss, Theorem 12 proved no quasi-concave-conditional-risk surrogate is calibrated, and Theorem 10 characterizes calibration via 'minima jump' conditions. File verdict is REJECT (linear-only theory, synthetic-only experiments, adversarial framing with no sports analogue).
equation: h(f(x),ρ): +1 if f(x)>ρ, ⊥ if |f(x)|≤ρ, −1 if f(x)<−ρ; ℓ_d^γ = (1−d)·sup_{B₂(x,γ)} 1{yf(x')<−ρ} + d·sup_{B₂(x,γ)} 1{yf(x')≤ρ}

claim: Candidate robust surrogates are shifted double sigmoid ell_ds^{mu,beta} and shifted double ramp ell_dr^{mu,beta} requiring shift beta >= gamma (mu=2.65 DSL, 0.95 DRL), validated only on synthetic 2-D data (100/class in reject band, 200/class outside, 5% label noise, 10 runs). Measured: shifted DRL (d=0.2, gamma_train=0.2, beta=0.1) gave 0.229 error / 0.904 accuracy / 0.895 reject rate flat across gamma_test in {0, 0.1, 0.2}, versus the non-robust beta=0 baseline 0.359/0.508/0.453; shifted DSL gave degenerate 0.2/0/1 (rejects everything); non-robust DSL error rose 0.338 (gamma_test=0) to 0.484 (gamma_test=0.2). Calibration of the proposed surrogates is conjectured from plots, not proven (future work).

The three-stream table-tennis stroke network fuses RGB cuboids (120x120x100) plus foreground optical-flow cuboids through 3D convolutions (30/60/80 filters of 3x3x3, max-pool 2x2x2, attention, FC-500) with a pose stream of 1D temporal convolutions over a 14x(x,y,score) descriptor (13 joints plus center); modalities are fused late with bilinear layers y = x1^T A x2 + b summed across modality pairs followed by softmax; ROI center x_roi = 0.6*f(x_max OF) + 0.4*f(x_gravity) with optical flow normalized v/(mu+3 sigma) clipped; training used SGD+Nesterov 0.5, weight decay 0.05, batch 5, cross-entropy, up to 1500 epochs with warm-restart LR (0.01 to 1e-5).

On TTStroke-21 (129 videos, 1,048 annotated strokes plus 106 negatives, 120 FPS, 21 classes; train/val/test 0.7/0.2/0.1; pose via PoseNet/PersonLab with 25% miss rate filled with ROI center plus score 0), pure classification test accuracy was three-stream 87.3% vs Twin-STCNN 81.9% vs RGB+Flow-I3D 75.9% (I3D overfit: 99.2 train to 75.9 test), and the three-stream model converged faster (epoch 1176 vs 1400+); detection+classification without the negative class was 85.6 vs twin 67.9 (up to +18 points from the pose stream); pose alone cannot converge (22% test accuracy); attention on all three branches was slightly worse than on RGB+optical-flow only; negative-class frame precision was 0.99 with recall 0.42 (F 0.59) - the model over-fires stroke labels.

Draw uncertainty for team i is defined as the standard deviation of its qualification probability across random draws: SD_i = sqrt((1/D) sum_d (q_id - qbar_i)^2), where q_id is the qualification probability under draw d; estimated with D=1,000 random draws times 1,000 outcome simulations each (independent Poisson from Elo expectancies) with bootstrap confidence intervals, plus a decomposition rerun under perfect (Elo) seeding with no playoffs to isolate the pure format effect. The new Champions League format reduced draw uncertainty 53% on average for 2024/25, but most of the reduction came from robustness to inaccurate UEFA seeding rather than a pure format advantage - under perfect Elo seeding with no playoffs the new format's pure advantage was much smaller ('the old format's problem wasn't the format, it was bad seeding').

The betting study defined classwise-ECE = (1/k) sum_i sum_j (|B_{j,i}|/n) |ybar_i(B_{j,i}) - pbar_i(B_{j,i})| with M=20 bins and a degenerate guard (<80% non-empty bins forces ECE=1); Kelly fraction k = (p*b - q)/b where p is model probability, b decimal-odds-minus-1, q = 1-p, with eighth-Kelly stakes (1/8)*k*bankroll. The pipeline (two parallel NBA pipelines, LR/RF/SVM/MLP, Spearman>0.7 feature filter, sequential forward selection under accuracy vs ECE objectives, BO-TPE tuning, KS covariate-shift screening at 1%) on 2018/19 NBA with Westgate closing odds, $10,000 bankroll, and bet-all-value-bets simulation (model prob > implied prob) used SVM in both branches: test accuracy 66.55%, test classwise-ECE 3.23%.

Selecting a sports-betting model by calibration instead of accuracy produced +34.69% average ROI (maximum 36.93% under eighth-Kelly, turning $10,000 into $13,693) while the accuracy-selected model lost -35.17% on average (best 5.56% fixed stakes; its Kelly counterpart lost 75.9% of the bankroll, down to $2,410). The mechanism: the accuracy-driven model was overconfident, with value bets clustering at probability extremes (more false positives), and Kelly sizing amplified the miscalibration into ruin; both systems bet roughly 88-90% of games, a single season only, and SVM won both branches (limiting model diversity).

The Factor Quantile (FQ) model forecasts entire joint distributions in three stages: per-margin univariate quantile regressions y_t = alpha^(tau) + B^(tau) x_t + eps_t^(tau) on a |Q|=9 tail-concentrated quantile grid {0.001, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.999} with latent PCA factors, PCHIP-interpolated into conditional marginal CDFs, then glued with a conditional copula Fhat(y|x*) = C(Fhat_1 ... Fhat_n | x*); FQ-A uses last principal components as latent factors while FQ-B uses bagging with 25M samples per margin. Evaluation used weighted CRPS C_w(F,y) = 2 integral_0^1 (1{y <= F^{-1}(alpha)} - alpha)(F^{-1}(alpha) - y) w(alpha) dalpha with weights w = 1, alpha(1-alpha), alpha^2/(1-alpha)^2, (2alpha-1)^2; energy score ES(F,y) = -1/2 E_F||Y-Y'|| + E_F||Y-y|| (insensitive to correlation misspecification per Pinson & Girard 2012); variogram score VS_p(F,y) = sum_{i,j}(|y_i-y_j|^p - E_F|Y_i-Y_j|^p)^2 as the dependence-structure check the energy score misses; and the Model Confidence Set protocol (Hansen et al. 2011) with sequential equivalence tests at 75%/90%, bootstrap variance and worst-model elimination.
equation: y_t = α^(τ) + B^(τ)x_t + ε_t^(τ); C_w(F,y) = 2∫₀¹(1{y≤F⁻¹(α)}−α)(F⁻¹(α)−y)w(α)dα; ES(F,y) = −½E_F‖Y−Y'‖ + E_F‖Y−y‖; VS_p(F,y) = Σ_{i,j}(|y_i−y_j|^p − E_F|Y_i−Y_j|^p)²

claim: On three 8-dimensional daily financial systems (8 USD FX rates 1999-2018, US Treasury term structure 1994-2018, 8 Bloomberg commodity indices 1991-2018, rolling 2000-obs recalibration, 250 for static models): the |Q|=9 PCHIP quantile grid reproduces the |Q|=500 distribution (a KS test cannot distinguish them at 1% significance), versus kernel needing 35 nodes and step-function needing 50 - a 4x or greater compute saving, with no quantile crossing observed; univariate CRPS put FQ-A(250) in the 90% model confidence set 50% of the time versus CCC-GARCH 37.5%, and FQ won rates decisively; multivariate results had FQ-A(250) best overall with 58.3% MCS inclusion versus DCC-GARCH 50%; FQ calibrated 30%+ faster than CCC-GARCH and 5x+ faster than DCC-GARCH with no convergence failures (DCC needed manual surgery on commodities); smaller 250-observation windows usually beat 2000-observation windows (long windows violate stationarity); and FQ-A >= FQ-B everywhere, so the simple alpha version dominates the complex bagging variant.

NFL fandom was mapped from geotagged Twitter Decahose tweets (random 10% sample, 2011-2014 regular seasons) with activity A(M_i) = Tweets(M_i)/Population(M_i) x 100,000 per metro, fandom radius defined as the first distance from the stadium where normalized activity falls below background (70% cumulative-population core threshold), sentiment measured on a hedonometer-style lexicon (~6.0 scale) in pregame/halftime/end-of-game windows of seven-day game windows; activity scales as population^alpha with alpha = 0.53 and R^2 = 0.64 (19,174 team-season-metro observations).
equation: A(M_i) = Tweets(M_i)/Population(M_i) × 100,000; activity ∝ population^α, α = 0.53, R² = 0.64

claim: Measured NFL fandom geography and sentiment (2011-2014, purely descriptive, no predictive validation): fandom radius ranged from Ravens 121 km to Seahawks 782 km; sentiment by winner/loser was pregame 6.14/6.09, halftime 5.86/5.80, end-of-game 6.12/5.77 - winners rebound, losers stay depressed (losses linger); inside-fandom versus overall sentiment Spearman rho = 0.85 (p<0.001); win percentage versus sentiment Pearson correlation 0.33. Limitations: decade-old data, hashtag-based team assignment, matchup tweets double-counted, lexicon fails on sarcasm, no code released.

True-positive head acceleration events (HAEs) were measured in NCAA Division I football (35 players, 4 games, 2022 Mountain West season, single team) with instrumented mouthguards triggering above 8g on any axis, video-adjudicating 1,101 triggered events to 828 true positives, with >= 90% wear-time criterion (64 eligible player-games) and analysis thresholds at 5g PLA and 400 rad/s^2 PAA at the head center of gravity. Results: sensitivity 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.92); positive predictive value 0.98/0.93/0.76 depending on the false-positive definition (the wide range is itself a finding). Per player-game incidence: >10g PLA defense 11.2, offense 11.3; >30g PLA defense 1.6, offense 2.6; >1.0 krad/s^2 PAA defense 5.5, offense 6.9; >2.0 krad/s^2 PAA defense 0.9, offense 1.4 - a counterintuitive asymmetry where offense shows higher high-magnitude incidence than defense at every threshold above the lowest. The paper makes no concussion link (exposure is not injury), and the sample is small (35 players, 1 team, 1 season) with limited NFL external validity.

Expected Possession Value (EPV) in soccer was extended with time-decayed within-possession credit PV(c_i) = 1 - product_j (1 - gamma^(t_j - t_i) * xG_j) over events j at or after time t_i with gamma = 0.95 per effective second (a stylistic, untuned choice); possession risk = own future decayed xG sum minus opponent's future decayed xG sum; duel possession value PV(d_i) = PV(e_{i+1}) if the same possession continues, else -PV(e_{i+1}); reward branches for DeltaEPV split into keep / turnover-penalized-twice / goal / duel-lead; Pass Carry Reward PCR(player) = 60 * sum DeltaEPV(pass or carry) / minutes. Duel skill used a modified Glicko-2 rating mu' = mu + phi'^2 g(phi_j) (s_j - E(mu + a, mu_j, phi_j)) with a = defender advantage term and context win-probability from LightGBM without skill features; league transfers got an ad-hoc bias correction PCR_adj = PCR * 0.8^(Delta ratings + pl). Custom losses were per-player-appearance-weighted (log-loss for xG, MSE for EPV), dividing by each player's appearance count.
equation: PV(c_i) = 1−Π_j(1 − γ^(t_j−t_i)·xG_j[t_j≥t_i]), γ=0.95; PV(d_i) = PV(e_{i+1}) if same possession, else −PV(e_{i+1}); PCR = 60·ΣΔEPV(pass∨carry)/minutes; μ' = μ + φ'²g(φ_j)(s_j − E(μ + a, μ_j, φ_j)); PCR_adj = PCR·0.8^(Δratings + pl)

claim: Predicting next-season Pass Carry Reward (per-60 DeltaEPV) from ~600 features with LightGBM beat naive carry-forward by about 38% RMSE: all data with >100 minutes, baseline RMSE 0.053 to model 0.033, MAE 0.036 to 0.023; >1000 minutes 0.042 to 0.031; hardest slice (new team and new league) 0.061 to 0.037; easiest (same team and league) 0.050 to 0.032. Duel ratings: van Dijk top aerial 1762 (2,167 duels, 71.9% wins), B. Ostojic top ground 1695 (279 duels, 73.1%); case study Zlatan aerial win 61.1% vs Leao 35.8% at similar a-priori difficulty (39.2 vs 40.5). No confidence intervals or significance tests were reported, gamma was untuned, and the 600-feature set details were partial (appendix truncated).

Two formulations integrate a reject option into node classification: NCwR-Cov (coverage-based) fixes the coverage rate as a business parameter then maximizes accuracy on posted samples, with objective E = selective risk r(f,g) + lambda*max(0, c - phi(g))^2, lambda = 32, target coverage c, and tau calibrated on validation to hit the coverage; NCwR-Cost treats rejection as a (K+1)-th softmax class with cost-aware cross-entropy ell_ce^d = -log f_y(h) - (1-d)*log f_{K+1}(h), where d=1 recovers standard cross-entropy and d < (K-1)/K is required for abstention to be relevant. Baselines were Softmax-Response (tau in 0.5-0.9) and CF-GNN conformal, over coverages 0.5-1.0 and d in {0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.85} with 10 random inits.
equation: E = r(f,g) + λ·max(0, c−φ(g))², λ=32; ℓ_ce^d = −log f_y(h) − (1−d)·log f_{K+1}(h); d < (K−1)/K

claim: On Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed citation networks (20 nodes/class train, 500 val, 1000 test) plus the ILDC Indian Legal Documents Corpus (7,593 labeled + 24,907 unlabeled cases): NCwR-Cost beat Softmax-Response at every coverage on all three datasets; NCwR-Cov on Cora reached coverage 0.5 -> 93.96 +/- 1.45 accuracy, 0.8 -> 89.12 +/- 0.8, 1.0 -> 81.65; NCwR-Cost d=0.5 -> 95.8 +/- 0.05 at 42.6% coverage, d=0.85 -> 87.2 +/- 0.06 at 90.5% coverage; on ILDC, NCwR-Cost d=0.25 -> 87.24 +/- 2.45 accuracy at 67.0 +/- 3.3% coverage and NCwR-Cov at 0.5 coverage -> 97.55 +/- 0.62. NCwR-Cov had high variance (std up to +/- 3.34) and tended to reject easy examples of particular classes; cost-based beat coverage-based at most operating points.

An agent-based model calibrated to Lorenz et al. (2011)'s crowd experiment used agent dynamics dx_i/dt = alpha_i(<x> - x_i) + beta_i(x_i(0) - x_i) + D xi_i(t), where alpha is social influence, beta individual conviction and D noise; collective error E(t) = (ln T - <ln x(t)>)^2, group diversity D(t) = (1/N) sum (ln x_i - <ln x>)^2, wisdom indicator W(t) = centrality of truth in the opinion distribution. The mechanism: coupling to the arithmetic mean while the truth-center is the geometric mean (AM > GM for log-normal opinions) drags the crowd rightward regardless of the truth. Simulations used N=100 agents, T=3000 steps, log-normal initial opinions, sweeping {alpha, beta}.
equation: dx_i/dt = α_i(⟨x⟩−x_i) + β_i(x_i(0)−x_i) + Dξ_i(t); E(t) = (ln T − ⟨ln x(t)⟩)²; D(t) = (1/N)Σ(ln x_i − ⟨ln x⟩)²

claim: Lorenz et al. (2011) experiment (144 ETH Zurich students, 12 sessions x 12 participants, 6 quantitative questions x 5 rounds, three information regimes) was reproduced showing three effects: social influence converges opinions without improving error; truth drifts to the periphery while the distribution narrows (range reduction); individuals grow more confident as the group drifts wrong (self-confidence effect). The aggregation metric matters: the arithmetic mean beat individuals' first estimates in 21.3% of cases while the geometric mean (log-transformed opinions) did so in 77.1%. An initially inaccurate crowd (E(0)=0.8) saw stronger social influence reduce long-run error across nearly the whole {alpha,beta} range, but an initially accurate crowd (E(0)=0.01-0.02) saw social influence increase error. The model has no score feedback - real forecasting markets have feedback, which changes the dynamics.

A theory paper proved a principled correspondence between proper scoring rules and opinion-pooling operators: quasi-arithmetic (QA) pooling with respect to a scoring rule's exposure function, where the Savage representation is s(p;j) = G(p) + <g(p), delta_j - p> with g the exposure function. The QA pool p* = argmin_x sum w_i D_G(x || p_i) minimizes the weighted Bregman divergence: the quadratic rule (g_quad(x)=2x) gives linear pooling sum w_i p_i; the log rule (g_log(x)=ln x + 1) gives logarithmic (geometric) pooling p*(j) = c * product_i p_i(j)^{w_i}. The max-min theorem states min_j u(p*;j) = sum w_i D_G(p* || p_i) >= 0, equal across outcomes with p*_j > 0; the no-regret theorem gives online gradient descent on simplex weights achieving regret <= 3*sqrt(m)*M*sqrt(T) versus the best mixture in hindsight; for the binary case (n=2) EVERY proper scoring rule has convex exposure, so all theorems apply to binary predictions regardless of rule. An informed-model contrast: experts at 0.1% vs 20% equal-weighted give linear ~10% (failure) versus log ~1.6%.
equation: s(p;j) = G(p) + ⟨g(p), δ_j − p⟩; p* = argmin_x Σw_i D_G(x∥p_i); p*(j) = cΠ_i p_i(j)^{w_i}; regret ≤ 3√m·M·√T

claim: Key aggregation discipline from the max-min/QA theory: never mix operator and rule - linear or log pooling under a mismatched scoring rule breaks concavity (explicit counterexamples given); the scoring rule encodes a value judgment, with the quadratic rule expressing even precision preference across [0,1] and the log rule expressing precision preference near 0 and 1. The Tsallis family corresponds to coordinate-wise power means (quadratic->arithmetic, log->geometric, gamma=0->harmonic), and six axioms exactly characterize the QA pooling class for n=2. No empirical validation was provided - proofs only.

A pure-theory paper proved that *difference queries* (asking expert i for the difference between its forecast and a peer's forecast) recover optimal Bayesian aggregation with only n queries, exponentially fewer than naive higher-order elicitation. In the partial-information model (n experts, independent mean-zero signals X_S indexed by expert subsets, target Y = sum_S X_S), the exact minimax worst-case error with query budget d < n is 1 - d/n; linear-aggregation regimes are: d = o(sqrt(n)) gives error 1 - Theta(d^2/n), d = Theta(sqrt(n)) gives a limit strictly in (0,1), and d = omega(sqrt(n)) gives exponentially decaying bounds. The proof reduces to constrained polynomial minimax via Chebyshev polynomials and equioscillation, assuming independent signals, truthful reporting and squared error; the correlated-signal extension is left open. These are worst-case bounds in the independent-signal model, not measured gains, and everything hinges on independent signals.
equation: error = 1 − d/n for d < n; d=o(√n) → 1−Θ(d²/n); d=Θ(√n) → (0,1); d=ω(√n) → exponential decay

claim: A spread-to-cover-probability conversion multiplies a zero-mean normal margin density by empirical key-number multipliers (historical probability divided by normal-implied probability per integer margin): 0:0, 1:0.9, 2:0.7, 3:2.7, 4:1.1, 5:0.7, 6:0.8, 7:2.1, 8:0.7, 9:0.4, 10:1.3, 11:0.7 (an SD=22 fit matched history best); the matrix has rows of margins -60..60 by columns of projected spreads -39..39, with cell = Normal(col, SD=15) mass over (s-0.5, s+0.5) times multiplier(s), column-normalized, with non-integer projections interpolated. Edge = cover% - break-even%, where break-even p = 100*|min(100,odds)|/(100+|odds|) (-110 needs 52.4%). Assumptions: the gambler's projection is the conditional mean, pushes are explicitly excluded, and an OT-rule-change caveat applies to margin 2.
equation: multiplier(s) = historical(s)/normal-implied(s); cell = N(col, SD=15) mass × multiplier(s); edge = cover% − break-even%; break-even p = 100·|min(100,odds)|/(100+|odds|)

claim: Key-number multipliers came from Boyd (2015) college football historical margins 1980-2014 (margin 3: 9.6%, 7: 7.3%, 10: 4.3%, 14: 4.3%, 1: 3.4%, 4: 3.9%) and 2021 CFB (SD 21.01 all games, 15.35 similar-spread), with Bill Connelly's SP+ used for illustration (HFA ~2-2.5); a worked example (Baylor -2.5, SP+ -2.9) gave plain-normal 51.06% versus key-number-adjusted 53.2% cover probability, i.e. a 0.8% edge (Baylor covered, won by 7 - anecdotal); a sanity example of projected to lose by 8 but bet at +7.5 gave a 1.2% edge under the method. No ROI, win-rate, or CLV was reported (paper states this explicitly); columns' expectations fell within 0.1-0.2 points of the projection as a fit check only. The reusable NFL port numbers: Stern's NFL conditional SD 13.861 (more recent estimates 13.5).

Kelly betting can be too conservative: maximizing g(K) = E[log(1+K^T X)] over the admissible set, the Restricted Betting Theorem says the optimizer satisfies h_X(-K) <= 1 (support-function confinement) with the feasible set convex and closed; a scalar lemma states that support [X_min, X_max] with X_min < 0 < X_max forces K in [-1/X_max, -1/X_min], and unbounded support on both sides forces the degenerate K* = 0 regardless of how large mu/sigma is. For toy Bernoulli X in {1, -x_0}, K* = (1 - eps(1+x_0))/x_0 < 1/x_0 regardless of how small eps is; bad-sample probability p_bad = 1 - (1-eps)^M (eps=0.001, M=50 gives ~0.05); the empirical counterpart Khat* comes from fhat_X = m^{-1} sum delta(x - x_i). Hypercube/hypersphere joint-support cases were also treated.

Empirically, for the normal family N(mu,1) with mu in [0,4] and 1M samples per mu, the empirical Kelly fraction Khat*(mu) rises 0 to ~0.9 as mu goes 0 to 4, while the theoretical K* = 0 for ALL mu and sigma - fitting an unbounded-support distribution (e.g. normal) to returns forces 'bet nothing' regardless of mu/sigma, while Kelly computed from the empirical return distribution gives sensible fractions. On AAPL tick data (2015-12-02, 110,000 ticks, X_min ~ -0.01), the empirical optimum was 82.4% of wealth versus theoretical GBM K*=0, matching Merton/Thorp continuous-time muhat/sighat^2 ~ 0.825. The paper honestly flags that the empirical PMF systematically underestimates tail risk (p_bad) and offers no correction. Sports-betting returns at fixed odds have bounded support by construction, so the pathology bites only if GSE fits unbounded models (normals) to residuals/returns or bets heavy-tailed parlays.

For the frequency-based Kelly-optimal portfolio over the unit simplex, maximizing g_n(K) = (1/n)*E[log(1+K^T X_n)] with X_{n,i} = product_{k=0}^{n-1}(1+X_i(k)) - 1, Theorem 3.1 gives a KKT-based necessary-and-sufficient optimality certificate: K* is optimal iff E[(1+X_{n,i})/(1+K*^T X_n)] = 1 when K_i* > 0 and <= 1 when K_i* = 0 (n=1 reduces to Cover-Thomas Theorem 16.2.1); Theorem 3.2 (Extended Dominant Asset, strengthened to necessity) states K* = e_j iff E[(1+X_i(0))/(1+X_j(0))] <= 1 for all i != j - 'invest everything in asset j is optimal iff j is dominant'; supporting lemmas are Lemma 3.3 (E[(1+K^T X_n)/(1+K*^T X_n)] <= 1 for all K), Lemma 3.4 (asymptotic relative optimality almost surely), and the simplex implies V(n) > 0 (survivability). A practical algorithm uses the sliding-window dominance ratio R_{ij}(k) = (1/M) sum_{l=0}^{M-1} (1+x_i(k-l))/(1+x_j(k-l)): if R_{ij} <= 1 for all i != j then set K_j*(k) = 1 (bang-bang all-in), else 0. Assumptions: i.i.d. returns, known bounded distribution (Xmin > -1), long-only simplex, log utility.

The Dominant Ratio Trading Algorithm backtest (VT, BND, BNDX daily closes, Feb 14 2019-Feb 14 2020, 252 trading days, Wharton Research Data Services; sliding window M=20, robustness M=1..60) gave V(0)=1 to V(252) ~ 1.23 (about 23% return) with M=20 versus lower buy-and-hold (exact not quoted), similar across M values (qualitative). The backtest is in-sample (rolling estimation equals evaluation), one year, three trending ETFs, no costs - the 23% is illustrative, not evidence. All-in bang-bang is optimal under the assumptions but reckless under estimation error; the paper's own survivability lemma guarantees only positivity, not drawdown control.

An exactly solvable Markov win-probability model for T20 cricket chases was built by backward induction over the acyclic (balls, wickets, runs-required) state graph with recursion V(s) = sum_o p_o(s)*V(s'_o), verified to machine precision 1e-9, with the martingale property E[V(next)|s] = V(s); leverage was defined as swing(s) = sum_o p_o(s) |V(s'_o) - V(s)| (conditional MAD), with leverage index LI normalized so the average delivery = 1 (reference 0.0170 WP/ball); WPA attributes DeltaV to the batsman and -DeltaV to the bowler (zero-sum per ball), telescoping to y - V(first ball), with state-conditional de-drifting (WP bins of width 0.02). The one-ball distribution p_o(s) came from RRR bins (6) x wickets x innings phase with two-level Dirichlet-style shrinkage and exponential recency weights (half-life 0.75 seasons). The core diagnosis: exact attribution and calibrated probability are mutually exclusive on the same state object, with unmodelled 3-5-event sequential scoring dependence as the mechanism.
equation: V(s) = Σ_o p_o(s)·V(s'_o); E[V(next)|s]=V(s); swing(s) = Σ_o p_o(s)|V(s'_o)−V(s)|; WPA = ΔV

claim: On IPL ball-by-ball 2008-2026 (Cricsheet-derived) second-innings chases - 1,162 chases, 130,029 legal deliveries, train on all but 2024-2026 (112,019 balls), held-out 2024-2026 (18,010 balls, 164 matches, realized win rate 0.498): held-out Brier/log-loss/ECE were RRR Markov+era 0.1489/0.4741/0.1310 versus logistic on RRR alone 0.1404/0.4379/0.0773 (the simple logistic beats the full Markov model); unconstrained XGBoost on identical (balls, wickets, runs) beat the exact Markov by 0.094 nats (CI [0.026, 0.174]); striker balls-faced added +0.0004 nats (CI [-0.0032, +0.0035]) - a decisive null. The calibration gap was worst at RRR 10-12 (-0.112; 18%-rated chases won 29%) with a held-out trough of -0.267 at RRR 8-10; the permutation decomposition showed innings heterogeneity explains ~18%, with residual 3-5-ball scoring persistence (lag-1 excess +0.036, lag-3 +0.021, lag-5 +0.008, null by lag 10-20) and wickets anti-clustering (lag-1 -0.009); block bootstrap K=20 reduced the slice gap 0.0613 to 0.0451 (26%, 6/6 seeds, saturating at K~20); leverage measured death-over mean LI 1.59 (final over 2.67) and Dhoni clutch +0.018/ball (CI [+0.004,+0.032]); era drift correction -0.057 nats (CI [-0.079,-0.035]).

A 2023 Soccer Prediction Challenge entry compared deep networks (Inception block + Transformer encoder + 10-layer MLP on a five-match recency matrix; LSTM+MLP and GRU+MLP baselines) against gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/CatBoost on 205 features including pi-rating features) on the 2023 Soccer Prediction Challenge dataset (51 leagues, 2001 to Apr 4 2023, 300,000+ matches; prediction set 736 matches Apr 14-26 2023). Evaluation: cumulative Rank Probability Score over ordered W/D/L for probabilities, RMSE for exact home/away goal counts. Training used three five-year windows, each with a preceding five-year train and time-ordered validation rounds (2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21). Baselines included league-average, team-average, pi-ratings alone, historical frequencies, and always-home-win.

Validation exact-score RMSE: Berrar pi-ratings 1.0047 beat team average 1.0206, XGBoost+Berrar 1.0212, selected-feature CatBoost 1.2162 and TE+MLP 1.5063 - pi-ratings alone beat every deep model on exact-score RMSE. Validation RPS: CatBoost+pi 0.2085, Inception+TE+MLP 0.2098, historical W/D/L 0.2303, always-home-win 0.4450. Challenge test (736 matches): authors 1.8169 RMSE / 0.2195 RPS versus winner 1.6235 versus bookmaker entry 0.2063 RPS - the bookmaker entry beat everything on RPS. Anti-patterns: 205-feature selection hurt (selected-feature CatBoost was the worst tree variant); deep models collapsed from validation to live (generalization issues conceded). The paper's real contribution is ratings-and-market baseline discipline plus the challenge protocol, not the architectures.

SPORTU is a large-scale multimodal sports-understanding benchmark for MLLMs: 900 text MCQs (5 sports) plus 1,701 slow-motion video clips with 12,048 QA pairs (10,973 MCQ + 1,075 open-ended, 7 sports), all expert-annotated by 9 experts (2 intercollegiate athletes with 12+ years, 7 players with 5+ years); difficulty split 25.36% easy / 50.22% medium / 24.42% hard, 300 multi-angle scenes; evaluation used zero-shot and five-shot, direct-answer vs rationale-first orderings, frame sampling 10 (GPT/Claude) / 16 (most open) / 100 (VideoChat) / whole video (Gemini), with open-ended scored by G-Eval (GPT-4o judge validated against humans at r=0.41). Dataset and eval code are public at github.com/chili-lab/SPORTU.

SPORTU results: best text score GPT-4o 71.00% (five-shot CoT); video direct-answer Qwen2-VL-72B 70.94% and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 70.18%; GPT-4o on hard video 57.84%; rationale-first prompting hurts accuracy (Claude example: 52.57% direct-answer vs 39.32% rationale-first); open-ended: GPT-4o G-Eval 1.84, and no model averaged above 3 out of 5; question-understanding failures and hallucination dominated errors. Caveats: frame-sampling differences confound the leaderboard, G-Eval/human r=0.41 is modest, American-football coverage depth is unclear, and contamination was not audited.

Local temperature scaling (LTS) extends temperature scaling from a single global scalar to a spatially-varying local temperature field T(x) predicted by a network H(alpha, z_i, I_i, x) from (logit map, image): Qhat_i(x, T_i(x)) = max_l sigma_SM(z_i(x)/T_i(x))(l) with T_i(x) in R+; T>1 damps overconfidence, T<1 boosts underconfidence, T->infinity gives uniform; because T(x) > 0 the class order is preserved, so calibration gains come with accuracy unchanged. Theorem 4 (Appendix E) gives an entropy-theoretic proof that temperature-scaling-style NLL minimization counteracts NLL's overconfidence pressure: when overconfident (entropy < cross-entropy), NLL minimization w.r.t. temperature-scaling parameters is equivalent to maximizing entropy under the overconfidence constraint; when underconfident, NLL coincides with entropy minimization; equilibrium is at the optimal T.
equation: Q̂ᵢ(x, Tᵢ(x)) = max_l σ_SM(zᵢ(x)/Tᵢ(x))(l); Tᵢ(x)∈R⁺; T>1 damps overconfidence, T<1 boosts underconfidence, T→∞→uniform

claim: LTS beat global temperature scaling on ECE/MCE/SCE/ACE (10 bins; All/Boundary/Local regions) across COCO (FCN+ResNet-101, 1000 test, mIoU 63.7%), CamVid (Tiramisu, 233 test) and LPBA40 (3D U-Net, 40 test) with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U + Benjamini/Hochberg FDR 0.05), against baselines including uncalibrated, global TS, IBTS (per-image T), isotonic, vector scaling, ensemble TS, Dirichlet calibration, and MMCE/focal-loss joint training each with LTS post-hoc. Measured ECE All (%): COCO UC 12.44 -> TS 12.53 -> IBTS 11.92 -> LTS 10.04; CamVid UC 7.79 -> TS 3.45 -> IBTS 3.63 -> LTS 3.40 (Boundary ECE UC 22.79 -> LTS 11.80); LPBA40 UC 5.58 -> TS 1.43 -> LTS 0.90; VoteNet+ UC 7.26 -> TS 5.07 -> IBTS 2.77 -> LTS 0.71; joint training CamVid ECE MMCE 4.45 -> MMCE+LTS 4.15, focal loss 3.47 -> FL+LTS 3.13. Downstream multi-atlas label-fusion Dice: 81.19 (UC) to 81.27 (LTS) - still far from theoretical upper bounds; MCE stays high everywhere (boundary annotation noise).

Forecast reconciliation for hierarchical/grouped time series is forecast combination: for each bottom-level series, the hierarchy constraints generate a candidate-forecast set, and combining them spans exactly the unbiased linear reconciliations - MSE-optimal weights recover MinT, and the full problem separates into per-series Bates-Granger problems. Coherence is y_t = S*b_t; the MinT closed form is P*_mint = (S' Sigma_h^{-1} S)^{-1} S' Sigma_h^{-1}; Theorem 3.1 states P satisfies PS=I iff P = Phi(w)C (combination is equivalent to unbiased linear reconciliation); Proposition 3.3 (separability) gives per-series w_i^sep = (C^{(i)} Sigma_h C^{(i)'})^{-1} 1 / (1' (C^{(i)} Sigma_h C^{(i)'})^{-1} 1), exactly Bates-Granger (1969); Proposition 3.4 states Phi(w*)C = P*_mint (MinT is per-series optimal combination). The modular framework combines covariance estimators (Raw / Diag-shrink / Factor-shrink / OLS) x weight penalties (egalitarian ridge toward equal weights eRidge, eLASSO) x implementation (Joint / Separate); existing MinT variants arise as unpenalized special cases.

Tested on Australian electricity generation (daily, Jun 11 2019-Jun 10 2020, 366 days; 67 rolling windows x h=1..7) and Australian labor-force grouped data (monthly; 21 rolling windows x h=1..12): electricity overall RMSE was Factor+Joint 11.08 vs MinT(Shrink) 11.09 (unpenalized best), and Factor+Separate+eRidge 11.06 matched or improved on the strongest benchmark at every hierarchy level; LCC-type methods were worse than unreconciled Base at Levels 1-2, and the proposed framework had uniformly lower overall RMSE than LCC-type methods. Gains over MinT(Shrink) were only ~0.3% relative - the headline is interpretability plus modularity, not big accuracy; labor-force Table 3 numbers were garbled in extraction (qualitative support only). Assumptions: unbiased base forecasts (breaks with biased sports models), Sigma-hat_h = Sigma-hat_1 one-step proxy unvalidated, point forecasts only.

An assumption-free characterization of the maximal asymptotic Kelly growth rate was given as the inf-KL rate to the bipolar of the null class: the polar S-degree is the set of valid e-variables and the bipolar S-degree-degree is the 'effective null' (TV-closed convex enlargement of the null class S); inf-KL is a_n(Q,P) = inf_{R in (P^n)^{oo}} KL(Q^n || R), superadditive so the rate d_inf-KL = lim (1/n) a_n exists by Fekete's lemma. Theorem 3.5 states sup over wealth processes of limsup (1/n) E_Q[log W_n] = d_inf-KL, achieved by repeating near-optimal m-block e-variables; Theorem 4.1 restores the KLinf identity under weak lower semicontinuity/weak compactness: if inf_{P in P} KL(R || P) is weakly l.s.c. at Q then lim (1/n)*inf-KL(Q^n,P^n) = KLinf(Q,P), with (1/n)*inf-KL <= KLinf always; Theorem 3.14 states power-one testing is equivalent to positive rate; binary KL is D(p||q) = p log(p/q) + (1-p) log((1-p)/(1-q)); for composite Q, d_rob = limsup (1/n)*sup_{E in (P^n)^o} inf_{Q in Q} E[log E] with d_rob <= d_wc and equality for finite Q or sub-exponential covering.
equation: a_n(Q,P) = inf_{R∈(Pⁿ)°°} KL(Qⁿ‖R); d_inf-KL = lim (1/n)a_n; sup limsup (1/n)E_Q[log W_n] = d_inf-KL; D(p‖q) = p log(p/q) + (1−p) log((1−p)/(1−q))

claim: The growth-rate theory's headline warning is Proposition 5.4: a counterexample where KLinf > 0 but every e-process grows at rate at most 0 (so d_inf-KL <= KLinf always, strict in general); all results are asymptotic (n -> infinity), assume i.i.d. (sports outcomes are not), the bipolar is uncomputable in practice, there is no finite-sample e-variable construction algorithm, and no prescription for choosing the null class P.

Monte Carlo Pass Search (MCPS) evaluates soccer passes counterfactually with three components: a policy samples pass variants, a learned discrete-token world model (SMART adapted from autonomous driving) rolls out trajectories, and a learned value model scores possession value - separating decision quality from execution quality and option quality (code + checkpoints released, CC BY 4.0). The value model is a Transformer on tracking windows with two BCE heads and PV(s) = P(ego scores in 10s) - P(opp scores in 10s), labeled by shots-in-10s weighted by an xG proxy; the world model is a decoder-only space-time Transformer with 8 history to 24 rollout tokens, player tokens as 10-dim velocities (2048-code k-means vocab) and ball tokens as 15-dim 3D velocities (1024-code vocab), plus a Player-to-Touch module (BCE hazard + weighted CE toucher ID) and a Ball-at-Touch module (diagonal-Gaussian NLL); search fits per-pass kick params via a CEM-style solver plus ball-flight simulator (gravity/drag/restitution/friction), sampling 256 local variants (execution noise) plus 256 global variants (alternative options); decision scores are DeltaPV(theta) = PV(s'(theta)) - PV(s), S_mean = DeltaPV_obs - (1/K) sum DeltaPV(theta^k), and S_pct = (1/K) sum 1[DeltaPV_obs >= DeltaPV(theta^k)]. Data: 7 German Bundesliga matches, 25 Hz all-22 + 3D ball (TRACAB Gen5), train/val/test 5/1/1 matches, held-out test Bochum vs Leverkusen 2022/23 with 512 accurately-inferred passes.
equation: PV(s) = P(ego scores in 10s) − P(opp scores in 10s); ΔPV(θ) = PV(s′(θ)) − PV(s); S_mean = ΔPV_obs − (1/K)ΣΔPV(θ^k); S_pct = (1/K)Σ1[ΔPV_obs ≥ ΔPV(θ^k)]

claim: MCPS measured on Bundesliga data: trajectory forecasting best-of-20 minADE20 2.4 (ours) vs Sports-Traj 4.2, naive Transformer 3.8, constant velocity 5.0, static 6.8; minFDE20 4.7 vs 6.9/7.5/10.1/13.4. Player-to-Touch: receiver top-1 0.605, pass-success accuracy 0.777, AUROC 0.799 - below Spearman/Anzer, honestly attributed to a harder penalized setting. Possession-value model: shot AUROC 0.73 vs ball-only EPV 0.78 (authors admit it does not improve shot discrimination); Brier 0.017 vs 0.022. Case study: local search exposes narrow success windows, global search flags missed alternatives, and the rankings separate execution skill (local percentile) from option selection (global mean-difference).

Deep Evidential Regression learns aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for regression in a single forward pass (no inference sampling, no OOD training data) by having the network output the four hyperparameters (gamma, nu, alpha, beta) of a Normal-Inverse-Gamma prior over a Gaussian likelihood: prediction E[mu] = gamma; aleatoric E[sigma^2] = beta/(alpha-1); epistemic Var[mu] = beta/(nu(alpha-1)); model evidence p(y|m) = St(y; gamma, beta(1+nu)/(nu*alpha), 2*alpha) (Student-t marginal). Training loss L = L^NLL + lambda*L^R with L^NLL = 1/2 log(pi/nu) - alpha log(Omega) + (alpha+1/2) log((y-gamma)^2 nu + Omega) + log(Gamma(alpha)/Gamma(alpha+1/2)), Omega = 2 beta(1+nu), and evidence regularizer L^R = |y-gamma|*(2 nu + alpha); assumes a Gaussian likelihood and alpha > 1, lambda must be tuned, and positivity constraints (softplus/exp) are required on nu, alpha, beta.
equation: E[μ]=γ; E[σ²]=β/(α−1); Var[μ]=β/(ν(α−1)); p(y|m) = St(y; γ, β(1+ν)/(να), 2α); L^NLL = ½log(π/ν) − α log(Ω) + (α+½)log((y−γ)²ν + Ω) + log(Γ(α)/Γ(α+½)), Ω=2β(1+ν); L^R = |y−γ|·(2ν+α)

claim: Deep evidential regression results (code at github.com/aamini/evidential-deep-learning): on the UCI-style benchmark suite (Boston, Concrete, Energy, Kin8nm, Naval, Power, Protein, Wine, Yacht), evidential models outperformed MC-dropout and deep ensembles on NLL and inference speed on ALL datasets with competitive RMSE; on NYU Depth v2 (>27k RGB-to-depth pairs) they showed a strong inverse confidence-vs-error relationship, a calibration curve near y=x with small calibration error, and uncertainty maps tracking actual error spatially; on ApolloScape outdoor driving (OOD) they showed a positive shift of the entropy CDF vs in-distribution and competitive OOD-detection AUC-ROC - without any OOD training data; adversarially, uncertainty rose steadily with perturbation magnitude, spatially aligned with error. Limitations from the paper's own section 6: NO calibration guarantee (conformalize before publishing), lambda is sensitive, and the Gaussian likelihood may miss heavy tails (blowouts).

Joint Bayesian model choice over the 2^p proportional-odds (PO) vs non-proportional-odds (NPO) configurations per variable in cumulative-link ordinal regression via reversible-jump MCMC, with stochastic ordering enforced by bounding proposals to a covariate-range hyper-rectangle. The cumulative-link model is logit(P(Y <= k|x)) = theta_k - x'beta (PO) or theta_k - x'beta_k (NPO), k=1..K-1, with stochastic ordering requiring theta_k - x'beta_k increasing in k (enforced over the observed covariate range only); RJ-MCMC uses dimension-matching PO<->NPO proposals with posterior model probabilities from chain occupancy and supports random effects (R code at github.com/tjmckinley/BayesOrd). The paper recommends LOO/WAIC comparison first and reserves RJ-MCMC for ambiguous cases.
equation: logit(P(Y≤k|x)) = θ_k − x'β (PO) or θ_k − x'β_k (NPO)

claim: Simulation results (100 datasets x 3 scenarios, n=1,000, 7 predictors, 3 ordinal levels, 200,000 MCMC updates, 10,000 burn-in): PO-truth misclassified 3/700 variable-classifications (0.43% error); NPO-truth misclassified 229/700 (33% - NPO structure is much harder to identify); mixed truth 124/700 (18%: 95 NPO->PO under-fits, 29 PO->NPO). On real data (738 dogs, repeated clinical measures, 500,000 iterations x 2 chains), there was strong posterior support for reproductive status, age, confinement and observed clinical signs, with most selected effects having PO structure. Limitations: ordering not guaranteed outside the observed covariate range, RJ-MCMC scales poorly (2^p space), no comparison to simpler LOO/WAIC alternatives, and only 3 ordinal levels were tested.

Hierarchical stacking (Yao, Pirs, Vehtari, Gelman 2021) generalizes Bayesian stacking from one global weight vector to an input-dependent weight function: p(ytilde|xtilde, w(.)) = sum_k w_k(xtilde) p(ytilde|xtilde, M_k), with LOO objective log p(w(.)|D) = sum_i log(sum_k w_k(x_i) p_{k,-i}) + log p^prior(w). Discrete cells use softmax w_jk = exp(alpha_jk)/sum_k exp(alpha_jk) with alpha_jk|mu_k, sigma_k ~ Normal(mu_k, sigma_k) (sigma_k -> infinity is no-pooling, sigma_k -> 0 is complete pooling); the posterior mean wbar is mandatory because MAP is degenerate at sigma=0; variants include additive ReLU features, GP priors, and time-series recency reweighting. Theorem 1: stacking weights approximately equal Pr(model k is locally best); Theorem 3: elpd gain over selection >= max(L(1-rho)(1-eps) - log K, 0) - largest when models are locally separated and no single model dominates; covariate-shift immunity holds if p(z|x) and p(y|x,z) are invariant (no reweighting needed, and reweighted complete pooling has inflated/infinite variance). Model checking: the PSIS-LOO elpd of the stacking model itself is nearly free via eq. 28.
equation: p(ỹ|x̃,w(·)) = Σₖ wₖ(x̃)p(ỹ|x̃,Mₖ); log p(w(·)|𝒟) = Σᵢ log(Σₖ wₖ(xᵢ)p_{k,−i}) + log p^prior(w); w_jk = exp(α_jk)/Σₖ exp(α_jk)

claim: Hierarchical stacking results: on Bangladesh well-switching (n=3020, 5 models, 50 random 2000/1020 splits), hierarchical stacking was best on test log predictive density, L1 calibration error (20 bins) and the 10-200 worst test points - no-pooling stacking had the highest calibration error despite beating selection on elpd (pure overconfidence); model selection plateaued early as n grew, no-pooling collapsed at small n, and hierarchical dominated everywhere. On Neal (1998) GP-regression bimodal data, hierarchical stacking beat complete pooling, mode-height and importance weighting under MAP/Laplace/importance resampling, and under covariate shift matched exact-MCMC in the bulk while beating it in the tails. On the 2016 US presidential election polling (8 models, one-week-ahead expanding-window backtest): hierarchical > complete-pooling > no-pooling > selection, with the advantage largest early in the cycle when polls were scarce; a state-correlated prior added a small gain in scarce-data regimes. Design rule from Theorem 3: add models that win somewhere, not models better everywhere.

The causal effect (ETT) of MLB's infield shift on change in run expectancy was estimated with three estimators with different identifying assumptions: estimand ETT = E[Y^{t=1} - Y^{t=0}|T=1] with outcome DeltaRE = RE_final - RE_initial + DeltaScore per PA; matching used k:1 nearest-neighbor on the linear propensity score with caliper 0.15 SD, 3:1 ratio, at most 5 re-uses, exact year match, run separately by batter handedness, with linear-regression outcome plus g-computation and robust SEs; IPTW used Horvitz-Thompson weighting-by-the-odds for ETT with 10,000 bootstraps; 2SLS IV used the fielding team's season-to-date shift propensity as a preference-based instrument, estimated per year and averaged over years by treated-PA share (allowing instrument-x-year interaction), with IV identification requiring relevance, effective random assignment, exclusion and no IV effect modification, and balance max |SMD| < 0.05. Data: MLB Statcast (public) via Petti & Gilani scraper, 2015-2022, pitch-level aggregated to PA; covariates included handedness, launch speed/angle/spray angle cumulative summaries, wOBA/BABIP/BB/K, pitcher release metrics, team shift rate and year; no analysis code linked.
equation: ETT = E[Y^{t=1}−Y^{t=0}|T=1]; ΔRE = RE_final − RE_initial + Δscore per PA

claim: All three estimators agreed the shift was effective versus left-handed batters: 95% CI upper bounds below 0 in every method, and point estimates lower for LHB than RHB in all methods; only IV suggested a non-zero effect versus righties. Magnitude: the most conservative estimate was ~10^-2 runs per targeted LHB PA; with LHB ~35-39% of team PAs and the shift used in up to 55% of those at peak, at most ~10^-1 expected runs per game were suppressed - a real but imperceptible advantage. First-stage IV strength: F = 1.18x10^5 unconditioned, partial F = 5.74x10^4 conditional (year + pitcher measures); a 0.25-SD caliper without replacement would have dropped 29,788/149,288 ~ 20% of treated LHB observations.

A prospective case-control study (n=54, 10-month follow-up) of Tunisian soccer players with non-time-loss groin pain vs matched healthy controls: static balance via force-platform single-leg stance with CoP velocity symmetry index (eyes open/closed x 3 trials; group-x-vision interaction F=4.508, p=0.03, eta_p^2=0.08); dynamic balance via the Y-Balance Test (anterior/posteromedial/posterolateral normalized to limb length) with pre-registered cutoffs >= 4 cm posteromedial asymmetry and <= 89.6% composite; statistics via G*Power a priori (26/group), repeated-measures ANOVA, t-tests + Cohen's d, and logistic regression for injury incidence. Recruitment: 27 groin-pain + 27 matched controls from Tunisian elite second division (Sfax), 10-month monthly phone/email surveillance; no public repo/code.

Results: Y-Balance Test asymmetries were higher in the groin-pain group in all directions (p<0.001): anterior d=2.23, posteromedial d=2.11, posterolateral d=1.53, composite d=2.83; injured-limb composite below 89.6% (p<0.001, d=-11.0); posteromedial asymmetry above 4 cm (p<0.001). Subsequent noncontact lower-extremity injury: 17/27 (63%) vs 5/27 (18.5%), p<0.001, V=0.45, odds ratio 7.48 [95% CI 2.15-26.00], p<0.01. Limitations: no exposure hours recorded, n=54 with a wide CI, no position stratification, monthly self-report, soccer-specific, and no causal-mechanism separation (asymmetry vs confounding).

An operational benchmarking protocol for AI weather models on the Indian monsoon evaluates on decision-relevant metrics (miss rate, false alarm rate) rather than generic skill scores, initializes hindcasts to expose false alarms and misses, checks probabilistic calibration via reliability diagrams, and blends models when no single one dominates. Deterministic metrics are MAE / miss rate / false alarm rate vs a climatology baseline; probabilistic metrics are Brier skill score, AUC, ranked probability skill score and reliability diagrams, with fair BSS/RPSS for unequal ensemble sizes; evaluation used multi-period out-of-sample windows (2019-2024, 1965-1978, 2004-2021) plus a live 2025 operational test.

On six open AIWP models (AIFS, FuXi, FuXi-S2S, GraphCast, GenCast, NeuralGCM) plus ECMWF IFS NWP against IMD 1-degree rain-gauge gridded truth (1901-2024): most models beat climatology by ~2 days MAE at 1-15-day leads in the core monsoon zone; IFS and GenCast retained skill to ~3 weeks on all three deterministic metrics; probabilistically the IFS ensemble, GenCast and NeuralGCM were skillful to 15 days, and IFS and NGCM had positive aggregated BSS over 1-30 days; ALL ensemble models were overconfident (predicted probabilities above observed frequencies), needing calibration/blending; no single model dominated across metrics/regions/periods, so the operational choice was a calibrated AIFS+NGCM blend; FuXi-S2S was skillful deterministically but had negative BSS at 15 days (deterministic and probabilistic skill can disagree). The framework informed real 2025 dissemination to 38 million farmers, and models captured anomalous early-onset-then-pause weeks ahead. Limitations: tiny test samples (~6 recent out-of-sample events), some models partly in-sample (marked), GenCast excluded on compute cost.

TwitterPaul extracted explicit predictions from tweets with a hand-built context-free grammar over prediction patterns (team mention + prediction verb + outcome), English only, with negation explicitly ignored and categories strong/weak/support/retweet/question; aggregation was per-match weighted voting under three schemes - unweighted, trust-weighted (user-history reliability), and logistic-regression-weighted (prediction strength + user features) - against baselines of the betting line, team-rank probability, and raw aggregations (all/strong/support). On the 2010 FIFA World Cup (16,157,749 tweets over 37 days; 538,000 extracted predictions, ~150,000 'strong'; extraction evaluated on 300 hand-labeled tweets; 64 matches with actual outcomes and pre-match betting lines; no public code/data), extraction quality was: strong predictions precision 0.886, recall 0.786, F1 0.833; all predictions precision 0.693, recall 0.931, F1 0.794.

TwitterPaul on the 2010 World Cup came close to the betting line but never beat it: RMSE (vs actual / vs market) was betting line 0.3959/0.0000, team-rank 0.4215/0.1614, strong predictions 0.4197/0.1159, trust-weighted 0.4147/0.1131, logistic-weighted 0.4183/0.1117, support-only 0.4416/0.2217; neither weighting scheme beat the market outright on outcome RMSE, and RMSE differences between schemes were within noise at n=64. Limitations: CFG English-only and negation-blind, no sarcasm handling, 2010 Twitter demographics unrepresentative, no calibration analysis; the density of 538K predictions over 64 matches (~8.4K per match) is what made aggregation work.

A formal equivalence between predictive accuracy and trading profit holds for any strictly proper scoring rule: the 'proper bet' s_G(p,q) = gradient G(p) - gradient G(q) earns positive expected profit whenever the forecaster beats the market under the scoring rule and liquidity suffices, and it is essentially the only robustly profitable strategy class. The profit decomposition is pi = [S(p,p*) - S(q,p*)] + D_G(q,p) - L_rho(s*,q): score gap (accuracy edge vs market) + Bregman divergence (divergence bonus, always >= 0) - liquidity cost (CLOB slippage). It was instantiated for Brier (bet proportional to p-q scaled), log and spherical rules with forecaster personas Conservative/Aggressive/Dispersed/Brittle; baselines were Brier-weighted allocation, Inverse-Margin, and Kelly (Kelly particularly poor - unstable under miscalibration). Data: 2,418 Kalshi markets via Prophet Arena (sports/politics/economics/crypto) with AI-model forecasts, contemporaneous bid/ask and realized outcomes; persona experiment 27,516 markets / 3,511 questions (Aug 2025-Apr 2026); live Gemini 3 deployment on Kalshi for 26 days with a $200 budget, 236 orders / 129 markets.

Live deployment of Gemini 3 on Kalshi (26 days, $200 budget): +80.33% ROI with Sharpe 3.35, decomposed as DeltaS = +0.7205 and D = +0.0828 - nearly all gains came from accuracy, not the divergence term. Offline: proper betting was the only strategy reliably converting accuracy into profit across thousands of AI forecasts; for stronger models Brier-weighted allocation was the only heuristic with consistent positive ROI; Inverse-Margin limited downside but capped upside; Kelly performed particularly poorly. Persona finding: Llama 4 Maverick had a worse Brier score gap than the spherical rule (-123.7 vs -53.3) but higher ROI (-13.1 vs -14.8) via a larger divergence term. Limitations: short live window (26 days, $200, one regime), Kalshi CLOB differs from sportsbook mechanics (the liquidity term must be re-mapped to book limits/juice), offline assumed zero price impact, and personas were synthetic.

An information-theoretic treatment of gambling on mutually-exclusive outcomes maximizes the one-parameter beta-utility family U_beta = (1/beta) log E[S^beta] = log[sum_i p_i (b_i o_i)^beta]^{1/beta} (Kelly at beta->0, expected return at beta=1), yielding a closed-form optimal allocation b^*(beta) = g with g_i proportional to p_i^{1/(1-beta)} o_i^{beta/(1-beta)}; beta->0 recovers Kelly b_i = p_i; beta >= 1 puts all wealth on one horse (ruinous); beta -> -infinity gives the risk-free b_i = c/o_i. Theorem 1 states (1/beta) log E[S^beta] = log c + D_{1/(1-beta)}(p||r) - D_{1-beta}(g||b): a three-term decomposition into bookmaker unfairness/vig (log c), bookmaker mispricing/edge in bits (D_{1/(1-beta)}(p||r)), and allocation error/staking mistake (-D_{1-beta}(g||b)). The paper introduced a novel conditional Renyi divergence D_alpha(p_{X|Y}||q_{X|Y}|p_Y) for side information (Theorem 6) and showed partial investment bets only when 1 - sum_{i in J} 1/o_i > 0 (Props 9-10). Pure theory, no empirical validation; assumptions: p_i, o_i > 0, i.i.d. races with constant odds for the growth claim, full reinvestment; the mutually-exclusive setup covers moneylines and parlay legs, not simultaneous independent bets.

AlphaPROBE reframes automated alpha (factor) mining as navigation of a DAG - factors as nodes, evolutionary links as edges - with a Bayesian Factor Retriever balancing exploitation (high |ICIR|) vs exploration (topology penalty, natural-language feedback) and a DAG-aware LLM generator conditioned on the full ancestral trace of the seed; seed quality = |ICIR| on train (Eq. 5), posterior retrieval decomposed into prior/likelihood/topology-penalty/NLF terms, embedding model Qwen3-Embedding-4B; the generator (DeepSeek V3.1 backbone) produces 5 candidates per step conditioned on the full ancestral trace (Eq. 14-15) with depth penalty gamma=0.05 and retrieval penalty omega=0.10; factor pool capacity 50, factor length <= 40, evicted factors retained in graph G for topology completeness, same dynamic factor integrator for all baselines. It beat Alpha158, AlphaGen, AlphaForge, AlphaQCM, AlphaSAGE, GP, AlphaAgent and R&D-Agent on IC/ICIR/RIC/RICIR/AR/MDD/SR across CSI 300/500/1000 (Qlib: train 2010-01-2020-12, validation 2021-01-2022-06, test 2022-07-2025-06; targets 20-day forward returns; code at github.com/gta0804/AlphaPROBE).

AlphaPROBE CSI300 ablation (IC/ICIR/RIC/RICIR %): full 5.84/39.02/7.20/46.94 vs random retriever 2.95/18.71/3.18/21.65, heuristic 4.54/35.15/5.92/35.71, MCTS 4.75/35.20/5.94/36.86, w/o prior 4.13/34.88/5.68/34.42, w/o likelihood 4.09/34.99/5.66/34.39, CoT generator 5.11/31.79/6.08/39.17 - every component contributed, with likelihood and prior mattering most; the same ordering held on CSI500 (6.26/52.39/8.78/73.18) and CSI1000 (9.04/70.49/11.35/88.02), with controlled drawdowns and faster recoveries in the 2023-2024 bear market and April 2025 tariff turmoil. Limitations: DeepSeek V3.1 was trained past the test window (LLM-knowledge caveat), |ICIR| quality bakes train-period bias, gamma/omega were hand-set without sensitivity analysis, and no transaction-cost schedule was quoted.

STaSy applies score-based generative models (SDEs) to tabular synthesis with T=50 diffusion steps: the forward SDE is dx = f(x,t)dt + g(t)dw with denoising score matching (Eq. 6); the reverse uses the probability-flow ODE dx = [f(x,t) - 1/2 g(t)^2 nabla_x log p_t(x)] dt with Hutchinson trace estimation for exact log-probabilities; a self-paced learning (SPL) curriculum (Eq. 13/15, Theorem 1) gives a closed-form soft record-weighting rule v_i* = 1 if l_i <= Q(alpha), 0 if l_i >= Q(beta), (l_i - Q(beta))/(Q(alpha) - Q(beta)) otherwise, with schedule alpha = alpha0 + log(1 + c((e-1)/S)(1-alpha0)), S=10,000, beta0 >= 0.8 (>=80% of records train from the start); fine-tuning (Algorithm 1) computes per-record exact log p under the probability-flow ODE and retrains with DSM loss on records with log p(x_i) < tau_i. Preprocessing used min-max for continuous and one-hot for categorical (weakest point - needs replacing); sampling via probability flow (best) or predictor-corrector solvers; score net with Squash/Concat/Concatsquash layers. It won the quality/diversity/time 'trilemma' versus 7 baselines (CTGAN, TVAE, TableGAN, OCT-GAN, RNODE, MedGAN, VEEGAN) on 15 real datasets (UCI/Kaggle: 7 binary, 6 multi-class, 2 regression), with strength concentrated on small (1.2-1.6K rows) and severely imbalanced (99.7/0.3) tables.
equation: dx = f(x,t)dt + g(t)dw; dx = [f(x,t) − ½g(t)²∇_x log p_t(x)]dt; v_i* = 1 if l_i ≤ Q(α); 0 if l_i ≥ Q(β); (l_i−Q(β))/(Q(α)−Q(β)) otherwise

claim: STaSy results: trilemma averages - STaSy quality 0.733 / diversity 0.658 / runtime 10.663s versus CTGAN 0.569/0.352/0.704s and TVAE 0.521/0.564/0.100s; aggregate TSTR (train-synthetic-test-real, DecisionTree/AdaBoost/LR/MLP/RF/XGBoost, 5 repeats): F1 0.792, AUROC 0.925, weighted F1 0.801, R^2 0.350, RMSE 4071.643 - STaSy best on all five. TSTR highlights: Credit 0.794 +/- 0.035 (synthetic beats real-data training 0.775 +/- 0.071); Shuttle 0.865 +/- 0.072 (naive 0.791 - biggest SPL+fine-tuning gain +0.074); Crowdsource 0.743 +/- 0.104 (smallest class 79 records); Contraceptive 0.451 +/- 0.017. Median test log-probability: STaSy 131.734 vs w/o fine-tuning 129.293 vs RNODE 59.327. Coverage: STaSy 0.658 vs CTGAN 0.352 - but Credit coverage was only 0.014 and Default 0.101, so diversity still collapses on the hardest imbalanced sets. Ablation: full STaSy beat all three ablations on all 7 reported datasets (both SPL and fine-tuning contribute). Sensitivity: SDE type is dataset-dependent (sub-VP for Spambase, VE for Crowdsource/Beijing); recommended alpha0 in {0.2, 0.25}, beta0 in {0.9, 0.95}.

TextGrad treats a compound AI system (prompts -> code -> evaluation) as a computation graph and does 'textual backpropagation': a Variable wraps any value with requires_grad plus a predecessor list, a forward pass (LLM call) registers predecessors, a backward pass has a backward-engine LLM (fixed glossary system prompt) produce per-predecessor natural-language criticism - the analogue of partial-L/partial-x, with the chain rule implemented by passing gradients to predecessors - and TGD.step (Eq. 9) is x_new = LLM('Below are the criticisms on {x}: {dL/dx}. Incorporate the criticisms, and produce a new variable.'); composability via textgrad.autograd.Function and tg.sum for minibatch losses, with the same backward engine across all applications 'without modifying the framework'; 3 LLM calls per iteration per variable with a 5-iteration budget in experiments. Results: LeetCode Hard (gpt-4o, 5 seeds) zero-shot 0.26, Reflexion 0.31 +/- 0.012, TextGrad (0 demos, 5 iters) 0.36 +/- 0.018 - a 20% relative gain over the best existing method with no demonstrations; GPQA 51% to 55% ('best known result'); MMLU Machine Learning 85.7% to 88.4%, College Physics 91.2% to 95.1%. Limitations: no convergence theory (metaphorical differentiation), the backward engine is the same LLM family as forward (self-critique bias), the LeetCodeHard re-extraction was disclosed (Reflexion comparison not on identical data), and gradients are only as good as the loss - with an LLM-judged loss the system hill-climbs the judge's biases. Data: LeetCode Hard 39 problems re-extracted (GPT-4 baseline ~7% completion), GPQA, MMLU subsets (Machine Learning, College Physics), druglikeness/binding-affinity molecules, prostate radiotherapy plans; framework released.
equation: x_new = LLM("Below are the criticisms on {x}: {∂L/∂x}. Incorporate the criticisms, and produce a new variable.")

claim: Flamingo (DeepMind, 2022) is a visual-language model for GPT-3-style few-shot learning over interleaved images/videos and text: a frozen NFNet vision encoder plus a frozen Chinchilla language model bridged by a Perceiver Resampler and gated cross-attention-dense layers (initialized to identity via tanh(alpha) with alpha=0); the Perceiver Resampler uses learned latent queries that cross-attend to variable-size visual features to produce a fixed 64 visual tokens (beats plain Transformer/MLP resamplers); per-image attention masking means at token l the model attends only the immediately preceding image (generalizes to 32 shots despite <= 5 images per sequence in training); the image-causal LM objective is Eq. 1 p(y|x) = product_l p(y_l | y_{<l}, x_{<=l}) and Eq. 2 sum_m lambda_m E[-sum_l log p(y_l | y_{<l}, x_{<=l})] with dataset weights lambda_m 'key to performance'; sizes 3B/9B/80B; video is 1-FPS frames plus learned temporal embeddings. Trained on proprietary web-scraped corpora M3W (~43M pages interleaved), ALIGN (1.8B image/alt-text pairs), LTIP (312M long-text/image pairs), VTP (27M short videos); no code/data release (open re-implementations exist).
equation: p(y|x) = Π_ℓ p(y_ℓ | y_{<ℓ}, x_{≤ℓ}); Σ_m λ_m E[−Σ_ℓ log p(y_ℓ|y_{<ℓ},x_{≤ℓ})]
