Flexible model aggregation for quantile regression uses weighted ensembles ĝ_w(x) = Σ_j w_j(x)·ĝ_j(x) with coarse (one weight per model), medium (per model × quantile level), or fine (per model × level × input level) weight granularity; non-crossing quantiles are enforced with a crossing penalty ρ(g) = ΣΣ (g(x;τ) − g(x;τ') + δ_{τ,τ'})_+ plus isotonization operators (Sort, PAVA, min-max sweep), and conformal CQR/CV+ give finite-sample coverage ≥ 1−α and ≥ 1−2α − √(2/n) respectively.
equation: ĝ_w(x) = Σ_j w_j(x)·ĝ_j(x); ρ(g) = ΣΣ (g(x;τ) − g(x;τ') + δ_{τ,τ'})_+

claim: Prior-agnostic robust forecast aggregation uses symmetric log-odds averaging with dampening: logit(f_α(x₁,x₂)) = α·logit(x₁) + α·logit(x₂). Optimized constants: α=0.585 for conditionally independent signals (regret 0.025512 vs lower bound 31/1326 ≈ 0.023379), α=0.5168 for known {0,1} state (regret 0.022599), and minimax ≈0.022542 for Blackwell-ordered signals.
equation: logit(f_α(x₁,x₂)) = α·logit(x₁) + α·logit(x₂); α=0.585 (regret 0.025512 vs lower bound 31/1326 ≈ 0.023379)

claim: An underdog achievement score (UAS) study of soccer's popularity defines a team as 'weak' if it ranks ≥ τ places below its opponent (τ = median rank difference per sport: soccer 7, water polo 2.5, others 3–5), with UAS = fraction of weak-team wins/draws among matches involving a weak team, and tests 14 hand-specified randomness factors in three groups (physical environment: ball lightness/velocity/geometry/bounciness, field/ball size, goal/ball size; player: BMI, body-ball interaction, dispossession, inexperience; team).

Under multiplicative asset dynamics p_i(t) = p_i(t−1)·e^{η_i(t)} with η_i ~ N(m_i, D_i), the Kelly portfolio maximizes v = E[ln W₁] with W₁ = 1 + Σq_iR_i, giving first-order conditions E[R_i/(1+Σq_jR_j)] = 0 for the optimal weights.
equation: p_i(t) = p_i(t−1)·e^{η_i(t)}, η_i ~ N(m_i, D_i); v = E[ln W₁], W₁ = 1 + Σq_iR_i; E[R_i/(1+Σq_jR_j)] = 0

claim: With no shorting or borrowing, the constrained N-asset Kelly-optimal portfolio condenses to q̂_i = 1/2 + (m_i + γ)/D_i with Σq̂_j = 1, solved by iteratively dropping assets with q̂_i ≤ 0 and re-solving — an analytic portfolio condensation rule.
equation: q̂_i = 1/2 + (m_i + γ)/D_i with Σq̂_j = 1; iteratively drop assets with q̂_i ≤ 0 and re-solve

claim: The Kelly criterion maximizes g(K) = E[log(1 + KᵀX)] with wealth recursion V(k+1) = (1 + KᵀX(k))V(k); its standard approximations are the Taylor form κTaylor = E[X]/E[X²] and the geometric-Brownian-motion form κGBM = μ/σ² — the latter being the classic mean-over-variance sizing rule.
equation: g(K) = E[log(1 + KᵀX)], V(k+1) = (1 + KᵀX(k))V(k); κTaylor = E[X]/E[X²]; κGBM = μ/σ²

claim: In Kelly betting with bounded payoffs, wealth stays positive on every path (survival) if and only if the fraction K lies in the interval −1/Xmax < K < 1/|Xmin|; the saturated Kelly fraction K*_sat,s := SAT_s[K*_approx] clamps the Taylor approximation K*_approx = E[X]/E[X²] = μ/(μ²+σ²) into that interval, and the N-step wealth variance is var(G_K(N)) = ((μ_K²+σ_K²)^N − μ_K^{2N})·V²(0) with μ_K = 1+Kμ, σ_K = Kσ.
equation: V(k) > 0 for all k and all paths iff −1/Xmax < K < 1/|Xmin|; K*_approx = E[X]/E[X²] = μ/(μ²+σ²); var(G_K(N)) = ((μ_K²+σ_K²)^N − μ_K^{2N})·V²(0)

claim: Learning-to-bet for anytime-valid hypothesis testing builds an e-process W_n(m) = W_{n-1}(m)(1 + λ_n(m)(X_n − m)) with W_0 = 1, rejecting at τ_m = inf{t ≤ N : W_t(m) ≥ 1/α} with anytime validity from Ville's inequality; an empirical-Kelly estimate λ̂_t(m) = clip(S_{t-1}/V_{t-1}, Λ_m) feeds a 3-action DQN over {λ̂/2, λ̂, λ_end} (MLP 22→256→128→3, Double DQN, Huber loss, AdamW lr 3e-4); e.g., α=0.05 rejects when W_t ≥ 20.

Hedged e-process mixtures W_t(m) = (1/K)Σ_k W_t^{(k)}(m) satisfy log W_t(m) ≥ max_k log W_t^{(k)}(m) − log K (with K = 6 ε-schedules), so mixing costs at most log K against the best schedule — the diversification mechanism behind the learning-to-bet DQN.
equation: W_t(m) = (1/K)Σ_k W_t^{(k)}(m); log W_t(m) ≥ max_k log W_t^{(k)}(m) − log K

claim: Competing probabilistic forecast models are evaluated as Kelly bettors with bankroll share as Bayesian credibility: Kelly with existing bets f = p − ((1−p)/o)(1 + w/b) (w = win shares, b = bankroll), binary market-clearing probability m = Σ pᵢbᵢ / (1 − Σ pᵢwᵢ), multinomial update wᵢ′ = (pᵢ/mᵢ) Σₖ mₖwₖ, and multinomial market-clearing m = eigenvector of pwᵀ with eigenvalue 1 (PageRank analogy) — shown identical to Bayes' theorem under the bankroll-as-credibility interpretation.
equation: f = p − ((1−p)/o)(1 + w/b); m = Σ pᵢbᵢ / (1 − Σ pᵢwᵢ); wᵢ′ = (pᵢ/mᵢ) Σₖ mₖwₖ

claim: Kelly betting identified the correct model more often than averaged log-loss/Brier in simulations: 55.1% vs 49.9% under wrong point probabilities, 96.0% vs 73.1%/80.2% under recency-bias misspecification, 74.4% vs 57.6%/58.3% under a non-predictive random walk; over 110 iterated scenarios Kelly led in 98 (89%) after 5 games, with only 2 scenarios not at least tied after 50 games.

The RAD forecast-trimming algorithm works in stages: (1) full forecaster pool; (2) Tukey's-fences robustness screen dropping forecasters whose absolute-error variance exceeds Q3+1.5·(Q3−Q1); (3–6) backward elimination on ADT(κ=1); (7) stop when the % ADT decrease falls below δ — evaluated with MASE, sMAPE, Bias, MSIS at α=0.05 and MCB significance tests.

A bookmaker pricing online against sequentially arriving Kelly bettors uses stochastic approximation a_{t+1} = a_t + η_t(p̄_t − a_t − G(a_t)) for unfair-odds profit maximization (guarantee E[u_T] ≥ u_t(a♯,b♯) − 7L_u·T^{−1/2}), and Follow-the-Leader with closed-form fair-odds price a⋆ = √(g·E[p_t]) / (√(g·E[p_t]) + √((1−g)(1−E[p_t]))) and regret REGRET(T) = O(√(T log T)).

The core economic result is that bookmaker profit hinges on the deviation between bettors' belief distribution and true beliefs — heavier tails in bettor beliefs imply higher profit — and that profit-maximization and information-elicitation are fundamentally incompatible for the market maker.

On ~588M Polymarket trades, the sign of longshot returns depends on the aggregation unit: with equal child-market weights longshots returned −6.30% [−8.38,−4.22]% and favorites +0.277% [0.242,0.312]%; pooled dollar-weighted purchases gave longshots −19.35% [−46.99,+8.30]% and favorites +0.83% [0.60,1.07]%; equal parent-event weights gave longshots +4.09% [1.29,6.90]% and favorites +0.392% [0.345,0.440]% — the measured tail return flips sign with the aggregation scheme.

Sports markets show no two-sided favorite-longshot bias: Sports longshots returned +2.43% [−0.93,5.79]% and favorites −0.230% under equal child-market weights, and pooled longshots +18.11% [−74.68,110.91]% with a huge confidence interval — a hard caution against importing generic longshot/favorite corrections into NFL moneyline modeling.

MOVDA is an Elo-style rating update that adds a margin-surprise term to the standard outcome-surprise update: expected margin E_MOV = α·tanh(β·ΔR) + γ + δ·I_HA (rating gap plus home indicator), surprise margin ΔMOV = TMOV − E_MOV, and rating update R'_A = R_A + K·(S_A − E_A) + λ·ΔMOV.
equation: E_MOV = α·tanh(β·ΔR) + γ + δ·I_HA; ΔMOV = TMOV − E_MOV; R'_A = R_A + K·(S_A − E_A) + λ·ΔMOV

claim: MOVDA's reported results (63.32 accuracy / 0.2258 Brier / 166 convergence games on 13,619 NBA games, beating Elo 62.77/0.2274/193, Glicko-2 63.18/0.2264/189, TrueSkill 62.66/0.2294/192) are untrustworthy: the ablation table contradicts the main table (63.24/0.2259), the abstract's '1.54% lower Brier, 0.58 pp higher accuracy vs TrueSkill' does not reproduce from its own table (1.57%/0.66pp), and '34 teams' appear in a 30-team league — adopt the method from the equations, never the numbers.

Ledger 1471 is a REJECT-as-duplicate entry for arXiv:0903.2910v1, already deep-read as ledger 1368 with an ADAPT verdict (dynamic Kelly fraction f*_t = R^{−1}c_t for mean-reverting log-price drift dx_t = (a − b x_t)dt + σdW_t, one-asset f*_t = (μ_t − r)/σ², and the estimation-sensitivity rule that 1% σ-error ≈ 2% drift-error); nothing new to intake, do not double-count.

H-scoring is a dynamic draft algorithm for head-to-head fantasy category leagues that re-optimizes strategy parameters per candidate pick via gradient descent: category-total differential X(j) = N(Xs + Xp + Xδ − XOm, 2N + (N−K−1)Xσ²), category win probabilities wc = ½[1 + erf(μ/(σ√2))], and objectives (Each Category V = Σc wc; Most Categories V = win-scenario product sum) optimized with Adam, jC re-normalized to sum 1.
equation: X(j) = N(Xs + Xp + Xδ − XOm, 2N + (N−K−1)Xσ²); wc = ½[1 + erf(μ/(σ√2))]

claim: Across 20 simulated NBA fantasy seasons (1,000 simulated seasons per draft seat), H-scoring achieved a 21.8% mean season-win rate (vs 8.3% random-chance) in Each Category and 37.7% in Most Categories; category punting emerged as learned behavior (~20% of category weights below 0.95, ~1–2 soft-punted categories); and turnovers were NOT down-weighted by default — gradient analysis showed turnovers ≈ as important as other counting stats, contrary to analyst folk wisdom.

In 1,660 Danish schoolchildren (286,536 child-weeks), a GAMM of acute:chronic workload ratio found injury risk ~3% for ACWR 0.8–1.5, minimum 1.5% at ACWR=0 (RR 0.5 vs ACWR=1), maximum 6% at ACWR=5 (RR 2.2) — 'only doubled despite a quintupling of activity' — but the pediatric musculoskeletal-pain outcome and session-count load have no NFL analogue, so the paper is REJECTed for player-availability modeling.

SUMMIR is a pipeline that scrapes sports news, extracts categorized insights, gates them against hallucination (FactScore + SummaC NLI), and ranks them with a PPO-fine-tuned permutation policy: ScoreNet weights w = softmax(ℓ), f_ℓ(x) = Σ_{j=1..6} w_j x_j; reward R = σ(0.7·N_gold + 0.3·N_SN) over NDCG_k = DCG/IDCG with DCG_k(p,r) = Σ_{t=1..k} (2^{r_{pt}}−1)/log2(t+1); PPO fine-tunes Llama 3.2 1B (lr 2e-5, target_kl 0.2).
equation: w = softmax(ℓ), f_ℓ(x) = Σ_{j=1..6} w_j x_j; R = σ(0.7·N_gold + 0.3·N_SN); DCG_k(p,r) = Σ_{t=1..k} (2^{r_{pt}}−1)/log2(t+1)

claim: On 281,163 insights across 800 cricket/soccer/basketball/baseball matches, SUMMIR reached NDCG@10 0.943 and Recall@10 0.960, beating NDCG-only (0.911/0.920) and Recall-only (0.910/0.860) rewards; GPT-4o was the best extractor (FactScore 95–97%, SummaC 60–72%); emotional intensity and named-entity popularity drove most ranking gain, and LLM gold labels were a noted noise source.

Enforcing tail calibration in probabilistic forecast training adds threshold-weighted CRPS (twCRPS = ∫[F−1{y≤x}]²w(x)dx with w(z)=1{z>t}) to the loss as CRPS+γ·twCRPS (a strictly proper sum), or adds a TMCB tail-miscalibration penalty (TMCB = ∫|R̂_t(u)−u|du, where R̂_t decomposes into exceedance-occurrence ratio Ô and CPIT uniformity).

On UK wind forecasts, twCRPS gave ~+45–49% tail-calibration skill with ≤0.15% overall CRPS loss across EMOS/DRN/CGM, while the TMCB penalty won bigger on the tail (+65%) but wrecked overall calibration (−187% MCB on EMOS); penalizing CPIT-uniformity alone 'severely deteriorates' all metrics by over-predicting extremes, and penalties can hurt already-tail-calibrated models.

A Bayesian spatial probit for goal conversion on MLS 2016/17 shots models r = Xθ + Az + w + e with Y_i = I(r_i>0), player random effects z ~ N(0, σ_p²I), and spatially correlated errors Cov(w_i,w_j) = σ_w² exp(−φ‖s_i−s_j‖), then decomposes player output into Shooting Prowess SP_k = posterior mean of z_k and Positioning Sense PS_k = (1/g_k) Σ p̂_i.
equation: r = Xθ + Az + w + e; Y_i = I(r_i>0); Cov(w_i,w_j) = σ_w² exp(−φ‖s_i−s_j‖); SP_k = posterior mean of z_k

claim: The spatial probit cut Brier ~30–33% and log score ~34–38% versus baselines with AUCs 0.937–0.952 vs ~0.75–0.79 — but the file flags these AUCs as suspicious (likely in-sample fit inflation); spatial correlation was effectively zero beyond ~4 yards for headers and ~6.7 yards for other shots.

Cricket player scores versus a specific opponent are modeled as Gamma(α,β) with α = Average/β and β chosen from 50,000 candidates in [0.01,5000] such that P(X > Highest score) ≤ 0.05; team win probability is the fraction of 10,000 Monte Carlo replications won.
equation: Runs ~ Gamma(α,β): α = Average/β; P(X > Highest score) ≤ 0.05; win prob = fraction of 10,000 Monte Carlo replications won

claim: Predicting IPL 2020 entirely from 2008–2019 data got the first three table positions 100% correct and 4 of the top 5, with title odds Mumbai Indians 73%, Delhi Capitals 27% (actual: Mumbai beat Delhi); adversarial notes: no posterior inference despite the title (moment/tail matching instead), batting only, and the 5% tail rule and β grid are arbitrary.

Regularized Ensemble Forecasting (REF) finds ensemble weights w* = argmin_w f(Σᵢ wᵢ²(µᵢ−E[µ])²) + λΦ(w) with Σwᵢ=1, wᵢ≥0, where Φ is an L2 penalty toward historical-performance priors Σ(wᵢ−sᵢ)² or an entropy penalty Σsᵢlog(1/wᵢ), λ from rolling validation; Theorem 1 gives MSPE = O(1/k)+σy², the same asymptotic rate as the simple mean.
equation: w* = argmin_w f(Σᵢ wᵢ²(µᵢ−E[µ])²) + λΦ(w), Σwᵢ=1, wᵢ≥0; MSPE = O(1/k)+σy²

claim: REF ranked 1st at every expert pool size on the M5 competition (+2.26% at k=5 → +6.22% at k=50 over the Simple Mean, best RMSSE 0.335 at k=15, p<0.001) and 1st on all three Survey of Professional Forecasters indicators (NGDP +4.08%, UNEMP +5.73%, CPI +2.53%); history-only weighting alone underperformed the Simple Mean in 8/9 SPF cases, yet REF still won by balancing both sources.

A two-tank Critical Power/Anaerobic Work Capacity fatigue model uses AWC = (P−CP)·Δt with depletion dW/dt = −(P−CP) for P>CP and recovery dW/dt = −(P_adj−CP) for P<CP with the experimentally fitted recovery law P_adj = aP+b, plus a concave quadratic max-power envelope P_max(t) = a₁W²(t) + a₂W(t) + CP; dynamic programming over a 32-velocity × 100-energy grid then yields the optimal pacing policy.
equation: AWC = (P−CP)·Δt; dW/dt = −(P−CP) for P>CP; dW/dt = −(P_adj−CP) for P<CP; P_adj = aP+b; P_max(t) = a₁W²(t) + a₂W(t) + CP

claim: For subject 9 (CP=234 W, AWC=9758 J), the DP-optimal policy beat the subject's own 10.3 km time-trial strategy 38:15 vs 41:17 (≈7.3% improvement) by inserting low-power recovery intervals the subject never used; recovery was slower than expenditure (a<1) and the max-power envelope was concave (a₁<0).

Projectile motion with quadratic drag R=mgkV² (k=1/V_term²) in constant horizontal wind is solved in closed elementary-function form by working in the wind-relative frame u⃗=V⃗−w⃗: the hodograph V(θ)=V0cosθ0/[cosθ·√(1+kV0²cos²θ0(f(θ0)−f(θ)))] with f(θ)=sinθ/cos²θ+ln tan(θ/2+π/4), plus explicit −(w/g)∫u/cosφ dφ drift terms.

The analytic formulas deviate at most 1% from 4th-order Runge-Kutta integration at any trajectory point across golf, tennis, and shuttlecock parameters with k spanning a 22× range — but only for constant horizontal wind (no gusts, swirl, vertical component, or Magnus lift).

Snow depth follows a physics-structured zero-inflated gamma regression: E(D_t|D_t>0)=e^μ + R_t·β₀·logit⁻¹(β₁+β₂T_t) + D_{t−1}·logit⁻¹(β₃+(β₄+β₅R_t)T_t) with variance scaling with expected CHANGE (Var=σ₁²+σ₂²(E−D_{t−1})², not level) and zero-probability P(D_t=0)=logit⁻¹(β₆+β₇·E); the standard constant-CV gamma was rejected as 'very poor'.

On three Norwegian locations (leave-one-year-out CV), 5-day-ahead MAE was 3–7 cm and 3-week-ahead 7–16 cm — roughly half the seasonal-trend-only baseline error — with ~uniform PIT histograms; Oslo's shallow intermittent pack (the NFL-stadium-like regime) had the largest relative errors.

A two-stage CRF event-selection → pointer-generator pipeline on 3,454 Finnish ice-hockey games reached CRF event-selection F-score 67.1% (end result 98.0%, goal 70.2%, penalty 20.1%, save 47.7%), test BLEU 19.67 / ROUGE-L 0.42, 84.7% of 510 events factually error-free, and journalist editing WER of 5.6% (annotator) to 22.0%/24.4% (direct machine-labeled publication) — 75–90% of generated text directly usable.

The key methodological finding is that models tuned by BLEU produced MORE fluent but MORE factually wrong text, so hyperparameters were hand-tuned for factuality balance instead — content models must be optimized and selected on factual-error rate, never BLEU alone; only ~34% of hockey events were alignable to text.

From a game-theoretic model of buyer/seller with uniformly distributed noisy beliefs (P_B,P_S ∼ U(L,H), L=P_T−E, H=P_T+E, E=ε·min(1−P_T,P_T)), zero-expectation odds must deviate from 1/P_C — longer than reciprocal when consensus P_C > 0.5, shorter when P_C < 0.5 — producing the favorite-longshot bias as an equilibrium of a fair market with no behavioral assumptions; Turing's weight-of-evidence map is P_{h1}=1/(10^{−WOE_{h1}}+1).

The seller's mean expected margin is negative for all true probabilities and noise levels (fair only at ε=0 or P_T=1), with maximum-unfairness point π̄_{So2}=ln(1−w_1)/w_1+1=−0.39 at w_1=1/2, ε=1, P_T→1/2; as market size grows ε→0 and the bias vanishes — the effect matters most in thin markets.

A drawdown-modulated feedback stake-scaling rule I(k)=γ·M(k)·V(k) with modulator M(k)=(dmax−d(k))/(1−d(k)) and drawdown d(k) = 1 − V(k)/max_{j≤k} V(j) shrinks positions to zero as drawdown approaches the cap, guaranteeing percentage drawdown ≤ dmax almost surely under bounded returns while keeping most of Kelly's growth.
equation: M(k) = (dmax−d(k))/(1−d(k)); I(k) = γ·M(k)·V(k); d(k) = 1 − V(k)/max_{j≤k} V(j)

claim: On TSLA data (dmax=.05, optimal γ*≈11.15 from 100,000 Monte Carlo paths over 60 returns), the modulated rule gave terminal wealth ≈1.005×10⁴ at drawdown ≈.05 versus classical Kelly ≈1.136×10⁴ at drawdown ≈.225 — about 12% less terminal wealth for a 5% vs 22.5% drawdown cap; the bounded-returns assumption does the heavy lifting.

A Serie A study (1,140 matches, 2011/12–2013/14) hand-coded an offensiveness index s = defenders×1 + midfielders×2 + forwards×3 (range 10–30) and estimated its effect on win probability with triple-outcome GLMs (OLS on goal difference, logit on home win, ordered logit P(y≤h)=g(π_h−Xθ)) with HC3 SEs, 1000-replicate nonparametric bootstrap BCa CIs, and Akaike-weight model averaging.

An aggressive opening raised win probability ≈9.44–16.17% (BCa, at the mean): initial scheme +0.30 goal diff (p<0.001) but final scheme −0.25 (p<0.001); crosses cost −0.01 per goal-diff unit (p<0.001), red cards −1.06 goal diff (p<0.001), and the stadium-filling index was insignificant at all powers (p>0.85) — the authors are unusually explicit about the coach-selection endogeneity problem.

A large-scale benchmark (Google Research, NeurIPS 2019) evaluated calibration under dataset shift with the Brier decomposition BS = |Y|⁻¹Σ_y(p(y|x,θ) − δ(y−y_n))² = |Y|⁻¹(1 − 2p(y_n|x,θ) + Σ_y p(y|x,θ)²) and ECE = Σ_b |acc_b − conf_b|·(n_b/n) over confidence bins, comparing vanilla, temperature scaling, MC-dropout, deep ensembles, and SVI across image, text, and ad-click modalities.
equation: BS = |Y|⁻¹Σ_y(p(y|x,θ) − δ(y−y_n))² = |Y|⁻¹(1 − 2p(y_n|x,θ) + Σ_y p(y|x,θ)²); ECE = Σ_b |acc_b − conf_b|·(n_b/n)

claim: Temperature scaling FAILS under shift — on Criteo it had a WORSE Brier score than vanilla softmax, so post-hoc calibration validated on i.i.d. data can actively harm calibration under shift; deep ensembles were consistently best across metrics and modalities (most gains with only 5 models), while last-layer dropout/SVI often scored worse than vanilla on shifted/OOD data.

Partially-factorized mean-field VB (PFM-VB) for dynamic probit smoothing uses the augmented model z_t = x_t'θ_t + ε_t (ε_t ~ N(0,1)), y_t = 1(z_t > 0), θ_t = Gθ_{t-1} + η_t (η_t ~ N(0,W)) — keeping the exact state|augmentation conditional via a Kalman smoother and factorizing only the truncated-normal marginals, since exact smoothing is a closed-form unified skew-normal with an intractable T-dimensional truncated-normal CDF.

On CAC40 daily opening direction (n=241), PFM-VB posterior-mean MAE versus exact sampling was 0.003/0.008 (θ_1/θ_2) versus 0.009/0.031 for full mean-field (~3–4× more accurate), with log-posterior-SD error 0.04/0.05 versus 0.14/0.16 (full MF over-shrinks uncertainty), and runtime 1.1 s versus 115.4 s for the exact sampler (~105× speedup).

BayesBlend is a pip-installable Python package for Bayesian model averaging/stacking with pseudo-BMA weights w_k = exp(elpd̂^k_{psis-loo}) / Σ_{k'} exp(elpd̂^{k'}_{psis-loo}), complete-pooling stacking ŵ = argmax_w Σ_i log Σ_k w_k p(y_i|y_{−i},M_k), and hierarchical (covariate-dependent) stacking w*_{ik} = α_k + β_k x_i with (β_1…β_K) ~ Normal(μ,σ) — the only implementation with Bayesian weight inference, hierarchical stacking, and a blend/predict step that loo/ArviZ lack.
equation: w_k = exp(elpd̂^k_{psis-loo}) / Σ_{k'} exp(elpd̂^{k'}_{psis-loo}); ŵ = argmax_w Σ_i log Σ_k w_k p(y_i|y_{−i},M_k); w*_{ik} = α_k + β_k x_i

claim: Hierarchical stacking achieved the highest blended ELPD on a drifting toy Bernoulli; on insurance loss development Bayesian stacking was best with hierarchical slightly better than non-hierarchical while pseudo-BMA performed WORSE than the best candidate; on leave-future-out loss forecasting only pseudo-BMA+ and MLE stacking beat the best single candidate (test-data winners don't generalize — blending lands close to the out-of-sample best without knowing it in advance).

Using inverse-propensity weighting (treated 1/π̂(X), control 1/(1−π̂(X)), propensity trimmed to [0.1,0.9]) on Retrosheet data for tied extra innings with the ghost runner, the causal odds ratio for bunting versus swinging away was 1.86 (95% CI 1.07–3.27) versus a crude OR of 2.13 (1.13–4.30) — bunting still significantly raises home win odds after adjusting for batter OPS, sac-bunt rate, and pitcher ERA.

Despite the edge, teams bunted in only 21% of such plate appearances (worth ~2 wins/season); bunters had more bunt experience while non-bunters were better hitters (higher OPS), and pitcher ERA did not differ — the IPW template ports directly to NFL coaching-strategy questions like fair-catch versus return on kickoffs.

Baseball flight follows v̇ = −g + (D+L)/m with drag D = −½ρ C_D A v² v̂ and lift L = −½ρ C_L A v² (v̂×ω̂_b); Denver's air density ρ = 0.91809 kg/m³ vs 1.0793 at sea level means ~15% less drag acceleration — the physics template for an altitude-adjusted FG/punt kicking model.
equation: v̇ = −g + (D+L)/m; D = −½ρ C_D A v² v̂; L = −½ρ C_L A v² (v̂×ω̂_b)

claim: Comparing 7 Coors seasons before vs 5 after the humidor against the NL baseline (≈0 NL change): HR/team-game 1.59→1.26 (−0.33), runs/team-game 6.94→5.87 (−1.07), average fly-ball distance 323→318 ft, Rockies ERA 6.14→5.34 (−0.80); only +0.9% extra spin was needed to overcome the aerodynamic break deficit, suggesting grip — not aerodynamics — is the real humidor mechanism.

Energy-efficient under-soil grass heating was evaluated with heating-degree-day normalization HDD = max(T_HDD,base − T̄_external, 0) with base 7°C, weather-normalized energy Q_grass,HDD7 = Q_grass/HDD (zero-HDD days excluded), and robust medians with Student-t or 10,000-replicate bootstrap percentile CIs — a portable, principled way to compare performance across weather regimes.
equation: HDD = max(T_HDD,base − T̄_external, 0), T_HDD,base = 7°C; Q_grass,HDD7 = Q_grass/HDD

claim: Across three winters at Frankfurt's Commerzbank Arena, median daily weather-normalized heating energy fell 66% (95% CI) in 2014/15 and reached 85% savings with predictive nighttime heating in 2015/16, while prior literature established that daily-mean air temperature is the DOMINANT meteorological variable for soil temperature (solar radiation, humidity, wind, precipitation minor) — direct feature-selection evidence for surface/field-condition models.

SportR is a multimodal-LLM sports-reasoning benchmark with progressive QA (infraction ID → foul classification → penalty prediction → explanation → bounding-box grounding with IoU = |pred∩gt|/|pred∪gt| → tactic ID) and an SFT+GRPO training recipe: J_GRPO(θ) = E[min(ρ_i A_i, clip(ρ_i,1−ε,1+ε)A_i) − β·D_KL(π_θ‖π_ref)] with advantage A_i = (r_i−μ_r)/σ_r and reward R(o|q) = 1.0·R_correct + 0.5·R_format.
equation: J_GRPO(θ) = E[min(ρ_i A_i, clip(ρ_i,1−ε,1+ε)A_i) − β·D_KL(π_θ‖π_ref)], A_i = (r_i−μ_r)/σ_r; R(o|q) = 1.0·R_correct + 0.5·R_format

claim: Zero-shot foul classification was hard everywhere (best 44.21) and ALL models scored <7% IoU on visual grounding; the SFT+GRPO-trained 7B model topped 5 of 7 categories (Q2 14.43→51.54, Q1 48.29→84.19); LLM-as-judge panels correlated with humans only at r ≈ 0.65 — too noisy as a sole production metric.

A liquidity-based-utility AMM framework for prediction markets defines the cost C(q) = min{Δx : u(x₀+Δx, y₀−s) ≥ u(x₀,y₀)} with marginal (instantaneous) price oracle π(q) = ∇C(q), bid/ask from one-sided directional derivatives of C, and liquidity add/remove priced at the current marginal oracle so existing LPs aren't diluted.
equation: C(q) = min{Δx : u(x₀+Δx, y₀−s) ≥ u(x₀,y₀)}; π(q) = ∇C(q)

claim: Backtested on Super Bowl LVII moneyline data, the optimal AMM fee was ≈1%, yielding 1–6% expected return over two weeks at tighter spreads than Bookmaker quoted — a 'win-win' where LPs earn fee income minus adverse-selection (loss-versus-rebalancing) cost while takers face a tighter market.

Joint diversification and leverage optimization in a utility framework separates the two knobs as w*_f = f*·w*: exponential (CARA) utility gives diversification weights w* (tractable under fat tails and uncertain covariance via compound distributions), while generalized-mean-variance log-utility gives the leverage scalar via μ = (1−f)r_0 + f μ_r, σ = f σ_r and MEU f* = (μ_r − r_0)/(σ_r² γ), with γ=1 → full Kelly and γ>1 → fractional Kelly.
equation: w = argmax_w (E[U(X|D)] − (λ/2)·Var[U(X|D)]); μ = (1−f)r_0 + f μ_r, σ = f σ_r; MEU f* = (μ_r − r_0)/(σ_r² γ)

claim: GMV log-utility leverage tempering endogenously produces half-Kelly-like behavior via the utility-variance penalty — a principled reason fractional Kelly exists, though only qualitative (no closed-form f*=½; solved numerically); the w*_f = f*·w* separation fills a documented GSE gap where nothing separates relative pick allocation across simultaneous picks from absolute bankroll fraction.

Jointly optimizing TWO correlated DFS lineups to maximize the expected value of the better one has a closed-form Gaussian objective E[max] = μ₁Φ(δ) + μ₂Φ(−δ) + θφ(δ) where δ = (μ₁−μ₂)/θ, θ = √(σ₁² + σ₂² − 2σ₁₂), Φ/φ = standard normal CDF/PDF, solved exactly with a cutting-plane MINLP loop adding cuts η ≤ E[max](x̂) + gᵀ(x−x̂).
equation: E[max] = μ₁Φ(δ) + μ₂Φ(−δ) + θφ(δ), δ = (μ₁−μ₂)/θ, θ = √(σ₁² + σ₂² − 2σ₁₂)

claim: Backtested with real money on 16 DraftKings NFL Showdown contests (2018), the exact E[max] method returned +$5,376 (+55.6% ROI on $9,674 fees) versus −$4,374 (−45.2%) for two independent max-EV lineups — even though the heuristic's EV was 1.19 points HIGHER, the exact method's E[max] objective was 6.68 points higher and its realized best entry outscored the heuristic's by 2.68 points.

Optimal reject-option strategies unify cost-based, bounded-improvement, and bounded-coverage formulations under one Bayes classifier with differing selection rules (bounded-coverage requires a randomized Bayes selection rule); two Fisher-consistent learned uncertainty scores are proposed for black-box predictors: REG regression F_REG(θ) = (C/2)‖θ‖² + (1/n) Σᵢ (ℓ(yᵢ, h(xᵢ)) − s_θ(xᵢ))² with s_θ(x) = ⟨θ, ψ(x)⟩, and SELE pairwise ranking F_SELE(θ) = (C/2)‖θ‖² + (1/P) Σ_p ψ_sele(s, T_n^p).
equation: F_REG(θ) = (C/2)‖θ‖² + (1/n) Σᵢ (ℓ(yᵢ, h(xᵢ)) − s_θ(xᵢ))², s_θ(x) = ⟨θ, ψ(x)⟩; F_SELE(θ) = (C/2)‖θ‖² + (1/P) Σ_p ψ_sele(s, T_n^p)

claim: On 11 classification datasets, average AuRC misclassification ranks were REG 1.09, SELE 2.09, baseline 2.82 (PHISHING: REG 0.72±0.12 vs baseline 6.37±0.44); on 11 ordinal-regression datasets SELE ranked best (1.27) and both beat the predictors' native scores most where the native score was poor — learned pick-gate scores beat probability-threshold gating.

JTSP jointly trains the classifier and the deferral (gate) policy with shared representations plus a policy-gradient loss term directly optimizing the selective-prediction reward (Algorithm 1, line 15); the policy-gradient term alone (JTSP vs the JTSP CE ablation without it) adds a consistent ~0.5–2.5 point gain, and both modules improve — not just the gate.

JTSP beat every post-hoc gate (max-prob threshold, logistic on softmax, separately-trained policy) on all four short-answer assessment datasets with both SFRN and BERT backbones — e.g., BEETLE selective accuracy/F1 85.33/79.63 at 8.20% deferral vs threshold 80.74/72.68 and no-deferral 79.35/70.73.

Pre-match hero-vector models on 1,933 DotA 2 replays (270 pro, 1,663 high-skill public, MMR >> 6000) achieved 58.75% accuracy on mixed-skill matches (logistic regression + wrapper selection) and 55.75% on pro matches (random forest + wrapper), versus in-game models up to 76.17% — hero/draft features alone are far less predictive than in-game features.
Hero vector encoding used in the DotA 2 match-prediction study: x_i = 1 if hero i is on Radiant, -1 if on Dire, 0 otherwise — a 113-dimensional tri-state representation of both drafts.
equation: x_i = 1 if hero i in Radiant, -1 if in Dire, 0 otherwise (113-dimensional tri-state)

claim: Per-minute in-game models M_t were trained on 5-minute sliding windows X_{rt} = {x_{i,t-4}, ..., x_{i,t}}, with 30 features per timestamp expressed as Dire, Radiant, R-D difference, and gradient forms.

The optimal algorithm class flipped between data tiers: pro in-game matches were best predicted by single-feature logistic regression on kill differential (75.22% accuracy), while mixed-skill in-game matches were best predicted by random forest + CFS (76.17%) — evidence the best model class can differ between regular and elite tiers.

Mixed-skill training data predicted held-out pro matches (Kiev Major, 113 matches) with only a small accuracy drop versus mixed-on-mixed (in-game 75.22 vs 76.17), showing abundant high-skill proxy data can substitute for scarce elite data; wrapper selection beat CFS on hero data while CFS beat wrapper on correlated in-game features.

The Bayesian partial-membership (PM) model for count data uses likelihood p(x_i|pi_i, Lambda) = product over j of Poisson(x_ij; product over k of lambda_kj^{pi_ik}) with pi_i ~ Dirichlet(delta), delta = 1, giving players interpretable fractional role assignments (a playmaker can be part-midfielder, part-attacker) distinct from uncertainty about a single role.
equation: p(x_i|pi_i, Lambda) = Prod_j Poisson(x_ij; Prod_k lambda_kj^{pi_ik}); pi_i ~ Dirichlet(delta), delta = 1

claim: In simulation, marginalized WAIC (WAICm) recovered the true number of profiles K=4 in 99/100 runs versus 79/100 for conditional WAIC, making WAICm the more reliable model-selection criterion for partial-membership models.

On 200 Serie A 2022/23 players with 22 count variables, the PM model selected 4 profiles — strikers (goals 20.91, shots 111.62), full-backs/dynamic mids (progressive carries 103.65, tackles 89.44), center-backs (clearances 133.32), goalkeepers — with true archetypes (Osimhen membership ~1.0), while mixed-membership capped at 0.565-0.686 membership with no true archetypes.
Model-fitting runtimes for K=2..8 on a MacBook Air M3 16GB: partial-membership 10.6h, mixed-membership 14.7h, finite mixture 7.3h.

Deep Symbolic Regression trains an autoregressive RNN emitting expression trees with a risk-seeking policy gradient that optimizes the conditional expectation of the top-epsilon quantile of rewards (best-case, not average-case): J_risk(theta; epsilon) = E_{tau ~ p(tau|theta)}[R(tau) | R(tau) >= R_epsilon(theta)], where R_epsilon is the (1-epsilon)-quantile of rewards under the current policy.
equation: J_risk(theta; epsilon) = E_{tau~p(tau|theta)}[R(tau) | R(tau) >= R_epsilon(theta)], R_epsilon = (1-epsilon)-quantile of rewards under current policy

claim: The risk-seeking policy gradient estimator: grad J_risk = E[(R(tau) - R_epsilon(theta)) * grad log p(tau|theta) | R(tau) >= R_epsilon(theta)], Monte-Carlo estimated as (1/(epsilon*N)) * sum_i [R(tau^(i)) - R_tilde_epsilon(theta)] * 1_{R(tau^(i)) >= R_tilde_epsilon(theta)} * grad log p(tau^(i)|theta) — only the top-epsilon fraction of each batch contributes, with a theoretically-prescribed quantile baseline, mirroring CVaR flipped to the risk-seeking side.
equation: grad_theta J_risk = E[(R(tau) - R_epsilon(theta)) . grad_theta log p(tau|theta) | R(tau) >= R_epsilon(theta)]; MC estimate (1/epsilon N) sum_i [R(tau^(i)) - R_tilde_epsilon(theta)] . 1_{R(tau^(i))>=R_tilde_epsilon(theta)} grad_theta log p(tau^(i)|theta)

claim: Deep Symbolic Regression significantly outperformed PQT, VPG, GP, Eureqa, and Wolfram on exact recovery across the 12-expression Nguyen benchmark suite (p < 10^-3), and beat all baselines at every Gaussian noise level, while Wolfram 'catastrophically fails for even the smallest noise level'.
On the harmonic series, DSR recovered the novel formula H_n ~ gamma + log(n) + 1/(2n) + 1/(11.3776n + 15.725) + 0.327981 with gamma ~ 0.57721 — a novel variant of Euler's 1755 expansion.

In-situ constraint masking enforces token constraints (arity, no nested trig, length limits, constant placement, no redundant subtrees) during expression generation rather than post-hoc, and ablations showed both the risk-seeking objective and in-situ constraints improve exact recovery.

Vertical Symbolic Regression replaces one-shot 'horizontal' search over all variables with control-variable experiments CvExp(phi, v_c, v_f, {T_k}_{k=1}^K): controlled variables v_c are fixed within each trial but varied across K trials while free variables v_f are random; each round learns a reduced form over 1-2 free variables, then extends: phi_{r+1} = extend(phi_r, new free variables).
equation: CvExp(phi, v_c, v_f, {T_k}_{k=1}^K); phi_{r+1} = extend(phi_r, new free variables)

claim: With v_c fixed, a ground truth like phi = x1*x3 - x2*x4 appears as a reduced form phi' = C1*x1 - C2; open constants are fit per trial by BFGS (500 iterations), and how those constants vary across trials reveals the next variable's role.
equation: phi = x1*x3 - x2*x4; reduced form phi' = C1*x1 - C2

claim: On the {sin,cos,+,-,x} operator set at complexity (3,2,2), VSR-MCTS achieved 100% exact recovery (R^2 >= 0.999) versus 20% for standard MCTS (8 vs 249 minutes, 61 vs 191 MB); the paper's theory (Section 5) proves VSR's search space is exponentially smaller than horizontal search for a class of expressions.

Interaction information for a feature pair is tau_ij = I(F_i; F_j; Y) = I(F_i; F_j | Y) - I(F_i; F_j) = H(F_i,F_j) + H(F_j,Y) + H(F_i,Y) - H(F_i) - H(F_j) - H(Y) - H(F_i,F_j,Y), interpretable as I(F_i; Y | F_j) - I(F_i; Y): the synergy a feature adds beyond its isolated effect.
equation: tau_ij = I(F_i; F_j; Y) = I(F_i; F_j | Y) - I(F_i; F_j) = H(F_i,F_j) + H(F_j,Y) + H(F_i,Y) - H(F_i) - H(F_j) - H(Y) - H(F_i,F_j,Y)

claim: IIFE took 10 top ranks with average rank 2.50 across public benchmarks (vs OpenFE 3.38, EAAFE 3.13, AutoFeat 3.08, DIFER 3.75, baseline 4.46), and IIFE+logistic-regression landed within 4.99% of tuned random forest — explainable linear models reaching near-nonlinear performance.

AutoFE literature hygiene audit: reporting cross-validation as the final metric inflates gains from 21.03% to 15.33% on holdout, and OpenFE's transductive groupby-then-* leakage inflates airfoil results by +14.01% and jungle chess by +1.95%.

The IIFE loop: (1) compute interaction information for all pairs O(|F|^2); (2) take the K highest-tau pairs times a bivariate-function set B, evaluate by parallel CV, keep the argmax; (3) apply univariate transforms to the winner; (4) add it to the pool and repeat with II computed only against the new feature O(|F|); stop when the mean of the recent P/2 CV scores is <= the mean of the previous P/2 (K=3, patience P=20/40).

Masked Trajectory Models tokenize trajectories as z_t^m = E_theta^m(x_t^m), flattened to sequence length N = M x T with sinusoidal timestep and learnable modality embeddings, and pretrain by maximizing E_tau sum_t sum_m log P_theta(z_t^m | Masked(tau)) (MSE implementation = Gaussian likelihood).
equation: z_t^m = E_theta^m(x_t^m), N = M x T; max_theta E_tau sum_t sum_m log P_theta(z_t^m | Masked(tau))

claim: MTM uses random-autoregressive masking: random masks with the constraint that at least one masked token has no future unmasked tokens (the last element of each sampled segment is necessarily masked).

One set of MTM weights serves zero-shot as forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, imitation policy, offline RL agent, or representation extractor — selected only by the inference-time masking pattern; on D4RL V2 it outperformed Decision Transformer and RvS and was competitive with specialized CQL and IQL despite purely self-supervised training.

Heteromodal MTM consistently beat MLP and action-labeled-only MTM, with the largest gap in low-data regimes — but only via a two-stage inference procedure: (1) predict future states from current state plus desired returns, (2) predict actions from current plus predicted future states; naive state-only mixing without the two-stage step did not always help.

MTM representations transferred to downstream TD3 on ExORL: Walk reached or exceeded asymptotic raw-state TD3 performance within 10% of the training budget, and state-action representations beat state-only representations on Run.

The PU-index is u_i = 1 - f_{y_i}(x_i): the probability mass the classifier assigns to everything except the true class. Theorems show identical PU-index histograms across two windows imply identical error rates and error standard deviations, while the converse is false — so the PU-index is provably at least as sensitive as error rate and fires while accuracy is still flat.

The PUDD detector slides windows with antiquated-data discard, buckets PU-index values with adaptive Ei-kMeans (k init 5, misclassified instances forced into one extra bin), and alarms via Pearson chi-square chi^2 = sum_i sum_j (T_ij^2/E_ij) - sum_i sum_j T_ij on a 2x(K+1) table when p < 10^(-X).
equation: chi^2 = sum sum (T_ij^2/E_ij) - sum sum T_ij

claim: PUDD ranked 1st in 17 of 24 dataset-by-classifier cases (top-3 in 20/24) against 7 classic and 5 state-of-the-art drift detectors; on airline incremental it scored 63.35 vs ADWIN 61.65 vs DDM 61.29, and PUDD-5 reached 98.49% accuracy, 2.8 points above the best SOTA on one dataset.

PUDD requires labels at detection time (u_i needs the true y_i), so it cannot do unsupervised pre-event detection — but it is valid for monitoring resolved weekly outcomes; and on the 679-feature airline dataset, tree ensembles that adapt rather than retrain (NS, ADLTER) beat PUDD.
FtaT adapts a trained tabular model at test time via a weighted-entropy loss: theta_{t+1} = argmin_theta sum_i W(x_i, D_t, theta_t) . Loss(f_hat_{theta_t}(x_i)).

FtaT's Confident Distribution Optimizer corrects label shift by post-processing predictions: f_hat_{theta_{t+1}}(x_k) = f_{theta_{t+1}}(x_k) o P_hat_t / P_0, where the shifted label distribution P_tilde_t is estimated from low-entropy predictions only (Entropy(f_hat(x_i)) < epsilon), debiased with the confusion matrix inverse C_hat_t^{-1}, and temporally smoothed.
equation: f_hat_{theta_{t+1}}(x_k) = f_{theta_{t+1}}(x_k) o P_hat_t / P_0 (Eq. 2); P_tilde_t = sum_i 1[Entropy(f_hat(x_i)) < epsilon] . f_hat(x_i) / sum_i 1[.] (Eq. 3)

claim: FtaT's Local Consistent Weighter assigns per-sample weight W = [max f_hat(x_k) - min f_hat(x_k)] . I(x_k, D_t, theta_t), where the consistency indicator I = 1 if ||f(x_k) - mean neighborhood prediction|| < beta, with neighborhood N(x_k, D_t) = {x : Dist(x, x_k) < mean pairwise Dist} (L2) — no augmentation needed.
equation: W = [max f_hat(x_k) - min f_hat(x_k)] . I(x_k, D_t, theta_t) (Eq. 6-8); I = 1 if ||f(x_k) - mean neighborhood prediction|| < beta

claim: On 6 TableShift benchmarks x 3 backbones, FtaT was best everywhere: MLP averaged 66.77/64.96/72.00 (Acc/BalAcc/F1) vs non-adaptation 62.45/64.61/60.59; naive FTTA actively hurt tabular models (TENT 58.43 MLP accuracy, worse than baseline; ODS collapsed to 43.10 vs 54.37 baseline on HELOC); stronger augmentation monotonically degraded CoTTA 60.46 -> 54.74 on DIABETE.

FtaT ablation showed removing the label-shift corrector hurt more than removing the neighborhood weighter (label shift is the bigger problem), and the Dynamic Model Ensembler (4 learning rates weighted by w_i proportional to 1 - R^i_t(D_t)) matched the best single tuned learning rate without tuning.
The TNP-KR KRBlock update is v'_i = sum_j K(q_i, k_j) / sum_m K(q_i, k_m) v_j — Nadaraya-Watson kernel-regression attention (Eq. 3).

Kernel-biased attention adds a learned RBF-network kernel bias on index sets: K(q,k,s_q,s_k) = SM(q^T k / sqrt(d_k) + sum_i alpha_i K_i(s_q,s_k)), with K(s,s') = sum_k a_k exp(-|b_k| (||s-s'||_2 - c_k)^2) using 5 learnable basis functions (Eq. 4).
equation: K(q,k,s_q,s_k) = SM(q^T k/sqrt(d_k) + sum_i alpha_i K_i(s_q,s_k)) (Eq. 4); K(s,s') = sum_k a_k exp(-|b_k| (||s-s'||_2 - c_k)^2)

claim: TNP-KR proposes enforcing temporal causality through the attention bias as K_t = -infinity whenever s_k(t) > s_q(t) (Eq. 5) — flagged as future work, not explored in the paper.
equation: K_t = -infinity when s_k(t) > s_q(t) (Eq. 5, proposed future work)

claim: On 1D GP (RBF) meta-regression, TNP-KR:DKA achieved NLL -0.464 +/- 0.002 (best) and SA -0.462, both below TNP-D and ConvCNP at -0.454 (paired p <= 0.039); on 2D GP, SA 0.460 +/- 0.002 vs ConvCNP 0.466 (p <= 0.002).

Scan Attention's translation-invariance headline: extrapolating from 64x64 training to 1024x1024 grids, SA scored NLL 0.307 +/- 0.006 while DKA hit 1.144 and NP/CNP collapsed to 27.2 (others OOM); SA processes 100K context points on 1M+ test points in under a minute on a single 24GB GPU.

In 1D Bayesian optimization, ConvCNP had the best regret (0.007 +/- 0.002) via better mean plus wider bounds under Expected Improvement — switching EI to UCB 'erased' the gap — a caution that better NLL sharpness does not imply better calibration.

The paper's unifying frame: every distributional-RL algorithm is a statistical estimator (a set of statistics of the return distribution) plus an imputation strategy (a rule generating a distribution consistent with those statistics), where statistics take the form s(mu) = E_{Z~mu}[h(Z)].

Theorem 4.3 (Bellman-closedness characterization): the only finite sets of statistics of the form s(mu) = E[h(Z)] that are exactly learnable via Bellman updates are those whose linear span equals the span of moment functionals {mu -> E_{Z~mu}[Z^l] | l = 0, ..., L} for some L <= K.

Lemma 4.4: C51 (CDRL) and QR-DQN (QDRL) statistic sets are NOT Bellman closed — 'the learnt values of statistics ... need not correspond exactly to the true underlying values for the MDP (even in tabular settings)'.

On a 5-state MDP with exponential terminal reward distributions, both CDRL and QDRL learned a sub-optimal greedy policy 'due to a lack of mean consistency' (C51: true support outside the [0,2] bins; QR-DQN: quantiles miss the tails), while expectile-based EDRL correctly learned the means of both return distributions and acted optimally.

On Atari-57 (3 seeds), ER-DQN — EDRL update plus QR-DQN-style architecture — substantially improved mean human-normalized score over both QR-DQN and naive ER-DQN without the imputation strategy, using only 11 expectiles versus QR-DQN's 200 quantiles, with per-update SciPy imputation described as low-overhead.

IRIS builds a sample-efficient world model as an autoregressive transformer over discrete tokens: a VQ-VAE-style discrete autoencoder tokenizes observations, a GPT-like transformer models interleaved frame/action/reward tokens, and an actor-critic is trained purely on imagined rollouts — the first method above human-level mean on the Atari 100k benchmark without lookahead search.

IRIS tokenizer: z_t^k = argmin_i ||y_t^k - e_i||_2 with y_t = CNN(x_t) in R^{Kx d} and codebook E in R^{N x d}; autoencoder loss L = ||x-D(z)||_1 + ||sg(E(x))-E(z)||^2_2 + ||sg(E(z))-E(x)||^2_2 + L_perceptual (L1 + VQ commitment + perceptual, straight-through estimator).

IRIS hyperparameters (Table 3): L=20 timesteps, embedding dim D=256, M=10 transformer layers, 4 attention heads, weight decay 0.01, embedding/attention dropout 0.1; RL objective maximize E_pi[sum_{t>=0} gamma^t r_t] with pi trained exclusively on imagined trajectories.

IRIS achieved mean human-normalized score 1.046, median 0.289, superhuman on 10 of 26 Atari games (5 seeds) — next-best mean in the table 0.616 with 6 superhuman games — surpassing SimPLe, DER, OTRainbow, DrQ, SPR, and CURL variants.

Paper-stated transfer insight: plays are already discrete tokens (play type, formation, result), so the VQ-VAE tokenizer problem disappears for football — the token-LM framing is arguably more natural for NFL than for Atari; limitations: VQ codebook collapse brittleness, weak long-horizon sparse-reward games, policy trained for control not unbiased simulation.
FootBots uses a Set Attention Block (SAB, Lee et al.): a transformer encoder block WITHOUT positional encoding over the agent set, giving permutation equivariance for varying player compositions.
equation: SAB: transformer encoder block without positional encoding over the agent set

claim: FootBots encoder applies sequentially decoupled attention: FFN + temporal positional encoding -> SAB_T (temporal dynamics) -> SAB_S (social interactions) -> context tensor C, cheaper than joint temporal-social attention; standard multi-head attention MHA: softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V.

FootBots' Conditioned Motion Prediction (CMP) predicts a subset of agents given known/predicted futures of others: CMP: f(X^P_{0:t} | X^C), with variants — predict players given ball; offense given ball+defense; defense given ball+offense; ball given all players — and decoder input H = C_{t-T:t} for MP vs H = FFN(X^C_{t+1:t+T}) union C^P_{t-T:t} for CMP.
equation: CMP: f(X^P_{0:t} | X^C); decoder H = C_{t-T:t} (MP); H = FFN(X^C_{t+1:t+T}) union C^P_{t-T:t} (CMP)

claim: FootBots outperformed non-social RNN, social pooling, GNN+recurrent, GAT+TCN, and prior transformer sports models on LaLiga 2022-2023 tracking data; limitations: ~4s prediction horizon, 2D only with no velocity/acceleration features, and CMP conditions on ground-truth futures while deployment would condition on hypothesized (counterfactual) futures.

ML4C orients edges in a causal skeleton by training a binary classifier (ML4C-Learner) to decide whether each Unshielded Triple (UT: X-Z-Y with X,Y nonadjacent) is a v-structure (X->Z<-Y), using 'latent vicinity' features (neighbors' conditional dependencies + structural entanglement); since v-structures fully determine the CPDAG given the skeleton (Markov completeness), one classifier serves both identifiability-determination and orientation, with v-structures + Meek rules producing the oriented CPDAG.

On the child benchmark network (20 nodes/25 edges), ML4C achieved SHD 0 / UT-level F1 1.0 versus PC 22/0.12, CPC 13/0.12, GMB 9/0.74, GES 15/0.47, GS 13/0.59; on insurance (27/52): ML4C 5/0.89 versus PC 36/0.39, GMB 19/0.76, GES 34/0.46, GS 28/0.56.

ML4C recasts PC and Majority-PC as hand-crafted special-case classifiers of unshielded triples within a discriminative-predicate formalism (weak vs strong predicates, Lemmas 4.2/4.3) and proves asymptotic correctness; it is robust to imperfect skeletons and across sample sizes where CI-test-based methods degrade.

ML4C limitations: discrete data only (sports indicators are continuous — discretization loses information), needs training DAGs (transfer depends on synthetic distribution matching reality), skeleton errors propagate, and it only orients what v-structures + Meek rules can reach — many edges stay undirected, an honest identifiability ceiling.

The paper runs multi-objective NAS+HPO over tabular architectures — MLP (875 combos of layers x widths), ResNet (350 combos), FT-Transformer (324 combos of attention blocks x heads x hidden dims) plus continuous training HPs (learning rate, weight decay, batch size, dropout) — jointly optimizing balanced accuracy plus a fairness metric via weighted mean-aggregation (scalarization) and ParEGO.

Reported claims: (1) 'significant variation and tradeoffs in the accuracy and fairness of the model predictions with changes in hyperparameters — certain subspaces of the search landscape are inherently fairer, more accurate, or both'; (2) joint NAS+HPO 'consistently Pareto dominate[s] state-of-the-art bias mitigation methods either in fairness, accuracy or both' (baselines: Reweighing, Disparate Impact Remover, Learning Fair Representations + LR); (3) 'models optimized solely for accuracy with NAS often fail to inherently address fairness concerns.'

The GSE-transferred warning from this paper: log-loss-only hyperparameter search likely leaves calibration on the table — post-hoc calibration fixes (isotonic, temperature scaling) are exactly the 'debiasing as post-processing' paradigm the paper argues against; instead search architectures that are inherently well-calibrated. Numeric tables were not extractable from the converted text.

The paper replaces the white-box gradient kernel in batch active-learning methods (BADGE, BAIT, BatchBALD, Core-Set, LCMD) with an empirical predictive covariance kernel: k_pred(x_i,x_j) = (1/K) sum_k (mu(x_i;omega_k) - mu-bar(x_i))(mu(x_j;omega_k) - mu-bar(x_j)) — the inner product of centered K-vectors, a valid PSD kernel — making them prediction-only methods that work with non-differentiable models like random forests and GBDTs.

Proposition 3.1: the posterior gradient kernel (first-order Taylor around BMA + GGN approximation) approximates the predictive covariance kernel — white-box gradient kernels are just an approximation of the prediction-covariance kernel. Proposition 3.2: for non-differentiable models, a Bayesian hypothesis-space view with latent hypothesis index Psi ~ Multinomial(q,1) over a fixed ensemble gives the predictive covariance kernel equal to the 'posterior' gradient kernel w.r.t. Psi EXACTLY.

Entropy bound for acquisition: H[Y_1:n|x_1:n] = 1/2 log det(Cov[mu(x_1)...mu(x_n)] + sigma^2 I) + C_n — acquisition-score log-determinants upper-bound expected information gain, since the multivariate normal is max-entropy for given covariance.
equation: H[Y_1:n|x_1:n] = 1/2 log det(Cov[mu(x_1)...mu(x_n)] + sigma^2 I) + C_n (Eq. 9)

claim: Across 15 large tabular regression datasets (UCI + OpenML), with 10-member DNN ensembles, black-box methods on average beat their white-box counterparts for all methods except ACS-FW and BAIT; with random-forest per-tree virtual ensembles, all black-box methods except BALD (top-k) beat uniform sampling.

Active-learning ablations: increasing ensemble size K improves acquisition for NNs and RFs (except LCMD, which improves then degrades); for CatBoost virtual ensembles K in [5,160] gives no boost; performance degrades with larger acquisition batches for all methods, and at the largest batch (4096) white-box catches up to black-box.

Delta Tensor proposes five Delta Lake layouts for dense/sparse tensors: FTSF (chunked dense format), COO, CSR/CSC, CSF (compressed sparse fiber), and BSGS (block sparse generic storage, mode-generic, enables slice-before-decode); compression ratio C_r = S_encode / S_binary; timing model t_write = t_ser + t_en(X), t_read_tensor = t_des + t_de(X_encode), t_read_slice = t_des + t_de(XS_encode).
equation: C_r = S_encode / S_binary; t_write = t_ser + t_en(X); t_read_tensor = t_des + t_de(X_encode); t_read_slice = t_des + t_de(XS_encode)

claim: On a dense FFHQ subset (5,000 images 1024x1024 RGB as a (5000,3,1024,1024) tensor, 14.6 GB serialized): chunking + metadata dictionary encoding shrank size to 13.3 GB (-8.90%) despite no compression; slice reads (100-image fiber) fell from 494.33s to 49.24s (-90.04%) because slice reads fetch only relevant chunks, while full-tensor reads rose +25.02% from Spark scheduling overhead.

On the sparse NYC Uber Pickups tensor (183,24,1140,1717 = 8,596,812,960 elements, 3,309,490 nonzeros = 0.038% nonzero): all methods were < 13.23% of PyTorch-PT size; BSGS had the best compression ratio C_r = 4.83%; CSF was most write-efficient (26.68% less than PT); BSGS most read/slice efficient (29.59% / 55.34% less than PT). Authors recommend CSF for write-heavy, BSGS for read/slice-heavy sparse workloads, FTSF for dense.

QuantFactor REINFORCE mines formulaic alpha factors as an MDP over RPN token sequences with deterministic (Dirac) transitions, dropping PPO's critic and using plain REINFORCE with a variance-bounded greedy-rollout subtractive baseline; objective J(theta) = E_{a_1:T ~ pi_theta}[r(a_1:T)] with sparse reward r = IC-bar of the completed formula vs 5-day returns at step T.
equation: J(theta) = E_{a_1:T ~ pi_theta}[r(a_1:T)]; r(a_1:T) = IC-bar of completed formula vs 5-day returns

claim: QFR shapes the reward with the factor's Information Ratio, gated by a delayed, ramped, capped IR test: delay alpha = 9e4 steps, ramp slope eta = 2.65e-6, cap delta = 0.3, weight lambda = 0.02 (eq. 11); hyperparameters: eta=2.65e-6 was the best trade-off and alpha below 7e4 harmed quality (IR test too early).
equation: IR shaping gated by delay alpha = 9e4 steps, ramp eta = 2.65e-6, cap delta = 0.3, weight lambda = 0.02 (eq. 11)

claim: QFR vs AlphaGen's PPO on six equity indices: QFR improved RankIC by 3.83% (headline claim), winning on all six; CSI300: QFR 0.0588/0.0602 (IC/RankIC) vs AlphaGen 0.0500/0.0540, GP 0.0445/0.0673; CSI500: QFR 0.0708/0.0674 vs AlphaGen 0.0544/0.0722. RankIC(z'_t, y_t) = IC(r(z'_t), r(y_t)) with r(.) the ranking operator.

QFR's mined factors gave the highest terminal cumulative return among all methods on CSI300 2021-2024 and the most PnL in all three CIMV volatility regimes, with the largest edge in the high-volatility period; ablation showed removing either the greedy baseline or the IR shaping degrades learning curves on all six indices. Caveats: backtest ignores transaction costs, shaping hyperparameters were tuned on the same indices used for evaluation.

FactorMiner is a self-evolving agent for financial alpha discovery with a modular skill architecture (60+ financial operator library, multi-stage validation pipeline) plus structured experience memory (successful templates + forbidden regions), run through a retrieve->generate->evaluate->distill 'Ralph Loop'; generation is steered by a global-library perspective — mining direction is chosen by how candidates complement the existing library (correlation-to-library as novelty gate), not individual quality.

Factor Library Top-40, 2025 out-of-sample (IC % / ICIR / avg |rho|): CSI500 — FactorMiner 8.25/0.77/0.31 vs AlphaAgent 5.90/0.46/0.32, GPLearn 6.04/0.43/0.44, Alpha101-Adapted 5.06/0.43/0.21, AlphaForge 4.48/0.38/0.36; CSI1000 7.78/0.76/0.30; HS300 7.46/0.38/0.31; crypto 3.82/0.28/0.25 (best everywhere, incl. cross-asset generalization).

Factor combination via frozen Top-40 equal-weight gave IC/ICIR 14.95/1.29 on CSI500 vs next-best Alpha101-Adapted 11.53/0.86; redundancy: FactorMiner avg |rho| ~0.30-0.31 vs GPLearn 0.44-0.45 (the 'Correlation Red Sea'), with the random-noise floor at 0.07-0.13; avg |rho| serves as the redundancy measure.

FactorMiner ledger caveats: the Top-40 were selected on CSI500-2024 then evaluated on 2025 including CSI500 (same-market overlap — the cross-dataset results are the cleaner read); absolute-value IC summaries hide sign instability across years; no portfolio backtest with costs; the 'self-evolving' claim sits atop a fixed hand-curated operator library.

TimeGrad is the first autoregressive denoising-diffusion forecaster for multivariate probabilistic time series: each time step's joint distribution is learned by a conditional DDPM conditioned on an RNN hidden state plus covariates known for the whole forecast horizon, with temporal factorization q(x_{t0:T}^0 | x_{1:t0-1}^0, c_{1:T}) = prod_{t=t0}^{T} q(x_t^0 | x_{1:t-1}^0, c_{1:T}) and encoder h_t = RNN_theta(concat(x_t^0, c_t), h_{t-1}).

TimeGrad DDPM backbone: forward q(x^n|x^{n-1}) = N(x^n; sqrt(1-beta_n) x^{n-1}, beta_n I); closed-form q(x^n|x^0) = N(x^n; sqrt(bar-alpha_n) x^0, (1-bar-alpha_n) I); reverse p_theta(x^{n-1}|x^n) = N(x^{n-1}; mu_theta(x^n,n), Sigma_theta I) with mu_theta(x^n,n) = (1/sqrt(alpha_n))(x^n - (beta_n/sqrt(1-bar-alpha_n)) epsilon_theta(x^n,n)); training objective E||epsilon - epsilon_theta(sqrt(bar-alpha_n) x_t^0 + sqrt(1-bar-alpha_n) epsilon, h_{t-1}, n)||^2.
equation: q(x^n|x^{n-1}) = N(x^n; sqrt(1-beta_n) x^{n-1}, beta_n I); mu_theta(x^n,n) = (1/sqrt(alpha_n))(x^n - (beta_n/sqrt(1-bar-alpha_n)) epsilon_theta(x^n,n))

claim: TimeGrad evaluation uses CRPS(F,x) = integral (F(z) - 1{x<=z})^2 dz and CRPS_sum = E_t[CRPS(F_hat_sum(t), sum_i x_{i,t}^0)] — a proper scoring rule chosen because likelihood is unusable when not all baselines yield analytic distributions.
equation: CRPS(F,x) = integral (F(z) - 1{x<=z})^2 dz; CRPS_sum = E_t[CRPS(F_hat_sum(t), sum_i x_{i,t}^0)]

claim: TimeGrad CRPS_sum (lower better, mean +/- se over 10 retrainings): Solar 0.287+/-0.02 (next: Transformer-MAF 0.301); Electricity 0.0206+/-0.001 (next 0.0207); Traffic 0.044+/-0.006 (next 0.056, -21%); Taxi 0.114+/-0.02 (next 0.179, -36%); Wikipedia 0.0485+/-0.002 (next 0.063, -23%) — SOTA on 5 of 6 datasets; Exchange was the loss (0.006 vs 0.005).

TimeGrad ablation: N~10 diffusion steps was already near-optimal and N~100 optimal (larger not beneficial) — a 10x sampling speedup is available; sampling uses annealed Langevin per step with S=100 trajectories for empirical quantiles; training ran on a single Nvidia V100 16GB.

DS-Agent is an LLM agent for automated data science structured by classical case-based reasoning — retrieve -> reuse -> revise -> retain — over a bank of expert Kaggle solutions: retriever p_R over the case bank given task tau and feedback l, LLM p_LLM generating solution y given tau/l/retrieved case c, evaluator p_E producing feedback l from y; iteration-t solution p_CBR(y^t|tau) marginalizes over retrieved-and-revised cases; it differs from RAG by the revise + retain steps.

DS-Agent's development stage retrieves top-k cases by embedding similarity, then ReviseRank re-ranks cases as '[2]>[1]>[3]...' conditioned on last iteration's execution feedback (p_RR(c|tau,l^{t-1}), no retriever fine-tuning), the planner reuses the top case, executes, feeds back, loops, and finally Retains the best solution in the bank — flexible learning without backprop; the deployment stage is simplified CBR (retrieve past successes, minor adaptation, single pass) designed for weak LLMs.

DS-Agent + GPT-4: 100% development success rate over all 12 data-science tasks with best performance in 9/12; DS-Agent + GPT-3.5 'consistently surpasses ResearchAgent with GPT-4 in all tasks' (ResearchAgent + GPT-3.5 'almost fails in every type of task'); deployment one-pass rate 85% (GPT-3.5) / 99% (GPT-4) vs best baseline 56%/60%; Mixtral-8x7b-Instruct lifted from 6% to 31% by simplified CBR.

DS-Agent costs: $1.60/run (GPT-4) / $0.06 (GPT-3.5) development; $0.135/$0.0045 low-resource deployment; average best mean rank improves monotonically with iteration steps; ledger limitations: the Kaggle bank may overlap pretraining (memorization unmeasured), ReviseRank ranking accuracy uncalibrated, and retaining by validation metric needs a locked holdout gate or the bank poisons itself.

VLMo's Mixture-of-Modality-Experts block: H'_l = MSA(LN(H_{l-1})) + H_{l-1}; H_l = MoME-FFN(LN(H'_l)) + H'_l, with FFN pool {V-FFN (vision), L-FFN (language), VL-FFN (fusion)} and deterministic routing by modality and layer — image/text-only inputs use V/L experts throughout, image-text pairs use V+L in bottom layers and the VL expert in top layers.
equation: H'_l = MSA(LN(H_{l-1})) + H_{l-1}; H_l = MoME-FFN(LN(H'_l)) + H'_l

claim: VLMo stagewise pre-training: (1) train V-FFN + shared attention on image-only data (BEiT masked image modeling); (2) freeze, train L-FFN on text-only data (MLM); (3) joint vision-language pre-training with three losses: image-text contrastive (ITC) + image-text matching (ITM) + MLM; configs Base = 12 layers/768 hidden/12 heads, Large = 24/1024/16 heads.

VLMo VQA test-dev/test-std: Base 76.64/76.89 (vs ALBEF-Base 74.54/74.70, ViLT-Base 71.26); Large 79.94/79.98; Large++ (1.0B noisy pairs) 82.88/82.78 vs Florence-Huge 80.16/80.36; COCO text-retrieval R@1/R@5/R@10 = 83.1/96.0/98.2 linear-time, beating fusion-rerank models; ablations: MoME 80.13/80.31 vs standard Transformer 78.81/79.27 on NLVR2.

Chronos reframes time-series forecasting as next-token prediction: scaling s = (1/C) sum_{i=1}^C |x_i| with x-tilde_i = x_i/s; quantization q(x-tilde) = argmin_b |x-tilde - c_b| with c_b uniformly spaced over [-15,15], B=4096 bins, out-of-range values clipped; objective theta* = argmin_theta -sum_{t=1}^{H} log p_theta(z_{C+t} | z_{1:C+t-1}) (categorical cross-entropy with label smoothing).
equation: s = (1/C) sum_{i=1}^C |x_i|; q(x-tilde) = argmin_b |x-tilde - c_b|, c_b uniform over [-15,15], B=4096; theta* = argmin_theta -sum_{t=1}^{H} log p_theta(z_{C+t} | z_{1:C+t-1})

claim: Chronos inference samples autoregressive paths (temperature/categorical), maps tokens back to values and unscales to form an empirical predictive distribution, with the median path as the point forecast; metrics are WQL over quantiles {0.1,...,0.9} and MASE vs seasonal-naive, aggregated by geometric mean relative to seasonal naive.

Chronos augmentation: TSMixup — 10M mixup augmentations combining k in {2,3} series with Dirichlet weights — plus 1M synthetic GP series via KernelSynth (length 1024, 9:1 real:synthetic); removing mixup/synthetic hurt zero-shot, with synthetic GP data helping most on small-data regimes.

Chronos results: zero-shot Chronos models ranked 2nd-4th in probabilistic (WQL) rankings with Chronos-T5 (Large, 710M) 2nd on point forecasting (MASE) — all zero-shot against per-dataset-trained models; fine-tuned Chronos-T5 (Small, 46M) was best on average across both metrics, beating supervised PatchTST/DeepAR with far cheaper training; llmtime (GPT-3.5/4) was far behind — text tokenization is a poor time-series tokenizer.

Chronos limitations: no covariates (cannot ingest weather, injuries, rest, line movement); mean scaling fragile on constant sequences; 4096-bin quantization caps precision — must be validated against market granularity (~0.5 pt) and key numbers 3/7; zero-shot results confound pretraining overlap (familiarity effects).

The contamination-free protocol places the entire test window after the last model's release date so nothing in the hold-out could have been memorized — yet a pretraining-familiarity advantage persists: within-family TimesFM vs Chronos on identical series, TimesFM outranked Chronos by -0.53 on Wikipedia vs -0.09 everywhere else (1,500 vs 754 series, Mann-Whitney p < 10^-5), with the advantage tracking corpus familiarity (Wikipedia pageviews are the bulk of TimesFM's pretraining corpus), not series properties.

Largest gain in the study: 28% lower MASE than the best classical method on weekly Wikipedia pageviews (TimesFM's pretraining domain); but pretrained models lost one of 7 groups to a Theta baseline (Electricity) and were indistinguishable from seasonal naive on daily exchange rates (Friedman does not reject — every method ties).

Negative results: seasonal strength and spectral entropy do NOT explain the familiarity pattern (seasonal strength if anything negatively associated), and most published-style gaps between leading pretrained models fall inside multiple-comparison rank intervals — i.e., leaderboard differences are often noise.

The paper's trust-signal mandates for foundation-model evaluation: (1) a published pretraining-corpus manifest per backbone; (2) domain holdouts relative to the corpus, not just later windows (e.g., pretrain on regular season, hold out playoffs); (3) any 'zero-shot' claim on a corpus-present domain relabeled 'familiar-domain'; (4) rank intervals, not decimal places, for model selection.

The DRO game is min_{x in X} sup_{P in A} E_{xi~P}[f_x(xi)] (Eq. 1); DRO-RoBAS centers the ambiguity set on a misspecification-robust posterior predictive from Bayesian Nonparametric Learning with MMD loss: min_x sup_{P: MMD(P, P-hat_n^{pred,NPL}) <= epsilon} E_{xi~P}[f_x(xi)] — the NPL-MMD posterior can be bimodal even when the model is unimodal, and there are tractable duals in the RKHS plus high-probability bounds on epsilon so the set contains the DGP and the DRO objective upper-bounds the true objective.
equation: min_{x in X} sup_{P in A} E_{xi~P}[f_x(xi)] (Eq. 1); DRO-RoBAS: min_x sup_{P: MMD(P, P-hat_n^{pred,NPL}) <= epsilon} E_{xi~P}[f_x(xi)]

claim: Competing formulations: BDRO: min_x E_{Pi(theta|xi_1:n)}[sup_{P: d_KL(P||P_theta) <= epsilon} E_P[f_x]] (Eq. 2); DRO-BAS_PP: KL ball around posterior predictive (Eq. 3); DRO-BAS_PE: expected-KL ball (Eq. 4). DRO-RoBAS works for any model family including likelihood-free models (DRO-BAS_PE is limited to exponential families).
equation: BDRO: min_x E_{Pi(theta|xi_1:n)}[sup_{P: d_KL(P||P_theta) <= epsilon} E_P[f_x]] (Eq. 2)

claim: Newsvendor test (cost f(x,xi)=h*max(x-xi,0)+b*max(xi-x,0), b=8, h=3, n=20, J=100 reps): under a bimodal-Gaussian DGP with a misspecified unimodal model, standard posteriors concentrate between the modes so DRO-BAS/BDRO need huge epsilon (conservative, high out-of-sample cost), while DRO-RoBAS's NPL-MMD posterior is bimodal and has consistently lower out-of-sample variance than empirical MMD (univariate).

Huber-contamination results (eta in {0,0.1,0.2}): at eta=0, DRO-BAS beats RoBAS — well-specified cases favor standard Bayes, robustness has a price; at eta>0, RoBAS shows the best out-of-sample mean-variance tradeoff, while even empirical MMD degrades; on portfolio with eta=0.1, empirical DRO degrades fast for epsilon<0.2 while RoBAS is unaffected, converging only at epsilon>=0.2.

RoBAS costs and caveats: computationally heavier (RKHS optimization + NPL sampling, Fourier-feature scaling left to future work); epsilon must still be chosen; guarantees are high-probability not exact; kernel choice affects everything and is not automated; the paper's contamination model assumes a clean test set, but in sports the 'test' (next week's games) can itself contain the outliers.
T-SHRED's SINDy latent loss: Xi^(i) = argmin ||z_{t+1} - (z_t + sum Theta(z_{t+ih}) Xi^(i) h)||^2_2 + ||Xi^(i)||_0 (Eq. 1), trained via l2 + pruning on Xi every 10 epochs as an l0 approximation.
equation: Xi^(i) = argmin ||z_{t+1} - (z_t + sum Theta(z_{t+ih}) Xi^(i) h)||^2_2 + ||Xi^(i)||_0 (Eq. 1)

claim: SINDy-Attention embeds symbolic regression inside each attention head: per-head Q^(h)=xW_{h,q}, K^(h)=xW_{h,k}, V^(h)=xW_{h,v} (Eq. 10); T^(h)=rowsoftmax(QK^T/sqrt(k))V (Eq. 11); S^(h)=Theta_SINDy(T^(h)')Xi^(h) (Eq. 12); S=concat(S^(h)) (Eq. 13); z=(SW_ff1)W_ff2 (Eq. 14); after training each head reads out as a coupled ODE over the latent space.
equation: Q^(h)=xW_{h,q}, K^(h)=xW_{h,k}, V^(h)=xW_{h,v} (Eq. 10); T^(h)=rowsoftmax(QK^T/sqrt(k))V (Eq. 11); S^(h)=Theta_SINDy(T^(h)')Xi^(h) (Eq. 12); S=concat(S^(h)) (Eq. 13); z=(SW_ff1)W_ff2 (Eq. 14)

claim: T-SHRED interpretability run on rotating shallow water: reducing latent 100->6 cost only ~2x test loss (7.76e-3) while model size fell 16x (28.51 MB vs 452.52 MB), and every head emitted a readable 3-variable linear ODE — e.g., SST L0H0: z-dot_0 = -0.699 z_0 + 0.275 z_2.

T-SHRED full-state prediction results (best-by-validation, 128 configs/dataset x 5 seeds): SST best overall = 1-layer GRU SHRED + MLP decoder 1.50e-3 (25.14 MB) vs best T-SHRED 1.87e-3 (75.31 MB); plasma best GRU 2.10e-4 vs T-SHRED 4.90e-4; within T-SHRED, SINDy-Attention beat all other transformer variants on all three datasets, with CNN decoders pairing best with transformer latents. Honest headline: transformers still lose to GRUs on next-step state prediction — the paper's contribution is the regularization mechanism, not SOTA forecasting.

The rotating shallow water dataset (PlanetSWE) used in T-SHRED follows du/dt = -u . grad u - g grad h - nu grad^4 u - 2 Omega x u; dh/dt = -H grad . u - grad . (h u) - nu grad^4 h + F; the three datasets were Sea Surface Temperature (1,400 weekly snapshots 1992-2019, 180x360 grid), complex plasma physics (2,000 timesteps x 14 fields, rSVD to 280-dim ROM), and rotating shallow water (10 tracks, 15.5 GB).
equation: du/dt = -u . grad u - g grad h - nu grad^4 u - 2 Omega x u; dh/dt = -H grad . u - grad . (h u) - nu grad^4 h + F

claim: Shapley value: phi_i = sum_{S subset N\{i}} |S|!(|N|-|S|-1)!/|N|! . (v(S union {i}) - v(S)); permutation form phi_i = 1/|Pi(N)| sum_{pi in Pi(N)} (v(P_i^pi union {i}) - v(P_i^pi)).
equation: phi_i = sum_{S subset N\{i}} |S|!(|N|-|S|-1)!/|N|! . (v(S union {i}) - v(S)); phi_i = 1/|Pi(N)| sum_{pi in Pi(N)} (v(P_i^pi union {i}) - v(P_i^pi))

claim: SHAPEffects per-observation effect: Effect_{var,x} = sgn(SHAP_var) . SHAP_var^2 (squaring amplifies the most influential), with group effect Ef_{var,group} = sum_{x in group} Effect_{var,x}; validation observations are classified by err(x,y) = y - y-hat(x) into Correctly/Over/Under-Predicted via error quantiles Q_low = Quantile(err, q_low), Q_high = Quantile(err, q_high), with bias translation when 0 is outside [Q_low, Q_high].
equation: Effect_{var,x} = sgn(SHAP_var) . SHAP_var^2; Ef_{var,group} = sum_{x in group} Effect_{var,x}; err(x,y) = y - y-hat(x)

claim: SHAPEffects negative-influence rule (5 cases): infinite if the variable has zero effect anywhere (pure noise/overfit — all such dropped at once); otherwise computed from how group effects align with the model's current bias direction (median error q_2(err)) — e.g., if the model over-predicts (q_2(err)<0) and the variable increases over-predictions while reducing under-predictions, negative influence = |Ef_O.P| - |Ef_U.P|; a variable worsening both tails gets |Ef_U.P| + |Ef_O.P|; drop the largest non-zero negative influence and iterate.

The TCN spin-prior network regresses initial ball spin from a 100-frame hip-centered pose-keypoint sequence (emphasizing the right arm: shoulder/elbow/wrist), with TCNs reported to beat RNNs/LSTMs for this task; results: training RMSE 2.95 Hz, validation RMSE 5.27 Hz, Pearson R 0.807 (novice) / 0.815 (competitive), p<0.001.

The paper reports the spin-prior system 'reduces the prediction error of landing positions by over 63.6% compared to a baseline method that utilized an adaptive extended Kalman filter'; the spin advantage appears mainly in second-bounce prediction; heavy-spin pro shots still underperform the labeled-spin oracle (attributed to limited training data and missing racket pose).

Calibration explainer: Brier = average of (p - y)^2 per settled pick (p = probability, y = 1 win / 0 loss), between 0 and 1; 0.25 = coin-flip baseline; Murphy identity: Brier ~= REL - RES + UNC; UNC = baseRate x (1 - baseRate), live ~0.25; REL = bin-average p error vs actual win rate, want low, live ~0.026; RES = bin win-rate spread vs overall average, want high, live ~0.002 (10 equal-width p buckets); Brier floor: <= 0.22 before PROVEN is even considered.
equation: Brier = average of (p - y)^2; Brier ~= REL - RES + UNC; UNC = baseRate x (1 - baseRate)

claim: Back-of-envelope: at UNC ~= 0.25 and residual REL ~= 0.02, hitting Brier <= 0.22 requires RES >= ~0.03 — about 15x the live 0.002; RES 0.002 = almost no ranking power ('the model is not ranking'); Murphy RES one-liner: 'When we group picks by confidence, do those groups actually win at different rates?'

Honest minimization order: (1) raise RES — fewer better picks, better ranking score, independent model probabilities, sport models, pause dead markets; (2) lower REL (Platt/temperature/isotonic) only after RES moves — 'maps alone cannot unlock PROVEN at RES~=0'; (3) UNC fixed by sample, not tunable with theater; autonomy rules: selective + pause + proven-path plan and metrics cron are automatic; PROVEN publish only on floors + GREENxK + AUTO_PUBLISH policy, never faked; founder needs no clicks for measurement or filtering.

Live calibration floors for the PROVEN trust ladder: Brier <= 0.22, ECE <= 0.05, Murphy REL <= 0.05, and n >= 100 settled picks; PERFORMANCE_STATS stays dark while the class is RED.

Honest-p resolver rule: for calibration sets prefer marketFairProb, then an independent trueProb, then MONEYLINE confidence only; never treat rank scores or confidence/100 as probabilities for SPREAD/TOTAL without a fair p, because that produced measured artificial overconfidence.

Measured 2026-08-09 live class: Brier 0.275 (floor 0.22), ECE 0.112 (floor 0.05), RES 0.002 - RED; root causes were confidence/100 used as p on SPREAD/TOTAL, 0% independent coverage, and calibration maps correctly OFF because rewriting p with isotonic to invent GREEN would be fabrication.

Calibration integrity rule: canonicalSettled was 1017 (515 wins + 499 losses + 3 pushes) but the calibration map n is 760 because pushes and rows with eligibleForLearning=false are excluded; PROVEN gating runs on the map metrics of learning-eligible WIN/LOSS only, never on the raw win rate.

Board honesty rules: the market board kills when odds are older than 240 minutes and the signal board kills when no fresh published pick exists within 240 minutes; model signals must be labeled 'Model signal' and never presented as book or exchange lines.
Ops memory pattern: Jarvis durable history is persisted to Neon as JarvisMemoryEvent rows with a trend-merge, giving the agent a durable cross-session history store.

Cryptographic proof roadmap: Merkle (live, SHA-256 per-pick receipts minted pre-kickoff, publicly verifiable by re-hash) -> Pedersen (dark, secp256k1, additively homomorphic commitment on the frozen slate's edge aggregate minted in the same atomic transaction as the Merkle root) -> Halo2 (constant ~3-5 KB proofs, <60 ms mobile verification, no trusted setup, fixed-point arithmetic scale 1e6 for the 52.4% boundary) -> STARK (hash-based, post-quantum, larger proofs); Halo2/IPA recursion is discrete-log-based and must never be labeled post-quantum.

Anti-cherry-picking mechanism: commit to the frozen aggregate before kickoff and open it after settlement; a mostly-settled slate is not partly openable and a mismatched opener is withheld, because an opening proves the aggregate was fixed pre-kickoff and unedited since - a binding check on the record, not a claim the picks were good.

Verification-before-adoption discipline: an AI-generated vendor/tooling research dump is held UNVERIFIED under the no-fake-data policy and nothing may be adopted, cited, or acted on until each named repo/claim passes citation verification; hallucination signatures flagged include hyper-precise unverifiable numbers and plausible-but-fake product names.

Engine/revenue structural separation: the affiliate odds widget is classified 'sportsbook' (not 'sports_data') and must never be wired into the prediction engine's import graph, sealed by an import-graph guard in both directions; widget copy must be labeled as bookmaker odds and never share pick-grade iconography.

Fail-closed eval rule for generation surfaces: when the model returns text that is not valid JSON, the runtime must reject with the JSON parse error, never infer fields from prose, and record a failed usage row.
Pre-mortem trigger rule: re-invoke the deterministic pre-mortem builder when an underlying PickSignalSnapshot factor moves by more than 0.15 before settlement.

ProofExplorer pattern: the public calibration panel shows real count-ups, a reliability curve from real buckets, and an honest building-state message when the sample is too small rather than showing untrustable numbers.

Method-tag continuity discipline: uniformMethodTags requires every aggregated line to be tagged before continuity claims propagate; continuous CLV cannot be claimed across untagged or mixed methods (sameMethodOrRefuse enforcement), and ClosingArchive persists methodTag/modelVersion and re-emits them.
shin_devig_v1 is inventoried as a tagged fair-probability devig method in the FairMethodTag union, alongside gamma, kalshi, model_prior, odds two-way, and demo.

Publish gate mechanics: Edge Index >= 2.5 publish minimum; the public explanation contract requires naming the top-3 evidence-ref factor scores with inline citations of the form (source: KIND at observedAt) and forbids outcome language and recommendation language.

Scoring formula from packages/prediction-engine/src/scoring.ts: consensus (max 30) + market depth (max 20) + edge (max 25) + volatility penalty (-15) + context (line movement, rest, schedule stress, H2H, venue form, cross-market, uncertainty) + flat +10 base, clamped 0-100; refuses below MIN_PUBLISH_CONFIDENCE=50 or MIN_BOOKMAKERS=2; MODEL_VERSION v5.0.0 stamped on every pick.

Core flaw verified in the audit: calibration sets expected = confidence/100, but confidence is a 0-100 heuristic quality score, not a calibrated win probability - fine for moneyline but misleading for spread/total (priced near 50% while confidence sits 65-90), producing systemic false 'overcalling'; interim fix was a market-neutral discrimination metric (improving | flat | inverted | insufficient-data).

Thin-evidence refusal doctrine: the refusal check runs before the model API call (cost-saving and explicit refusal), returning an exact refusal copy with publicReady false and no attempt to infer content from unparseable or absent evidence.

Publication voice discipline: published picks are posted as past-tense, third-person ledger entries (e.g., 'Published BOS -3.5 at 73% confidence (SOLID_PLAY)') pointing to a canonical game-room URL, with engagement-bait, first-person voice, and comparisons to other operators hard-forbidden by regex.

Measured 2026-09-13 calibration baseline on 2,641 settled WIN/LOSS + 13 PUSH: overconfidence worsens at the top - the 80-89 confidence bucket went 0.497 actual vs 84.0 confidence (+0.343 gap, n=189), and the 90-99 bucket went 0.532 vs 93.4 (+0.402, n=47); the book path is inverted at the top while the signal path calibrates honestly (80-89: signal 0.678 on n=59 vs book 0.415 on n=130).

Fitted book-path calibrator (temporal split, winner: logistic on confidence + sport + market, log-loss 0.6678 vs identity 0.7608): the mapping is FLAT - book confidence 50 maps to 0.449, confidence 100 maps to 0.536, i.e., a '100' book pick is roughly a 54% proposition; the signal path must be left alone.

NFL calibration head constraint: with only 70 settled NFL picks total (SPREAD n=15 at 0.133 win rate), the NFL head must be CLV-only or pooled until far more games settle - do not fit an NFL realized-results head on n=70.

Labeling discipline: CLV is the primary label (available within hours), realized results are the slow-loop validation label; both are always reported, and premium/free discrimination was only 56.4% (n=784) vs 53.4% (n=1857).

Bridge audit result: 285 rows x 285 distinct game_ids, 0 duplicates, probability range 0.18944950 to 0.88231212 from a logistic-IRLS fit on 1999-2024 (6,955 training rows) with a 2025-only holdout; sample_count=6955 on every row is the training-fit size (a model property, never read as per-game sample size).

Coverage-soft-spot method: grade weekly matchup assets by mapping positional defensive leaks against opponent weaknesses (e.g., TE vs CIN 27th DVOA vs TEs; pass-rush mismatch JAX 53.1% pressure vs DEN 56.3% pressure allowed; Bears CBs allowing 113.7 and 158.3 passer ratings outside) - directly reusable as a weekly matchup feature.
