Empirical-Bayes bucket: p-hat = (w + M*p-hat_parent)/(n + M) with pseudocount M = 25, hierarchical shrinkage from the global rate downward. Teacher construction: training plays binned by score margin (14 bins), time remaining (7 bins), pregame spread (9 bins); bin value = fraction of training plays the possession team won; sparse bins shrunk toward coarser parents; test plays read targets from the training-season table only. Data: NFL regular-season play-by-play 2015-2024 (nflfastR), disjoint season splits: train 2015-2022 (40,246 states), selection 2023 (5,241), test 2024 (5,185).

On 5,185 NFL test plays (2024), Brier scores [paired-bootstrap CIs]: direct RLVR 0.1443 [0.1394, 0.1491] (ECE 0.0292, MCE 0.0596, acc 0.784, resolution 0.1058); masked-CoT RLVR 0.1522 [0.1466, 0.1577]; DeepSeek-V4 zero-shot 0.1438 [0.1392, 0.1483] (acc 0.790); empirical-rate teacher 0.1432 [0.1384, 0.1480]; market 0.1355 [0.1307, 0.1403] (ECE 0.0273, acc 0.799, resolution 0.1148); untrained base Qwen2.5-7B 0.2057; nflverse WP 0.1562; GBM all-features 0.1584. Paired differences: Direct-Masked = -0.0079* [-0.0101, -0.0057]; Direct-Market = +0.0088* [0.0068, 0.0107]; Direct-DeepSeek-V4 = +0.0005 (not significant). Three static estimators converge ~0.143-0.144 and trail the market by the same 0.008 - the gap is resolution/information, not calibration. Reward-target ablation: realized outcome -> Brier 0.166/ECE 0.10; half-blend -> 0.181/0.121; empirical rate -> 0.154/0.050. Full-completion CoT training decalibrated (Brier 0.25->0.34) from gradient on reasoning tokens, not the reward; masked training cut inconsistent completions 22.4% -> 4.4% in a blinded judge. Adding field position + down did not improve the teacher. The direct model was better calibrated than its own teacher (ECE 0.029 vs 0.044) - policy smooths the bucketed target.

The empirical-Bayes bucketed rate used as the verifiable-reward teacher: p-hat = (w + M*p-hat_parent)/(n + M) with pseudocount M = 25, i.e. sparse bucket rates are shrunk toward their coarser parent buckets. The paper's own Section 7 caveat: the method works 'only where the public state already carries most of the predictive signal, and where outcomes are dense and resolved quickly enough to estimate a reliable empirical rate; sparse or long-horizon events would weaken both the reward and the comparison against a market.' A model trained on p-hat can never be better calibrated than p-hat's information content (smoothness gains only).

Dombry & Zaoui (2025, arXiv:2503.23782v1) extend the reject option (abstention) to distributional regression with an OPTIMAL rule at a fixed, exactly controlled rejection rate epsilon: reject when the predictive distribution's CRPS entropy exceeds a threshold lambda_epsilon. CRPS: CRPS(H,y) = integral (H(u) - 1{y<=u})^2 du. Average-CRPS decomposition: CRPS-bar(H,K) = ent(K) + Div(H,K) with ent(K) = integral K(u)(1-K(u)) du and Div(H,K) = integral (H(u)-K(u))^2 du (Lemma 5); E[CRPS(F*_X, Y) | X] = ent(F*_X) (Lemma 1). Risk with rejection cost: R_lambda(Gamma_F) = E[CRPS(F_X,Y) * 1{Gamma_F(X) != reject}] + lambda * r(Gamma_F).

Optimal distributional reject rule (Dombry & Zaoui, Prop. 1): Gamma*_lambda(X) = F*_X iff ent(F*_X) <= lambda, else reject. Fixed-rate rule (Prop. 3): Gamma*_epsilon = Gamma*_{lambda_epsilon} with lambda_epsilon = G_ent^{-1}(1-epsilon), achieving exactly rejection rate epsilon. Excess risk (Thm. 1): E[excess_{lambda_epsilon}(Gamma-hat_epsilon)] <= 2E[Div(F-hat_{n,X}, F*_X)] + E[|ent(F-hat_{n,X}) - ent(F*_X)|] + MC/sqrt(N) + u; Cor. 1 bounds it by 3E[W_1(F-hat, F*)] + MC/sqrt(N) + u; distributional KNN rate <= n^{-h/(2h+d)} + N^{-1/2} for d>=2 (Cor. 3). Plug-in entropy for weighted-average estimators (Lemma 6): ent(F-hat_{n,X}) = sum_i sum_j w_i w_j (Y_j - Y_i) 1{Y_i < Y_j}. Rejection-rate control is distribution-free: E[|r(Gamma-hat_epsilon) - epsilon|] <= C N^{-1/2} (Prop. 5); randomization zeta ~ U[0,u] ensures exact rate attainment.
equation: Γ*_λ(X) = F*_X iff ent(F*_X) ≤ λ, else reject

claim: On three UCI regression benchmarks, distributional random forest error fell sharply with the reject option: Airfoil Self-Noise Err 1.53(0.05) at epsilon=0 -> 1.11(0.06) at epsilon=0.5 -> 0.78(0.09) at epsilon=0.9; Concrete 3.55(0.14) -> 1.92(0.22) at epsilon=0.9; QSAR 0.65(0.04) -> 0.37(0.09). Rejection rates tracked targets almost exactly with only 20% unlabeled calibration data: epsilon=0.1 -> r-hat=0.10(0.02); 0.5 -> 0.50(0.04); 0.9 -> 0.90(0.02). DRF uniformly beat distributional KNN; the authors conclude calibration of the entropy threshold matters more than estimator choice. Limitations: KNN minimax rate suffers the curse of dimensionality; Lemma 6's plug-in is only for local-average estimators (no closed form for neural/GNN distributional models); exact-epsilon is asymptotic; no comparison against thresholding predictive variance.

Guo, Pleiss, Sun & Weinberger (2017, arXiv:1706.04599v2) is the canonical calibration paper: perfect calibration means P(Y-hat=Y | P-hat=p) = p for all p in [0,1]. Metrics: ECE = sum_m (|B_m|/n) |acc(B_m) - conf(B_m)|; MCE = max_m |acc-conf|; NLL = -sum_i log pi-hat(y_i|x_i) (Table 1 uses M=15 bins). Temperature scaling: q-hat_i = max_k softmax(z_i/T)^{(k)}, T chosen to minimize validation NLL; T does not change the argmax, so accuracy is unchanged. Entropy-maximization derivation: temperature scaling is the unique max-entropy distribution subject to E[true-class logit] = E[weighted logit] (Claim 1). Comparators: histogram binning, isotonic regression, BBQ (Bayesian binning into quantiles), Platt variants (matrix/vector scaling).

Temperature scaling results (ECE %, M=15): CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 16.53% -> temp 1.26% (histogram binning 2.66%, isotonic 4.99%, BBQ 5.46%, vector 1.32%, matrix 25.49%); CIFAR-10 ResNet-110 4.60% -> 0.83%; DenseNet-40 3.28% -> 0.33%; ImageNet ResNet-152 5.48% -> 1.86%; DenseNet-161 6.28% -> 1.99%; Birds ResNet-50 9.19% -> 1.85%; Cars 4.30% -> 2.35%; 20 News DAN-3 8.02% -> 4.11%; SVHN 0.44% -> 0.17%; Reuters 0.85% -> 0.91% (already calibrated - post-processing unnecessary). Miscalibration drivers: ECE grows with depth and width; BatchNorm increases miscalibration even as accuracy improves; more weight decay monotonically improves calibration well past the accuracy optimum; NLL overfits during training (CIFAR-100: test error drops 29%->27% while NLL overfits). Matrix scaling fails on 1000-class ImageNet (quadratic parameter blowup); vector scaling's learned vector is nearly constant, so miscalibration is intrinsically low-dimensional; binning methods change class predictions and hurt accuracy. Temperature scaling is a 1-D convex optimization (~10 conjugate-gradient iterations, fraction of a second); BBQ is ~3 orders of magnitude slower.

The NLL-vs-accuracy disconnect in Guo et al. (2017): on CIFAR-100, test error drops 29%->27% while NLL overfits - explaining why a model with good classification accuracy can still produce terrible probability-based sizing. The brief's sequencing lesson: measure ECE (M=15) on emitted probabilities first; if below ~1% (the Reuters case), post-hoc calibration is unnecessary; post-hoc calibration assumes train/validation/test come from the same distribution and breaks under distribution shift.

Jonkers, Van Wallendael, Duchateau & Van Hoecke (2024, arXiv:2404.15018) restore valid conformal predictive distributions under covariate shift by weighting calibration conformity scores with the estimated test-vs-calibration covariate likelihood ratio w-hat(x): the weighted conformal predictive system (WSCPS) outputs Q-hat(y|x_{n+1}) = sum_i p_i^w(x_{n+1}) * 1{C_i <= C(x_{n+1},y)} + ..., with normalized weights p_i^w proportional to w-hat(x_i). The likelihood ratio w(x) = dP_test/dP_cal is estimated via a probabilistic classifier (test-vs-calibration discriminator). Assumptions: covariate shift ONLY - P(Y|X) is invariant, only P(X) changes; the likelihood ratio is estimable (needs overlap/support). Conjecture 3.5 (UNPROVED): the WSCPS output is asymptotically uniformly distributed (probabilistically valid) under consistent w-hat estimation.

Airfoil self-noise under induced exponential-tilt covariate shift (N=1,503, 25/25/50 train/calibration/test splits, 1,000 Monte Carlo trials): unweighted CPS coverage collapses below nominal; WSCPS restores average coverage to the desired 80% and slightly lowers CRPS vs unweighted CPS; Kang-Schafer synthetic benchmark shows the same pattern. Only the 80% nominal level was tested; interval widths stayed reasonable. Limitations flagged: weight estimation is the whole game (a bad discriminator gives bad weights and no validity); assumes P(Y|X) invariance - in the NFL a QB change arguably changes P(Y|X) itself (concept drift), which WSCPS does not handle; small datasets mean weight-estimation variance is a real concern; the probabilistic-validity claim is a conjecture, empirically supported but unproved.

Kampakis (2016, UCL PhD thesis, arXiv:1609.07480v1) Investigation 2: GP regression with a dynamic-time-warping kernel for days-to-first-injury from variable-length exposure records. DTW-RBF kernel: k(x_i, x_j) = exp(-gamma * DTW(x_i, x_j)), gamma > 0 constrained so predictive variances stay positive; composite kernel over two exposure series: K(x_i,x_j) = 1/2 [k_train(x_i,x_j) + k_match(x_i,x_j)]. DTW distance: DTW(X,Y) = min over warping paths of sum d(x_i, y_j) - admitting different-length histories. Data: 35 THFC first-team players' daily training+match exposure minutes, 2012-13 pre-season; after cleaning 29 players, 21 injured; response = days to first injury (range 14-312, mean 91.73, median 49.5).

Kampakis thesis Investigation 2 (GP-DTW, leave-one-out CV with the test subject's record truncated at T, T-1, ..., T-12 days before injury - a forecast-horizon/landmark evaluation): concordance correlation coefficient 0.95-0.98 from T down to T-12; best MAE ~11 days (response mean 91.7, median 49.5); skill deteriorates with truncation and MAE is minimized at T-3. The author flagged single-club generalizability concerns and noted training subjects contribute full records while the test subject is truncated (population-future schedule leakage). Concordance correlation coefficient: ccc = 2 rho sigma_x sigma_y / (sigma_x^2 + sigma_y^2 + (mu_x - mu_y)^2).

Kampakis thesis Investigation 3 (STATSports Viper10 GPS, 29 THFC players, 1,310 session rows x 69 features, weekly aggregation): supervised PCA (Bair et al. 2006 - screen by univariate |x_j^T y|, PCA on survivors) was best by kappa in both approaches - Approach A kappa 0.21+-0.04 (acc 88.8%, precision 0.55, recall 0.33); ridge logistic second (0.16+-0.33); RF/SVM/GP/MLP/k-NN all ~= 0. Approach B: supervised PCA kappa 0.14+-0.09 despite 97.07% accuracy - accuracy alone is misleading for imbalanced injury classification. SPCA interpretation: PC1 = 'absence of high-speed running' (DistanceZone5, r=-0.764); PC2 = 'medium-speed sprinting'. Investigation 1 recovery-time ML (10x10-fold CV): RF best - RMSE 30.1, corr 0.471+-0.341, ccc 0.406; SVM poly3 RMSE 28.8, corr 0.511; classification kappa best = RF 0.256; ordinal severity regression was rejected (kappa 0.31-0.40). Significant recovery covariates (>50% of tests): recurrence 6/6, phase of play 6/6, body part 5/6, injury diagnosis 5/6, stage of season 3/4.

Siqueira Neto & Fontanari (2022, arXiv:2207.08924v2) test the 'wisdom of crowds' on 15,455 Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Survey of Professional Forecasters contests (20 economic indicators, 1968:Q4-2020:Q4, mean 35 participants per contest, 5 horizons). Odds the crowd beats ALL participants: mean aggregation 0.015, median 0.026 (median ~1.7x better). The median beats the majority BY CONSTRUCTION (no contest with fraction-beaten xi_median > 0.5); the mean beats the majority in only 67% of contests. Mean relative errors: mean aggregation 0.20 +- 0.01, median 0.19 +- 0.01, winners 0.15 +- 0.01, random forecaster 0.22 +- 0.01, ARIMA 0.31 +- 0.01. Median vs mean head-to-head: errors correlated r = 0.98; median beats mean in 50.4% of contests. ARIMA beats a random expert in 35% of contests and the crowd in 28%. 58% of contests have crowd error <=5%; 28% have error >10% - accuracy is good but 'hardly miraculous.'

Siqueira Neto & Fontanari (2022) debunk the 'unbiased estimates / error cancellation' explanation of crowd wisdom: Pearson correlation between unsigned skewness |mu_3| of the forecast distribution and collective error is r = 0.03 - no meaningful correlation. Skewness defined as mu_3 = (1/n) sum((g_i - <g>_n)/delta^{1/2})^3; mean individual error epsilon = (1/n) sum |g_i - G| equals the expected error of a random forecaster; median defined as F_n^{-1}(1/2). The authors' own caveat on Page's diversity prediction theorem (gamma_mean^2 = epsilon_quad - delta): delta and epsilon_quad cannot be varied independently, so the 'more diversity = better' reading is wrong. ARIMA benchmark is a weak strawman (fixed 12-quarter window, univariate).

Zhao & Jiang (2024, arXiv:2409.13888, RecSys 2024) introduce two model-free filter scores that rank candidate context features by the heterogeneous treatment effect they induce across bandit arms (features that change WHICH arm is optimal), rather than by outcome correlation. Heterogeneous Incremental Effect: FI_HIE(x) = sum_{b=1}^{m_x} (N_b/N) * (P_{w_b}(Y=1) - P_{w*}(Y=1)), with w_b = argmax_{i in {1..k}} P_{b_i}(Y=1) (per-bin winning arm) and w* the global winning arm - the sample-weighted incremental gain of using per-bin winners over the global winner. Each feature is binned into m_x bins (each of size N_b) to capture nonlinearity and handle continuous/categorical features uniformly.

Heterogeneous Distribution Divergence (Zhao & Jiang 2024): FI_HDD(x) = sum_b (N_b/N) * D_b(P_{b_1},...,P_{b_k}) - D(P_1,...,P_k), where D_b = sum_{i,j} (N_{b_i} N_{b_j}/N_b^2) * sum_{v in {0,1}} P_{b_i}(Y=v) * log(P_{b_i}(Y=v)/P_{b_j}(Y=v)) is the pairwise KL over binary outcomes within bins - i.e., the sample-weighted contextual KL divergence between arm reward distributions within bins minus the non-contextual (pooled) divergence: how much MORE the arm distributions diverge once conditioned on the feature. Combined score FI(x) = alpha1 * normalized-HIE + alpha2 * normalized-HDD, min-max normalized, alphas as hyperparameters.

Zhao & Jiang (2024) computational finding: model-free HIE/HDD feature selection took 2.7s per trial vs LinUCB 647.3s, nonlinear LinUCB 665.5s, CohortMAB 82.5s (10 features x 50,000 samples) - the model-free screen is ~240x faster than LinUCB-based selection and ~30x faster than CohortMAB, while matching or beating model-embedded selection on downstream contextual multi-armed bandit reward (synthetic CausalML data with 5 true HTE features, plus a real Roblox randomized experiment with 4 arms and 600,000 samples where the added irrelevant random feature ranked lowest). Transfer risks flagged: GSE has no randomized pick-assignment log, so per-bin arm-conditional probabilities would be confounded by selection bias; derivation is binary-reward only; the planned online validation (10k contents x CMAB) was not yet run.

Peterson (2017, arXiv:1710.00431) derives 'decoupled' vs 'coupled' Kelly return functions. Decoupled return: R_avg = sum_{i=1}^N f_i * exp(E[ln(1+f_i X_i)]) - 1 (Eq. 10) - each term needs only the marginal p(X_i), cost N*T. Coupled return: R_c = exp(E[ln(1+sum F_i X_i)]) - 1 (Eq. 11) - requires the N-dimensional integral over the joint distribution p(X), cost T^N. The decoupled form ignores cross-asset dependence in the return term (only the risk term has the cross moments M_ij) - for correlated outcomes this is a real approximation error the paper does not quantify vs the coupled form.

Peterson's decoupled Kelly portfolio model (Eq. 17): max_f P * sum f_i (exp(E[ln(1+f_i X_i)]) - 1) - (1-P) * sum (f_i^4 M_ii + 2 sum_{j>i} f_i^2 f_j^2 M_ij), subject to sum f_i^2 = 1, K_min <= f_i^2 <= K_max (cardinality bounds); wealth fraction in asset i is f_i^2. The risk term: Var[R] = sum (f_i^4 M_ii + 2 sum_{j>i} f_i^2 f_j^2 M_ij) (Eq. 14). GBM calibration: X_i(t+Delta t) = exp((mu_i - sigma_i^2/2) Delta t + sigma_i sqrt(Delta t) * y) - 1; mu_i = ln(1+Avg[R]), sigma_i = (ln(Var[R] e^{-2 mu_i} + 1))^{1/2}. Solver: differential evolution (DE/rand/1/bin, C=0.75, ~100s per run on a 2.4 GHz dual-core).

Peterson (2017) results on 10 stocks (monthly returns): the mean-variance model converged to the same portfolio at all P - heavily concentrated on stock X_10 (weight ~= 0.55, the highest drift-to-vol ratio), all others at the 0.05 lower bound. Decoupled Kelly matched the MV portfolio at P=0.3 and P=0.5 (X_10 ~= 0.55/0.53); at P=0.1 gave a more diversified, lower-return/lower-risk portfolio (X_5=0.1438, X_10=0.4339); converged slowly at P=0.7; MIS-CONVERGED at P=0.9 (lower return AND higher risk - author flags a possible local-maximum trap), confirmed by Monte Carlo return-to-risk ratios. Limitations: single 10-stock dataset, no out-of-sample test; Kelly fractions can exceed 1 (leverage-factor issue); asymptotic (n->infinity) justification while sports slates are finite.

Pagolu, Challa, Panda & Majhi (2016, arXiv:1610.09225v1) build a tweet sentiment analyzer for Microsoft: random forest / logistic regression / SMO on human-annotated tweets, with word2vec (300-dim, summed per tweet) + RF selected (70.18%) over n-gram + RF (70.49%) 'for semantic sustainability'. Per-day features = total positive/negative/neutral counts over a 3-day window; logistic regression and LibSVM predict next-day up/down; 80/20 and 90/10 splits; 355 instances. Data: 250,000 tweets about Microsoft 2015-08-31 to 2016-08-25; MSFT daily open/close from Yahoo Finance; weekend/holiday gaps filled by (x+y)/2 averaging (Goel's method). No equations stated in the paper.

Pagolu et al. (2016) results: sentiment classification word2vec+RF accuracy 70.18% (precision 0.711, recall 0.702, F 0.690); n-gram+RF 70.49% (0.719/0.705/0.694); logistic 62.42%/57.14%; SMO 62.42%/65.84%. Sentiment-classifier ROC AUCs: positive 0.772, neutral 0.778, negative 0.828. Direction prediction: logistic regression 69.01% accuracy; LibSVM (90% train) 71.82%. Human concordance benchmark cited from literature: 70-79% agreement - the sentiment classifier sits at the human-agreement boundary. Limitations: single stock, single year; direction split not stated as time-ordered (random split on a time series = likely lookahead leakage); 71.82% on the 90/10 split is ~36 test points (+-15pp noise); weekend-gap interpolation fabricates price continuity; no naive baseline reported.

Brahma, Das & Magdon-Ismail (2010, arXiv:1009.1446) compare inventory-based (Hanson LMSR) vs information-based market makers in simulation and live human trading, and build a Bayesian market maker (BMM) that converges tightly in equilibrium yet adapts to repeated shocks via a consistency-index detector. LMSR spot: rho(q_t) = e^{q_t/b}/(1+e^{q_t/b}); trade cost C(Q;q_t) = b*ln(1+e^{(q_t+Q)/b}) - b*ln(1+e^{q_t/b}); max loss = b*ln 2 (~8664.34 at b = 125). Zero-profit Glosten-Milgrom baseline: Gaussian belief p_t(v) = N(mu_t, sigma_t^2); trader signal s ~ N(V, sigma_eps^2); information disadvantage rho_t = sigma_t/sigma_eps; ask = mu_t + sigma_eps * Q(rho_t) * sqrt(1+rho_t^2) (universal Q-function); range-based Bayesian belief updates from observed buy/sell/no-trade with bounds (z^-, z^+). The ZP converges fast initially but adapts exponentially slowly after later shocks (overconfidence).

Brahma et al. BMM shock adaptation via consistency index: C(history) = L(mu_t, 2 sigma_t) - L(mu_t, sigma_t), where L(mu,sigma) = integral N(v;mu,sigma) * prod_{i=1}^{W} (Phi(z^+_i, v, sigma_eps) - Phi(z^-_i, v, sigma_eps)) dv over a window W of recent trades; if C > 0, sigma_{t+1} = 2 sigma_t. BMM belief update: mu_{t+1} = mu_t + sigma_t * B/A; sigma_{t+1}^2 = sigma_t^2 (1 - (AC+B^2)/A^2), with A,B,C functions of (z^-, z^+, mu_t, rho_t, sigma_eps); spread = ask - mu_t = sigma_eps * Q(rho_t) * sqrt(1+rho_t^2). Arbitrary trade sizes handled via mini-order heuristic: split Q into chunks of size alpha, quote VWAP of sequential fictitious ZP executions. General law established: inherent tradeoff between adaptability to shocks and convergence in equilibrium (and expected loss); W is the master tradeoff knob. Single-spot-price interface: trader sees only the infinitesimal price, requests a side and size, gets a VWAP quote, may accept or cancel - canceled trades are informative (z^- = p_t, z^+ = p(Q)).

Brahma et al. (2010) results: simulations (1,000 runs x 200 steps; true value ~ N(50,12) truncated to [0,100]; jump prob 0.01 with Gaussian jumps sigma_j=5 or adversarial uniform redraws): Gaussian shocks, matched average spread - BMM profit +2081.35 vs LMSR -2457.30; RMSD 2.92 vs 5.38; BMM max loss 9479.82 vs LMSR 8662.32 (~LMSR's theoretical bound 8664.34). Uniform (adversarial) shocks: BMM profit +603.40 vs -1897.98; RMSD 8.78 vs 10.79; but BMM max loss 50,183.77 vs 8,384.42 - BMM is NOT loss-bounded (worst case ~6x LMSR's bound). Live trading (6 experiments, 9-17 human traders): BMM profit beats LMSR in 5 of 6 experiments (e.g., Equilibrium(1): 47,231.77 vs -1,350.12, though ~30,000 came from one rogue trader buying at 100); post-convergence RMSD_eq strongly favors BMM (LimitedInformation: 0.93 vs 14.56; Equilibrium(5): 1.00 vs 8.15). Counter-case Equilibrium(4): BMM lost -10,588.86 vs LMSR -2,619.07 (misled when the true value was below the 50 starting point and traders had to sell endowments).

Migliorati (2021, arXiv:2111.09695v1) runs a deep-learning feature-selection horse race on NBA game outcomes (2004/05-2019/20, 16 seasons, ~18,000 games): single-feature Elo / relative-win-frequency models beat all Four-Factors-based deep models. Best dynamic Elo (depth 2): AUC 0.7117, accuracy 0.6736. Historical Elo (20% offseason regression to mean, HFA=40, K=30): AUC 0.7117, accuracy 0.6721 - near-identical to depth-2. Elo update used: R <- R + K*(outcome - 1/(1+10^(-(R_opp - R + HFA)/400))). No odds comparison, no calibration metrics (accuracy/AUC only), no properly tabulated walk-forward results; cross-validation over pooled seasons without strict time ordering allows temporal leakage, and feature selection was done on the same data used to report performance.

Byanna & Klabjan (2016, arXiv:1603.07593v2) evaluate NFL offensive linemen without film grades in a five-stage pipeline: (1) stepwise OLS salary model Salary_i = X_i' beta + epsilon learns what the salary market prices; (2) five 'differential statistics' (each = to-side minus not-to-side, or allowed-rate ratios) control for teammates: stuff % differential, yards/attempt differential, successful-run % differential, pressures-allowed %, sack % - the line split into 5 directional splits (LS, L, M, R, RS); (3) k-means (Hartigan-Wong) on standardized salary-model predictors; (4) parametric salary-distribution fits per cluster (Lognormal, Gamma, Beta, Pareto, Weibull); (5) anomaly rule flagging players with P(salary >= S) < 5% (one-sided) as over/undervalued, plus a silhouette gate s(i) > sample mean. Data: STATS LLC play-by-play aggregated game-by-game, every OL with >=1 snap in 2013-14 and 2014-15 (5,383 player-game data points x 44 variables).

Byanna & Klabjan (2016) salary model (Table 11, adj. R^2 = 0.50): intercept 5,399,261 (p=2.12e-15); avg PFF prior to contract +56,697 (p=0.00268); experience -199,134 (p=0.00831); draft round -264,405 (p=5.38e-5); Pro Bowl selections +624,910 (p=0.000338); stuff % differential -82,247 (p=0.012284); yds/attempt differential +382,197; sack % -2,516 (p=0.022994). Current-year PFF rating NOT significant (dropped) - differential stats beat PFF for salary explanation; adding not-to-side terms raised adj. R^2 from 0.47 to 0.50 with opposite-signed not-to-side coefficients as the control logic predicts. Clusters k=7 (n=133): sizes 25/17/18/23/24/8/18; salary means $5.12M/$2.97M/$3.84M/$2.21M/$2.53M/$6.66M/$3.10M; mean silhouette ~= 0.16 (weak; Kaufman-Rousseeuw suggest >0.25). Flagged: undervalued John Jerry (NYG G, 2014, $795,635), Mike McGlynn (KC G, 2014, $1,037,594); overvalued Scott Wells (STL C, 2013&2014, $5,283,150), Davin Joseph (TB G, 2013, $6,889,518); PFF ranks corroborated 4 of 5 in direction; the paper's headline finding N is internally inconsistent (abstract says five players, conclusion says 3+3).

Sobkowicz et al. (2019, arXiv:1910.03400, Physica A 2020) model tournament performance as a linear talent-luck mix: P_j(t) = a * T_j + (1 - a) * L_j(t), with T_j in [0,1] fixed per agent (symmetric, centered at 0.5; uniform or truncated Gaussian with sigma_T in {0.1, 0.2}) and L_j(t) ~ U(0,1) i.i.d. per round. Tournament: 1,000,000 agents grouped in tens, highest performance advances, 6 rounds select a winner; repeated 1000 times per configuration. Since talent is fixed and the weighted luck component is U(0, 1-a), the difference of two subsequent runs has a symmetric triangular distribution on [-(1-a), (1-a)] with SD = (1-a)/sqrt(6). Fitted to empirical Olympic 100m results from 13 Olympic Games (1968-2016), with performance rescaled p = t_WR/t (world-record time at race date / run time).

Sobkowicz et al. (2019) best-fit parameters: men sigma_T = 0.15, a = 0.96; women sigma_T = 0.14, a = 0.94 - random luck accounts for ~4% of performance for men and ~6% for women at the Olympic level, presented as a strong lower bound for less controlled domains. Stage averages (empirical men: RO+QF 0.934 (SD 0.032), SF 0.959 (0.014), FIN 0.975 (0.013); model: 0.935/0.968/0.975 - agreement within ~0.007 everywhere). Individual run-to-run variability: empirical SD ~= 0.012-0.013 both sexes; model-predicted SD = 0.04/sqrt(6) ~= 0.016 (men), 0.06/sqrt(6) ~= 0.024 (women) - the women's empirical value is notably below the model prediction. Lucky-streaks (sigma_T=0.2, a=0.5): of 1000 final winners, 852 were 'moderately lucky' (L > 0.5) in all 6 rounds; 232 'very lucky' (L > 0.75) in all 6; almost no final winner was moderately lucky in fewer than 5 of 6 rounds. Talent cutoffs: practically no agent with talent < 0.5 won round 3 despite 50% luck weight; cutoffs ~0.7 (round 4), ~0.8 (round 5) - talent gates late-stage participation even when luck dominates individual rounds. Injustice metric Z_t = Q/Delta-TL_t with Delta-TL_t = TL(t+1) - TL(t) reached 2700 for finalists vs the winner under linear payoff growth (a=1, sigma_T=0.2).
equation: Z_t = Q / ΔTL_t, ΔTL_t = TL(t+1) − TL(t)

claim: Tang, Wang & Jin (2025, arXiv:2502.10985) ask why Elo beats more complex systems (mElo/Elo2k, pairwise) at prediction despite every dataset rejecting the Bradley-Terry model Elo assumes; answer: Elo = online gradient descent on convex log-loss with a regret bound, and data sparsity (t/N) decides the complexity winner. Elo update: p_t = sigma(theta_t[i_t] - theta_t[j_t]); theta_{t+1}[i] <- theta_t[i] + eta_t (o_t - p_t). BT model: P(o_t=1|i,j) = sigma(theta*[i] - theta*[j]). Loss decomposition: L_T = model misspecification error + Regret_T. Theorem 1: OGD with eta_t = D/(G sqrt(t)) gives Regret_T <= (3/2) G D sqrt(T); for Elo, empirical ||theta||_inf <= 5 so D = 10 sqrt(N), G <= sqrt(2), giving (1/T) Regret_T <= C sqrt(N/T) with eta_t = sqrt(N/t) - holds under misspecification and non-stationarity. Hessian: grad^2 f_t = p_t(1-p_t)(e_i - e_j)(e_i - e_j)^T >= 0 (convexity); Elo2k loss is non-convex - no OGD guarantee.

Tang et al. (2025) learning-rate schedule replacing hand-tuned K: eta_t = sqrt(aN/(t+b)), standard eta in [10/C ~= 0.06, 40/C ~= 0.23] with C = 400/ln 10; hyperparameters chosen by minimizing L(v) = sum_{i=1}^{30} (CE_i + 5(CE_i - ln2) 1{CE_i > ln2}) - penalizing overfitting across 30 checkpoints. BT rejection test (logistic-regression form of BT, likelihood-ratio statistic Lambda ~ chi^2_2 with Wilks, Sur et al. 1.25 chi^2_2 correction for high-dim; second martingale test using online Elo ratings robust to adaptive matchmaking) rejects the BT model on all 8 datasets at eta = 0.08. Theorem 2/G.1: under product matchmaking q_ij = q_i q_j (incl. uniform), population BT-MLE theta* induces the same ranking as average win rate; under SST, Elo recovers the true ranking asymptotically - but Example 1 (SST 5-player + structured matchmaking Q) shows Elo/MLE can be ranking-inconsistent with ground truth under arbitrary matchmaking (theta^mle = [5.48, 0.89, 4.60, 0.04, 0], ranking 1>3>2>4>5 vs truth), with bootstrap CIs confirming.

Tang et al. (2025) empirical sparsity rule on 8 real datasets (N players, 2T/N games-per-player): BT rejected everywhere (p < 10^-4, most < 10^-10). Table 2 average CE loss - Elo-family best or tied in all 6 sparse datasets: Renju 0.6039 (Pairwise 0.6688), Chess 0.6391, Tennis 0.6242 (Pairwise 0.6820), Scrabble 0.6730, StarCraft 0.5713 (Pairwise 0.6753), Go 0.6443. Only in dense sets does Elo2k win: Hearthstone 0.6847 vs 0.6898 (also AlphaStar-dense, go-dense, mixedchess-dense). Sparsity rule (empirical, not derived): t/N < 1000 -> Elo/Elo2k/pairwise ordering favors Elo (regret dominates); t/N > 1000 -> model capacity wins when Elo2k's hindsight baseline is better. Blotto sparse vs 10x dense: same underlying non-BT model, different winner - sparsity, not model, decides. NFL implication: N=32 teams, T~=285 games/season -> t/N ~= 9 (extreme-sparse) -> Elo-family only, no pairwise/head-to-head parameters, no per-QB-matchup matrices. Pairwise ranking inconsistency tau is strongly correlated with prediction performance.

Landry, Charantonis & Monteleoni (2024, arXiv:2406.02141) turn a single deterministic NWP forecast into a calibrated probabilistic one (no ensemble needed) with a Bernstein Quantile Network (BQN). Bernstein quantile function: Q(tau) = sum_{j=0}^{d} theta_j C(d,j) tau^j (1-tau)^{d-j}, degree d = 16, sorted theta => monotone Q. Uncertainty representations compared: deterministic (RMSE loss); EMOS/DRN (Normal via Y_obs ~ N(theta_1 x_nwp + theta_2, exp(theta_3 log sigma-hat + theta_4)) with sigma-hat = error SD when no ensemble, CRPS loss); LQR/QRN (quantile regression, quantile loss, n quantiles at tau = i/(n+1)); LBQ/BQN (Bernstein polynomial quantile function, degree 16, coefficient sorting for monotonicity, sampled at 98 tau values, quantile loss). Models: linear MOS-style and MLP (4x256, SiLU, batch norm; station + lead-time embeddings added after the first linear layer); NNs trained 5x and parameter-averaged (Vincentization for quantiles); Adam, 100 epochs, OneCycleLR, weight decay 1e-5. Data: GDPS deterministic surface-temperature forecasts at 1,066 METAR stations across Canada/US; 25 predictors; train 2019-2020, test Jan-Nov 2021.

Landry et al. (2024) CRPS (all stations x lead times): raw 2.925 -> naive 1.921 -> MOS 2.467 -> EMOS 1.700 -> DNN 2.315 -> DRN 1.633, BQN 1.622 (best), QRN 1.635. CRPSS = 1 - CRPS_model/CRPS_baseline vs naive: EMOS 0.115, DRN 0.150, BQN 0.156, QRN 0.149 - NN BQN ~= 15-16% CRPS reduction vs the naive probabilistic baseline. NN gains over EMOS significant at early leads, shrinking to ~2.5% at late leads. Joint multi-lead-time training with lead-time embeddings beats per-lead-time partitioning (DRN 1.655 -> 1.634; BQN 1.641 -> 1.622); embedding alone ~= predictor alone; joint best in central lead times. ENS10 ablation: adding the 2nd ensemble member gives a sharp CRPSS jump even with postprocessing; diminishing returns after; member impact grows with lead time. Calibration: all models flatten central rank histograms vs naive; BQN's Bernstein edges show slight artifacts. Extremes: all models degrade at forecast tails; the Feb 2021 Texas cold event was out-of-distribution (CRPSS collapse in low winter percentiles) - the model cannot invent tails it has not seen. Naive baseline = station/init-hour/lead-time/month-debiased NWP + Normal(0, error SD). Leakage caveat: train/validation split not fully independent (late leads of training days overlap early leads of validation days).

Flepp, Pawlowski & Richardson (2025, arXiv:2506.21253v1) replace classical outcome uncertainty with two within-match belief-path entertainment metrics from Ely, Frankel & Kamenica (2015, JPE), validated on 25,389 real men's matches (2010/11-2023/24), 725 women's matches (2023/24), and 13.26M simulated matches. Surprise (backward-looking belief shift summed over 90 minute-periods): Surprise = sum_{t=1}^{90} sqrt((p_t^H - p_{t-1}^H)^2 + (p_t^D - p_{t-1}^D)^2 + (p_t^A - p_{t-1}^A)^2). Suspense (forward-looking variance of next-period beliefs given a home-score or away-score event): Suspense = sum_{t=1}^{90} sqrt(sum_{j in {H,D,A}} [p_{t+1}^{HS} ((p_{t+1}^j|HS_{t+1}) - p_t^j)^2 + p_{t+1}^{AS} ((p_{t+1}^j|AS_{t+1}) - p_t^j)^2]).

Suspense and surprise empirical results (Flepp et al. 2025): benchmark ranges from perfectly balanced matches (lambdaH=lambdaA) at 10th (0.5) and 90th (2.5) percentiles of empirical goals/team/match: suspense [6.03, 6.89] (low-scoring 6.89, high-scoring 6.03), surprise [1.17, 1.74] (low 1.17, high 1.74). Empirical top-5-league average suspense 5.85 (SD 2.14) - significantly BELOW the benchmark lower bound 6.03 (p<0.01) in every league (EPL lowest 5.74, Ligue 1 highest 5.99); average surprise 1.41 (SD 0.80) - inside the benchmark. Classical outcome-uncertainty (absolute pre-match win-probability difference) correlates only -0.39 with suspense and -0.18 with surprise and is NON-SIGNIFICANT in the TV-demand regression, while ln(suspense) beta=0.042 (p=0.015) and ln(surprise) beta=0.050 (p=0.004) on ln(audience) - an empirical refutation of pre-match-uncertainty-as-demand-proxy. Trends: EPL suspense -0.6%/season overall driven entirely by Man City (-3.9%/season suspense, -2.5%/season surprise); Bundesliga -0.7%/-0.5% not top-team driven; La Liga +0.6% baseline (Real Madrid +4.5%/season, Barcelona +5.6%); PSG -3.1%/-2.4%. Simulation tradeoff: suspense peaks at lambdaH=lambdaA=0.5 and is ZERO at (0,0) even though perfectly balanced; raising one team's scoring rate moves suspense and surprise in OPPOSITE directions.

Shekhar, Ghavamzadeh & Javidi (2019, arXiv:1905.09561v1) derive the Bayes-optimal classifier under a bounded-rate abstention constraint (abstain on at most fraction delta, no per-abstention cost) plus a semi-supervised plug-in rule that sets the abstention threshold from UNLABELED data with minimax-near-optimal excess-risk bounds. Bayes-optimal threshold: gamma_delta = sup{gamma>0 : P_X(|eta(X)-1/2| <= gamma) <= delta} - partition by ambiguity |eta(x)-1/2|: predict +-1 outside, abstain inside. Randomized boundary rule: c_0 = (delta - delta_1)/(delta_2 - delta_1) - randomize on boundary shells where the ambiguity cdf jumps, to hit the rate exactly. Reduces to Chow 1957 / Denis & Hebiri 2015 when the cdf of |eta-1/2| is continuous, but holds for arbitrary distributions. Plug-in: estimate eta with an adaptive histogram (Lepski-type data-driven bandwidth balancing stochastic error ~(nh^D)^-1/2 against Holder bias ~h^beta, optimal h ~= n^{-1/(2beta+D)}), then set the abstention threshold from m UNLABELED samples via the empirical cdf of |eta-hat - 1/2| - satisfies the delta constraint with high probability and handles cdf discontinuities. Theorem 2: excess-risk upper bound under Holder + margin assumptions; Theorem 3: minimax lower bound - near-optimal rates.

Shekhar et al. (2019) experiment on UCI PIMA (768x8), delta in {0.1,...,0.6}: accuracy rises MONOTONICALLY with delta (more abstention -> higher accuracy on decided points); the plug-in rule's achieved rejection rate tracks delta TIGHTLY, while the convex-surrogate baseline is conservative (achieves less than delta). Limitations: the histogram plug-in is a theoretical device intractable in high dimensions; bounded-rate assumes the delta budget is the right primitive (in wagering the cost of a skip is economic, not a hard rate); no calibration discussion - the rule needs accurate |eta-hat - 1/2|, i.e., calibrated probabilities. The threshold is set from unlabeled data, so there is no label leakage by construction.

Cheng Yana / Xin Li / Guoqiang Li (2020, arXiv:2012.00253) build a hierarchical three-level (player -> frame -> short-segment) Boolean voting pipeline on YOLOv3 + OpenPose that clips rally highlights from full table-tennis broadcasts. Highlight = partition of playing segments: S = {Sp1, Snp1, Sp2, Snp2, ...}, SP = {Sp1, Sp2, ...} (Eq 1-2). Middle-level per-frame: YOLO rule - frame is playing iff sum P_playing(p) > sum P_non-playing(p) (Eq 3); OpenPose rule - frame is playing iff a playing action exists among the first 2 detected humans (Eq 4). High-level segment voting: a k-frame window s is playing iff Prp(s) > Prc, where Pr_play(s) = (1/k) sum_i Bp_i (Eq 5-6), emitting interval set {t_start, t_end} (Eq 7). Action merge: delete the gap between consecutive segments if (t_begin^{i+1} - t_end^i) < Delta t (Eq 8), producing final clip intervals (Eq 9). Labels: binary 'playing' (serve, push, loop, etc.) vs 'non-playing' (ball-picking, shoe-lacing, rest, preparation). Validation metrics: precision P = Rcd/Rd, recall R = Rcd/Ra, combined C = 2PR/(P+R) on rally detection (Rcd = correctly detected rallies, Rd = detected, Ra = actual).
equation: f playing iff Σ P_playing(p) > Σ P_non-playing(p)

claim: Cheng et al. (2020) rally-detection results (10 table-tennis videos, 640x352 @25fps, ~640k frames total): YOLOv3 average P 96.4%, R 96.2%, C 96.2%; OpenPose average P 95.7%, R 87.3%, C 90.7%. Initial frame-level accuracy (before voting) was only ~80% for both models - the voting cascade lifts frame-level ~80% to rally-level ~96% C. Runtimes: OpenPose 1870 s vs YOLOv3 782 s on the 518-image benchmark - the paper claims OpenPose is '1.39x slower' but its own arithmetic gives 2.39x (flagged as a suspect arithmetic slip). Training: YOLOv3 - 689 manually annotated images (518 'playing' vs 205 'non-playing'); OpenPose - 15,216 action feature vectors from a single 10-minute match video. Limitations: single sport, low-res, one visual style, no cross-dataset validation, arXiv-only with sloppy presentation; rally-level metrics inflate over frame-level error (a 1-frame miss inside a rally still counts as detected). Baselines claimed beaten: Chakraborty & Zhang 2016 (58.58% P / 49.58% R), Gygli 2018 (86% P / 90.8% R), Liu et al. 2009 (86% P / 84.8% R), Tang et al. 2011 (12.1% error).

Martin et al. (arXiv:2301.13576v1, MediaEval 2022) define the Sport Task benchmark protocol: fine-grained table-tennis stroke detection/classification on TTStroke-21 with two subtasks. Subtask 1 (classification): global + per-class accuracy on trimmed clips; 21 classes (20 stroke classes - 8 services, 6 offensive, 6 defensive, Forehand/Backhand super-classes - + non-stroke); 1,155 trimmed videos (>210K frames), 807 train / 230 val / 118 test. Subtask 2 (detection): COCO-style temporal mAP - AP averaged over 20 IoU thresholds {0.50, 0.55, ..., 0.95} (step 0.05); detection = True when temporal IoU >= threshold; frame-wise temporal IoU as secondary metric; 28 untrimmed videos, 100 minutes, >718K frames at 120 FPS, 16/6/6 train/val/test (videos disjoint; players may repeat). Protocol: up to 5 runs per subtask via XML submission; fully automatic; working-notes paper required; pre-trained models on prior years' TTStroke-21 FORBIDDEN (keeps yearly comparisons honest). Baseline code: github.com/ccp-eva/SportTaskME22. License terms have EXPIRED (data destruction was required by 2023-01-30); faces blurred via SSD+ResNet detector + tracking; annotations by professional players.

MediaEval Sport Task 2021 reference results: classification - best 74.2% global accuracy (Qian et al., SWIN-Transformer, long-tail-aware), ResNet-50 68.8%, baseline 20.4%; detection - NO submission beat the baseline mAP; best frame-wise IoU 0.247 (YOLOv5) vs baseline 0.144. Transferable lessons flagged: long-tail-aware training decides fine-grained sports classification (the >=30-point per-class head-vs-tail accuracy spread is the health check for any GSE fine-grained classifier - judged on per-class accuracy, not just global); a trivial baseline must score near chance on classification to validate task difficulty; the 'forbid pre-training on prior benchmark years' rule plus mandatory working-notes documentation is a governance template for honest year-over-year model comparison; boundary-precision scoring (mean absolute boundary error in frames) should be added since downstream clip products care about exact cut points, not just IoU-thresholded mAP.

Csato & Gyimesi (arXiv:2601.09673v3) formalize match classification by incentive structure: six classes (competitive, unimportant, offensive-incentive, defensive-incentive, collusion-vulnerable, asymmetric) derived from each team's (G, L) position, from simulated prize probabilities under W/D/L outcomes. Gain from offensive play: G = P(prize | W) - P(prize | D); loss: L = P(prize | D) - P(prize | loss avoided); indifference threshold = the (G, L) point where a team is indifferent between attacking and defending; incentive strength kappa = distance from indifference (quantifies how far a match is from indifference). Simulation: 500 pre-final-round scenarios x 1,000 final-round outcome simulations; fixed Elo strengths; independent Poisson scores; UEFA-style tournament structures; complete vs incomplete round-robin designs compared on class mix. No code or data released.
equation: G = P(prize | W) − P(prize | D); L = P(prize | D) − P(prize | loss avoided)

claim: Csato & Gyimesi (2601.09673v3) directional finding: incomplete round robins produce FEWER unimportant matches but MORE offensive and MORE defensive/collusion-vulnerable matches than complete ones (no hard numeric given in the file). Limitations: static pre-match incentives - no in-match updating (a team leading 2-0 has different incentives than the pre-match class says); naive/level-1 behavior assumed (teams maximize own prize probability without strategic interaction); simplified prizes, fixed Elo, trained on old UEFA formats; six classes are a discretization of a continuous incentive space. The paper's setup is ex-ante simulation from pre-round standings (no result leakage). NFL analogues flagged: rest-vs-seed final-week games, tanking-adjacent fixtures, playoff-scenario games - the same (G, L) machinery applies with playoff-prize probabilities under W/D/L. This was a fresh-search replacement for 1311.1131v1 (already in done-ids.txt - assigned duplicate, not a REJECT).

Qi, Cai, Hu & Shen (2025, arXiv:2506.11399v1) propose DYNAMO - causal-structure learning for non-stationary time series estimating time-varying causal DAGs - and apply it to 760 EPL matches to decompose home-field advantage into a referee-bias pathway (crowd pressure -> opponent fouls/yellow cards -> xG) versus a performance pathway. Model: x_t := f(Pa(x_t), eps_t; theta(tau_t)), tau_t = t/T; parents from instantaneous + L lagged variables; causal structure theta(tau_t) varies smoothly with t. Assumptions: (1) unconfoundedness (no unobserved confounders), (2) per-time-point DAG acyclicity, (3) locally stationary causality (Lipschitz contraction sum alpha_j(theta) < 1, parameter-space Lipschitz), (4) symmetric Lipschitz kernel with bandwidth h, (T,h) -> (infty,0), Th -> infty. Theorem 1: structural identifiability under Assumptions 1-4 with no faithfulness assumption. Theorem 2: theta-hat(tau_t) -> theta(tau_t) with probability -> 1 as (T,h) -> (infty,0), Th -> infty, Th^7 -> 0.
equation: x_t := f(Pa(x_t), ε_t; θ(τ_t)), τ_t = t/T

claim: DYNAMO loss: L_t(theta) = (1/Th) sum_l l(x_l, Y_{l-1}; theta) K_h(tau_l - tau_t). Linear variant (eq. 4): NOTEARS loss ||x_l - W_t^T x_l - A_t^T Y_{l-1}||_2^2 K_h + lambda_1 ||W_t|| + lambda_2 ||A_t|| + (rho/2) H(W_t)^2 + alpha H(W_t), with the acyclicity trace-exponential H(W) = tr(e^{W o W}) - d, solved via W = W_+ - W_- split with L-BFGS-B. Nonlinear variant (eq. 5): NTS-NOTEAR loss with neural net g_t and induced graph W_t(g_t). Bandwidth via quasi-k-fold CV minimizing L_CV^t(h); Epanechnikov kernel recommended. Props 1-2: a stationary approximation x-tilde_t(tau) exists per tau with identical causal structure and ||x_t - x-tilde_t(tau_t)||_q = O(T^-1).
equation: ℒ_t(ϑ) = (1/Th) Σ_l ℓ(x_l, Y_{l−1}; ϑ) K_h(τ_l − τ_t)

claim: DYNAMO empirical findings on 760 EPL matches (>1.6M within-game events, proprietary Hudl & Wyscout data; 2020-21 closed doors vs 2021-22 with spectators; variables per minute per team as home-away differences demeaned vs opponent): 2020-21 empty stadiums - home win 37.9% vs away win 40.3% (home advantage collapsed below away); 2021-22 crowds back - home win 43.0%, +9 points over away. Referee-bias pathways (opponent fouls/yellows -> xG) are time-varying within matches and team-specific: Liverpool steady escalating bias with crowds (Anfield); Man City early opponent yellows then second-half fouls; Arsenal flipped from second-half favoritism (empty) to performance-driven bias (crowded); non-relegated teams shifted from opponent fouls (empty) to opponent yellow cards (crowded) - crowd pressure makes refs punish away teams more harshly; lower-ranked/relegated teams barely changed. DYNAMO-predicted minute-level xG beat DYNOTEARS and raw xG on goal-prediction MSE for all 4 studied teams across both seasons; Arsenal 2021-22 MSE 0.00079 vs 0.00106 (DYNOTEARS) vs 0.00111 (raw xG) ~= 29% improvement (worst-team MSE 0.00079 used as the numeric gate; absolute improvements are small, e.g. Arsenal 2020-21: 0.00046 vs 0.00063). Simulation used self-generated ER graphs (T=500, cosine time-varying weights), flagged as circular evaluation; the 4-team deep dive is cherry-picked with 16-team summary compressed into an unfetched appendix.

Jain & Saha (2016, arXiv:1601.04203v2) design DFS tournament payout structures in two stages: fit a power-law 'ideal' payout curve via binary search, then bucket/round it into legal payouts minimizing squared distance to the ideal. Ideal payout: pi_i = E + (P1 - E)/i^alpha, where E = entry fee (minimum payout), P1 = first prize, i = place. Budget identity: B - N*E = sum_{i=1..N} (P1 - E)/i^alpha (B = total prize pool, N = paid places); RHS strictly decreasing in alpha -> binary search finds alpha. Optimization: minimize sum_i (p_i - pi_i)^2 subject to sum_i p_i = B; p_1 >= p_2 >= ... >= p_N (monotonicity); p_i >= E; p_i in a nice-number set; constant payout within each of r contiguous buckets. Three algorithms: (a) exact DP over bucket boundaries and payout values - time O(r N^3 B log^2 B), space O(r N^2 B log B) (impractical at scale); (b) integer linear program; (c) four-stage production heuristic (Yahoo's deployed version: greedy bucket formation + local adjustments + extra-winner redistribution).

Jain & Saha (2016) DFS payout findings: power-law fit across real tournaments - average p-value .237 (fit not rejected). Production heuristic runtime under 1.5 seconds even on the hardest contests tested (2.6 GHz i7, 16 GB RAM); DraftKings 125,000-winner contest: heuristic solution cost 78.7k, runtime 1,700 ms, zero extra winners added. Limitations: power-law ideal validated on a small set of observed tournaments; the squared-distance objective is a modeling choice, not derived from player-behavior data (no A/B or elasticity evidence the shape maximizes entries/revenue); optimizes a fixed contest, not an operator's contest portfolio; nothing about player skill distributions or payout-driven entry behavior; no code or dataset released. The brief verdicts this as contest-economics/product IP (pick'em pools, subscriber tournaments, leaderboard payouts), not engine prediction IP - it fills the research map's Gap 10 (DFS-specific optimization literature).

Cui et al. (2026, arXiv:2606.09941v1) build a deep generative model (Time VQ-VAE tokenization + MaskGIT bidirectional transformer) for synthesizing minute-by-minute wind-vector time series at one Oklahoma site. Masked token-wise NLL: L(theta) = -sum_i sum_{t:m=1} sum_k 1(s_t^{(i)}=k) log p(s_t^{(i)}=k | s_{1:C}^{(i-1)}, s_{m(1:T)}^{(i)}); sampling via iterative MaskGIT decoding. Energy score: ES(F,y) = (1/m) sum ||Xi - y|| - (1/2m^2) sum sum ||Xi - Xj||. Quantile-regression volatility diagnostic: minimize sum rho_tau(d_t - beta^T f(.)), rho_tau(u) = u(tau - 1{u<0}). Data: US DOE ARM facility, Lamont, Oklahoma, 1 Hz surface meteorology to minute scale, June only 1994-2025 (June to suppress seasonality); train June 1-21, 1998-2020 (474 days); validation June 22-30; test 1994-1997 + 2021-2025 (185 days); gaps <=20 min imputed with Brownian bridges. Two temporal modes (independent days vs consecutive-day conditioning on last 60 min of prior day); weather-state variants None / as-Feature / Embedded.

Cui et al. (2026) wind-generator evaluation: discriminator (bidirectional LSTM, real vs synthetic, best variant Embedded+Consecutive, 50 seeds) - real 0.766 (0.052), synthetic 0.744 (0.081): well above 0.5 chance, so synthetic days are detectable; high-pass-filtered accuracy 0.896 on synthetic. Energy scores (Embedded+Independent): median +0.55% vs training baseline, IQR [-2.12%, +3.12%]. Volatility: Embedded generator replicates the 42.0% C_0.9 reduction (achieves 40.6%); Features generator underestimates baseline volatility by ~26%. TAILS: no generated wind speed exceeds the 22.7 m/s training max in 50,000 days (Embedded: 3 exceedances); observations exceed 20 m/s 28 times. Authors' conclusion: nonparametric generators are 'understandably unable to reproduce extreme winds accurately.' Day-boundary transitions unrealistic (RMS day-boundary wind-speed change 1.17-1.34 vs 0.73 observed). The brief verdicts REJECT for GSE: the generator explicitly fails on extreme winds - the exact tail regime that would matter for game-day applications (kicking game, deep passing) - and minute-scale single-site simulation has no path to NFL prediction value; the weather/wind lane is carried by ledgers 1098/1305 instead.

Liu, Jiang, Wang & Li (2020, arXiv:2010.00526v1) introduce LiveQA, a sports question-answering dataset over live NBA broadcast text - 1,670 documents, 1,786,616 sentences, 117,050 quizzes - requiring tracking entities across a ~1,070-sentence timeline plus inference and calculation, not just span extraction. Scale: per-document averages 1,069.83 sentences, 70.09 quizzes. Evidence location: contextual 68.6%, after game 30.6%, impossible 0.8%. Question-type distribution: comparison 16.6%, calculation 25.4%, inference 28.5%, tracking 29.5%. Baselines: random 50.0%, dominant-option 56.4%, gated-attention reader 53.1% - the neural reader LOSES to the dominant-option heuristic, showing how hard timeline reasoning over 1,000+ sentences is. Limitations: dominant-option beating the neural model is a red flag for dataset bias (answer-distribution artifacts); NBA-only, broadcast-text only; exact train/dev/test split not recorded; impossible-answer rate 0.8% too low to test abstention; models are 2020-era - modern long-context LLMs need re-benchmarking. Code: github.com/PKU-TANGENT/GAReader-LiveQA; data: github.com/PKU-TANGENT/LiveQA. The transferable artifact is the dataset taxonomy (comparison/calculation/inference/tracking) and the timeline-evidence-location labeling design, not the 2020-era reader architectures.

Rendar & Ma (2022, arXiv:2207.00585v1) is a two-page podium abstract predicting ulnar collateral ligament (Tommy John) injury in rookie MLB pitchers from rookie-season tabular stats - 8,503 pitchers debuting after 1974, 826 positive / 7,677 negative (~1:10 imbalance), 47 Stathead features -> K-best 13 -> six models, best MLP at ROC-AUC 0.674. Method: 80/20 split 'according to year' (split years not stated); oversampling applied to training set; models KNN, Naive Bayes, XGBoost, Random Forest, Decision Tree, MLP (hyperparameters not stated); metric ROC-AUC; no cross-validation, no confidence intervals, no calibration. ROC-AUC: KNN 0.5702; Naive Bayes 0.5463; XGBoost 0.6068; Random Forest 0.6143; Decision Tree 0.6329; MLP 0.6740 (best). Limitations: no feature list, no split years, no hyperparameters, no uncertainty intervals - nothing independently reproducible; name-join label noise between Stathead and the TJ repository directly corrupts labels; AUC 0.674 is modest and at 1:10 imbalance precision at any usable recall is likely poor (not reported); 'split according to year' without years - temporal cleanliness unverifiable; no trivial baseline (e.g., innings-pitched workload alone). The brief verdicts ADAPT as a compact, honest tabular injury-prediction protocol for NFL rookie injury risk, treating the missing details as gaps to fill rather than results to trust.

The full-read ledger of arXiv:2511.04361v2 (ATSCM, Adaptive Time-varying Structural Causal Model for energy market regime detection), a 5-page workshop paper, was verdict REJECT: it contains zero empirical content - no dataset, no experiment, no baseline, no number - with authors deferring 'empirical validation' to future work; its abstract claim of 'competitive forecasting performance' is flagged as unsupported. Conceptual architecture only: three levels (interpretable factors W^t in R^27, latent dynamics I^t, observations V^t in R^35); time-varying causal graph G^t = f_discovery(V^{1:t}, W^{1:t}; theta_disc); objective = reconstruction + causal + counterfactual + discovery losses; no theorems, no identification assumptions stated. Per the program's replace-on-reject rule, a replacement full read is owed on reserve ledger 1318.

FanCric (Bhatnagar 2024, arXiv:2410.01307), verdict ADAPT, is a six-agent LLM pipeline for fantasy cricket teams orchestrated via LangGraph: Supervisor, Researcher (venue/home-away, weather both innings - temp, wind, cloud cover, dew, humidity; pitch reports; win odds), Career Profiler (career stats + strengths/weaknesses using ESPN Cricinfo player IDs instead of names to avoid LLM name bias), Form Assessor (recent form, home/away, batting first/second splits), Strategizer, Selector (rule compliance via agentic search, generates n teams, iterative refinement reviewed by the stronger GPT-4o while all other agents used GPT-4o-mini - a model-strength confound), Evaluator (post-match fantasy-point backtest). No equations are stated (LLM-prompted system, not a statistical model).

FanCric evaluated on a single IPL 2023 match (Lucknow vs Mumbai, May 16, 2023) against 12.7M Dream11 crowd entries: crowd mean 501.54, std 89.02, median 512, min 0, max 811.5, ex-post optimal 'Dream Team' 832.5 (KS statistic 0.14, p=0.0, non-normal, left-skewed). Prompt-engineering baseline (gpt-4o-mini, temperature=1, few-shot, n=10): mean 512.9 (50.4 percentile), win rate 70%, best 634 (95.1 percentile). FanCric (n=10): mean 528.55 (58.6 percentile), win rate 80%, best 644 (96.3 percentile), 'Strategic Strikers' with Marcus Stoinis (C), 6/11 Dream Team players. Ablation n=20: FanCric avg points 528.5, avg rank 56.9, win% 75%, highest rank 99.9 percentile with 722 points vs prompt-engineering 481.6 / 42.9 / 50% / 95.9; n=5: FanCric 507.7 / 53.0 / 60% / 86.3 vs prompt 501.7 / 55.1 / 80% / 86.1; n=1: FanCric 522.5 / 55.6 / 100% / 55.6 vs prompt 535.5 / 61.9 / 100% / 61.9 (the only n where prompt engineering won). Limitations: n=1 match with no confidence intervals or multiple-comparison correction; salary-cap optimization (the core of NFL DFS) absent - Dream11's constraint is credit-based quotas, not dollar salary.

Gayen, Pal, Manwani & Sharma (2025, arXiv:2501.08397v1) graft coverage-constrained abstention (reject option) onto temporal GNN encoders (TGN, GraphMixer, DyGFormer) for continuous-time dynamic graphs. Objective (eq. 1): max_{f,q} P(f(x)=y | q(x)=0) = max_{f,q} P(f(x)=y | a(x) ≤ θ), θ in (0,1). Link-prediction loss (eq. 2): L^E_t(f,q) = r-hat(f,q|E_t) + λΨ(c − φ-hat(q|E_t)), Ψ(b) = max(0,b)^2. Empirical selective risk (eq. 3): r-hat(f,q|E_t) = Σ_{(u,v,t) in E_t} ℓ(f(z_u(t),z_v(t)), y_{E_t})(1 − q(z_u(t),z_v(t))) / (|E_t| φ-hat(q|E_t)). Empirical coverage (eq. 4): φ-hat(q|E_t) = (1/|E_t|) Σ_{(u,v,t) in E_t (1 − q(z_u(t),z_v(t))). Combined (eq. 5): L^E_t = α L^E_t(f,q) + (1−α) L^E_{h,t} (auxiliary head = plain BCE on ALL samples with no coverage gating, so the model still sees rejected samples). Architecture: prediction head f(x) + abstention head q(x) in {0,1} producing scalar score a(x) in [0,1]; scores sorted on validation, threshold θ chosen to hit target coverage c; abstain iff a(x) > θ.
equation: max_{f,q} P(f(x)=y | q(x)=0) = max_{f,q} P(f(x)=y | a(x) ≤ θ), θ ∈ (0,1)

claim: Node-classification mirror losses (eqs. 6-9) plus imbalance-weighted auxiliary loss (eq. 10): L^V_{h,t} = β L^V_{h,minor,t} + L^V_{h,major,t}, β > 1. Training hyperparameters (verbatim): Adam (link prediction; node classification on Wikipedia) / SGD (Reddit node classification), 75 epochs, early stopping patience 10, batch 200, λ=32, α=0.5, 100-dim time encoding, 172-dim output; 5 seeds (0-4), mean ± std reported. Class imbalance: searched β in [2,100]; best β = 2 or 5, results degrade for β ≥ 10 (Table 5). Coverage sweep 100%, 90%, 80%, 70%, 60%, 50% (θ re-set per coverage on validation-sorted scores). Metrics: AP and AUC-ROC for link prediction under random/historical/inductive negative sampling; AUC-ROC for node classification. Baselines: TGN and GraphMixer without reject option (= 100% coverage row), DyGFormer in appendix.

Gayen et al. (2025) abstention results: transductive link-pred AP (Table 1, random NSS), TGN - Wikipedia 98.56 ± 0.06 (100% coverage) → 99.88 ± 0.02 (60%); Reddit 98.63 ± 0.02 → 99.86 ± 0.04; UN Trade 64.87 ± 1.93 → 81.46 ± 1.81; Can. Parl. 74.14 ± 1.51 → 90.19 ± 3.50 (paper claims ≈16.05-point AP gain). Inductive link-pred AUC (Table 2), TGN Reddit: 97.17 ± 0.04 (100%) → 99.73 ± 0.13 (60%), claimed ≈2.56-point gain. Node classification AUC (Table 3, TGN): Wikipedia 86.23 ± 3.30 (100%) → 89.78 ± 2.76 (60%, β=1) → 89.86 ± 2.52 (β>1); Reddit 63.08 ± 1.48 → 66.03 ± 3.45 (60%, β=1) → 69.58 ± 2.96 (60%, β=5) - the β=5 minority-weighting adds ≈3.55 points on the extreme-imbalance (0.05%) Reddit task. Performance peaks then declines as coverage keeps dropping; DyGFormer on UN Trade is erratic (AP 65.37 → 61.02 → 67.45 → 77.76 → 62.40 → 60.21, std up to ±11.67). Compute (Table 6, Can. Parl. link pred): TGN 9 s/epoch, 668 MB GPU; DyGFormer 91 s/epoch, 18,326 MB. Caveats: AP/AUC computed only on non-abstained samples (improvement with lower coverage is mechanically guaranteed); no comparison to plain softmax-threshold abstention or Monte-Carlo dropout; θ set post-hoc on validation so test-time realized coverage drifts; no abstention calibration (no coverage guarantee, unlike conformal methods); fixed λ=32, α=0.5 with no sensitivity analysis; external validity to NFL is zero (datasets are Wikipedia/Reddit/Parliament/UN-trade interaction streams) - the portable artifact is the selective-loss machinery.

The ledger's GSE integration plan for the coverage-constrained abstention method (fills existing-research map gap item 4, 'learning-to-abstain with coverage-risk curves'): add a lightweight selection head g(x) alongside the pick classifier, train selective risk + λ·max(0, c−coverage)² + (1−α)·BCE-on-all-samples starting at λ=32, α=0.5 with coverage targets {0.9, 0.8, 0.7}; at inference sort selection scores and abstain below the validation-calibrated θ_c. ADOPT iff at matched realized coverage (±2 pts) selective ROI beats the softmax-threshold baseline by ≥ 3 ROI points on the chronological test block AND realized coverage stays within ±3 pts of target over the last 4 weeks. Suggested improvement: replace the fixed quadratic penalty with a Lagrangian dual update (learn λ online to pin exact coverage) and per-market coverage budgets (spread vs total vs moneyline get separate θ). The β ∈ {2,5} minority-weighting result (degrades at β ≥ 10) applies to rare high-edge markets such as upset moneylines.

Arieli, Babichenko & Smorodinsky (2018, arXiv:1710.02838v3) study robust forecast aggregation: what an 'ignorant aggregator' (seeing only experts' probabilities, not their information structure or the common prior) can guarantee under square loss vs an omniscient expert. Relative loss (Lemma 1): L(f,P) = E[(f(x(s)) − x-hat(s))²]; regret R_C(f) = sup_{P in C} L(f,P). Two-expert schemes for Blackwell-ordered signals: the precision scheme f_pre with weights proportional to φ(x) = 1/(x(1−x)) when |x_1−x_2| ≤ 0.4 and to √φ(x) when |x_1−x_2| > 0.4, adopting 0/1 forecasts at extremes and 1/2 on (0,1)/(1,0). For conditionally independent signals: the average-prior scheme f_avg applies Bordley's Bayes formula with a dummy prior = (x_1+x_2)/2, P(ω=1|s) = (1−μ)^{n−1}Πx_i / [(1−μ)^{n−1}Πx_i + μ^{n−1}Π(1−x_i)] (prior + forecasts sufficient). Assumptions: binary state, common prior, non-strategic experts, square loss, one-shot interaction; the many-expert result additionally needs conditional i.i.d. signals.

Arieli et al. (2018) robust aggregation theorems: Theorem 1 (Blackwell) - min regret = (1/8)(5√5−11) ≈ 0.0225, achieved by the precision scheme; naive schemes worse: DeGroot simple average = 1/16 = 0.0625, follow-the-most-extreme = 0.0714 (worse than averaging). Theorem 2 (conditionally independent) - R(f_avg) = 0.0260, lower bound 0.0225 (gap 0.0035); Prop. 2 variant e_p (dummy prior 0.49(x_1+x_2), +0.02 if sum > 1) → 0.0250; Conjecture 3 (UNPROVEN): 0.0225 tight for i.i.d. Theorem 4 (many i.i.d. experts) - R ≥ 1/4 − 3√(log n/n) → 1/4 as n→∞: with many conditionally-i.i.d. experts and unknown prior, no scheme beats predicting 1/2. Precision weighting cuts worst-case regret by ~3× vs averaging; following the sharper forecast is worse than simple averaging. Caveats: worst-case regret not average-case (minimax-optimal against adversarial structures; on typical structures simpler schemes may do as well, but ordering precision > average > extreme-following is informative); binary state only; square loss only; two-expert results; one-shot (GSE is repeated and can learn the prior - the paper itself notes prior knowledge suffices for optimal aggregation, so these results matter for combining sources with unknown joint structure like a new market or model); Prop. 1: with unrestricted correlation, nothing beats 1/2 - schemes need Blackwell or conditional-independence structure.

Arieli et al. (2018) GSE integration: replace the simple average of the GSE model probability p_G and market-implied probability p_M with the precision scheme (w_i proportional to 1/(p_i(1−p_i)) when |p_G−p_M| ≤ 0.4, to 1/√(p_i(1−p_i)) beyond; snap to 0/1 at extremes), or the average-prior scheme (dummy prior μ-hat = (p_G+p_M)/2 in Bordley's formula) where a base rate is unavailable; ADOPT the precision scheme iff it beats simple averaging on backtested Brier score (~1 day, both schemes closed-form). Guardrails: REJECT 'follow the most extreme forecast' as a combination rule (0.0714 > 0.0625) and REJECT averaging >~3 correlated sub-model outputs without a fitted prior - Theorem 4 says it is provably vacuous; instead select the single best-calibrated expert or fit the joint structure first. Since GSE is not one-shot, fit the empirical prior μ-hat per market/week from historical data and plug into the exact Bordley formula (optimal given prior + forecasts under conditional independence), then test whether learned-prior Bordley beats the minimax schemes and measure the crossover of how much history is needed before learned-prior wins.

Fakoor, Kim, Mueller, Smola & Tibshirani (2023, JMLR 24:1-41, arXiv:2103.00083v5) aggregate any number of conditional quantile models into one estimator with per-model × per-quantile-level × per-input weights, guaranteed non-crossing isotonization, and conformal calibration. Pinball loss ψ_τ(Z−q) = τ|Z−q| (Z≥q), (1−τ)|Z−q| (Z<q) (eq. 3); E[ψ_τ] minimized at the true quantile. CRPS(F,Y) = ∫(F(y)−1{Y≤y})²dy = 2∫_0^1 ψ_τ(Y−F^{−1}(τ))dτ (eqs. 5–6). WIS(F^{−1},Y) = Σ_{α in A} {α(u_α−ℓ_α) + 2·dist(Y,[ℓ_α,u_α])} = 2Σ_{τ in T} ψ_τ(Y−F^{−1}(τ)) (eqs. 7–8) - optimizing pinball loss is equivalent to optimizing WIS. Aggregator: weighted linear ensembles ĝ_w(x) = Σ_j w_j(x)·ĝ_j(x); coarse (eq. 16): one weight w_j per model, Σw_j=1; medium: weight w_{jτ} per model × quantile level, Σ_j w_{jτ}=1 per τ (Hadamard product); fine: weight w_{jτ,ν} per model × output level τ × input level ν, Σ_jΣ_ν w_{jτ,ν}=1 per τ (matrix-vector product - aggregate median informed by all quantiles of all models). Global weights fit by SGD on pinball loss with softmax parametrization; local weights w^τ(x) = SoftMax(W^τ f_θ(x)) (eq. 17), trained end-to-end (eq. 18) - mixture-of-experts/attention interpretation.

Fakoor et al. (2023) non-crossing machinery: crossing penalty ρ(g) = Σ_{x in X0}Σ_{τ<τ'} (g(x;τ) − g(x;τ') + δ_{τ,τ'})_+ (eq. 19); adaptive margins δ_{τ,τ'} = δ_0(Q_{τ'}({R_i}) − Q_τ({R_i}))_+ from pilot residuals (eq. 21); isotonization operators - Sort (12), IsoProj/PAVA (13), new min-max sweep (23): cumulative max upward / cumulative min downward from the median; usable post hoc (guaranteed) or end-to-end as differentiable layers (eq. 22). Proposition 2 (NEW): Σ_τ ψ_τ(y−g-tilde(x;τ)) ≤ Σ_τ ψ_τ(y−ĝ(x;τ)) for g-tilde = Sort(ĝ) or IsoProj(ĝ); with T symmetric, WIS can only improve; strict if sorting nontrivial. Prop. 1: ℓ_p error can only improve for any p≥1. Prop. 4: probability and quantile averages have equal means; quantile average always sharper: m_k(F-bar) ≤ m_k(F) for even k≥2. Prop. 5 (NEW): p=2, f_2(v)=o(f_1(v)), f_1 log-concave → quantile-averaged density f-bar(v)=o(f_1(v)) (thinner tails) vs probability average f(v) ~ w_1·f_1(v) (same tail order).

Fakoor et al. (2023) conformal calibration: CQR (eq. 26) with finite-sample coverage ≥ 1−α (eq. 27), upper-bounded by 1−α+1/(n_2+1); CV+ (eq. 28) with guarantee ≥ 1−2α − min{2(1−1/K)/(n/K+1), (1−K/n)/(K+1)} ≥ 1−2α − √(2/n) (eq. 29); nested CV+ scheme exploiting ĝ_j^{−k,ℓ} = ĝ_j^{−ℓ,k} symmetry → base models trained K(K−1)/2 times instead of K(K−1) or K². Assumptions: i.i.d. train/test for conformal guarantees (marginal, not conditional - conditional coverage is impossible distribution-free); K-fold OOF predictions prevent ensemble overfitting. Benchmark protocol: 34 datasets (8 UCI ML Repository + 26 AutoML Benchmark for Regression/OpenML); 5 random train/val/test splits (72%/18%/10%) per dataset; features and response standardized; base models tuned by validation WIS; m = 99 quantile levels T = {0.01,...,0.99}; p = 6 base models (CGN, SQR, DQR, quantile RandomForest, ExtraTrees, LightGBM); aggregation weights trained on out-of-fold (K=5) base predictions (eq. 15); metric WIS averaged over out-of-sample predictions. Code: https://github.com/amazon-research/quantile-aggregation.

Fakoor et al. (2023) quantile-aggregation findings: DQA (local-fine, CrossPenalty+PostSort) best average relative WIS across all 34 datasets (Figs. 1, 6); QRA/FQRA runners-up, up to 50% worse than DQA on some datasets (relative factor 1.5), never beating DQA. Flexibility trend (Fig. 7): local > global and fine > medium > coarse, especially at higher PVE (higher signal-to-noise); local-fine best overall. Isotonization (Fig. 8): all methods improve on 'none' but second-order (relative WIS range ~0.90–1.10) vs first-order DQA-vs-base gains; AdaptCrossPenalty + GradMinMax best average; paper standardizes on CrossPenalty + PostSort. Prop. 2 verification (Fig. 9): PostSort and PostPAVA never hurt WIS on any of the 34 datasets; PostMinMax hurts on a few (dataset 19 most noticeable). Conformal (Figs. 10–11, nominal 0.8): raw DQA hits ~0.8 averaged over datasets but misses per-dataset; conformalized DQA achieves ≥0.8 coverage on every individual dataset; interval inflation never more than 75% (factor 1.75), typically 0–30%; Average/Median overcover; QRA/FQRA cover on average but miss on several datasets. Conformalized DQA is the only method robust to base-model miscalibration. Caveats: fine/local variants have p×m×m weights (up to 6×99×99) and rely on SGD implicit regularization + early stopping - risky on small samples (ledger rejects fine aggregation unless sample exceeds ~10× parameter count); conformal guarantees are marginal not conditional; CV+ guarantee weaker (1−2α) than split CQR (1−α); end-to-end isotonization loses the Prop. 2 guarantee - only post hoc sorting/PAVA is guaranteed; min-max sweep not WIS-guaranteed post hoc. GSE's target is probabilities of discrete outcomes, not continuous quantiles - maps to interval/prop-distribution outputs. The CQR/CV+ treatment is the reference for repairing GSE's cqr.ts (live bug clamping rank to n−1, falsely certifying 90% coverage at 83.33%); post-sort isotonization is ADOPT-ready (~30 min, guaranteed no WIS downside); medium w_{jτ} aggregation ADOPT iff it beats equal-weight quantile average on 2025 WIS by ≥3%.

Chen, Peng & Tang (2026, arXiv:2604.24517v2) study prior-agnostic minimax aggregation of two experts under squared loss. Aggregator (verbatim): `logit(f_α(x_1,x_2)) = α·logit(x_1) + α·logit(x_2)` - symmetric log-odds averaging with shrinkage α < 1 (dampening/extremizing correction). Known-marginals variant: same rule but subtracts `γ·logit(μ)` where μ = known marginal mean forecast (base-rate correction). Practical rule of thumb supported: α ≈ 0.5–0.6 log-odds dampening is near-minimax across all tractable regimes. Numerical protocol: heuristic global search over information structures + grid refinement at 10^-5; authors flag claims as numerical, not analytic, certificates.

Chen, Peng & Tang (2026) two-expert minimax constants by information-structure regime: conditionally independent signals - α = 0.585, worst-case regret 0.025512 vs analytic lower bound 31/1326 ≈ 0.023379 (gap ≈ 0.0021); known {0,1} state - α = 0.5168, regret 0.022599; Blackwell-ordered - exact minimax ≈ 0.022542 (attained near the same family); unrestricted (adversarially correlated experts) - exact minimax 0.25, aggregation provably hopeless; known marginals - α = 0.656089, γ = 0.498268, regret 0.022763. The worst-case regret floor for combining two binary forecasts under squared loss is ~0.0225–0.0255 regardless of structure. Rule is two lines of code; generalization to n experts proposed heuristically: round-robin pairwise f_α over all components, then average pairwise outputs. Limitations: two experts only (n-expert extension heuristic, no theory); regrets are numerical; squared loss only - log-loss case untouched; no real-data validation; the 0.585 constant's transfer to real correlated model panels is untested (paper's CI analysis excludes correlation).

The ledger's GSE integration for Chen, Peng & Tang (2026): implement f_α with α=0.585 as a two-line challenger combiner for the two strongest engine components, and the marginal-corrected variant (α=0.656089, γ=0.498268, μ = de-vigged market consensus) as a market-aware challenger - the minimax-theoretic analogue of market-relative modeling: de-vigged consensus as base rate with a multiplicative correction, derived from theory rather than heuristics. Proposed gates: ADOPT pair combiner if it beats simple average (α=1) by ≥0.002 Brier on 2025 walk-forward (DM p<0.05) with no log-loss regression; ADOPT marginal-corrected variant if it additionally beats plain α=0.585 rule by ≥0.001 Brier. Improvement direction: fit α empirically on GSE data rather than using 0.585, and derive a correlation-adjusted α as a decreasing function of component forecast correlation - converting the worst-case constant into a data-adaptive combiner.

Vicente et al. (2024, arXiv:2404.06626v1), verdict REJECT: a descriptive study quantifying 'underdog achievement' across 12 international team-ball sports with a 14-factor randomness model, but no predictive model, no calibration, no market path, and American football explicitly excluded (no suitable international competitions). Underdog achievement score (UAS): a team is 'weak' in edition e if its rank is ≥ τ places below the opponent's (τ = median of the sport's rank-difference distribution; soccer τ=7, water polo τ=2.5, all others 3–5); UAS = (# victories or draws by weak teams) / (# matches containing a weak team), aggregated over editions (eqs. 3.2–3.4), 95% CIs per sport. Weighted ranking: wr≤e_h(i) = (N_eh − c(i, R_eh)) + λ·wr≤e_{h−1}(i), c(i,R) ∈ [1,N] rank position, λ ∈ {1, 0.5, 0} testing history-weighting sensitivity, weakness judged on ranking through the previous edition only (no current-edition leakage). Min-max normalization: a′ = (a − min(a)) / (max(a) − min(a)). Pearson correlation: cov(X,Y)/(σ_X·σ_Y), range [−1,1].
equation: UAS = (# victories or draws by weak teams) / (# matches containing a weak team)

claim: Vicente et al. (2024) findings: UAS by sport (Table 3; λ=1 / 0.5 / 0) - Water Polo 0.37/0.34/0.32; Soccer 0.36/0.27/0.22; Field Hockey 0.31/0.22/0.20; Ice Hockey 0.30/0.21/0.18; Basketball 0.25/0.19/0.16; Volleyball 0.22/0.11/0.07; Handball 0.21/0.17/0.11; Futsal 0.17/0.13/0.07; Cricket 0.15/0.11/0.08; Lacrosse 0.08/0.07/0.06; Rugby 0.07/0.04/0.03; Roller Hockey 0.05/0.02/0.01. Kruskal–Wallis test on UAS across sports: p = 2.47×10⁻¹⁰ (significant at 5%). Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction significant pairs include soccer vs cricket (0.01239), lacrosse (0.00007), roller hockey (0.00002), rugby (0.00011); water polo vs lacrosse (0.00160), roller hockey (0.00044), rugby (0.00161). PCA: first two components explain 56% of the 14-factor variance. Correlation with UAS: strongest positive = GS/NPG (goal size/defenders); strongest negative = NRAM/NRPM, PI, BG; weaker negative = SI, PP, FS/BS, BL; positive-impact factors named: GS/NPG, NP/FS, PBD, PBH, BB, and to a lesser extent GS/BS and BV. Limitations: the 14 factors are hand-authored, hand-scored per-sport constants chosen because they plausibly drive upsets - finding they correlate with upsets is weak, near-circular evidence; negative correlations reinterpreted post-hoc as 'weaker effect' rather than theory falsification; soccer's high UAS (0.36) is driven by low scoring and draws - opposite of NFL structure; data: match scores scraped from Wikipedia, companion dataset ISE Technical Report 24T-003 (Lehigh), code github.com/thaksheel/randomness-team-ball-sports.

Laureti, Medo & Zhang (2009, arXiv:0712.2771v3) analyze the Kelly-optimal portfolio for lognormally-distributed asset returns, including the 'condensation' phenomenon (under-diversification) and whether the Kelly portfolio lies on Markowitz's Efficient Frontier. Model: p_i(t) = p_i(t−1)·e^{η_i(t)}, η_i ~ N(m_i, D_i), independent (eq. 1); returns R_i = e^{η_i}−1 lognormal with mean μ_i = exp(m_i+D_i/2)−1, variance σ_i² = (exp(D_i)−1)exp(2m_i+D_i). Kelly objective: maximize v = E[ln W₁], W₁ = 1 + Σq_iR_i (eq. 2); first-order conditions E[R_i/(1+Σq_jR_j)] = 0 (eq. 6). One risky asset (verbatim): q̂ = 1/2 + m/D (eq. 7); invest nothing if m < −D/2 (m_<), everything if m > D/2 (m_>). Constrained (no short/borrow) N assets: q̂_i = 1/2 + (m_i + γ)/D_i, γ from Σq̂_j = 1 (eq. 9); iteratively drop any asset with q̂_i ≤ 0 and re-solve (eq. 13 form for equal volatility: include M assets where M is the largest with m_M + (1/M)Σᵢ₌₁ᴹ m_i > D/M). Kelly-on-EF theorem: for μ_i, σ_i → 0, the constrained Kelly portfolio satisfies the constrained Efficient Frontier. Assumptions: investor knows true (m_i, D_i); lognormal returns; infinite divisibility; no dividends/costs/taxes; zero risk-free rate; no shorting/borrowing (forced by log-wealth being undefined on bankruptcy).

Laureti, Medo & Zhang (2009) condensation findings: two-asset condensation - invest fully in asset 1 when m′₁ = m₂ + (D₁+D₂)/2 (eq. 12); both assets held only for m″₁ < m₁ < m′₁ (Fig. 4 phase diagram). Many assets, equal volatility D, uniform m ∈ [a,b]: typical portfolio size M_T = √(2ND/(b−a)) (eq. 14, third branch); inverse participation ratio R = 1/Σq_i² ≈ 4M_T/3 (eq. 15); relative size M_T/N ∼ 1/√N → condensation in the large-N limit. Power-law tail f(m) = Cm^{−α−1}: condensation to a single asset when m̃₁−m̃₂ > D, with medians m̃₁ = m_min(Nr/ln2)^{1/α}, m̃₂ = m_min(Nr/1.68)^{1/α} (Sec. 2.4.2, Fig. 6). Logarithmic Efficient Frontier (minimize E[(lnW₁)²]−E[lnW₁]² s.t. E[lnW₁]=v_P, Σq_i=1, eqs. 16–18) ≈ classic EF: 'the difference between the traditional M-V approach and the modification proposed here is very small and does not justify the additional complexity' (Sec. 4). Verification: eq. 7 matches the numerical optimum across 2m/D ∈ [−1,1] for D = 0.25 and 1.0 (Fig. 2), relative error ≤3% at D=0.01; uniform-m case (N=1000, D=0.01, x=−0.05): M_T follows eq. 14 and R ≈ 4M_T/3 matches 10,000-repetition Monte Carlo (Fig. 5). Competing formula q̂′ = μ/(μ²+σ²) from [13] errs ~50% at D=0.25. Critical limitation: estimation error (the dominant real-world issue) explicitly deferred to references [20, 23, 24]; the lognormal formulas do NOT apply to binary sports bets.

The ledger's GSE integration for Laureti, Medo & Zhang (2009): the Kelly-consistent pick-inclusion rule is the actionable item - for each day's candidate pick set (model prob p_i, decimal odds o_i), compute binary-outcome Kelly fractions under a Σq≤1 constraint, iteratively drop the pick with the most-negative constrained fraction and re-solve (GSE analog of eq. 13's elimination loop) until all included picks have q̂_i > 0, replacing ad-hoc 'top-N picks' cutoffs with a Kelly-consistent selection. Use the inverse participation ratio R = 1/Σq_i² as a concentration monitor on the posted card: flags days when the portfolio condensates to 1–2 picks (R ≈ 1), triggering the fractional-Kelly haircut from ledger 0171's protocol. Appendix B's correlated-returns sketch extends to correlated binary bets (same-game / correlated legs): replace the diagonal-D assumption with an outcome-correlation matrix estimated from the engine's joint simulations. CAUTION: the paper's exact formulas (eq. 7, eq. 9, eq. 12) are for continuous lognormal returns and must NOT be ported verbatim to binary bets - ledger 0813's exact binary-outcome Kelly fractions are the correct base, with only the eq.-13 elimination logic and eq.-15 IPR metric transferred.

Hsieh & Barmish (2017, arXiv:1710.01787) demonstrate that common closed-form approximations to the Kelly fraction (Taylor quadratic expansion, GBM μ/σ²) can be catastrophically wrong - even sign-wrong - and quantify the severe drawdown exposure of exact full Kelly. Kelly objective: choose K to maximize g(K) = E[log(1 + K^T X)], wealth recursion V(k+1) = (1 + K^T X(k))V(k). Taylor approximation: maximize K·E[X] − (1/2)K²·E[X²], optimum κTaylor = E[X]/E[X²]. GBM approximation: κGBM = μ/σ². Drawdown analysis: coin-flip gamble with ±1 outcomes, win probability p = 0.99, horizon N = 252; Kelly problem re-solved under expected-maximum-drawdown constraint E[D(K)] ≤ d. Assumptions: i.i.d. returns, known distribution, log utility, no transaction costs - the paper's point is that the approximations add unstated error beyond these.

Hsieh & Barmish (2017) findings: Gamble A (X = 0.15 w.p. 0.95, X = −0.95 w.p. 0.05) - κTaylor = 1.4286 → saturated K_Taylor = 1, exact expected growth ≈ −0.017; κGBM = 1.6529 → saturated at 1, exact expected growth ≈ −0.017; true optimum K* = 0.6667 with g(K*) ≈ 0.0404. The approximations turn a +4% growth opportunity into −1.7% expected growth. Annualized: true r(K*) ≈ 10.384 vs ≈ −3.443 for both approximations. Coin gamble (N = 252, p = 0.99, K* = 0.98): 92% chance the maximum drawdown exceeds 98%. Expected maximum drawdown of the Kelly bettor: E[D(K*)] ≈ 0.903; for the approximation at K = 1 it is ≈ 1.0. Imposing E[D(K)] ≤ 0.2 reduces the optimal fraction to ≈ 0.1. Takeaway as stated: never serve Taylor/GBM closed forms directly - approximation error can flip a +4% edge into −1.7% growth and push drawdown to near-certain ruin levels; exact convex optimization on the empirical/simulated return distribution is the required path, plus explicit drawdown constraints.
