Gradient (Proposition 1): ∇_θ J_risk(θ;ε) = E_{τ∼p(τ|θ)}[(R(τ)−R_ε(θ))·∇_θ log p(τ|θ) | R(τ) ≥ R_ε(θ)]. Monte-Carlo estimate: (1/εN) Σ_i [R(τ⁽ⁱ⁾) − R̃_ε(θ)] · 1_{R(τ⁽ⁱ⁾) ≥ R̃_ε(θ)} ∇_θ log p(τ⁽ⁱ⁾|θ). Differs from REINFORCE in two ways: (a) theoretically-prescribed baseline (the quantile); (b) only the top-ε fraction of each batch contributes to the gradient. Mirror-image of CVaR (risk-averse, bottom ε) — DSR is risk-seeking (top ε). In-situ constraints: arity enforcement by node type (e.g. cosine = unary → one child), no nested trig, length limits, constant placement, no redundant subtrees — masked at generation time, not post-hoc penalties. RNN emits tokens conditioned on previously sampled tokens; parent and sibling embeddings fed as RNN inputs. Reward = normalized RMSE-based fitness.

DSR (arXiv:1912.04871) findings: DSR significantly outperforms all five baselines (PQT, VPG, GP, Eureqa, Wolfram) in exact recovery rate across the Nguyen suite, p < 10⁻³ (Table 1; bold across all benchmarks). Noise: Wolfram “catastrophically fails for even the smallest noise level”; DSR outperforms all baselines at every noise level and dataset size; with 10× data, recovery improves across noise levels (Fig. 4). Literature comparisons: DSR “greatly outperforms each study's published results” — Table 8: DSR median RMSE 0 on Neat-1, Neat-2 vs Neat-GP's 0.0779, 0.0579. Ablation: risk-seeking objective beats standard policy gradient; in-situ constraints improve recovery. Harmonic series: rediscovered H_n ≈ γ + log(n) + 1/(2n) + 1/(11.3776n + 15.725) + 0.327981 with γ ≈ 0.57721 (Euler–Mascheroni constant) emerging naturally — a novel variant of Euler's 1755 formula. Data: Nguyen symbolic regression benchmark suite (Uy et al. 2011): 12 community-vetted benchmark expressions. Literature-reported values from Neat-GP, GrammarVAE, BSR, Eureqa setups (recapitulated per their papers). Hyperparameter tuning done on Nguyen-7 and Nguyen-10 only (grid search: 800 combos GP, 81 each for DSR/PQT/VPG); the other 10 benchmarks effectively held out. Noisy runs use exact equivalence anywhere on the reward–complexity Pareto front (to avoid rewarding overfit). Limitations noted in the file: benchmark suite is tiny (12 expressions, 1–2 variables); exact-recovery metric is the wrong objective for GSE (predictive metrics matter, not rediscovery); constants are harder for DSR than PySR's BFGS loop (RNN must emit constant tokens); RNN training is sequential and sample-hungry vs embarrassingly parallel GP; literature comparisons recapitulated from papers (reproduction fidelity risk); real sports data has correlated features, regime breaks, measurement error — none tested. Reference implementation exists as open-source deep-symbolic-regression package (recorded as unverified in file). GSE implementation spec in file: risk-seeking fine-tuning as a PySR post-pass — embed PySR hall-of-fame expressions, run small RL loop (REINFORCE with top-ε quantile baseline, ε ≈ 0.2) mutating expressions, reward = held-out-season predictive r, hard constraint mask (forbid: >1 nested trig, single-input expressions, >15 nodes). Alt: DSR-lite in PyTorch (LSTM over prefix-notation token sequences, reward = −NMSE + complexity penalty). Data: nflverse team-season pipeline. Effort: ~2 engineer-days for post-pass; ~1 week from scratch. Acceptance gate in file: ADOPT if best ≤15-node expression beats best PySR-only ≤15-node expression by ≥0.03 test r on 2024–2025 with constraint mask preventing degenerate solutions; REJECT if RL loop collapses to PySR's hall-of-fame or underperforms. Improvement experiment in file: risk-seeking CVaR scheduling — anneal ε from 0.5 → 0.05 over training (broad exploration early, elite exploitation late), mirroring simulated annealing's temperature schedule. CONTRADICTION: the file claims DSR “greatly outperforms” PySR-family GP methods, yet GSE's own stance (in this file's GSE-overlap section) keeps PySR as the production engine — the resolution stated is that DSR's *ideas* port as a post-pass, not that DSR replaces PySR on noisy tabular sports data; untested on sports data.

Vertical Symbolic Regression (arXiv:2312.11955): instead of searching all variables at once (“horizontal”), it runs controlled experiments round-by-round — freeze most variables, learn reduced forms over 1–2 free variables, then extend each round by freeing more variables. Its theory proves exponential search-space shrinkage, and VSR-MCTS empirically dominates horizontal GP/MCTS on multi-variable recovery. Control Variable Experiment: CvExp(φ, v_c, v_f, {T_k}_{k=1}^K) — trial expression φ, controlled variables v_c (fixed within a trial, varied across K trials), free variables v_f (random). Assumes a data oracle (simulator) generating data at arbitrary controlled settings. Reduced-form expressions: controlling v_c={x2,x3,x4} with v_f={x1} makes ground truth φ=x1x3−x2x4 look like φ′=C1x1−C2 (open constants fit by BFGS); constants' variation across trials reveals the next variable's role. Vertical framework: round 1 = SR over 1–2 free variables; each round adds freed variables, extending previous expressions; search stays in small hypothesis spaces early. Two regressors: VSR-GP and VSR-MCTS (MCTS over context-free-grammar expressions). Vertical extension: φ_{r+1} = extend(φ_r, new free variables). Theory (Sec. 5): VSR search space exponentially smaller than horizontal for a class of expressions. Recovery criterion: R² ≥ 0.999 = exact recovery, hand-checked; BFGS optimizer (500 iters). No verbatim loss equations given beyond the CvExp/extend notation.

VSR (arXiv:2312.11955) findings: Table 4 (recovery % | time min | peak MB, 48h limit) — {inv,+,−,×}, (3,2,2): VSR-GP 70% vs GP 40% (10 vs 21 min); VSR-MCTS 70% vs MCTS 40% (5 vs 38 min). {sin,cos,+,−,×}, (3,2,2): VSR-MCTS 100% vs MCTS 20% (8 vs 249 min, 61 vs 191 MB); VSR-GP 50% vs GP 40%. {sin,cos,inv,+,−,×}, (3,2,2): VSR-MCTS 70% vs MCTS 0% (17 vs 287 min); VSR-GP 20% vs GP 30% (GP slightly better here, but VSR-GP expressions hand-checked as shorter/simpler, e.g. x+x instead of 2x). VSR-MCTS uses less time/memory than MCTS across the board; hand-checks confirm VSR finds shorter, simpler equivalents. Noise-rate and quartile ablations performed (results not numerically extracted in file). Limitations: the data oracle is the whole game — without a simulator, vertical SR collapses to observational conditioning and the exponential-shrinkage theory assumes true control; synthetic trig equations only; no real-world validation; GP slightly beat VSR-GP on hardest set (30% vs 20%) — vertical isn't universally better, MCTS benefits more; 48-hour compute budgets; reduced-form identification under noise is fragile — misidentified early rounds poison later ones (no backtracking described). GSE implementation spec in file: VSR-PySR — round r runs PySR restricted to feature subset S_r (S_1 ⊂ S_2 ⊂ ...); seed round r+1's population with round r's hall-of-fame; “control” approximated by residualizing (regress target on controlled features' current best form, search free features against residuals); observational control = bin controlled variables (e.g. down/distance buckets), fit reduced forms per bin. Data: nflverse play-level (EPA/play), 6–10 features. Reproducible test in file: nflverse 2015–2022 plays (target EPA/play), 2023–2025 test; horizontal PySR vs VSR-PySR (3 rounds); metrics = test R², expression length, wall-clock time, recovery of known structure (does it find success-rate + explosiveness decomposition?). Acceptance gate in file: ADOPT if VSR-PySR matches or beats horizontal test R² with ≤50% of the expression length or ≤50% of the compute time; REJECT if horizontal wins on both accuracy and simplicity. Improvement experiment in file: “Regime-vertical SR” — run vertical rounds over GAME REGIMES (round 1: neutral-script plays only; round 2: add trailing; round 3: add leading) to test whether football relationships are regime-decomposable; stable round-1 equations across regimes = regime-robust metrics, differences = content (“the equation changes when trailing”). CONTRADICTION: VSR-MCTS dominates (100% vs 20%, 70% vs 0%) while VSR-GP only roughly matches or loses to GP (20% vs 30% on hardest) — so the vertical benefit is regressor-dependent, and GSE's PySR (a GP-family engine) may see little gain; the file's own spec should arguably target an MCTS-based SR rather than VSR-PySR (INFERENCE).

IIFE (arXiv:2409.04665, Northwestern/Allstate): automated feature engineering that pre-selects which feature pairs to combine using interaction information (synergy beyond individual contributions), iteratively building arbitrarily high-order features; it also audits the AutoFE literature and quantifies how much published gains are inflated by bad experimental hygiene (CV-as-metric, transductive leakage). Interaction information (Algorithm 1): τ_ij = I(F_i; F_j; Y) = I(F_i; F_j | Y) − I(F_i; F_j) = H(F_i,F_j) + H(F_j,Y) + H(F_i,Y) − H(F_i) − H(F_j) − H(Y) − H(F_i,F_j,Y). Symmetric in all three variables; interpretable as I(F_i; Y | F_j) − I(F_i; Y): the information F_i shares with Y *given* F_j minus without — synergy beyond isolation. IIFE loop (Algorithm 3): (1) compute II for all pairs (O(|F|²); prefilter to F̃ = top-50 by RF impurity importance if |F| too large); (2) loop: take K highest-τ pairs, apply all bivariate functions B, evaluate each candidate by cross-validated downstream-model performance V_M in parallel, keep the argmax; (3) apply univariate functions U to the new feature, keep argmax; (4) add to pool; next iteration computes II only for (new feature × existing) — O(|F|). Stop (Algorithm 2): patience P — stop if mean of recent P/2 CV scores ≤ mean of previous P/2. Order cap optional for interpretability. II as accelerator (§IV-D): restrict expand-reduce methods' expansion (OpenFE, AutoFeat) to high-II pairs → “OpenFE-II”/“AutoFeat-II”: pair set reduced ~5×, similar-or-better test scores, much shorter runtimes. II computed via nearest-neighbor CMI estimator (Mesner & Shalizi, ref [14]) on a random 3,000-sample subset. Named statistics: F1-micro (classification), 1 − relative absolute error (regression); RF impurity importance for prefiltering. Operators used: num-num (+,−,×,min,max,x1/(|x2|+1),%,reverse), num-cat/cat-num groupbythen{min,max,mean,median,std}, univariate (x²,|x|,x,1/(1+e^(−x)),1/x); Lasso drops ÷ and 1/x (division-by-zero). Implementation parameters: K = 3, stop patience P = 20 (P = 40 for cal housing/openml586/jm1); RF on large sets n_estimators=50, max_samples=0.25; unseen-category encoding = train max|value| + 10%·i (or 0); hardware Intel Xeon Silver 4108 @ 1.80GHz, 8 cores, Ray-parallel. LightGBM retune ranges: learning_rate loguniform(0.001,1), subsample/colsample uniform(0.1,0.9), reg_lambda loguniform(0.001,100), num_leaves randint(8,64). Assumptions (stated): high-II pairs are good combination candidates; entropy estimation on discretized/continuous features is reliable; patience stop detects convergence; prefiltering to top-50 doesn't drop synergistic pairs.
equation: τ_ij = I(F_i; F_j; Y) = I(F_i; F_j | Y) − I(F_i; F_j)

claim: IIFE (arXiv:2409.04665) findings: Table I (all public datasets/models) — IIFE 10 top ranks, average rank 2.50 (1.64) vs OpenFE 3.38, EAAFE 3.13, AutoFeat 3.08, DIFER 3.75, baseline 4.46. Average % change over baseline: 26.88% (90.6) vs AutoFeat 20.62%, DIFER 9.02%, OpenFE 8.26%, EAAFE 7.11%. Excluding the OpenML-586 outlier: 8.74% vs 5.63–7.16%. By model: linear-only 72.42% (AutoFeat 59.44%), RF-only 5.20%, LGBM-only 3.02% (OpenFE marginally better at 3.11%). Linear-model gap closure (Fig. 3): IIFE+LR reduces the gap to RF* to 4.99% and to LGBM* to 5.35%; IIFE+Lasso → RF* 4.94%, → LGBM* 10.15% — linear models reach near-nonlinear performance while staying explainable. Standout wins (Table IV, 25 runs per cell): OpenML 586 (Lasso) IIFE 0.7494 vs OpenFE 0.2150 vs AutoFeat 0.6235 vs DIFER 0.3261 (baseline 0.1383); Jungle Chess (LR) 0.7988 vs OpenFE 0.7543; Jungle Chess (RF) 0.9396 vs OpenFE 0.8391; Airfoil (Lasso) 0.6468 vs AutoFeat 0.6349; Bikeshare (RFR) 0.9955 vs OpenFE 0.9898. OpenFE occasionally beats IIFE (Cal Housing Lasso 0.5260 > 0.5076; Jungle Chess LGBM: EAAFE 0.9873 > IIFE 0.9701 > OpenFE 0.9481). Large-scale proprietary (Table II): IIFE +6.21% in 5.33h vs OpenFE-II +1.16% (4.17h) vs AutoFeat-II +4.23% (5.75h). Literature-hygiene quantifications (§IV-C): CV-as-final-metric inflates gains 21.03% → 15.33% on holdout (a 5.7pp inflation); OpenFE's transductive groupby-then-* (test samples in aggregates) inflates airfoil by +14.01% and jungle chess by +1.95% vs the inductive fix. Combining methods (§IV-E): IIFE+AutoFeat (LR) +1.51%, IIFE+EAAFE (RF) +0.31%, IIFE+OpenFE (LGBM) +0.20% over the second-best single method. Synthetic verification: II ranks the true pair at/near rank 0 across all f (Fig. 5 histograms). Key property: builds increasingly complex features iteratively (Jungle Chess: best feature reached order 10 — beyond any competitor's cap) while stopping at low order when the model doesn't benefit (Airfoil/RF case). Runtimes (Table V): TOTAL avg — IIFE 1.58h, OpenFE 1.45h, AutoFeat 1.53h, EAAFE 1.31h, DIFER 4.55h (slowest everywhere; LGBMclass avg 7.07h). On large data, OpenFE/AutoFeat without II-acceleration “cannot complete within several weeks.” Appendix C (Wine Quality-Red): all AutoFE methods score below baseline as classification; reframing as regression gives +4.43% over baseline — the deficit is the modeling choice, not AutoFE. Data: Airfoil (1,503×5, reg), Credit Default (30k×23, clf), Bikeshare (17,389×13, reg), Wine Quality Red (999×12, clf), California Housing (20,640×8, reg), OpenML 586 (1k×25, reg), JM1 (10,885×22, clf), Jungle Chess (44,819×6, clf); proprietary Allstate-scale regression dataset (100s of thousands of samples, ~1,000s of features). Downstream models: LR/Lasso, RF, LightGBM — hyperparameter-tuned (random search, 100 iterations, 5-fold CV) *before* AutoFE and *after* AutoFE. 25 runs per dataset/model. Limitations (adversarial read in file): (a) IIFE's internal selection still uses CV scores on train for the keep decision (V_M), holdout only at end — the 26.88% headline still carries selection bias; (b) the transductive fix (train-only aggregates applied to test) is exactly what ledger 1842's OpenFE implementation must enforce — cross-ledger dependency; (c) the 72.42% linear-only gain is dominated by datasets where linear baselines were terrible (huge std 153) — gap-closure framing is fairer; (d) II estimation via nearest-neighbor MI is noisy at small N, no discretization sensitivity analysis; (e) prefiltering to top-50 by RF importance can drop pure-interaction pairs (XOR-type) — the exact pairs II is supposed to find; untested failure mode; (f) proprietary dataset unverifiable; (g) anonymous code link (github.com/2oppy67zj4ky/Appendix) in v1 may be dead. GSE implementation spec in file: “GSE-IIFE” — (1) pair screening: compute τ_ij for all candidate feature pairs on training seasons only (2020–2022) via Mesner–Shalizi nearest-neighbor CMI; skip RF-importance prefiltering (the XOR-blindspot — NFL feature counts in the hundreds, O(|F|²) affordable); (2) iterative construction: top-K pairs × bivariate set {+, −, ×, ÷, diff-vs-opponent, ratio-to-league-avg} → LightGBM CV on 2023 → keep argmax; univariate {log, sqrt, z-score, sigmoid} on winner; patience P = 5; (3) inductive enforcement: every groupby-then-* aggregate computed on training seasons only, mapped onto validation/test; (4) run separately for public explainable LR model and LightGBM engine model. Effort: ~4–5 days. Reproducible test in file: nflverse 2020–2024 game-level, kickoff cutoffs; IIFE loop on 2020–2022 (II) / 2023 (V_M selection); frozen feature set; evaluate LR and LightGBM on held-out 2024 (log-loss) vs no-FE baseline. Controls: (a) transductive-aggregates arm to replicate the +14% inflation finding in sports; (b) random-pair baseline (same K) to prove II prioritization beats chance; (c) leakage audit on all groupby features. Acceptance gate in file: ADAPT iff (a) 2024 held-out log-loss improves ≥ 0.003 for LightGBM, AND (b) II-prioritized arm beats random-pair arm by ≥ 0.002, AND (c) the transductive-control arm demonstrably inflates, AND (d) LR arm closes ≥ 50% of the LR→LightGBM gap. REJECT if II doesn't beat random pairs, any inductive violation, or >8h per model arm.
equation: τ_ij = I(F_i; F_j | Y) − I(F_i; F_j)

claim: MTM tokenizes trajectories with modality-specific encoders flattened to a 1-D sequence of length N = M x T, adding fixed sinusoidal timestep embeddings plus learnable modality-type embeddings; modalities M = {state, action, return-to-go}.

MTM training objective is to maximize expected summed log-likelihood of masked tokens over trajectories and modalities, implemented as MSE loss under a Gaussian probabilistic model, using an MAE-style encoder-decoder of bidirectional transformers where the encoder processes unmasked tokens only.
equation: max_θ E_τ Σ_{t=1}^T Σ_{m=1}^M log P_θ(z_t^m | Masked(τ))

claim: MTM uses random autoregressive masking: random masks constrained so at least one masked token has no future unmasked tokens (the last element of each sampled segment is necessarily masked); input sequences are contiguous fixed-length sub-segments of episodes.

One MTM model serves four inference roles via masking patterns: RCBC mask yields an offline RL policy, BC mask yields behavior cloning/policy init, forward-dynamics mask (unmask actions, mask states) yields a world model, and inverse-dynamics mask (current state plus desired future state) yields action recovery/goal-reaching.

MTM finding on D4RL locomotion V2: MTM with RCBC inference outperforms Decision Transformer and RvS and is competitive with specialized CQL and IQL despite training with a purely self-supervised objective without any explicit RL components.

MTM heteromodality finding: heteromodal MTM (trained on ~1% fully-labeled data plus ~95% state-only data) consistently beats MLP and action-labeled-only MTM, with a 'quite substantial' gap in low-data regimes; however, naive addition of state-only data without the paper's two-stage inference did NOT always help RCBC - the two-stage procedure was required.

MTM representation-transfer finding: TD3 trained on MTM latent representations learns 'significantly' faster on all 3 ExORL tasks (Stand, Walk, Run); on Walk it reaches or exceeds asymptotic raw-state TD3 performance within 10% of the training budget, and state-action reps beat state-only reps on Run asymptotic performance.

PUDD (Early Concept Drift Detection via Prediction Uncertainty, arXiv:2412.11158) is built on the PU-index: for instance x_i with true class y_i, the probability mass the classifier assigns to not the true class.

PUDD theory: identical PU-index histograms across two windows imply identical error rates and error standard deviations, but equal error rates/stds do NOT imply identical PU-index histograms - so the PU-index is provably at least as sensitive as error rate and can fire while accuracy is unchanged.
PUDD drift test uses expected contingency frequency and a chi-square statistic over windowed PU-index buckets, with the p-value from the chi-square CDF with w = (cols-1)x(rows-1) degrees of freedom.
equation: E_{ij} = (Σ_j T_{ij} × Σ_i T_{ij}) / Σ_{ij} T_{ij}; χ² = Σ_i Σ_j (T_{ij}² / E_{ij}) − Σ_{ij} T_{ij}

claim: PUDD finding: ranks 1st in 17 of 24 dataset-x-classifier cases and top-3 in 20 of 24 in the incremental regime; in the train-once-until-alarm regime, 1st in 15 cases and top-3 in 19 (vs 7 classic detectors ADWIN/DDM/EDDM/HDDM-A/HDDM-W/KSWIN/PH and 5 SOTA MCDD/AMF/IWE/NS/ADLTER).

PUDD finding: PUDD-5 reaches 98.49% accuracy, 2.8% higher than the best SOTA method on one dataset; the exception is the airline dataset, where NS and ADLTER beat PUDD - attributed to airline's 679 tabular attributes favoring tree ensembles.

PUDD example results (mean accuracy over 100 seeds): elec2 incremental PUDD-5 = 74.92 vs ADWIN 71.94; powersupply mixed PUDD-5 = 82.81 vs ADWIN 78.45; airline PUDD-5 = 63.35 vs ADWIN 61.65 vs DDM 61.29.

PUDD limitations: the PU-index requires true labels at detection time (drift can only be checked after outcomes resolve), and chi-square validity requires observed counts > 50 and expected > 5 per cell, enforced by Adaptive PU-index Bucketing; drift is chunk-level with fixed-size chunks (1000; 100 for CIFAR-10-CD).

FtaT (Fully Test-Time Adaptation for tabular data) corrects label shift with a Confident Distribution Optimizer: the next-step prediction is the current prediction elementwise-multiplied by the ratio of the estimated shifted label distribution to the source label distribution.

FtaT finding: best on all 3 backbones averaged over datasets - MLP 66.77/64.96/72.00 (Acc/BalAcc/F1) vs non-adaptation baseline 62.45/64.61/60.59; TabTransformer 66.14/64.40/69.03; FT-Transformer 64.01/62.54/69.56 (TableShift protocol, no source access at test).

FtaT cautionary finding: existing test-time adaptation methods FAIL on tabular data - TENT 58.43 MLP accuracy (worse than the 62.45 baseline), LAME 59.48, ODS collapses on HELOC (43.10 vs 54.37 baseline), CoTTA ≈ baseline (61.59), SAR ≈ baseline.

FtaT finding: stronger data augmentation monotonically degrades CoTTA on tabular data, from 60.46 down to 54.74 on DIABETE; as shifts grow (DIABETE to HELOC to ASSIST), both parameter-optimizing and prediction-optimizing FTTA degrade below baseline.
FtaT per-dataset wins (MLP): HELOC 64.09 vs 54.37 baseline; Health Insurance 72.42 vs 65.79; Hypertension 62.20 vs 58.76 with F1 73.77 vs 55.46; competitive on DIABETE 61.66 vs 60.81.

FtaT ablation: removing the Confident Distribution Optimizer hurts more than removing the Local Consistent Weighter, so label shift is the bigger problem on tabular data, though both components are needed for best results.

FtaT Dynamic Model Ensembler: M models with learning rates {1e-3, 1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-5}, ensemble weights proportional to one minus each model's current-batch loss, final prediction = sum of weighted predictions; it matches the best single tuned LR without any tuning.

TNP-KR (Transformer Neural Process - Kernel Regression, arXiv:2411.12502v4) builds each KRBlock as Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression: the output is a kernel-weighted average of context values with weights normalized over all context points.

TNP-KR attention adds a learnable kernel-based bias to scaled dot-product attention: the bias is a weighted sum of RBF-network kernels over index sets, with the RBF network using 5 learnable basis functions and different kernels acting on different index-set components (spatial plus temporal).
equation: 𝒦(q,k,s_q,s_k) = SM(qᵀk/√d_k + Σ_i α_i 𝒦_i(s_q,s_k)); K(s,s′) = Σ_k a_k exp(−|b_k|(‖s−s′‖₂−c_k)²)

claim: TNP-KR encodes temporal causality as an attention bias set to negative infinity when the key's time exceeds the query's time, eliminating the need for masking; the authors flag this as proposed but NOT explored in the paper.

TNP-KR finding on 1D GP RBF (NLL): TNP-KR:DKA -0.464 ± 0.002 (best), SA -0.462 ± 0.002, PERF -0.459 ± 0.002 vs ConvCNP/TNP-D -0.454 ± 0.002, BANP -0.335, ANP -0.298; all TNP-KR variants beat TNP-D and ConvCNP (paired p ≤ 0.039), at ~0.5M params with 5 seeds and 100K batches of 32.

TNP-KR translation-invariance headline: trained on 64x64 grids and tested on 1024x1024, Scan Attention gets NLL 0.307 ± 0.006 while DKA gets 1.144, PERF 1.457, and everything else OOMs or collapses to 27.2 (NP/CNP) - because token embeddings exclude the index set and the bias kernels are translation invariant.

TNP-KR scale finding: Scan Attention processes a 1M+ pixel image in about 50 seconds; DKA/PERF do it in about 0.3 ms; 100K context plus 1M test points run in under a minute on one 24GB GPU; DKA beats PERF on nearly every benchmark (paired p < 0.001 to 0.047), making DKA the linear-time default when SA's O(n_c²) is too slow.

TNP-KR nuance: on BO regret under Expected Improvement, ConvCNP 0.007 ± 0.002 beats SA 0.013 ± 0.003, but switching EI to UCB 'erases' the gap - a better-mean/worse-calibration trade-off showing an NLL/sharpness edge does not automatically mean a decision-quality edge.
Distributional-RL statistics theory: a statistic of the return distribution has the general form of the expectation of a function of the return variable.

Theorem 4.3 (Bellman-closedness characterization): the only finite sets of statistics of this form that are Bellman closed are those whose linear span equals the span of moment functionals for l = 0..L with L ≤ K - highlighting how rare Bellman-closed statistics are.

Lemma 4.4: the statistic sets learned under CDRL (C51) and QDRL (QR-DQN) are NOT Bellman closed - their learnt statistic values need not correspond to the true underlying values for the MDP even in tabular settings.

EDRL (expectile DRL): learn K expectiles of the return distribution with an asymmetric-least-squares loss, using a sample-based imputation strategy (SciPy root-finding/optimization per update) to construct Bellman targets consistent with the learned expectiles; the expectile imputation PRESERVES the mean, while C51 (support clipping) and QR-DQN (quantiles miss tails) do NOT.

EDRL finding on a 5-state MDP: due to lack of mean consistency, both CDRL and QDRL learn a sub-optimal greedy policy (CDRL's true support falls outside its [0,2] bins; QDRL's quantiles miss the tails), while EDRL correctly learns the means of both return distributions and acts optimally.

EDRL finding on Atari-57 (3 seeds): ER-DQN is a 'substantial improvement' over QR-DQN in mean human-normalized score using only 11 expectiles vs QR-DQN's 200 quantiles; the imputation adds low training overhead but per-update numerical optimization is a serving-latency concern.

IRIS (Transformers are Sample-Efficient World Models) tokenizer: a VQ-VAE-style discrete autoencoder mapping image frames to K tokens from a vocabulary of size N, with each token the nearest codebook entry to the CNN-encoded frame patch.
equation: E: R^{h×w×3} → {1..N}^K; z_t^k = argmin_i ‖ y_t^k − e_i ‖_2

claim: IRIS autoencoder loss: L1 reconstruction plus two VQ commitment terms (stop-gradient on either side) plus perceptual loss, all equally weighted, trained with a straight-through estimator.

IRIS world model: a GPT-like transformer over sequences of (frame tokens, action, reward, termination), trained on segments of L=20 timesteps with cross-entropy for next-token transitions and termination, MSE or cross-entropy for rewards; the RL objective maximizes discounted return with the policy trained exclusively on imagined rollouts.

IRIS finding on the Atari 100k benchmark (26 games, 100k steps ≈ 2 hours each, 5 seeds): mean human-normalized score 1.046, median 0.289, superhuman on 10 of 26 games - a new state of the art for methods without lookahead search, surpassing SimPLe, DER, OTRainbow, DrQ, SPR, CURL (next-best mean 0.616, next-best superhuman count 6).
IRIS sample-efficiency datapoint: after only 120 training games on Pong, the world model reenacts a test trajectory 'pixel perfect', including the scoreboard-update game mechanic.

IRIS hyperparameters (Table 3): L=20 timesteps, embedding dim D=256, M=10 layers, 4 attention heads, weight decay 0.01, embedding/attention dropout 0.1; limitation: the VQ tokenizer is brittle (codebook collapse kills the world model), and long-horizon sparse-reward games remain weak for this architecture.

FootBots Set Attention Block (SAB): a transformer encoder block WITHOUT positional encoding applied over the agent set, giving permutation equivariance so no agent ordering is needed for multi-agent motion prediction.

FootBots encoder: FFN plus temporal positional encoding, then SAB_T for temporal dynamics, then SAB_S for social interactions - sequentially decoupled, which is cheaper than joint temporal-social attention; the decoder is a Multi-Attention Block Decoder with cross-attention.

FootBots defines two tasks: standard motion prediction of future positions from past positions, and Conditional Motion Prediction (CMP) predicting a subset of agents conditioned on the known future of another subset.

FootBots multi-head attention is standard scaled dot-product attention with softmax; the CMP conditioning tasks in the paper include: predict players given ball position, predict offense given ball+defense, predict defense given ball+offense, and predict ball given all players.

FootBots finding: 'outperforms baselines in motion prediction and excels in conditioned tasks' on LaLiga data, with synthetic-dataset insights confirming the social attention mechanism's effectiveness and the value of CMP; exact numeric tables were not extracted, so magnitudes are uncertain. Stated assumptions: prediction horizon ≤ observation length, and temporal/social attention can be decoupled sequentially without loss.

ML4C-Learner is a binary classifier on per-UT (unshielded triple) feature vectors with labels v-structure/not from ground-truth DAGs; classified v-structures get oriented, and v-structures plus Meek rules produce the CPDAG output.

ML4C theoretical justification: by Markov completeness, v-structures are invariant across the Markov equivalence class and fully determine the CPDAG given the skeleton, so one classifier serves both the identifiability-determination and orientation phases.
ML4C finding on the child benchmark network (20 nodes / 25 edges), reported as SHD / UT-F1: ML4C 0 / 1.0 vs PC 22 / .12, CPC 13 / .12, GMB 9 / .74, GES 15 / .47, GS 13 / .59.

ML4C finding on the insurance benchmark network (27 nodes / 52 edges), SHD / UT-F1: ML4C 5 / .89 vs PC 36 / .39, GMB 19 / .76, GES 34 / .46, GS 28 / .56; the paper states ML4C 'significantly outperforms all competitors, with the highest average F1-score and consistent performance across all datasets'.

ML4C learnability studies: the ML4C-Learner beats individual weak/strong discriminative predicates, is robust across sample sizes where CI-test-based methods degrade, and tolerates imperfect skeleton inputs; weak predicates satisfy (false implies non-v-structure) and strong predicates are sound and complete, with PC and Majority-PC recast as hand-crafted special-case classifiers.

Supervised causal learning theory from the ML4C paper: supervised causal learning targeting a non-identifiable edge is no better than random guessing - the motivating observation for its two-phase paradigm; the paper also flags sample bias in synthetic training data as an explicitly named failure mode.

Tabular-NAS fairness paper (Das & Dooley, arXiv:2310.12145): multi-objective NAS+HPO over MLP (875 architectural combos), ResNet (350 combos), and FT-Transformer (324 combos) search spaces built on the rtdl package, plus continuous training HPs (learning rate, weight decay, batch size, dropout).

Tabular-NAS fairness paper uses two multi-objective strategies - weighted mean-aggregation (scalarization) and ParEGO (multi-objective extension of efficient global optimization) - jointly optimizing balanced accuracy and one fairness metric (disparate impact, statistical parity difference, average odds difference, or equal opportunity difference).

Tabular-NAS fairness thesis: post-hoc bias-mitigation is 'debiasing as post-processing'; the paper argues for architectures that are inherently fair, with Pareto-front comparisons against bias-mitigation baselines (Reweighing, Disparate Impact Remover, Learning Fair Representations + LR) and against single-objective accuracy-only NAS runs.

Black-box batch active learning for regression: the empirical predictive covariance kernel is the average over K ensemble members of centered prediction products, equivalently an inner product of centered K-vectors and a valid PSD kernel.

Black-box active learning theory Prop 3.1: the posterior gradient kernel (first-order Taylor around the BMA plus GGN approximation) approximates the predictive covariance kernel - so white-box gradient kernels are just an approximation of the prediction-covariance kernel.

Black-box active learning theory Prop 3.2: for non-differentiable models, a Bayesian hypothesis-space view with latent hypothesis index over the fixed ensemble gives the predictive covariance kernel equal to the 'posterior' gradient kernel w.r.t. the hypothesis index exactly; a Dirichlet/BMC mixture variant gives the same.

Black-box active learning entropy bound: the joint entropy of n targets given inputs equals half the log-determinant of the predictive covariance plus noise variance times identity, plus a constant - so acquisition-score log-determinants of the kernel Gram matrix upper-bound expected information gain (multivariate normal is max-entropy for a given covariance).

Black-box active learning finding on DNN 10-member ensembles: black-box is competitive with white-box for BALD, BatchBALD, BAIT, BADGE, and Core-Set, and on average black-box BEATS white-box for all but ACS-FW and BAIT (hypothesis: the white-box implicit Fisher-information approximation is poor in the low-data regime).

Black-box active learning finding on tree ensembles: for random forests with a per-tree virtual ensemble, all black-box methods except BALD (top-k) beat uniform sampling; for bagged RFs and CatBoost virtual ensembles only LCMD, BADGE, and Core-Set beat uniform - attributed to low disagreement among virtual/bagged members.

Black-box active learning ablations: increasing ensemble size K improves acquisition for NNs and RFs (except LCMD, which first improves then degrades); for CatBoost virtual ensembles K in [5,160] gives no boost; performance degrades with larger acquisition batches for all methods, and at the largest batch (4096) white-box catches up to black-box.

Black-box active learning failure mode and assumption: low inter-member disagreement means active learning adds nothing over uniform sampling (monitor mean pairwise |μ_k − μ̄|); the regression model assumes homoscedastic Gaussian noise Y|x,ω ~ N(μ(x;ω), σ_N²); the method scales in number of drawn predictions K, not in parameter count.

Delta-tensor storage paper defines compression ratio as encoded size over naive binary serialization size, with write time = serialization plus encode time, tensor-read time = deserialize plus decode time, and slice-read time = deserialize plus decode of the sliced encoding.
equation: C_r = S_encode / S_binary; t_write = t_ser + t_en(X); t_read_tensor = t_des + t_de(X_encode); t_read_slice = t_des + t_de(XS_encode)

claim: Delta-tensor dense finding (FFHQ subset, 5000 1024x1024 RGB images, 14.6 GB serialized): chunking plus metadata dictionary encoding shrinks 14.6 GB to 13.3 GB (-8.90%) with no compression; write slows 135.69s to 251.77s (+85.52% overhead, authors attribute ~60.7 points to a removable Python for-loop RDD construction); read-full-tensor slows 379.51s to 474.51s (+25.02% from Spark scheduling); but read-slice drops 494.33s to 49.24s (-90.04%) - the payoff case.

Delta-tensor sparse finding (NYC Uber pickups tensor of shape (183, 24, 1140, 1717) = 8,596,812,960 elements with 3,309,490 nonzeros, i.e. 0.038% nonzero): all sparse methods use under 13.23% of PyTorch PT size; BSGS has the best compression ratio at 4.83%; CSF is most write-efficient (26.68% less time than PT); BSGS is most efficient for read-full (29.59% less) and read-slice (55.34% less).

Delta-tensor authors' recommendation: CSF for write-heavy sparse workloads, BSGS (Block Sparse Generic Storage, partitioning-before-encoding, which enables slice-before-decode) for read/slice-heavy sparse workloads, and FTSF (Flattened Tensor Storage Format) for dense; encoding-before-partitioning (CSR, CSF) vs partitioning-before-encoding (BSGS) is the key design split.

QuantFactor REINFORCE (QFR, Zhao et al., arXiv:2409.05144v3): an RL miner for formulaic alpha factors over RPN token sequences that replaces AlphaGen's PPO with plain REINFORCE plus a theoretically variance-bounded greedy-policy baseline - dropping the critic because deterministic transitions plus trajectory-level feedback make PPO's critic add bias without benefit.

QFR MDP formulation: states are partial RPN token sequences, actions are the next token from the operator/feature vocabulary (cross-sectional operators Abs/Log/+/-/x/div/Larger/Smaller and time-series operators Ref/Mean/Median/Sum/Std/Var/Max/Min/Mad/Delta/WMA/EMA/Cov/Corr with lookback), transitions are deterministic (Dirac), and reward is sparse (zero except at the terminal sequence).

QFR evaluation metric is RankIC - the information coefficient of the ranked factor values against ranked forward returns - over six equity-index constituent panels (CSI300, CSI500, CSI1000, SPX, DJI, NDX) with six features (open, close, high, low, volume, vwap), target 5-day forward return, train 2016-01-01 to 2020-01-01.
equation: RankIC(z'_t, y_t) = IC(r(z'_t), r(y_t)), r(·) = ranking operator

claim: QFR finding (Table V, IC / RankIC, 5-seed std): CSI300 QFR 0.0588(0.0022)/0.0602(0.0014) vs AlphaGen 0.0500/0.0540, GP 0.0445/0.0673, XGB 0.0192/0.0241; headline claim: QFR improves RankIC by 3.83% vs AlphaGen's PPO, winning on all six indices with the largest margin late in training.

QFR IR reward shaping: a shaped term rewarding the Information Ratio of the mined factor, gated by an 'IR test' that activates after time delay α = 9×10⁴ steps, ramps with slope η = 2.65×10⁻⁶, is capped at δ = 0.3, and is weighted by λ = 0.02; ablation shows removing either the greedy baseline or the IR shaping degrades learning curves on all six indices.

QFR shaping-hyperparameter findings: η = 2.65×10⁻⁶ is the best trade-off; α below 7×10⁴ harms quality (IR test fires too early); results are robust to δ (settled at 0.3); backtest shows QFR's mined factors give the highest terminal cumulative return on CSI300 2021-2024 and the most PnL in all three CIMV volatility regimes, with the largest edge in the high-volatility period.

FactorMiner (arXiv:2602.14670v2, 2026): a self-evolving financial factor-mining agent with a modular skill architecture (60+ curated operator library plus multi-stage validation pipeline: IC screening → correlation checking → deduplication → full validation) and a structured experience memory, mined via the Ralph Loop: retrieve patterns from memory → generate candidates → evaluate in parallel → distill outcomes back into memory.

FactorMiner summary metrics: absolute-IC metrics |E[IC_t]| and |E[IC_t]|/std(IC_t) (ICIR on absolute IC), and redundancy as avg |ρ| (mean absolute pairwise correlation across the factor library); the experience memory stores successful patterns plus forbidden regions (factor families highly correlated with the existing library), and mining direction is chosen by how candidates COMPLEMENT the library.

FactorMiner findings (IC / ICIR / avg-|ρ|, Top-40 selected once on CSI500-2024, frozen, evaluated out-of-sample 2025): CSI500 FactorMiner 8.25/0.77/0.31 vs AlphaAgent 5.90/0.46/0.32, GPLearn 6.04/0.43/0.44, Alpha101-Adapted 5.06/0.43/0.21, AlphaForge 4.48/0.38/0.36; CSI1000 7.78/0.76/0.30; HS300 7.46/0.38/0.31; crypto 3.82/0.28/0.25 (cross-asset generalization).

FactorMiner combination finding: equal-weight combination of the frozen Top-40 on CSI500 gives IC/ICIR 14.95/1.29 vs next-best Alpha101-Adapted 11.53/0.86; redundancy avg |ρ| ≈ 0.30-0.31 sits near the low-redundancy random-exploration floor (0.07-0.13, random noise, not useful) while GPLearn hits 0.44-0.45 (the 'Red Sea').

FactorMiner integrity flags: Top-40 selected on CSI500-2024 was then tested on 2025 INCLUDING CSI500 (same-market selection/evaluation overlap; CSI1000/HS300/crypto are the cleaner read), and IC values are absolute-value summaries (|E[IC]|) so sign flips are hidden - a factor flipping sign year to year still scores; no portfolio backtest with costs was run.
TimeGrad (autoregressive diffusion for multivariate time series): the forward diffusion step is Gaussian with mean scaled by √(1-β_n) and variance β_n I.
TimeGrad closed-form forward marginal: the n-step diffused variable is Gaussian with mean √ᾱ_n times the clean series and variance (1-ᾱ_n) I.
TimeGrad reverse step: Gaussian with learned mean and fixed covariance, where the learned mean is expressed through the noise-prediction network ε_θ.

TimeGrad training objective: expected squared error between the true diffusion noise and the network's noise prediction, conditioned on the noised series, the RNN hidden state, and the diffusion step.

TimeGrad model factorization: the joint distribution over the forecast window given history and covariates factorizes autoregressively as a product of per-step conditionals on all past values and known-future covariates.
TimeGrad temporal encoder: the hidden state is a 2-layer LSTM over concatenated observations and covariates, living in R^40.
equation: h_t = RNN_θ(concat(x_t^0, c_t), h_{t−1}), h_t ∈ ℝ^40

claim: TimeGrad evaluation metric: CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) as a proper scoring rule in place of likelihood, and CRPS_sum for the multivariate joint - expected CRPS of the predicted sum distribution against the realized sum across entities.

TimeGrad architecture and training: ε_θ is a conditional 1-D dilated ConvNet (WaveNet/DiffWave style) with 8 residual blocks, 8 residual channels, gated activation σ(·)⊙tanh(·), bidirectional dilated convolution with dilation 2^{i%2}, and 8 summed skip connections; N=100 diffusion steps with linear β schedule 1e-4→0.1; batch 64, Adam 1e-3, early stopping on validation, single Nvidia V100 16GB.

TimeGrad findings (CRPS_sum, lower better, 10-run mean±se): Exchange 0.006±0.001 (NOT best - VES/VAR/Transformer-MAF at 0.005, the only dataset not won); Solar 0.287±0.02 (best); Electricity 0.0206±0.001 (best); Traffic 0.044±0.006 (best, -21% vs next Transformer-MAF 0.056); Taxi 0.114±0.02 (best, -36% vs 0.179); Wikipedia 0.0485±0.002 (best, -23% vs 0.063) - SOTA on 5 of 6 benchmarks vs 11 baselines (VAR, VAR-Lasso, GARCH, VES, KVAE, Vec-LSTM variants, GP variants, Transformer-MAF).

TimeGrad ablation: diffusion steps N can drop to ~10 without significant loss on Electricity (10x sampling speedup available); N≈100 is optimal; scaling each series by its context-window mean (or 1 if zero) 'significantly improves performance'.

DS-Agent (arXiv:2402.17453) replaces ungrounded experiment planning with classical case-based reasoning: a retriever p_R over the case bank given task τ and feedback l, an LLM p_LLM generating solution y given τ, l and retrieved case c, and an evaluator p_E producing feedback l from y.

DS-Agent formalization: the iteration-t solution distribution p_CBR(y^t|τ) marginalizes over retrieved-and-revised cases, which differs from RAG by the revise plus retain steps (RAG only retrieves/reuses once).
DS-Agent ReviseRank: the LLM re-ranks candidate cases as '[2]>[1]>[3]...' conditioned on the last iteration's execution feedback, enabling dynamic case adjustment WITHOUT retriever fine-tuning.

DS-Agent development-stage loop: (1) retrieve top-k by embedding similarity, (2) ReviseRank, (3) planner reuses top case to write experiment plan, (4) execute and get feedback l^t, (5) loop, (6) Retain - the best solution is added to the case bank, giving flexible learning without backprop. Deployment stage is simplified CBR: retrieve past successful development solutions, reuse with minor adaptation, single pass, designed for weak LLMs.

DS-Agent case bank: technical reports of winning teams plus top-ranked public-leaderboard code from several recently completed Kaggle competitions (text, time-series, tabular); reports cleaned to core insights and code summarized to textual insights via GPT-3.5. Code open-sourced at https://github.com/guosyjlu/DS-Agent.

DS-Agent development findings (30 data-science tasks, 12 development + 18 deployment): DS-Agent + GPT-4 achieves 100% success rate over all 12 development tasks and best performance in 9/12; DS-Agent + GPT-3.5 is second-best overall and 'consistently surpasses ResearchAgent with GPT-4 in all tasks'; ResearchAgent + GPT-3.5 'almost fails in every type of task'.

DS-Agent deployment findings: one-pass rate 85% (GPT-3.5) / 99% (GPT-4) over 18 tasks vs best baseline 56% / 60%; Mixtral-8x7b-Instruct is lifted from 6% to 31% by the simplified CBR (36% average one-pass-rate improvement across alternative LLMs); average best mean rank improves monotonically with iteration steps; cost is $1.60/run (GPT-4) / $0.06 (GPT-3.5) for development and $0.135 / $0.0045 in low-resource deployment.

VLMo (unified vision-language pre-training with mixture-of-modality-experts): each block applies multi-head self-attention on the layer-normalized input with a residual, then a MoME feed-forward network on the normalized result with a residual.
equation: H'_l = MSA(LN(H_{l−1})) + H_{l−1}; H_l = MoME-FFN(LN(H'_l)) + H'_l

claim: VLMo uses three experts - V-FFN (vision), L-FFN (language), VL-FFN (vision-language fusion) - with shared multi-head self-attention across modalities and the experts replacing the FFN per block; routing is deterministic by input modality and layer index: image/text-only inputs use V/L experts throughout, while image-text pairs use V+L experts in bottom layers and the VL expert in top layers (top-2 for base, top-3 for large).

VLMo stagewise pre-training: (1) train V-FFN plus shared self-attention on image-only data via BEiT masked image modeling; (2) freeze those and train L-FFN on text-only data via MLM; (3) train the full model with three losses - image-text contrastive (ITC), image-text matching (ITM), masked language modeling.

VLMo configs: Base = 12 layers, 768 hidden, 12 heads, FFN 3072; Large = 24 layers, 1024 hidden, 16 heads, FFN 4096; 224x224 images, 16x16 patches, RandAugment, BERT-uncased tokenizer, max text length 40, whole-word masking; 200k steps, batch 1024, AdamW (β1=0.9, β2=0.98), LR 2e-4. Two serving modes: dual-encoder (separate encoding, dot-product similarity, linear-time retrieval) and fusion-encoder (joint encoding, [T_CLS] to classifier).

VLMo VQA findings (Table 1): VLMo-Base 76.64/76.89 on test-dev/test-std vs ALBEF-Base 74.54/74.70 and ViLT-Base 71.26; VLMo-Large 79.94/79.98; VLMo-Large++ 82.88/82.78 vs Florence-Huge 80.16/80.36 and SimVLM-Huge 80.03/80.34.

VLMo NLVR2 and retrieval findings: NLVR2 dev/test-P Base 82.77/83.34 (vs ALBEF-Base 80.24/80.50), Large 85.64/86.86, Large++ 88.62/89.54 (vs SimVLM-Huge 84.53/85.15); VLMo-Large++ COCO text-retrieval R@1/R@5/R@10 = 83.1/96.0/98.2 and image-retrieval = 65.2/86.5/92.2, Flickr30K TR = 96.8/100.0/100.0 and IR = 88.1/98.4/99.3 - beating Florence-Huge (COCO TR 81.8/95.2, IR 63.2/85.7) with linear-time retrieval.

VLMo ablations: stagewise image+text init NLVR2 82.09/82.49 vs image-only init 80.33/81.06; MoME 80.13/80.31 vs standard Transformer 78.81/79.27; all three losses together best (ITC alone 73.91/73.75 → ITC+ITM+MLM 80.13/80.31). ImageNet acc@1: VLMo-Base 85.5 (vs BEiT-Base 85.2, ViT-Base 83.6); ADE20K mIoU 53.4 (vs BEiT 52.8).
Chronos (learning the language of time series): mean scaling divides each value by the mean absolute value over the context window.
Chronos quantization: each scaled value is assigned to the nearest of B=4096 uniformly spaced bin centers over [-15,15], with values outside [c_1,c_B] clipped.
equation: q(x̃) = argmin_b |x̃ − c_b|, c_b uniformly spaced over [−15,15], B=4096

claim: Chronos training objective: minimize negative log-likelihood of future tokens given all preceding tokens - categorical cross-entropy with label smoothing; the model is a series-to-token pipeline feeding a T5 encoder-decoder (20M/46M/200M/710M = Mini/Small/Base/Large) or GPT-2 (90M).

Chronos inference: sample autoregressive paths (temperature or categorical samples) from the token distribution, map tokens back to values, unscale - giving empirical predictive distributions; the point forecast is the median path. Metrics: WQL over quantiles {0.1,...,0.9} and MASE vs seasonal-naive, aggregated by geometric mean relative to seasonal naive.

Chronos training config and data: 200K steps, batch 256, AdamW, LR 0.001→0 linear decay, weight decay 0.01; context length 512, horizon 64 at train time; 28 datasets, ~890K univariate time series, ~84B observations; augmentation = TSMixup (10M mixups combining k∈{2,3} series with Dirichlet weights) plus 1M synthetic KernelSynth GP series at 9:1 real:synthetic sampling; weights released on Hugging Face as autogluon/chronos-t5-*.

Chronos findings: zero-shot Chronos models ranked 2nd-4th in probabilistic (WQL) rankings and Chronos-T5 (Large) ranked 2nd on point forecasting (MASE) - all zero-shot against per-dataset trained models; in-domain Chronos beat almost all task-specific models on both WQL and MASE with the largest (710M) best; fine-tuned Chronos-T5 (Small) was THE BEST method on average across both metrics, beating supervised PatchTST/DeepAR with far cheaper training.

Chronos negative-control finding: llmtime via GPT-3.5/4 is far behind Chronos on both metrics despite being much larger language models - text tokenization is a poor time-series tokenizer; and the TSMixup ablation shows removing mixup/synthetic hurts zero-shot performance, with synthetic GP data with realistic kernels helping most in small-data regimes.

Contamination-free holdout paper (domain familiarity): the protocol makes the entire test window postdate the last evaluated model's release date so window memorization is impossible by construction; comparison is rank-based with multiple-comparison rank intervals, Friedman test per group plus corrected paired post-hoc tests (not decimal-place metric gaps).

Contamination-free holdout findings: pretrained time-series models win 5 of 7 groups but lose one to a Theta baseline (Electricity) and on daily exchange rates are indistinguishable from seasonal naive (Friedman test does not reject; every method ties); the largest gain is 28% lower MASE than the best classical method on weekly Wikipedia pageviews - TimesFM's pretraining domain. Evaluated 13 forecasters (4 classical, 3 trained-per-dataset, 6 pretrained) on 7 groups from 5 domains, all rebuildable without an API key.

Domain-familiarity contrast: TimesFM outranks Chronos by -0.53 on Wikipedia vs -0.09 everywhere else (1500 vs 754 series, Mann–Whitney p < 10⁻⁵) - the advantage tracks corpus familiarity, not series properties (TimesFM's authors describe Wikipedia pageviews as the bulk of its pretraining corpus); seasonal strength and spectral entropy do NOT explain the familiarity pattern, and most published-style gaps between leading pretrained models fall inside multiple-comparison rank intervals, i.e. leaderboard differences are often noise.

DRO-RoBAS (robust Bayesian ambiguity sets): the standard DRO game minimizes worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set; BDRO takes the expectation over the posterior of the worst case inside a KL ball around each posterior draw; DRO-RoBAS instead takes the worst case inside an MMD ball around the posterior predictive of the NPL-MMD robust Bayesian posterior, with a tractable dual in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space and high-probability bounds on ε so the ambiguity set contains the true distribution.
equation: min_{x∈X} sup_{P∈A} E_{ξ∼P}[f_x(ξ)]; BDRO: min_x E_{Π(θ|ξ_{1:n})}[sup_{P: d_KL(P‖P_θ)≤ε} E_P[f_x]]; DRO-RoBAS: min_x sup_{P: MMD(P, P̂_n^{pred,NPL}) ≤ ε} E_{ξ∼P}[f_x(ξ)]

claim: DRO-RoBAS newsvendor setup: cost = h·max(x−ξ,0) + b·max(ξ−x,0) with b=8, h=3; MMD discrepancy with a Gaussian kernel; simulations only - newsvendor demand ξ with n=20 observations, J=100 repetitions, D=1 and 5; portfolio with 5-D Gaussian returns, n=100; Huber contamination η∈{0,0.1,0.2} and a bimodal-Gaussian-DGP vs unimodal-model misspecification case.

DRO-RoBAS bimodal-misspecification finding: with a bimodal demand DGP and a misspecified unimodal Gaussian model, standard posteriors concentrate between the modes so DRO-BAS/BDRO need huge ε and become conservative with high out-of-sample cost, while DRO-RoBAS's NPL-MMD posterior is bimodal despite the unimodal model and gives consistently lower out-of-sample cost.

DRO-RoBAS contamination findings: at η=0 DRO-BAS beats RoBAS - the well-specified case favors standard Bayes; at η>0 RoBAS shows the best out-of-sample mean-variance tradeoff and even empirical MMD degrades; in the portfolio case at η=0.1, for ε<0.2 empirical DRO degrades fast while RoBAS is unaffected, at ε≥0.2 they converge, and at η=0.2 the gap magnifies. RoBAS is computationally heavier (RKHS optimization + NPL sampling) and the paper's contamination model assumes the test set is clean, which is flagged as mismatched to sports where the next week's games can themselves contain the outliers.

T-SHRED (symbolic-regression-regularized model discovery with a transformer): the SINDy latent loss learns sparse coefficients Ξ^(i) minimizing next-step reconstruction error in a sparse library plus an ℓ₀ sparsity penalty.

T-SHRED SINDy-Attention: each head computes standard Q/K/V projections and attention output, then passes the attention output through a SINDy library with sparse coefficients; heads are concatenated and passed through two feed-forward matrices.
equation: Q^(h)=xW_{h,q}, K^(h)=xW_{h,k}, V^(h)=xW_{h,v}; T^(h)=rowsoftmax(QKᵀ/√k)V; S^(h)=Θ_SINDy(T^(h)′)Ξ^(h); S=concat(S^(h)); z=(SW_ff1)W_ff2

claim: T-SHRED shallow-water ground truth equations: the u-momentum equation has advection, pressure-gradient, hyperviscosity, and Coriolis terms; the height equation has divergence, flux-divergence, hyperviscosity, and forcing terms.

T-SHRED experimental scale: 8 encoders (GRU/LSTM/vanilla-transformer/SINDy-loss-transformer/SINDy-attention-transformer/SINDy-attention+loss) × 2 decoders (MLP/CNN, CNN decoder y = σ(Conv₁(σ(Conv₂(z))))) × layers {1–4} × lr {1e-2, 1e-3} = 128 configs per dataset with 5 seeds, best-by-validation reported as mean±std test loss, on three dynamical systems with 50 random persistent sensors, temporal lag 50, next-step full-state prediction, 80/10/10 time splits.

T-SHRED datasets: Sea Surface Temperature (NOAA) - 1,400 weekly snapshots 1992–2019, 180×360 grid (44,219 ocean points), 179 MB; complex plasma physics - 2,000 timesteps × 14 fields of 257×256 points, rSVD-reduced to a 280-dim ROM, 785 MB; rotating shallow water equations (PlanetSWE, from 'The Well') - 10 tracks, 15.5 GB total. Code: https://github.com/yyexela/T-SHRED.

T-SHRED findings: SST best = 1-layer GRU SHRED + MLP decoder, test loss 1.50×10⁻³ (25.14 MB); best T-SHRED = 1-layer SINDy-Attention + CNN decoder, 1.87×10⁻³ (75.31 MB); Plasma best = 3-layer GRU SHRED + MLP, 2.10×10⁻⁴ (0.74 MB); best T-SHRED = SINDy-Attention + CNN, 4.90×10⁻⁴ (1.23 MB); PlanetSWE best = 1-layer SINDy-loss GRU SHRED + MLP, 2.49×10⁻³ (151.86 MB); best T-SHRED = SINDy-Attention + CNN, 3.58×10⁻³ (452.52 MB). The ledger's honest headline: transformers still lose to GRUs on next-step state prediction on all three datasets - the win is interpretability plus SINDy-Attention dominance among transformer variants.

T-SHRED interpretability run: shrinking the latent from 100 to 6 cost only ~2x test loss on PlanetSWE (7.76×10⁻³) while model size fell 16x (28.51 MB vs 452.52 MB), and every head emitted a readable 3-variable linear ODE; training uses ℓ₂ + pruning on Ξ every 10 epochs as an approximation of the ℓ₀ SINDy loss under the Takens-embedding regime (lag 50 suffices) with sensors fixed in space.

SHAPEffects (Shapley-value feature selection robust to concept shift): the Shapley value of feature i is the weighted average of its marginal contributions over all subsets, equivalently the average marginal contribution over all permutations.

SHAPEffects effect definitions: the per-observation effect is the signed square of the SHAP value (squaring amplifies the most influential observations), and the group effect sums per-observation effects over the group.
equation: Effect_{var,x} = sgn(SHAP_var(x,y,ŷ)) · SHAP_var(x,y,ŷ)²; Ef_{var,group} = Σ_{x∈group} Effect_{var,x}

claim: SHAPEffects error grouping (Definition 1): validation observations are classified by prediction error err(x,y) = y − ŷ(x) into Correctly Predicted / Over-Predicted / Under-Predicted using error quantiles Q_low and Q_high - correctly predicted iff err ∈ [Q*_low, Q*_high], under-predicted iff err > Q*_high, over-predicted iff err < Q*_low. The method is two-phase: (1) optional Boruta-style preprocessing adding a random permuted copy of the most influential variable and dropping variables whose mean global influence ≤ the random variable's, (2) backward elimination driven by negative influence (Definition 2); a variable with zero effect anywhere is treated as pure noise/overfit and dropped. Code: https://github.com/CCaribe9/SHAPEffects.

SHAPEffects synthetic benchmark: f(x_t) = 2x_{1,t} + λ₁x²_{2,t} + 3sin(2πx_{3,t}) − 0.4x_{4,t} + λ₂x²_{5,t} + (same 5 terms at t−1) + ε_t with ε~N(0,0.01), x_i ~ U(0,1) for i=1..10 (only the first 5 informative) plus a lag of the target; over 81 sudden-shift and 81 incremental-shift scenarios the MAE-difference histograms are predominantly negative (SHAPEffects better), positive differences 'practically negligible', and sudden vs incremental results nearly identical.

SHAPEffects real shift case 1 (sudden, Spanish day-ahead electricity price with 335 explanatory variables; concept shift = June 15, 2022 Iberian gas-price cap decree): SHAPEffects(0.1–0.9) test MAE 12.61, RMSE 15.60, R² −0.99 vs Boruta 13.41/17.14/−1.40, PIMP 13.39/17.11/−1.39, Best Lasso(0.001) 13.41/17.14/−1.40, Shapicant 19.27/22.30/−3.07 - about 6% MAE improvement over the best SOTA selector; real case 2: SHAPEffects(0.2–0.8) MAE 12.97, RMSE 15.98, R² −1.09 vs Boruta-Shap 13.71/17.52/−1.51, PIMP 13.65/17.44/−1.49; R² is negative for all methods post-shift (relative superiority only); quantile parameters matter, with (0.1–0.9) best in real case 1; on static benchmarks (CAT Scan, Appliances, Max Planck Weather) it is comparable to SOTA.
Multi-camera asynchronous ball localization (2203): the factor graph factorizes as a product of factors over variable subsets, with each factor a Gaussian potential on its residual error.
Ball-localization projection factor: 3D location projects through camera matrix K[R T], and the projection residual is the detected 2D point minus the projected location.
Ball-localization motion factor: the predicted next location is current location plus velocity times the inter-detection time gap, with residual against the next location variable.

Ball-flight aerodynamics factors: drag opposes velocity quadratically and lift depends on the cross product of spin and velocity; acceleration is (drag+lift)/mass plus gravity, and the aero prediction advances velocity by acc·Δt.
equation: F_D(V)=−½ρ_air A C_D‖V‖V; F_L(V,W)=½ρ_air A C_L‖V‖²U, U=W×V; acc=(F_D+F_L)/m+g; π^aero(V_s,W_j)=V_s+acc·Δt; err^aero=V_{s+1}−π^aero

claim: Ball bounce factor (eqs. 12–19): post-bounce horizontal velocities mix pre-bounce spin and velocity through the ball-radius ratio term, vertical velocity flips with restitution e_z, and spin updates from the new velocities with z-spin unchanged.

Ball-flight ODE prediction (eq. 21): position derivative = velocity, velocity derivative = aero acceleration, spin derivative = 0, propagated with 4th-order Runge-Kutta; on ground contact (V_z<0, L_z<z_ground) integration terminates, bounce dynamics apply, and integration restarts.

Ball-localization incremental inference: each new detection triggers relinearized incremental optimization (ISAM2) approximating the MAP problem as a linear least-squares problem - no camera synchronization is needed because every single detection updates the graph. Variables: camera poses (priors from extrinsic calibration), ball 3D location L_t, 3D velocity V_t, 3D spin W_j (constant between bounces, changing only at ground contact).

Ball-localization TCN spin-prior network: a temporal convolutional network regresses ball spin from a 100-frame human-pose sequence (hip-centered, right-arm shoulder/elbow/wrist keypoints); the authors report TCNs beat RNNs/LSTMs for this task. Training RMSE 2.95 Hz, validation RMSE 5.27 Hz; Pearson R 0.807 (novice) / 0.815 (competitive), p<0.001. Headline claim: spin priors reduce landing-position RMSE by over 63.6% vs an adaptive-EKF baseline.

Ball-localization experimental setup and limitations: indoor tennis court, 6 Blackfly S cameras at 5.5 m height on back walls (3 per side, overlapping coverage), each with a Jetson Xavier; intrinsic calibration via checkerboard, extrinsic via AprilTag + court keypoints; tools GTSAM (factor graphs) and AlphaPose; supported by a Google grant; no author code or dataset link stated. Limitations: spin labels are self-distilled from the same factor-graph inference being evaluated (circularity risk), the dataset is small, proprietary, and single-venue, and bounce-model coefficients required ad-hoc modification.

RESCUE note measurement doctrines: (1) Murphy decomposition from arXiv:2607.00164 (Verifiable Rewards for Calibrated Probabilistic Forecasting) - the identity brier − (reliability − resolution + uncertainty) is NOT zero on a sample in general; the residual SUM_b (n_b/n)·var_p(b) is asserted via two independent routes agreeing to 1e-12, and a single sign error in any of the four terms fails the suite. (2) BigInt-exact Wilson from arXiv:2505.23703 - reduced Wilson fractions carry z² with denominator 10^30 through n² and every add/multiply, so 96 bits was far too tight; a 4096-bit runaway guard is used, documented as non-precision (BigInt never silently rounds). (3) Relabeling null from arXiv:2603.03613 - a uniformly-better candidate gives p ~ 1 under every relabeling (maximally robust) vs a lucky arrangement giving low p; the API reports survivesRelabeling as the gate-able verdict with p shipped beside it. (4) The opponent-adjusted NFL pass blocking/rushing paper (arXiv:2604.01491, 153k interactions from 266 games) landed as clusterBootstrap + decide, establishing that uncertainty must come from end-to-end game resampling and that an interval covering zero is 'directional, not decisive'.

Short-week road-deficit backtest (2026-09-28): corpus = nflverse games.csv (CC-BY 4.0), n = 2,622 settled NFL regular-season games 2015–2024, rest days read from the source's own home_rest/away_rest columns; sides playing on ≤4 days rest graded against the closing spread, control = all games where both teams had >4 days rest. Results: short-week n=157, mean −0.471 vs closing spread, sd 12.206; control n=2,465, mean +0.063, sd 12.815. Raw differential: −0.534 points. Welch t = −0.53 - not statistically distinguishable from zero.

Short-week road-deficit verdict: the shipped live signal claims road teams on 4 days rest underperform their baseline spread by −1.75 points (code constant, plus −0.65 over 1500 miles of travel and −0.50 when the opponent rested normally, emitted via spreadPointAdjustment) against a docstring claim of −1.85 to −2.30 points plus a 34% increase in 4th-quarter explosive plays. The backtest supports neither at face value - the shipped penalty is 3.3x the measured point estimate (1.75/0.534 ≈ 3.28). The effect points the claimed direction (sign is not the problem): short-week teams do underperform (−0.471 vs +0.063). Verdict: 'not backwards — roughly a third of the claimed size, and the claimed size is not real.' A closing line is a near-perfect market estimate: a genuine 1.75-point rest edge would show up as a large t, not sub-1.

Short-week road-deficit backtest bugs and discipline: Bug 1 (self-confirming backtest) - the first version added spreadPointAdjustment to the observed margin then compared groups, returning ~−1.77 BY CONSTRUCTION ('confirmed' the −1.75 perfectly); deliberately not done - raw margin only. Bug 2 (sign error exposed by the control) - the first raw run used margin + line, but nflverse spread_line is positive when the home team is favored and must be subtracted; it produced an impossible control mean of −3.483 (closing lines average ~0 by construction) - which is why a control group exists. Deliberate non-action: the magnitude is NOT being changed on one backtest - per law 3, rescale is a founder decision; the three honest options recorded are (a) rescale the penalty to the measured effect and widen the interval, (b) demote the signal to an unweighted logged observation, (c) widen the corpus (play-level, more seasons) and re-measure. The nflverse spread_line sign convention (positive = home favored, must subtract) is a concrete wiring fact: a wrong sign does not crash, it silently inverts.

Advanced-metrics catalog definitions (compiled 2026-09-17): EPA = change in Expected Points from before a play to after it, where Expected Points = the historical average net point value of a game state defined by down, distance, and field position; EPA per play = total ÷ play count. Success rate has three conventions: (1) nflfastR - play is successful if EPA > 0; (2) Football Outsiders - gain ≥40% of line-to-gain on 1st down, ≥60% on 2nd, 100% on 3rd/4th; (3) Bill Connelly/college - 50%/70%/100%. CPOE = actual completion outcome (or rate) minus the model's estimated completion probability, where the expected rate reflects throw difficulty (air yards, field placement, other variables).

Advanced-metrics catalog definitions continued: DAVE decay schedule (verified from FTN live tables) - after Week 1 of 2026, DAVE was 83% preseason forecast for offense and 98% for defense/special teams; by Week 11 of 2025 it was 12% offense / 35% defense+ST. The EPA+CPOE composite's canonical weighting/formula is unverified - no primary source for the exact weights was found. PRWR = how often a rusher beats his blocker within 2.5 seconds; PBWR = how often a blocker sustains for at least 2.5 seconds (2026 methodology added/refined bull rushes, chips, stunts). RBWR/RSWR: defender wins by defeating/displacing a blocker, forcing the runner to alter the lane, or making a tackle within three yards; the responsible blocker receives the inverse result. Situation-neutral pace (Football Outsiders): exclude 4th quarter and final five minutes of the first half, require score within six points. Explosive-play rate (4for4): pass gains ≥15 yards and rush gains ≥10 yards. Havoc rate: defensive plays with a tackle for loss, forced fumble, or defended pass, divided by total defensive plays (family - no NFL standard). Stuff rate: share of rushes stopped for no gain or negative yardage (boundary varies by provider). Fourth-down aggressiveness: observed go-for-it rate vs a WP/EP model's recommended action, controlling for field position, yards to go, score, clock, timeouts.

Advanced-metrics catalog FPI prior and NGS definitions: ESPN FPI's preseason prior is anchored on Vegas expectations (win totals, moneylines) plus prior-year unit efficiencies, returning starters, coaching/coordinator/QB changes, and QB injuries; it adjusts for altitude, seasonal effects, and QB injury/suspension/absence probability. NGS Average Separation = distance between WR/TE and nearest defender at catch/incompletion; Average Cushion = same distance at the snap; ESPN's all-routes (untargeted included) Open/Catch/YAC approach is the most predictive-flavored. Time to throw is descriptive, not normative - no 'good' time to throw; it must be paired with pressure data.

Advanced-metrics catalog predictive findings: dropback (passing) EPA correlation with wins is ~0.53–0.61 vs rushing efficiency ~0.13–0.19 (Advanced Football Analytics expected-wins model); a 2026 early-season study found passing EPA predicts future point differential at r ≈ 0.42. Offensive success rate reaches ~r = 0.60 stability by game 6 but is less predictive of future scoring than passing EPA. ESPN FPI in 2016: favorites won 73% of regular-season games, beating the Vegas closing line's hit rate that year. Special-teams EPA: the Wharton Special Teams Performance Index cut prediction RMSE by 1.9% when added to offense/defense ratings; special teams are ~15% of plays. Turnover luck: season-to-date turnover differential regresses toward zero (PMC meta-review) - called 'the single biggest upgrade available to an Elo-based engine' because record-based ratings like Elo systematically undervalue efficient teams with bad turnover luck.

Advanced-metrics catalog coaching/scheme findings: fourth-down aggressiveness captures 0.5–1.5 points/game of systematic value the market is slow to price; Aaron Schatz's red-zone critique - red-zone efficiency is close to noise while red-zone trip rate (opportunity) is the stickier part; a 2012 hierarchical-Bayes study found raw third-down conversion rate 'a nearly meaningless measure of the efficiency of an offense', while all-downs efficiency (first downs per play) has 8-game predictive correlation with wins of ~0.36, the highest of the common measures; a 2024 arXiv study estimates the historical bye-week advantage largely disappeared after the 2011 CBA, mini-byes showed no obvious benefit, and Monday-rest differential was small; PFF research - pressure creation is more repeatable and predicts future sacks better than prior sack totals, while pressure-to-sack conversion is noisy and heavily QB/scheme-influenced.

Advanced-metrics catalog data-source and licensing facts: free tier = nflverse (play-by-play 1999+, rosters, schedules, stats, depth charts, injuries 2009+, snap counts 2012+, participation 2016+, NGS passing/receiving/rushing 2016+, PFR advanced-stats mirror 2018+, draft/combine/contracts); paid tier = PFF at $9.99/mo monthly, $99.99/yr annual, $199.99/yr PFF Pro (Sep 2026 price drop, Pro includes programmatic data access for modeling), grades 0–100 on a −2 to +2 per-play scale; Stathead at $8/mo single sport, $16/mo all sports; scraped/social-only (research only, no redistribution) = ESPN published rankings, FTN DVOA tables, X charting accounts, Substacks/newsletters. Licensing reality: facts aren't copyrightable; compiled databases and proprietary grades/metrics (PFF grades, DVOA, FPI, Total Points) are protected IP - computing your own EPA from nflverse play-by-play is clean, republishing PFF's grades table is not. DVOA: proprietary formula expressed as a percentage with league average 0%; FTN implementation is canonical now; weekly numbers move retroactively with opponent adjustments; no public API.

Advanced-metrics catalog gap list and caveats: the 12-item ranked gap list for engine v5.2.7 (expected lift for moneyline/spread/total, thin sample) ranks 1. opponent-adjusted efficiency (HIGH), 2. turnover regression (HIGH), 3. dropback vs. rush EPA split (HIGH), 4. explosive-play differential (HIGH), 5. early-season shrinkage (HIGH). Standing caveat: predicting team quality ≠ predicting covers - efficient markets already price public info (open EPA, FPI, PFF grades), so metrics enter as feature candidates for a spread/total model and the edge is implementation quality (opponent adjustment, shrinkage, weighting). Weather caveat: the clearest weather relationship is wind vs. passing and kicking production and totals; effects are nonlinear and interact with stadium/roof, direction, precipitation, and offensive style - avoid fixed rules like 'X mph = Y points'. Altitude: no robust NFL-specific coefficient verified - assigning a number without backtesting is fabrication.

Neon max-leverage audit (2026-09-28) cost equations: Compute billed as CU-hours = compute size × hours running, where 1 CU ≈ 4 GB RAM + CPU + local SSD and the minimum size is 0.25 CU; the central cost equation is `0.25 CU × ~730 hrs/mo = ~182.5 CU-hours/mo` → Launch ≈ $19.35/mo for compute alone, Scale ≈ $40.50/mo; on the Free plan, 182.5 CU-hrs exceeds the 100 CU-hr allowance so compute suspends mid-month until the next billing period (a hard outage). Storage is billed in GB-months at $0.35/GB-mo on Launch/Scale (Free: 0.5 GB/project). Public network transfer (egress) shares a 500 GB/project/mo allowance across Postgres, Object Storage, and Functions, then $0.10/GB (Launch); Free: 5 GB/project/mo.

Neon audit pricing and scale-to-zero mechanics: each branch beyond 10/project (Launch) or 25/project (Scale) costs $1.50/branch-month (~$0.002/hr) prorated hourly, and every branch bills while awake - each forgotten branch with an awake compute is a second ~$19/mo leak. Instant restore (PITR) costs $0.20/GB-mo and defaults to a 1-day window on paid plans; snapshots cost $0.09/GB-mo (billing began May 1, 2026); Object Storage costs $0.023/GB-mo with no per-operation charge; Functions cost $0.10 active / $0.025 waiting per Cap-Hr plus $0.60/M invocations on Launch. Scale-to-zero suspends compute after 5 minutes of inactivity, but any DB traffic resets the idle timer and logical-replication subscribers pin the compute awake. A signals-writer cron hitting the DB more often than ~every 6 minutes keeps compute at ~100% duty cycle (≈ $19/mo on Launch at the 0.25 CU floor); a 0.25 CU floor spiking to 4 CU during a backfill bills 16x for those hours.

Neon audit connection-pooling rule: Neon plans are now Free / Launch / Scale (legacy auto-migrated February 2026), all usage-based with no monthly minimum on Launch/Scale. Connection pooling uses PgBouncer in transaction mode with 10,000 client connections on the `-pooler` hostname; direct connections are limited to max_connections of only 104 at 0.25 CU - unpooled Vercel fan-out can fail under concurrency exactly when traffic spikes (game windows). Read replicas are their own compute billed in CU-hours - they offload storage, not compute, so they are NOT a cost saver at this workload's read volume. The audit deliberately does NOT recommend the Scale plan (2.1x the compute rate, $0.222 vs $0.106) or disabling scale-to-zero on Launch.

Convergent calibration evidence (2026-09-04): three independent measurements on three different populations using three different methods converge on the verdict that the confidence score has no resolution and the ≥80 tier is inverted. Measurement 1 (tail win rate vs claimed rate): 152 graded picks at confidence ≥80, live production, read 2026-09-02 → 61 wins = 40.13% vs mean claimed 86% (inverted; corrected from an earlier 37% report); production re-read 2026-09-03 confirmed the verdict with 0 bootstrap/unpublished/seed rows in the population. Measurement 2 (Brier decomposition): 1,663 graded WIN/LOSS picks, live production → resolution term 0.0054 (≈0); Murphy uncertainty 0.2493 vs base rate 52.6%. Measurement 3 (replay discrimination): 13,646 spread/total picks, 1999–2025 replay of the frozen model → AUC (Mann-Whitney) 0.4965, seeded permutation p = 0.4113 (no discrimination); controls: |line| magnitude 0.4982, rest 0.5019, week 0.5073 - all ≈0.50. No equation was written in the file; terms stated verbatim.

Convergent calibration evidence consequences: the 1999–2025 replay's blended win rate was 52.70% but the honest ROI is −5.48% per unit staked (the blended rate is an artifact of averaging markets priced differently). The replay's synthetic pricing (both sides at −110) cannot explain the live measurements away - the live ≥80 tail is inverted on its own and the live resolution term is ≈0 on its own. Decisions taken: calibration floors of Brier ≤ 0.22 / ECE ≤ 0.05; nothing calibrated is published; PERFORMANCE_STATS, LIVE_BOARD, and PUBLISH_LEDGER stay closed and the honest 'collecting' state is published instead; the inverted ≥80 tail is monitored but never shipped as probability; corpus-poisoning gate - any measurement predating the nflverse `spread_line` sign fix (PR #695) is void (none of the three predates it in derivation). Correction recorded: confidence is NOT 'mildly anti-informative' from the 70–79 band (corrected in #698 by its own author); the correct statement is no discrimination (AUC ≈ 0.5).

Symbolic regression REPORT (engine/research/2026-09-13/symbolic-regression/REPORT.md): method = symbolic regression via `gplearn` (pure Python, free); function set {+, −, ×, ÷(protected), √|·|, log|·|, |·|, −, 1/·, max, min, sin, cos}; search budget population 3,000 × 150 generations × 2 seeds per target, tournament size 50, parsimony 0.0001. Target A: play EPA from pre-snap features only (no leakage: down, distance, yardline, time remaining, quarter, score differential, shotgun, no-huddle; play type deliberately excluded as decided at/after the snap); train n=165,330 plays / holdout n=82,261. Target B: drive ends in score (TD/FG=1) from drive-start state (yardline, time, quarter, score diff, down, distance); time-censored 'End of half' drives excluded; train n=22,810 drives / holdout n=11,271; base rate 40.8%. Data: nflverse play-by-play parquet, seasons 2020–2025.

Symbolic regression results: Target A (play EPA from pre-snap state): NULL (confirmed). Dumb baseline (train mean): holdout R² 0.0000. Best GP-discovered formula (2 seeds × 3,000 pop × 150 gen): holdout R² −0.0222. Gradient-boosting reference: R² 0.0078. All top-5 'discoveries' were cosmetic rewrites of the same constant prediction - identical R² and MAE. Football translation: the strongest single linear correlate (|r| = 0.022, distance) explains 0.05% of EPA variance; 99%+ of play EPA is decided after the snap - by execution, not situation; even a 3,000-tree gradient booster explains 0.8%. Target B (drive scores from drive-start state): INTERESTING (not a breakthrough). Dumb baseline (40.8% base rate): holdout AUC 0.5000. Best GP formula (seed 42): AUC 0.5818; runner-up (seed 7): AUC 0.5661; gradient-boosting reference: AUC 0.6268. Correction note: an early aborted run logged HGB AUC 0.5645 - a measurement bug (`predict()` class labels instead of `predict_proba()`); the correct reference is 0.6268 and both CSVs carry the corrected number.

Symbolic regression football insight: the Target B formula captures only ~65% of the ranking signal a plain gradient booster finds ((0.5818−0.5)/(0.6268−0.5)). Football translation: scoring chance is governed by a min-bottleneck between field position and distance - the drive is only as promising as the worse of (how far from the end zone) and (how much is needed on this down) - passed through a saturating squashing function (the `sin(√|·|)` wrapper is a machine-built sigmoid substitute). Verdict: Target A NULL (confirmed twice, plus 3,000-tree GBM at R² 0.008); Target B INTERESTING (novel min-bottleneck formula, stable across seeds and held-out seasons); no breakthrough - nothing beats standard ML or changes how football should be measured today. Next-try items: (1) richer targets with real signal - EPA²/WPA²-style leverage targets (variance more predictable than mean; a big play's leverage is largely situational), 4th-down go/for-go decision surfaces, red-zone TD rate; (2) richer pre-snap-legal features. The report's 'Verdict' and 'Next steps' reproducibility stubs are empty placeholders - stale since the run did complete (doc hygiene gap).

claim: Calibration uncertainty stack EB-τ and isotonic-vs-Platt rules: EB-τ hierarchical adjustment - group random effects u_g ~ N(0,τ²), τ̂ estimated by moment matching and clamped to [0.05, 2]; unknown group → u = 0 (no adjustment).
